   Migraine Prophylaxis

   8 years or older: 1 mg/kg/day orally in combination with cognitive behavioral therapy 4 ,5

   Pain, Chronic

   6 years or older, less than 35 kg: 10 mg orally once daily 6

   6 years or older, 35 kg or greater: 25 mg orally once daily 6

   Discontinuation: Avoid abrupt discontinuation; taper dose gradually; if intolerable symptoms,
   resume previous dose followed by smaller decreases 7
   Withdrawal following long-term antidepressant use (eg, longer than 6 months) should always
   be gradual with dosage reduction over at least 3 months (4 to 6 months may be necessary)
   monitoring for withdrawal syndromes and return of disease symptoms Perioperative management: Tricyclic antidepressant (TCA) medications are generally contin-
   ued in the perioperative period to prevent symptoms of withdrawal 8 , 9 or relapse TCAs

 should be continued until the day of surgery and restarted after surgery with oral intake
   (Strength of Recommendation: D) Electrocardiogram should be closely monitored for ar-
   rhythmias Patients taking TCAs may have increased minimal alveolar concentrations (MAC)
   or total anesthetic requirements 8 , Dose adjustments
   Renal impairment (estimated GFR 60 mL/min or less): No adjustment necessary based on
   data from a systematic review of pharmacokinetics, efficacy and safety from the European
   Renal Best Practice (ERBP); this recommendation is based on extrapolated and/or indirect data
   only Renal replacement therapy (hemodialysis, peritoneal dialysis, or hemodiafiltration): No ad-
   justment necessary based on data from a systematic review of pharmacokinetics, efficacy and
   safety from the ERBP Hepatic impairment: Patients with liver disease may require reduced doses 12

   Pharmacogenomic Dosage Adjustments

   CYP2C19 Phenotypes
   • Gene-based dosing guidelines apply when a higher initial dose is warranted, such as treating
   major depression 12 ; however, no specific definition of a higher initial dosage is provided.
   • Although data on the relationship of CYP2C19 genotype and TCA treatment outcomes are
   scarce in pediatric patients, children may have increased CYP2C19 activity compared with
   adults. There is no current evidence to preclude extrapolation of dosing guidelines based on
   adult data to pediatric patients • Ultrarapid or rapid metabolizers: Avoid use of a tertiary amine because of risk for decreased
   efficacy. Consider alternative TCA therapy with nortriptyline or desipramine. If a tertiary amine
   is needed, titrate dose to clinical response with symptom improvement and minimal (if any)
   side effects. Use therapeutic drug monitoring to guide dose adjustments • Intermediate or normal metabolizer: No adjustment to the recommended initial or steady-state
   doses are necessary; titrate over several days to the steady-state dosage • Poor metabolizers: Avoid use of a tertiary amine because of risk for sub-optimal response.
   Consider alternative TCA therapy with nortriptyline or desipramine. If a tertiary amine is neces-
   sary, consider reducing recommended steady-state dose by 50%; begin with a low initial dose
   and titrate to clinical response using therapeutic drug monitoring to guide dose adjustments 2/15
 CYP2D6 Phenotypes

   • Gene-based dosing guidelines apply when a higher initial dose is warranted, such as treating
   major depression 12 ; however, no specific definition of a higher initial dosage is provided.
   • Although data on the relationship of CYP2D6 genotype and TCA treatment outcomes are
   scarce in pediatric patients, CYP2D6 activity is mature in early childhood. There is no current
   evidence to preclude extrapolation of dosing guidelines based on adult data to pediatric pa-
   tients • Ultrarapid metabolizers: Avoid use of TCAs because of potential lack of efficacy. If use is neces-
   sary, consider titrating to a higher target dosage to achieve clinical response. Use therapeutic
   drug monitoring to guide dose adjustments • Extensive metabolizers: No adjustment to the recommended initial or steady-state doses are
   necessary; titrate over several days to the steady-state dosage • Intermediate metabolizers: Consider reducing recommended steady-state dose by 25%; begin
   with a low initial dose and titrate over several days to clinical response. Use therapeutic drug

drugs.uses_raw:
Cyclic Vomiting Syndrome; Prophylaxis

   Guidelines: Amitriptyline is the first-line choice for prophylaxis of cyclic vomiting syndrome in
   patients older than 5 years according to a consensus statement by the North American Society
   for Pediatric Gastroenterology, Hepatology, and Nutrition (NASPGHAN). Propranolol is the sec-
   ond-line option. For children 5 years or younger, cyproheptadine is the first-line drug and pro-
   pranolol is second-line. Initiate prophylaxis if episodes occur frequently (more than every 1 to
   2 months), cause repeated hospitalizations and school absences, or if abortive therapy is not
   effective. Treat with the goal therapeutic dose of the prophylaxis agent for at least 2 cycles; if
   ineffective, switch to another medication Major Depressive Disorder
   Guidelines: The American Academy of Pediatrics recommends that patients 10 to 21 years old
   with major depressive disorder in the primary care setting should receive psychotherapy (eg,
   cognitive behavioral therapy or interpersonal psychotherapy for adolescents) and/or treat-
   ment with an SSRI. Tricyclic antidepressants were not included in the most recent guidelines
   because of a lack of efficacy demonstrated in clinical trials for this class of antidepressants Evidence: A systematic review and network meta-analysis (71 included studies; 9510 patients;
   median age, 14 years; median duration of treatment, 8 weeks) found treatment efficacy (mean
   overall change in symptoms after treatment) of amitriptyline for major depressive disorder in

 children and adolescents was not significantly different when compared with 15 antidepres-
   sants, 7 psychotherapeutic modalities, and 5 combinations of antidepressant plus psychother-
   apeutic modality. Fluoxetine and fluoxetine plus CBT were the only treatment groups signifi-
   cantly more effective than pill placebo and psychological controls Migraine Prophylaxis
   Guidelines: Amitriptyline plus cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) may be a treatment option
   for migraine prophylaxis when patients have ready access to CBT, and after discussion of the
   risks of amitriptyline therapy Evidence: Amitriptyline 1 mg/kg/day combined with CBT has been reported to decrease the
   frequency of migraine or headache days (high confidence), reduce headache frequency by at
   least 50% (high confidence), and decrease migraine-related disability (moderate confidence)
   compared with amitriptyline without CBT Additionally, similar outcomes for amitriptyline
   prophylaxis without CBT were not significantly different when compared with placebo Pain, Chronic
   Functional abdominal pain disorders: Significantly more patents achieve at least a 50% re-
   duction in pain from baseline with amitriptyline compared with placebo (76% vs 9%) in a 12-
   week randomized study of pediatric patients 8 years or older (median age, 3 years) with
   functional abdominal pain disorders (N=168). Pain intensity, frequency, and duration scores
   and quality of life were significantly improved with amitriptyline, and few amitriptyline-treated
   patients required further analgesics. Common adverse events were weight gain, vomiting, and
   constipation. Amitriptyline dosage was 10 mg/day if weight was less than 35 kg and 25 mg/day
   if weight was 35 kg or greater. A smaller, 4-week study reported no significant difference in
   pain improvement compared with placebo, 6 while another small, 8-week study reported sig-
   nificantly improved quality of life with amitriptyline compared with placebo Dosages were
   similar to those used in the 12-week study 6 ,18 .
   Neuropathic pain: In a 6-week, randomized controlled trial of gabapentin versus amitriptyline
   for neuropathic pain (N=34), there was no significant difference between the two study groups
   in pain intensity decrease. Patients on both drugs had important reductions in pain, surpass-
   ing the minimally important difference (MID) of 1 point on the Coloured Analogue Scale (CAS;
   10-point pain scale). There was no significant difference in sleep scores (n=26) or the incidence
   of adverse events between the groups. Included patients were 8 to 17 years with a median age
   of 6 years in the gabapentin group and 5 years in the amitriptyline group. Gabapentin
   dose was 300 mg orally 3 times daily, and amitriptyline dose was 10 mg daily at bedtime Despite limited data, in a survey of 117 pediatric providers treating pediatric pain, amitriptyline

 was reported as one of the top three most frequently used medications for the treatment of
   moderate and severe neuropathic pain FDA Approved Pediatric Uses: Amitriptyline is indicated for the relief of symptoms of depres-
   sion in patients 12 years or older Administration
   Extemporaneous Oral Compounds

   20 mg/mL Suspension 13
   • Use correct number of amitriptyline 100 mg tablets for desired quantity of 20 mg/mL suspen-
   sion and grind to a fine powder with a mortar and pestle.
   • Add a sufficient amount of vehicle, either a 10:1 mixture of Simple Syrup NF and 1%
   methylcellulose or a 1:1 mixture of OraSweet:and OraPlus, to wet powder and mix into
   paste.
   • Transfer to plastic prescription bottle and prepare suspension with chosen vehicle to in-
   tended volume.
   • Label the container with "Shake well before using."
   • With OraPlus and OraSweet vehicle: Stable for 91 days at room temperature (25°C) and
   under refrigeration (4°C).
   • With Simple Syrup NF and 1% methylcellulose vehicle: Stable for 28 days at room temper-
   ature (25°C) and 42 days under refrigeration (4°C).

   10 mg/mL Suspension (300 mL) in SyrSpend SF PH4™ 14 :
   • Weigh out 3 g amitriptyline hydrochloride active pharmaceutical ingredient powder and
   transfer to a low-actinic prescription bottle.
   • Add SyrSpend SF PH4™ to the bottle using a volumetric pipette to achieve a final volume of
   300 mL.
   • Shake bottle until the suspension is optically uniformly dispersed.
   • Label the container with "Shake well before using" and "Protect from light."

   • Stable for up to 90 days under refrigeration (2 to 8°C) or at room temperature (20 to 25°C).

   1 mg/mL Suspension (100 mL) 15

   • Mix 100 mg of amitriptyline hydrochloride powder with a flavoring agent and 2 mL glycerin.

 • Add a sufficient amount of simple syrup to yield 100 mL and mix well.
   • May add 100 mg edetate disodium to increase length of stability.

   • Label the container with "Shake well before using."
   • Without edetate disodium: Stable for 21 days at room temperature in amber glass bottles.

   • With edetate disodium: Stable for at least 37 days at room temperature in amber glass
   bottles.

drugs.contraindications_raw:
Common: Weight gain, constipation, xerostomia, dizziness, extrapyramidal movements,
   headache, somnolence, blurred vision 1

   Black Box Warning
   Suicidality and Antidepressant Drugs
   Antidepressants increased the risk compared to placebo of suicidal thinking and behavior (sui-
   cidality) in children, adolescents, and young adults in short-term studies of major depressive
   disorder (MDD) and other psychiatric disorders. Anyone considering the use of amitriptyline
   hydrochloride tablets or any other antidepressant in a child, adolescent, or young adult must
   balance this risk with the clinical need. Short-term studies did not show an increase in the risk
   of suicidality with antidepressants compared to placebo in adults beyond age 24; there was a
   reduction in risk with antidepressants compared to placebo in adults aged 65 and older.
   Depression and certain other psychiatric disorders are themselves associated with increases in
   the risk of suicide. Patients of all ages who are started on antidepressant therapy should be
   monitored appropriately and observed closely for clinical worsening, suicidality, or unusual
   changes in behavior. Families and caregivers should be advised of the need for close observa-
   tion and communication with the prescriber. Amitriptyline hydrochloride tablets are not ap-
   proved for use in pediatric patients Monitoring
   Therapeutic Drug Monitoring

   Depression: Amitriptyline plus nortriptyline, 80 to 200 nanograms/milliliter (ng/mL) 21
   • In a consensus guideline, the use of therapeutic drug monitoring (TDM) with amitriptyline is
   rated as 1, strongly recommended for dose titration and for special indications. At drug con-

 centrations in blood within the reported therapeutic reference range, highest probability of re-
   sponse or remission can be expected Toxic Monitoring
   • Perform baseline screening of sodium level and after 3 to 4 weeks in high-risk patients (eg,
   previous history of antidepressant-induced hyponatremia, low body weight, concomitant use
   of thiazides or other hyponatremia-inducing agents), especially during the first 3 weeks follow-
   ing initiation • Monitor all patients starting antidepressant therapy for clinical worsening, suicidality, or un-
   usual changes in behavior, especially at the initiation of therapy or when the dose increases or
   decreases Such monitoring should include at least weekly face-to-face contact with patients
   or their family members or caregivers during the initial 4 weeks of treatment, then visits every
   other week for the next 4 weeks, then at 12 weeks, and then as clinically indicated beyond 12
   weeks 23,24 . More frequent monitoring may be required in more severely depressed or suici-
   dal patients • Screen patients for bipolar disorder risk factors prior to initiating therapy. Screening should
   include a family history of suicide, bipolar disorder, and depression, and monitor for
   mania/hypomania activation • Monitor blood pressure at baseline, with significant dose increases, and every 3 to 6 months
   once stabilized • Monitor hyperthyroid patients or those receiving thyroid medication • Evaluate ECG for QT prolongation at baseline, at steady state, after initial dose titration, with
   dose changes, and especially with higher doses and in children • Monitoring of the metabolic profile to detect early weight gain may be advisable at 3, 6, and
   12 months, then yearly, in all patients (not just in patients who are obese or overweight) and if
   receiving combination therapy, especially with atypical antipsychotics

   Amphetamine sulfate has a high potential for abuse and misuse, which can lead to the devel-
   opment of a substance use disorder, including addiction. Misuse and abuse of CNS stimulants,
   including amphetamine sulfate, can result in overdose and death, and this risk is increased
   with higher doses or unapproved methods of administration, such as snorting or injection.
   Before prescribing amphetamine sulfate, assess each patient’s risk for abuse, misuse, and ad-
   diction. Educate patients and their families about these risks, proper storage of the drug, and
   proper disposal of any unused drug. Throughout amphetamine sulfate treatment, reassess

Common Hypokalemia (37% vs 55%), chills (29% vs 68%), vomiting (27% vs 55%), and hyper-
   tension (10% vs 21%) were reported for amphotericin liposome compared with amphotericin B
   deoxycholate in a double-blind study in 95 children 16 years or younger Endocrine/Metabolic:
   •Hypokalemia occurred at the end of treatment in 2% (7 out of 33 pediatric patients) in the
   liposomal amphotericin B group compared with 6% (16 out of 56 pediatric patients) for the
   conventional amphotericin B group when drugs were administered as recommended (3 to 5
   mg/kg/day over at least 1 hour for liposomal and 5 to 5 mg/kg/day over at least 4 hours for
   conventional). Potassium replacement therapy was administered to 9% of patients in the li-
   posomal amphotericin B group and 3% of patients in the conventional group. In those
   younger than 90 days (n=16), 100% vs 5%, respectively, received potassium replacement
   therapy Hepatic:

   •Hepatotoxicity was more common in pediatric patients who received liposomal amphotericin
   B compared with conventional amphotericin B in a retrospective study; but when concomitant
   hepatotoxic drugs were accounted for there was no difference. Additionally, the majority of
   these children with hepatoxicity had at least 1 enzyme abnormality at baseline. Of 65 pediatric
   patients with baseline and end-of-treatment liver function test, amphotericin-related hepato-

 toxicity was 8% (24/29) for liposomal amphotericin B and 6% (20/36) for conventional
   amphotericin B (OR 8 (1.2 to 3; p=0.024)). The LFTs that were different between the 2
   groups were gamma-glutamyl transferase (GGT) and bilirubin; GGT was up to 5 x the upper
   limit of normal (ULN) in 4% in the liposomal group compared with 7% (p=0.049) in the
   conventional group and bilirubin was more than 3 to 10 x the ULN in 2% and 0%, respec-
   tively Infusion-Related Reactions:
   •Infusion-related reactions (rigors, fever, tachycardia, and rash) occurred in 1% (3 out of 33
   pediatric patients) in the liposomal amphotericin B group compared with 2% (13 out of 56
   pediatric patients; p=0.15) for the conventional amphotericin B group when drugs were admin-
   istered as recommended (3 to 5 mg/kg/day over at least 1 hour for liposomal and 5 to 5
   mg/kg/day over at least 4 hours for conventional). None of the reactions occurred in children
   younger than 90 days (n=16) •In a comparative clinical trial (n=343 adults and pediatric patients; more than 75% of patients
   were older than 13 years of age), amphotericin liposome appears to be less toxic than conven-
   tional amphotericin B, with a lower incidence of infusion-related reactions (20.6% vs 2%, re-
   spectively). Dose reductions due to toxicity (infusion- and non-infusion-related) were more fre-
   quent for conventional amphotericin B versus liposomal (29% vs 10%) Renal:
   •Compared with older individuals, pediatric patients appear to have more tolerance for the
   nephrotoxic effects of amphotericin B deoxycholate Creatinine elevation (doubling of base-
   line serum creatinine concentration) occurred in 2% (7 out of 33 pediatric patients) in the li-
   posomal amphotericin B group compared with 3% (8 out of 56 pediatric patients; p=0.4) for
   the conventional amphotericin B group when drugs were administered as recommended (3 to
   5 mg/kg/day over at least 1 hour for liposomal and 5 to 5 mg/kg/day over at least 4 hours
   for conventional). The mean number of concomitant nephrotoxic drugs was 5 for the liposo-
   mal group compared with 2 for the conventional group •In a comparative clinical trial (n=343 adults and pediatric patients; more than 75% of patients
   were older than 13 years of age), amphotericin liposome appears to be less toxic than conven-
   tional amphotericin B, with a lower incidence nephrotoxicity (serum creatinine greater than 2
   times baseline, 7% vs 7%, respectively) . Dose reductions due to toxicity (infusion- and

Acinetobacter baumannii infection, carbapenem-resistant (CRAB): Guidance from the Infectious Disease Society
  of America (IDSA) recommends a sulbactam-containing agent in combination with a second agent for the treatment of
  infections caused by CRAB. Sulbactam/durlobactam in combination with imipenem/cilastatin or meropenem is pre-
  ferred; polymyxin B, high-dose minocycline, tigecycline, or cefiderocol may be substituted for imipenem/cilastatin or
  meropenem. If sulbactam/durlobactam is unavailable, high-dose ampicillin/sulbactam in combination with polymyxin

 B, high-dose minocycline, tigecycline, or cefiderocol is an alternative. If prolonged therapy is necessary (eg, osteomyeli-
  tis), the second agent may be discontinued after clinical improvement occurs and the sulbactam-containing agent con-
  tinued as monotherapy to complete the course of therapy. High dose ampicillin-sulbactam (ie, 300 to 450 mg/kg/day)

  Staphylococcus aureus (most common), Kingella kingae (common in patients 6 months to 5 years of age), and
  Streptococcus pyogenes (second most common causative organism in older children). Haemophilus influenza type b and
  Streptococcus pneumoniae are rare 17,9 .
   ●   First-line agent: Cefazolin is the first-line agent for the treatment of acute hematogenous osteomyelitis due to me-
       thicillin-sensitive-S aureus, K kingae, and S pyogenes .
   ●   Alternative agents: Alternative agents include nafcillin (preferred) or oxacillin; ampicillin/sulbactam (in patients
       who cannot tolerate or are allergic to first-line therapy); clindamycin (option for S pyogenes and option for methi-
       cillin-sensitive-S aureus, but not first-line); and vancomycin (when methicillin-resistent S aureus (MRSA) is greater
       than approximately 10% for skin infections or confirmed MRSA infection, in patients with signs of potential sepsis,
       significant disease burden, and/or have a high risk of MRSA).
   ●   Adjunct: Rifampin may be used as an adjunct (for example, persistent bacteremia despite appropriate antimicrobial
       therapy).
   ●   IV to oral therapy: Switch to oral therapy when clinical response is evident. Additionally, C-reactive protein (CRP)
       may assist in determining switching to oral therapy (50% reduction of the maximum CRP value or CRP reduction to
       less than 2 mg/dL). Options for oral therapy include cephalexin, cefadroxil, and amoxicillin/clavulanate.
   ●   First-line agents for MRSA: Vancomycin or clindamycin.
   ●   Second-line agents for MRSA: Daptomycin or linezolid (when no response or intolerance to vancomycin or clin-
       damycin). Ceftaroline may be considered as a last line agent when other treatments for MRSA failed.

  central catheter (PICC) in a retrospective cohort study (n=2060). Furthermore, there was a significantly higher risk of re-
  quiring a return emergency department visit or rehospitalization for any adverse outcome in the PICC group. The pri-
  mary discharge antibiotics were clindamycin and cephalexin for oral therapy and clindamycin, cefazolin, ceftriaxone,
  and vancomycin for PICC therapy. Infants (younger than 1 year) were underrepresented (4.8%) in this study 7/15

drugs.uses_raw:
Anacaulase-bcdb is indicated for eschar removal in adult and pediatric patients with deep par-
   tial thickness and/or full thickness thermal burns Limitations

   Safety and effectiveness have not been established for treatment of the following 1 :
   ●   Chemical or electrical burns
   ●   Burns on the face, perineum, or genitalia
   ●   Burns on the feet of patients with diabetes mellitus or on the feet of patients with occlusive
       vascular disease
   ●   Circumferential burns
   ●   Burns in patients with significant cardiopulmonary disease, including inhalation injury

   Administration
   Application

 • To prepare the wound area before application, clean the wound to remove any charred tis-
   sue, blisters, and any topical products, then apply a dressing soaked with an antibacterial solu-
   tion to the treatment area for at least 2 hours • At least 15 minutes prior to application, ensure adequate pain control measures are in place;
   maintain pain management throughout the application as practiced for an extensive dressing
   change of burn wounds • Protect any open wounds (eg, laceration, abraded skin, or escharotomy incision) with skin
   protectant ointments or ointment gauze to prevent possible exposure • Ensure the wound bed is clear of any remnants of topical agents (eg, silver sulfadiazine or
   povidone iodine) • Before application, apply an ointment skin protectant (eg, petrolatum) 2 to 3 cm around the
   treatment area to create an ointment barrier; avoid applying the ointment to the treatment
   area itself, as this would impede direct contact with the eschar. • Moisten the treatment area by sprinkling sterile 9% Sodium Chloride Irrigation onto the
   burn wound • Within 15 minutes of mixing, use a sterile tongue depressor to apply a 3-mm thick layer of
   the mixed product to completely cover an area of up to 15% body surface area (BSA); if wound
   area is greater than 15% BSA, apply in 2 separate sessions 24 hours apart and do not exceed a
   total treatment area of 20% BSA • Cover the treated wound with a sterile occlusive film dressing; gently press the dressing at
   the area of contact with the ointment barrier to ensure adherence between the dressing and
   the ointment barrier and to achieve complete containment of the product on the treatment
   area. The gel should fill the entire volume of the treatment area, and there should be no visible
   air under the occlusive film dressing • Cover the dressed wound with a sterile loose, thick, fluffy dressing and secure with a sterile
   bandage. Leave the dressing and the gel in place for 4 hours; discard any unused portions of
   the product • Monitor patients for signs of local or systemic allergic reactions; if a hypersensitivity reaction
   occurs, remove the gel from the treatment area and initiate appropriate therapy Removal of Product

   • Remove the gel after 4 hours • While implementing and maintaining pain management as practiced for an extensive dress-
   ing change of burn wounds and using aseptic technique, remove the occlusive dressing, the

 ointment barrier, and the dissolved eschar by scraping with a sterile blunt-edged instrument • Wipe the wound thoroughly with a large sterile dry gauze, then wipe with a sterile gauze that
   has been soaked with sterile 9% Sodium Chloride Irrigation. Rub the treated area until the
   appearance of a clean dermis or subcutaneous tissues with pinpoint bleeding. To remove rem-
   nants of dissolved eschar, apply a dressing soaked with an antibacterial solution for at least 2
   hours Wound Care After Removal
   • Following eschar removal, continue wound care based on clinical judgement (eg, observe for
   spontaneous re-epithelization or proceed with autograft)

   sion at 2 mg/kg/hr. The appropriate amount of anakinra was diluted to a total volume of 100
   mL and infused over 12-hour intervals One institution has reported the following procedure for continuous IV infusion: Each 100 mg

   lution chosen should allow the infusion rate to be at least 5 mL/hr, and each infusion bag
   should last for no more than 8 hours. Protect both the bag and tubing from light; stable for 8

drugs.uses_raw:
Zaire ebolavirus: A total of 54 pediatric subjects (birth to less than 18 years of age; including
   neonates born to a mother who is RT-PCR positive for Zaire ebolavirus infection) were included
   in a randomized clinical trial of ansuvimab-zykl. In this study, adults and pediatric patients who
   tested positive for Ebola virus RNA and were treated with ansuvimab-zykl (n=174) had a signifi-
   cantly lower 28-day mortality rate compared with those treated with ZMapp (another triple
   monoclonal antibody combination used as a control group) (n=154); the mortality rates were 1% and 7%, respectively, for a treatment difference of -14.6 percentage points (95% CI,
   -25.2 to -1.7). A difference was observed in patients with low or high viral loads, with 28-day
   mortality rates ranging from 9% to 9% for the ansuvimab-zykl group and 5% to 5%
   for the ZMapp group. Serious adverse events resulting in death occurred in 2 patients in the
   ZMapp treatment group (including worsening gastrointestinal symptoms, hypotension, and hy-
   poxia); these events were not obviously distinguishable from the symptoms of existing Ebola
   virus disease FDA Approved Pediatric Indication

   Ansuvimab-zykl is indicated for the treatment of infection caused by Zaire ebolavirus in pedi-
   atric patients, including neonates born to a mother who is RT-PCR positive for Zaire ebolavirus
   infection Limitations of Use

   The efficacy of ansuvimab-zykl has not been established for other species of the Ebolavirus and
   Marburgvirus genera Zaire ebolavirus can change over time, and factors such as emergence of resistance, or changes
   in viral virulence could diminish the clinical benefit of antiviral drugs. Consider available infor-

 mation on drug susceptibility patterns for circulating Zaire ebolavirus strains when deciding
   whether to use ansuvimab-zykl Administration
   • Infuse diluted solution immediately. Do not mix with or administer as an infusion with other
   medicinal products. Do not coadminister other drugs simultaneously through the same infu-
   sion line • IV solution can be infused via a central line or peripheral catheter with a 2-micron in-line fil-
   ter extension set • May slow or stop Infusion if necessary, to alleviate any side effects • At the end of the infusion, if a syringe pump was used, flush the line with 2 to 5 mL of diluent,
   not to exceed the total infusion volume. If an infusion bag was used, flush the line by infusing
   at least 25 mL of the diluent, to ensure complete product administration

drugs.contraindications_raw:
Common, adults: Headache (20.4%), nausea (9.3%), infusion site pain (9.3%), infusion site
   swelling (7.4%), and back pain (3.7%) Black Box Warning
   Interactions with Glucose Monitoring and Thrombosis

   • Maltose in immune globulin products, including anthrax immune globulin, may give falsely
   high blood glucose levels with some blood point-of-care glucose testing systems (for example
   those based on the GDH-PQQ or glucose-dyeoxidoreductase methods) resulting in inappropri-
   ate administration of insulin and life-threatening hypoglycemia. To avoid interference by mal-
   tose contained in anthrax immune globulin, perform blood glucose measurements in patients
   receiving anthrax immune globulin with a glucose-specific method (monitor and test strips).

   • Thrombosis may occur with immune globulin products, including anthrax immune globulin.
   Risk factors may include advanced age, prolonged immobilization, hypercoagulable conditions,
   history of venous or arterial thrombosis, use of estrogens, indwelling vascular catheters, hy-
   perviscosity, and cardiovascular risk factors. Thrombosis may occur in the absence of known
   risk factors.

   • For patients at risk of thrombosis, administer anthrax immune globulin at the minimum infu-
   sion rate practicable. Ensure adequate hydration in patients before administration. Monitor
   for signs and symptoms of thrombosis and assess blood viscosity in patients at risk of hyper-
   viscosity Monitoring
   Laboratory Monitoring

 • Assess renal function, including BUN and serum creatinine, at baseline and periodically
   thereafter. Additionally assess urine output periodically in patients at risk for acute renal fail-
   ure • In patients at risk for hyperviscosity (eg, patients with cryoglobulins, fasting chylomicronemia
   or markedly high triglycerides, monoclonal gammopathies), conduct baseline assessment of
   blood viscosity • In patients at higher risk for hemolysis, consider lab tests (including Hb or HCT) at baseline,
   within 36 to 96 hours after infusion, and 7 to 10 days post-infusion with additional testing for
   signs or symptoms of hemolysis or substantial drop in Hb or HCT • Perform glucose measurement with a glucose-specific method, as maltose in anthrax im-
   mune globulin may interfere with glucose dehydrogenase pyrroloquinolinequinone (GDH-
   PQQ) or glucose-dye-oxidoreductase methods Physical Monitoring

   • Evaluate all patients for signs and symptoms of acute allergic reactions both during and after
   infusion, especially patients with antibodies against IgA . 1

   • Monitor vital signs for signs and symptoms of infusion-related reactions during and immedi-
   ately after infusion • In patients with signs and symptoms of aseptic meningitis syndrome, conduct cerebrospinal
   fluid studies and a detailed neurological exam Monitor patients for pulmonary adverse reactions and transfusion-related acute lung injury. If
   transfusion-related acute lung injury is suspected, test for anti-HLA and anti-neutrophil anti-
   bodies in the product • Monitor for signs and symptoms of thrombosis • Monitor for clinical signs and symptoms of hemolysis and hemolytic anemia 1

drugs.pharmacokinetics_summary:
Pharmacology
  Mechanism of action
  Antihemophilic Factor VIII is an essential cofactor in the activation of Factor X which leads to the formation of thrombin and fibrin. Von
  Willebrand Factor (VWF) promotes platelet aggregation and adhesion to damaged endothelium. It also serves as a stabilizing carrier protein for
  the procoagulant protein Factor VIII. Together, Factor VIII and VWF temporarily replace the missing coagulation Factor VIII and VWF needed for
  effective hemostasis 2 ,4 ,3 .

Venous thromboembolism; treatment or prophylaxis to reduce risk of recurrent venous
   thromboembolism

   A randomized open-label study in children (N=229) with confirmed venous thromboembolism
   (VTE) describing the use of apixaban in comparison with usual care (eg, heparin, LMWH, war-
   farin) demonstrated a similar rate of symptomatic and asymptomatic recurrent VTE after 6 to
   12 weeks of overall anticoagulation. Overall composite rates of symptomatic and asympto-
   matic recurrent VTE were 6% with apixaban and 7% with usual care; no VTE-related mortal-
   ities occurred in either group. Median age was 2 years (range, 04 to 18 years) and 9%
   of the patients were female. There were 48 children under 2 years old, 16 of whom were less
   than 27 days old. Most were White (76.4%), Black (13.5%), or Asian (3.9%). 1 , Thromboembolism; prophylaxis in children with congenital or acquired cardiac disease
   The composite endpoint of major bleeding plus clinically-relevant nonmajor bleeding was re-
   ported in 8% of patients treated with apixaban compared with 8% treated with standard of
   care (warfarin or low-molecular-weight heparin) in the phase 2, open-label SAXOPHONE trial.
   No thromboembolic events or thromboembolism-related deaths were reported in either treat-
   ment group. Pediatric patients (mean age 8 years; range 4 to 17 years) with congenital or
   acquired cardiac disease were randomized to apixaban prophylaxis (n=129) or standard of
   care (n=63). Apixaban dosage was as follows: 10

   levels. Non-bleeding-related adverse events included rash (1%) and leukopenia (1%) Primary thromboprophylaxis in patients with acute lymphoblastic leukemia or lym-
   phoma: Apixaban did not significantly reduce the risk of thromboembolism (composite end-

   compared with standard of care (no prophylaxis) in the randomized, open-label PREVAPIX-ALL
   study of pediatric patients 1 year or older (median, 6 years) with newly diagnosed acute lym-
   phoblastic leukemia or lymphoma and a newly inserted central venous line undergoing induc-
   tion chemotherapy (N=512). The composite outcome was reported in 12% of the apixaban
   group compared with 18% of the standard of care group (relative risk, 69; 95% CI, 45 to 05). Major bleeding was reported in 2 patients in each group while clinically-relevant nonma-

   twice daily. Treatment was continued until day 28 of the induction cycle 11

   bolism and for reduction in the risk of recurrent venous thromboembolism use in pediatric pa-

 Black Box Warning
   Premature discontinuation of apixaban increases the risk of thrombotic events
   Premature discontinuation of any oral anticoagulant, including apixaban, increases the risk of
   thrombotic events. If anticoagulation with apixaban is discontinued for a reason other than
   pathological bleeding or completion of a course of therapy, consider coverage with another
   anticoagulant.
   Spinal/epidural hematoma
   Epidural or spinal hematomas may occur in patients treated with apixaban who are receiving
   neuraxial anesthesia or undergoing spinal puncture. These hematomas may result in long-
   term or permanent paralysis. Consider these risks when scheduling patients for spinal proce-
   dures. Factors that can increase the risk of developing epidural or spinal hematomas in these
   patients include:
   • use of indwelling epidural catheters
   • concomitant use of other drugs that affect hemostasis, such as nonsteroidal anti- inflamma-
   tory drugs (NSAIDs), platelet inhibitors, other anticoagulants
   • a history of traumatic or repeated epidural or spinal punctures
   • a history of spinal deformity or spinal surgery
   • optimal timing between the administration of apixaban and neuraxial procedures is not
   known
   Monitor patients frequently for signs and symptoms of neurological impairment. If neurologi-
   cal compromise is noted, urgent treatment is necessary.
   Consider the benefits and risks before neuraxial intervention in patients anticoagulated or to
   be anticoagulated Monitoring
   Therapeutic Monitoring
   • Routine monitoring of coagulation to guide direct oral anticoagulant (DOAC) therapy is not
   generally required 12,13 . Measuring DOAC plasma levels and anticoagulant effects may be use-
   ful in emergency situations (eg, serious bleeding, urgent surgery, acute thrombotic events) or
   special situations (eg, before elective surgery with unknown/uncertain time since last intake or
   concerns about drug clearance; very obese or underweight patients). Monitoring of drug

 plasma levels by a coagulation expert or reverting to vitamin K antagonist therapy may be rea-
   sonable in the rare patients with multiple factors that interfere with pharmacokinetics of the
   drug (eg, very obese; uncontrolled cancer patients receiving therapy for malignancy, use of an-
   tineoplastics with unknown pharmacokinetic interactions) Coagulation test monitoring may
   be performed to ensure efficacy in those with a history of nonadherence, drug interactions, as-
   sess bleeding potential (renal failure, overdose), and to assist in drug-selection decisions (such
   as to access if drug failure occurred in acute thrombosis) • Chromogenic anti-FXa assay is the preferred method for quantitative assessment. However,
   it must be calibrated for a specific anticoagulant and cannot be used to assess the anticoagula-
   tion effect of other agents not previously calibrated. Low and high plasma concentrations can
   be measured with acceptable interlaboratory precision. Trough range for apixaban (at 12
   hours post-dose) was 4 to 8 international units/mL. In the absence of a calibrated test, a
   standard chromogenic anti-FXa assay calibrated to unfractionated or low molecular weight
   heparins may be used for qualitative assessment to measure the presence or absence of anti-
   coagulant effect • When using prothrombin complex concentrate as a reversal agent for the anti-factor Xa activ-
   ity of apixaban, monitoring for the anticoagulation effect of apixaban using a clotting test (pro-
   thrombin time, INR, or aPTT) or anti-factor Xa activity is not useful and is not recommended • All patients on indefinite antithrombotic therapy for secondary prevention of recurrent VTE
   should be reevaluated at least annually for changes in clinical indication Toxic Monitoring
   • Assess renal function prior to initiation of therapy and periodically during treatment.
   Frequency of monitoring depends on individual patient factors, including baseline renal func-
   tion, concomitant drug therapy, comorbidities, and age, but it is recommended to monitor re-
   nal function at least every 6 months and every 3 to 6 months in patients with renal impairment
   (CrCl less than 60 mL/min) or during an acute illness that may worsen renal function (infec-
   tions, acute heart failure). In the frail, increased monitoring is recommended. Elderly may re-
   quire more frequent monitoring (every 3 to 6 months) and measurement of a 24-hour CrCl • Evaluate liver function at baseline and periodically monitor tests for any significant change in
   function. In general, healthy patients may be monitored yearly, however more frequent moni-
   toring may be required in patients at risk of hepatic dysfunction. Elderly patients (75 years or
   older) at high risk should have their hepatic function monitored regularly and may require
   more frequent monitoring (every 3 to 6 months) • Bleeding risk in high-risk patients may be evaluated at every followup with the HAS-BLED risk
   score (hypertension, abnormal renal and liver function, stroke, bleeding, labile INRs, elderly,

 and drugs or alcohol) • Evaluate baseline CBC during initiation and at regular intervals (at least yearly) to assess any
   trends in hemoglobin/hematocrit. Evaluate more frequently if needed, especially in patients
   with active bleeding symptoms • Plasma concentration of apixaban can be measured using liquid chromatography-tandem
   mass spectrometry. The mean peak and trough concentrations were 50 and 30 nanogram/mL,
   respectively • For cardiac surgery in adults, monitoring of apixaban levels are helpful in emergency cases, in
   patients with an unclear history of drug intake and in patients with organ dysfunction, as
   bioavailability and plasma concentration may vary depending on renal and hepatic function • Bleeding risk in adult high-risk patients has been evaluated at every followup with the HAS-
   BLED risk score (hypertension, abnormal renal and liver function, stroke, bleeding, labile INRs,
   elderly, and drugs or alcohol) • Promptly evaluate signs and symptoms of blood loss • Monitor patients undergoing concomitant neuraxial anesthesia or spinal puncture frequently
   for neurological impairment (eg, leg numbness or weakness, bowel or bladder dysfunction) in-
   dicating possible spinal or epidural hematoma • All patients on indefinite antithrombotic therapy for secondary prevention of recurrent VTE
   should be reevaluated at least annually for changes in bleeding risk factors and assessed for
   new bleeding complications Coagulation Assays

   • Assessment of the anticoagulant effect using coagulation testing is useful in emergency situa-
   tions (trauma), urgent surgery, urgent invasive procedures, major bleeding, overdose/ at-
   tempted suicide, acute thrombosis, renal failure, liver failure, adherence verification, and po-
   tential drug-drug interactions • Proper timing of the blood draw for the coagulation test is necessary to effectively evaluate
   the maximum effect, which is at the maximum plasma concentration (peak 1 to 4 hours after
   apixaban dose) • Chromogenic anti-FXa assay is the preferred method for quantitative assessment. However,
   it must be calibrated for a specific anticoagulant and cannot be used to assess the anticoagula-
   tion effect of other agents not previously calibrated. Low and high plasma concentrations can
   be measured with acceptable interlaboratory precision. Trough range for apixaban (at 12
   hours post-dose) was 4 to 8 international units/mL. In the absence of a calibrated test, a
   standard chromogenic anti-FXa assay calibrated to unfractionated or low molecular weight

 heparins may be used for qualitative assessment to measure the presence or absence of anti-
   coagulant effect • Activated partial thromboplastin time (aPTT), dilute thrombin time (dTT), Ecarin clotting time
   (ECT), HepTest, international normalized ratio (INR), prothrombin time (PT), prothrombinase-
   induced clotting time (PiCT) and thrombin time (TT) are not recommended for qualitative or
   quantitative evaluation of apixaban

drugs.dosing_raw:
Thrombosis; Prophylaxis or Treatment - Heparin-Induced Thrombocytopenia (HIT)
   initial, 75 mcg/kg/min continuous IV infusion; adjust in increments of 1 to 25 mcg/kg/min
   to achieve aPTT of 5 to 3 times the initial baseline value (not to exceed 100 seconds) 1 ,2 ,3 . In
   a multicenter, open-label study (n=18) in infants and children (10 days to 16 years of age) re-
   ceiving argatroban, approximately 61% reached the target aPTT (1.5 to 3 times the baseline;
   maximum 100 seconds) with a dose of 75 mcg/kg/min and nearly all achieved the target
   aPTT with a maximum dose of 2 mcg/kg/min Pharmacologic Reversal
   An antidote to argatroban is not available. To control excessive anticoagulation (with or
   without bleeding), discontinue argatroban or decrease the infusion dosage. Anticoagulation
   parameters returned to baseline within 2 to 4 hours after discontinuing argatroban in clinical
   studies; hepatic impairment prolongs reversal of anticoagulation Conversion to Oral Anticoagulant
   Coadministration of argatroban and warfarin includes the potential prolonging INR beyond
   that produced by warfarin alone. A loading dose of warfarin should not be used. Initiate ther-
   apy using the expected daily dose of warfarin Warfarin therapy is not recommended until
   the platelet count has recovered to 150,000 cells/mm3 5 ,6 .

   Argatroban Up to 2 mcg/kg/min
   The relationship between INR obtained on combined therapy and INR obtained on warfarin
   alone is dependent on both the dose of argatroban and the thromboplastin reagent used. The
   INR value on warfarin alone can be calculated from the INR value on combination argatroban
   and warfarin therapy. The following equations can be used to predict the INR on warfarin
   alone 4 :
   ●   Thromboplastin, ISI = 88: INRW = 19 + 57 (INRWA)
   ●   Thromboplastin, ISI = 78: INRW = 18 + 45 (INRWA)
   ●   ISI = International Sensitivity Index

 ●   INRW = INR on warfarin alone
   ●   INRWA = INR on warfarin and argatroban combined

   INR should be measured daily while argatroban and warfarin are co-administered. In general,
   with doses of argatroban up to 2 mcg/kg/min, argatroban can be discontinued when the INR is
   greater than 4 on combined therapy A minimum overlap of 5 days between nonheparin an-
   ticoagulation and warfarin therapy is recommended After argatroban is discontinued, re-
   peat the INR measurement in 4 to 6 hours. If the repeat INR is below the desired therapeutic
   range, resume the infusion of argatroban and repeat the procedure daily until the desired
   therapeutic range on warfarin alone is reached Argatroban Greater than 2 mcg/kg/min
   For doses greater than 2 mcg/kg/min, the relationship of INR between warfarin alone to the
   INR on warfarin plus argatroban is less predictable. In this case, in order to predict the INR on
   warfarin alone, temporarily reduce the dose of argatroban to a dose of 2 mcg/kg/min. Repeat
   the INR on argatroban and warfarin 4 to 6 hours after reduction of the argatroban dose and
   follow the process outlined above for administering argatroban at doses up to 2 mcg/kg/min

The most commonly reported adverse effects in pediatric patients with autistic disorder as-

   blurred vision (8%), salivary hypersecretion (6%), and dizziness (5%) 4 ,2 ,3 .
   The most commonly reported adverse effects (greater than 5%) in pediatric patients with
   schizophrenia were extrapyramidal disorder, somnolence and tremor 4 ,2 ,3 .

   The most commonly reported adverse effects in pediatric patients with Tourette's syndrome
   were sedation (13%), somnolence (13%), nausea (11%), headache (10%), nasopharyngitis (9%),
   fatigue (8%), and increased appetite (7%) 2 , The odds ratio for cumulative type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM) risk was 09 (95% CI, 5 to 9) in antipsychotic-exposed youth compared with psychiatric controls in a meta-analysis (n=7
   studies); although the absolute incidence rate of T2DM compared with all controls (3.09 cases
   (95% CI, 35 to 82) per 1000 patients-years) was small over the mean follow-up period of 7
   years (n=13 studies). Important differences among studies included may affect the validity of
   this finding. The majority of antipsychotic agents were second-generation agents (risperiDONE,
   QUEtiapine, ARIPiprazole, and OLANZapine) 8/15
 In a meta-analysis of 24 pediatric studies (n=3048), weight gain was -0.04 kg (95% CI, -0.38 to

   Suicidal Thoughts and Behaviors

   Antidepressants increased the risk of suicidal thoughts and behavior in children, adolescents,
   and young adults in short-term studies. These studies did not show an increase in the risk of
   suicidal thoughts and behavior with antidepressant use in patients over age 24; there was a re-
   duction in risk with antidepressant use in patients aged 65 and older 5 ,23 .

   In patients of all ages who are started on antidepressant therapy, monitor closely for worsen-
   ing, and for emergence of suicidal thoughts and behaviors. Advise families and caregivers of
   the need for close observation and communication with the prescriber 5 , Monitoring
   Therapeutic Monitoring

   • Periodically reassess the need for continued treatment 7 ,5 ,2 .

   Toxic Monitoring

   • Monitor patients for clinical worsening, suicidality, and unusual changes in behavior, during
   therapy, especially during the initial months of treatment and with dose adjustments, and in
   patients younger than 24 years of age 7 ,5 .

   • Screen for bipolar disorder (eg, detailed psychiatric history, including family history of suicide,
   bipolar disorder, and depression) prior to initiation in patients with depressive symptoms 7 , • CBC, in patients with a history of clinically significant low WBC/ANC or drug-induced
   leukopenia/neutropenia; Frequently monitor during first few months of therapy 7 ,5
   • Monitor for fever or other signs or symptoms of infection in patients with significant neu-
   tropenia 7 ,5

   • Fasting blood glucose, fasting lipid profile, and blood pressure: Measure in all patients at
   baseline and after 3 months of treatment. If the glucose and blood pressure are normal after 3
   months of treatment, then monitor annually. If the lipids are normal after 3 months, then

 monitor at least every 5 years However, other experts do not recommend monitoring lipids
   or glucose at 3 months and there is only weak evidence to support monitoring at 6 months for
   ARIPiprazole. They do recommend monitoring fasting plasma glucose and lipids at 12 months.
   Beyond 1 year monitoring is based on previous results • Monitor for symptoms of hyperglycemia, including polydipsia, polyuria, polyphagia, and
   weakness, in all patients 7 , 5 , • Fasting blood glucose, in patients with an established diagnosis of diabetes: Monitor regularly
   for worsening of glucose control 7 ,5 ,2 .
   • Fasting blood glucose, in patients with risk factors for diabetes: Measure fasting blood glu-
   cose at baseline and periodically during treatment 7 ,5

   • Fasting blood glucose: Measure in patients who develop symptoms of hyperglycemia during
   treatment 7 , 5

   • Clinically monitor weight 7 ,5 . Monitor body mass index at baseline and at 4, 8, and 12 weeks,
   and at least every 3 months thereafter, or more often as indicated • Evaluate for abnormal movements (eg, dystonia, akathisia, tardive dyskinesia) and neurolep-
   tic malignant syndrome 16 at baseline, 3 months, and 12 months • Complete fall risk assessment in patients with diseases, conditions or concomitant medica-
   tions that may exacerbate antipsychotic effects (eg, somnolence, orthostatic hypotension, mo-
   tor instability), when initiating treatment and recurrently in patients on long-term therapy 7 ,5 .

   Therapeutic Drug Monitoring
   • Psychosis: 100 to 350 nanograms/milliliter (ng/mL; aripiprazole); 150 to 500 ng/mL (aripipra-
   zole plus dehydroaripiprazole) 22

   • In a consensus guideline, the use of therapeutic drug monitoring (TDM) with aripiprazole is
   rated as 2, recommended for dose titration and for special indications or problem solving.
   TDM will increase the probability of response in non-responders • The antipsychotic therapeutic reference range for aripiprazole is 100 to 350 ng/mL, and for
   aripiprazole plus dehydroaripiprazole is 150 to 500 ng/mL, with a laboratory alert level of 1000
   ng/mL for both analyses. Therapeutic reference ranges were obtained from drug concentra-
   tions at therapeutically effective doses and related to clinical effects; there are reports of de-
   creased tolerability or adverse effects at supratherapeutic drug concentrations in blood

drugs.uses_raw:
Perinatal/infantile-onset Hypophosphatasia:
   •Skeletal signs, respiratory function, and growth improved and were sustained for a median of 3 years
   and up to 6 years of treatment with asfotase alfa in an open-label study of 69 children 5 years or
   younger with signs and symptoms of hypophosphatasia before 6 months of age. Median (range) age at
   enrollment was 16 months (0.3 to 2 months). Median (range) Radiographic Global Impression of
   Change (RGI-C) score at 6 months of treatment was +2 (-1.7 to +3) (p less than 0001) and at 1 year was
   +2 (-2.3 to +3) (p less than 0001). At baseline, 24 of the 69 (35%) patients required respiratory support
   and at the last assessment 11 (46%) no longer required respiratory support. In general, z scores im-
   proved for height and weight over time. Overall survival rate at year 6 was 80% •Asfotase alfa significantly improved overall survival compared with a historical control of untreated pa-
   tients at 1 year (95% vs 42%) and at 5 years (84% vs 27%) in open-label, multicenter, multinational, inter-
   ventional studies (n=85). Additionally, 16 of 21 treated patients who needed ventilator support at base-
   line survived. Of those 16 survivors, 12 were able to be weaned from the ventilator. Comparatively only
   1 out of 20 of historical patients, who required ventilatory support, survived Juvenile-onset Hypophosphatasia: In a 24-week prospective trial, all patients who received asfotase
   alfa were considered Radiographic Global Impression of Change responders (minimum increase of 2 on
   scale) by month 54 compared with 6% of control patients after 56 months. An increase in step length by
   at least 1 point in either foot was also noted in 6 of 8 patients who received asfotase alfa compared
   with 1 of 6 control patients 1

   Pediatric FDA approved indication:
   Asfotase alfa is indicated for treatment of perinatal/infantile- or juvenile-onset hypophosphatasia in pe-
   diatric patients 1 day or older Administration
   • Administer within 3 hours of removing vials from refrigerator • Administer subQ using a 1-mL syringe and 5-inch injection needles, (25 to 29 gauge); use a larger
   bore needle for medication withdrawal (eg, 25 gauge) and use a smaller bore needle (eg, 29 gauge) for
   the injection • MAX volume to inject subQ is 1 mL; if more than 1 mL is required, split the volume equally between 2
   syringes and give 2 injections at different sites • Rotate injection sites including, thighs, abdomen, deltoid, or buttocks; do not administer in areas that
   are reddened, inflamed, or swollen

   with aspirin is unknown and is dependent on underlying conditions and risk of recurrent
   stroke; however, experts recommend continuing aspirin for at least 2 years Kawasaki Disease (KD): The initial treatment of KD is IV immune globulin and aspirin. Aspirin

   term treatment. Patients with coronary artery aneurysms require long-term and potentially in-

   During the acute phase, moderate-dose (30 to 50 mg/kg/day) 3 ,5 or high-dose (80 to 100
   mg/kg/day) aspirin is recommended No data to support superiority of either dose 3 , but
   there is some evidence that a high-dose is unnecessary 21 , 22 , 23 , A meta-analysis (all
   Japanese and North American studies) revealed that outcomes in KD were directly associated
   with IVIG dose and that the initial dose of aspirin administered (high-dose aspirin (80 to 100
   mg/kg/day) vs lower-dose aspirin (30 to 50 mg/kg/day)) did not affect coronary outcomes In
   a multicenter retrospective study (n=1213), low-dose (3 to 5 mg/kg/day) was not inferior to
   high-dose aspirin (80 mg/kg/day) for reducing the risk of coronary artery abnormalities during
   the acute phase of KD when used with IV immunoglobulin 21

   Thrombosis; Prophylaxis: Aspirin is recommended as thromboprophylaxis after Fontan sur-
   gery, in patients with systemic-to-pulmonary shunts, in patients after ventricular assist device
   placement, and in patients with mechanical heart valves who have had thrombotic events
   while receiving therapeutic antithrombotic therapy or patients in whom there is a contraindi-
   cation to full-dose vitamin K antagonists 6 , 7 , 8 , 9 , In a prospective, multicenter, randomized
   study (n=111) of warfarin vs aspirin for primary thromboprophylaxis in children after Fontan
   surgery, the thrombosis event rate at 2 years was 19% with no significant difference between
   warfarin and aspirin therapy (24% vs 14%; p=0.45); minor bleeding was more common in the
   warfarin group (33% vs 14%) Administration
   Oral: Aspirin should be taken with a full glass of water (8 ounces or more) 12,13 . Do not break
   extended-release tablets, such as Zorprin®; swallow intact Take with food to minimize GI
   upset.

A meta-analysis of 9 randomized, placebo-controlled trials reported the most common ad-
   verse events with atomoxetine in children included gastrointestinal (abdominal pain, appetite
   decrease, dyspepsia, vomiting), somnolence, dizziness, and fatigue Adverse reactions re-
   ported in at least 2% of child and adolescent poor metabolizers and at a significant greater fre-
   quency than extensive metabolizers include insomnia (11%), weight loss (7%), constipation
   (7%), depression (7%), tremor (5%), excoriation (4%), middle insomnia (3%), conjunctivitis (3%),
   syncope (3%), early morning waking (2%), mydriasis (2%), and sedation (4%) Black Box Warning
   Suicidal Ideation in Children and Adolescents

   Atomoxetine increased the risk of suicidal ideation in short-term studies in children or adoles-
   cents with Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD). Anyone considering the use of ato-
   moxetine in a child or adolescent must balance this risk with the clinical need. Comorbidities
   occurring with ADHD may be associated with an increase in the risk of suicidal ideation and/or
   behavior. Patients who are started on therapy should be monitored closely for suicidality (sui-
   cidal thinking and behavior), clinical worsening, or unusual changes in behavior. Families and
   caregivers should be advised of the need for close observation and communication with the
   prescriber. Atomoxetine is approved for ADHD in pediatric and adult patients. Atomoxetine is
   not approved for major depressive disorder. Pooled analyses of short-term (6 to 18 weeks)
   placebo-controlled trials of atomoxetine in children and adolescents (a total of 12 trials involv-
   ing over 2200 patients, including 11 trials in ADHD and 1 trial in enuresis) have revealed a
   greater risk of suicidal ideation early during treatment in those receiving atomoxetine com-
   pared to placebo. The average risk of suicidal ideation in patients receiving atomoxetine was 4% (5/1357 patients), compared to none in placebo-treated patients (851 patients). No sui-
   cides occurred in these trials 1

 Monitoring
   Monitor blood pressure at baseline, following dose increases, and periodically during therapy Monitor for the development of symptoms suggestive of cardiac disease throughout ther-
   apy 5 ,6 ,7 ,8 . Monitor closely for clinical worsening, suicidality, and unusual changes in behavior,
   especially during the first few months of therapy or at times of dose changes. Families or care-
   givers should observe daily. Monitor for symptoms that may represent precursors to emerging
   suicidality (eg, aggressiveness, agitation, akathisia, anxiety, hostility, impulsivity, insomnia, irri-
   tability, mania or hypomania, panic attacks). Monitor for appearance or worsening of aggres-
   sive or hostile behavior. Monitor liver enzymes if signs or symptoms of liver dysfunction occur
   (eg, dark urine, jaundice, pruritus, right upper quadrant tenderness, unexplained "flu-like"
   symptoms). Monitor height and weight changes for growth development. Periodically reevalu-
   ate continued need for atomoxetine when used for extended duration

   Data suggests that statin use in those 8 to 18 years of age had similar adverse-event profiles
   and efficacy when compared to adult studies 2 , however, randomized controlled trials in chil-
   dren have been limited to patients with hereditary familial hypercholesterolemia for a maxi-
   mum duration of 2 years. Data are lacking for children with secondary dyslipidemias. Long-
   term safety, especially with regard to growth and sexual development, is unknown A double-blind, placebo-controlled, 26-week study (n=187) followed by an open-label phase
   found that atorvastatin significantly decreased plasma levels of total-C, LDL-C, triglycerides,
   and apolipoprotein B in boys and postmenarchal girls 10-17 years of age. The mean achieved

 LDL-C value was 7 mg/dL in the atorvastatin group compared with 5 mg/dL in the
   placebo group. Long-term reduction of morbidity and mortality into adulthood is unknown Heterozygous Familial Hypercholesterolemia

   Statin therapy for 6 to 96 weeks significantly improved LDL-C and other lipid parameters (ex-
   cept triglycerides) and was well-tolerated in a metaanalysis of 9 studies in 1191 pediatric pa-
   tients (mean age, 3 +/- 5 years; mean BMI, 3 +/- 7 kg/m(2) based on 6 studies) with
   heterozygous familial hypercholesterolemia. At the end of treatment, the observed differences
   in lipid parameters for statins vs placebo were: Total cholesterol (9 studies) -79.3 mg/dL (95%
   CI, -93.9 to -64.7 mg/dL); LDL-C (9 studies) -78.5 mg/dL (95% CI, -93.2 to -63.8 mg/dL);
   Triglycerides (8 studies) -4.8 mg/dL (95% CI, -9.7 to 1 mg/dL); Apolipoprotein B (8 studies)
   -49.6 mg/dL (95% CI, -60.4 to -38.8 mg/dL); HDL-C (8 studies) 2 mg/dL (95% CI, 08 to 29
   mg/dL). In subgroup analysis, statins showed a dose-dependent effect on achievement of the
   LDL-C target. Important differences among studies may affect the validity of the total choles-
   terol, LDL-C, and apolipoprotein B results. Lovastatin 10 to 40 mg/day was given in 2 studies,
   pravastatin 10 to 40 mg/day in 2 studies, simvastatin 10 to 40 mg/day in 2 studies, pitavastatin
   1 to 4 mg/day in 1 study, atorvastatin 10 to 20 mg/day in 1 study, and rosuvastatin 5 to 20
   mg/day in 1 study Prevention of Pediatric Graft Coronary Artery Disease (GCAD)

   Early initiation of atorvastatin therapy in the post-transplant course reduced angiographic-evi-
   dent GCAD in a retrospective study (n=65). Patients were divided into two groups, those receiv-
   ing atorvastatin within 9 weeks post transplantation (age at transplantation = 3 ± 7 years;
   n=33) and those who did not receive atorvastatin within 9 weeks post transplantation (age at
   transplantation 4 ± 1 years; n=32). The median time to starting atorvastatin in the control
   group was 6 weeks (9 to 338 weeks). Atorvastatin was initiated at a 2 ± 1 mg/kg/day and
   rounded to the nearest dividable dose based off of a 10 mg tablet (2.5, 5, 5, and 10 mg). LDL
   levels were found to be significantly lower at one year post transplantation but not statistically
   lower at post transplantation years 2 to GCAD occurred in 2 subjects initiated early with
   atorvastatin and 12 in the control group (p less than 005). Subjects treated with atorvastatin
   experienced significantly fewer episodes of treated rejection in the first year post transplant as
   compared with placebo (p=0.0005). This significantly improved the freedom from the develop-
   ment of GCAD compared with patients who had at least one episode of treated rejection in the
   same time period (p=0.0001) Hyperlipidemia Secondary to Pediatric Renal Transplantation

   A retrospective study evaluating the effect of atorvastatin on lipid profiles in children with hy-
   perlipidemia secondary to pediatric renal transplantation found atorvastatin to be safe and ef-

 fective for this use (n=38 with n=5 receiving atorvastatin therapy). Atorvastatin was initiated at
   10 mg/day in children with elevated LDL (>130 mg/dL) following 6 months of nutritional coun-
   seling. Atorvastatin was found to be safe and effective as there was significant reduction in
   participants total cholesterol, LDL, VLDL, and triglyceride levels after 3 to 6 months of treat-
   ment (p less than 05) A prospective study looking at the prevalence of hyperlipidemia in pediatric transplant pa-
   tients and the treatment of persistently elevated cholesterol and/or LDL found that atorvas-
   tatin (n=8) was effective at reducing total cholesterol (p less than 01), LDL (p less than 01),
   and triglycerides (p=0.05) when compared with pre-treatment levels. The study found no ad-
   verse effects on allograft function or cyclosporin levels in their patients Pediatric FDA approved indication:

   • Indicated as an adjunct to diet to reduce low-density lipoprotein cholesterol (LDL-C) in pedi-
   atric patients aged 10 years or older with heterozygous familial hypercholesterolemia (HeFH)
   4,1

   • Indicated as an adjunct to other LDL-C lowering therapies, or alone if such treatments are un-
   available, to reduce LDL-C in pediatric patients 10 years or older with homozygous familial hy-
   percholesterolemia (HoFH)) 4 ,1

   Administration
   Tablets

   ach (ie, 1 hour before or 2 hours after a meal) • Missed dose: Take as soon as possible. If dose was missed by more than 12 hours, do not
   take the missed dose and resume with the next scheduled dose

drugs.uses_raw:
Neuromuscular blockade: Neuromuscular blockade (NMB) agents include atracurium,
   cisatracurium, pancuronium, rocuronium, and vecuronium. Studies have shown the most com-
   monly used NMB agents are vecuronium, pancuronium, or atracurium; however, a large, re-
   cent prospective observational study in 20 pediatric intensive care units in the United Kingdom
   showed substantial variation in practice, but that vecuronium was the most commonly used
   agent In a blinded, comparative study of atracurium, rocuronium, and vecuronium (total
   n=60; age 18 to 72 months), the quality of intubation conditions at the point of successful intu-
   bation were rated in the following order (better to worse): rocuronium > vecuronium >
   atracurium. The mean time to 95% NMB was longer for atracurium (124 seconds) as compared
   to rocuronium (92 seconds) or vecuronium (112 seconds) Slower onset was confirmed in a
   further comparative study of atracurium and rocuronium (n=30, age 18 months to 67 months),
   with a mean time to 95% NMB of 126 seconds for atracurium vs 86 seconds for rocuronium Atracurium or vecuronium are recommended for the majority of critically ill patients when
   continuous NMB is required Use in patients following liver transplant is safe and effective,
   with mean infusion rate of 24 (range 8 to 52) mcg/kg/min required Neuromuscular blockade, critically ill patients in ICU: In critically ill pediatric patients, the
   lowest effective dose of neuromuscular blockade (NMB) agent to achieve desired clinical ef-
   fects and manage breakthrough movement is recommended to balance the use of neuromus-
   cular blockade (NMB) agents (eg, optimization of patient-ventilator synchrony, reduction of
   oxygen consumption, and prevention of unintended extubation or device removal) with com-
   plications (eg, residual neuropathy or weakness) and lighter sedation strategies for neurocog-
   nitive recovery. Adequate sedation and analgesia during NMB agent use is recommended to
   prevent patient awareness Neuromuscular blockade, sepsis and acute respiratory distress syndrome:
   Neuromuscular blockade is recommended in pediatric patients with sepsis and acute respira-
   tory distress syndrome (ARDS) based on indirect evidence from randomized clinical trials in
   adults, which suggests improved 90-day survival and shorter duration of mechanical ventila-
   tion without increasing muscle weakness. One retrospective study of 317 pediatric patients

 with ARDS that reported lower mortality in patients treated with neuromuscular blockade
   (8.8% vs 7%), but a longer duration of mechanical ventilation. Most adult and pediatric data
   support a neuromuscular blockade duration of 24 to 48 hours after ARDS onset Pediatric Approved FDA Indications
   Adjunct to general anesthesia, to facilitate endotracheal intubation, and to provide skeletal
   muscle relaxation during surgery or mechanical ventilation in patients 1 month or older Administration
   Do not administer atracurium until the patient has been adequately sedated or is un-
   conscious For IV administration only; do not administer by IM route. Administer bolus injection over 10
   to 15 seconds 7 ,5 . For continuous infusion, concentrations of 2 to 1 mg/mL have been used
   4 ,8 ,5
             . Do not mix in the same syringe or administer through the same needle as alkaline solu-
   tions (eg, sodium bicarbonate, barbiturate solutions) The use of passive eyelid closure and eye lubrication for prevention of corneal ulcers is recom-
   mended in critically ill patients receiving neuromuscular blockade agents

   Black Box Warning
   Hypersensitivity Reactions including Anaphylaxis

   • Patients treated with avalglucosidase alfa-ngpt have experienced life-threatening hypersensi-
   tivity reactions, including anaphylaxis. Appropriate medical monitoring and support measures,
   including cardiopulmonary resuscitation equipment, should be readily available during aval-
   glucosidase alfa-ngpt administration. If a severe hypersensitivity reaction (eg, anaphylaxis) oc-
   curs, discontinue avalglucosidase alfa-ngpt immediately and initiate appropriate medical treat-
   ment. In patients with severe hypersensitivity reaction, a desensitization procedure to avalglu-
   cosidase alfa-ngpt may be considered.

   Infusion-Associated Reactions (IARs)

   • Patients treated with avalglucosidase alfa-ngpt have experienced severe IARs. If severe IARs
   occur, consider immediate discontinuation of avalglucosidase alfa-ngpt, initiation of appropri-
   ate medical treatment, and the benefits and risks of readministering avalglucosidase alfa-ngpt
   following severe IARs. Patients with an acute underlying illness at the time of avalglucosidase
   alfa-ngpt infusion may be at greater risk for IARs. Patients with advanced Pompe disease may
   have compromised cardiac and respiratory function, which may predispose them to a higher
   risk of severe complications from IARs.

   Risk of Acute Cardiorespiratory Failure in Susceptible Patients

   • Patients susceptible to fluid volume overload, or those with acute underlying respiratory ill-
   ness or compromised cardiac or respiratory function for whom fluid restriction is indicated

 may be at risk of serious exacerbation of their cardiac or respiratory status during avalglucosi-
   dase alfa-ngpt infusion. More frequent monitoring of vitals should be performed during aval-
   glucosidase alfa-ngpt infusion in such patients Monitoring
   • Frequently monitor vitals of patients who are susceptible to fluid volume overload, or those
   with acute underlying respiratory illness or compromised cardiac or respiratory function for
   whom fluid restriction is indicated • Observe for hypersensitivity reactions, including anaphylaxis.
   • Assess for infusion-associated reactions.

   mortar and pestle.

The most frequently reported adverse effects when used for juvenile idiopathic arthritis (JIA)

   Malignancy
   Chronic immunosuppression with azaTHIOprine, a purine antimetabolite, increases risk of ma-
   lignancy in humans. Reports of malignancy include post-transplant lymphoma and hep-
   atosplenic T-cell lymphoma (HSTCL) in patients with inflammatory bowel disease. Physicians
   using this drug should be very familiar with this risk as well as with the mutagenic potential to
   both men and women and with possible hematologic toxicities. Physicians should inform pa-
   tients of the risk of malignancy with azaTHIOprine 25,5 ,20 .

   ●    Patients with nosocomial infections
   ●    Patients with known or suspected bacteremia
   ●    Patients requiring hospitalization
   ●    Elderly or debilitated patients
   ●    Patients with significant underlying health problems that may compromise their ability to

 Literature
   • A systematic review and meta-analysis of 136 studies evaluating the toxicity of azithromycin
   in the setting of mass drug administration (control of trachoma) and non-mass drug adminis-
   tration found that the main adverse events reported in pediatric patients were diarrhea, ab-
   dominal pain, and vomiting. In the setting of non-mass drug administration, the most com-
   monly reported serious adverse events were cardiac adverse events, including QT-prolonga-
   tion and infantile hypertrophic pyloric stenosis. Increasing doses of azithromycin were associ-
   ated with a higher incidence of adverse events. Diarrhea, vomiting, fever, and rash were more
   common in the high-dosage group (greater than 30 mg/kg) than in the low- or medium-dosage
   groups (10 mg/kg or less and 10 to 30 mg/kg, respectively). The incidence of prolonged QT and
   increased eosinophils was higher in the medium-dosage group than in the low-dosage group • The use of macrolide antibiotics was associated with infantile hypertrophic pyloric stenosis
   with a 30-fold increased risk in infants exposed at 0 to 13 days of age and 3-fold increased risk
   in infants exposed at 14 to 120 days of age in an observational study (n=6591) Similar out-
   comes (highest risk of pyloric stenosis when exposed within the first couple weeks of life; al-
   though risk still present at 6 weeks of life) were demonstrated in another observational study
   (n= 4875 exposed to azithromycin) Solution Compatibility

   tam, potassium chloride, ticarcillin-clavulanate, and tobramycin.

   mg 3 times daily for 3 days, 15 mg 3 times daily for 3 days, 20 mg 3 times daily for 3 days.
   Additional increases may be necessary up to Maximum 80 mg/day given as 20 mg orally 4
   times daily (FDA dosage) 6 ,7 ,8 .

   Intrathecal
   4 Years or Older
   Intrathecal test dose: 25 to 50 mcg intrathecally given over at least 1 minute; may increase
   dosage by 25-mcg increments every 24 hours, Maximum 100 mcg. Observe for response 4 to
   8 hour after administration. Patients must have a positive clinical response to a single bolus
   dose of no greater than 100 mcg/2 mL to be acceptable candidates for chronic therapy with
   the intrathecal infusion pump 9 , Post-implant titration: After the first 24 hours, the intrathecal daily dose should be increased
   slowly by 5% to 15% only once every 24 hours, until the desired clinical effect is achieved 9 ,10 .
   Post-implant maintenance: Intrathecal daily dose may be increased by 5% to 20% (maxi-
   mum, 20%) during periodic pump refills. Dose may be reduced by 10% to 20% as needed.
   Intrathecal formulations are most often administered in a continuous infusion mode immedi-
   ately following implant. Most patients require gradual increase in dose over time to maintain
   optimal response. The average maintenance dose for children younger than 12 years is 274

 mcg/day (range 24 to 1199 mcg/day). Dosage requirements for children over 12 years of age
   do not seem to be different than adults. The reported range for maintenance dose for adults
   is 90 to 703 mcg per day, with a range of 22 to 1400 mcg/day for cerebral origin spasticity and
   300 to 800 mcg/day, with a range of 12 mcg/day to 2003 mcg/day for spinal cord spasticity
   9 ,10
           .

   Dose Adjustment
   Post-implant titration: Dose adjustment should allow for some spasticity to support circula-
   tory function, possibly prevent deep vein thrombosis, and optimize the activities of daily living
   and ease of care. Careful dose titration should be considered when spasticity is necessary to
   sustain upright posture and balance in locomotion or whenever spasticity is used to obtain op-
   timal function and care 9 ,10 .

   Tolerance in chronic use: A drug holiday of gradual reduction of intrathecal baclofen over 2
   to 4 weeks, plus switching to alternative methods to manage spasticity, has been used for tol-
   erance treatment. After the drug holiday, intrathecal baclofen may be resumed with the initial
   continuous infusion dose 9 , Discontinuation: Slowly reduce dose if the drug needs to be discontinued for any reason 6 ,
   except in overdose related situations Renal Impairment: Cautious use is recommended in patients with renal insufficiency because
   the drug is primarily excreted unchanged in the urine; 6 , 9 dosage reduction may be necessary
   6 ,9 ,11
                   .
   Patients with overt or subclinical renal insufficiency may develop toxicity at therapeutic doses
   12,13
               .

   Hepatic Impairment: Baclofen is metabolized only to a limited extent 14 ; no dose reductions
   are required in patients with hepatic insufficiency.

   Hemodialysis: Use lower initial doses and increase gradually, only as needed and tolerated 15

   Management of severe spasticity in pediatric patients 4 years or older. Response to an in-
