   cal administration 9 ,10 .

   Oral
   Orally administered baclofen is indicated for the treatment of spasticity resulting from multiple
   sclerosis, particularly flexor spasms and concomitant pain, clonus, and muscular rigidity, and
   spinal cord injuries/diseases in patients 12 years and older 6 ,7 ,8

   Limitations of Use

   Baclofen is not indicated in the treatment of muscle spasm resulting from rheumatic disorders
   6 ,7
          .

   Administration
   Intrathecal

   •For the screening phase, use the 1 mL (50 mcg/mL) ampule 9 or single-use syringe •Administer the screening bolus over at least 1 minute into the intrathecal space by barbotage.
   During dose increases, if significant improvements do not occur, check for proper pump func-
   tion and catheter patency 9 , •If using the prefilled syringe for the screening bolus dose: use 1 mL of the prefilled syringe for
   a 50-mcg bolus screening dose, use 5 mL of 50 mcg/mL baclofen injection for a 75 mcg dose,
   and use 2 prefilled syringes for 100 mcg dose 3/13
 •Intrathecal baclofen is intended for use as a single bolus test dose or for chronic use with an
   implantable pump labeled for intrathecal use 9 ,10 , or with the Medtronic SynchroMed® II
   Programmable Pump •Delivery of more drug volume than the programmed rate (overinfusion) can result in unex-
   pected overdose or withdrawal caused by early emptying of the pump reservoir; refill the
   reservoir per the pump manual Delivery Regimen: Intrathecal formulations are most often administered in a continuous infu-
   sion mode immediately following implant. Patients with programmable pumps who have re-
   ceived satisfactory control on continuous infusion may benefit from using more complex
   schedules of intrathecal baclofen delivery. For patients who experience increases spasms at
   night, they may benefit from a schedule that will allow a 20% increase in their hourly infusion
   rate. Changes in flow rate should be programmed to start two hours before the time of de-
   sired effect 9 ,10 .
   •Chronic intrathecal administration should only be used with pumps specifically FDA approved
   for the administration of intrathecal baclofen. There are numerous pumps available with vary-
   ing reservoir volumes and refill kits; refer to the manufacturer's manual for the implantable
   pump approved for intrathecal infusion •Only refill pump through the reservoir refill septum. For pumps with a catheter access port
   that allows direct access to the intrathecal catheter, extreme care should be taken Preparation

   Intrathecal

   •The specific concentration that should be used will depend on the total daily dose required,
   as well as the delivery rate of the pump. Intrathecal formulations may require dilution when
   used with certain implantable pumps. Consult the pump's manufacturer's manual for specific
   recommendations 9 ,10 .
   •For maintenance patients who require concentrations other than 500 mcg/mL, 1000 mcg/mL,
   or 2000 mcg/mL, dilute intrathecal baclofen with sterile preservative-free NS 16,9

       muscle rigidity, that in rare cases has advanced to rhabdomyolysis, multiple organ-system

   ●   Prevention of abrupt discontinuation of intrathecal baclofen requires careful attention to
       programming and monitoring of the infusion system, refill scheduling and procedures, and
       pump alarms. Patients and caregivers should be advised of the importance of keeping
       scheduled refill visits and should be educated on the early symptoms of baclofen with-
       drawal. Special attention should be given to patients at apparent risk (eg, spinal cord in-

drugs.uses_raw:
Influenza
   Summary: Baloxavir marboxil significantly reduced the time to symptom alleviation by about
   a day compared with placebo, and baloxavir marboxil time to symptom alleviation was similar

 to that of oseltamivir in otherwise healthy adolescents 2 , but not in a limited number of ado-
   lescents with high risk for developing influenza-related complications Recommendations
   Consider an antiviral for any previously healthy, symptomatic outpatient not at high risk for in-
   fluenza complications, who is diagnosed with confirmed or suspected influenza, on the basis
   of clinical judgement, if treatment can be started within 48 hours of illness onset 4

   Preferred Agents: 4
    ●   Hospitalized: Oral oseltamivir
    ●   Outpatients with acute uncomplicated influenza: Oral oseltamivir, inhaled zanamivir, IV
        peramivir, or oral baloxavir
    ●   Pregnant women: Oral oseltamivir
    ●   Severe or complicated illness with suspected or confirmed influenza who are not hospitalized:
        Oral or enterically administered oseltamivir

   In a randomized, active- and placebo-controlled trial of adult and adolescent patients with
   PCR-confirmed influenza who were at high risk of developing influenza-related complications
   (N=1158), the median time to improvement of influenza symptoms was significantly shorter in
   the baloxavir marboxil group compared with placebo (73 vs 102 hours) and similar to that
   achieved with oseltamivir (81 hours). However, in the small subset of adolescent patients
   (n=38) the median time to improvement was similar in those treated with baloxavir (188 hours)
   or placebo (191 hours). Patients received 1 dose of weight-based oral baloxavir marboxil (40
   mg or 80 mg), oseltamivir 75 mg daily for 5 days, or placebo; all were treated within 48 hours
   of symptom onset In the randomized CAPSTONE-1 study of patients 12 to 64 years old with influenza during the
   2016 to 2017 season (N=1436), treatment with baloxavir marboxil significantly reduced the
   median time to symptom alleviation compared with placebo (65.4 hours vs 6 hours); time to
   sympton alleviation was similar with baloxavir marboxil and oseltamivir (53.5 hours and 8
   hours). When only patients with RT-PCR confirmed influenza infection were analyzed, median
   time to symptom alleviation was 7 hours with baloxavir marboxil and 2 with placebo.
   The difference in time to symptom alleviation between baloxavir marboxil and placebo was 6 hours in adolescents 2 (n=118; 80 received baloxavir marboxil and 38 received placebo 5 ).
   The difference in time to alleviation between baloxavir marboxil and placebo was greater in
   those initiating baloxavir marboxil within 24 hours (median difference, 8 hours) compared
   with those initiating therapy later (median difference, 2 hours). After 1 day of treatment, vi-
   ral loads declined significantly more with baloxavir marboxil compared with placebo or os-
   eltamivir. Resistance-associated PTI38T/M substitutions were detected in 7% of those treated

 with baloxavir marboxil compared with no patients given placebo. Adverse effects related to
   the study drug occurred in 4% of the baloxavir marboxil group compared with 4% of the
   oseltamivir group and 9% of the placebo group. Included patients were symptomatic for no
   more than 48 hours; acetaminophen use was allowed. Patients were randomized to receive
   baloxavir marboxil 40 or 80 mg as a single dose (dependent on weight; followed by 4 days of
   placebo; n=610), oseltamivir 75 mg twice daily for 5 days (n=513), or placebo (n=309). About
   half of the patients started their treatment regimen within 24 hours of symptom onset. Most
   had influenza A(H3N2) virus In a randomized, double-blind trial in household contacts (n=749) of patients with confirmed
   influenza (index patients; n=545), administration of a single dose of weight-based baloxavir
   marboxil was associated with a significantly lower rate of laboratory-confirmed clinical in-
   fluenza (1.9%) compared with placebo (13.6%) for an adjusted risk ratio of 14 (95% CI, 06 to 3). Confirmed clinical influenza was defined as positive RT-PCR for influenza viral RNA along
   with fever and at least 1 moderate-to-severe respiratory symptom; 5% of household con-
   tacts received the study drug within 24 hours after illness onset in the index patients. Mean
   age of index patients was 3 years, while mean age of household contacts was 5 to 6
   years (mostly parents or siblings of index patients). Among patients aged 12 years or older (for
   whom baloxavir marboxil is FDA-approved), 3% developed laboratory-confirmed clinical in-
   fluenza in the baloxavir group (n=303) compared with 2% for placebo (n=304), for an ad-
   justed risk ratio of 1 (95% CI, 04 to 28). In patients aged less than 12 years, 2% devel-
   oped laboratory-confirmed clinical influenza in the baloxavir group (n=71) compared with 5% for placebo (n=71), for an adjusted risk ratio of 27 (95% CI, 08 to 9). Influenza A
   virus infection was present in 6% of the index patient population (mostly H1N1pdm09 and
   H3N2 subtypes). Adverse events occurred at similar rates in baloxavir and placebo groups
   (20.5% to 2%), and included headache, hematuria, pharyngitis, and increased ALT; 1 case of
   hematuria was deemed related to baloxavir treatment Influenza Transmission Reduction

   In a phase 3b, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial conducted across the 2019 to
   2024 influenza seasons (N=1457, ages 5 to 64 years), a single oral dose of baloxavir marboxil
   significantly reduced influenza transmission in household contacts by day In the primary
   analysis population, which included unvaccinated household contacts who were negative for
   influenza at baseline, the adjusted incidence of laboratory-confirmed influenza transmission
   by day 5 was 5% in the baloxavir marboxil group compared with 4% in the placebo group
   (adjusted odds ratio (OR), 68; 95% CI, 5 to 93), reflecting a 29% relative risk reduction
   (95% CI, 12 to 45). However, the incidence of symptomatic transmission by day 5 did not differ
   significantly between groups, with a 8% adjusted incidence in the baloxavir group compared

 with 6% in the placebo group (OR, 75; 95% CI, 5 to 12). These findings were consistent
   across prespecified subgroups based on age, timing of treatment initiation, influenza subtype,
   and season. Similar results were observed in the broader full analysis population, which in-
   cluded vaccinated household contacts and those without confirmed influenza-negative status
   at baseline. Findings through day 9 were also consistent with the primary analysis, showing a
   statistically significant reduction in overall influenza transmission with baloxavir compared
   with placebo (10.8% vs. 4%; OR, 66; 95% CI, 48 to 91), and a non-significant reduction
   in symptomatic transmission (6.2% vs. 3%; OR, 73; 95% CI, 49 to 09) FDA Pediatric Approval
   Baloxavir marboxil is indicated to treat acute uncomplicated influenza in patients 5 years or
   older who have been symptomatic for no more than 48 hours and who are otherwise healthy
   or at high risk of developing influenza-related complications Baloxavir marboxil is indicated for post-exposure prophylaxis of influenza in persons aged 5
   years or older following contact with an individual who has influenza Influenza viruses change over time, and factors such as the virus type or subtype, emergence of re-
   sistance, or changes in viral virulence could diminish the clinical benefit of antiviral drugs. Consider
   available information on drug susceptibility patterns for circulating influenza virus strains when de-

Coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19): The safety and effectiveness of bamlanivimab plus
   etesevimab have not been assessed in pediatric patients. The adult dosing regimen is ex-
   pected to result in comparable serum exposures of bamlanivimab in patients 12 years or older
   and weighing at least 40 kg as observed in adults, based on a pharmacokinetic modeling ap-
   proach which accounted for effect of body weight changes associated with age on clearance
   and volume of distribution Emergency Use for COVID-19 Infection
   Bamlanivimab in combination with etesevimab are authorized for emergency use by the US
   Food and Drug Administration (FDA) for the treatment of mild to moderate COVID-19 in pedi-
   atric patients with positive results of direct SARS-CoV-2 viral testing, who are at high risk for
   progressing to severe COVID-19 and/or hospitalization Limitations of Authorized Use

   Bamlanivimab and etesevimab are not authorized for treatment of mild to moderate COVID-19
   in geographic regions where infection is likely to have been caused by a nonsusceptible SARS-
   CoV-2 variant based on available information including variant susceptibility to these drugs
   and regional variant frequency Bamlanivimab and etesevimab are NOT authorized for use in patients 5 :
   ●   2 years or older who are hospitalized due to COVID-19, OR
   ●   Who require oxygen therapy due to COVID-19, OR
   ●   Who require and increase in baseline oxygen flow rate due to COVID-19 in those on chronic
       oxygen therapy due to underlying non-COVID-19 related comorbidity

 Benefit of treatment with etesevimab and bamlanivimab has not been observed in patients
   hospitalized due to COVID-19. Monoclonal antibodies, such as etesevimab and bamlanivimab,
   may be associated with worse clinical outcomes when administered to hospitalized patients
   with COVID-19 requiring high flow oxygen or mechanical ventilation Emergency Use for Post-Exposure Prophylaxis of COVID-19

   Bamlanivimab plus etesevimab is authorized for emergency use by the US Food and Drug
   Administration (FDA) for post-exposure prophylaxis of COVID-19 in individuals who are at high
   risk of progression to severe COVID-19, including hospitalization or death 6

   Patients who meet the following criteria are considered at high risk of progression to severe
   COVID-19 6
   ●   Not fully vaccinated OR are not expected to mount an adequate immune response to SARS-
       CoV-2 vaccination (eg, individuals with immunocompromising conditions including those
       taking immunosuppressive medications) AND
   ●   Have been exposed to an individual infected with SARS-CoV-2 consistent with close contact
       criteria per CDC OR
   ●   Who are at high risk of exposure to an individual infected with SARS-CoV-2 because of oc-
       currence of SARS-CoV-2 infection in other individuals in the same institutional setting (eg,
       nursing homes, prisons)

   Bamlanivimab and etesevimab are not authorized for use in geographic regions where expo-
   sure is likely to have been to a nonsusceptible SARS-CoV-2 variant based on available informa-
   tion including variant susceptibility to these drugs and regional variant frequency Post-exposure prophylaxis with bamlanivimab and etesevimab is not a substitute for vaccina-
   tion against COVID-19 Bamlanivimab and etesevimab are not authorized for pre-exposure prophylaxis for prevention
   of COVID-19 Administration

drugs.contraindications_raw:
Common, adults: ALT greater than or equal to 3x ULN (18%), AST greater than or equal to 3x
   ULN (11.5%), thrombocytosis (8.2%), creatine phosphokinase greater than 5x ULN (3.7%), neu-
   tropenia (2.2%), deep vein thrombosis (1.5%), pulmonary embolism (1.4%), urinary tract infec-
   tion (1.3%) 1

   Black Box Warning

   Serious Infections

   • Patients treated with baricitinib are at risk for developing serious infections that may lead to
   hospitalization or death. Most patients who developed these infections were taking concomi-
   tant immunosuppressants such as methotrexate or corticosteroids.

   If a serious infection develops, interrupt baricitinib until the infection is controlled.
   • Reported infections include active tuberculosis, which may present with pulmonary or extra-
   pulmonary disease. Patients should be tested for latent tuberculosis before initiating barici-
   tinib and during therapy. Treatment for latent infection should be considered prior to barici-
   tinib use.

   • Reported infections include invasive fungal infections, including candidiasis and pneumocys-
   tosis. Patients with invasive fungal infections may present with disseminated, rather than local-
   ized, disease.

   • Reported infections include bacterial, viral, and other infections due to opportunistic
   pathogens.

   • The risks and benefits of treatment with baricitinib should be carefully considered prior to
   initiating therapy in patients with chronic or recurrent infection.
   • Patients should be closely monitored for the development of signs and symptoms of infec-
   tion during and after treatment with baricitinib including the possible development of tubercu-
   losis in patients who tested negative for latent tuberculosis infection prior to initiating therapy.
   Mortality

 • In a large, randomized, postmarketing safety study in rheumatoid arthritis (RA) patients 50
   years of age and older with at least one cardiovascular risk factor comparing another Janus ki-
   nase (JAK) inhibitor to tumor necrosis factor (TNF) blockers, a higher rate of all-cause mortality,
   including sudden cardiovascular death, was observed with the JAK inhibitor.

   Malignancies

   • Lymphoma and other malignancies have been observed in patients treated with baricitinib.
   In RA patients treated with another JAK inhibitor, a higher rate of malignancies (excluding non-
   melanoma skin cancer (NMSC)) was observed when compared with TNF blockers. Patients who
   are current or past smokers are at additional increased risk.
   Major Adverse Cardiovascular Events

   In RA patients 50 years of age and older with at least one cardiovascular risk factor treated
   with another JAK inhibitor, a higher rate of major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE) (de-
   fined as cardiovascular death, myocardial infarction, and stroke) was observed when com-
   pared with TNF blockers. Patients who are current or past smokers are at additional increased
   risk. Discontinue baricitinib in patients that have experienced a myocardial infarction or stroke.

   Thrombosis

   • Thrombosis, including deep venous thrombosis and pulmonary embolism, has been ob-
   served at an increased incidence in patients treated with baricitinib compared to placebo. In
   addition, there were cases of arterial thrombosis. Many of these adverse events were serious
   and some resulted in death. In RA patients 50 years of age and older with at least one cardio-
   vascular risk factor treated with another JAK inhibitor, a higher rate of thrombosis was ob-
   served when compared with TNF blockers. Avoid baricitinib in patients at risk. Patients with
   symptoms of thrombosis should discontinue baricitinib and be promptly evaluated Monitoring
   Toxic Laboratory Monitoring

   • Screen for viral hepatitis prior to initiation of therapy 1

   • Monitor for expression of hepatitis B virus DNA in patients with positive hepatitis B surface
   antibody and hepatitis B core antibody, without hepatitis B surface antigen • Monitor CBC, including absolute neutrophil count, absolute lymphocyte count, and Hb prior
   to initiation and thereafter during routine patient management and closely monitor patients
   with abnormal baseline and post-baseline values • Evaluate liver enzymes prior to initiation and thereafter during routine patient management
   and closely monitor patients with abnormal baseline and post-baseline values 6/9
 • Monitor for signs and symptoms of new infections during and after treatment • Evaluate estimated GFR prior to initiation and closely monitor patients with abnormal base-
   line and post-baseline laboratory values Toxic Physical Monitoring

drugs.uses_raw:
Systemic lupus erythematous: In a study of pediatric patients with systemic lupus erythe-
   matosus (SLE; N=93; median age, 15 years; range, 6 to 17 years), treatment with IV belimumab
   improved the proportion of patients achieving an SLE Responder Index-4 (SRI-4) response at
   week 52 compared with placebo (53% vs 44%), although the difference was not significant be-
   tween groups. Patients receiving belimumab had a 62% lower risk of experiencing a severe
   flare (incidence of at least 1 severe flare, 23% vs 43%), as measured by the modified Safety of
   Estrogen in Lupus Erythematosus National Assessment (SELENA)-SLE Disease Activity Index
   (SLEDAI) Flare Index. Of the patients that experienced a severe flare, the median time to first
   severe flare was 160 days in the belimumab group and 82 days in the placebo group. Patients
   received belimumab 10 mg/kg IV plus standard therapy or placebo plus standard therapy 2/9
 Use of belimumab SUBQ in pediatric patients (5 to less than 18 years of age and weighing at
   least 15 kg) with SLE is supported by evidence from an open-label pharmacokinetic trial (SUBQ
   administration of belimumab in pediatric patients with SLE) and a separate pharmacokinetic,
   efficacy, and safety study of intravenous dosing in pediatric patients with SLE. The pharmacoki-
   netics of belimumab, following SUBQ administration in pediatric patients, are estimated to be
   similar to adults who receive belimumab SUBQ and pediatric patients who receive belimumab
   IV The prefilled syringe (SUBQ) has not been studied in pediatric patients less than 18 years of
   age Active lupus nephritis: Use of belimumab in pediatric patients with active lupus nephritis is
   based on the extrapolation of efficacy from the IV study in adults with active lupus nephritis
   (N=224), and supported by pharmacokinetic data from IV studies in adults with active lupus
   nephritis (N=224) and from pediatric patients with systemic lupus erythematosus (N=53).
   Estimated belimumab exposures for pediatric patients were comparable to adults with active
   lupus nephritis Use of belimumab, administered SUBQ in pediatric patients 5 years of age and older who
   weigh at least 15 kg with active lupus nephritis, is based on the extrapolation of efficacy from
   the IV trial in adults with active lupus nephritis, and is supported by pharmacokinetic data de-
   rived from the same adult trial, a pharmacokinetic, efficacy, and safety IV trial in pediatric sub-
   jects with active SLE, and an open-label SUBQ trial in pediatric subjects with active SLE.
   Belimumab exposures for pediatric patients with active lupus nephritis following SUBQ admin-
   istration are estimated to be comparable to adults with active lupus nephritis who receive beli-
   mumab IV The prefilled syringe (SUBQ) has not been studied in pediatric patients less than 18 years of
   age Pediatric Approved FDA Indications

   Belimumab is indicated for the treatment of patients aged 5 years or older with active systemic
   lupus erythematous or active lupus nephritis who are receiving standard therapy Administration
   Intravenous

   time Subcutaneous

   ministration or start a new weekly schedule from the day that missed dose was administered;

drugs.uses_raw:
Beremagene geperpavec-svdt is indicated for the treatment of wounds in adult and pediatric
   patients with dystrophic epidermolysis bullosa (DEB) with mutation(s) in the collagen type VII
   alpha 1 chain (COL7A1) gene Administration
   • Only a healthcare professional should apply gel • Use the gel in the administration syringes immediately after preparation 1
   • Apply gel to the selected wound(s) in droplets spaced evenly within the wound, approxi-
   mately 1 cm-by-1 cm apart. The resulting droplet pattern should loosely resemble a grid. Avoid
   touching the administration syringe to the skin or wound 1

   • Use the clean scissors to cut the hydrophobic dressing to a size slightly larger than the
   wound and place the dressing atop the gel droplets 1
   • Use the scissors to cut the standard dressing used by the patient to a size slightly larger than
   the hydrophobic dressing and place the standard dressing atop the hydrophobic dressing 1
   • Clean all surfaces that may have come in contact with gel and treat all spills with a virucidal
   agent such as 70% isopropyl alcohol, 6% hydrogen peroxide or 4% ammonium chloride. Blot
   using absorbent materials. Dispose all materials (eg, syringe, cleaning materials) that may have
   come in contact with biological suspension or gel into a biohazard bag or container. Discard
   unused administration syringes containing the gel after preparation into a biohazard bag or
   container 1

   • Leave dressing in place until the next dressing change after beremagene geperpavec-svdt gel
   application 1

   • It may not be possible to apply gel to all the wounds at each treatment visit 1

 • Apply gel to wounds until they are closed before selecting new wound(s) to treat. Prioritize
   weekly treatment to previously treated wounds if they re-open 1

   Preparation
   • Prepare beremagene geperpavec-svdt gel at pharmacy by mixing the biological suspension
   into the excipient gel for immediate use within 8 hours of preparation • Only a healthcare professional should apply gel • Individuals who are pregnant should not prepare or apply gel and should avoid direct contact
   with the treated wounds or dressings from treated wounds • Remove both vials from the carton and thaw biological suspension vial and the excipient gel
   vial at room temperature for at least 20 minutes; excipient gel is more viscous and will take
   longer to thaw • Invert the biological suspension vial 4 to 5 times; do not invert the excipient gel vial • Aseptically connect an 18-gauge needle to the 3 mL preparation syringe • Remove the needle cap and puncture biological suspension vial stopper; hold the vial at 45 to
   90 degrees and withdraw 1 mL of biological suspension into the preparation syringe • Remove the preparation syringe (still connected to the needle) containing 1 mL of biological
   suspension from the vial; do not engage the safety lock • Puncture the clean excipient gel vial stopper and transfer biological suspension into the ex-
   cipient gel vial • Without removing the needle from the excipient gel vial, lift the tip of the needle above the
   liquid and pull the plunger back to the 1 mL mark to vent the gel vial • Remove the preparation syringe with the 1 mL of air and engage the safety lock • Place a 70% isopropyl alcohol pad on top of the excipient gel stopper and hold it tightly in
   place; shake vigorously for 10 seconds • Aseptically connect an 18-gauge needle to the first 1 mL administration syringe and insert the
   needle into the excipient vial containing beremagene geperpavec-svdt gel; tilt the vial 45 to 90
   degrees and withdraw 5 mL of beremagene geperpavec-svdt gel • Do not remove the needle from the vial; lift the tip of the needle above the beremagene
   geperpavec-svdt gel and disconnect the administration syringe containing 5 mL of mixed
   beremagene geperpavec-svdt. Leave needle in the vial stopper • Do not flick the syringe to remove the air pocket. Manipulate the plunger up and down, until
   all air pockets have been removed 3/6
 • Cap the administration syringe and set aside • Connect a new 1 mL administration syringe to the needle that remains in the excipient gel
   vial stopper (with the tip of the needle ABOVE the beremagene geperpavec-svdt gel 1

   • Place the tip of the needle in the beremagene geperpavec-svdt gel, tilt the vial 45 to 90 de-
   grees and withdraw 5 mL of beremagene geperpavec-svdt gel into the administration sy-
   ringe. Complete preparation of the administration syringe as described above 1
   • Repeat steps if 2 additional administration syringes are required (each containing 5 mL of
   gel) 1
   • Discard the excipient gel vial (with the needle within the vial stopper) into the biohazard con-
   tainer 1

   • Place capped administration syringes into a sealable plastic bag. Place the sealable plastic
   bag into an appropriate insulated secondary container at 2 to 8°C (35.6 to 4°F) for transport
   from the preparation site to the administration site 1
   • Clean all surfaces that may have come in contact with gel and treat all spills with a virucidal
   agent such as 70% isopropyl alcohol, 6% hydrogen peroxide or 4% ammonium chloride. Blot

drugs.uses_raw:
Hereditary angioedema
   • In a randomized trial of patients 12 years or older with Type 1 or 2 hereditary angioedema
   (HAE) due to C1 inhibitor deficiency (N=120), treatment with berotralstat 150 mg daily and 110
   mg daily significantly reduced investigator confirmed HAE attack rate compared with placebo
   over a 24-week period (1.31 and 65 vs 35 attacks per month; attack rate ratio relative to
   placebo, 56 [95% CI, 41 to 77] and 7 [95% CI, 51 to 95], respectively). The overall
   Angioedema Quality of Life Questionnaire (AE-QoL; scores range from 0 to 100 with higher
   scores indicating greater impairment) total score and mean change from baseline were not
   significantly different from placebo in both the 110-mg and 150-mg groups; the mean change
   from baseline at 24 weeks did exceed the minimal clinically important difference of 6 points
   with berotralstat 110 mg (LSM, -12.46 points), berotralstat 150 mg (LSM, -14.59 points), and
   with placebo (LSM, -9.69 points; no significant difference from placebo in both groups). A
   prospective run-in period of up to 70 days was used to determine baseline attack rate and the
   mean was approximately 3 attacks per month across all treatment groups. The HAE attack rate
   was significantly reduced in the 150-mg group regardless if patients experienced 2 or more at-
   tacks at baseline (attack rate, 76 vs 92) or fewer than 2 attacks at baseline (attack rate, 5
   vs 45); however, in the 110-mg group only patients with 2 or more attacks per month at
   baseline had a significant reduction. The reduction in mean attack rate began within the first
   month and was sustained throughout the 24-week period. Patients could use standard medi-
   cations for breakthrough HAE attacks throughout the study. The most frequent treatment
   emergent adverse events with berotralstat were abdominal pain, vomiting, diarrhea, and back
   pain. The overall risk versus benefit profile favored the 150 mg/day dose The lower studied
   dose of 110 mg/day is FDA approved for use in patients requiring dosage adjustments, eg due
   to moderate to severe hepatic impairment, persistent gastrointestinal adverse events, or cer-
   tain concomitant drugs • Use in pediatric patients 2 to less than 12 years is supported by efficacy data from the ade-
   quate and well-controlled study in adults and pediatric patients 12 years or older, and pharma-
   cokinetic and safety data from a multicenter, single-arm, open-label study (N=29) with addi-
   tional support from population pharmacokinetic analyses. Patients were treated for at least 12
   weeks, with 17 patients completing 48 weeks of treatment. No new safety signals were ob-
   served 2/7
 FDA Approved Pediatric Indication

   Berotralstat is indicated for prophylaxis to prevent attacks of hereditary angioedema (HAE) in
   adults and pediatric patients 2 years of age and older Limitations of Use

   The safety and effectiveness for the treatment of acute HAE attacks have not been established.
   Berotralstat should not be used for treatment of acute HAE attacks Additional doses or doses of berotralstat higher than the prescribed once daily dose are not
   recommended due to the potential for QT prolongation Administration
   Oral tablets

   • Take with food Oral pellets

   • Administer immediately before or after a meal • Do not crush or chew oral pellets; doing so results in a bitter taste from disruption of the film
   coating • Pour the entire contents of packet directly into mouth and swallow immediately with a non-
   acidic liquid (eg, water or milk) • Alternatively, may sprinkle the packet contents over 1 tablespoon (15 mL) of soft, non-acidic
   food (eg, pudding, mashed potatoes, creamed corn, pureed peas, pureed bananas, or pureed
   carrots) at or below room temperature. Consume immediately; if not consumed within 10 min-
   utes, discard. Acidic foods (eg, yogurt and applesauce) can dissolve the film coating, resulting
   in a bitter taste

drugs.uses_raw:
Atopic dermatitis, active inflammatory disease: For acute flares, use of topical corticos-
   teroids is recommended daily until inflammatory lesions are significantly improved and less
   thick, for up to several weeks at a time. During significant flares, the use of mid- or higher po-
   tency topical corticosteroids for short courses may be appropriate to gain rapid control of
   symptoms Atopic dermatitis, relapse prevention: In patients who experience frequent, repeat out-
   breaks at the same body site, maintenance therapy with topical corticosteroids once to twice
   weekly may reduce the rates of relapse and increase the time to first flare relative to the use of
   moisturizers alone. For long-term management, the least potent corticosteroid that is effective
   should be used to minimize the risk of adverse effects 5/18
 Infantile hemangioma

   Guidelines: Intralesional injection of betamethasone or triamcinolone or a combination of
   both may be used to treat focal, bulky infantile hemangiomas during proliferation or in certain
   critical anatomic locations, such as the lip or nose. Local skin adverse effects, such as dermal
   atrophy or pigmentary changes, failure to thrive, and transient Cushingoid features are com-
   mon adverse events with intralesional administration Evidence:

   •A meta-analysis of 22 studies found that 71% of subjects treated with intralesional corticos-
   teroid injection (mostly with triamcinolone monotherapy or triamcinolone plus betametha-
   sone) achieved greater than 75% regression in infantile hemangioma size •The combination of a high-potency steroid (betamethasone) and a long-acting steroid (triam-
   cinolone) may maximize early regression and decrease rebound growth 9 , as well reduce the
   required number of injections and risk of side effects FDA approved pediatric indications

   Betamethasone dipropionate augmented

   •Betamethasone dipropionate augmented cream, gel lotion, and ointment are approved for
   approved for the relief of inflammatory and pruritic symptoms of corticosteroid-responsive
   dermatoses in patients 13 years old or older 5 ,2 ,6 ,4 .

   toms of corticosteroid-responsive dermatoses of the scalp 7

   Betamethasone injection is approved for the following indications when oral therapy is not
   feasible 8 :
   •Severe allergic conditions nonresponsive to conventional therapy including: seasonal or
   perennial allergic rhinitis, asthma, atopic or contact dermatitis, drug hypersensitivity reactions
   and serum sickness, and transfusion reactions 8

 •Dermatologic diseases: Bullous dermatitis herpetiformis, exfoliative erythroderma, mycosis
   fungoides, pemphigus, severe erythema multiforme (Stevens-Johnson syndrome) 8
   •Intralesional treatment of alopecia areata, keloids, discoid lupus erythematosus, localized hy-
   pertrophic, infiltrated, inflammatory lesions of granuloma annulare, lichen planus, lichen sim-
   plex chronicus (neurodermatitis), and psoriatic plaques, necrobiosis lipoidica diabeticorum 8

   •Endocrine disorders: Congenital adrenal hyperplasia, hypercalcemia associated with cancer,
   and nonsuppurative thyroiditis 8
   •Gastrointestinal diseases: Regional enteritis and ulcerative colitis, to tide the patient over a
   critical part of the disease 8
   •Hematologic disorders: Autoimmune hemolytic anemia, Diamond-Blackfan anemia, pure red
   cell aplasia, and selected cases of secondary thrombocytopenia 8

   •Trichinosis with neurologic or myocardial involvement 8
   •Tuberculosis meningitis with subarachnoid block or impending block when used in conjunc-
   tion with appropriate antituberculous therapy 8

   •Neoplastic diseases: Palliative management of lymphomas or leukemias 8

   •Nervous system diseases: Acute exacerbations of multiple sclerosis, cerebral edema associ-
   ated with primary or metastatic brain tumor or craniotomy 8
   •Ophthalmic diseases: Sympathetic ophthalmia, temporal arteritis, uveitis, and ocular inflam-
   matory conditions unresponsive to topical corticosteroids 8
   •Renal diseases: To induce diuresis or remission of proteinuria in patients with idiopathic
   nephrotic syndrome or that due to lupus erythematosus 8

   •Respiratory diseases: Berylliosis, fulminating or disseminating pulmonary tuberculosis when
   used concurrently with appropriate antituberculosis chemotherapy, idiopathic eosinophilic
   pneumonias, and symptomatic sarcoidosis 8
   •Rheumatic disorders: Short-term administration in the treatment of acute rheumatic carditis,
   ankylosing spondylitis, psoriatic arthritis, dermatomyositis, and polymyositis; systemic lupus
   erythematosus 8

   acute and subacute bursitis 8

   cizumab 625 mg/0.025 mL was administered in each eye under IV ketamine (0.3 mg) and lo-
   cal atropine (0.25%). Feeding intolerance, hypotension (42/24 mmHg), and oxygen desatura-
   tion (arterial oxygen saturation, 80%) were observed 22 hours after bevacizumab administra-
   tion and continued the following day. Shortness of breath with apnea and lethargy were also
   noted. Intubation for mechanical ventilation, treatment with DOPamine, and prophylactic an-
   tibiotics were instituted. Blood pressure normalized on day 3 and his general condition im-
   proved. On day 6, DOPamine and antibiotics were discontinued. He was successfully extu-
   bated on day 7 and arterial oxygen saturation was normal. The sibling received bevacizumab
   with no episodes of hypotension 19

   Musculoskeletal: Non-mandibular osteonecrosis has been reported in patients younger than
   18 years who received IV bevacizumab Neurologic: In a retrospective study (n=125), the adjusted odds ratio was 1 (95% CI, 2 to 4) for severe neurodevelopmental disability in intravitreal bevacizumab-treated compared
   with laser-treated preterm infants at 18 months corrected age after adjusting for gestational
   age, gender, maternal education, Score for Neonatal Acute Physiology-II score, bronchopul-
   monary dysplasia, sepsis, and severe brain injury Ophthalmic: More high myopia was seen in eyes treated with bevacizumab (14.6%) than
   those treated with ranibizumab (0%; p=0.03) at 1 year of age in a retrospective study (n=37 in-
   fants) Black Box Warning
   IV Administration

   Gastrointestinal Perforations: The incidence of gastrointestinal perforation, some fatal, in
   patients receiving bevacizumab ranged from 3 to 3%. Discontinue bevacizumab in patients
   who develop gastrointestinal perforation.

   Surgery and Wound Healing Complications: The incidence of wound healing and surgical
   complications, including serious and fatal complications, is increased in patients receiving be-
   vacizumab. Discontinue bevacizumab in patients who develop wound healing complications
   that require medical intervention. Withhold bevacizumab at least 28 days prior to elective sur-
   gery. Do not administer bevacizumab for at least 28 days after surgery and until the wound is
   fully healed.

 Hemorrhages: Severe or fatal hemorrhage, including hemoptysis, gastrointestinal bleeding,
   hematemesis, central nervous systems (CNS) hemorrhage, epistaxis, and vaginal bleeding oc-
   cur up to 5-fold more frequently in patients receiving bevacizumab. Do not administer beva-
   cizumab to patients with a recent history of hemoptysis. Discontinue in patients who develop
   Grade 3 to 4 hemorrhage 15

   Solution Compatibility
   NS

   Solution Incompatibility
   D5W

   Monitoring
   The duration for follow-up is unknown but will require longer follow-up compared with laser
   treatment 12,8 due to delayed or incomplete vascularization, significant rates of recurrence
   and need for retreatment, and potential for developmentally abnormal or atypical retinal vas-
   cular features In a retrospective case series recurrent ROP occurred a mean of 2 weeks (range, 7 to 9 weeks) adjusted age after intravitreal bevacizumab in 20 infants Additionally retinal
   detachment had occurred in 2 treated patients at the age of 5 years 16 and 3 years

drugs.uses_raw:
Recurrent Clostridioides difficile infection: The safety and pharmacokinetics of bezlotox-
   umab in pediatric patients aged 1 year or older were evaluated in a randomized, double-blind,
   placebo-controlled, multi-center trial. Enrolled patients had a diagnosis of Clostridioides diffi-
   cile infection (CDI) and received standard of care (vancomycin, metronidazole, or fidaxomicin)
   for the baseline CDI episode. In this trial, 143 patients were randomized and treated, of whom
   107 received a single infusion of bezlotoxumab 10 mg/kg and 36 received a placebo infusion.
   Of these randomized patients, 58% were 1 to less than 12 years, 52% were male, 80% were
   white, and 7% were multi-racial. The majority (94%) of patients had one or more risk factors for
   CDI recurrence. Five of 107 pediatric patients (5%) receiving bezlotoxumab and one of 36 pedi-
   atric patients receiving placebo (3%) died in this trial. There were no treatment discontinua-
   tions due to adverse reactions. The adverse reactions observed in pediatric patients were com-
   parable to those observed in adult patients. The most common adverse reactions were pyrexia
   (18%) and headache (14%); 1 pediatric patient (1%) experienced an infusion-related adverse
   reaction. FDA Approved Indications
   Bezlotoxumab is indicated to reduce recurrence of Clostridioides difficile infection (CDI) in
   adults and pediatric patients aged 1 year or older who are receiving antibacterial drug treat-
   ment for CDI and are at a high risk for CDI recurrence 1

   Limitations of Use

 Bezlotoxumab is not indicated for the treatment of Clostridioides difficile infection (CDI).
   Bezlotoxumab is not an antibacterial drug. Bezlotoxumab should only be used in conjunction
   with antibacterial drug treatment of CDI 1

   Administration
   • Do not freeze diluted solution; allow to reach room temperature before infusion 1

   • Administer as an IV infusion over 60 minutes via peripheral or central line using sterile, non-
   pyrogenic, low-protein binding 2 to 5 micron in-line or add-on filter; do not give other medi-
   cations through the same IV line simultaneously 1

drugs.contraindications_raw:
Common, pediatric: Abdominal pain, insomnia, and anxiety 1

   Endocrine and metabolic
   Dyslipidemia has been reported with the use of tenofovir alafenamide. Assess all patients with
   dyslipidemia for additional atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease (ASCVD) risk factors (patients
   with HIV are considered at moderate risk for ASCVD). If LDL-C is 130 mg/dL or more but less
   than 250 mg/dL, refer to the NHLBI guidelines on a treatment approach with lifestyle modifica-
   tions and drug therapy. Persistent dyslipidemia may lead to premature ASCVD

   Gastrointestinal
   Pancreatitis has been reported with the use of NRTIs and ritonavir-boosted PIs; discontinue
   the offending agent and avoid reintroduction Lactic acidosis
   Lactic acidosis has been reported with emtricitabine and tenofovir alafenamide use. Consider
   discontinuing ARV drugs temporarily in patients with a lactate 1 to 5 mmol/L (confirmed with
   second test) while conducting additional diagnostic work-up. In patients with a lactate 5
   mmol/L or greater (confirmed with second test) or 10 mmol/L (any one test), discontinue all
   ARV drugs and provide supportive therapy (eg, IV fluids, sedation, respiratory support).
   Following resolution of clinical and laboratory abnormalities, resume therapy with either an
   NRTI-sparing regimen or a revised NRTI-containing regimen. Monitor lactate monthly for 3
   months or more Psychiatric
   Neuropsychiatric symptoms (eg, depression or exacerbation of depression, suicide
   ideation/attempt, schizoaffective disorders, anxiety) have been reported with bictegravir use.
   For persistent or severe neuropsychiatric symptoms, consider discontinuing bictegravir if a
   suitable alternative exists. For mild symptoms, advise patient that symptoms likely will resolve
   with time

   Black Box Warning
   Warning: Post Treatment Acute Exacerbation of Hepatitis B
   •Severe acute exacerbations of hepatitis B have been reported in patients who are coinfected
   with HIV-1 and hepatitis B virus (HBV) and have discontinued products containing emtric-
   itabine (FTC) and/or tenofovir disoproxil fumarate (TDF), and may occur with discontinuation of
   bictegravir/emtricitabine/tenofovir alafenamide.

 •Closely monitor hepatic function with both clinical and laboratory follow-up for at least sev-
   eral months in patients who are coinfected with HIV-1 and HBV and discontinue
   bictegravir/emtricitabine/tenofovir alafenamide. If appropriate, anti-hepatitis B therapy may
   be warranted Monitoring

drugs.uses_raw:
Constipation and Fecal Disimpaction
   Guidelines: According to NASPGHAN guidelines, initial treatment of functional constipation in-
   cludes education, diary use (to evaluate dietary and fluid intake, especially in patients less than
   6 months), and oral treatment in patients 6 months or older. Oral medication or occasional

 suppositories may be started in patients less than 6 months if initial treatment is ineffective.
   The recommended initial treatment of choice for fecal disimpaction is polyethylene glycol
   (PEG) or enemas. For maintenance therapy, PEG with or without electrolytes is the first-line
   treatment; if PEG is not available, the recommended replacement is lactulose. Other laxatives
   (milk of magnesia, mineral oil, and stimulant laxatives) may be considered as additional or sec-
   ond-line treatments Duration of therapy: Initial therapy for fecal disimpaction should be 2 to 6 days. Maintenance
   therapy should be continued for at least 2 months or at least 1 month after a good response
   to therapy 2 ,1 . Medications should be weaned gradually and may need to be continued for
   months to years in some patients. Relapses are common and may be treated with mainte-
   nance or disimpaction therapy as needed 1

   Administration
   Oral

   • Administer with water 3 ,4 .
   • Delayed release tablet: Swallow tablets whole, do not chew or crush. Do not take within 1
   hour after taking an antacid or milk Rectal

   • Suppository for rectal use only • Remove one suppository from the strip • Remove wrapper before inserting into rectum • Carefully insert the pointed end first of the suppository well into the rectum • Retain suppository in rectum for about 15 to 20 minutes

drugs.contraindications_raw:
The most frequently reported adverse effects during pediatric clinical trials were abdominal
   pain, vomiting 15 , edema, flushing, headache, and transaminase elevations Transaminase
   elevations occur in 7% to 8% of patients, with a higher incidence reported in adolescents
   than children Black Box Warning
   Risks of hepatotoxicity and embryo-fetal toxicity 16
   ●   Because of the risks of hepatotoxicity and birth defects, bosentan is available only through a
       restricted program called the Bosentan REMS Program. Under the Bosentan REMS, pre-
       scribers, patients, and pharmacies must enroll in the program.
   Hepatotoxicity 16
   ●   In clinical studies, bosentan caused at least 3-fold upper limit of normal (ULN) elevation of
       liver aminotransferases (ALT and AST) in about 11% of patients, accompanied by elevated
       bilirubin in a small number of cases. Because these changes are a marker for potential seri-
       ous hepatotoxicity, serum aminotransferase levels must be measured prior to initiation of
       treatment and then monthly. In the postmarketing period, in the setting of close monitor-
       ing, rare cases of unexplained hepatic cirrhosis were reported after prolonged (greater than
       12 months) therapy with bosentan in patients with multiple comorbidities and drug thera-
       pies. There have also been reports of liver failure. The contribution of bosentan in these
       cases could not be excluded.
   ●   In at least one case, the initial presentation (after greater than 20 months of treatment) in-
       cluded pronounced elevations in aminotransferases and bilirubin levels accompanied by
       non-specific symptoms, all of which resolved slowly over time after discontinuation of
       bosentan. This case reinforces the importance of strict adherence to the monthly monitor-
       ing schedule for the duration of treatment and the treatment algorithm, which includes

 stopping bosentan with a rise of aminotransferases accompanied by signs or symptoms of
       liver dysfunction.
   ●   Elevations in aminotransferases require close attention. Bosentan should generally be
       avoided in patients with elevated aminotransferases (greater than 3 times ULN) at baseline
       because monitoring for hepatotoxicity may be more difficult. If liver aminotransferase ele-
       vations are accompanied by clinical symptoms of hepatotoxicity (such as nausea, vomiting,
       fever, abdominal pain, jaundice, or unusual lethargy or fatigue) or increases in bilirubin
       greater than or equal to 2 times ULN, treatment with bosentan should be stopped. There is
       no experience with the reintroduction of bosentan in these circumstances.

   Embryo-fetal Toxicity 16
   ●   Bosentan is likely to cause major birth defects if used by pregnant females based on animal
       data. Therefore, pregnancy must be excluded before the start of treatment with bosentan.
       Throughout treatment and for 1 month after stopping bosentan, females of reproductive
       potential must use 2 reliable methods of contraception unless the patient has an intrauter-
       ine device (IUD) or tubal sterilization, in which case no other contraception is needed.
       Hormonal contraceptives, including oral, injectable, transdermal, and implantable contra-
       ceptives should not be used as the sole means of contraception because these may not be
       effective in patients receiving bosentan. Obtain monthly pregnancy tests

   Monitoring
   Monitor liver transaminases (ALT, AST) and bilirubin concentrations at baseline and then
   monthly If values at baseline or if values elevated during therapy more than 3 times ULN, re-
   fer to the Dose Adjustments section above for recommendations. Monitor hemoglobin after 1
   and 3 months, and every 3 months thereafter 3 , Monitor for symptoms of liver injury (ab-
   dominal pain, fever, jaundice, nausea, unusual fatigue or lethargy, vomiting). Exclude preg-
   nancy prior to treatment and obtain monthly pregnancy tests in females of childbearing po-
   tential

   Injection route
   Buprenorphine hydrochloride exposes patients and other users to the risks of opioid addic-
   tion, abuse, and misuse, which can lead to overdose and death. Assess each patient’s risk prior
   to prescribing buprenorphine hydrochloride, and monitor all patients regularly for the devel-
   opment of these behaviors and conditions. Serious, life-threatening, or fatal respiratory de-
   pression may occur with use of buprenorphine hydrochloride. Monitor for respiratory depres-
   sion, especially during initiation of buprenorphine hydrochloride or following a dose increase.
   Prolonged use of buprenorphine hydrochloride during pregnancy can result in neonatal opioid
   withdrawal syndrome, which may be life-threatening if not recognized and treated, and re-
   quires management according to protocols developed by neonatology experts. If opioid use is
   required for a prolonged period in a pregnant woman, advise the patient of the risk of neona-
   tal opioid withdrawal syndrome and ensure that appropriate treatment will be available.
   Concomitant use of opioids with benzodiazepines or other central nervous system (CNS) de-
   pressants, including alcohol, may result in profound sedation, respiratory depression, coma,
   and death. Reserve concomitant prescribing of buprenorphine hydrochloride and benzodi-
   azepines or other CNS depressants for use in patients for whom alternative treatment options
   are inadequate. Limit dosages and durations to the minimum required. Follow patients for
   signs and symptoms of respiratory depression and sedation 7/13

   Insertion and removal of the buprenorphine implant are associated with the risk of implant
   migration, protrusion, and expulsion resulting from the procedure. Rare but serious complica-
   tions including nerve damage and migration resulting in embolism and death may result from
   improper insertion of drug implants inserted in the upper arm. Additional complications may
   include local migration, protrusion, and expulsion.

   available only through a restricted program called the PROBUPHINE REMS Program. All health-

   Antidepressants increased the risk of suicidal thinking and behavior in children, adolescents,
   and young adults in studies of major depressive disorder and other psychiatric disorders.
   Monitor patients closely for clinical worsening, suicidality, or unusual changes in behavior.
   Families and caregivers should be advised of the need for close observation and communica-
   tion with the prescriber. Not approved for use in pediatric patients 10,11,7 ,8 ,12,14,4 ,5 .
   Serious neuropsychiatric events (eg, depression, mania, psychosis, hallucinations, hostility,
   anxiety, panic, suicidal ideation), have been reported in patients with and without preexisting
   psychiatric disease who were taking buPROPion for smoking cessation; some patients experi-
   enced worsening of their psychiatric illnesses. Most symptoms occurred during therapy, but
   some were following discontinuation of buPROPion. All patients should be observed for emer-
   gence of neuropsychiatric reactions even if they are not using buPROPion for smoking cessa-
   tion. If such reactions occur, promptly notify the prescriber 10,11,8 ,10,14,4 ,5 .

       XL®. Antidepressants increased the risk of suicidal thoughts and behavior in children, ado-

       risk of suicidal thoughts and behavior with antidepressant use in subjects over age 24; there
       was a reduction in risk with antidepressant use in subjects aged 65 and older.

drugs.uses_raw:
Hereditary angioedema, treatment: In a double-blind, randomized, prospective, multina-
   tional, parallel-group, dose finding study (n=124; 6 to 72 years of age) of human C1 esterase in-
   hibitor (Berinert®) for the treatment of acute abdominal or facial attacks of hereditary an-
   gioedema (HAE), patients treated with Berinert® 20 units/kg achieved a significant decrease in
   time to onset of relief of symptoms of HAE attack compared with placebo (median of 30 min-
   utes for Berinert® versus 5 hours for placebo; p=0.0025) In a 52-week, open-label extension of the COMPACT study of patients 6 years or older (N=126;
   mean age, 5 years) , the proportion of patients who achieved a time-normalized reduction
   to less than 1 attack/month was 79% with a dosage of 40 international units/kg twice weekly
   (mean, 4 attacks/month) and 86% with 60 international units/kg twice weekly (mean 5
   attacks/month). Responder rates (50% or greater reduction in the time-normalized number of
   HAE attacks) were 94% in the 40 international units/kg group and 92% in the 60 international
   units/kg group; severe attacks were reported in 19% and 27%, respectively; and 3% and 7% of angioedema attacks were treated (mean number of medications/month, 3). The ad-
   verse event rate was 5 events per patient-year with 60 international units/kg and 3 events
   per patient-year with 40 international units/kg; serious adverse events were reported in 1%
   overall. The most common adverse event was injection-site reaction, and other common ad-
   verse events were nasopharyngitis, upper respiratory tract infections, and headache. There
   were no cases of thromboembolic events (except an unrelated myocardial infarction) or ana-
   phylaxis, and no neutralizing bodies were observed. Patients had type I (90%) or type II HAE,
   C1-INH functional levels below 50%, and at least 4 attacks within 2 consecutive months (mean, 8 attacks in 3 months before screening). They had either completed the COMPACT study or
   were study treatment-naïve; 8% of each group were previously treated with C1-esterase in-
   hibitor, and a stable regimen of oral prophylactic medication was continued in 24% of study-
   treatment-naïve patients. Patients who had 12 or more HAE attacks during a 4-week period in
   the first 24 weeks of the study were eligible for incremental dose increases of 10 international
   units/kg up to a maximum of 80 international units/kg. Patients in the United States were al-
   lowed to continue treatment for up to an additional 88 weeks IV Route

   FDA Approved Indication:
   Berinert®

   and pediatric patients with hereditary angioedema Limitations of Use

      Key: ART = antiretroviral therapy, ARV = Antiretroviral, AST = aspartate amino-
      transferase, ALT = alanine aminotransferase, BUN = blood urea nitrogen, CAB-LA
      = cabotegravir long-acting, CBC = complete blood count; DAA = direct-acting an-
      tiviral; HCV = hepatitis C virus, IN = integrase, INSTI = integrase strand transfer
      inhibitor, PrEP = pre-exposure prophylaxis

      (a) If ART is initiated soon after HIV diagnosis and entry into care, repeat baseline labora-
      tory testing is not necessary.
      (b) ART is indicated for all people with HIV and should be started as soon as possible.
      However, if ART initiation is delayed, patients should be retained in care, with periodic
      monitoring as noted above.
      (c) After 2 years of consistently suppressed HIV RNA, less frequent monitoring (eg, every 6
      months) may be considered.
      (d) After 2 years of ART with consistently suppressed viral load: CD4 count 300 to 500
      cells/mm(3), monitor every 12 months; CD4 count greater than 500 cells/mm(3), CD4 mon-
      itoring is optional.
      (e) If HIV RNA is detectable at 4 to 8 weeks, repeat every 4 to 8 weeks until viral load is
      suppressed to less than 50 copies/mL, then every 3 to 6 months.
      (f) For patients on ART, viral load is typically measured every 3 to 6 months. More frequent
      monitoring may be considered in individuals having difficulties with ART adherence or at
      risk for nonadherence. However, for adherent patients with suppressed viral load and sta-
      ble immunological status for more than 1 year, monitoring can be extended to 6-month
      intervals.
      (g) Standard genotypic drug-resistance testing in ARV-naïve persons should focus on test-
      ing for mutations in the PR and RT genes. If transmitted INSTI resistance is a concern, or if
      a person has a history of INSTI use as PrEP or treatment, or a person presents with
      viremia while on an INSTI, providers should also test for resistance mutations in the IN
      gene. In ARV-naïve patients who do not immediately begin ART, repeat testing before initi-
      ation of ART is optional if drug-resistance testing was performed at entry into care. For vi-
      rologically suppressed patients who are switching therapy for toxicity or convenience, viral
      amplification will not be possible and therefore resistance testing should not be per-
      formed. Results from prior resistance testing can be used to help in the construction of a

 new regimen.
      (h) If infected with hepatitis B virus, tenofovir disoproxil fumarate or tenofovir alafe-
      namide plus either emtricitabine or lamivudine should be used as part of the ART regimen
      to treat both hepatitis B virus and HIV infections.
      (i) If HBsAg, and HBsAb, and HBcAb are negative at baseline, administer hepatitis B vac-
      cine series. Also, consult Guidelines for Opportunistic Infections.
      (j) Typically HBV infection has resolved with loss of HBsAb despite isolated HBcAb; confirm
      with an HBV viral load if wanted. A positive HBV viral load is indicative of acute infection
      (other symptoms will be present usually) or chronic infection. Vaccinate the patient when
      viral load is negative. Also, consult Guidelines for Opportunistic Infections.
      (k) In patients with recent HCV infection (acquired in last 6 months) or advanced immun-
      odeficiency (CD4 count less than 100 cells/mm(3)), the HCV antibody test may not be ade-
      quate for screening. HCV RNA screening is indicated in persons who have been success-
      fully treated for HCV or who spontaneously cleared prior infection. HCV antibody-negative
      patients with elevated ALT may need HCV RNA testing.
      (l) At-risk populations: injection drug users, persons with a history of incarceration, men
      with HIV who have unprotected sex with men, and persons with percutaneous/parenteral
      exposure to blood in unregulated settings are at risk of HCV infection.
      (m) Serum sodium, potassium, bicarbonate, chloride, blood urea nitrogen, creatinine, glu-
      cose (preferably fasting). Monitor serum phosphorus concentrations in patients with
      chronic kidney disease who are on tenofovir-containing regimens. Renal function determi-
      nation should include creatinine monitoring and estimation of the glomerular filtration
      rate.
      (n) Consult recommendations of the HIV Medicine Association of the Infectious Diseases
      Society of America for patients with renal disease. More frequent monitoring may be indi-
      cated for patients with evidence of kidney disease (eg, proteinuria or decreased glomeru-
      lar function) or increased risk of renal insufficiency (eg. patients with diabetes or hyper-
      tension).
      (o) CBC with differential should be done when a CD4 count is performed. When CD4 count
      is no longer being monitored, the recommended frequency of CBC with differential is
      once a year. More frequent monitoring may be for patients receiving medications that po-
      tentially cause cytopenia (eg, trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole)
      (p) If random lipids are abnormal, fasting lipids should be obtained. Consult the ACA/AHA
      recommendations for diagnosis and management of patients with dyslipidemia.
      (q) If random glucose is abnormal, fasting glucose should be obtained. HgbA1C is not
      longer recommended for diagnosis of diabetes in patients with HIV on ART.
      (r) Assess urine glucose and protein before initiating tenofovir-containing regimens and
      monitor during treatment with these regimens.
      (s) In women with child-bearing potential.

   Calcitriol is the active form of vitamin D3 (cholecalciferol). The known sites of action are intes-
   tine, bone 2 , kidney, and parathyroid gland Vitamin D3 is metabolically activated in the liver
   and kidney prior to being an active calcium and phosphorous metabolism regulator 3 , Physiological daily production of calcitriol is 5 to 1 mcg. This may be higher during periods of
   increased bone synthesis Calcitriol is rapidly absorbed from the intestine; Tmax is 3 to 6 hours.

Common, adult: Female genital mycotic infections, urinary tract infection, increased urination,
   diarrhea, nausea, vomiting, flatulence, asthenia, indigestion, abdominal discomfort, and
   headache 1 ,2
   The safety profile of pediatric patients treated with canagliflozin was similar to that observed
   in adults with type 2 diabetes 1 ,2 .

   In clinical trials with metFORMIN HCl immediate-release tablets in pediatric patients with type
   2 diabetes, the profile of adverse reactions was similar to that observed in adults 1 , Black Box Warning
   Warning: Lactic Acidosis 1 ,2

 ●   Postmarketing cases of metFORMIN-associated lactic acidosis have resulted in death, hy-
        pothermia, hypotension, and resistant bradyarrhythmias. The onset of metFORMIN-associ-
        ated lactic acidosis is often subtle, accompanied only by nonspecific symptoms such as
        malaise, myalgias, respiratory distress, somnolence, and abdominal pain. metFORMIN-asso-
        ciated lactic acidosis was characterized by elevated blood lactate levels (greater than 5
        mmol/L), anion gap acidosis (without evidence of ketonuria or ketonemia), an increased
        lactate/pyruvate ratio; and metFORMIN plasma levels generally greater than 5 mcg/mL.
    ●   Risk factors for metFORMIN-associated lactic acidosis include renal impairment, concomi-
        tant use of certain drugs (eg, carbonic anhydrase inhibitors such as topiramate), age 65
        years old or greater, having a radiological study with contrast, surgery and other proce-
        dures, hypoxic states (eg, acute congestive heart failure), excessive alcohol intake, and he-
        patic impairment.
    ●   Steps to reduce the risk of and manage metFORMIN-associated lactic acidosis in these high
        risk groups are provided in the full prescribing information.
    ●   If metFORMIN-associated lactic acidosis is suspected, immediately discontinue
        canagliflozin/metFORMIN hydrochloride and institute general supportive measures in a hos-
        pital setting. Prompt hemodialysis is recommended.

   Monitoring
   Therapeutic Monitoring

   •Monitor HbA1c every 3 months if possible. A reasonable HbA1c goal for most patients is less
   than 5%, but HbA1c goals may be more or less stringent and should be individualized to
   each patient 11,10
   • Perform self-monitoring of blood glucose (SMBG) as needed to assist in meeting goals of
   therapy; SMBG should be individualized to each patient 11,10 .

   Toxic Monitoring

   • Obtain estimated GFR (eGFR) prior to initiation of treatment and at least annually thereafter;
   monitor more frequently in patients at increased risk of renal impairment (eg, elderly) 1 , • Reassess eGFR 48 hours after an iodinated contrast imaging procedure if therapy was discon-
   tinued (ie, in patients with an eGFR between 45 and 60 mL/min/1.73 m(2); in patients with a
   history of liver disease, alcoholism, or heart failure; or in patients who received intra-arterial
   iodinated contrast) 1 ,2 .

   • Measure hematologic parameters annually during therapy 1 ,2 .

 • Measure serum vitamin B12 in 2- to 3-year intervals in patients with insufficient vitamin B12
   or calcium intake or absorption 1 ,2 .

   • Consider ketone monitoring in patients at risk for ketoacidosis 1 ,2

   • Prior to initiation, evaluate factors that may increase the risk of amputation, such as a history
   of prior amputation, peripheral vascular disease, neuropathy, and diabetic foot ulcers 1 , • Prior to initiation, assess volume status and correct if necessary; especially in patients with
   renal impairment (estimated GFR less than 60 mL/min/1.73 m(2)), elderly patients, or patients
   on loop diuretics 1 ,2 .

   • Prior to initiation, evaluate factors that may contribute to bone fracture risk 1 ,2 .

   • Assess for necrotizing fasciitis (Fournier's Gangrene) in patients who present with pain or ten-
   derness, erythema, or swelling in the genital or perineal area, along with fever or malaise 1 , • Assess for ketoacidosis regardless of presenting blood glucose levels in patients who present
   with signs and symptoms consistent with severe metabolic acidosis 1 ,2 .
   • Monitor for signs and symptoms of volume depletion during treatment, including sympto-
   matic hypotension or acute changes in SCr 1 ,2 .

   • Monitor for signs and symptoms of hypotension during treatment 1 , • Monitor for infection (including osteomyelitis) during treatment (including new pain or ten-
   derness or sores or ulcers involving the lower limbs) 1 ,2 .

   • Monitor for genital mycotic infections during treatment 1 ,2 .

Cryopyrin-Associated Periodic Syndromes: Rapid and sustained remission of symptoms and
   laboratory values (C-reactive protein and serum amyloid A protein) were achieved in a 3-part,
   48-week, double-blind, placebo-controlled, randomized withdrawal study (n=35; 9 to 74 years
   of age). After an open-label, single-dose, the complete response rate was 97%. Improvement
   was noted within 24 hours with optimal benefit by 8 days for most patients. In the random-
   ized, double-blind, placebo-control phase (n=31), remission rates were 100% and 19% (p less
   than 001) for canakinumab and placebo, respectively. Disease activity was absent or minimal

 in 97% of patients who entered the open-label phase In an open-label study of pediatric
   (n=47) and adult patients (n=119), 7% of the pediatric patients (3 years or older) remained
   relapse-free after a median treatment duration of 290 days (29 to 625 days). On at least one
   occasion, 4 patients received 8 mg/kg and 2 patients received 10 mg/kg IV Similar results
   were demonstrated in an open-label study of 18 Japanese patients (2 years or older). The dos-
   ing protocol allowed titration up to 600 mg every 8 weeks (or 8 mg/kg for patients weighing 40
   kg or less) for those who did not achieve a complete response by day 8 or day 15 or for those
   who relapsed prior to their next scheduled dose. The mean final dose was 250 mg (6 mg/kg) Studies demonstrated that higher doses were required in younger patients and in those with
   more severe disease, without evidence of increased adverse events 2 ,3 .

   Renal impairment: No specific recommendations are available. No clinically significant differ-
   ence in pharmacokinetics was reported in those with mild, moderate, or severe renal impair-
   ment compared with normal renal function 1

   Hepatic impairment: No specific recommendations are available. The effect on pharmacoki-
   netics is unknown. There is a potential increased risk for bleeding with severe hepatic impair-
   ment that requires close monitoring 1

   Other Dose Adjustments

   Bleeding: Interrupt use if clinically significant bleeding occurs 1
   Disease recurrence: If patient experiences more than 2 recurrences of acquired thrombotic
   thrombocytopenic purpura, discontinue use 1

   Surgery and other interventions: Withhold treatment for 7 days prior to elective surgery,
   dental procedures or other invasive interventions. If emergency surgery is required, von
   Willebrand factor concentrate may be considered to rapidly correct hemostasis 1

   toxic epidermal necrolysis) have been reported, especially in patients with the inherited allelic

   mainly Caucasian populations. Screen genetically at-risk patients prior to receiving therapy and
   do not initiate in patients who test positive for the allele, unless the benefit clearly outweighs
   the risk. Discontinue use if a serious dermatologic reaction is suspected 2 ,24,25 . .

   ●   Obesity or being overweight (eg, aged 12 to 17 and have BMI 85th percentile or greater for

   ●   Diabetes

       vere), interstitial lung disease, cystic fibrosis, and pulmonary hypertension)
   ●   Sickle cell disease
   ●   Neurodevelopmental disorders (eg, cerebral palsy) or other conditions that confer medical
       complexity (eg, genetic or metabolic syndromes and severe congenital anomalies)
   ●   Medical-related technological dependence (eg, tracheostomy, gastrostomy, or positive pres-
       sure ventilation (not related to COVID-19))

   Casirivimab and imdevimab is not authorized for the treatment of mild to moderate COVID-19
   in geographic regions where infection is likely to have been caused by a non-susceptible SARS-

   COVID-19 requiring high flow oxygen or mechanical ventilation This emergency use authorization (EUA) for casirivimab plus imdevimab is authorized only for

   serotypes of Streptococcus pneumoniae and lacks efficacy against Haemophilus influenzae 2/8
 The American Academy of Pediatrics recommends antibiotics for children 6 months or older
   with severe signs or symptoms of unilateral or bilateral AOM or in children 6 months through
   23 months of age for bilateral AOM without severe signs or symptoms. Antibiotics or observa-
   tion with close follow-up is recommended in children 6 months to 23 months of age with non-
   severe unilateral AOM and in children 24 months or older with nonsevere, unilateral or bilat-

   Short-course therapy: Compared with a 10-day course, a 5-day course of amoxicillin,
   amoxicillin/clavulanate, or cefdinir was found to be a safe and effective treatment in young
   children with uncomplicated outpatient CAP who demonstrated early clinical improvement.
   Relatively healthy children younger than 6 years (mean age 7 months) with outpatient CAP
   who showed clinical improvement during the first 5 days of antibiotic therapy (N=380) were
   randomized to standard (10-day) or short (5-day) course of amoxicillin, amoxicillin/clavulanate,
   or cefdinir. Fewer than 10% of participants in both groups demonstrated inadequate clinical
   response or persistent symptoms. The short-course strategy was associated with a signifi-
   cantly lower frequency of antibiotic-resistant genes detected in throat swabs at the end of
   treatment Results of a meta-analysis found shorter courses of amoxicillin or cotrimoxazole
   non-inferior to longer courses among children 2 to 59 months old with non-severe CAP
   (N=11,143). A 3-day course of antibiotic treatment was non-inferior to a 5-day course for the
   outcome of treatment failure (RR, 01; 95% CI, 91 to 12), and a 5-day course was non-infe-

drugs.contraindications_raw:
Common:
   In clinical trials, common adverse events included rash (5% to 13%), abdominal pain (7%), vom-
   iting (6%), diarrhea (7%), and fever (5% to 9%) 16,15 . Local reactions (3%) and phlebitis (1.3%)
   have also been reported Hepatic:
   Acute liver injury with cefepime was described in a 5-year old boy with significant medical ill-
   ness. After 2 doses of cefepime 50 mg/kg, the metabolic panel increased from normal to AST
   1387 units/L, ALT 795 units/L, and alkaline phosphatase 376 units/L; new-onset jaundice and
   mild right-upper quadrant tenderness were noted. Viral hepatitis panels were negative and bil-
   iary obstruction was ruled out by liver ultrasound. Cefepime was stopped and lab parameters
   gradually normalized Renal:
   Acute kidney injury occurred in 5% of piperacillin-tazobactam treated patients compared
   with 2% of cefepime treated patients in a single center, retrospective cohort study of 71 pe-
   diatric patients with cystic fibrosis who were also on concomitant vancomycin and tobramycin Solution Compatibility
   D5W, D10W, D5LR, D5NS, and NS.
