drugs.uses_raw:
Empiric antibacterial therapy for well-appearing febrile infant
   29 to 60 days of age: The American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP) recommends initiating par-
   enteral empiric antibiotics in febrile infants 29 to 60 days old if cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) analy-
   sis suggests bacterial meningitis and/or any inflammatory marker (IM) obtained is abnormal.
   Oral antibiotic therapy with cephalexin or cefixime should be initiated if CSF and any IMs ob-
   tained are normal but the urinalysis result is positive. CefTRIAXone is recommended as first-

 line antibacterial therapy in patients with suspected urinary tract infection or if no focus is
   identified. For suspected bacterial meningitis, cefTRIAXone or the combination of cefTAZidime
   and vancomycin may be used Drug-resistant pathogens: In communities with circulation of extended-spectrum beta-lacta-
   mase producing strains of E. coli, gentamicin should be used instead of cefTAZidime for treat-
   ment of suspected bacteremia or sepsis, and meropenem should be used in stead of cef-
   TAZidime when bacterial meningitis is suspected. Fourth or fifth generation cephalosporins
   may also be considered in consultation with an expert Duration of therapy: Empiric antimicrobials should be continued until blood and cere-
   brospinal fluid cultures are negative for 24 to 36 hours. If cultures are positive, antimicrobial
   therapy should be modified to targeted therapy for the duration of time consistent with the
   nature of the disease, identified organism, and response of the infant to treatment Prophylaxis for sexually transmitted diseases in victims of sexual assault: Due to resis-
   tance, cefixime is no longer part of the empiric regimen Treatment of febrile neutropenia in cancer patients: In a randomized controlled trial, oral
   cefixime following 48 hours of appropriate IV antibiotic therapy (n=100) was as successful as
   continued IV antibiotic therapy (n=100) for empiric therapy in febrile neutropenic children
   (ages 6 months to 21 years). Patients randomized to IV/oral therapy were switched to oral
   therapy if cultures were negative and there were no specific risk factors for breakthrough bac-
   teremia. Treatment success was 72% and 73% for the IV/oral and continued IV groups, respec-
   tively In another randomized, controlled trial in low risk patients, IV antibiotics for 3 days
   then cefixime for an additional 4 days (n=74) was similarly efficacious to 7 days of IV antibiotic
   therapy (n=80). Eligible patients were afebrile at 48 hours and had negative cultures at 72
   hours. A favorable outcome was reported in 98% of patients in each group Treatment of group A streptococcal pharyngitis in patients with penicillin allergy: More
   narrow-spectrum cephalosporins (cephalexin or cefadroxil) are preferred 13,6 . A meta-analysis
   including 35 clinical trials found clinical and bacteriologic failure was less likely when a
   cephalosporin was used to treat group A streptococcal tonsillopharyngitis compared with peni-
   cillin Current guidelines recommend penicillin V or amoxicillin as drugs of choice in patients
   with no penicillin allergy 13 , Treatment of pyelonephritis:Cefixime has been used successfully as an oral agent adminis-
   tered after 2 to 4 days of initial intravenous therapy for the treatment of children with
   pyelonephritis 15,16,17,18,19 . Has also been used successfully as oral therapy alone compared
   with initial intravenous (cefotaxime or ceftriaxone) then oral therapy in infants and young chil-

 dren with an initial episode of pyelonephritis, ages 1 month to 36 months without anatomical
   abnormalities or clinical hemodynamic impairment. An initial dose of 8 mg/kg orally, followed
   by 4 mg/kg every 12 hours for a total of 10 to 14 days of therapy has been used successfully in
   clinical trials 15,19 .

   Treatment of acute bacterial sinusitis:Amoxicillin, with 20,1 or without 20 clavulanate, is rec-
   ommended for first-line treatment of bacterial sinusitis. The American Academy of Pediatrics
   (AAP) considers amoxicillin the agent of choice in those communities where antimicrobial re-
   sistance is not suspected due to its narrow spectrum, efficacy, safety, low cost, and palatability In contrast, the Infectious Disease Society of America (IDSA) recommends the combination
   product due to concerns of an increased prevalence of ß-lactamase producing Haemophilus
   influenzae Cefixime is no longer recommended for empiric monotherapy for acute bacterial sinusitis due
   to highly variable activity against S pneumoniae. Combination therapy with cefixime and either
   clindamycin 20,1 or linezolid 20 is recommended for failure of initial therapy with
   amoxicillin/clavulanate 20 , Cefixime and clindamycin may also be used in children with non-
   type I penicillin allergy or children from areas with high rates of penicillin-resistant S pneumo-
   niae. Treatment duration of 10 to 14 days is recommended Treatment of uncomplicated gonococcal infections. Ceftriaxone plus azithromycin is the
   recommended regimen for the treatment of uncomplicated gonococcal infections of the
   cervix, urethra, and rectum; cefixime plus azithromycin is an alternative regimen when ceftri-
   axone is not available Urinary Tract Infections
   Short-course treatment: In a randomized clinical trial (N=664), children with symptomatic uri-
   nary tract infection assigned to standard-course 10-day therapy with amoxicillin-clavulanate,
   cefixime, cefdinir, cephalexin, or trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole had lower rates of treatment
   failure (0.6%) than children assigned to short-course 5-day antibiotic therapy (4.2%). However,
   the low failure rate of short-course therapy suggests it may be considered for children exhibit-
   ing clinical improvement after 5 days of antimicrobial treatment Pediatric FDA-Approved Indications - 6 months or older

   Acute exacerbations of chronic bronchitis caused by susceptible isolates of Streptococcus pneu-
   moniae and Haemophilus influenzae Otitis media caused by susceptible isolates of H influenzae, Moraxella catarrhalis, and
   Streptococcus pyogenes 3 ,21,22 .

   Uncomplicated gonorrhea (cervical/urethral) caused by susceptible isolates of Neisseria gonor-
   rhoeae (penicillinase- and non-penicillinase-producing isolates) Uncomplicated urinary tract infections caused by susceptible isolates of Escherichia coli and
   Proteus mirabilis 3 , Administration
   May be taken without regard to food Chewable tablets must be chewed or crushed prior to swallowing

   amoxicillin/clavulanate Acute otitis media (AOM), Uncomplicated: Amoxicillin is the preferred first-line treatment
   for initial or delayed antibiotic treatment. Amoxicillin/clavulanate may be considered in pa-
   tients who have received amoxicillin in the previous 30 days or who have the otitis-conjunctivi-
   tis syndrome. In penicillin allergic patients, treatment options are cefdinir, cefuroxime, cefpo-
   doxime, or ceftriaxone; these cephalosporins are highly unlikely to be cross-reactive due to
   their distinct chemical structures. For failure of initial antibiotic treatment (after a 48 to 72
   hour course), the first-line treatment is amoxicillin/clavulanate for those initially treated with
   amoxicillin or a 3-day course of ceftriaxone in those initially treated with
   amoxicillin/clavulanate or oral third-generation cephalosporins. An alternative is clindamycin
   with or without a third-generation cephalosporin. Importantly, clindamycin may not be effec-
   tive for the multidrug-resistant serotypes of Streptococcus pneumoniae and lacks efficacy
   against Haemophilus influenzae 2/7
 The American Academy of Pediatrics recommends antibiotics for children 6 months or older
   with severe signs or symptoms of unilateral or bilateral AOM or in children 6 months through
   23 months of age for bilateral AOM without severe signs or symptoms. Antibiotics or observa-
   tion with close follow-up is recommended in children 6 months to 23 months of age with non-
   severe unilateral AOM and in children 24 months or older with nonsevere, unilateral or bilat-
   eral AOM. The above recommendations apply to otherwise healthy children without comor-
   bidities that may alter the natural course of AOM Group A streptococcal pharyngitis in patients with penicillin allergy. More narrow-spectrum

   minister both antibiotics simultaneously via Y-site Preparation
   •Reconstitute vial with 10 mL of sterile water, 9% sodium chloride for injection, D5W, LR, or

   chloride •Gently mix •The reconstituted vial yields a final volume of approximately 12 mL with a concentration of

   tration of cefTAZidime 8 to 40 mg/mL and avibactam 2 to 10 mg/mL •Diluted solutions are stable for 12 hours when stored at room temperature •Diluted solutions may be refrigerated between 2 and 8°C (36 and 46° F) for up to 24 hours.

Acute bacterial sinusitis: Amoxicillin, with 9 ,18 or without 18 clavulanate, is recommended for
   first-line treatment of acute bacterial sinusitis.

   Cefuroxime monotherapy should only be used for patients with penicillin allergy who reside in
   communities with a low level of S pneumoniae resistance Where resistance is a concern,
   clindamycin plus either cefixime 18 , 9 or cefpodoxime 9 , or linezolid plus cefixime is recom-
   mended 18 ; levofloxacin is also an option 18,9 .

   Acute otitis media (AOM), Uncomplicated: Amoxicillin is the preferred first-line treatment
   for initial or delayed antibiotic treatment. Amoxicillin/clavulanate may be considered in pa-
   tients who have received amoxicillin in the previous 30 days or who have the otitis-conjunctivi-
   tis syndrome. In penicillin allergic patients, treatment options are cefdinir, cefuroxime, cefpo-
   doxime, or ceftriaxone; these cephalosporins are highly unlikely to be cross-reactive due to
   their distinct chemical structures. For failure of initial antibiotic treatment (after a 48 to 72
   hour course), the first-line treatment is amoxicillin/clavulanate for those initially treated with
   amoxicillin or a 3-day course of ceftriaxone in those initially treated with
   amoxicillin/clavulanate or oral third-generation cephalosporins. An alternative is clindamycin
   with or without a third-generation cephalosporin. Importantly, clindamycin may not be effec-
   tive for the multidrug-resistant serotypes of Streptococcus pneumoniae and lacks efficacy
   against Haemophilus influenzae The American Academy of Pediatrics recommends antibiotics for children 6 months or older
   with severe signs or symptoms of unilateral or bilateral AOM or in children 6 months through
   23 months of age for bilateral AOM without severe signs or symptoms. Antibiotics or observa-
   tion with close follow-up is recommended in children 6 months to 23 months of age with non-
   severe unilateral AOM and in children 24 months or older with nonsevere, unilateral or bilat-
   eral AOM. The above recommendations apply to otherwise healthy children without comor-
   bidities that may alter the natural course of AOM Lyme disease: Joint guidelines from the Infectious Diseases Society of America (IDSA),
   American Academy of Neurology (AAN), and American College of Rheumatology (ACR) recom-
   mend doxycycline, amoxicillin or cefuroxime as the preferred treatment for many manifesta-
   tions of Lyme disease. IV ceftriaxone is preferred when treating manifestations with parenchy-
   mal involvement of the brain or spinal cord, hospitalized patients with Lyme carditis, or in pa-
   tients with Lyme arthritis and no or minimal response to oral antibiotics. IV therapy may be
   transitioned to oral therapy once there is evidence of clinical improvement. Alternative IV med-
   ications include cefotaxime and penicillin G, and azithromycin may used as an alternative oral
   medication when other antibiotics are contraindicated 4/14
 Duration: Patients with erythema migrans are treated for 7 to 14 days, depending on which
   antibiotic was chosen; cefuroxime should be given for 14 days for erythema migrans. Other
   manifestations of Lyme disease are typically treated for 14 to 21 days depending on the mani-
   festation. Lyme arthritis is treated with oral therapy for 28 days. If Lyme arthritis persists with
   no or minimal response, a second course of IV antibiotics for 2 to 4 weeks is recommended Otitis media with effusion: Antibiotics are not recommended for asymptomatic otitis media
   with effusion Surgical prophylaxis The American Society of Health-System Pharmacists (ASHP) in collabora-

   urinary tract infections treated with a short course of antibiotic therapy (5 days or less) had a
   61% increased risk of treatment failure compared with children treated for 7 to 10 days.
   Treatment failure rates were 8% with short-course therapy compared with 4% with longer
   courses (RR, 61; 95% CI 15 to 27). There was no significant difference between groups in
   relapse rates (9.6% with short-course vs 1% with longer course) or reinfection rates (10% vs 2%) FDA-Approved Indications - Intravenous :

 Black Box Warning
   Serious Infections

   Patients treated with certolizumab pegol are at increased risk for developing serious infections
   that may lead to hospitalization or death. Most patients who developed these infections were
   taking concomitant immunosuppressants such as methotrexate or corticosteroids.

   Certolizumab pegol should be discontinued if a patient develops a serious infection or sepsis.
   Reported infections include:

   • Active tuberculosis, including reactivation of latent tuberculosis. Patients with tuberculosis
   have frequently presented with disseminated or extrapulmonary disease. Patients should be
   tested for latent tuberculosis before certolizumab pegol use and during therapy. Treatment
   for latent infection should be initiated prior to certolizumab pegol use.

   • Invasive fungal infections, including histoplasmosis, coccidioidomycosis, candidiasis, as-
   pergillosis, blastomycosis, and pneumocystosis. Patients with histoplasmosis or other invasive
   fungal infections may present with disseminated, rather than localized disease. Antigen and
   antibody testing for histoplasmosis may be negative in some patients with active infection.
   Empiric anti-fungal therapy should be considered in patients at risk for invasive fungal infec-
   tions who develop severe systemic illness.

   • Bacterial, viral and other infections due to opportunistic pathogens, including Legionella and
   Listeria.
   The risks and benefits of treatment with certolizumab pegol should be carefully considered
   prior to initiating therapy in patients with chronic or recurrent infection.

   Patients should be closely monitored for the development of signs and symptoms of infection
   during and after treatment with certolizumab pegol, including the possible development of tu-
   berculosis in patients who tested negative for latent tuberculosis infection prior to initiating
   therapy.
   Malignancy

   Lymphoma and other malignancies, some fatal, have been reported in children and adoles-
   cent patients treated with TNF blockers, of which certolizumab pegol is a member Monitoring
   Toxic Laboratory Monitoring

   rate can occur weeks or months after chloramphenicol treatment. Peripheral pancytopenia if
   often observed, but in rare cases only 1 or 2 of the 3 major cell types (erythrocytes, leukocytes,
   platelets) may be depressed • Reversible, dose-related bone marrow suppression can occur. This is characterized by vac-
   uolization of the erythroid cells, reduction or reticulocytes, and leukopenia. It is reversible
   upon discontinuation of chloramphenicol "Gray baby" syndrome

   • In many cases, chloramphenicol was initiated within the first 48 hours of life However, this
   syndrome is not restricted to neonates and has been reported in older children 15,19 .

   • Symptoms appeared after 3 to 4 days of high dose treatment, and appeared in the following
   order: Abdominal distention with or without emesis, progressive pallid cyanosis, vasomotor
   collapse and irregular respiration, and death within a few hours of symptom onset • Symptom progression accelerated with higher doses • Associated with serum chloramphenicol levels greater than 50 mcg/mL 15,19 ; levels in some
   patients were greater than 90 mcg/mL after multiple doses • Discontinuation of therapy upon early evidence of symptoms often reversed the process with
   complete recovery Black Box Warning
   Serious and fatal blood dyscrasias (aplastic anemia, hypoplastic anemia, thrombocytopenia
   and granulocytopenia) are known to occur after the administration of chloramphenicol. In ad-
   dition, there have been reports of aplastic anemia attributed to chloramphenicol which later
   terminated in leukemia. Blood dyscrasias have occurred after both short term and prolonged
   therapy with this drug. Chloramphenicol must not be used when less potentially dangerous
   agents will be effective. It must not be used in the treatment of trivial infections or where it is
   not indicated, as in colds, influenza, infections of the throat; or as a prophylactic agent to pre-
   vent bacterial infections Precautions: It is essential that adequate blood studies be made during treatment with the
   drug. While blood studies may detect early peripheral blood changes, such as leukopenia,
   reticulocytopenia or granulocytopenia, before they become irreversible, such studies cannot

 be relied on to detect bone marrow depression prior to development of aplastic anemia. To fa-
   cilitate appropriate studies and observation during therapy, it is desirable that patients be hos-
   pitalized Solution Compatibility

   • Susceptibility testing should be performed concurrently with initiation of therapy if the choice
   to use chloramphenicol was based on clinical impression Toxic Monitoring

   • Obtain adequate blood studies at baseline and approximately every 2 days during therapy • Obtain chloramphenicol blood levels at appropriate intervals during therapy. Close followup
   with available microtechniques is recommended in patients with impaired metabolic pro-
   cesses (eg, liver or kidney dysfunction), including immature metabolic processes of the new-
   born infant Therapeutic Drug Monitoring
   • Monitor chloramphenicol blood levels, particularly in premature and term neonates and in-
   fants and children with immature metabolic processes or impaired renal or hepatic function 11/15
 • In 17 pediatric patients (age range, 1 month to 6 years) the total body clearance, half life, and
   Vd of chloramphenicol varied significantly between patients, making the prediction of standard
   dose and interval difficult • Maintain serum levels between 10 and 30 mcg/mL. 15,16,10 Serum levels greater than 50
   mcg/mL are associated with a greatly increased incidence of toxic effects, particularly gray
   baby syndrome in infants less than 6 months old. Serum levels should be measured 1 and 6
   hours after dosage is initiated. Pre- and post-dose levels should be determined at regular in-
   tervals (2 to 3 days) throughout the treatment period 16
   • Meningitis: In a study evaluating 70 pediatric cases of pediatric meningitis it was recom-
   mended that chloramphenicol concentrations be kept in the range of 15 to 25 mcg/mL by as-
   saying levels at 48 hour intervals at the beginning of treatment. To ensure adequate concen-
   trations in the CSF while avoiding toxicity, the dosage of chloramphenicol should be increased
   when the peak falls below 20 mg/L and decreased when the trough serum concentration ex-
   ceeds 15 mg/L or the peak concentration exceeds 30 mg/L

Chloroquine phosphate is indicated in infants and children for the treatment of uncomplicated
   malaria due to susceptible strains of Plasmodium falciparum, P malariae, P ovale, and P vivax.
   Chloroquine is also indicated for prophylaxis of malaria in geographic areas where resistance
   to chloroquine is not present Limitations of Use
   • Do not use chloroquine phosphate for the treatment of complicated malaria (high-grade par-
   asitemia and/or complications, eg, cerebral malaria or acute renal failure) • Do not use chloroquine phosphate for malaria prophylaxis in areas where chloroquine resis-
   tance occurs. Resistance to chloroquine phosphate is widespread in Plasmodium falciparum,

 and is reported in P vivax • Concomitant therapy with an 8-aminoquinoline drug is necessary for the treatment of the
   hypnozoite liver stage forms of P vivax and P ovale Administration
   Oral

   • Do not take antacids or kaolin within 4 hours before or after dose 1

   • Do not take ampicillin within 2 hours before or after dose 1

   • Shake suspension well 6 ,7 .

   Preparation

   Extemporaneous oral compound

   10 mg chloroquine base/mL suspension (60 mL) 6
   • Triturate two 500-mg chloroquine phosphate tablets (each tablet contains 300 mg chloro-
   quine base) in a mortar after removing the film coating.
   • Levigate with a small amount of sterile water.

   • Add a sufficient amount of cherry syrup and levigate until a uniform mixture is obtained.
   • Transfer contents of the mortar to a conical graduate cylinder.

   • Add sufficient quantity of cherry syrup to a final volume of 60 mL.
   • Pour into an amber glass bottle and shake vigorously

   • Label the container with "Shake well before using."
   • Stable for up to 28 days when stored under refrigeration (4°C), at room temperature (22 to
   25°C), and at 29°C.

   Other concentrations
   • A 9 mg chloroquine base/mL suspension (15 mg chloroquine phosphate/mL) may be com-
   pounded by suspending chloroquine phosphate in SyrSpend SF PH4. This suspension is stable
   for 90 days under refrigeration (2 to 8°C) or at room temperature (20 to 25°C) • A 15 mg chloroquine base/mL suspension may also be compounded by pulverizing two 500-
   mg chloroquine phosphate tablets in a mortar, levigating with water or glycerin, and adding 13
   mL methylcellulose. Transfer to a conical graduate cylinder and add sufficient quantitiy of a 2:1

 mixture of simple syrup and cherry syrup to a final volume of 40 mL. Label with "Shake well
   before using." The suspension is stable for 3 days under refrigeration

drugs.contraindications_raw:
Reported adverse reactions for chloroquine or other 4-aminoquinoline compounds:
   Maculopathy and macular degeneration (may be irreversible), urticaria, anaphylactic reaction
   including angioedema, tinnitus, sensorimotor disorders, vomiting, diarrhea, erythema multi-
   forme, Stevens-Johnson syndrome, pancytopenia, aplastic anemia, neuropsychiatric changes,
   hypotension electrocardiographic changes, hypoglycemia 13

   Monitoring
   Toxic Laboratory Monitoring

   • CBC periodically during prolonged therapy 2

   Toxic Physical Monitoring

   • Monitor for signs and symptoms of cardiomyopathy • Monitor knee and ankle reflex periodically for muscle weakness during prolonged therapy Ophthalmologic Screening

   • Perform a baseline ophthalmologic examination within the first year 9 in all patients begin-
   ning long-term therapy to document any complicating ocular conditions and to document the

 appearance of the fundus and functional status Include best corrected distance visual acu-
   ity (BCVA), automated threshold visual field (VF) of the central 10 degrees (central 24 degrees
   recommended if of Asian descent), and spectral domain ocular coherence tomography (SD-
   OCT) Most critical is the fundus evaluation of the macula to rule out underlying disease or
   preexisting tissue damage. Although baseline visual fields and SD-OCT are always useful, it is
   not critical to obtain at baseline unless abnormalities are present (eg, focal macular lesion,
   glaucoma, etc) that might affect screening tests • Annual ophthalmologic screening may be deferred until there have been 5 years of exposure,
   however, more frequent screening repeated annually should be considered in patients with
   significant risk factors (eg, daily dose greater than 5 mg/kg base using actual body weight, sub-
   normal GFR, concomitant use of tamoxifen citrate, concurrent macular disease, or greater
   than 5 years of therapy) 9 ,10 . Including best corrected distance visual acuity (BCVA), automated
   threshold visual field (VF) of the central 10 degrees (central 24 degrees recommended if of
   Asian descent), and SD-OCT Ophthalmologic Examination Techniques

   • Use of both automated visual fields (appropriate to race; wider test patterns looking beyond
   the central macular are needed for Asian patients) and spectral domain ocular coherence to-
   mography (SD-OCT) is suggested for routine primary screening. Other tests may be used as
   needed or available, including multifocal electroretinogram (mfERG) and fundus autofluoresce,
   which is especially useful in a topographic view of damage across the posterior fundus and
   wide-angle images can show extramacular patterns of damage in Asian eyes. Central visual
   field testing is very sensitive in reliable patients. White SITA testing with pattern deviation plots
   is recommended, which distinguish regional loss from background sensitivity better than the
   grey scale. The 10-2 field pattern has high resolution within the macula and is excellent for
   non-Asian patients. However, wider test patterns (24-2 or 30-2) are needed for Asian patients
   in whom toxicity often manifests beyond the macula. Microperimetry and adaptive optics reti-
   nal imagining are newer techniques to consider. Special cameras with enhanced optics to re-
   duce wave-front distortion can image the cone array directly and show cone damage with
   early disease. However, distinguishing damage from artifact is still difficult with current instru-
   ments • Questionable test results should be repeated or validated with additional procedures to
   avoid unnecessary cessation of valuable medication • Multifocal electroretinograph was found to be more sensitive than visual acuity test, ophthal-
   moscopy, fluorescein angiography, color vision tests, and visual field test in detecting hydroxy-
   chloroquine-induced retinal dysfunction in a study 6/9
 Ophthalmologic Tests Not Recommended for Screening

   The following are not recommended as screening tools 10 :
   ●   Ophthalmoscopy is not a screening tool because photoreceptor damage is detectable with
       other techniques well before visible changes in the fundus.
   ●   A time-domain optical coherence tomography's resolution is not sufficient to detect early
       toxic changes.
   ●   Fluorescein angiography can recognize retinal pigment epithelium defects, but these are
       late changes and not appropriate for screening.
   ●   Full-field electroretinogram will show abnormalities in only very late toxicity.
   ●   Amsler grid is not consistent enough for reliable screening of subtle scotomas.
   ●   Color vision testing errors may occur but are not sensitive or specific.
   ●   The electro-oculogram has not been validated as a reliable screening test.

   ChlorproMAZINE should generally not be used in pediatric patients under 6 months of age ex-

   Administration

   •Discontinue 48 hours prior to myelography and resume at least 24 hours after procedure 6 ,4 .

   •Do not administer subQ IM Injection

   •Reserve parenteral administration for bedfast patients or for acute ambulatory cases •Keep patient lying down for at least one-half hour after injection to avoid hypotension •Inject slowly, deep into upper outer quadrant of buttock •If irritation occurs, may dilute injection with NS or 2% procaine •Mixing with other agents in the syringe is not recommended 5/11
 •Avoid contact of solution on hands or clothing due to possibility of contact dermatitis IV Administration

   •Use IV only for treating tetanus and during surgery 4

   •Avoid injecting undiluted solution into a vein; dilute in NS to final concentration of 1 mg/mL •If used for treating tetanus, dilute to 1 mg/mL and administer at a rate of 1 mg per 2 minutes
   4

   •Reserve parenteral administration for bedfast patients or for acute ambulatory cases •Keep patient lying down for at least one-half hour after injection to avoid hypotension •Avoid contact of solution on hands or clothing due to possibility of contact dermatitis Preparation
   IV

   •Avoid injecting undiluted solution into a vein; dilute in NS to final concentration of 1 mg/mL Extemporaneous Preparation

   100 mg/mL Oral Solution (20 mL), using USP pure chlorproMAZINE HCl powder 7
   • Calibrate and mark a suitable amber plastic prescription bottle for 20 mL.

   • Weigh out 2 g of pure USP chlorproMAZINE HCl powder and transfer into the pre-calibrated
   amber plastic bottle.

   • Add 15 mL of Ora-Sweet to the bottle.
   • Apply moderate intermittent agitation until the drug powder dissolves (approximately 30
   minutes).

   • Add enough Ora-Sweet to reach the 20 mL mark and mix well.
   • Label the bottle with a 90 day beyond-use date and store at room temperature.

   • Product is stable in amber plastic prescription bottles at both refrigeration and room temper-
   ature for up to 3 months.

   • Note: Commercial chlorpromazine HCl tablets were not selected due to the presence of insol-
   uble excipients.

   sponded to cholic acid treatment. Response was determined by a combination of lab values
   (AST/ALT reduction, total bilirubin level 1 mg/dL or less, no cholestasis on liver biopsy) and clin-
   ical outcomes (increased body weight, survival for more than 3 years). Pre- and post-treatment
   liver biopsies (n=6) generally revealed improvements in inflammation and giant cell formation,
   and no progression of fibrosis. Survival for greater than 3 years was reported in 67% (41 of 62)
   of subjects, and 32% (13 of 41) of the surviving subjects were "long-term survivors" who lived
   10 to 24 years on treatment Disorder of peroxisomal function, with liver disease manifestations, steatorrhea, or
   complications due to decreased absorption of fat-soluble vitamins: Of 24 evaluable pa-
   tients, 46% responded to cholic acid treatment. Response was determined by a combination of
   lab values (AST/ALT reduction, total bilirubin level 1 mg/dL or less, no cholestasis on liver
   biopsy) and clinical outcomes (increased body weight, survival for more than 3 years). Pre- and
   post-treatment biopsies (n=9) were generally unchanged. Survival for greater than 3 years was
   reported in 42% (13 of 31) of subjects, and 62% (8 of 13)of the surviving subjects were "long-
   term survivors" who lived 10 to 17 years on treatment; this was not an improvement com-
   pared with historical controls Pediatric Approved FDA Indications

   months of age 1 ,3 .

   intubation, and to provide skeletal muscle relaxation during surgery or mechanical ventilation

 in children 2 to 12 years of age 1 ,3 .

   Administration
   Do not administer cisatracurium until the patient has been adequately sedated or is
   unconscious 1 ,3 ,5 . For IV use

   1 month or older: 1 to 15 mg/kg IV 1 ,2 ,3 ,4 ,5 ,6 .

   1 month or older: 1 to 3 mcg/kg/min by continuous IV infusion 1 ,3 ,5 .

   An initial infusion rate of 3 mcg/kg/min may be required to rapidly counteract the spontaneous
   recovery of neuromuscular function, thereafter, 1 to 2 mcg/kg/min may be adequate to main-
   tain desired level of effect

   While clarithromycin is labelled for use in acute bacterial sinusitis 2 ,3 , current treatment guide-
   lines do not recommend the use of macrolides, including clarithromycin, for empiric
   monotherapy due to high levels of S pneumoniae resistance 21,20 .

 Treatment of acute otitis media (AOM): Amoxicillin is the preferred first-line treatment for
   initial or delayed antibiotic treatment. Amoxicillin/clavulanate may be considered in patients
   who have received amoxicillin in the previous 30 days or who have the otitis-conjunctivitis syn-
   drome Macrolide antibiotics have limited activity against 2 of the 3 most common causative AOM or-
   ganisms (Haemophilus influenza and Streptococcus pneumoniae). In penicillin allergic patients,
   treatment options are cefdinir, cefuroxime, cefpodoxime, or ceftriaxone; these cephalosporins
   are highly unlikely to be cross-reactive due to their distinct chemical structures In a meta-
   analysis comparing first-line recommended antibiotics (amoxicillin or amoxicillin-clavulanate)
   with macrolides for the treatment of acute otitis media, the risk for clinical failure was higher
   with the use of macrolides than with the use of amoxicillin and amoxicillin-clavulanate (RR 31; 95% CI, 07 to 6) Treatment of community acquired pneumonia (CAP): There was no difference in the length
   of hospital stay between empirical beta-lactam monotherapy and combination macrolide plus
   beta-lactam therapy in children, median age 27 months, with radiologically confirmed CAP in a
   prospective observational study (n=1418; median length of stay, 55 vs 59 hours). Additionally
   no difference was detected in subgroup analysis of those 5 years or older, those with atypical
   bacteria, or those admitted to the intensive care unit Combination therapy of a macrolide
   antibiotic plus ceftriaxone did not reduce the length of stay compared with ceftriaxone alone
   in children (1 to 17 years of age) admitted to the hospital with pneumonia in a retrospective
   study (n=13,593). The mean length of stay was 4 days (median 2 days) in both groups Treatment of otitis media with effusion: Antibiotics are not recommended for asympto-
   matic otitis media with effusion Treatment of bartonellosis in HIV-infected patients. Clarithromycin is considered an alterna-
   tive agent; erythromycin or doxycycline is the preferred treatment Helicobacter pylori infection: Testing for H. pylori infection is recommended in patients with
   gastric or duodenal ulcers and/or erosions; if endoscopy is indicated after failure of therapy
   for iron deficiency anemia; and in children with a history of gastric cancer in a first-degree rela-
   tive. Treatment should be guided by antimicrobial susceptibility testing. For clarithromycin-
   susceptible strains, 14 days of triple therapy with high dose amoxicillin, a high dose proton
   pump inhibitor (PPI), and clarithromycin is recommended. For clarithromycin-resistant strains
   or in cases where susceptibility testing is not performed, 14 days of quadruple therapy with
   bismuth subsalicylate, high dose amoxicillin, a high dose PPI, and metroNIDAZOLE is recom-

 mended. Testing for H. pylori eradication is recommended 6 to 8 weeks after completion of

   States and countries in Europe Clarithromycin resistance may be higher in children than in
   adults, in patients previously treated for H. pylori, and varies by geographic region
   27 , 28 , 29 , 30 , 31 , 32 , Penicillin allergy: For patients with a confirmed penicillin allergy, triple therapy with clar-
   ithromycin, metroNIDAZOLE, and a high dose PPI is recommended if the H. pylori strain is clar-
   ithromycin-susceptible. If the strain is clarithromycin-resistant, quadruple therapy with bis-
   muth subsalicylate, tetracycline, a high dose PPI, and metroNIDAZOLE is recommended Sequential therapy: 5 days of amoxicillin plus a PPI, followed by another 5 days of clar-
   ithromycin plus a nitroimidazole antibiotic (metroNIDAZOLE or tinidazole) plus a PPI, improved
   eradication rates by 14% when compared with standard simultaneous therapy of 7 or 10 days
   duration consisting of a PPI and 2 to 3 antibiotics in a meta-analysis (n=1221 children, 12 trials) However, sequential quadruple therapy increases the risk of antibiotic resistance, perturba-

drugs.contraindications_raw:
Hypersensitivity reactions, jaundice, liver function test abnormalities, acute kidney injury have been reported in association with clin-
  damycin therapy Black Box Warning
  Clostridioides difficile associated diarrhea (CDAD) has been reported with nearly all antibacterial agents, including clindamycin phosphate,
  and may range in severity from mild diarrhea to fatal colitis. Treatment with antibacterial agents alters the normal flora of the colon, lead-
  ing to overgrowth of C difficile.

  Because clindamycin phosphate therapy has been associated with severe colitis which may end fatally, it should be reserved for serious in-
  fections where less toxic antimicrobial agents are inappropriate. It should not be used in patients with nonbacterial infections such as most
  upper respiratory tract infections. C difficile produces toxins A and B, which contribute to the development of CDAD. Hypertoxin producing
  strains of C difficile cause increased morbidity and mortality, as these infections can be refractory to antimicrobial therapy and may require
  a colectomy. CDAD must be considered in all patients who present with diarrhea following antibiotic use. Careful medical history is neces-
  sary since CDAD has been reported to occur over two months after the administration of antibacterial agents.

  If CDAD is suspected or confirmed, ongoing antibiotic use not directed against C difficile may need to be discontinued. Appropriate fluid and
  electrolyte management, protein supplementation, antibiotic treatment of C difficile, and surgical evaluation should be instituted as clini-
  cally indicated Solution Compatibility
  D5W, D10W, and NS.

  Terminal Injection Site Compatibility
  Acyclovir, amikacin, amiodarone, ampicillin, aztreonam, caffeine citrate, cefazolin, cefepime, cefotaxime, cefoxitin, ceftazidime, ceftriaxone,
  cimetidine, enalaprilat, esmolol, gentamicin, heparin, hydrocortisone succinate, linezolid, magnesium sulfate, metoclopramide, metronida-
  zole, midazolam, milrinone, morphine, netilmicin, nicardipine, penicillin G, piperacillin, piperacillin/tazobactam, potassium chloride, propo-
  fol, prostaglandin E1, ranitidine, remifentanil, sodium bicarbonate, tobramycin, and zidovudine.

  Terminal Injection Site Incompatibility
  Aminophylline, azithromycin, barbiturates, caspofungin, fluconazole, and phenytoin.

  Monitoring
  Therapeutic Laboratory Monitoring

  • Monitor CBC periodically in patients on prolonged therapy • Perform bacteriologic studies (ie, culture and susceptibility) to determine the causative organisms and their susceptibility to clindamycin Toxic Laboratory Monitoring

  • Monitor CBC periodically during prolonged therapy • Monitor liver tests periodically in patients with severe liver disease and during prolonged therapy • Monitor renal function periodically during prolonged therapy Toxic Physical Monitoring
  • Careful medical history is necessary since Clostridioides difficile-associated disease (CDAD) has been reported to occur over two months af-
  ter the administration of antibacterial agents • Monitor organ system function in patients up to 16 years of age 15/21

Common adverse events reported during pediatric clinical trials include somnolence or exces-
   sive sedation, irritability, behavioral abnormalities, dizziness, ataxia, vomiting, and salivation or
   drooling, which are similar to adverse events reported with other benzodiazepines, but with
   lower severity 22,28,6 ,23,7 ,8 ,9 .

   Black Box Warning
   Warning: Risks from Concomitant Use with Opioids; Abuse, Misuse, and Addiction; and
   Dependence and Withdrawal Reactions: 4 , 3
   ●   Concomitant use of benzodiazepines and opioids may result in profound sedation, respira-
       tory depression, coma, and death. Reserve concomitant prescribing of these drugs for pa-
       tients for whom alternative treatment options are inadequate. Limit dosages and durations
       to the minimum required. Follow patients for signs and symptoms of respiratory depression
       and sedation.
   ●   The use of benzodiazepines, including cloBAZam, exposes users to risks of abuse, misuse,
       and addiction, which can lead to overdose or death. Abuse and misuse of benzodiazepines
       commonly involve concomitant use of other medications, alcohol, and/or illicit substances,
       which is associated with an increased frequency of serious adverse outcomes. Before pre-
       scribing clobazam and throughout treatment, assess each patient's risk for abuse, misuse,
       and addiction.
   ●   The continued use of benzodiazepines, including cloBAZam, may lead to clinically significant
       physical dependence. The risks of dependence and withdrawal increase with longer treat-
       ment duration and higher daily dose. Abrupt discontinuation or rapid dosage reduction of
       cloBAZam after continued use may precipitate acute withdrawal reactions, which can be

 life-threatening. To reduce the risk of withdrawal reactions, use a gradual taper to discon-
       tinue clobazam or reduce the dosage.

   Monitoring
   Toxic Physical Monitoring
   • Monitor for respiratory depression, somnolence, and sedation, especially with concomitant
   use of other CNS depressants 3 ,4 .
   • Monitor for signs and symptoms of Stevens-Johnson syndrome or toxic epidermal necrolysis,
   especially during the first 8 weeks of therapy or upon drug reintroduction 1 ,17 .

   • Monitor for signs and symptoms of CNS depression 1 , • Monitor for suicidal behavior and ideation (emergence or worsening of depression, suicidal
   thoughts or behaviors, and unusual changes in mood or behavior) 3 ,4 .
   • Assess patient's risk for abuse, misuse, and addiction using a standardized screening tool,
   prior to initiation and throughout treatment 3 ,4 .

   • Monitor for signs and symptoms of abuse, misuse, and addiction, especially in at-risk patients

   Mechanism of action:

   Clobetasol propionate is a synthetic corticosteroid that has anti-inflammatory, antipruritic, and
   vasoconstrictive properties. Its anti-inflammatory effect is thought to be due to its ability to
   control biosynthesis of potent mediators of inflammation. It stimulates phospholipase A(2) in-
   hibitory proteins and subsequently blocks the release of arachidonic acid, which is a common
   precursor to leukotrienes and prostaglandins

drugs.uses_raw:
Tuberculosis, active; drug-resistant: Drug-resistant TB is treated with a combination of at
   least 4 or 5 drugs susceptible to the tuberculosis strain being treated. Shorter-course (6 to 9
   months), all oral standardized regimens are preferred when patients meet eligibility criteria
   (no extensive disease, no extrapulmonary disease except for TB lymphadenopathy, no prior
   exposure to components (exposure = more than 1 month of use). Longer course regimens are
   necessary for those not meeting eligibility criteria 5 ,6 ,3 ,2 ,4 .
   Longer-course regimen building: Regimens are built using the World Health Organization
   groupings. Group A drugs are levofloxacin/moxifloxacin, bedaquiline, and linezolid. Group B
   drugs are clofazimine and cycloserine/terizidone. Group C drugs are ethambutol, delamanid,
   pyrazinamide, imipenem/cilastatin or meropenem (both used in combination with
   amoxicillin/clavulanate), ethionamide/prothionamide, and p-aminosalicylic acid. Injectable

 drugs such as amikacin, streptomycin, kanamycin, and capreomycin are not recommended for
   treating pediatric patients. Ethionamide/prothionamide and p-aminosalicylic acid are only to
   be used if better options are not possible or available. Regimen building is undertaken as fol-
   lows 3 ,2 :
   • Preferred: All 3 Group A agents and at least 1 Group B agent.
   • If only 1 or 2 Group A drugs are able to be used: Use available Group A drug(s) and both
   Group B drugs.

   • Use Group C drugs if unable to complete a 4 or 5 drug regimen using only Group A and B
   drugs.

   Treatment duration is generally 18 to 24 months total, and 15 to 17 months after culture con-
   version. Durations may be extended depending on patient response.
   TB meningitis: Take into consideration the cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) penetration of available
   drugs. Levofloxacin, moxifloxacin, linezolid, cycloserine, pyrazinamide, and
   ethionamide/prothionamide have good CSF penetration.

   FDA Approved Pediatric Uses: Clofazimine is not FDA-approved for use in pediatric patients.
   Clofazimine may be obtained in the United States only via a single patient Investigational New
   Drug (SPIND) expanded access/compassionate use program.

   Administration
   • Take with meals • Clofazimine tablets will disperse slowly over approximately 5 minutes in water (5 mL for 50
   mg tablet; 10 mL for 100 mg tablet). Stir just prior to administration

The most commonly reported adverse effects are drowsiness (50%), ataxia (30%), and behav-

 Black Box Warning
   Oral Tablet

   Risks From Concomitant Use With Opioids; Abuse Misuse, and Addiction; and
   Dependence and Withdrawal Reactions: 4
   ●   Concomitant use of benzodiazepines and opioids may result in profound sedation, respira-
       tory depression, coma, and death. Reserve concomitant prescribing of these drugs for use
       in patients for whom alternative treatment options are inadequate. Limit dosages and dura-
       tions to the minimum required. Follow patients for signs and symptoms of respiratory de-
       pression and sedation.
   ●   The use of benzodiazepines, including clonazepam, exposes users to risks of abuse, misuse,
       and addiction, which can lead to overdose or death. Abuse and misuse of benzodiazepines
       commonly involve concomitant use of other medications, alcohol, and/or illicit substances,
       which is associated with an increased frequency of serious adverse outcomes. Before pre-
       scribing clonazepam and throughout treatment, assess each patient's risk for abuse, mis-
       use, and addiction.
   ●   The continued use of benzodiazepines, including clonazepam, may lead to clinically signifi-
       cant physical dependence. The risks of dependence and withdrawal increase with longer
       treatment duration and higher daily dose. Abrupt discontinuation or rapid dosage reduction
       of clonazepam after continued use may precipitate acute withdrawal reactions, which can
       be life-threatening. To reduce the risk of withdrawal reactions, use a gradual taper to dis-
       continue clonazepam or reduce the dosage.

   Dine plus methylphenidate, and placebo in patients with ADHD and Tourette's syndrome. The
   combination provided benefits for impulsivity, hyperactivity, inattention, and tic severity; how-
   ever, increased sedation was reported with the combination Caudal block, adjunct: The addition of cloNIDine to local anesthetics for caudal blockade in
   infants and children has been associated with a local anesthetic sparing effect and an increase
   in duration of analgesia. Duration of analgesia increases with the increased mcg/kg dose of
   cloNIDine; however, adverse effects such as sedation are also increased 8 ,27 . Caudal cloNIDine
   has also been associated with less postoperative nausea and vomiting, and pruritus when
   compared with caudal hydromorphone or morphine cloNIDine has been used with bupiva-
   caine, levobupivacaine, and ropivacaine with epinephrine

   Hypertension: CloNIDine may be an appropriate oral antihypertensive for difficult to control
   or severe hypertension in children 28 , 13 , Premedication for postoperative pain, adjunct: Oral clonidine improved postoperative pain
   in children undergoing surgery, particularly tonsillectomies, in a meta-analysis (n=11 studies;
   742 children). Clonidine appeared to be well tolerated; however, most children additionally re-
   ceived atropine Sedation in critically ill patients, Guidelines: Alpha-2 agonists, primarily cloNIDine and

   tion with midazolam following congenital cardiac surgery, scoliosis surgery, burn injury, and
   among general PICU patients. One prospective cohort and 2 randomized clinical trials reported
   significant reductions in opioid and benzodiazepine exposure with the addition of scheduled
   enteral cloNIDine Sevoflurane-induced Agitation - Post-Anesthesia; Prevention:

   Summary
    ●   Recommendation: May be used in children younger than 8 years; optimal route, dose, and
        timing of dose needs to be established.
    ●   Strength of Evidence: Double-blind, randomized studies.
    ●   Efficacy: Favors Efficacy

   Oral 30 , IV 31,32,33 , or caudal 32 clonidine administered preoperatively 30 or intraoperatively
   31 , 33
         in children younger than 8 years of age reduced postoperative sevoflurane-induced
   agitation.

   Intraoperative IV clonidine 3 mcg/kg significantly reduced the incidence of sevoflurane-induced
   agitation in healthy children (1 to 5 years of age) undergoing non-cardiac, elective surgery in a
   double-blind, randomized study (n=290; 80% boys). At least 1 episode of postoperative agita-
   tion occurred in 25% of the clonidine group and 47% of the placebo group (RR 56; 95% CI 43 to 73). These results were mostly based on there being a significant effect in boys (RR 43; 95% CI 3 to 61); there was no significant effect when the 73 girls were assessed. Less
   opioids were used during and after surgery in the clonidine group compared with placebo
   group. Blood pressure and heart rate were reduced in the clonidine group; no hemodynamic
   interventions were necessary Preoperative oral clonidine reduced the frequency of sevoflurane-induced agitation in children
   (1 to 6 years old) undergoing circumcision, in a double-blind, randomized study (n=60).
   Children were randomized to 1 of 3 oral premedication (30 minutes prior to induction of anes-
   thesia): midazolam 5 mg/kg (up to a maximum of 15 mg), clonidine 2 mcg/kg, or clonidine 4
   mcg/kg. Anesthesia was induced and maintained with sevoflurane. Children were excluded if
   they had an inadequate penile block. A modified objective pain scale (3 of the 5 items) was
   used as the assessment of agitation. The items assessed were tears, movements, and behavior
   on a scale of 0 (absent) to 3 (most severe). A total score of 3 or more was classified as agita-
   tion. The agitation score was significantly lower in the clonidine 4 mcg/kg group compared with
   midazolam group (median (interquartile range) 3 (0 to 6) vs 5 (2.8 to 8), p=0.015, respec-
   tively). A significant difference was not demonstrated between clonidine 2 mcg/kg and midazo-

 lam (median (interquartile range) 5 (0 to 7) vs 5 (2.8 to 8), respectively). During the first
   postoperative hour, the proportion of children with agitation was significantly lower in the
   clonidine 4 mcg/kg group compared with the midazolam group (p=0.025). Compared with mi-
   dazolam, the proportion of children experiencing agitation that lasted 15 minutes or more was
   significantly lower in the clonidine 4 mcg/kg group (p=0.047). The quality of induction was esti-
   mated to be good in 70%, 50%, and 30% of the midazolam, clonidine 2 mcg/kg, and clonidine 4
   mcg/kg group, respectively. No difference in hemodynamic measurements, including blood
   pressure and heart rate, was demonstrated among the groups Clonidine, when administered intravenously or caudally, significantly reduced postanesthesia
   agitation in children. In a randomized, patient-blinded trial, 78 children (aged 3 to 8 years) who
   were undergoing surgery under sevoflurane anesthesia were all given caudal epidural block
   with bupivacaine 175%, 1 mL/kg. Each patient was assigned to one of 4 groups (18
   patients/group) to receive, in addition, caudal clonidine 1 mcg/kg (Group 1), caudal clonidine 3
   mcg/kg (Group 2), intravenous clonidine 3 mcg/kg (Group 3), or no additional treatment
   (Group 4). Groups 2, 3, and 4 received intravenous saline placebo. Postanesthesia agitation oc-
   curred in 4 patients in Group 1, none in Group 2, 1 in Group 3, and 7 in Group Clonidine 3
   mcg/kg, regardless of route of administration, was significantly better than placebo at prevent-
   ing agitation (p less than 05), whereas clonidine 1 mcg/kg was not significantly better than
   placebo. Respiratory depression was not observed Intravenous (IV) clonidine was safe and reduced sevoflurane-induced agitation in males 2 to 7
   years of age undergoing circumcision, according to a small, double-blind study (n=40). All pa-
   tients received oral midazolam 5 milligram/kilogram (mg/kg) 30 minutes before induction of
   anesthesia, and single-agent sevoflurane was used for both induction and maintenance of
   anesthesia. For pain treatment, a penile block was performed before surgery using 5% bupi-
   vacaine 1 mL/kg and an acetaminophen suppository 15 mg/kg was inserted. Subjects were
   randomized to IV clonidine 2 mcg/kg diluted in 5 mL normal saline or to IV placebo (normal
   saline), both delivered over 5 minutes starting 5 minutes after the initiation of surgery. Overall,
   16 patients in the placebo group and 2 patients in the clonidine group were judged to be agi-
   tated (p less than 001). IV midazolam was to be given to agitated subjects who could not be
   easily calmed. Six patients in the placebo group and none in the clonidine group required post-
   operative midazolam (p=0.02). During the recovery period, heart rate and blood pressure were
   significantly less in clonidine-treated subjects (p less than 05), though none exhibited brady-
   cardia or hypotension. All subjects met the discharge criteria at the end of the 2-hour observa-
   tion period Pediatric FDA-Approved Indications

   •Attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) as monotherapy or as adjunctive therapy to
   stimulant medications 3 ,1 .

 •Cancer pain: Continuous epidural clonidine should be restricted to pediatric patients with se-
   vere intractable pain from malignancy that is unresponsive to epidural or spinal opiates or
   other more conventional analgesic techniques. Effectiveness has been established in patients
   old enough to tolerate placement and management of an epidural catheter, based on evi-
   dence from adequate and well controlled studies in adults and experience with the use of
   clonidine in the pediatric age group for other indications Administration
   Epidural: The 500 mcg/mL-strength must be diluted with NS to a final concentration not ex-
   ceeding 100 mcg/mL prior to use. Do not use with preservative-containing diluents Extended-release tablets: May be taken with or without food. Do not crush, chew, or break
   before swallowing. Substitution of extended-release tablets with other cloNIDine formulations
   on a mg-per-mg basis is not recommended Extended-release suspension (0.1 mg/mL; 100 mcg/mL):

   been associated with a dose-dependant increase in sedation 8 ,27 .

   Black Box Warning
   Epidural Injection

   The 500 mcg/mL strength product should be diluted prior to use in an appropriate solution Epidural cloNIDine is not recommended for obstetrical, postpartum, or peri-operative pain
   management. The risk of hemodynamic instability, especially hypotension and bradycardia,
   from epidural cloNIDine may be unacceptable in these patients. However, in a rare obstetrical,
   postpartum or peri-operative patient, potential benefits may outweigh the possible risks Monitoring
   Therapeutic Monitoring
   Sedation in critically ill patients in ICU
   • Assessment of the level of sedation in mechanically ventilated pediatric patients is recom-
   mended, using the Comfort-B Scale, State Behavioral Scale, or Richmond Agitation-Sedation
   Scale 16
   • All pediatric patients requiring mechanical ventilation should be assigned a target depth of
   sedation and evaluated at least once daily with a validated sedation assessment tool 16

   Toxic Monitoring

 Epidural injection: Monitor vital signs frequently during the first few days of epidural therapy.
   Careful monitoring of epidural pump function and catheter placement is required to avoid the
   risk of abrupt, inadvertent interruption of treatment and risk of withdrawal Oral: Monitor blood pressure and heart rate prior to therapy initiation, following dose in-
   creases, and periodically during therapy Oral: Monitor for hypotension and bradycardia in patients with preexisting renal impairment Oral: Frequently monitor vital signs in patients with cardiac conduction abnormalities or those
   on concomitant sympatholytic drugs, 1 and in patients at risk for hypotension, heart block,
   bradycardia, syncope, cardiovascular disease, vascular disease, cerebrovascular disease, or
   chronic renal failure Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD): 34 , 35 :
   • Conduct a thorough examination prior to initiating cloNIDine therapy for a diagnosis of
   ADHD. Special attention should be given to symptoms indicative of a cardiac condition, includ-
   ing palpitations, near syncope, or syncope 34,35 .
   • Obtain a complete family and patient history for conditions associated with sudden cardiac
   death, and determine current use of any other prescription or over-the-counter medications
   34,35
             .

   • Conduct a complete physical evaluation of the patient for hypertension, cardiac murmurs,
   physical findings associated with Marfan syndrome, and signs of irregular cardiac rhythms
   34 , • Perform further evaluation if family history, patient history or physical exam is suggestive of
   cardiac disease during initial visit or at follow up visits, and if indicated, consult pediatric cardi-
   ologist 34,35 .
   • Continue to assess the patient for cardiac symptoms and any changes in family history at fol-
   low up visits 34,35 .

   • Evaluate blood pressure and heart rate at baseline, during routine follow-up within 1 to 3
   months, at follow up visits every 6 to 12 months, and when the patient is weaned from cloNI-
   Dine. Decreases in blood pressure and heart rate have been reported with the use of certain
   ADHD drugs 34 , • When discontinuing cloNIDine therapy, taper drug to avoid rebound hypertension and moni-
   tor blood pressure 34,35 .
   Sedation in critically ill patients in ICU

 • Assessment of the level of sedation in mechanically ventilated pediatric patients is recom-
   mended, using the Comfort-B Scale, State Behavioral Scale, or Richmond Agitation-Sedation
   Scale 16
   • All pediatric patients requiring mechanical ventilation should be assigned a target depth of
   sedation and evaluated at least once daily with a validated sedation assessment tool 16

Bleeding and thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura are the most common hematological ad-
   verse events 8 , Anemia, neutropenia, and leukopenia have also been reported. Other ad-
   verse events reported in children include headache, skin bruising, skin rash, and hair loss 3 ,4 ,6 .

   Black Box Warning
   The effectiveness of clopidogrel hydrogen sulfate results from its antiplatelet activity, which is
   dependent on its conversion to an active metabolite by the cytochrome P450 (CYP) system,
   principally CYP2C19. Clopidogrel hydrogen sulfate at recommended doses forms less of the
   active metabolite and so has a reduced effect on platelet activity in patients who are homozy-
   gous for nonfunctional alleles of the CYP2C19 gene, (termed “CYP2C19 poor metabolizers”).
   Tests are available to identify patients who are CYP2C19 poor metabolizers. Consider use of
   another platelet P2Y12 inhibitor in patients identified as CYP2C19 poor metabolizers Monitoring
   Measure bleeding time prior to therapy initiation and 3 to 7 days after therapy initiation to as-
   sess drug efficacy. Platelet aggregation assay studies may be useful in some patients to evalu-

 ate response Monitor hematological parameters closely during the first few months of ther-

Drug-resistant schizophrenia
   Guideline: A trial of cloZAPine should be considered for youth with treatment-resistant
   schizophrenia spectrum disorders, following 2 or more failures of a first-line antipsychotic
   agent (clinical standard, based on rigorous empirical evidence and/or overwhelming clinical
   consensus) 17
   Literature: In a systematic review that identified 18 studies of cloZAPine in childhood- and
   adolescent-onset schizophrenia, meta-analysis found cloZAPine significantly reduced the Brief
   Psychiatric Rating Scale (BPRS) score compared with control (mean difference, 48 [95% CI, 04 to 91]; 3 double-blind, randomized studies, 6- to 12-week duration, in 85 inpatients aged
   6 years or older). In open-label (n=4) and observational studies (n=7), BPRS and Positive and
   Negative Syndrome Scale (PANSS) scores were also significantly improved with cloZAPine, in-
   cluding some with long-term followup (2 to 6 years). cloZAPine dosage specifics for initiation,
   titration, and maintenance were unavailable Administration
   • May be administered with or without food 5 ,13,14

   • Orally disintegrating tablets: Consume tablet immediately once it is removed from the blis-
   ter unit (do not push tablet through, pull back foil on blister); tablets disintegrate in the mouth
   and can be swallowed subsequently with saliva or liquid; may be chewed if desired 14
   • Suspension: Shake bottle for 10 seconds prior to each use; administer dose using only the
   provided oral syringes; consume the prepared dose immediately; suspension stable 100 days
   after initial opening 5

   Preparation

   Extemporaneous Oral Preparations

 • An oral suspension of cloZAPine 20 mg/mL was stable for 63 days and retained at least 97% of the initial cloZAPine concentration when stored in amber plastic containers at 23°C
   and prepared in any of the following suspending vehicles: Ora-Sweet, Ora-Plus, a 1-to-1 mix-
   ture of Ora-Sweet plus Ora-Plus, or simple syrup. The containers were not protected from light • A 20-mg/mL oral suspension prepared from crushed tablets in a pediatric mixture base (con-
   taining syrup, carboxymethylcellulose, methylhydroxybenzoate and propylhydroxybenzoate)
   was found to be chemically stable for 18 days at room temperature. However, an expiration
   date of 7 days was recommended due to lack of microbial testing

drugs.contraindications_raw:
Common (adults): Hypotension (9% to 13%), syncope (6%), tachycardia (17% to 25%), sweating
   (6%), increased weight (4% to 31%), excessive salivation (13% to 48%), nausea (5% to 17%), dry
   mouth (5% to 6%), dizziness (14% to 27%), headache (7% to 10%), sedation (21%), somnolence
   (up to 46%), visual disturbances (5%), fever 5% to 13%) 28,8 ,9

   Black Box Warning
   Severe Neutropenia; Orthostatic Hypotension, Bradycardia, and Syncope; Seizure;
   Myocarditis, Pericarditis, and Cardiomyopathy

   Severe Neutropenia

   • cloZAPine treatment has caused severe neutropenia, defined as an absolute neutrophil count
   (ANC) less than 500/mcL. Severe neutropenia can lead to serious infection and death. Prior to
   initiating treatment with cloZAPine a baseline ANC must be at least 1500/mcL for the general
   population; and must be at least 1000/mcL for patients with documented Benign Ethnic
   Neutropenia (BEN). During treatment, patients must have regular ANC monitoring. Advise pa-

 tients to immediately report symptoms consistent with severe neutropenia or infection (eg,
   fever, weakness, lethargy, or sore throat).

   • Because of the risk of severe neutropenia, cloZAPine is available only through a restricted
   program under a Risk Evaluation Mitigation Strategy (REMS) called the CloZAPine REMS
   Program.

   Orthostatic Hypotension, Bradycardia, Syncope

   • Orthostatic hypotension, bradycardia, syncope, and cardiac arrest have occurred with cloZA-
   Pine treatment. The risk is highest during the initial titration period, particularly with rapid
   dose escalation. These reactions can occur with the first dose, with doses as low as 5 mg
   per day. Initiate treatment at 5 mg once or twice daily; titrate slowly; and use divided
   dosages. Use cloZAPine cautiously in patients with cardiovascular or cerebrovascular disease
   or conditions predisposing to hypotension (eg, dehydration, use of antihypertensive
   medications).

   Seizures
   • Seizures have occurred with cloZAPine treatment. The risk is dose-related. Initiate treatment
   at 5 mg, titrate gradually, and use divided dosing. Use caution when administering cloZAP-
   ine to patients with a history of seizures or other predisposing risk factors for seizure (CNS
   pathology, medications that lower the seizure threshold, alcohol abuse). Caution patients
   about engaging in any activity where sudden loss of consciousness could cause serious risk to
   themselves or others.

   Myocarditis, Pericarditis, Cardiomyopathy, and Mitral Valve Incompetence

   • Fatal myocarditis and cardiomyopathy have occurred with cloZAPine treatment. Discontinue
   cloZAPine and obtain a cardiac evaluation upon suspicion of these reactions. Generally, pa-
   tients with cloZAPine-related myocarditis or cardiomyopathy should not be rechallenged with
   cloZAPine. Consider the possibility of myocarditis, pericarditis, or cardiomyopathy if chest pain,
   tachycardia, palpitations, dyspnea, fever, flulike symptoms, hypotension, or ECG changes occur
   25,21,26
              .

   Monitoring
   Therapeutic drug monitoring

   Psychosis: 350 to 600 nanograms/milliliter (ng/mL) 18
   • In a consensus guideline, the use of therapeutic drug monitoring (TDM) with cloZAPine is
   rated as 1, strongly recommended for dose titration and for special indications. The highest

 probability of response or remission can be expected at drug concentrations within the re-
   ported therapeutic reference range 18
   • Antipsychotic therapeutic reference range for cloZAPine is 350 to 600 ng/mL when used as an
   antipsychotic, with a laboratory alert level of 1000 ng/mL. Reported therapeutic reference
   ranges are established. Controlled clinical trials have shown beneficial effects of TDM. Reports
   on decreased tolerability or intoxications exist • In patients with schizophrenia, achieving a cloZAPine plasma level in the range of 250 to 400
   nanograms/milliliter (ng/mL) increases the likelihood of a clinical response • Obtain a cloZAPine trough level in patients that have failed to demonstrate an adequate re-
   sponse. If the trough level is less than 350 nanograms/mL, a dose increase may be warranted
   to the extent side effects are tolerated CloZAPine to norclozapine ratio

   • Assessing the cloZAPine to N-desmethylclozapine (norclozapine) ratio (CLZ:NDMC) during
   treatment may be helpful in assessing cognitive improvements, maximizing efficacy, and mini-
   mizing adverse effects. The optimal CLZ:NDMC ratio has not been established; however, a ratio
   of approximately 2 may be associated with effectiveness and tolerability. Lower ratios are as-
   sociated with clinical improvement in schizophrenia-symptom rating scales including Scale for
   Assessment of Positive Symptoms (SAPS), and Scale for Assessment of Negative Symptoms
   (SANS) in pooled results from 3 studies; however, 3 other studies did not find this correlation.
   In 5 of 6 studies, lower ratios were associated with improved cognitive performance (executive
   functioning, working memory, decision making, social cognition, improved attention, and cog-
   nitive flexibility) • CLZ:NDMC ratio less than 2 might indicate presence of additional factors inducing cloZAPine-
   metabolizing enzymes. The use of fluvoxamine to increase the CLZ:NDMC ratio via inhibition of
   CYP1A2-mediated cloZAPine metabolism was associated with a reduction in cardiometabolic
   adverse events (reduction in body weight, fasting serum insulin, glucose, and serum triglyc-
   erides). Concurrent fluvoxamine should be used cautiously because the degree of effect on
   cloZAPine metabolism is unpredictable making on-going monitoring of serum cloZAPine levels
   in addition to CLZ:NDMC ratio likely necessary • CLZ:NDMC ratio greater than 2 is suggestive of a non-trough sample, recent missed dose, or
   the CYP1A2 or other CYP450 enzyme systems may be saturated or inhibited Laboratory monitoring for neutropenia 7

   Baseline: Obtain CBC including differential and ANC at baseline and weekly for the first 6
   months to ensure ANC is at least 1500/mcL. If ANC is at least 1500/mcL for the first 6 months

 of treatment, monitoring frequency may be reduced to once every 2 weeks for the next 6
   months. Thereafter, if ANC is at least 1500/mcL, monitoring frequency can be reduced to once
   a month for the duration of therapy Baseline: In patients with benign ethnic neutropenia (BEN), obtain CBC including differential
   and ANC at least twice at baseline and then once weekly for the first 6 months to ensure ANC
   is at least 1000/mcL. If ANC is at least 1000/mcL for the first 6 months of treatment, monitoring
   frequency may be reduced to once every 2 weeks for the next 6 months. Thereafter, if ANC is
   at least 1000/mcL, monitoring frequency can be reduced to once a month for the duration of
   therapy Interruptions in therapy: In patients with a normal ANC range (with or without benign ethnic
   neutropenia), if treatment is interrupted for less than 30 days, continue ANC monitoring as be-
   fore the interruption. If treatment is interrupted for 30 days or more, restart ANC monitoring
   regimen as if the patient is new to the drug 21
   Abnormal blood counts: General population

   • Mild Neutropenia (ANC between 1000 and 1499/mcL): Confirm with repeat ANC measure-
   ment within 24 hours; obtain ANC 3 times/week until ANC is at least 1500/mcL, then return to
   last "normal range" ANC monitoring schedule.
   • Moderate Neutropenia (ANC between 500 and 999/mcL): Confirm with repeat ANC measure-
   ment within 24 ours; obtain ANC daily until ANC is at least 1000/mcL, then 3 times/week until
   at least 1500/mcL. Once ANC is 1500/mcL, obtain ANC weekly for 4 weeks, then return to "nor-
   mal range" ANC monitoring schedule if clinically appropriate.

   • Severe Neutropenia (ANC less than 500/mcL): Confirm with repeat ANC measurement within
   24 ours; obtain ANC daily until ANC is at least 1000/mcL, then 3 times/week until at least
   1500/mcL. Once ANC is 1500/mcL, monitor as a new patient under the "normal range" ANC
   monitoring schedule if patient is rechallenged..
   Abnormal blood counts: Benign Ethnic Neutropenia (BEN)
   • Normal Range (ANC at least 1000/mcL): Obtain ANC at baseline and weekly until month 6,
   then every 2 weeks until month 12, then monthly thereafter.
   • Neutropenia (ANC between 500 and 999/mcL): Confirm with repeat ANC measurement within
   24 hours; obtain ANC 3 times/week until ANC is at least 1000/mcL or patient's baseline. Once
   ANC is 1000/mcL or at patient's baseline, obtain ANC weekly for 4 weeks then return to last
   "normal range" ANC monitoring schedule if clinically appropriate.
   • Severe Neutropenia (ANC less than 500/mcL): Confirm with repeat ANC measurement within
   24 hours; obtain ANC daily until ANC is at least 500/mcL. Once ANC is at least 500/mcL, obtain
   ANC 3 times/week until ANC is at patient's baseline. Once ANC is 1000/mcL or at patient's

 baseline, monitor as a new patient under the "normal range" ANC monitoring schedule if pa-
   tient is rechallenged.

   Discontinuation: If abrupt discontinuation is unrelated to neutropenia, continue current mon-
   itoring of CBC with differential and ANC until ANC has reached at least 1500/mcL (general pop-
   ulation) or at least 1000/mcL or the patient's baseline (BEN patients). Also monitor for the re-
   currence of psychotic symptoms or cholinergic rebound symptoms (profuse sweating,
   headache, nausea, vomiting, or diarrhea) Fever:

   • Obtain an ANC level in those who develop temperature of 3°F (38.5°C) or greater • Initiate appropriate workup for infection in patients with BEN and an ANC less than 1000/mcL Laboratory Monitoring

   • Measure fasting plasma glucose at baseline 21,22 , at week 12 , then annually thereafter, or
   more frequently in patients with a higher baseline risk for the development of diabetes Patients with diabetes mellitus should be regularly monitored for worsening of glucose control
   21,22

   • Measure fasting lipid profile at baseline 21 , 22 , at week 12 , and then every 5 years or periodi-
   cally thereafter. Repeat testing should be done more frequently as clinically indicated • Screen for gestational diabetes early in pregnancy • Consider obtaining baseline serum chemistry panel. Obtain baseline measurements of potas-
   sium and magnesium, and periodically monitor electrolytes during treatment • Perform serum tests for liver injury, including transaminases • Monitor for signs or symptoms of hepatotoxicity, including coagulopathy • Actively monitor for cloZAPine-related myocarditis by measuring serum C reactive protein
   (CRP) and troponin levels at baseline, day 7, day 14, day 21, and day If mild elevation of
   serum CRP or troponin levels, persistent tachycardia, or signs and symptoms of acute infection
   occur, monitor serum CRP and troponin levels daily until specific clinical feature resolves •

   Physical Monitoring
   • Examine patient for tardive dyskinesia before initiation and then annually. Patients at higher
   risk for tardive dyskinesia (ie, patients who have experienced acute dystonic reactions,

 akathisia, or other clinically significant extrapyramidal side effects) should be examined every
   6 months throughout the duration of treatment • Perform baseline ECG 21 and repeat if myocarditis is suspected. Monitor vital signs, including
   blood pressure, pulse, body temperature, and respiration rate, at least every second day for
   the first 28 days • Complete fall risk assessment in patients with conditions or concomitant medications that
   may exacerbate antipsychotic effects (eg, somnolence, postural hypotension, motor and sen-
   sory instability) when initiating treatment and recurrently in patients on long-term therapy • Monitor for signs or symptoms of hepatotoxicity, including fatigue, malaise, anorexia, nau-
   sea, jaundice, and hepatic encephalopathy • Prior to initiating therapy, screen for constipation and reassess bowel function frequently
   with careful attention to any changes in the frequency or character of bowel movements, as
   well as signs and symptoms of complications of hypomotility (eg, nausea, vomiting, abdominal
   distension, abdominal pain). If constipation or gastrointestinal hypomotility are identified,
   monitor closely • Carefully evaluate patients with fever to rule out severe neutropenia or infection • Based on available data on the use of atypical antipsychotics, the American Diabetes
   Association, the American Psychiatric Association, the American Association of Clinical
   Endocrinologists, and the North American Association for the Study of Obesity developed a
   consensus position statement that recommends baseline and periodic monitoring for obesity
   and diabetes, as listed below 22 :
    ●   Obtain personal and family history of obesity, diabetes mellitus, dyslipidemia, hypertension,
        and cardiovascular disease, prior to treatment and review annually with patient
    ●   Track weight and BMI at baseline, at week 4, at week 8, at week 12, following initiation or
        change in therapy, and quarterly thereafter
    ●   Measure waist circumference at baseline and annually thereafter
    ●   Measure blood pressure at baseline, at week 12, then annually thereafter, or more fre-
        quently in patients with a higher baseline risk for the development of hypertension
