      Key: ART = antiretroviral therapy, ARV = Antiretroviral, AST = aspartate amino-
      transferase, ALT = alanine aminotransferase, BUN = blood urea nitrogen, CAB-LA
      = cabotegravir long-acting, CBC = complete blood count; DAA = direct-acting an-
      tiviral; HCV = hepatitis C virus, IN = integrase, INSTI = integrase strand transfer
      inhibitor, PrEP = pre-exposure prophylaxis

      (a) If ART is initiated soon after HIV diagnosis and entry into care, repeat baseline labora-
      tory testing is not necessary.
      (b) ART is indicated for all people with HIV and should be started as soon as possible.
      However, if ART initiation is delayed, patients should be retained in care, with periodic
      monitoring as noted above.
      (c) After 2 years of consistently suppressed HIV RNA, less frequent monitoring (eg, every 6
      months) may be considered.
      (d) After 2 years of ART with consistently suppressed viral load: CD4 count 300 to 500

 cells/mm(3), monitor every 12 months; CD4 count greater than 500 cells/mm(3), CD4 mon-
      itoring is optional.
      (e) If HIV RNA is detectable at 4 to 8 weeks, repeat every 4 to 8 weeks until viral load is
      suppressed to less than 50 copies/mL, then every 3 to 6 months.
      (f) For patients on ART, viral load is typically measured every 3 to 6 months. More frequent
      monitoring may be considered in individuals having difficulties with ART adherence or at
      risk for nonadherence. However, for adherent patients with suppressed viral load and sta-
      ble immunological status for more than 1 year, monitoring can be extended to 6-month
      intervals.
      (g) Standard genotypic drug-resistance testing in ARV-naïve persons should focus on test-
      ing for mutations in the PR and RT genes. If transmitted INSTI resistance is a concern, or if
      a person has a history of INSTI use as PrEP or treatment, or a person presents with
      viremia while on an INSTI, providers should also test for resistance mutations in the IN
      gene. In ARV-naïve patients who do not immediately begin ART, repeat testing before initi-
      ation of ART is optional if drug-resistance testing was performed at entry into care. For vi-
      rologically suppressed patients who are switching therapy for toxicity or convenience, viral
      amplification will not be possible and therefore resistance testing should not be per-
      formed. Results from prior resistance testing can be used to help in the construction of a
      new regimen.
      (h) If infected with hepatitis B virus, tenofovir disoproxil fumarate or tenofovir alafe-
      namide plus either emtricitabine or lamivudine should be used as part of the ART regimen
      to treat both hepatitis B virus and HIV infections.
      (i) If HBsAg, and HBsAb, and HBcAb are negative at baseline, administer hepatitis B vac-
      cine series. Also, consult Guidelines for Opportunistic Infections.
      (j) Typically HBV infection has resolved with loss of HBsAb despite isolated HBcAb; confirm
      with an HBV viral load if wanted. A positive HBV viral load is indicative of acute infection
      (other symptoms will be present usually) or chronic infection. Vaccinate the patient when
      viral load is negative. Also, consult Guidelines for Opportunistic Infections.
      (k) In patients with recent HCV infection (acquired in last 6 months) or advanced immun-
      odeficiency (CD4 count less than 100 cells/mm(3)), the HCV antibody test may not be ade-
      quate for screening. HCV RNA screening is indicated in persons who have been success-
      fully treated for HCV or who spontaneously cleared prior infection. HCV antibody-negative
      patients with elevated ALT may need HCV RNA testing.
      (l) At-risk populations: injection drug users, persons with a history of incarceration, men
      with HIV who have unprotected sex with men, and persons with percutaneous/parenteral
      exposure to blood in unregulated settings are at risk of HCV infection.
      (m) Serum sodium, potassium, bicarbonate, chloride, blood urea nitrogen, creatinine, glu-
      cose (preferably fasting). Monitor serum phosphorus concentrations in patients with
      chronic kidney disease who are on tenofovir-containing regimens. Renal function determi-

 nation should include creatinine monitoring and estimation of the glomerular filtration
      rate.
      (n) Consult recommendations of the HIV Medicine Association of the Infectious Diseases
      Society of America for patients with renal disease. More frequent monitoring may be indi-
      cated for patients with evidence of kidney disease (eg, proteinuria or decreased glomeru-
      lar function) or increased risk of renal insufficiency (eg. patients with diabetes or hyper-
      tension).
      (o) CBC with differential should be done when a CD4 count is performed. When CD4 count
      is no longer being monitored, the recommended frequency of CBC with differential is
      once a year. More frequent monitoring may be for patients receiving medications that po-
      tentially cause cytopenia (eg, trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole)
      (p) If random lipids are abnormal, fasting lipids should be obtained. Consult the ACA/AHA
      recommendations for diagnosis and management of patients with dyslipidemia.
      (q) If random glucose is abnormal, fasting glucose should be obtained. HgbA1C is not
      longer recommended for diagnosis of diabetes in patients with HIV on ART.
      (r) Assess urine glucose and protein before initiating tenofovir-containing regimens and
      monitor during treatment with these regimens.
      (s) In women with child-bearing potential.

   Product-Specific Monitoring
   •Assess estimated CrCl prior to or when initiating therapy, and during treatment on a clinically
   appropriate schedule. When interpreting changes in estimated CrCl, consider comorbidities or
   concomitant drugs due to cobicistat's inhibition of tubular secretion of creatinine without af-
   fecting actual renal glomerular function. If there is an increase in serum creatinine of greater
   than 4 mg/dL from baseline, monitor closely for renal safety •When coadministered with tenofovir disoproxil fumarate, evaluate estimated CrCl, urine glu-
   cose, and urine protein at baseline and routinely during therapy and assess serum phospho-
   rous in patients at risk for or with chronic kidney disease

   tients, even if the needle is changed Administration

   are moles, scars, or stretch marks • Instruct children and lean patients to use injection techniques that minimize risk of intramus-
   cular injection, eg, injecting into a pinched fold of skin • Use with NovoFine(R) or NovoFine(R) Plus needles with a gauge of 32 and a length of 4 mm. If
   needles longer than 4 mm are used, injection techniques that minimize the risk of IM injection
   should be used • Missed dose during initial 4 weeks of treatment: Once-daily dosing during initial 4 weeks of

drugs.contraindications_raw:

   and rash Monitoring
   Concurrent use with cortisone, hydrocortisone, spironolactone, or estrogen may alter the test
   results Cortisol levels: Measure at baseline and again at exactly 30 and 60 minutes after administra-
   tion. A post-administration cortisol level of less than 18 mcg/dL at either time point is sugges-
   tive of adrenocortical insufficiency Method Options
   Rapid Screening Test (Intramuscular Injection)

   Collect blood sample of 6 to 7 mL in a heparinized tube before IM cosyntropin and exactly 30
   minutes after IM cosyntropin. Refrigerate blood samples until sent to the laboratory.
   Determine plasma cortisol response by some appropriate method. If it is not possible to send
   them to the laboratory or perform the fluorimetric procedure within 12 hours, then the
   plasma should be separated and refrigerated or frozen until ready to assay Alternative Test (Intravenous Injection)
   Measure adrenal response by urinary steroid excretion at baseline and after treatment or
   measure plasma cortisol levels at baseline and after the end IV infusion. Measurement of
   plasma cortisol levels is preferable because urinary steroid excretion does not always accu-
   rately reflect adrenal or plasma cortisol response to ACTH. Draw plasma between 30 to 60
   minutes; difference between 30 and 60 minutes may not be significant. If plasma is drawn 60
   minutes after treatment, then the criterion for a normal response is an approximate doubling

 of the basal plasma cortisol value Based on a study performed in 49 healthy adult volun-
   teers administered low-dose (1 mcg) cosyntropin IV, a falsely low cortisol value may occur if a
   sample is drawn after 30 minutes
drugs.pharmacokinetics_summary:
Pharmacology
   Mechanism of action: Cosyntropin, a synthetic subunit of natural adrenocorticotrophic hor-
   mone (ACTH), stimulates adrenal gland to secrete 17-OH corticosteroids, 17-ketosteroids,
   and/or 17-ketogenic steroids. Extra-adrenal effects include increased melanotropic activity, in-
   creased growth hormone secretion and an adipokinetic effect.

   conditions that lead to vitamin B12 malabsorption (eg, autoimmune gastritis/pernicious ane-

   necessary for those not meeting eligibility criteria 7 ,8 ,3 ,1 ,2 .
   Longer-course regimen building: Regimens are built using the World Health Organization
   groupings. Group A drugs are levofloxacin/moxifloxacin, bedaquiline, and linezolid. Group B
   drugs are clofazimine and cycloserine/terizidone. Group C drugs are ethambutol, delamanid,
   pyrazinamide, imipenem/cilastatin or meropenem (both used in combination with
   amoxicillin/clavulanate), ethionamide/prothionamide, and p-aminosalicylic acid. Injectable
   drugs such as amikacin, streptomycin, kanamycin, and capreomycin are not recommended for
   treating pediatric patients. Ethionamide/prothionamide and p-aminosalicylic acid are only to
   be used if better options are not possible or available. Regimen building is undertaken as fol-
   lows 3 ,1 :

   • Preferred: All 3 Group A agents and at least 1 Group B agent.

   • If only 1 or 2 Group A drugs are able to be used: Use available Group A drug(s) and both
   Group B drugs.

   • Use Group C drugs if unable to complete a 4 or 5 drug regimen using only Group A and B
   drugs.
   Treatment duration is generally 18 to 24 months total, and 15 to 17 months after culture con-
   version. Durations may be extended depending on patient response.

   TB meningitis: Take into consideration the cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) penetration of available
   drugs. Levofloxacin, moxifloxacin, linezolid, cycloserine, pyrazinamide, and
   ethionamide/prothionamide have good CSF penetration.

   Black Box Warning

 Sandimmune®
   cycloSPORINE should be administered with adrenal corticosteroids but not with other im-
   munosuppressive agents. Increased susceptibility to infection and the possible development
   of lymphoma may result from immunosuppression. Sandimmune® is not bioequivalent to
   Neoral® and Gengraf® and cannot be used interchangeably without physician supervision.
   Monitor cycloSPORINE blood levels to avoid toxicity due to high levels and possible organ re-
   jection due to low levels as a result of the erratic absorption of cycloSPORINE during chronic
   administration of Sandimmune® Neoral® and Gengraf®
   cycloSPORINE, a systemic immunosuppressant, may increase the susceptibility to infection and
   development of neoplasia. Hypertension and nephrotoxicity can occur at recommended
   dosages, and the risk increases with increasing dose and duration of cycloSPORINE therapy.
   Monitor blood levels and renal function to avoid toxicity. Neoral® and Gengraf® are not bioe-
   quivalent with Sandimmune® and cannot be used interchangeably without physician supervi-
   sion. Psoriasis patients previously treated with PUVA and to a lesser extent, methotrexate or
   other immunosuppressive agents, UVB, coal tar, or radiation therapy, are at an increased risk
   of developing skin malignancies when taking cycloSPORINE 1 ,4 .

   Monitoring
   Monitor renal function (BUN and creatinine) 35 , 3 and hepatic function tests (serum bilirubin
   and liver enzymes) frequently during therapy Serum lipids, magnesium, and potassium
   should also be monitored Observe patients for signs and symptoms of anaphylaxis (eg, facial and upper thorax flushing,
   non-cardiogenic pulmonary edema, dyspnea, wheezing, blood pressure changes, and tachy-
   cardia) for at least 30 minutes after starting an IV infusion and frequently thereafter Monitor for signs or symptoms of opportunistic infection (eg, activation of latent viral infection
   including BK virus-associated neuropathy which may lead to renal allograft loss) Therapeutic Drug Monitoring
   Close monitoring of blood levels is recommended when drugs or dietary supplements that in-
   hibit or induce the CYP3A4 isoenzyme, modify efflux of the P-glycoprotein transporter, or both,
   are either added to or discontinued from cycloSPORINE therapy 1 ,3 ,4 .

   Atopic Dermatitis

 Obtain whole-blood cyclosporine trough concentrations, when clinical response is inadequate
   or concomitant use of potentially interacting drugs Transplantation

   consistent and are not interchangeable. HPLC is the preferred method but the monoclonal an-

drugs.uses_raw:
• Dabigatran etexilate mesylate is indicated for reduction in risk of recurrent VTE in previously
   treated pediatric patients. Oral pellets are indicated in patients 3 months to less than 12 years,
   and oral capsules are indicated in patients 8 to less than 18 years 1 , • Dabigatran etexilate mesylate is indicated for treatment of VTE in pediatric patients who have
   been treated with a parenteral anticoagulant for at least 5 days. Oral pellets are indicated in
   patients 3 months to less than 12 years, and oral capsules are indicated in patients 8 to less
   than 18 years 1 ,2 .

   Administration
   Capsules

   • Dispense in the manufacturer's original bottle • Open one bottle of medication or remove one capsule at a time from the blister package.
   Once the bottle has been opened, use within 4 months for maximum potency. Immediately
   close bottle tightly after use to avoid exposure to moisture 9/17
 • Administer twice daily, 1 dose in the morning and 1 dose in the evening, at approximately the
   same time every day. The dosing interval should be as close to 12 hours as possible • Take capsule with a full glass of water, with or without food • Capsules should be swallowed whole. Do not break, chew, or empty contents of the capsule
   as this may result in increased drug exposure Pellets

   • Do not administer using a syringe and do not administer via feeding tube • Do not administer with milk, milk products, or soft foods that contain milk products • The prepared dose should be given before meals to ensure the patient receives the full dose • Administer twice daily, 1 dose in the morning and 1 dose in the evening, at approximately the
   same time every day. The dosing interval should be as close to 12 hours as possible • Oral pellets may be mixed with 2 teaspoons of the following soft foods at room temperature:
   Mashed carrots, apple sauce, mashed banana • Oral pellets may be spooned directly into the patient's mouth and swallowed with apple juice
   or added to approximately 1 to 2 ounces of apple juice for drinking • Administer immediately or within 30 minutes after mixing. Discard and prepare a new dose if
   not administered within 30 minutes after initial preparation 2

drugs.contraindications_raw:
Common: Bleeding (22%), dyspepsia (9%), vomiting (8%), upper abdominal pain (5%), nausea
   (5%), diarrhea (5%) 1 ,2

   Black Box Warning
   Premature Discontinuation Increases The Risk Of Thrombotic Events 1 , 2
    ●   Premature discontinuation of any oral anticoagulant, including dabigatran etexilate, in-
        creases the risk of thrombotic events. If anticoagulation with dabigatran etexilate is discon-

 tinued for a reason other than pathological bleeding or completion of a course of therapy,
        consider coverage with another anticoagulant.

   Spinal/Epidural Hematoma 1 ,2
    ●   Epidural or spinal hematomas may occur in patients treated with dabigatran etexilate who
        are receiving neuraxial anesthesia or undergoing spinal puncture. These hematomas may
        result in long-term or permanent paralysis. Consider these risks when scheduling patients
        for spinal procedures. Factors that can increase the risk of developing epidural or spinal
        hematomas in these patients include: use of indwelling epidural catheters; concomitant use
        of other drugs that affect hemostasis, such as NSAIDs, platelet inhibitors, other anticoagu-
        lants; a history of traumatic or repeated epidural or spinal punctures; a history of spinal de-
        formity or spinal surgery; optimal timing between administration of dabigatran etexilate
        and neuraxial procedures is not known. Monitor patients frequently for signs and symp-
        toms of neurological impairment. If neurological compromise is noted, urgent treatment is
        necessary. Consider the risks and benefits before neuraxial intervention in patients antico-
        agulated or to be anticoagulated.

   Monitoring
   Therapeutic Laboratory Monitoring
   • Routine monitoring is not required. Coagulation test monitoring may be performed to ensure
   efficacy in those with a history of nonadherence, drug interactions, assess bleeding potential
   (renal failure, overdose), and to assist in drug-selection decisions Therapeutic Physical Monitoring
   • All patients on indefinite antithrombotic therapy for secondary prevention of recurrent VTE
   should be reevaluated at least annually for changes in clinical indication 7

   Toxic Laboratory Monitoring
   • Assess renal function prior to initiation of therapy and periodically during treatment as clini-
   cally indicated, such as situations where renal function may decline 1 ,2 . Frequency of monitor-
   ing depends on individual patient factors, including baseline renal function, concomitant drug
   therapy, comorbidities, and age, but it is recommended to monitor renal function at least ev-
   ery 6 months and every 3 to 6 months in patients with renal impairment (CrCl less than 60
   mL/min) or during an acute illness that may worsen renal function (infections, acute heart fail-
   ure). In the frail, increased monitoring is recommended • Check serum creatinine several days prior to elective surgery 12/17
 • Evaluate liver function at baseline and periodically monitor tests for any significant change in
   function. In general, healthy patients may be monitored yearly, however more frequent moni-
   toring may be required in patients at risk of hepatic dysfunction • Bleeding risk in high-risk patients may be evaluated at every followup with the HAS-BLED risk
   score (hypertension, abnormal renal and liver function, stroke, bleeding, labile INRs, and drugs
   or alcohol) • Evaluate baseline CBC during initiation and at regular intervals (at least yearly) to assess any
   trends in hemoglobin/hematocrit. Evaluate more frequently if needed, especially in patients
   with active bleeding symptoms • Plasma concentrations of dabigatran can be measured using liquid chromatography-tandem
   mass spectrometry. Dabigatran 150 mg twice daily is expected to have a median steady state
   peak and trough concentrations of 184 and 90 nanograms(ng)/mL, respectively. In the PETRO
   trial, patients receiving dabigatran 150 mg twice daily had a peak dabigatran concentration of
   64 to 443 ng/mL and trough of 31 to 225 ng/ml (range 5th to 95th percentile) Coagulation Assays
   • In general, assessment of the extent of anticoagulation is not necessary; however, if needed,
   the ecarin clotting time (ECT) or aPTT should be utilized (INR does not accurately measure the
   effects of dabigatran) 1 ,2 .

   • Routine anticoagulant monitoring is not required, however there are situations where assess-
   ment of the anticoagulant effect using coagulation testing is useful and includes emergency
   situations (trauma), urgent surgery, urgent invasive procedures, major bleeding, overdose/ at-
   tempted suicide, acute thrombosis, renal failure, liver failure, adherence verification, and po-
   tential drug-drug interactions • Proper timing of the blood draw for the coagulation test is necessary to effectively evaluate
   the maximum effect, which is at the maximum plasma concentration (peak 2 hours after dabi-
   gatran dose) • Activated partial thromboplastin time (aPTT), prothrombin time (PT), and thrombin time (TT)
   should be used only as qualitative tests to confirm if there is an anticoagulant effect. An analy-
   sis showed an aPTT range of 46 to 54 seconds corresponding to a therapeutic dabigatran con-
   centration of 90 to 180 nanograms/mL. However dabigatran affects aPTT with insensitivity at
   supra-therapeutic concentrations and therefore may underestimate high concentrations.
   When the more sensitive assays Ecarin clotting time (ECT) and dilute thrombin time (dTT) are
   unavailable, the aPTT may provide qualitative assessment of dabigatran. Sensitivity of different
   assays vary, checking the sensitivity of aPTT to dabigatran at each institution is recommended.
   A normal aPTT does not exclude clinically relevant dabigatran activity 13/17
 • Ecarin clotting time (ECT), diluted thrombin time (dTT), and anti-FXa concentrations are pre-
   ferred methods for use as quantitative tests to measure anticoagulant intensity. ECT median
   trough 63 seconds (10th to 90th percentile range, 44 to 103 seconds) in patients receiving
   dabigatran 150 mg twice a day. A normal dTT, and an ECT near baseline indicates no clinically
   relevant anticoagulation from dabigatran • TT is highly sensitive and may be oversensitive. It is not suited for quantitative assessment in
   the doses expected with clinical use. Very sensitive to the presence of dabigatran; a normal TT
   excludes even low dabigatran concentrations Toxic Physical Monitoring
   • Frequently monitor patients receiving epidural or spinal anesthesia or lumbar puncture for
   signs or symptoms of neurological impairment (ie, midline back pain, sensor or motor deficits)
   1,2
         .

   • Immediately evaluate any signs or symptoms of blood loss 1 ,2 .
   • Bleeding risk in high-risk patients may be evaluated at every followup with the HAS-BLED risk
   score (hypertension, abnormal renal and liver function, stroke, bleeding, labile INRs, elderly,
   and drugs or alcohol) • All patients on indefinite antithrombotic therapy for secondary prevention of recurrent VTE
   should be reevaluated at least annually for changes in bleeding risk factors and assessed for
   new bleeding complications

drugs.uses_raw:
Dalteparin is indicated for the treatment of symptomatic venous thromboembolism (VTE) to
   reduce the recurrence of VTE in pediatric patients 1 month or older Administration
   •Administer only by subcutaneous (subQ) route; do not administer by intramuscular injection •Whenever possible, administer benzyl alcohol-free formulations (prefilled syringes) to pedi-
   atric patients •Should not be mixed with other injections or infusions unless specific compatibility data are
   available that support such mixing •Dalteparin should be administered by deep subQ injection to patients who are sitting or lying
   down. •Injection site may be in a U-shaped area around the navel, the upper outer side of the thigh,
   or the upper outer quadrangle of the buttock; the injection site should be varied daily. The en-
   tire length of the needle should be inserted at a 45- to 90-degree angle. When the area around
   the navel or the thigh is used, using the thumb and forefinger, lift up a fold of skin while giving
   the injection •To ensure delivery of the full content of fixed-dose syringes, do not expel the air bubble from
   the prefilled syringe before injection. The entire dose should be injected. The needle guard will
   not be activated unless the entire dose has been given •For graduated syringes, prepare the syringe for injection by expelling the air bubble and then
   continuing to push the plunger to the desired dose or volume. The remaining volume should
   then be injected. The needle guard will not be activated unless the entire remaining dose is
   given

   tients (n=50) Serious: Major bleeding (intestinal hematoma) occurred in one pediatric patient (2%) Black Box Warning
   Warning: Spinal/Epidural Hematomas

   •Epidural or spinal hematomas may occur in patients who are anticoagulated with low molecu-
   lar weight heparins (LMWH) or heparinoids and are receiving neuraxial anesthesia or undergo-
   ing spinal puncture. These hematomas may result in long-term or permanent paralysis.

 Consider these risks when scheduling patients for spinal procedures. Factors that increase the
   risk of developing epidural or spinal hematomas in these patients include:

   Use of indwelling epidural catheters

   Concomitant use of other drugs that affect hemostasis, such as non-steroidal anti-inflamma-
   tory drugs (NSAIDs), platelet inhibitors, other anticoagulants.

   A history of traumatic or repeated epidural or spinal procedures

   A history of spinal deformity or spinal surgery

   Optimal timing between the administration of dalteparin sodium and neuraxial procedures is
   not known

   •Monitor patients frequently for signs and symptoms of neurological impairment. If neurologi-
   cal compromise is noted, urgent treatment is necessary.
   •Consider the benefits and risks before neuraxial intervention in patients anticoagulated or to
   be anticoagulated for thromboprophylaxis 1

   transient, occurring early in treatment, and can often be minimized by starting low and slowly

   Common: Loss of grip strength and weakness in the legs, drowsiness, and dizziness may occur
   in conscious patients. Other common adverse effects are nausea, thrombophlebitis, tissue
   necrosis secondary to extravasation, urticaria and erythema, and injection site reactions Cardiovascular: Thrombophlebitis has been reported 1 ,6 .
   Respiratory: Pulmonary edema has been rarely reported; both Dantrium® and Revonto®
   contain mannitol, which may have contributed to the edema 1 ,6 .

   Black Box Warning
   Oral

   Dantrolene sodium has a potential for hepatotoxicity, and should not be used in conditions
   other than those recommended. Symptomatic hepatitis (fatal and non-fatal) has been re-
   ported at various dose levels of the drug. The incidence reported in patients taking up to 400
   mg/day is much lower than in those taking doses of 800 mg or more per day. Even sporadic
   short courses of these higher dose levels within a treatment regimen markedly increased the
   risk of serious hepatic injury. Liver dysfunction as evidenced by blood chemical abnormalities
   alone (liver enzyme elevations) has been observed in patients exposed to dantrolene sodium
   for varying periods of time. Overt hepatitis has occurred at varying intervals after initiation of
   therapy, but has been most frequently observed between the third and twelfth month of ther-

 apy. The risk of hepatic injury appears to be greater in females, in patients over 35 years of
   age, and in patients taking other medication(s) in addition to dantrolene sodium.

   Spontaneous reports suggest a higher proportion of hepatic events with fatal outcome in el-
   derly patients receiving dantrolene sodium. However, the majority of these cases were compli-
   cated with confounding factors such as intercurrent illnesses and/or concomitant potentially
   hepatotoxic medications. Dantrolene sodium should be used only in conjunction with appro-
   priate monitoring of hepatic function including frequent determination of SGOT and SGPT. If
   no observable benefit is derived from the administration of dantrolene sodium after a total of
   45 days, therapy should be discontinued. The lowest possible effective dose for the individual
   patient should be prescribed 2

   infection (5.5-6.1%), diarrhea (4.2-5.9), headache (3.3-5.4%), and nausea/vomiting (2.6-3.9%) 1
   In separate trials evaluating dapagliflozin or immediate-release metFORMIN in pediatric pa-
   tients with type 2 diabetes, the adverse event profiles were similar to that observed in adult tri-
   als Black Box Warning
   Black Box Warning

   Postmarketing cases of metFORMIN-associated lactic acidosis have resulted in death, hy-
   pothermia, hypotension, and resistant bradyarrhythmias. The onset of metFORMIN-associated
   lactic acidosis is often subtle, accompanied only by nonspecific symptoms such as malaise,
   myalgias, respiratory distress, somnolence, and abdominal pain. metFORMIN-associated lactic

 acidosis was characterized by elevated blood lactate levels (greater than 5 mmol/Liter), anion
   gap acidosis (without evidence of ketonuria or ketonemia), an increased lactate/pyruvate ratio;
   and metFORMIN plasma levels generally greater than 5 mcg/mL.

   Risk factors for metFORMIN-associated lactic acidosis include renal impairment, concomitant
   use of certain drugs (eg, carbonic anhydrase inhibitors such as topiramate), having a radiologi-
   cal study with contrast, surgery and other procedures, hypoxic states (eg, acute congestive
   heart failure), excessive alcohol intake, and hepatic impairment.

   Steps to reduce the risk of and manage metFORMIN-associated lactic acidosis in these high
   risk groups are provided in the full prescribing information.
   If metFORMIN-associated lactic acidosis is suspected, immediately discontinue
   dapagliflozin/metFORMIN hydrochloride and institute general supportive measures in a hospi-
   tal setting. Prompt hemodialysis is recommended Monitoring
   Therapeutic Laboratory Monitoring
   Monitor HbA1c at least twice yearly in patients who are well-controlled, every 3 months if not
   meeting treatment goals or when there is a change of therapy, or more frequently as clinically
   warranted Perform blood glucose monitoring as needed to assist in meeting goals of therapy Toxic Laboratory Monitoring

   Assess renal function, including estimated GFR (eGFR), prior to initiation of treatment and at
   least annually thereafter. More frequent monitoring is recommended in patients with in-
   creased risk of renal impairment (eg, elderly) Reassess eGFR 48 hours after an iodinated contrast imaging procedure if therapy was discon-
   tinued (ie, in patients with a history of liver disease, alcoholism, or heart failure; or in patients
   who received intra-arterial iodinated contrast) Assess for ketoacidosis in patients who present with signs and symptoms consistent with se-
   vere metabolic acidosis Monitor hematologic parameters annually Monitor for signs of lactic acidosis Monitor vitamin B(12) levels every 2 to 3 years in patients predisposed to low vitamin B(12) lev-
   els, including those with inadequate vitamin B(12) or calcium intake or absorption 5/10
 Monitor for signs and symptoms of acute kidney injury Toxic Physical Monitoring

   Assess volume status prior to initiating therapy in patients who are predisposed to volume de-
   pletion (eg, patients with renal impairment [estimated GFR less than 60 mL/min/1.73 m(2)],
   concomitant loop diuretics, elderly patients) Monitor for hypotension during treatment Monitor for genital mycotic infections Assess for urinary tract infections in symptomatic patients Assess for necrotizing fasciitis

   •Add small amount of SyrSpend SF PH4 in the mortar and mix to form a smooth paste.

   •Add and mix geometric proportions of the vehicle.
   • Label the container with "Shake well before using."

 • Stable for 90 days at room temperature (24 degrees C) or under refrigeration (4 degrees C) in

   2 mg/mL Suspension using Ora-Plus and Ora-Sweet (200 mL) 8
   •Crush sixteen 25-mg dapsone tablets to a fine powder.

   •Then, add sufficient quantity to final volume of 200 mL while mixing.

   *An alternative to Ora-Plus/Ora-Sweet is citric acid (1 g dissolved in 50 mL of distilled water),

  Administer daptomycin 50 mg/mL by IV, diluted in a 50-mL bag of NS and infuse over 30 minutes in patients 7 to 17 years of age or diluted
  in a 25-mL bag of NS and infused over 60 minutes in patients 1 to 6 years of age 9 ,2 ,10 .

  Do not use ReadyMED® elastomeric infusion pumps (Cardinal Health, Inc.) to store/deliver DAPTOmycin doses; mercaptobenzothiazole
  (MBT) has been detected in drug samples tested from these pumps 5 ,11,10 .

Pharmacology
  Mechanism of action: DAPTOmycin, a cyclic lipopeptide, has rapid, concentration-dependent, bactericidal activity against multidrug-resis-
  tance Gram-positive organisms. It inhibits DNA, RNA, and protein synthesis and causes cell death by binding to bacterial membranes and
  causing a rapid depolarization of membrane potential Protein binding of DAPTOmycin is 90% to 93%, mainly to albumin. Excretion is primarily by the kidneys (approximately 78% and 7% of the
  administered dose

drugs.uses_raw:
Anemia associated with chronic kidney disease (CKD): Darbepoetin alfa was noninferior to
   epoetin alfa in a 28-week clinical study of 124 children 1 year or older with CKD, receiving or

 not receiving dialysis, randomized to continue epoetin alfa (EPO) or to convert to darbepoetin
   alfa. Transfusion were necessary in 14% and 6% of patients receiving EPO and darbepoetin, re-
   spectively Target hemoglobin levels of 10 to 13 g/dL were achieved with darbepoetin in 2
   non-randomized studies (n=65) of pediatric patients (1 to 18 years of age), EPO naive or EPO-
   experienced, with anemia due to CKD, on dialysis and not on dialysis 3 ,4 . Darbepoetin alfa has
   been used in infants younger than 1 year, not on dialysis and erythropoiesis stimulating agent-
   naive. In a study of 6 infants 9 to 9 months of age with CKD, 3 infants (stable outpatients)
   achieved target Hb levels of 100 to 110 g/L within 6 weeks, while the other 3 infants had unsta-
   ble medical conditions and low iron stores. Initial doses were approximately 5 mcg/kg/week,
   and the mean dose of the 3 infants attaining target Hb levels was reduced to 25
   mcg/kg/week and the dosing interval was increased to every 3 to 4 weeks during the 20-week
   study Transfusion, adjunct: Very low birth weight infants (age, 5 to 6 weeks) requiring red blood cell
   transfusion experienced less suppression of the reticulocyte count and increased hematocrit
   when darbepoetin was administered at the time of transfusion in a randomized pilot study
   (n=20; gestational age 29 to 30 weeks). At 7 to 10 days after darbepoetin 10 mcg/kg subQ, the
   reticulocyte count increased, but decreased in the control group (+ 177 x 3 mcL vs - 85 x 3
   mcL). Likewise, the hematocrit increased more in the darbepoetin group (12.4%) compared
   with the control group (8.1%) Pediatric FDA-Approved Indication:

   Darbepoetin alfa administered IV or subQ is indicated for treatment of anemia associated with
   chronic kidney disease (CKD) in pediatric patients (1 to 18 years of age) being converted from
   epoetin alfa to darbepoetin alfa, including patients receiving or not receiving dialysis Administration
   Do not dilute and do not administer with other drug solutions. IV administration is recom-
   mended for patients on hemodialysis Intraperitoneal administration in 50 mL of peritoneal dialysis fluid at the end of a nightly inter-
   mittent dialysis period was effective and safe in a study of 19 children receiving peritoneal dial-
   ysis

   Erythropoiesis-stimulating agents (ESAs) increase the risk for death, myocardial infarction,
   stroke, and other serious cardiovascular events. Patients with chronic kidney disease (CKD)
   were at a greater risk for death, serious adverse cardiovascular reactions, and stroke when ad-
   ministered ESAs to target Hb levels of greater than 11 g/dL in clinical studies. No trial has iden-
   tified a Hb target level, ESA dose, or dosing strategy that does not increase these risks. In CKD
   patients, use the lowest sufficient dose to reduce the need for RBC transfusions. In cancer pa-
   tients with certain tumor types (ie, breast, non-small cell lung, head and neck, lymphoid, cervi-
   cal), ESAs shortened overall survival and increased the risk of tumor progression or recurrence
   in clinical studies. In cancer patients, use the lowest dose needed to avoid RBC transfusions to
   reduce these risks and the risk of serious cardiovascular and thromboembolic reactions. Use
   ESAs only for treatment of anemia due to concomitant myelosuppressive chemotherapy, and
   discontinue following the completion of a chemotherapy course. Patients receiving myelosup-
   pressive therapy when the anticipated outcome is cure should not be treated with ESAs Solution Incompatibility

drugs.contraindications_raw:
Common, darunavir, greater than or equal to 5%, greater than or equal to Grade 2:
   Diarrhea, nausea, rash, headache, abdominal pain, and vomiting 2
   Safety analyses of darunavir/cobicistat in pediatric patients did not identify new safety con-
   cerns compared to the known safety profile of darunavir/cobicistat in adult patients Dyslipidemia: Dyslipidemia has been reported with the use of protease inhibitors. Assess all
   patients with dyslipidemia for additional atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease (ASCVD) risk
   factors (patients with HIV are considered at moderate risk for ASCVD). Consider ARV regimen
   changes, especially if the patient is receiving an older protease inhibitor (eg, lopinavir/ritonavir)
   and/or ritonavir-boosting. If LDL-C is 130 mg/dL or more but less than 250 mg/dL, refer to the
   NHLBI guidelines on a treatment approach with lifestyle modifications and drug therapy.
   Persistent dyslipidemia may lead to premature ASCVD Osteopenia and osteoporosis: Osteopenia and osteoporosis has been reported with
   darunavir. To help prevent osteopenia or osteoporosis from occurring, ensure that the patient

 has sufficient intake and levels of calcium and vitamin D, encourage weight-bearing exercise,
   minimize modifiable risk factors (eg, smoking, low BMI, use of steroids or medroxyproges-
   terone), and consider switching from darunavir to rilpivirine or an unboosted INSTI. If osteope-
   nia or osteoporosis does occur, consider switching the ARV regimen and supplementing with
   vitamin D3 to raise serum 25-OH-vitamin D concentrations to 30 nanograms (ng)/mL Serious skin reactions: Stevens-Johnson syndrome, toxic epidermal necrolysis, and erythema
   multiforme major has been reported with darunavir use. Discontinue all ARV drugs and other
   possible causative agents if confirmed. Provide intense supportive care, including IV hydration,
   aggressive wound care, eye care, labial adhesion preventative care, pain management, and an-
   tipyretics. Parenteral nutrition and antibiotics may also be needed. Consult with a specialist to
   determine if corticosteroids and/or IVIG is appropriate. Do not reintroduce the offending medi-
   cation Drug reaction with eosinophilia and systemic symptoms (DRESS): DRESS is a rare but seri-
   ous adverse effect that has been reported with darunavir use. Discontinue all ARV drugs and
   other possible causative agents if confirmed. Consult with a specialist to determine if corticos-
   teroids and/or IVIG is appropriate. Provide supportive care of end-organ disease and do not
   reintroduce the offending agent Monitoring

      (a) If ART is initiated soon after HIV diagnosis and entry into care, repeat baseline labora-

      (b) ART is indicated for all people with HIV and should be started as soon as possible.
      However, if ART initiation is delayed, patients should be retained in care, with periodic
      monitoring as noted above.
      (c) After 2 years of consistently suppressed HIV RNA, less frequent monitoring (eg, every 6
      months) may be considered.
      (d) After 2 years of ART with consistently suppressed viral load: CD4 count 300 to 500
      cells/mm(3), monitor every 12 months; CD4 count greater than 500 cells/mm(3), CD4 mon-
      itoring is optional.
      (e) If HIV RNA is detectable at 4 to 8 weeks, repeat every 4 to 8 weeks until viral load is
      suppressed to less than 50 copies/mL, then every 3 to 6 months.
      (f) For patients on ART, viral load is typically measured every 3 to 6 months. More frequent
      monitoring may be considered in individuals having difficulties with ART adherence or at
      risk for nonadherence. However, for adherent patients with suppressed viral load and sta-
      ble immunological status for more than 1 year, monitoring can be extended to 6-month
      intervals.

      ation of ART is optional if drug-resistance testing was performed at entry into care. For vi-
      rologically suppressed patients who are switching therapy for toxicity or convenience, viral
      amplification will not be possible and therefore resistance testing should not be per-
      formed. Results from prior resistance testing can be used to help in the construction of a

 new regimen.
      (h) If infected with hepatitis B virus, tenofovir disoproxil fumarate or tenofovir alafe-
      namide plus either emtricitabine or lamivudine should be used as part of the ART regimen

      viral load is negative. Also, consult Guidelines for Opportunistic Infections.

      with HIV who have unprotected sex with men, and persons with percutaneous/parenteral
      exposure to blood in unregulated settings are at risk of HCV infection.

      cose (preferably fasting). Monitor serum phosphorus concentrations in patients with
      chronic kidney disease who are on tenofovir-containing regimens. Renal function determi-
      nation should include creatinine monitoring and estimation of the glomerular filtration
      rate.
      (n) Consult recommendations of the HIV Medicine Association of the Infectious Diseases
      Society of America for patients with renal disease. More frequent monitoring may be indi-
      cated for patients with evidence of kidney disease (eg, proteinuria or decreased glomeru-
      lar function) or increased risk of renal insufficiency (eg. patients with diabetes or hyper-
      tension).

Use the minimum effective dose to achieve a trend of decreasing ferritin 1 ,2 .
   Estimated glomerular filtration rate should be greater than 60 mL/min/1.73 m2 before initiating

   EXJADE®
   Transfusional iron overload
   2 years or older: 20 mg/kg/day orally administered once daily, round to the nearest whole
   tablet. Adjust dose in increments of 5 or 10 mg/kg y based on clinical response and therapeu-
   tic goals every 3 to 6 months; maximum 40 mg/kg/day in patients not adequately controlled
   (for example, serum ferritin concentrations consistently greater than 2500 mcg/L and no evi-
   dence of declining) Non-transfusion dependent thalassemia syndromes

   10 years or older: 10 mg/kg/day orally administered once daily, round to the nearest whole
   tablet. If the baseline liver iron concentration (LIC) is greater than 15 mg Fe/g dry weight (dw),
   consider increasing the dose to 20 mg/kg/day after 4 weeks; if after 6 months of therapy, if the
   LIC remains greater than 7 mg Fe/g dw, increase the dose of deferasirox to a maximum of 20
   mg/kg/day; otherwise continue at no more than 10 mg/kg/day if the LIC is 3 to 7 mg Fe/g dw JADENU™
   Transfusional iron overload
   2 years or older: 14 mg/kg/day orally administered once daily, rounded to the nearest whole
   tablet or whole sachet. Adjust dose in increments of 5 or 7 mg/kg based on clinical response
   and therapeutic goals every 3 to 6 months; maximum 28 mg/kg/day in patients not ade-
   quately controlled (for example, serum ferritin concentrations consistently greater than 2500
   mcg/L and no evidence of declining) Non-transfusion dependent thalassemia syndromes

 10 years or older: 7 mg/kg/day orally administered once daily, rounded to the nearest whole
   tablet or whole sachet. If the baseline liver iron concentration (LIC) is greater than 15 mg iron/g
   dry weight (dw), consider increasing the dose to 14 mg/kg/day after 4 weeks; if after 6 months
   of therapy, if the LIC remains greater than 7 mg iron/g dw, increase the dose of deferasirox to
   a maximum of 14 mg/kg/day; otherwise continue at no more than 7 mg/kg/day if the LIC is 3
   to 7 mg iron/g dw Conversion from Exjade to Jadenu
   Dose of Jadenu should be about 30% lower (round to the nearest whole tablet or nearest
   whole sachet content for granules) 2 ,1 .

   Dose adjustments

   Baseline hepatic impairment: 2 , 1
    ●   Mild (Child-Pugh A): No dose adjustment is necessary.
    ●   Moderate (Child-Pugh B): Reduce the starting dose by 50%.
    ●   Severe (Child-Pugh C): Avoid deferasirox.
   Baseline renal impairment:
   Use with caution in pediatric patients with estimated GFR 40 to 60 mL/min/1.73 m2 (in adults,
   the dose is reduced by 50%). Do not use in patients with estimated GFR less than 40
   mL/min/1.73 m2 2 ,1 .
   Increases in Serum Creatinine

   Transfusional iron overload
   Pediatric patients (2 to 17 years of age): Reduce the dose by 7 mg/kg (JADENU™) or 10
   mg/kg (EXJADE®) if serum creatinine increases to greater than 33% above the average base-
   line measurement 2 ,1 .

   Interrupt therapy for acute illnesses which can cause volume depletion, such as vomiting, diar-
   rhea, or prolonged decreased oral intake, and monitor more frequently. Resume therapy as
   appropriate, based on assessments of renal function, when oral intake and volume status are
   normal. Avoid use of other nephrotoxic drugs 2 , In the setting of decreased renal function, evaluate the risk benefit profile of continued de-
   ferasirox use. Use the minimum effective dose and monitor renal function more frequently, by
   evaluating tubular and glomerular function. Titrate dosing based on renal injury. Consider
   dose reduction or interruption and less nephrotoxic therapies until improvement of renal
   function. If signs of renal tubular or glomerular injury occur in the presence of other risk fac-

 tors such as volume depletion, reduce or interrupt deferasirox to prevent severe and irre-
   versible renal injury 2 ,1 .
   Non-transfusion dependent thalassemia syndromes
   Pediatric patients (10 to 17 years of age): Reduce the dose by 5 mg/kg (JADENU™) or 5
   mg/kg (EXJADE®) if serum creatinine increases to greater than 33% above the average base-
   line measurement 2 ,1 .

   Increase monitoring frequency for pediatric patients who have acute illnesses which can cause
   volume depletion, such as vomiting, diarrhea, or prolonged decreased oral intake. Consider
   dose interruption until oral intake and volume status are normal. Avoid use of other nephro-
   toxic drugs 2 , In the setting of decreased renal function, evaluate the risk benefit profile of continued de-
   ferasirox use. Use the minimum effective dose and monitor renal function more frequently, by
   evaluating tubular and glomerular function. Titrate dosing based on renal injury. Consider
   dose reduction or interruption and less nephrotoxic therapies until improvement of renal
   function. If signs of renal tubular or glomerular injury occur in the presence of other risk fac-
   tors such as volume depletion, reduce or interrupt deferasirox to prevent severe and irre-
   versible renal injury 2 ,1 .

   Concomitant medications: Avoid concomitant use with either UDP-glucuronosyltransferases
   (UGT) inducers or bile acid sequestrants. If concomitant treatment is required with either UGT
   inducers (such as rifampicin, phenytoin, phenobarbital, and ritonavir) or bile acid sequestrants
   (such as cholestyramine, colesevelam, colestipol), consider increasing the initial dose of de-
   ferasirox by 50% 3 ,4 .

   Low Ferritin Concentrations

   Transfusional-dependent:
   Consider dose reduction, it the serum ferritin concentrations are below 1000 mcg/L at 2 con-
   secutive visits, especially when doses are greater than 5 mg/kg/day (Jadenu) or 25
   mg/kg/day (Exjade) 2 , Interrupt deferasirox if the ferritin concentrations are consistently below 500 mcg/L 2 ,1 .
   Non-transfusion dependent: Interrupt therapy when serum ferritin is less than 300 mcg/L.
   When the liver iron concentration is less than 3 mg iron/g dry weight (dw) , interrupt treatment
   and continue to monitor LIC. Restart when the LIC increases to more than 5 mg Fe/g dw 3 ,4 .

drugs.contraindications_raw:
In clinical studies, the most frequent adverse effects were abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting,
   diarrhea, skin rashes, and increases in serum creatinine occurring in greater than 5% of pa-
   tients. Gastrointestinal symptoms, increases in serum creatinine, and skin rash were dose re-
   lated In transfusional iron overload patients (more than 5,000) treated with deferasirox during clini-
   cal trials, adverse reactions (0.1% to 1%) included gastritis, edema, sleep disorder, pigmenta-
   tion disorder, dizziness, anxiety, maculopathy, cholelithiasis, pyrexia, fatigue, pharyngolaryn-
   geal pain, early cataract, hearing loss, gastrointestinal hemorrhage, gastric ulcer (including
   multiple ulcers), duodenal ulcer, and renal tubulopathy (Fanconi’s syndrome) A prospective study of long-term deferasirox use in pediatric and adult patients (n=555) with
   transfusion dependent thalassemia suggests treatment for 5 years or greater is generally well
   tolerated. It was additionally reported that drug-related adverse events, including increased
   blood creatinine (11.2%), abdominal pain (9%), and nausea (7.4%), were generally mild to mod-
   erate, transient, and reduced in frequency over time. No adverse effect on pediatric growth or
   adolescent sexual development was observed Serum zinc levels were found to be 8 +/- 8 mcg/dL with deferasirox, which is statistically
   lower than in the control population (149 +/- 3 mcg/dL) (p less than 05) in a study aimed
   to examine the effects of oral chelators on serum and urine zinc levels in thalassemia major
   patients Renal toxicity, renal failure and proteinuria
   Postmarketing experience showed that most fatalities occurred in patients with multiple co-
   morbidities and who were in advanced stages of their hematological disorders. In clinical trials,
   patients experienced dose-dependent increases in serum creatine. Frequency was observed at
   38% and 36% in two separate studies.
   Renal tubular damage, including Fanconi’s Syndrome, has been reported most commonly in
   children and adolescents with β-thalassemia and serum ferritin levels less than 1500 mcg/L.
   Intermittent proteinuria (urine protein/creatinine ratio greater than 6 mg/mg) occurred in 6% of treated patients. In clinical trials in patients with transfusional iron overload, treat-

 ment was temporarily withheld until the urine protein/creatinine ratio fell below 6 mg/mg.
   Clinical significance of the proteinuria is undetermined Hepatic toxicity and failure
   A multicenter, open-label, randomized, active comparator control study reported that 4 pa-
   tients (1.3%) discontinued treatment because of hepatic toxicity (drug-induced hepatitis in 2
   patients and increased serum transaminases in 2 additional patients). Hepatic toxicity appears
   to be more common in patients greater than 55 years of age. Hepatic failure was more com-
   mon in patients with significant comorbidities, including liver cirrhosis and multiorgan failure Gastrointestinal hemorrhage
   GI hemorrhage, including deaths, has been reported, especially in elderly patients who had ad-
   vanced hematologic malignancies and/or low platelet counts. Nonfatal upper GI irritation, ul-
   ceration and hemorrhage have been reported in patients, including children and adolescents,
   receiving treatment Bone marrow suppression
   Neutropenia, agranulocytosis, worsening anemia, and thrombocytopenia, including fatal
   events, have been reported. The risk is increased with preexisting hematologic disorders Hypersensitivity
   Serious hypersensitivity reactions (such as anaphylaxis and angioedema) can occur, with the
   onset of the reaction usually occurring within the first month of treatment Auditory and ocular abnormalities

   Auditory disturbances (high frequency hearing loss, decreased hearing), and ocular distur-
   bances (lens opacities, cataracts, elevations in intraocular pressure, and retinal disorders) were
   reported at a frequency of less than 1% with therapy in the clinical studies Overchelation

   For patients with transfusional iron overload, overchelation of iron is possible Black Box Warning
   Renal Failure 1 ,2 ,12
    ●      Deferasirox can cause acute renal failure and death, particularly in patients with comorbidi-
           ties and those who are in the advanced stages of their hematologic disorders.

 ●   Evaluate baseline renal function prior to starting or increasing deferasirox dosing in all pa-
        tients. Deferasirox is contraindicated in adult and pediatric patients with estimated GFR less
        than 40 mL/min/1.73 m2. Measure serum creatinine in duplicate prior to initiation of ther-
        apy. Monitor renal function at least monthly. For patients with baseline renal impairment or
        increased risk of acute renal failure, monitor renal function weekly for the first month, then
        at least monthly. Reduce the starting dose in patients with pre-existing renal disease. During
        therapy, increase the frequency of monitoring and modify the dose for patients with an in-
        creased risk of renal impairment, including use of concomitant nephrotoxic drugs, and pedi-
        atric patients with volume depletion or overchelation.

   Hepatic Failure 1 ,2 ,12
    ●   Deferasirox can cause hepatic injury including hepatic failure and death
    ●   Measure serum transaminases and bilirubin in all patients prior to initiating treatment, ev-
        ery 2 weeks during the first month, and at least monthly thereafter.
    ●   Avoid use of deferasirox in patients with severe (Child-Pugh C) hepatic impairment and re-
        duce the dose in patients with moderate (Child Pugh B) hepatic impairment.

   Gastrointestinal Hemorrhage 1 ,2 ,12
    ●   Deferasirox can cause gastrointestinal (GI) hemorrhages, which may be fatal.
    ●   Monitor patients and discontinue deferasirox for suspected GI ulceration or hemorrhage

   Monitoring
   All Patients
   Monitor serum creatinine weekly during the first month after initiation or modification of ther-
   apy and at least monthly thereafter. Monitor renal function more frequently in patients with
   pre-existing renal disease or decreased renal function. Monitor renal function more frequently
   during acute illnesses which can cause volume depletion such as vomiting, diarrhea, or pro-
   longed decreased oral intake. Monitor more frequently in patients receiving 14 to 28
   mg/kg/day (Jadenu) or 20 to 40 mg/kg/day (Exjade) and when iron burden is approaching nor-
   mal 2 , .
   Measure transaminases (AST and ALT) and bilirubin in all patients before the initiation of treat-
   ment and every 2 weeks during the first month and at least monthly thereafter Monitor
   more frequently in patients receiving 14 to 28 mg/kg/day (Jadenu) or 20 to 40 mg/kg/day
   (Exjade) and when iron burden is approaching normal 2 ,1 .

   Monitor for signs and symptoms of GI ulceration and hemorrhage during therapy and
   promptly initiate additional evaluation and treatment if a serious GI adverse event is sus-

 pected Monitor blood counts in all patients monthly Perform auditory and ophthalmic testing (including slit lamp examinations and dilated fun-
   doscopy) before starting treatment and thereafter at regular intervals (every 12 months). If dis-
   turbances are noted, monitor more frequently and consider dose reduction or interruption Measure serum ferritin monthly Monitor zinc levels regularly and start zinc replacement at an early age Transfusional iron overload 2

    ●   Serum ferritin level
    ●   Baseline serum creatinine in duplicate (due to variations in measurements) and calculate

        patients)
    ●   Urinalysis and serum electrolytes to evaluate renal tubular function
    ●   Serum transaminases and bilirubin
    ●   Baseline auditory and ophthalmic examinations

   Non-transfusion dependent thalassemia syndromes 2
   Prior to starting therapy, obtain:
    ●   Liver iron concentration by liver biopsy or by an FDA-cleared or approved method for identi-
        fying patients for treatment with deferasirox therapy
    ●   Serum ferritin level on at least 2 measurements one month apart
    ●   Baseline serum creatinine in duplicate (due to variations in measurements) and calculate

    ●   Urinalysis and serum electrolytes to evaluate renal tubular function
    ●   Serum transaminases and bilirubin
    ●   Baseline auditory and ophthalmic examinations

    ●   Liver iron concentration every 6 months

   Black Box Warning
   Agranulocytosis and Neutropenia

   • Deferiprone can cause agranulocytosis that can lead to serious infections and death.
   Neutropenia may precede the development of agranulocytosis.
   • Measure the absolute neutrophil count (ANC) before starting deferiprone therapy and moni-
   tor regularly while on therapy.

   • Interrupt deferiprone therapy if neutropenia develops.

   • Interrupt deferiprone if infection develops, and monitor the ANC more frequently.
   • Advise patients taking deferiprone to report immediately any symptoms indicative of infec-
   tion 1 ,2 .

   Monitoring

 Therapeutic Laboratory Monitoring

   • Monitor the serum ferritin concentration every 2 to 3 months to assess body iron stores for
   efficacy 1 ,2 .

   Toxic Laboratory Monitoring
   • Measure the absolute neutrophil count (ANC) before starting therapy, then weekly during
   therapy 1 ,2 .

   • Monitor serum ALT levels monthly during therapy 1 , • Monitor plasma zinc concentrations during therapy 1 ,2 .

drugs.uses_raw:
Hepatic veno-occulsive disease, severe: Survival at 100 days post-HSCT was significantly im-
   proved by an estimated 23% in adult and pediatric patients with severe hepatic VOD and multi-
   organ failure who received defibrotide (n=102; 1% were 16 years or younger) compared
   with historical controls who did not receive defibrotide (n=32; 8% were 16 years or
   younger). The absolute survival rate was 2% for defibrotide and 25% for controls. Complete
   response (CR), which included resolution of parameters used to document VOD with organ
   dysfunction within a window of +/- 14 days, occurred in 5% of treated patients and in 5%

 of controls, for an estimated significant difference of 19%. Median time to CR was 5 days in
   treated patients In another prospective study (N=75; 29% were younger than 17 years of age) and an expanded
   access program (N=351; 54% were younger than 17 years of age) in adult and pediatric pa-
   tients with hepatic VOD and multi-organ dysfunction following HSCT, the survival rates at 100
   days post-transplantation were 44% and 45%, respectively. The expected survival rates in pa-
   tients who receive supportive care or interventions other than defibrotide sodium are 21% to
   31% Hepatic veno-occulsive disease (VOD); prophylaxis: Defibrotide should be used for prophy-
   laxis of VOD in pediatric patients undergoing allogeneic HSCT who have risk factors 2 :
    ●   pre-existing hepatic disease
    ●   second myeloablative transplant
    ●   allogeneic transplant for leukemia that is beyond second relapse
    ●   conditioning with busulfan-containing regimens
    ●   prior treatment with gemtuzumab ozogamicin
    ●   diagnosis of primary hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis, adrenoleukodystrophy, or
        osteopetrosis

   Defibrotide should typically be reserved for patients undergoing myeloablative chemotherapy
   but may be considered in patients with high-risk features who are undergoing reduced inten-
   sity conditioning regimens. In addition, defibrotide may be considered in patients undergoing
   autologous HSCT when using high-risk conditioning regimens. Combination therapy with ur-
   sodeoxycholic acid is an option in high-risk patients In a meta-analysis of 5 comparative clinical trials (one randomized, 4 cohorts) that included
   643 pediatric and adult patients undergoing hematopoietic stem cell transplantation (HSCT),
   the use of defibrotide significantly reduced the risk of developing hepatic veno-occlusive dis-
   ease (VOD)/sinusoidal obstruction syndrome by 53% (RR 47, 95% CI 31 to 73). In the ran-
   domized trial (356 pediatric patients), VOD occurred in 12% of the defibrotide group versus
   20% of the control group (ie, no defibrotide). Across the 4 cohort trials (287 adult and pediatric
   patients), the rates of VOD were 5% with defibrotide and 2% with historical controls who
   did not receive defibrotide. No significant difference was found in the rate of severe VOD, de-
   fined as the presence of multiorgan failure or death, in patients who received defibrotide pro-
   phylaxis (0% with defibrotide vs 3% with historical controls; 4 cohort studies, n=287). VOD
   morbidity and mortality, measured with a composite score, was significantly improved with de-
   fibrotide in the randomized trial. In total, the systematic review also included 8 case series of
   patients (n=587) receiving defibrotide prophylaxis and found an incidence of VOD of 9%.

 Across all 13 studies (N=1230), the incidence of VOD with defibrotide prophylaxis was 7%.
   Patients in 7 of the 13 studies were considered at high risk for VOD with at least one risk fac-
   tor. Types of transplants, conditioning regimens, patient characteristics, dosage of defibrotide,
   criteria to diagnose VOD, and the use of heparin varied across studies but no significant het-
   erogeneity was noted in the 5 comparative trials. In most studies, defibrotide was started with
   the first day of the conditioning regimen and continued to at least day +20 after HSCT. No in-
   crease in bleeding or other adverse events with defibrotide were noted Pediatric Approved FDA Indications

   Defibrotide is indicated for the treatment of hepatic veno-occlusive disease, also known as si-
   nusoidal obstruction syndrome, in patients with renal or pulmonary dysfunction following
   hematopoietic stem-cell transplantation Administration
   Administer diluted solution in a concentration of 4 mg/mL to 20 mg/mL as a 2-hour continuous
   infusion using an infusion set equipped with a 2 micron in-line filter Flush IV line (peripheral or central) with D5W or NS immediately before and after administra-
   tion of defibrotide sodium Do not coadminister with other drugs within the same IV line

drugs.uses_raw:
Tuberculosis, active; drug-resistant: Drug-resistant TB is treated with a combination of at
   least 4 or 5 drugs susceptible to the tuberculosis strain being treated. Shorter-course (6 to 9
   months), all oral standardized regimens are preferred when patients meet eligibility criteria
   (no extensive disease, no extrapulmonary disease except for TB lymphadenopathy, no prior
   exposure to components (exposure = more than 1 month of use). Longer course regimens are
   necessary for those not meeting eligibility criteria 6 ,7 ,4 ,2 ,5 . If delamanid is used in a regimen
   containing a fluoroquinolone, levofloxacin is suggested over moxifloxacin as there may be a
   higher risk of QT prolongation with moxifloxacin Longer-course regimen building: Regimens are built using the World Health Organization
   groupings. Group A drugs are levofloxacin/moxifloxacin, bedaquiline, and linezolid. Group B

 drugs are clofazimine and cycloserine/terizidone. Group C drugs are ethambutol, delamanid,
   pyrazinamide, imipenem/cilastatin or meropenem (both used in combination with
   amoxicillin/clavulanate), ethionamide/prothionamide, and p-aminosalicylic acid. Injectable
   drugs such as amikacin, streptomycin, kanamycin, and capreomycin are not recommended for
   treating pediatric patients. Ethionamide/prothionamide and p-aminosalicylic acid are only to
   be used if better options are not possible or available. Regimen building is undertaken as fol-
   lows 4 ,2 :
   • Preferred: All 3 Group A agents and at least 1 Group B agent.

   • If only 1 or 2 Group A drugs are able to be used: Use available Group A drug(s) and both
   Group B drugs.
   • Use Group C drugs if unable to complete a 4 or 5 drug regimen using only Group A and B
   drugs.

   Treatment duration is generally 18 to 24 months total, and 15 to 17 months after culture con-
   version. Durations may be extended depending on patient response.

   TB meningitis: Take into consideration the cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) penetration of available
   drugs. Levofloxacin, moxifloxacin, linezolid, cycloserine, pyrazinamide, and
   ethionamide/prothionamide have good CSF penetration.

   FDA Approved Pediatric Uses: Delamanid is not approved for use by the FDA. Delamanid
   may be obtained in the United States only via a single patient Investigational New Drug (SPIND)
   expanded access/compassionate use program.

   Administration
   • Administer by directly observed therapy (DOT) • Administer with food • Dispersible tablets: Disperse in 10 to 15 mL of water per each 25-mg tablet and ingest imme-
   diately; add another 10 to 15 mL of water per tablet to cup and ingest immediately to ensure
   entire dose is administered Extemporaneous oral compound

   5 mg/mL Suspension (100 mL) 8

   • Triturate 10 50-mg tablets of delamanid to a fine powder using a glass mortar and pestle.
   • Add approximately 20 mL of simple syrup to wet the powder and mix into a fine paste.

 • Add an additional 77 mL of simple syrup in geometric proportions while mixing thoroughly,
   to bring the total volume in the mortar to 100 mL.

   • Transfer to an appropriately sized amber bottle.
   • Label the container with "Shake well before using."

   • Stable for 15 days at room temperature (22 to 24°C) or at 30°C.

   Sugar-free oral compound

   5 mg/mL Suspension (100 mL) 8
   • Prepare Thick & Easy® vehicle by adding 5 grams Thick & Easy® Instant Food and
   Beverage Thickening Powder to 236 mL distilled water; mix with a spoon for 30 seconds and
   let the mixture sit for at least 5 minutes before use. Mix again just prior to use.
   • Triturate 10 50-mg tablets of delamanid to a fine powder using a glass mortar and pestle.

   • Add the following to the ground tablets in the mortar: Methylparaben 100 mg, potassium sor-
   bate 100 mg, citric acid 125 mg, and sodium saccharin 125 mg. Mix all the powders well using
   the pestle.
   • Add 50 mL of distilled water to the mortar and allow to sit for 5 minutes. After the 5 minutes
   have elapsed, mix well to form a uniform mixture.
   • Add 47 mL of prepared Thick & Easy® vehicle to bring the total volume in the mortar to 100
   mL, and mix to form a uniform suspension.

   • Transfer to an appropriately sized amber bottle.
   • Label the container with "Shake well before using."

   • Stable for 30 days at room temperature (22 to 24°C) or at 30°C.

Common: Nausea, vomiting, headache, sleep disorders/disturbances, dizziness, gastritis, de-
   creased appetite, hallucinations, nightmares 1

   QT interval prolongation: Prolongation may increase slowly over first 6 to 10 weeks of treat-
   ment, then remains stable. Associated with the delamanid metabolite DM-6705; this
   metabolite's formation and metabolism is regulated by plasma albumin and CYP3A4 In clinical trials of patients treated with an optimized background regimen plus either dela-
   manid 200 mg/day or placebo, the following results were reported 1 :

 • Mean placebo-corrected increase in QTcF from baseline: 6 to 6 msec after 1 month of de-
   lamanid, and 3 to 1 msec after 2 months • Incidence of QTcF greater than 500 msec: 6 to 1% with delamanid compared with 0% to 2% with placebo • QTcF change from baseline greater than 60 msec: 1 to 3% with delamanid compared
   with 0% to 1% with placebo • Palpitations: 6% with delamanid compared with 7% with placebo Monitoring
   Therapeutic Monitoring
   • Monitor for clinical (eg, decrease in cough and systemic symptoms, increase in weight), radio-
   logic, and bacteriologic response to treatment 5

   • Obtain sputum culture prior to initiation, then monthly during treatment. If cultures remain
   positive after 3 months, repeat susceptibility testing • Monitor body weight monthly; adjust doses accordingly 2

   Toxic Monitoring

   • Measure serum electrolytes at baseline and correct if abnormal 1

   • Obtain ECG prior to initiation, then monthly while receiving treatment. Consider more fre-
   quent monitoring if the QTc interval exceeds 450 msec in women or 470 msec in men. and in
   patients with hypoalbuminemia, known congenital QT prolongation, history of cardiac arrhyth-
   mias, clinically relevant bradycardia, or conditions predisposing arrhythmia, or electrolyte dis-
   turbances, or serum albumin concentrations less than 4 g/dL, or concomitant use of agents
   known to prolong the QTc interval 1
   •

   Therapeutic Drug Monitoring

   Consider monitoring therapeutic drug concentrations in patients with the following conditions
   5
       :
   • Gastrointestinal problems that may increase the risk of malabsorption
   • Concurrent HIV infection
   • Impaired renal function

 • Diabetes
   Some experts use therapeutic drug monitoring for all patients with resistant TB early in treat-
   ment to identify poor responses earlier

drugs.uses_raw:
Attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD)
   Guidelines: The recommended first-line treatment for children and adolescents with ADHD is
   age dependent. For children 4 to 6 years, parent training in behavioral management (PTBM)
   and/or behavioral classroom interventions is the treatment of choice. In moderate-to-severe
   cases, methylphenidate may be considered if the behavioral interventions are unsuccessful.
   For children 6 to 12 years, the combined treatment of an FDA-approved stimulant drug for
   ADHD and PTBM and/or behavioral classroom intervention (preferably both) is preferred. In
   children 12 years or older, the preferred treatment is an FDA-approved stimulant drug A meta-analysis that included 6 trials with 216 participants 6 to 17 years old demonstrated that
   short-term (2 to 6 weeks) treatment with desipramine improves the core symptoms of ADHD
   as assessed by parents, teachers, and clinicians, but that its effects on the cardiovascular sys-
   tem are a concern. All studies evaluated the severity of ADHD symptoms but trial investigators
   used different scales and raters, making it difficult to combine results. In 3 trials, the Clinical

 Global Impression (CGI) response rates for tricyclic antidepressants (TCA; desipramine and
   nortriptyline) were more efficacious than placebo (OR 5, 95% CI 29 to 39); the calcu-
   lated number needed to treat for benefit was 2, which was consistent for both TCAs.
   Desipramine was more efficacious than placebo for reducing ADHD symptoms as assessed by
   clinicians (OR 41, 95% CI 41 to 18), by parents (standard mean difference (SMD) -1.42,
   95% CI -1.99 to -0.85), and by teachers (SMD -0.97, 95% CI -1.66 to -0.28). There was only 1
   study comparing desipramine with clonidine in which desipramine was more efficacious in re-
   ducing ADHD symptoms (SMD -0.9, 95% CI -1.4 to -0.4). No serious adverse effects occurred
   during the studies, however desipramine had significantly higher rates of appetite suppres-
   sion, diastolic blood pressure increases, and pulse rate increases. The authors note that other
   first-line pharmacological interventions for ADHD (methylphenidate, amphetamine derivatives,
   atomoxetine, alpha agonists) have been studied comprehensively for this indication and
   should be considered before TCAs due to their safer side-effect profile Comorbid tic diagnosis: Patients with a diagnosis of both ADHD and tics receiving de-
   sipramine are probably more likely than those receiving placebo to have a reduced tic severity
   but are also more likely to have an increase in diastolic blood pressure and increased heart
   rate. Desipramine is now rarely used in children after several case reports of sudden death as-
   sociated with the use of this medication Major depressive disorder: The American Academy of Pediatrics recommends that patients
   10 to 21 years old with major depressive disorder in the primary care setting should receive
   psychotherapy (eg, cognitive behavioral therapy or interpersonal psychotherapy for adoles-
   cents) and/or treatment with an SSRI. Tricyclic antidepressants were not included in the most
   recent guidelines because of a lack of efficacy demonstrated in clinical trials for this class of
   antidepressants FDA Approved Indications

   lished. Therefore, desipramine is not recommended for use in children. Anyone considering
   the use of desipramine in children or adolescents must balance the risks with the clinical need Desipramine is indicated for the treatment of depression

   Suicidality and Antidepressant Drugs

   Antidepressants increased the risk compared to placebo of suicidal thinking and behavior (sui-
   cidality) in children, adolescents, and young adults in short-term studies of major depressive
   disorder (MDD) and other psychiatric disorders. Anyone considering the use of desipramine or
   any other antidepressant in a child, adolescent, or young adult must balance this risk with clini-
   cal need. Short-term studies did not show an increase in the risk of suicidality with antidepres-
   sants compared to placebo in adults beyond age 24; there was a reduction in risk with antide-
   pressants compared to placebo in adults aged 65 or older. Depression and certain other psy-
   chiatric disorders are themselves associated with increased in the risk of suicide. Patients of all
   ages who are started on antidepressant therapy should be monitored appropriately and ob-
   served closely for clinical worsening, suicidality, or unusual changes in behavior. Families and
   caregivers should be advised of the need for close observation and communication with the
   prescriber. Desipramine is not approved for use in pediatric patients Monitoring

 Toxic Monitoring
   •Monitor sodium level at baseline and after 3 to 4 weeks, especially during the first 3 weeks fol-
   lowing initiation Depression
   •Monitor patients receiving antidepressants for worsening of depression, suicidality, or un-
   usual changes in behavior, especially at the initiation of therapy or when the dose increases or
   decreases. Such monitoring should include at least weekly face-to-face contact with patients or
   their family members or caregivers during the initial 4 weeks of treatment, then visits every
   other week for the next 4 weeks, then at 12 weeks, and then as clinically indicated beyond 12
   weeks. Families and caregivers should be advised of the need for close observation (i.e., daily
   observation) of patients and communication with the prescriber. More frequent monitoring
   may be required in more severely depressed or suicidal patients 3 ,9 ,10 .

   •Patients who experience symptoms of anxiety, agitation, panic attacks, insomnia, irritability,
   hostility, impulsivity, akathisia, hypomania, or mania may be at an increased risk for worsening
   depression or suicidality. If these symptoms are observed, therapy should be re-evaluated and
   it may be necessary to discontinue medications when symptoms are severe, sudden in onset,
   or were not part of the patient's initial symptoms •Monitor blood pressure at baseline, with significant dose increases, and every 3 to 6 months
   once stabilized •Evaluate ECG for QT prolongation at baseline, at steady state, after initial dose titration, with
   dose changes, and especially with higher doses and in children •Monitoring of the metabolic profile to detect early weight gain may be advisable at 3, 6, and

   •Obtain a complete family and patient history for conditions associated with sudden cardiac
   death (SCD), and determine current use of any other prescription or over-the-counter medica-
   tions 11,12 .

 •Conduct a complete physical evaluation of the patient for hypertension, cardiac murmurs,

   •Continue to assess the patient for cardiac symptoms and any changes in family history at fol-

   Injection

   4 years or older: Initial, 10 mcg/dose intranasally in 1 nostril daily; may titrate up to 30 mcg
   once daily or 30 mcg in 2 divided doses (20 mcg in the morning and 10 mcg at nighttime).
   Adjust dose as needed to achieve adequate duration of sleep and adequate (not excessive)
   water turnover; adjust each divided dose separately to account for adequate diurnal rhythm of
   water turnover. Do not use nasal spray for doses less than 10 mcg or doses that are not multi-
   ples of 10 mcg. Increased dosage may be necessary after prolonged treatment as response
   may decrease over time Oral solution
   Younger than 3 months: Initial, 1 to 5 mcg/day orally of a 10 mcg/mL solution (1:10 dilution
   of desmopressin 100 mcg/mL nasal solution with NS) 3 divided into 2 doses given every 12
   hours. Adjust based on clinical response; monitor to maintain adequate but not excessive hy-
   dration (include weight, urine volume, specific gravity, and serum sodium measurements) 4 ;
   stabilizing doses were 2 to 5 mcg twice daily in a case series that included 4 neonates 6 days or
   older Oral tablets
   4 years or older: Initial, 05 mg/dose (one-half of the 1 mg tablet) orally twice daily. Adjust
   dose up to 2 mg/day (given in 2 or 3 divided doses) to achieve therapeutic goals; optimal
   dosing range in studies was 1 to 8 mg/day. Adjust each divided dose separately to account
   for adequate diurnal rhythm of water turnover Switching between formulations
