drugs.uses_raw:
Injection solution: Treatment of central diabetes insipidus in children 12 years or older, treat-
   ment of hemophilia A with Factor VIII coagulant activity levels greater than 5% in children 3
   months or older, and treatment of mild to moderate classic von Willebrand's disease (Type I)
   with Factor VIII levels greater than 5% in children 3 months or older. Desmopressin is not indi-
   cated for the treatment of hemophilia A with Factor VIII coagulant activity of 5% or less, or for
   the treatment of hemophilia B, or in patients who have Factor VIII antibodies. It is also not indi-
   cated for the treatment of severe classic von Willebrand's disease (Type 1), and is ineffective
   for the treatment of nephrogenic diabetes insipidus Desmopressin nasal spray: Treatment of central diabetes insipidus in children 4 years or
   older 6/17
 Desmopressin is not indicated for nephrogenic diabetes insipidus, primary nocturnal enuresis,
   for use in patients with conditions that compromise the intranasal route of administration
   (e.g., severe nasal congestion and blockage, nasal mucosa atrophy, severe atrophic rhinitis, re-
   cent nasal surgery such as transsphenoidal hypophysectomy), for use in patients with an im-
   paired level of consciousness, or for use in patients requiring doses less than 10 mcg or doses
   that are not multiples of 10 mcg Stimate® nasal spray: Treatment of hemophilia A with Factor VIII coagulant activity levels
   greater than 5% in children 11 months or older and treatment of mild to moderate classic von
   Willebrand's disease (Type I) with Factor VIII levels greater than 5% in children 11 months or
   older. Stimate® Nasal Spray is not indicated for the treatment of hemophilia A with Factor VIII
   coagulant activity of 5% or less, or for the treatment of hemophilia B, or in patients who have
   Factor VIII antibodies. It is also not indicated for the treatment of severe classic von
   Willebrand's disease (Type 1) Oral tablet: Treatment of central diabetes insipidus in children 4 years or older and treatment
   of primary nocturnal enuresis in children 6 years or older. Desmopressin is ineffective for the
   treatment of nephrogenic diabetes insipidus Administration
   All formulations require careful fluid intake restriction to prevent possible water intoxication
   and hyponatremia 7 ,11,12,12,13 .

   Injection

   • Administer IV or SUBQ 1

   • Central diabetes insipidus: Administer undiluted 1
   • Hemophilia A or von Willebrand disease: For patients weighing 10 kg or less, dilute in 10 mL
   NS. For patients weighing more than 10 kg, dilute in 50 mL NS. Infuse slowly over 15 to 30 min-
   utes. If used preoperatively, administer 30 minutes prior to scheduled procedure • Limit fluid intake to a minimum from 1 hour before administration until the next morning (at
   least 8 hours after administration) 1

   Nasal spray

   • Prior to first use, prime the pump by pressing down on the pump 5 times; if not used for one
   week or longer, reprime by pressing down on the pump once 2

 • Discard after 50 sprays as any amount delivered after that may be substantially less than the
   appropriate dose 2
   • Stimate® nasal spray: Prime the nasal spray pump prior to first use by pressing down 4
   times; the bottle will then deliver 150 mcg/spray of drug. Discard 6 months after opening or af-
   ter the administration of 25 sprays; amount delivered thereafter may be less than 150 mcg. If
   used preoperatively, administer 2 hours prior to scheduled procedure. Limit fluid intake to a
   minimum from 1 hour before administration to at least 24 hours after administration Oral tablet:

   • May be taken without regard to food • Primary nocturnal enuresis: Limit fluid intake to a minimum from 1 hour before administra-
   tion until the next morning (at least 8 hours after administration) 5

   Preparation

   Extemporaneous intranasal compound
   Desmopressin 033 mg/mL nasal solution: Use a sterile syringe and needle to draw up 5
   mL of sodium chloride 9% solution and add to 5 mL of desmopressin solution 1 mg/mL.
   Filter the solution into a sterile container through a 2 micrometer filter Extemporaneous oral compound
   Desmopressin 10 mcg/mL oral solution: Dilute nasal desmopressin in the original vial. Store
   in the refrigerator (2 to 8°C) and protect from light for a maximum of 28 days Precautions
   must be taken to avoid contamination because the preservative in the original product is di-
   luted in conjunction with the desmopressin

drugs.contraindications_raw:
Postmarketing reports: Hypertension, hypotension, flushing, headache, nausea, abdominal
   cramps 2 ,5 ,1 . Nasal congestion, rhinitis, nosebleed, and cough have been reported with the
   nasal spray Long-term studies of patients with central diabetes insipidus reported transient increases in
   AST up to 5 x ULN, which returned to the normal range despite continuation of therapy Black Box Warning
   Warning: Hyponatremia
   Desmopressin acetate can cause hyponatremia. Severe hyponatremia can be life-threatening,
   leading to seizures, coma, respiratory arrest, or death.

   Desmopressin acetate is contraindicated in patients at increased risk of severe hyponatremia,
   such as patients with excessive fluid intake, illnesses that can cause fluid or electrolyte imbal-
   ances, and in those using loop diuretics or systemic or inhaled glucocorticoids.

   Ensure the serum sodium concentration is normal before starting or resuming desmopressin
   acetate. Measure serum sodium within 7 days and approximately 1 month after initiating ther-
   apy, and periodically during treatment. More frequently monitor serum sodium in patients 65
   years or age and older and in patients at increased risk of hyponatremia.
   If hyponatremia occurs, desmopressin acetate may need to be temporarily or permanently
   discontinued Solution Compatibility
   NS

 Compatibility information refers to physical compatibility and is derived from Trissel’s™ 2
   Clinical Pharmaceutics Database. The determination of compatibility is based on concentra-
   tions for administration recommended herein. Drug compatibility is dependent on multiple
   factors (eg, drug concentrations, diluents, storage conditions). This list should not be viewed as
   all-inclusive and should not replace sound clinical judgment. The user is referred to Trissel’s™ 2
   for more complete details.

   Trissel’s™ 2 Clinical Pharmaceutics Database, version updated on 06/15/2012.

   Monitoring
   Therapeutic Monitoring

   • Central diabetes insipidus: Assess urine osmolality, urine volume, serum sodium, and in
   some cases, plasma osmolality prior to and during therapy 31,1 ,5 .
   • Hemophilia A: Verify factor VIII coagulant activity levels are greater than 5%, exclude the
   presence of factor VIII autoantibodies, and assess serum sodium and aPTT prior to treatment.
   Monitor levels of factor VIII coagulant activity, factor VIII antigen, and factor VIII ristocetin co-
   factor (von Willebrand factor) during therapy • von Willebrand disease: Verify factor VIII coagulant activity levels are greater than 5% and
   exclude severe von Willebrand disease (Type I) and presence of abnormal molecular form of
   factor VIII antigen prior to therapy. Monitor serum sodium, bleeding time, levels of factor VIII
   coagulant activity, factor VIII ristocetin cofactor activity, and factor VIII von Willebrand factor
   antigen during therapy Response to desmopressin therapy may be assessed by blood sam-
   ple 45 to 60 minutes after the completion of desmopressin infusion 32

   Toxic Monitoring
   • Monitor patients for signs and symptoms of hyponatremia, including decreased serum
   sodium levels 1 ,5 .

   • Monitor serum sodium concentration within 1 week and approximately 1 month of initiation
   of therapy, and periodically thereafter depending on risk of hyponatremia • Perform more frequent monitoring of serum sodium levels in patients with conditions associ-
   ated with fluid and electrolyte imbalance (cystic fibrosis, heart failure, renal disorders, habitual
   or psychogenic polydipsia) and in patients taking concomitant drugs that may cause hypona-
   tremia (eg, tricyclic antidepressants, SSRIs, opiate analgesics, NSAIDs, lamotrigine, oxybutynin,
   carbamazepine) • Monitor urine osmolality, and in some cases, plasma osmolality during therapy 1 ,5 .

 • Monitor urine volume during therapy 1 ,33 .

   • Monitor blood pressure and pulse during IV infusion

 Foam: In a clinical trial of 387 patients treated with desonide foam, the most common adverse
   reactions (>greater than 1%) included upper respiratory tract infection, cough, application site
   burning, viral infection, elevated blood pressure, and headache Post market reports of adverse effects include application site irritation and erythema, skin re-
   actions, and facial swelling 3

   Gel: In a clinical trial of 425 patients treated with desonide gel, the most common adverse re-
   actions (greater than 1%) included headache, application site burning, and rash Lotion: Total incidence of adverse effects was approximately 8% and included

   sient erythema, and dryness/scaliness 5
   Ointment: Total incidence of adverse effects was approximately 6% and included erythema,

   Toxic Monitoring

   • Monitor for elevated sodium and decreased potassium levels • Monitor for signs and symptoms of adrenal insufficiency after corticosteroid withdrawal,
   Cushing syndrome, and hyperglycemia during therapy • Monitor for the development of infection • In a patient with unexplained diarrhea or who has spent time in the tropics, exclude latent or

   plications fail to improve after 2 days 32

The most commonly reported (greater than or equal to 5%) adverse effects in pediatric patients were headache, abdomi-
  nal pain, diarrhea, nasopharyngitis, and oropharyngeal pain Serious infectious disease: In pediatric patients with gastroesophageal reflux disease or other gastric acid-related disor-

  justed HR, 34; 95% CI, 32 to 36) compared with no PPI use. In sub-group analysis similar results were observed for in-
  fections of the digestive tract (adjusted HR, 52; 95% CI, 48 to 55); ear, nose, and throat (adjusted HR, 47; 95% CI, 41 to 52); lower respiratory tract (adjusted HR, 22; 95% CI, 19 to 25); kidneys or urinary tract (adjusted HR, 2;
  95% CI, 15 to 25); and nervous system (adjusted HR, 31; 95% CI, 11 to 54) and for both bacterial (adjusted HR, 56; 95% CI, 50 to 63) and viral infections (adjusted HR, 3; 95% CI, 28 to 33). The median follow-up time was 8
  years, median age at index date was 84 days (range, 44 to 210 days), gestational age was full-term in 1%, and 8%
  were male. Of the children who received PPIs, the median duration of treatment was 118 days In a retrospective, single-center, observational, case-control study of 136 children (1 year or older) having protracted diar-
  rhea and stool analysis for Clostridium difficile, the use of PPI therapy was significantly higher in the patients with C difficile-
  associated diarrhea compared to the control group (22% vs 6%; odds ratio of 5 (95% CI, 4 to 4; p=0.006)) Monitoring

  Consider obtaining serum magnesium levels prior to initiating treatment and then periodically during treatment in pa-
  tients expected to be on prolonged therapy or who use digoxin or other drugs that may cause hypomagnesemia (eg, di-
  uretics) Consider monitoring magnesium and calcium levels prior to initiating treatment and then periodically during treatment in
  patients with a preexisting risk of hypocalcemia (eg, hypoparathyroidism)

Adverse effects reported in 5% or more of patients who received dexmethylphenidate tablets,
   and at least twice the incidence of placebo during clinical trials included abdominal pain,
   anorexia, fever, and nausea. The most common reasons for discontinuation were anorexia, in-
   somnia, tachycardia, and twitching (eg, motor or vocal tics) Adverse effects reported in 5% of
   more of patients who received extended-release capsules, and at least twice the incidence of
   placebo during clinical trials included anxiety, decreased appetite, dyspepsia, and headache.
   Dose-related adverse events included depression, insomnia, irritability, mood swings, nasal
   congestion, pruritus, and vomiting Cases of painful and prolonged penile erections (ie, more than 4 hours) and priapism have
   been reported with use of methylphenidate products following dose increases, with longer
   than usual dosing intervals, and after temporary or permanent drug withdrawal. Some cases
   required surgical intervention. Inform male patients and caregivers of the signs and symptoms
   of priapism and the need for immediate medical evaluation if the condition occurs 17,18 .
   In an FDA analysis, 15 cases of priapism associated with methylphenidate were reported over
   a 15-year period, with the majority of affected patients under age 18 (median age, 5 years;
   range, 8 to 33 years). Some cases required inpatient care, including surgical treatment in 2 pa-
   tients (ie, shunt placement, needle aspiration of the corpus cavernosum). Priapism developed
   following methylphenidate withdrawal in 4 cases. Priapism resolved after the drug was
   restarted in some patients 19

   Black Box Warning
   Abuse, Misuse, and Addiction
   Dexmethylphenidate hydrochloride has a high potential for abuse and misuse, which can lead
   to the development of a substance use disorder, including addiction. Misuse and abuse of CNS
   stimulants, including dexmethylphenidate hydrochloride, can result in overdose and death,
   and this risk is increased with higher doses or unapproved methods of administration, such as
   snorting or injection.
   Before prescribing dexmethylphenidate hydrochloride, assess each patient’s risk for abuse,
   misuse, and addiction. Educate patients and their families about these risks, proper storage of
   the drug, and proper disposal of any unused drug. Throughout dexmethylphenidate hy-

 drochloride treatment, reassess each patient’s risk of abuse, misuse, and addiction and fre-
   quently monitor for signs and symptoms of abuse, misuse, and addiction Monitoring
   Toxic Physical Monitoring

   • Assess for risk of abuse, misuse, and addiction prior to initiation and monitor for signs and
   symptoms of abuse, misuse, and addiction 1 ,2 .

   • Assess for cardiac disease before therapy initiation (eg, a careful history, family history of
   sudden death or ventricular arrhythmia, and physical exam) 1 , • Monitor all patients for potential tachycardia and hypertension 1 ,2 .
   • The American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP) does not recommend the routine use of ECGs or
   routine subspecialty cardiology evaluations (which were previously recommended by the
   American Heart Association (AHA) scientific statement 9 ,10 to detect cardiac conditions that
   might place the child at risk for sudden cardiac death [SCD]) before initiating stimulant therapy
   to treat ADHD in most children. The APA cited specific reasons for changing the recommenda-
   tion including: lack of evidence establishing a relationship between stimulant drugs used to
   treat ADHD and SCD, the frequency of sudden unexpected deaths among patients taking stim-
   ulant drugs is not higher than that in the general population of children, and lack of cost-effec-
   tive analysis to support ECG screening or special evaluation by pediatric cardiologist Based
   on the AAP and the AHA consensus statements, the following cardiac monitoring recommen-
   dations have been established to assist clinicians in the evaluation of children treated with
   stimulant drugs, including dextroamphetamine sulfate, for ADHD 9 ,10 :
   ●   - Conduct a thorough examination prior to initiating stimulant therapy for a diagnosis of
       ADHD. Special attention should be given to symptoms indicative of a cardiac condition, in-
       cluding palpitations, near syncope, or syncope.
   ●   - Obtain a complete family and patient history for conditions associated with sudden cardiac
       death (SCD), and determine current use of any other prescription or over-the-counter
       medications.
   ●   - Conduct a complete physical evaluation of the patient for hypertension, cardiac murmurs,
       physical findings associated with Marfan syndrome, and signs of irregular cardiac rhythms.
   ●   - Perform further evaluation if family history, patient history or physical exam is suggestive
       of cardiac disease during initial visit or at follow up visits, and if indicated, consult pediatric
       cardiologist .

 ●   - Continue to assess the patient for cardiac symptoms and any changes in family history at
       follow up visits.
   ●   - Blood pressure and heart rate should be evaluated at baseline, during routine follow-up
       within 1 to 3 months, and at follow up visits every 6 to 12 months. Increases in blood pres-
       sure and heart rate have been reported with stimulant use.
   • Prior to initiating treatment, screen patients for risk factors for developing a manic episode
   (eg, comorbid or history of depressive symptoms or a family history of suicide, bipolar disor-
   der, or depression) 1 ,2 .
   • Monitor growth determinations (body weight and height) in pediatric patients during treat-
   ment 1 ,2 .

   • Carefully observe for signs and symptoms of peripheral vasculopathy, including Raynaud's
   phenomenon (ie, digital changes) during treatment 1 , • Assess the family history and clinically evaluate patients for motor or verbal tics or Tourette’s
   syndrome prior to initiation and monitor patients for the emergence or worsening of tics or
   Tourette’s syndrome during therapy 1 ,2 .

   and the extent of absorption • Disposal: Fold so that the adhesive side of the system adheres to itself and placed in a lidded

   Black Box Warning
   Abuse, Misuse, and Addiction

   Dextroamphetamine has a high potential for abuse and misuse, which can lead to the devel-
   opment of a substance use disorder, including addiction. Misuse and abuse of CNS stimulants,
   including dextroamphetamine, can result in overdose and death, and this risk is increased with
   higher doses or unapproved methods of administration, such as snorting or injection.
   Before prescribing dextroamphetamine, assess each patient’s risk for abuse, misuse, and ad-
   diction. Educate patients and their families about these risks, proper storage of the drug, and
   proper disposal of any unused drug. Throughout dextroamphetamine treatment, reassess
   each patient’s risk of abuse, misuse, and addiction and frequently monitor for signs and symp-
   toms of abuse, misuse, and addiction Monitoring
   Therapeutic Physical Monitoring

   • Periodically re-evaluate the need for continued use Toxic Physical Monitoring
   • Prior to initiation of therapy, assess the risk of abuse, misuse, and addiction, and monitor for
   signs of abuse and dependence during therapy • Assess for cardiac disease (eg, perform careful history, family history of sudden death or ven-
   tricular arrhythmia, and physical exam) prior to initiation 7/11
 • Monitor blood pressure for potential hypertension • Monitor pulse for potential tachycardia • Prior to initiating treatment, screen patients for risk factors for developing a manic episode
   (eg, comorbid or history of depressive symptoms or a family history of suicide, bipolar disor-
   der, and depression) • Closely monitor growth (height and weight) in pediatric patients 9 ,10 .

   • Carefully observe patients for digital changes during treatment • Assess the family history and clinically evaluate patients for tics or Tourette's syndrome and
   regularly monitor for the emergence or worsening of tics or Tourette's syndrome • Narcolepsy: Polysomnographic reevaluation should be considered if symptoms of new or in-
   creased sleep abnormalities are noted 11

   Dextrose restores blood glucose levels in hypoglycemia and provides a source of carbohydrate
   calories. Intravenous dextrose provides 4 kcal/g and oral glucose provides 4 kcal/g 17,14 .

   sodium-potassium (Na-K) adenosine triphosphatase pump (ATP) leading to an intracellular
   shift of potassium 7 , 23 ,

Anxiety and sedation: Not a preferred agent for sedation in the intensive care setting or for
   procedural sedation. Because of the long half-life of diazePAM and its metabolites, repeat ad-
   ministration can lead to prolonged sedation 37,38 . Midazolam is preferred for procedural seda-
   tion due to its short half-life and the ability to give midazolam by multiple routes Acute seizures: Intravenous and rectal diazePAM are appropriate for the treatment of acute
   seizures. Both routes have been compared with buccal or intranasal midazolam. Buccal mida-
   zolam has been reported to be safe and at least as effective as, or more effective than, rectal
   diazePAM in randomized studies in the emergency department setting 19 , 20 , Intranasal mi-

 dazolam has been reported to be safe and at least as effective as, or more effective than, rec-
   tal diazePAM in randomized studies in the community and emergency department settings
   40,21,41
              .

   Generalized spasticity in children with cerebral palsy (CP): According to the American
   Academy of Neurology, diazePAM can be considered for the short-term treatment of spasticity
   in children with CP In a randomized, placebo-controlled trial, bedtime diazePAM was associ-
   ated with decreased tone, increased spontaneous movement, and improvement in passive
   range-of-motion. Patients less than 12 years of age with CP received diazePAM for 4 weeks on
   and 2 weeks off for 3 cycles until physical therapy was well-established Convulsive Status Epilepticus: The proposed treatment algorithm for status epilepticus
   (seizures greater than 30 minutes duration) in children and adults was developed by a litera-
   ture review. Initiate treatment for seizures of greater than 5 minute duration as there is a
   greater likelihood of seizures progressing to status epilepticus when a seizure goes beyond 5
   minutes 27 :
   ●   First-Line Therapy (first 5 to 20 minutes of continued seizures): Choose One of the follow-
       ing options
   ●   IM midazolam as a single dose OR
   ●   IV LORazepam, may repeat with one dose OR
   ●   IV diazePAM, may repeat with one dose
   ●   Alternatives, if none of the above are available:
   ●   IV PHENobarbital as a single dose; OR rectal diazePAM as a single dose; OR intranasal mida-
       zolam; OR buccal midazolam
   ●   Effectiveness between IV LORazepam and IV diazePAM was similar. Midazolam by IM, intranasal,
       or buccal may be more effective than diazePAM IV or rectal.
   ●   Second-Line Therapy (20 to 40 minutes of continued seizures) based on expert opinion:
       Choose One of the following options
   ●   IV fosphenytoin as a single dose (IV phenytoin is an acceptable alternative)
   ●   IV valproic acid as a single dose
   ●   IV levETIRAcetam as a single dose
   ●   Alternative, if none of the above are available:
   ●   IV PHENobarbital (if not already administered)
   ●   Third-Line Therapy (40 minutes or more of seizures)

 ●   No data to provide definitive recommendations. May repeat second-line therapy or use
       anesthetic doses of thiopental, midazolam, PENTobarbital, or propofol while continuously
       monitoring EEG

   Intravenous diazePAM is an appropriate medication for initial treatment of status epilepticus;
   however, intravenous lorazepam has been suggested as a first-line agent due to a more sus-
   tained duration of action and a decreased need for additional anticonvulsants when compared
   with diazePAM IV 43,44,29,45 . However, lorazepam IV was not superior to diazePAM IV for status
   epilepticus in 272 pediatric patients (3 months to younger than 18 years of age) in a random-
   ized trial. There was no significant difference in the rates of cessation of status epilepticus
   within 10 minutes without recurrence within 30 minutes (primary efficacy outcome), which was 9% with lorazepam 1 mg/kg IV (maximum 4 mg/dose) and 1% with diazePAM 2 mg/kg
   (maximum 8 mg/dose). At 5 minutes, half the original dose was repeated if cessation of
   seizures were not attained. Also, there was no significant difference in assisted ventilation (pri-
   mary safety outcome), which was required in 6% and 16%, respectively Lorazepam IV
   may be preferred over rectal diazePAM in the Emergency Department setting Sedation in Critically Ill Patients in ICU: Most patients requiring mechanical ventilation will
   receive sedation to reduce anxiety, maintain ventilator-patient synchrony, and facilitate neces-
   sary care procedures, however, minimizing benzodiazepine-based sedation when feasible in
   critically ill pediatric patients is recommended to decrease incidence and/or duration or sever-
   ity of delirium. Benzodiazepines are not recommended as first-line sedation therapy; consider
   alpha blockers (first-line), propofol, or dexmedetomidine prior to benzodiazepines. The ideal
   depth of sedation has significant intra- and inter-patient variability based on the disease being
   treated, stage of disease evolution, invasiveness of therapy required, and developmental abili-
   ties to cooperate with treatments and therapies. Protocolized sedation is recommended in all
   critically ill pediatric patients requiring sedation and/or analgesia during mechanical ventila-
   tion; daily sedation interruption as a part of this protocol is not suggested due to lack of im-
   provement in outcomes Pediatric FDA-Approved Indications
   Rectal gel, 2 years and older: Acute treatment of intermittent, stereotypic episodes of fre-
   quent seizure activity (ie, seizure clusters, acute repetitive seizures) that are distinct from a
   patient's usual seizure pattern in patients with epilepsy 2 years or older 6 ,7

   Nasal spray, 2 years and older: Acute treatment of intermittent, stereotypic episodes of fre-
   quent seizure activity (eg, seizure clusters, acute repetitive seizures) that are distinct from a
   patient's usual seizure pattern in patients with epilepsy 2 years or older 7/22
 Oral, 6 months and older: Diazepam is indicated as adjunct therapy for the relief of skeletal
   muscle spasms due to reflex spasm to local pathology (eg, inflammation of the muscles or
   joints, secondary to trauma), spasticity due to upper motor neuron disorders (eg, cerebral
   palsy, paraplegia), athetosis, and stiff-man syndrome. Diazepam is also indicated as an adjunct
   treatment for convulsive disorders and the management of anxiety disorder for the short-term
   relief of anxiety symptoms 4 ,5 .

   Parenteral, 30 days and older: Diazepam is indicated for the treatment of muscle spasm as-
   sociated with local pathology, cerebral palsy, athetosis, stiff-man syndrome or tetanus, as well
   as status epilepticus and severe recurrent convulsive seizures 1 ,2 .

   Buccal mucosa, 2 to 5 years of age: Diazepam is indicated for the acute treatment of inter-

   Warning: Risks From Concomitant Use with Opioids; Abuse, Misuse, and Addiction; and
   Dependence and Withdrawal Reactions 8 , 4
   ●   Concomitant use of benzodiazepines and opioids may result in profound sedation, respira-
       tory depression, coma, and death. Reserve concomitant prescribing of these drugs for pa-
       tients for whom alternative treatment options are inadequate. Limit dosages and durations
       to the minimum required. Follow patients for signs and symptoms of respiratory
       depression.
   ●   The use of benzodiazepines, including diazepam, exposes users to risks of abuse, misuse,
       and addiction, which can lead to overdose or death. Abuse and misuse of benzodiazepines
       commonly involve concomitant use of other medications, alcohol, and/or illicit substances,
       which is associated with increased frequency of serious adverse outcomes. Before prescrib-
       ing diazepam and throughout treatment, assess each patient's risk for abuse, misuse, and
       addiction.

 ●   The continued use of benzodiazepines, including diazepam, may lead to clinically significant
       physical dependence. The risks of dependence and withdrawal increase with longer treat-
       ment duration and higher daily dose. Abrupt discontinuation or rapid dosage reduction of
       diazepam may precipitate acute withdrawal reactions, which can be life-threatening. To re-
       duce the risk of withdrawal reactions, use a gradual taper to discontinue diazepam or re-
       duce the dosage.

 Black Box Warning
   Warning: Risk of Serious Cardiovascular and Gastrointestinal Events 17
   Cardiovascular Thrombotic Events
    ●   Nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) cause an increased risk of serious cardiovas-
        cular thrombotic events, including myocardial infarction and stroke, which can be fatal. This
        risk may occur early in treatment and may increase with duration of use.
    ●   Diclofenac is contraindicated in the setting of coronary artery bypass graft (CABG) surgery.

   Gastrointestinal Bleeding, Ulceration, and Perforation
    ●   NSAIDs cause an increased risk of serious gastrointestinal (GI) adverse events including
        bleeding, ulceration, and perforation of the stomach or intestines, which can be fatal. These
        events can occur at any time during use and without warning symptoms. Patients with a
        prior history of peptic ulcer disease and/or GI bleeding are at greater risk for serious GI
        events.

   Monitoring
   Monitor for signs and symptoms of gastrointestinal bleeding. CBC and chemistry panel (includ-
   ing transaminase levels) should be checked periodically when on long-term therapy. Monitor
   renal function in advanced renal disease. Monitor platelet function in patients with coagulation
   disorders or those receiving anticoagulants concomitantly. Monitor heart rate and blood pres-
   sure at baseline and throughout the course of diclofenac therapy 1 ,2 ,4 ,3 .

 • Triturate twenty-four 50 mg tablets of dipyridamole to a fine powder using a mortar and

drugs.contraindications_raw:
The most commonly reported adverse effects were dry mouth (32%), urinary hesitancy (14%),
   and constipation (11%) 1 ,2 .

   Black Box Warning
   Mortality

   In the National Heart, Lung and Blood Institute's Cardiac Arrhythmia Suppression Trial (CAST),
   a long-term, multi-center, randomized, double-blind study in patients with asymptomatic non-
   life-threatening ventricular arrhythmias who had a myocardial infarction more than 6 days but
   less than 2 years previously, an excessive mortality or non-fatal cardiac arrest rate (7.7%) was
   seen in patients treated with encainide or flecainide compared with that seen in patients as-
   signed to carefully matched placebo-treated groups (3%). The average duration of treatment
   with encainide or flecainide in this study was 10 months.

   The applicability of the CAST results to other populations (e.g., those without recent myocar-
   dial infarction) is uncertain. Considering the known proarrhythmic properties of disopyramide
   and the lack of evidence of improved survival for any antiarrhythmic drug in patients without
   life-threatening arrhythmias, the use of disopyramide as well as other antiarrhythmic agents
   should be reserved for patients with life-threatening ventricular arrhythmias 1 , Monitoring
   Laboratory Parameters

   •Closely monitor disopyramide levels and therapeutic response 1 ,2
   •Carefully monitor blood glucose levels in patients with congestive heart failure, chronic mal-
   nutrition, hepatic or renal disease, or concomitant use of agents that can compromise preser-
   vation of normal glucoregulatory mechanisms in the absence of food 1 ,2

   Physical Findings
   •Carefully monitor patients receiving concomitant antiarrhythmic agents as this may produce
   serious negative inotropic effects or excessively prolong conduction 1 , 4/6
 •Measure intraocular pressure prior to initiating treatment in patients with a family history of
   glaucoma 1 ,2 .
   •Monitor ECG for prolongation of the PR interval, evidence of QRS widening, or other signs of
   overdose in patients with impaired renal function or hepatic impairment 1 ,2 .

   • Vials must be diluted prior to use in compatible diluent up to a concentration of 4000
   mcg/mL. Solutions containing DOBUTamine may exhibit a pink color which will increase with
   time due to oxidation of the drug. There is no significant loss of potency over 24 hours • Standard concentration: The recommended standard concentrations are 500, 1000, 2000,
   and 4000 mcg/mL Solution Preparation Calculations
   To calculate the AMOUNT of drug needed per defined final fluid volume:

   Desired final concentration (mg/mL) x defined final fluid volume (mL) = AMOUNT of drug to
   add to final infusion solution (mg).
   To calculate the VOLUME of drug needed per defined final fluid volume:

   *AMOUNT of drug to add (mg) ÷ drug (vial) concentration (mg/mL) = VOLUME of drug to add
   (mL)

   Example (for DOBUTamine): 30 mL of 2000 mcg/mL solution using DOBUTamine concentra-
   tion of 5 mg/mL.

   2000 mcg/mL = 2 mg/mL

   2 mg/mL x 30 mL = 60 mg DOBUTamine
   *60 mg ÷ 5 mg/mL = 8 mL of DOBUTamine

   Add 8 mL of DOBUTamine (12.5 mg/mL) to 2 mL of compatible solution (eg, D5 W) to yield
   30 mL of infusion solution with a concentration of 2000 mcg/mL.

    ●   All patients with HIV-1 should be tested for the presence of HBV prior to or when initiating
        dolutegravir/lamiVUDine. Emergence of lamiVUDine-resistant HBV variants associated with
        lamiVUDine-containing antiretroviral regimens has been reported. If
        dolutegravir/lamiVUDine is used in patients co-infected with HIV-1 and HBV, additional
        treatment should be considered for appropriate treatment of chronic HBV; otherwise, con-
        sider an alternative regimen.
    ●   Severe acute exacerbations of HBV have been reported in patients who are co-infected with
        HIV-1 and HBV and have discontinued lamiVUDine, a component of
        dolutegravir/lamiVUDine. Closely monitor hepatic function in these patients and, if appro-

      suppressed to less than 50 copies/mL, then every 3 to 6 months.
      (f) For patients on ART, viral load is typically measured every 3 to 6 months. More frequent
      monitoring may be considered in individuals having difficulties with ART adherence or at
      risk for nonadherence. However, for adherent patients with suppressed viral load and sta-
      ble immunological status for more than 1 year, monitoring can be extended to 6-month
      intervals.
      (g) Standard genotypic drug-resistance testing in ARV-naïve persons should focus on test-
      ing for mutations in the PR and RT genes. If transmitted INSTI resistance is a concern, or if
      a person has a history of INSTI use as PrEP or treatment, or a person presents with
      viremia while on an INSTI, providers should also test for resistance mutations in the IN
      gene. In ARV-naïve patients who do not immediately begin ART, repeat testing before initi-
      ation of ART is optional if drug-resistance testing was performed at entry into care. For vi-
      rologically suppressed patients who are switching therapy for toxicity or convenience, viral
      amplification will not be possible and therefore resistance testing should not be per-
      formed. Results from prior resistance testing can be used to help in the construction of a
      new regimen.
      (h) If infected with hepatitis B virus, tenofovir disoproxil fumarate or tenofovir alafe-
      namide plus either emtricitabine or lamivudine should be used as part of the ART regimen
      to treat both hepatitis B virus and HIV infections.
      (i) If HBsAg, and HBsAb, and HBcAb are negative at baseline, administer hepatitis B vac-
      cine series. Also, consult Guidelines for Opportunistic Infections.
      (j) Typically HBV infection has resolved with loss of HBsAb despite isolated HBcAb; confirm
      with an HBV viral load if wanted. A positive HBV viral load is indicative of acute infection
      (other symptoms will be present usually) or chronic infection. Vaccinate the patient when
      viral load is negative. Also, consult Guidelines for Opportunistic Infections.
      (k) In patients with recent HCV infection (acquired in last 6 months) or advanced immun-
      odeficiency (CD4 count less than 100 cells/mm(3)), the HCV antibody test may not be ade-
      quate for screening. HCV RNA screening is indicated in persons who have been success-
      fully treated for HCV or who spontaneously cleared prior infection. HCV antibody-negative
      patients with elevated ALT may need HCV RNA testing.
      (l) At-risk populations: injection drug users, persons with a history of incarceration, men
      with HIV who have unprotected sex with men, and persons with percutaneous/parenteral
      exposure to blood in unregulated settings are at risk of HCV infection.
      (m) Serum sodium, potassium, bicarbonate, chloride, blood urea nitrogen, creatinine, glu-
      cose (preferably fasting). Monitor serum phosphorus concentrations in patients with
      chronic kidney disease who are on tenofovir-containing regimens. Renal function determi-

 nation should include creatinine monitoring and estimation of the glomerular filtration
      rate.
      (n) Consult recommendations of the HIV Medicine Association of the Infectious Diseases
      Society of America for patients with renal disease. More frequent monitoring may be indi-
      cated for patients with evidence of kidney disease (eg, proteinuria or decreased glomeru-
      lar function) or increased risk of renal insufficiency (eg. patients with diabetes or hyper-
      tension).
      (o) CBC with differential should be done when a CD4 count is performed. When CD4 count
      is no longer being monitored, the recommended frequency of CBC with differential is
      once a year. More frequent monitoring may be for patients receiving medications that po-
      tentially cause cytopenia (eg, trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole)
      (p) If random lipids are abnormal, fasting lipids should be obtained. Consult the ACA/AHA
      recommendations for diagnosis and management of patients with dyslipidemia.
      (q) If random glucose is abnormal, fasting glucose should be obtained. HgbA1C is not
      longer recommended for diagnosis of diabetes in patients with HIV on ART.
      (r) Assess urine glucose and protein before initiating tenofovir-containing regimens and
      monitor during treatment with these regimens.

Cardiogenic shock (PALS guidelines): DOBUTamine , EPINEPHrine, DOPamine, or milrinone
   may be used as inotropic infusions in pediatric patients with cardiogenic shock Renal-dose DOPamine: Although low-dose DOPamine (2 to 5 mcg/kg/minute) is used in chil-
   dren to improve renal function and urine volume, clinical evidence to support this use is pres-
   ently lacking 6 ,7 ,8 . In a randomized study (n=147) in children undergoing open-heart surgery
   with cardiopulmonary bypass, low-dose DOPamine was not superior to low-dose
   DOBUTamine for renal function protection and offered no clinical benefit compared with
   DOBUTamine In a multicenter, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled study in
   adults (n=328) with early renal dysfunction, low-dose DOPamine (2 mcg/kg/minute) did not of-
   fer clinically significant protection from renal dysfunction. Peak serum creatinine concentra-
   tion during treatment (primary endpoint) was not significantly different between the
   DOPamine and placebo groups (245 vs 249 micromole/L; p=0.93); other measures of renal
   function were not significantly different between the 2 groups Severe sepsis and septic shock
   Surviving Sepsis Campaign guidelines: Vasoactive medications should be given to patients
   with septic shock after 40 to 60 mL/kg of fluid resuscitation if there is evidence of abnormal
   perfusion, or sooner if fluid overload develops or other concerns for fluid administration

   EPINEPHrine vs DOPamine:Within the first hour of resuscitation the resolution rate was bet-
   ter with EPINEPHrine (41%) than DOPamine (13%) (OR 8, 95% CI 3 to 2) in 60 children (3
   months to 12 years of age) with fluid-refractory cold septic shock. Doses were initiated and
   titrated as needed every 10 minutes for DOPamine (10 to 15 to 20 mcg/kg/min) and
   EPINEPHrine (0.1 to 2 to 3 mcg/kg/min) As a first-line vasoactive agent for fluid refrac-
   tory septic shock, DOPamine was associated with an increased 28-day mortality rate compared
   with EPINEPHrine in a double-blind, randomized trial (n=120 children 1 month to 15 years of
   age). The odds ratio for death at 28 days for DOPamine compared with EPINEPHrine was 51
   (95% CI, 12 to 8). IV or intraosseous doses were 5 to 10 mcg/kg/min of DOPamine and 1
   to 3 mcg/kg/min for EPINEPHrine Administration

   to central line when available • Vials must be diluted prior to use in compatible diluent up to a concentration of 3200

   not respond to therapy, suspect occult hypovolemia. Acidosis may reduce the effectiveness of
   DOPamine • When discontinuing, gradually reduce the infusion rate to avoid hypotension after abrupt dis-

   D5W; D5NS; D5-0.45%NaCl; D5LR; sodium lactate USP 1/6 molar; or LR • Recommended concentrations are 200 mcg/mL to 3200 mcg/mL. Higher concentration solu-

   To calculate the AMOUNT of drug needed per defined final fluid volume:

   Desired final concentration (mg/mL) × defined final fluid volume (mL) = AMOUNT of drug to

   To calculate the VOLUME of drug needed per defined final fluid volume:

   *AMOUNT of drug to add (mg) ÷ drug (vial) concentration (mg/mL) = VOLUME of drug to add
   (mL)
   Example (for DOPamine): Mix 30 mL of 800 mcg/mL solution using DOPamine concentration

drugs.contraindications_raw:
Cardiovascular: Arrhythmias, hypotension, hypertension, and vasoconstriction Arrhythmias generally occur at doses greater than 10 mcg/kg/minute Dermatologic: Tissue ischemia due to peripheral extravasation of DOBUTamine Black Box Warning
   Tissue sloughing may occur with IV infiltration. According to the manufacturer's black box
   warning, to prevent sloughing and necrosis in areas of extravasation, the area should be infil-
   trated as soon as possible with a saline solution containing phentolamine mesylate Suggested treatment for extravasation: Inject a 5- to 1-mg/mL solution (5 to 10 mg in 10
   mL of normal saline) of phentolamine subcutaneously into the affected area. Inject 2 to 1 mL
   at a time into extravasated area until entire site is infiltrated. Usual amount needed is 1 to 5
   mL, depending on the size of the infiltrate, but a higher amount may be needed. Should be in-
   jected into area of extravasation within 12 hours. May be repeated if necessary 14,15,16 .

   Monitoring
   Continuous heart rate and intra-arterial blood pressure monitoring is preferable. Assess urine
   output, cardiac output, pulmonary wedge pressure, and peripheral perfusion frequently.
   Observe IV site closely for blanching and infiltration 13,3 .

   Warning: Posttreatment Acute Exacerbations of Hepatitis B
   Severe acute exacerbations of hepatitis B (HBV) have been reported in patients who are coin-
   fected with HIV-1 and HBV and have discontinued lamivudine or tenofovir disoproxil fumarate
   (TDF), which are components of doravirine/lamivudine/tenofovir disoproxil fumarate oral
   tablets. Hepatic function should be monitored closely with both clinical and laboratory follow-
   up for at least several months in patients who are coinfected with HIV-1 and HBV and discon-
   tinue doravirine/lamivudine/tenofovir disoproxil fumarate oral tablets. If appropriate, initiation
   of anti-hepatitis B therapy may be warranted Monitoring

      (a) If ART is initiated soon after HIV diagnosis and entry into care, repeat baseline labora-
      tory testing is not necessary.
      (b) ART is indicated for all people with HIV and should be started as soon as possible.
      However, if ART initiation is delayed, patients should be retained in care, with periodic
      monitoring as noted above.
      (c) After 2 years of consistently suppressed HIV RNA, less frequent monitoring (eg, every 6
      months) may be considered.
      (d) After 2 years of ART with consistently suppressed viral load: CD4 count 300 to 500
      cells/mm(3), monitor every 12 months; CD4 count greater than 500 cells/mm(3), CD4 mon-
      itoring is optional.
      (e) If HIV RNA is detectable at 4 to 8 weeks, repeat every 4 to 8 weeks until viral load is
      suppressed to less than 50 copies/mL, then every 3 to 6 months.
      (f) For patients on ART, viral load is typically measured every 3 to 6 months. More frequent
      monitoring may be considered in individuals having difficulties with ART adherence or at
      risk for nonadherence. However, for adherent patients with suppressed viral load and sta-
      ble immunological status for more than 1 year, monitoring can be extended to 6-month
      intervals.
      (g) Standard genotypic drug-resistance testing in ARV-naïve persons should focus on test-
      ing for mutations in the PR and RT genes. If transmitted INSTI resistance is a concern, or if
      a person has a history of INSTI use as PrEP or treatment, or a person presents with
      viremia while on an INSTI, providers should also test for resistance mutations in the IN
      gene. In ARV-naïve patients who do not immediately begin ART, repeat testing before initi-
      ation of ART is optional if drug-resistance testing was performed at entry into care. For vi-
      rologically suppressed patients who are switching therapy for toxicity or convenience, viral
      amplification will not be possible and therefore resistance testing should not be per-
      formed. Results from prior resistance testing can be used to help in the construction of a

 new regimen.
      (h) If infected with hepatitis B virus, tenofovir disoproxil fumarate or tenofovir alafe-
      namide plus either emtricitabine or lamivudine should be used as part of the ART regimen
      to treat both hepatitis B virus and HIV infections.
      (i) If HBsAg, and HBsAb, and HBcAb are negative at baseline, administer hepatitis B vac-
      cine series. Also, consult Guidelines for Opportunistic Infections.
      (j) Typically HBV infection has resolved with loss of HBsAb despite isolated HBcAb; confirm
      with an HBV viral load if wanted. A positive HBV viral load is indicative of acute infection
      (other symptoms will be present usually) or chronic infection. Vaccinate the patient when
      viral load is negative. Also, consult Guidelines for Opportunistic Infections.
      (k) In patients with recent HCV infection (acquired in last 6 months) or advanced immun-
      odeficiency (CD4 count less than 100 cells/mm(3)), the HCV antibody test may not be ade-
      quate for screening. HCV RNA screening is indicated in persons who have been success-
      fully treated for HCV or who spontaneously cleared prior infection. HCV antibody-negative
      patients with elevated ALT may need HCV RNA testing.
      (l) At-risk populations: injection drug users, persons with a history of incarceration, men
      with HIV who have unprotected sex with men, and persons with percutaneous/parenteral
      exposure to blood in unregulated settings are at risk of HCV infection.
      (m) Serum sodium, potassium, bicarbonate, chloride, blood urea nitrogen, creatinine, glu-
      cose (preferably fasting). Monitor serum phosphorus concentrations in patients with
      chronic kidney disease who are on tenofovir-containing regimens. Renal function determi-
      nation should include creatinine monitoring and estimation of the glomerular filtration
      rate.
      (n) Consult recommendations of the HIV Medicine Association of the Infectious Diseases
      Society of America for patients with renal disease. More frequent monitoring may be indi-
      cated for patients with evidence of kidney disease (eg, proteinuria or decreased glomeru-
      lar function) or increased risk of renal insufficiency (eg. patients with diabetes or hyper-
      tension).
      (o) CBC with differential should be done when a CD4 count is performed. When CD4 count
      is no longer being monitored, the recommended frequency of CBC with differential is
      once a year. More frequent monitoring may be for patients receiving medications that po-
      tentially cause cytopenia (eg, trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole)
      (p) If random lipids are abnormal, fasting lipids should be obtained. Consult the ACA/AHA
      recommendations for diagnosis and management of patients with dyslipidemia.
      (q) If random glucose is abnormal, fasting glucose should be obtained. HgbA1C is not
      longer recommended for diagnosis of diabetes in patients with HIV on ART.
      (r) Assess urine glucose and protein before initiating tenofovir-containing regimens and
      monitor during treatment with these regimens.
      (s) In women with child-bearing potential.

   Renal impairment: No specific recommendations are available 1

   Hepatic impairment: No specific recommendations are available 1
   Liver test abnormalities: If signs or symptoms consistent with liver injury are observed, inter-
   rupt treatment until liver transaminase and total bilirubin levels have either returned to base-
   line or stabilized at a new baseline value. Consider restarting doxecitine/doxribtimine at the
   last tolerated dose and increase the dose based on tolerability. Consider permanently discon-
   tinuing use if signs or symptoms consistent with liver injury persist or worsen 1

   Other Dose Adjustments
   Gastrointestinal adverse events: Reduce the dose of doxecitine/doxribtimine or interrupt
   treatment until diarrhea and/or vomiting improves or returns to baseline. Consider restarting
   doxecitine/doxribtimine at the last tolerated dose and increase the dose based on tolerability.

   ●   Rocky Mountain spotted fever, typhus fever and the typhus group, Q fever, rickettsialpox,
       and tick fevers caused by Rickettsiae
   ●   Respiratory tract infections caused by Mycoplasma pneumoniae
   ●   Lymphogranuloma venereum caused by Chlamydia trachomatis
   ●   Psittacosis (ornithosis) caused by Chlamydophila psittaci
   ●   Trachoma caused by Chlamydia trachomatis, although the infectious agent is not always
       eliminated, as judged by immunofluorescence
   ●   Inclusion conjunctivitis caused by Chlamydia trachomatis
   ●   Uncomplicated urethral, endocervical, or rectal infections in adults caused by Chlamydia
       trachomatis.
   ●   Nongonococcal urethritis caused by Ureaplasma urealyticum
   ●   Relapsing fever due to Borrelia recurrentis
   ●   Chancroid caused by Haemophilus ducreyi
   ●   Plague due to Yersinia pestis (formerly Pasteurella pestis)
   ●   Tularemia due to Francisella tularensis (formerly Pasteurella tularensis)
   ●   Cholera caused by Vibrio cholerae (formerly Vibrio comma)
   ●   Campylobacter fetus infections caused by Campylobacter fetus (formerly Vibrio fetus)
   ●   Brucellosis due to Brucella species (in conjunction with streptomycin)
   ●   Bartonellosis due to Bartonella bacilliformis
   ●   Granuloma inguinale caused by Klebsiella granulomatis
   ●   Uncomplicated gonorrhea caused by Neisseria gonorrhoeae

   Treatment of the following infections when penicillin is contraindicated 57 , 19 , 39 , 43 :
   ●   Syphilis caused by Treponema pallidum
   ●   Yaws caused by Treponema pallidum subspecies pertenue
   ●   Listeriosis due to Listeria monocytogenes

 ●   Vincent’s infection caused by Fusobacterium fusiforme
   ●   Actinomycosis caused by Actinomyces israelii
   ●   Infections caused by Clostridium species

   Treatment of the following infections (when bacteriologic testing indicates appropriate suscep-
   tibility to doxycycline) 19,20,39,43 :
   ●   Escherichia coli
   ●   Enterobacter aerogenes (formerly Aerobacter aerogenes)
   ●   Shigella species.
   ●   Acinetobacter species (formerly Mima species and Herellea species)
   ●   Respiratory tract infections caused by Haemophilus influenzae
   ●   Respiratory tract and urinary tract infections caused by Klebsiella species
   ●   Upper respiratory infections caused by Streptococcus pneumoniae (formerly Diplococcus
       pneumoniae)
   ●   Anthrax due to Bacillus anthracis, including inhalational anthrax (post-exposure): to reduce
       the incidence or progression of disease following exposure to aerosolized Bacillus anthracis

   As an adjunct to amebicides in acute intestinal amebiasis 19,20,39,43 .

   Adjunctive therapy in severe acne 19 , 20 , Use of doxycycline is not recommended in infants and children younger than 8 years, except
   when the potential benefits are expected to outweigh the risks in severe or life-threatening
   conditions (e.g., anthrax, Rocky Mountain spotted fever) 58,29 .

   minimize esophageal irritation/ulceration Administer with food or milk if gastric irritation

   or magnesium, bismuth subsalicylate, and iron-containing preparations and when taken with
   food, especially calcium-containing food Acticlate/Acticlate CAP

   milk 40,41

   Swallow capsules whole. Do not break, chew or dissolve 41

   Doryx®: May be administered by carefully breaking up tablets and sprinkling delayed-release
   pellets on a spoonful of cool applesauce. Do not crush or damage pellets. Swallow without
   chewing and follow with water, if desired. Use immediately. Do not store for later use Doryx MPC: (doxycycline hyclate delayed-release tablets): Do not chew or crush. Administer
   with an adequate amount of fluid to wash down doxycycline and reduce the risk of esophageal

   infusion duration is generally 1 to 4 hours. Recommended minimum infusion time is 1 hour for
   100 mg of a 5 mg/mL solution 42 , IV: Avoid rapid administration Extravasation Management:Although not pediatric-specific, the following are recommenda-
   tions for extravasation of acidic agents (doxycycline pH ranges from 8 to 3) 45 :
   ●   General:
   ●   Stop and disconnect infusion; do not remove the cannula or needle
   ●   Attempt to gently aspirate as much extravasated agent as possible; avoid manual pressure
   ●   Remove cannula or needle
   ●   Dry heat and elevation
   ●   Closely monitor for signs of coagulation and ischemia
   ●   Avoid attempt at pH neutralization (doxycycline - pH 8 to 3)
   ●   Monitor and consider the need for surgical management such as surgical flushing with nor-
       mal saline or debridement and excision of necrotic tissue (especially if pain persists for 1 to
       2 weeks). In cases of compartment syndrome, surgical decompression may be required
   ●   Refractory Events:
   ●   Hyaluronidase 15 units intradermally along injection site and edematous area. Give as five, 2 mL intradermal injections along extravasation site and edematous tissue.

 ●   Inadvertent Intraarterial Administration:
   ●   Leave inadvertent intraarterial line in place for diagnostics
   ●   Systemic heparin titrated to therapeutic anticoagulant effect.
   ●   Stellate ganglion block

   Preparation

   Intravenous
   • Reconstitute vial with 10 mL (100-mg vial) or 20 mL (200 mg vial) SWFI for a concentration of
   10 mg/mL 46
   • Further dilute with 100 to 1000 mL (100-mg vial) or 200 to 2000 mL (200-mg vial) of a compat-
   ible solution (ie, NS, D5W, LR) for a final concentration of 1 mg/mL to 1 mg/mL 46

   • Stable for 48 hours at 25°C under fluorescent light when diluted with NS or D5W; protect
   from direct sunlight during storage and infusion. May store for 72 hours if refrigerated and
   protected from sunlight and artificial light; in this situation, infusion time should not exceed 12
   hours 46
   • When diluted with solutions other than NS or D5W (eg, LR), storage and stability information
   may differ. Please consult the manufacturer's product information 46

   Extemporaneous oral compound
   Note: Powder for oral suspension (25 mg/5 mL) and oral syrup (50 mg/5mL) are commercially
   available.
   Emergency extemporaneous preparation

   Intended for use during a public health emergency for those who cannot swallow pills 47 :

   • Place one 100-mg doxycycline hyclate tablet in a small bowl.

   • Add 20 mL water to bowl and allow to soak for at least 10 minutes to soften tablet.
   • Crush tablet with back of a metal spoon until there are no visible pieces of tablet left; stir to
   mix.
   • Measure the appropriate dosage and place into a second small bowl.
   • Mix with 3 teaspoons of milk, formula, breastmilk, chocolate milk, chocolate pudding, or a so-
   lution of apple juice plus 2 to 4 teaspoons of sugar; stir well.

   • For children 23 kg or less, may store leftover doxycycline and water mixture in a covered
   bowl or cup at 20 to 25°C (68 to 77°F) for 24 hours.

   in patients aged 65 or older 6/10

   prescriber 17

Common, study 1 (greater than 20%): Abdominal pain, diarrhea, vomiting, pyrexia, upper
   respiratory tract infection, nasopharyngitis, cough. Study N=22; 18 patients were younger than

   years, 10 patients were 2 to less than 12 years 1

   Black Box Warning
   Warning: Serious Meningococcal Infections 1
   Eculizumab, a complement inhibitor, increases the risk of serious infections caused by
   Neisseria meningitidis. Life-threatening and fatal meningococcal infections have occurred in pa-
   tients treated with complement inhibitors. These infections may become rapidly life-threaten-
   ing or fatal if not recognized and treated early.

   • Complete or update vaccination for meningococcal bacteria (for serogroups A, C, W, Y, and B)
   at least 2 weeks prior to the first dose of eculizumab, unless the risks of delaying therapy with
   eculizumab outweigh the risk of developing a serious infection. Comply with the most current
   Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices (ACIP) recommendations for vaccinations
   against meningococcal bacteria in patients receiving a complement inhibitor.

 • Patients receiving eculizumab are at increased risk for invasive disease caused by N meningi-
   tidis, even if they develop antibodies following vaccination. Monitor patients for early signs and
   symptoms of serious meningococcal infections and evaluate immediately if infection is
   suspected.

   Because of the risk of serious meningococcal infections, eculizumab is available only through a
   restricted program under a Risk Evaluation and Mitigation Strategy (REMS) called Ultomiris and
   Soliris REMS.

   Monitoring
   Therapeutic Monitoring

   Monitor for signs and symptoms of thrombotic microangiopathy (TMA) complications during
   therapy and for at least 12 weeks after discontinuation, including changes in mentals status,
   seizures, angina, dyspnea, or thrombosis Measure serial platelet count, serum LDH levels, and serum creatinine levels for response dur-
   ing therapy and for at least 12 weeks after discontinuation. The occurrence of 2, or repeated
   measure of any of 1 of the following changes in laboratory parameters may indicate TMA
   complications: • decrease in platelet count by 25% or more compared to baseline or the peak platelet count
   during eculizumab treatment

   • increase in serum creatinine by 25% or more compared to baseline or nadir during
   eculizumab treatment

   • increase in serum LDH by 25% or more over baseline or nadir during eculizumab treatment

   Toxic Monitoring

   • Consider monitoring liver function tests based on case reports of liver injury 8
   • Closely monitor all patients for early signs and symptoms of meningococcal infections
   throughout therapy. Other infections, particularly those associated with encapsulated bacteria,
   should also be considered • Observe all patients for signs and symptoms of infusion reactions for at least 1 hour follow-
   ing completion of each infusion Therapeutic Drug Monitoring
   Although optimal therapeutic concentrations of eculizumab and complement (C5b-C9) block-
   ade for atypical hemolytic uremic syndrome (aHUS) are unknown, consider confirming comple-

 ment blockade by CH50 4 and measuring plasma drug concentrations Complete blockade
   was achieved at CH50 of 10% or less 4 ; however, in a 9-year-old girl who was successfully

drugs.contraindications_raw:
Common, study 1 (greater than 20%): Abdominal pain, diarrhea, vomiting, pyrexia, upper
   respiratory tract infection, nasopharyngitis, and cough. Study N=22; 18 patients were younger
   than 12 years Common, study 2 (greater than 20%): Pyrexia, diarrhea, vomiting, upper respiratory tract in-
   fection, cough, nasal congestion, tachycardia. Study N=19; 5 patients were younger than 2
   years, 10 patients were 2 to less than 12 years 1

   Black Box Warning
   Warning: Serious Meningococcal Infections 1
   Eculizumab, a complement inhibitor, increases the risk of serious infections caused by
   Neisseria meningitidis. Life-threatening and fatal meningococcal infections have occurred in pa-
   tients treated with complement inhibitors. These infections may become rapidly life-threaten-
   ing or fatal if not recognized and treated early.

   • Complete or update vaccination for meningococcal bacteria (for serogroups A, C, W, Y, and B)
   at least 2 weeks prior to the first dose of eculizumab, unless the risks of delaying therapy with
   eculizumab outweigh the risk of developing a serious infection. Comply with the most current
   Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices (ACIP) recommendations for vaccinations
   against meningococcal bacteria in patients receiving a complement inhibitor.

 • Patients receiving eculizumab are at increased risk for invasive disease caused by N meningi-
   tidis, even if they develop antibodies following vaccination. Monitor patients for early signs and
   symptoms of serious meningococcal infections and evaluate immediately if infection is
   suspected.

   Because of the risk of serious meningococcal infections, eculizumab is available only through a
   restricted program under a Risk Evaluation and Mitigation Strategy (REMS) called Ultomiris and
   Soliris REMS.

   Monitoring
   Therapeutic Monitoring

   Monitor for signs and symptoms of thrombotic microangiopathy (TMA) complications during
   therapy and for at least 12 weeks after discontinuation, including changes in mentals status,
   seizures, angina, dyspnea, or thrombosis Measure serial platelet count, serum LDH levels, and serum creatinine levels for response dur-
   ing therapy and for at least 12 weeks after discontinuation. The occurrence of 2, or repeated
   measure of any of 1 of the following changes in laboratory parameters may indicate TMA
   complications: • decrease in platelet count by 25% or more compared to baseline or the peak platelet count
   during eculizumab treatment

   • increase in serum creatinine by 25% or more compared to baseline or nadir during
   eculizumab treatment

   • increase in serum LDH by 25% or more over baseline or nadir during eculizumab treatment

   Toxic Monitoring

   • Consider monitoring liver function tests based on case reports of liver injury 8
   • Closely monitor all patients for early signs and symptoms of meningococcal infections
   throughout therapy. Other infections, particularly those associated with encapsulated bacteria,
   should also be considered • Observe all patients for signs and symptoms of infusion reactions for at least 1 hour follow-
   ing completion of each infusion Therapeutic Drug Monitoring
   Although optimal therapeutic concentrations of eculizumab and complement (C5b-C9) block-
   ade for atypical hemolytic uremic syndrome (aHUS) are unknown, consider confirming comple-

 ment blockade by CH50 4 and measuring plasma drug concentrations Complete blockade
   was achieved at CH50 of 10% or less 4 ; however, in a 9-year-old girl who was successfully
   treated for aHUS with eculizumab, CH50 activity was 25% to 30% Complete complement
   (C5b-C9) blockade was achieved when peak and trough plasma concentrations of eculizumab
   was 35 mcg/mL or above in adults with paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria

drugs.contraindications_raw:
Common: Adverse events in pediatric patients were similar to those seen in adults, which in-
   cluded diarrhea, nausea, fatigue, headache, dizziness. Additionally, anemia (7%) and hyperpig-
   mentation (32%) were reported in pediatric patients Rash was more common in pediatric patients (32%) compared with adults (26%) with a higher
   frequency of grade 3 or 4 rash (3% vs 9%) Drug reaction with eosinophilia and systemic symptoms (DRESS): DRESS is a rare but seri-
   ous adverse effect that has been reported with efavirenz use. Discontinue all ARV drugs and
   other possible causative agents if confirmed. Consult with a specialist to determine if corticos-
   teroids and/or IVIG is appropriate. Provide supportive care of end-organ disease and do not
   reintroduce the offending agent Gastrointestinal

   Pancreatitis has been reported with the use of NRTIs and ritonavir-boosted PIs; discontinue
   the offending agent and avoid reintroduction Lactic acidosis

   Lactic acidosis has been reported with emtricitabine and tenofovir disoproxil fumarate use.
   Consider discontinuing ARV drugs temporarily in patients with a lactate 1 to 5 mmol/L (con-
   firmed with second test) while conducting additional diagnostic work-up. In patients with a lac-
   tate 5 mmol/L or greater (confirmed with second test) or 10 mmol/L (any one test), discontinue
   all ARV drugs and provide supportive therapy (eg, IV fluids, sedation, respiratory support).
   Following resolution of clinical and laboratory abnormalities, resume therapy with either an

 NRTI-sparing regimen or a revised NRTI-containing regimen. Monitor lactate monthly for 3
   months or more Musculoskeletal

   Osteopenia and osteoporosis has been reported with efavirenz and tenofovir disoproxil fu-
   marate. To help prevent osteopenia or osteoporosis from occurring, ensure that the patient
   has sufficient intake and levels of calcium and vitamin D, encourage weight-bearing exercise,
   minimize modifiable risk factors (eg, smoking, low BMI, use of steroids or medroxyproges-
   terone), consider using rilpivirine or an unboosted protease inhibitor with tenofovir disoproxil
   fumarate, consider switching tenofovir disoproxil fumarate to tenofovir alafenamide when
   possible, and consider measuring vitamin D levels and supplementing with vitamin D3 if a defi-
   ciency is identified. If osteopenia or osteoporosis does occur, consider switching the ARV regi-
   men and supplementing with vitamin D3 to raise serum 25-OH-vitamin D concentrations to 30
   nanograms (ng)/mL Neurologic

   Neuropsychiatric symptoms (eg, abnormal dreams, psychosis, suicidal ideation or attempted
   suicide) and other CNS manifestations (eg, dizziness, somnolence, insomnia, impaired concen-
   trations, seizures, cerebellar dysfunctions) have been reported with efavirenz use. In one case-
   series, 24% of children receiving efavirenz experienced CNS manifestations, with 18% of pa-
   tients requiring discontinuation. In a separate study, 11% of patients experienced new-onset
   seizures after receiving efavirenz The incidence of CNS symptoms has ranged from 14% to
   30% Black Box Warning
   Posttreatment Acute Exacerbation of Hepatitis B 1
    ●   Severe acute exacerbations of hepatitis B virus (HBV) have been reported in patients who
        are coinfected with HIV-1 and HBV and have discontinued products containing emtricitabine
        (FTC) and/or tenofovir disoproxil fumarate (TDF), which are components of
        efavirenz/emtricitabine/tenofovir disoproxil fumarate.
    ●   Closely monitor hepatic function with both clinical and laboratory follow-up for at least sev-
        eral months in patients who are coinfected with HIV-1 and HBV and discontinue
        efavirenz/emtricitabine/tenofovir disoproxil fumarate. If appropriate, initiation of anti-hep-
        atitis B therapy may be warranted.

      (a) If ART is initiated soon after HIV diagnosis and entry into care, repeat baseline labora-

      (b) ART is indicated for all people with HIV and should be started as soon as possible.
      However, if ART initiation is delayed, patients should be retained in care, with periodic
      monitoring as noted above.
      (c) After 2 years of consistently suppressed HIV RNA, less frequent monitoring (eg, every 6
      months) may be considered.
      (d) After 2 years of ART with consistently suppressed viral load: CD4 count 300 to 500
      cells/mm(3), monitor every 12 months; CD4 count greater than 500 cells/mm(3), CD4 mon-
      itoring is optional.
      (e) If HIV RNA is detectable at 4 to 8 weeks, repeat every 4 to 8 weeks until viral load is
      suppressed to less than 50 copies/mL, then every 3 to 6 months.
      (f) For patients on ART, viral load is typically measured every 3 to 6 months. More frequent
      monitoring may be considered in individuals having difficulties with ART adherence or at
      risk for nonadherence. However, for adherent patients with suppressed viral load and sta-
      ble immunological status for more than 1 year, monitoring can be extended to 6-month
      intervals.
      (g) Standard genotypic drug-resistance testing in ARV-naïve persons should focus on test-
      ing for mutations in the PR and RT genes. If transmitted INSTI resistance is a concern, or if
      a person has a history of INSTI use as PrEP or treatment, or a person presents with
      viremia while on an INSTI, providers should also test for resistance mutations in the IN

 gene. In ARV-naïve patients who do not immediately begin ART, repeat testing before initi-
      ation of ART is optional if drug-resistance testing was performed at entry into care. For vi-
      rologically suppressed patients who are switching therapy for toxicity or convenience, viral
      amplification will not be possible and therefore resistance testing should not be per-
      formed. Results from prior resistance testing can be used to help in the construction of a
      new regimen.
      (h) If infected with hepatitis B virus, tenofovir disoproxil fumarate or tenofovir alafe-
      namide plus either emtricitabine or lamivudine should be used as part of the ART regimen
      to treat both hepatitis B virus and HIV infections.
      (i) If HBsAg, and HBsAb, and HBcAb are negative at baseline, administer hepatitis B vac-
      cine series. Also, consult Guidelines for Opportunistic Infections.
      (j) Typically HBV infection has resolved with loss of HBsAb despite isolated HBcAb; confirm
      with an HBV viral load if wanted. A positive HBV viral load is indicative of acute infection
      (other symptoms will be present usually) or chronic infection. Vaccinate the patient when
      viral load is negative. Also, consult Guidelines for Opportunistic Infections.
      (k) In patients with recent HCV infection (acquired in last 6 months) or advanced immun-
      odeficiency (CD4 count less than 100 cells/mm(3)), the HCV antibody test may not be ade-
      quate for screening. HCV RNA screening is indicated in persons who have been success-
      fully treated for HCV or who spontaneously cleared prior infection. HCV antibody-negative

      with HIV who have unprotected sex with men, and persons with percutaneous/parenteral

drugs.contraindications_raw:
The most commonly reported adverse reactions were rash (18%), headache (14%), pain (13%),
   diarrhea (11%), depression (11%), back pain (9%), fever (8%), and nausea (8%). Additional ad-
   verse reactions included abdominal pain, asthenia, dyspepsia, vomiting, arthralgia, myalgia, in-
   somnia, dizziness, anxiety, and pneumonia Lactic Acidosis

   Lactic acidosis has been reported with lamivudine and tenofovir disoproxil fumarate use.
   Consider discontinuing ARV drugs temporarily in patients with a lactate 1 to 5 mmol/L (con-
   firmed with second test) while conducting additional diagnostic work-up. In patients with a lac-
   tate 5 mmol/L or greater (confirmed with second test) or 10 mmol/L (any one test), discontinue
   all ARV drugs and provide supportive therapy (eg, IV fluids, sedation, respiratory support).
   Following resolution of clinical and laboratory abnormalities, resume therapy with either an
   NRTI-sparing regimen or a revised NRTI-containing regimen. Monitor lactate monthly for 3
   months or more Musculoskeletal

   Osteopenia and osteoporosis has been reported with efavirenz and tenofovir disoproxil fu-
   marate. To help prevent osteopenia or osteoporosis from occurring, ensure that the patient
   has sufficient intake and levels of calcium and vitamin D, encourage weight-bearing exercise,
   minimize modifiable risk factors (eg, smoking, low BMI, use of steroids or medroxyproges-
   terone), and consider measuring vitamin D levels and supplementing with vitamin D3 if a defi-
   ciency is identified. If osteopenia or osteoporosis does occur, consider switching the ARV regi-
   men and supplementing with vitamin D3 to raise serum 25-OH-vitamin D concentrations to 30
   nanograms (ng)/mL Neurologic

   Neuropsychiatric symptoms (eg, abnormal dreams, psychosis, suicidal ideation or attempted
   suicide) and other CNS manifestations (eg, dizziness, somnolence, insomnia, impaired concen-
   trations, seizures, cerebellar dysfunctions) have been reported with efavirenz use. In one case-
   series, 24% of children receiving efavirenz experienced CNS manifestations, with 18% of pa-
   tients requiring discontinuation. In a separate study, 11% of patients experienced new-onset
   seizures after receiving efavirenz Black Box Warning

 Warning: Post treatment acute exacerbation of hepatitis B

   Severe acute exacerbations of hepatitis B have been reported in patients who are co-infected
   with hepatitis B virus (HBV) and human immunodeficiency virus (HIV-1) and have discontinued
   lamivudine or tenofovir disoproxil fumarate, two components of
   efavirenz/lamivudine/tenofovir disoproxil fumarate oral tablets. Monitor hepatic function
   closely in these patients and, if appropriate, initiate anti-hepatitis B treatment 1 ,2 .

      (a) If ART is initiated soon after HIV diagnosis and entry into care, repeat baseline labora-
      tory testing is not necessary.
      (b) ART is indicated for all people with HIV and should be started as soon as possible.
      However, if ART initiation is delayed, patients should be retained in care, with periodic
      monitoring as noted above.
      (c) After 2 years of consistently suppressed HIV RNA, less frequent monitoring (eg, every 6
      months) may be considered.
      (d) After 2 years of ART with consistently suppressed viral load: CD4 count 300 to 500

 cells/mm(3), monitor every 12 months; CD4 count greater than 500 cells/mm(3), CD4 mon-
      itoring is optional.
      (e) If HIV RNA is detectable at 4 to 8 weeks, repeat every 4 to 8 weeks until viral load is
      suppressed to less than 50 copies/mL, then every 3 to 6 months.
      (f) For patients on ART, viral load is typically measured every 3 to 6 months. More frequent
      monitoring may be considered in individuals having difficulties with ART adherence or at
      risk for nonadherence. However, for adherent patients with suppressed viral load and sta-
      ble immunological status for more than 1 year, monitoring can be extended to 6-month
      intervals.
      (g) Standard genotypic drug-resistance testing in ARV-naïve persons should focus on test-
      ing for mutations in the PR and RT genes. If transmitted INSTI resistance is a concern, or if
      a person has a history of INSTI use as PrEP or treatment, or a person presents with
      viremia while on an INSTI, providers should also test for resistance mutations in the IN
      gene. In ARV-naïve patients who do not immediately begin ART, repeat testing before initi-
      ation of ART is optional if drug-resistance testing was performed at entry into care. For vi-
      rologically suppressed patients who are switching therapy for toxicity or convenience, viral
      amplification will not be possible and therefore resistance testing should not be per-
      formed. Results from prior resistance testing can be used to help in the construction of a
      new regimen.

      namide plus either emtricitabine or lamivudine should be used as part of the ART regimen
      to treat both hepatitis B virus and HIV infections.

      cine series. Also, consult Guidelines for Opportunistic Infections.
      (j) Typically HBV infection has resolved with loss of HBsAb despite isolated HBcAb; confirm
      with an HBV viral load if wanted. A positive HBV viral load is indicative of acute infection
      (other symptoms will be present usually) or chronic infection. Vaccinate the patient when
      viral load is negative. Also, consult Guidelines for Opportunistic Infections.
      (k) In patients with recent HCV infection (acquired in last 6 months) or advanced immun-
      odeficiency (CD4 count less than 100 cells/mm(3)), the HCV antibody test may not be ade-
      quate for screening. HCV RNA screening is indicated in persons who have been success-

      patients with elevated ALT may need HCV RNA testing.

      with HIV who have unprotected sex with men, and persons with percutaneous/parenteral

      cose (preferably fasting). Monitor serum phosphorus concentrations in patients with

 nation should include creatinine monitoring and estimation of the glomerular filtration
      rate.

      Society of America for patients with renal disease. More frequent monitoring may be indi-
      cated for patients with evidence of kidney disease (eg, proteinuria or decreased glomeru-

      tension).
