drugs.uses_raw:
Eladocagene exuparvovec-tneq is indicated for the treatment of adult and pediatric patients
   with aromatic L-amino acid decarboxylase (AADC) deficiency This indication is approved under accelerated approval based on the change from baseline in
   gross motor milestone achievement at 48 weeks post-treatment. Continued approval for this
   indication may be contingent upon verification and description of clinical benefit in a confirma-
   tory clinical trial Administration
   Preparation

   Strictly observe aseptic technique Use of the syringe (ie, connecting the syringe to the syringe pump and priming of the cannula)
   should begin within 6 hours of starting product thaw Thawing vial: Coordinate timing of thaw and infusion. Eladocagene exuparvovec-tneq should
   be used within 6 hours of starting product thaw. Infusion takes 4 hours. The maximum time
   from thaw to completion of infusion should be no more than 10 hours Thawing vial: Thaw upright at room temperature approximately 15 minutes before use; do not
   thaw or warm any other way. Gently invert vial 3 times; do not shake. Inspect visually for par-
   ticulate matter and discoloration; appearance should be clear/colorless to slightly
   opaque/faint white suspension. Do not use if particulates or discoloration are visible • Preparing in syringe 1 :
   ●   Open syringe, label as product-filled syringe, attach filter needle.
   ●   Draw full volume of vial into syringe; invert vial and syringe, partially withdraw or angle the
       needle as necessary to maximize product recovery.
   ●   Draw air into syringe to empty needle of product. Remove needle from syringe, purge the
       air from syringe and cap.
   ●   Place syringe in plastic bag, seal, place in appropriate secondary container and deliver to
       surgical site for immediate use.

   Maintain at room temperature until use; do not refreeze thawed product Dispose any remaining product and materials in compliance with institutional policy Administration

 For single-dose intraputaminal infusion only, in a medical center which specializes in stereotac-
   tic neurosurgery Strictly observe aseptic technique Administer using an FDA-authorized cannula for intraparenchymal infusion (ie, ClearPoint
   SmartFlow Neuro Cannula Part Number NGS-NC-01-EE or 122 NGS-NC-02-EE) Eladocagene exuparvovec-tneq is intended to be administered with an infusion pump capable
   of infusing at a rate of 003 mL/min. Administer at an infusion rate of 003 mL/min to each
   target point, with a dose duration for infusion at each target point of 27 minutes Using standard neurosurgical stereotactic procedure, brain imaging for stereotactic planning
   and intraoperative navigation should be done prior to the procedure. After stereotactic regis-
   tration is complete, mark the entry point on the skull. Surgical access through the skull bone
   and dura should be performed Administer by bilateral intraputaminal infusion using a single infusion cannula in one surgical
   session at two sites (anterior and posterior) per putamen. The infusion cannula is placed and
   infusion performed separately for each target point 1 :
   ●   Tightly connect syringe with prepared eladocagene exuparvovec-tneq to Luer Lock connec-
       tor at proximal end of infusion cannula.
   ●   Load syringe onto infusion pump and secure appropriately.
   ●   Set infusion pump occlusion limit to highest level to prevent pump from alarming or dis-
       rupting infusion.
   ●   Prime at rate of up to 003 mL/minute (0.18 mL/hour), until first drop of the product can be
       seen at tip of needle (place sterile absorbent pad or gauze under cannula tip to contain any
       liquid emerging during priming).
   ●   Run infusion pump prior to insertion of cannula to ensure prepared product is flowing from
       the tip immediately before insertion.
   ●   Place infusion SmartFlow Neuro Cannula at the designation point in the putamen using
       stereotactic tools based on pre-planned stereotactic trajectories.
   ●   Starting with the first target site, insert cannula through a burr hole into the putamen and
       then incrementally withdraw cannula along the intraputaminal infusion track, distributing
       the 08 mL (infused at a rate of 003 mL/min) of eladocagene exuparvovec-tneq per puta-
       men across the planned trajectory to optimize distribution across the target site. The pump
       should run continuously throughout the 27-minute infusion, including during the reposi-
       tioning to the designated sites along the infusion track.
   ●   Once infusion is complete, stop pump and leave cannula in place for 5 minutes before with-
       drawing. Re-zero the total delivered volume setting on infusion pump as soon as cannula is

 inserted to target and perform infusion. Reinsert at next target point, repeating the same
       procedure for the other 3 target points.
   ●   After standard neurosurgical closure procedures, carry out a postoperative brain imaging
       examination of the patient to ensure there are no complications (eg, bleeding).

Chronic Hepatitis C Virus (HCV) Infection

   Sustained virologic response at 12 weeks after treatment cessation (SVR12) was achieved in
   100% of pediatric patients aged 12 to less than 18 years with chronic hepatitis C virus (HCV)
   genotype 1 or genotype 4 infection who received elbasvir 50 mg/grazoprevir 100 mg once daily
   for 12 weeks (N=22; median age, 5 years), in an open-label trial. The trial included patients
   with genotype 1 (n=21) or genotype 4 (n=1) infection without cirrhosis who were either treat-
   ment-naive (64%) or treatment-experienced (36%). Patients with genotype 1a infection with
   one or more baseline NS5A resistance-associated substitutions (RAS) were excluded from the
   study Guideline Recommendations: Direct-acting antiviral (DAA) treatment with an approved regi-
   men is recommended for all children and adolescents with HCV infection 3 years or older, as
   they will benefit from antiviral therapy, regardless of disease severity. The presence of extra-
   hepatic manifestations (eg, cryoglobulinemia, rash, and glomerulonephritis) or advanced fibro-
   sis should lead to early antiviral therapy to minimize future morbidity and mortality. Selection

drugs.contraindications_raw:
12 years or older, greater than or equal to 5%: Headache (14%) and nausea (9%) 1
   Adverse reactions observed in pediatric patients 12 years or older were consistent with those
   observed in clinical trials of elbasvir/grazoprevir in adults Black Box Warning
   Risk of Hepatitis B Virus Reactivation in Patients Coinfected with HCV and HBV

   Test all patients for evidence of current or prior hepatitis B virus (HBV) infection before initiat-
   ing treatment with elbasvir/grazoprevir. HBV reactivation has been reported in HCV/HBV coin-
   fected patients who were undergoing or had completed treatment with HCV direct acting an-
   tivirals and were not receiving HBV antiviral therapy. Some cases have resulted in fulminant
   hepatitis, hepatic failure, and death. Monitor HCV/HBV coinfected patients for hepatitis flare or
   HBV reactivation during HCV treatment and post-treatment follow-up. Initiate appropriate pa-
   tient management for HBV infection as clinically indicated Monitoring
   Therapeutic Laboratory Monitoring

 • Determine hepatitis C genotype and test for presence of virus with NS5A resistance-associ-
   ated polymorphisms in patients with genotype 1a infection prior to initiation to determine
   dosage Toxic Laboratory Monitoring

   • Prior to initiation, screen all patients for current or prior hepatitis B virus (HBV) infection us-
   ing hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg) and hepatitis B core antibody (anti-HBc) • Prior to initiation, measure HBV DNA in patients with evidence of current or prior HBV infec-
   tion • In patients with evidence of current or prior HBV infection, monitor for hepatitis flare or HBV
   reactivation (HBsAg, HBV DNA, aminotransferase levels, and bilirubin) throughout therapy and
   during post-treatment follow-up • Perform hepatic function tests prior to therapy, at treatment week 8, treatment week 12 (if
   receiving 16 weeks of therapy), and as clinically indicated • Assess severity of hepatic disease at baseline and monitor for worsening hepatic function
   during treatment by evaluating liver function tests, especially in patients with pre-existing liver
   disease or certain risk factors including hepatocellular carcinoma or alcohol abuse Toxic Physical Monitoring
   • In patients with evidence of current or prior HBV infection, monitor for clinical signs of hep-
   atitis flare or reactivation (eg, yellow eyes or skin) • Evaluate for hepatic disease at baseline and monitor for signs and symptoms of hepatic de-
   compensation during treatment (eg, jaundice, ascites, encephalopathy, variceal hemorrhage)
   1
       , especially in patients with pre-existing liver disease or certain risk factors including hepato-
   cellular carcinoma or alcohol abuse In patients with compensated cirrhosis (Child-Pugh A) or
   evidence of advanced liver disease, such as portal hypertension, more frequent hepatic labo-

   Black Box Warning
   Warning: Drug-Induced Liver Injury and Liver Failure 1

   • Elexacaftor/tezacaftor/ivacaftor can cause serious and potentially fatal drug-induced liver in-
   jury. Cases of liver failure leading to transplantation and death have been reported in patients
   with and without a history of liver disease taking elexacaftor/tezacaftor/ivacaftor, in both clini-
   cal trials and the postmarketing setting. Liver injury has been reported within the first month
   of therapy and up to 15 months following initiation of elexacaftor/tezacaftor/ivacaftor.
   • Assess liver function tests (ALT, AST, alkaline phosphatase, and bilirubin) in all patients prior
   to initiating elexacaftor/tezacaftor/ivacaftor. Assess liver function tests every month during the
   first 6 months of treatment, then every 3 months for the next 12 months, then at least annu-
   ally thereafter. Consider more frequent monitoring for patients with a history of liver disease
   or liver function test elevations at baseline.
   • Interrupt elexacaftor/tezacaftor/ivacaftor for significant elevations in liver function tests or in
   the event of signs or symptoms of liver injury. Consider referral to a hepatologist. Follow pa-
   tients closely with clinical and laboratory monitoring until abnormalities resolve. If abnormali-

 ties resolve, resume treatment only if the benefit is expected to outweigh the risk. Closer mon-

drugs.uses_raw:
Aplastic Anemia, Severe, First-line Therapy
   Complete hematological response was achieved by 7 pediatric patients and 17 achieved over-
   all response with combination eltrombopag, horse antithymocyte globulin, and cyclosporine
   for first-line treatment of severe aplastic anemia in an open-label cohort study (n=25 younger
   than 18 years). Patients had not received prior treatment with any antithymocyte globulin,
   alemtuzumab, or high-dose cyclophosphamide. Complete response was defined as absolute
   neutrophil count (ANC) greater than 1000/mcL, platelet count greater than 100 x 10(9)/L, and
   Hb greater than 10 g/dL. Partial response was defined as blood counts no longer meeting the
   standard criteria for severe pancytopenia in severe aplastic anemia (ANC greater than 500
   mcL, platelet count greater than 20 x 10(9)/L , or reticulocyte count greater than 60,000 mcL.
   Both complete and partial response required 2 consecutive serial blood count measurements
   meeting the criteria at least 1 week apart. The starting dose for patients 12 years or older was
   150 mg orally once daily (a reduced dose of 75 mg was administered for East and Southeast
   Asians). Patients 6 to 11 years received 75 mg once daily (37.5 mg for East and Southeast
   Asians), and patients 2 to 5 years received 5 mg/kg once daily (1.25 mg/kg in East and
   Southeast Asians). Duration of therapy was 6 months. Dose was adjusted for elevated platelet
   counts and hepatic impairment. Horse antithymocyte globulin was administered as 40
   mg/kg/day (actual body weight) IV on Days 1 to 4 of the 6-month treatment period.
   Cyclosporine was administered as 3 mg/kg (actual body weight) orally every 12 hours for 6
   months starting on Day 1 in those 12 years or older, except if the body mass index (BMI) was
   greater than the 95th percentile, then adjusted body weight was used. In those 2 to 11 years of
   age, the dose was 6 mg/kg orally every 12 hours, based on actual body weight for BMI at or be-
   low the 95th percentile, otherwise based on adjusted body weight. Cyclosporine was adjusted
   to maintain target therapeutic trough levels between 200 and 400 mcg/L. Following the study
   period, patients who achieved a hematologic response were permitted to receive cyclosporine
   maintenance dosing of 2 mg/kg/day orally as a fixed dose for an additional 18 months Persistent or Chronic Immune Thrombocytopenia
   Platelet counts of 50 x 109/L or greater for at least 6 out of 8 weeks (between weeks 5 and 12)
   were achieved in 41% of patients who received eltrombopag compared with 3% who received

 placebo in a randomized study (N=92). Patients were refractory to or had relapsed to one or
   more prior immune thrombocytopenia (ITP) treatments, mainly corticosteroids and im-
   munoglobulins. Response to eltrombopag by age was 36% (1 to 5 years), 44% (6 to 11 years),
   and 42% (12 to 17 years). During an open-label phase, 53% of patients receiving concomitant
   corticosteroids (n=15) were able to discontinue or reduce the dose of the steroid without need
   for rescue therapy Pediatric FDA approved indications:

   Promacta(R)
   • Severe aplastic anemia in combination with standard immunosuppressive therapy for first-
   line treatment in pediatric patients 2 years or older • Thrombocytopenia in pediatric patients 1 year or older with persistent or chronic immune
   thrombocytopenia who have had an insufficient response to corticosteroids, immunoglobu-
   lins, or splenectomy. Limit use to patients with an increased risk of bleeding because of their
   degree of thrombocytopenia and clinical condition Alvaiz(TM)
   • Thrombocytopenia in pediatric patients 6 years or older with persistent or chronic immune
   thrombocytopenia (ITP) who have had an insufficient response to corticosteroids, im-
   munoglobulins, or splenectomy. Should be used only in patients with ITP whose degree of
   thrombocytopenia and clinical condition increase the risk for bleeding Limitations of Use
   • Eltrombopag is not indicated for the treatment of patients with myelodysplastic syndromes Administration
   • Administer without a meal or with a meal low in calcium (up to 50 mg). Separate administra-
   tion of eltrombopag by at least 2 hours before or 4 hours after antacid medications, calcium-
   rich foods (more than 50 mg) including dairy products or calcium-fortified juices, certain fruits
   and vegetables, and supplements containing polyvalent cations (eg, iron, calcium, aluminum,
   magnesium, selenium, zinc) 5

   Suspension

   • Use only water to prepare oral suspension. Do not use hot water 7/13
 • Give immediately after preparation and discard any suspension not administered within 30
   minutes after preparation • Use a new single-use oral dosing syringe to prepare each dose for oral suspension Tablets

   • Take tablets whole. Do not split, crush or mix tablets with food or liquids 1 ,

Common, 1 year or older: Upper respiratory tract infection (17%), nasopharyngitis (12%),
   cough (9%), diarrhea (9%), pyrexia (9%), abdominal pain (8%), oropharyngeal pain (8%),

 In patients with chronic hepatitis C, eltrombopag in combination with interferon and ribavirin
   may increase the risk of hepatic decompensation. Eltrombopag may increase the risk of severe
   and potentially life-threatening hepatotoxicity. Monitor hepatic function and discontinue dos-
   ing as recommended Monitoring
   Therapeutic Laboratory Monitoring
   Immune Thrombocytopenia: Obtain CBC with differential, including platelet count, weekly during
   the dose adjustment phase until a stable platelet count (50 x 109/L or greater) has been estab-
   lished, then monthly thereafter during treatment Severe Aplastic Anemia: Regularly monitor platelet count during treatment Toxic Laboratory Monitoring
   Obtain CBC with differential, including platelet count, weekly during the dose adjustment
   phase until a stable platelet count (50 x 109/L or greater) has been established, then monthly
   thereafter during treatment. Following discontinuation of treatment, monitor CBC with differ-
   ential, including platelet counts, weekly for at least 4 weeks Monitor platelet counts weekly for first 2 weeks when switching between oral suspension and
   tablet formulations Monitor liver tests, including ALT, AST, and bilirubin, prior to initiation of treatment, every 2
   weeks during dose adjustment phase, then monthly thereafter. If restarting therapy after in-
   terruption for liver function abnormalities, monitor serum liver tests weekly during the dose
   adjustment phase Closely monitor patients with renal impairment during therapy Toxic Physical Monitoring
   Perform ocular examination at baseline, and monitor for signs and symptoms of cataracts reg-
   ularly during therapy

Common: The most commonly reported adverse effects were nausea (11%), diarrhea (7%),
   headache (6%), and fatigue (5%). The safety profile in pediatric patients 12 to younger than 18

   Dyslipidemia has been reported with the use of tenofovir alafenamide. Assess all patients with

   with HIV are considered at moderate risk for ASCVD). If LDL-C is 130 mg/dL or more but less

   Gastrointestinal

   Pancreatitis has been reported with the use of NRTIs and ritonavir-boosted PIs; discontinue
   the offending agent and avoid reintroduction 4

   Lactic acidosis

   Lactic acidosis has been reported with tenofovir alafenamide use. Consider discontinuing ARV
   drugs temporarily in patients with a lactate 1 to 5 mmol/L (confirmed with second test) while
   conducting additional diagnostic work-up. In patients with a lactate 5 mmol/L or greater (con-
   firmed with second test) or 10 mmol/L (any one test), discontinue all ARV drugs and provide
   supportive therapy (eg, IV fluids, sedation, respiratory support). Following resolution of clinical
   and laboratory abnormalities, resume therapy with either an NRTI-sparing regimen or a re-
   vised NRTI-containing regimen. Monitor lactate monthly for 3 months or more Black Box Warning
   Severe acute exacerbations of hepatitis B have been reported in patients who are coinfected
   with HIV-1 and HBV and have discontinued products containing emtricitabine and/or tenofovir
   disoproxil fumarate (TDF), and may occur with discontinuation of
   elvitegravir/cobicistat/emtricitabine/tenofovir alafenamide. Hepatic function should be moni-
   tored closely with both clinical and laboratory follow-up for at least several months in patients
   who are coinfected with HIV-1 and HBV and discontinue
   elvitegravir/cobicistat/emtricitabine/tenofovir alafenamide. If appropriate, anti-hepatitis B
   therapy may be warranted Monitoring

   Administration

   • Administer as a central or peripheral IV infusion over 1 hour • Administer through an IV line containing a sterile, non-pyrogenic, low-protein binding 2 mi-

   sion bag or syringe • Do not store any unused portion of infusion solution for reuse Preparation

   weight • 5 mg/mL vials: Withdraw the necessary amount of solution and dilute with NS to a maxi-
   mum concentration of 5 mg/mL; do not dilute to less than 25 mg/mL. The diluted solution
   may be placed in either a syringe or an infusion bag, depending on the volume needed. When
   using a syringe, use a gamma irradiated or ethylene oxide sterilized latex-free, polyvinyl chlo-
   ride (PVC)-free syringe. When using an infusion bag, use a non-PVC polyolefin infusion bag 6/10

   olefin infusion bag made from either polyethylene or ethylene/propylene copolymer • Discard any unused portion remaining in vials • If not administered immediately, store the diluted solution under refrigeration at 2 to 8°C (36

   were common in adults MetFORMIN monotherapy: Similar to adults; diarrhea, nausea/vomiting, flatulence, abdomi-

   Black Box Warning
   Black Box Warning

   Lactic Acidosis

   • Postmarketing cases of metFORMIN-associated lactic acidosis have resulted in death, hy-
   pothermia, hypotension, and resistant bradyarrhythmias. The onset of metFORMIN-associated
   lactic acidosis is often subtle, accompanied only by nonspecific symptoms such as malaise,
   myalgias, respiratory distress, somnolence, and abdominal pain. MetFORMIN-associated lactic
   acidosis was characterized by elevated blood lactate levels (greater than 5 mmol/L), anion gap
   acidosis (without evidence of ketonuria or ketonemia), an increased lactate/pyruvate ratio, and
   metFORMIN plasma levels generally greater than 5 mcg/mL.

   • Risk factors for metFORMIN-associated lactic acidosis include renal impairment, concomitant
   use of certain drugs (eg, carbonic anhydrase inhibitors such as topiramate), age 65 years old or
   greater, having a radiological study with contrast, surgery and other procedures, hypoxic
   states (eg, acute congestive heart failure), excessive alcohol intake, and hepatic impairment.
   • Steps to reduce the risk of and manage metFORMIN-associated lactic acidosis in these high
   risk groups are provided in the full prescribing information.

   • If metFORMIN-associated lactic acidosis is suspected, immediately discontinue
   empagliflozin/metFORMIN hydrochloride and institute general supportive measures in the
   hospital setting. Prompt hemodialysis is recommended Monitoring
   Therapeutic Monitoring

   •Monitor HbA1c every 3 months if possible. A reasonable HbA1c goal for most patients is less
   than 5%, but HbA1c goals may be more or less stringent and should be individualized to
   each patient 4 ,3
   •Perform self-monitoring of blood glucose (SMBG) as needed to assist in meeting goals of ther-
   apy; SMBG should be individualized to each patient 4 ,3 .

   • Assess renal function before treatment initiation and as clinically indicated, especially in pa-
   tients with impaired renal function (estimated GFR less than 60 mL/min/1.73 m(2)) or patients
   on loop diuretics • Reassess estimated GFR 48 hours after an iodinated contrast imaging procedure if therapy
   was discontinued (ie, patients with an estimated GFR less than 60 mL/min/1.73 m(2); those
   with a history of liver disease, alcoholism, or heart failure; or those who received intra-arterial
   iodinated contrast) to determine if renal function is stable enough to restart therapy • Measure hematologic parameters annually • Measure serum vitamin B12 levels every 2 to 3 years, especially in patients predisposed to
   decreased levels (those with inadequate vitamin B12 or calcium intake or absorption) • Assess volume status prior to therapy initiation in patients with impaired renal function (esti-
   mated GFR less than 60 mL/min/1.73 m(2)), elderly patients, or patients on loop diuretics • Monitor for signs and symptoms of volume depletion after therapy initiation Assess for ketoacidosis in patients who present with signs and symptoms consistent with se-

      transferase, ALT = alanine aminotransferase, BUN = blood urea nitrogen, CAB-LA
      = cabotegravir long-acting, CBC = complete blood count; DAA = direct-acting an-

      inhibitor, PrEP = pre-exposure prophylaxis

      (a) If ART is initiated soon after HIV diagnosis and entry into care, repeat baseline labora-
      tory testing is not necessary.
      (b) ART is indicated for all people with HIV and should be started as soon as possible.
      However, if ART initiation is delayed, patients should be retained in care, with periodic
      monitoring as noted above.
      (c) After 2 years of consistently suppressed HIV RNA, less frequent monitoring (eg, every 6
      months) may be considered.
      (d) After 2 years of ART with consistently suppressed viral load: CD4 count 300 to 500
      cells/mm(3), monitor every 12 months; CD4 count greater than 500 cells/mm(3), CD4 mon-
      itoring is optional.
      (e) If HIV RNA is detectable at 4 to 8 weeks, repeat every 4 to 8 weeks until viral load is
      suppressed to less than 50 copies/mL, then every 3 to 6 months.
      (f) For patients on ART, viral load is typically measured every 3 to 6 months. More frequent
      monitoring may be considered in individuals having difficulties with ART adherence or at
      risk for nonadherence. However, for adherent patients with suppressed viral load and sta-
      ble immunological status for more than 1 year, monitoring can be extended to 6-month
      intervals.
      (g) Standard genotypic drug-resistance testing in ARV-naïve persons should focus on test-
      ing for mutations in the PR and RT genes. If transmitted INSTI resistance is a concern, or if
      a person has a history of INSTI use as PrEP or treatment, or a person presents with
      viremia while on an INSTI, providers should also test for resistance mutations in the IN
      gene. In ARV-naïve patients who do not immediately begin ART, repeat testing before initi-
      ation of ART is optional if drug-resistance testing was performed at entry into care. For vi-

 rologically suppressed patients who are switching therapy for toxicity or convenience, viral
      amplification will not be possible and therefore resistance testing should not be per-
      formed. Results from prior resistance testing can be used to help in the construction of a
      new regimen.
      (h) If infected with hepatitis B virus, tenofovir disoproxil fumarate or tenofovir alafe-
      namide plus either emtricitabine or lamivudine should be used as part of the ART regimen
      to treat both hepatitis B virus and HIV infections.
      (i) If HBsAg, and HBsAb, and HBcAb are negative at baseline, administer hepatitis B vac-
      cine series. Also, consult Guidelines for Opportunistic Infections.
      (j) Typically HBV infection has resolved with loss of HBsAb despite isolated HBcAb; confirm
      with an HBV viral load if wanted. A positive HBV viral load is indicative of acute infection
      (other symptoms will be present usually) or chronic infection. Vaccinate the patient when
      viral load is negative. Also, consult Guidelines for Opportunistic Infections.
      (k) In patients with recent HCV infection (acquired in last 6 months) or advanced immun-
      odeficiency (CD4 count less than 100 cells/mm(3)), the HCV antibody test may not be ade-
      quate for screening. HCV RNA screening is indicated in persons who have been success-
      fully treated for HCV or who spontaneously cleared prior infection. HCV antibody-negative
      patients with elevated ALT may need HCV RNA testing.
      (l) At-risk populations: injection drug users, persons with a history of incarceration, men
      with HIV who have unprotected sex with men, and persons with percutaneous/parenteral
      exposure to blood in unregulated settings are at risk of HCV infection.
      (m) Serum sodium, potassium, bicarbonate, chloride, blood urea nitrogen, creatinine, glu-
      cose (preferably fasting). Monitor serum phosphorus concentrations in patients with
      chronic kidney disease who are on tenofovir-containing regimens. Renal function determi-
      nation should include creatinine monitoring and estimation of the glomerular filtration
      rate.
      (n) Consult recommendations of the HIV Medicine Association of the Infectious Diseases
      Society of America for patients with renal disease. More frequent monitoring may be indi-
      cated for patients with evidence of kidney disease (eg, proteinuria or decreased glomeru-
      lar function) or increased risk of renal insufficiency (eg. patients with diabetes or hyper-
      tension).
      (o) CBC with differential should be done when a CD4 count is performed. When CD4 count
      is no longer being monitored, the recommended frequency of CBC with differential is
      once a year. More frequent monitoring may be for patients receiving medications that po-
      tentially cause cytopenia (eg, trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole)
      (p) If random lipids are abnormal, fasting lipids should be obtained. Consult the ACA/AHA
      recommendations for diagnosis and management of patients with dyslipidemia.
      (q) If random glucose is abnormal, fasting glucose should be obtained. HgbA1C is not
      longer recommended for diagnosis of diabetes in patients with HIV on ART.

 (r) Assess urine glucose and protein before initiating tenofovir-containing regimens and
      monitor during treatment with these regimens.

The most commonly reported adverse effect in treatment-naive adult patients was nausea
   (10%) In trials of pediatric patients, the safety profile of emtricitabine and tenofovir alafe-
   namide was similar to that in adults, with the exception of a cohort of patients age 6 to less

   namide for preexposure prophylaxis was diarrhea (5%). Black Box Warning
   Post-Treatment Acute Exacerbation of Hepatitis B and Risk of Drug Resistance with use
   Emtricitabine/Tenofovir Alafenamide for HIV-1 Preexposure Prophylaxis (PrEP) in
   Undiagnosed Early HIV-1 Infection

   Severe acute exacerbations of hepatitis B virus (HBV) have been reported in individuals with
   HBV who have discontinued products containing emtricitabine (FTC) and/or tenofovir diso-
   proxil fumarate (TDF) and may occur with discontinuation of emtricitabine/tenofovir alafe-
   namide. Hepatic function should be monitored closely with both clinical and laboratory follow-
   up for at least several months in individuals with HBV who discontinue emtricitabine/tenofovir
   alafenamide. If appropriate, initiation of anti-hepatitis B therapy may be warranted.
   Emtricitabine/tenofovir alafenamide used for HIV-1 pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP) must only
   be prescribed to individuals confirmed to be HIV-negative immediately prior to initiating and at
   least every 3 months during use. Drug-resistant HIV-1 variants have been identified with use of
   emtricitabine/tenofovir alafenamide during use. Drug-resistant HIV-1 variants have been iden-
   tified with use of FTC/TDF for HIV-1 PrEP following undetected acute HIV-1 infection. Do not ini-

 tiate emtricitabine/tenofovir alafenamide for HIV-1 PrEP if signs or symptoms of acute HIV-1 in-
   fection are present unless negative infection status is confirmed Monitoring

      transferase, ALT = alanine aminotransferase, BUN = blood urea nitrogen, CAB-LA
      = cabotegravir long-acting, CBC = complete blood count; DAA = direct-acting an-
      tiviral; HCV = hepatitis C virus, IN = integrase, INSTI = integrase strand transfer
      inhibitor, PrEP = pre-exposure prophylaxis

      (a) If ART is initiated soon after HIV diagnosis and entry into care, repeat baseline labora-
      tory testing is not necessary.
      (b) ART is indicated for all people with HIV and should be started as soon as possible.
      However, if ART initiation is delayed, patients should be retained in care, with periodic
      monitoring as noted above.
      (c) After 2 years of consistently suppressed HIV RNA, less frequent monitoring (eg, every 6
      months) may be considered.
      (d) After 2 years of ART with consistently suppressed viral load: CD4 count 300 to 500

 cells/mm(3), monitor every 12 months; CD4 count greater than 500 cells/mm(3), CD4 mon-
      itoring is optional.
      (e) If HIV RNA is detectable at 4 to 8 weeks, repeat every 4 to 8 weeks until viral load is
      suppressed to less than 50 copies/mL, then every 3 to 6 months.
      (f) For patients on ART, viral load is typically measured every 3 to 6 months. More frequent
      monitoring may be considered in individuals having difficulties with ART adherence or at
      risk for nonadherence. However, for adherent patients with suppressed viral load and sta-
      ble immunological status for more than 1 year, monitoring can be extended to 6-month
      intervals.
      (g) Standard genotypic drug-resistance testing in ARV-naïve persons should focus on test-
      ing for mutations in the PR and RT genes. If transmitted INSTI resistance is a concern, or if
      a person has a history of INSTI use as PrEP or treatment, or a person presents with
      viremia while on an INSTI, providers should also test for resistance mutations in the IN
      gene. In ARV-naïve patients who do not immediately begin ART, repeat testing before initi-
      ation of ART is optional if drug-resistance testing was performed at entry into care. For vi-
      rologically suppressed patients who are switching therapy for toxicity or convenience, viral
      amplification will not be possible and therefore resistance testing should not be per-
      formed. Results from prior resistance testing can be used to help in the construction of a
      new regimen.
      (h) If infected with hepatitis B virus, tenofovir disoproxil fumarate or tenofovir alafe-
      namide plus either emtricitabine or lamivudine should be used as part of the ART regimen
      to treat both hepatitis B virus and HIV infections.
      (i) If HBsAg, and HBsAb, and HBcAb are negative at baseline, administer hepatitis B vac-
      cine series. Also, consult Guidelines for Opportunistic Infections.
      (j) Typically HBV infection has resolved with loss of HBsAb despite isolated HBcAb; confirm
      with an HBV viral load if wanted. A positive HBV viral load is indicative of acute infection
      (other symptoms will be present usually) or chronic infection. Vaccinate the patient when
      viral load is negative. Also, consult Guidelines for Opportunistic Infections.
      (k) In patients with recent HCV infection (acquired in last 6 months) or advanced immun-
      odeficiency (CD4 count less than 100 cells/mm(3)), the HCV antibody test may not be ade-
      quate for screening. HCV RNA screening is indicated in persons who have been success-
      fully treated for HCV or who spontaneously cleared prior infection. HCV antibody-negative
      patients with elevated ALT may need HCV RNA testing.
      (l) At-risk populations: injection drug users, persons with a history of incarceration, men
      with HIV who have unprotected sex with men, and persons with percutaneous/parenteral
      exposure to blood in unregulated settings are at risk of HCV infection.
      (m) Serum sodium, potassium, bicarbonate, chloride, blood urea nitrogen, creatinine, glu-
      cose (preferably fasting). Monitor serum phosphorus concentrations in patients with
      chronic kidney disease who are on tenofovir-containing regimens. Renal function determi-

 nation should include creatinine monitoring and estimation of the glomerular filtration
      rate.
      (n) Consult recommendations of the HIV Medicine Association of the Infectious Diseases
      Society of America for patients with renal disease. More frequent monitoring may be indi-
      cated for patients with evidence of kidney disease (eg, proteinuria or decreased glomeru-
      lar function) or increased risk of renal insufficiency (eg. patients with diabetes or hyper-
      tension).

   Administration
   May be given with or without food 16,17 .

   Preparation

   Extemporaneous oral compounds
   Note: A 1 mg/mL oral solution is available commercially.

 1 mg/mL oral suspension in SyrSpend SF PH4 (300 mL) 18 :
   • Weigh out 300 mg enalapril maleate active pharmaceutical powder and transfer to a low-ac-
   tinic prescription bottle.
   • Gradually add SyrSpend SF PH4 with a volumetric pipette to achieve a final volume of 300
   mL.
   • Shake bottle until powder is uniformly dispersed.

   • Label the container with "Shake well before using."
   • Stable for 90 days at controlled room temperature (20 to 25° C) or under refrigeration (2 to 8°
   C). Protect from light.

   1 mg/mL oral suspension in Bicitra and Ora-Sweet SF (200 mL) 17

   • Place ten 20-mg enalapril tablets in a standard polyethylene terephthalate bottle.

   • Add 50 mL of Bicitra® (sodium citrate 500 mg/5 mL and citric acid 334 mg/5 mL).
   • Shake for at least 2 minutes; let concentrate stand for 60 minutes; then shake for at least 1
   additional minute.

   • Add 150 mL of Ora-Sweet SF® to the concentrate, shake well.
   • Label with "Shake well before use" and "Protect from light."

   • Product stability is 30 days when refrigerated at 2 to 8° C (36 to 46° F)

   1 mg/mL oral solution in Citrate buffer solution, Sweetened suspending agent, or De-
   ionized water (200 mL) 19
   • Place twenty 10-mg enalapril tablets into a mortar and crush to a powder.
   • Add a small amount of vehicle to powder and triturate into a smooth paste. Vehicle options
   include deionized water, citric acid buffer solution, or a 1:1 mixture of Ora-Sweet® and
   Ora-Plus®.
   • Add vehicle in increasing volumes to make the enalapril liquid pourable. Transfer liquid to
   graduated cylinder.

   • Add enough vehicle to bring final volume to 200 mL and transfer to prescription bottle.
   • Label with "Shake well before use" and "Protect from light."

   • Stable for 91 days at room temperature (25° C) and under refrigeration (4° C) if prepared with
   citrate buffer solution or sweetened suspending agent.

   • Stable for 91 days under refrigeration (4° C) or 56 days at room temperature (25° C) if pre-
   pared with deionized water for storage in the refrigerator or for 56 days for storage at room

 temperature.

drugs.uses_raw:
Acute anticoagulation for children with ischemic stroke and cerebral venous sinus thrombosis
   (CVST), and for long-term anticoagulation in children with a substantial risk of recurrent car-
   diac embolism, CVST, and selected hypercoagulable states 3 , 4 , Multisystem Inflammatory Syndrome in Children, associated with COVID-19: Enoxaparin
   may be used for prophylactic or therapeutic anticoagulation in patients older than 2 months
   with multisystem inflammatory syndrome in children (MIS-C) associated with SARS-CoV-2
   (COVID19) Therapeutic anticoagulation should be administered to those with large coro-
   nary artery aneurysms (CAA; coronary artery z-score 10 or more) per the American Heart
   Association Kawasaki disease guidelines 17,18 , moderate to severe left ventricular dysfunction

 (unless contraindicated due to bleeding risk factors) 17 , with an ejection fraction of less than
   35%, or with documented thrombosis until resolution of thrombosis For patients without
   large coronary artery aneurysms or moderate to severe left ventricular dysfunction, consider
   prophylactic or therapeutic anticoagulation based on individual risk factors for thrombosis Antithrombotic treatment should also include low-dose aspirin in patients without risk factors
   for bleeding Venous Thromboembolism; Prophylaxis, in Hospitalized Patients with COVID-19:
   For hospitalized children with COVID-19, indications for VTE prophylaxis should be the same as
   those for children without COVID-19 For hospitalized pediatric patients with acute COVID-19 or multisystem inflammatory syn-
   drome (MIS-C) and 1 or more additional risk factors associated with hospital-acquired VTE or
   markedly elevated D-dimer, thromboprophylaxis with LMWH is suggested in combination with
   mechanical prophylaxis when feasible for patients not at high risk for bleeding. Additional risk
   factors for hospital-acquired VTE include central venous catheter, age older than 12 years, im-
   mobility, mechanical ventilation, history of VTE, obesity, and active malignancy. Do not use
   thromboprophylaxis in hospitalized pediatric patients who have an incidental finding of
   asymptomatic SARS-CoV-2 in the absence of other VTE factors that warrant prophylaxis. Post-
   discharge thromboprophylaxis may be considered on an individual basis in highly select pedi-
   atric patients with multiple ongoing risk factors Prophylaxis of venous thromboembolism in high-risk patients 2 ,8 ,25 . Enoxaparin is recom-
   mended for prophylaxis in high-risk pediatric patients undergoing major orthopedic or general
   surgery Has also been used successfully in thrombosis prophylaxis in pediatric cardiac
   catheterization 26 , and in at-risk patients with acute lymphoblastic leukemia Dosing Issues

   Once-daily prophylactic doses have been used in children 12,25,5 ,27 . Based on pharmacoki-
   netic data, doses of 1 mg/kg sub Q once daily in children 2 months or younger, and 5 mg/kg
   subQ once daily in children older than 2 months have been suggested for thromboprophylaxis In a pharmacokinetic study of children (N=126; median age 9 years) once-daily enoxa-
   parin for secondary thromboembolic prophylaxis resulted in median 24-hour trough levels
   above the desired anti-FXa activity level in over half of the subjects (53.2%). Once-daily dosing
   with frequent monitoring may be appropriate for some patients One pilot study success-
   fully used prophylactic doses of 1 mg/kg every 24 hours after initial treatment doses for chil-
   dren with deep vein thrombosis In another open label pilot study in children (n=80) with
   deep vein thrombosis, after a 2-week, twice-daily treatment period, patients received once-

 daily enoxaparin dosing (1.5 mg/kg/day) or twice-daily dosing (1 mg/kg every 12 hours). No sig-
   nificant differences were found between the 2 groups for post-thrombotic syndrome, re-
   thrombosis, bleeding, or therapy-related death Another study comparing antithrombin (AT)
   supplementation plus enoxaparin with AT supplementation alone used prophylactic enoxa-
   parin doses of 1 mg/kg every 24 hours in children with acute lymphoblastic leukemia. The
   enoxaparin/AT group had no thromboembolisms (TE) while the AT-only group had nine cases
   of TE Treatment of venous thromboembolism 2 , 8 , 28 , 5 , 27 , Enoxaparin has been safely adminis-
   tered to children with deep vein thrombosis receiving chemotherapy, maintaining anticoagula-
   tion with minimal risks Dosing Issues

   Several retrospective studies have suggested that higher initial doses are required to more
   quickly achieve therapeutic anti-Xa levels and reduce the number of dosage adjustments. In
   one retrospective study in children (n=192), higher initial doses (1.7 mg/kg every 12 hours for
   children 3 months of age and younger; 2 mg/kg every 12 hours for children greater than 3
   months of age) achieved more rapid therapeutic anti-factor Xa levels resulting in fewer
   venipunctures, without an increase in adverse events, compared with standard doses.

drugs.uses_raw:
Hepatitis B infection, chronic: Following 48 weeks of entecavir treatment, HBV DNA levels of
   less than 50 international units/mL and normalization of ALT were achieved by 58% (14/24)
   and 83% (20/24) of treatment-naïve patients and 47% (9/19) and 95% (18/19) of lamiVUDine-
   experienced patients with HBeAg-positive chronic HBV infection and compensated liver dis-
   ease (age 2 to 18 years). Daily doses were 015 mg/kg and 03 mg/kg daily, respectively. In a
   randomized, trial, HBV DNA less than 50 international units/mL (46% vs 2%), ALT normalization
   (67% vs 22%), and HBeAg seroconversion (24% vs 12%) were achieved following 48 weeks of
   entecavir 015 mg/kg daily (maximum dose 5 mg) compared with placebo in treatment-
   naïve patients with HBeAg-positive chronic hepatitis B infection, compensated liver disease,
   and elevated ALT (n=180; age 2 to 18 years) There are limited data available on use in lamiVUDine-experienced patients; use only if poten-
   tial benefit justifies potential risk However, in a observational study (n=27) of children (2.1 to 6 years of age) who have developed lamiVUDine-resistant chronic hepatitis B, there was no
   significant difference in virologic response to entecavir monotherapy compared with adefovir
   added-on to lamiVUDine therapy. Furthermore, both therapies were significantly superior to

 adefovir monotherapy, which served as a control. The mean follow-up period was 7 months
   (11.6 to 3 months) Hepatitis B with HIV co-infection: If treatment for both HIV and hepatitis B is required,
   lamiVUDine is recommended as the first-line agent as part of a fully suppressive antiretroviral
   therapy (ART) regimen. Emtricitabine is considered an effective alternative agent to lamiVU-
   Dine. In patients 2 years and older, not already receiving lamiVUDine or emctricitabine, and 14
   kg or greater, tenofovir alafenamide or tenofovir disoproxil fumarate should also be given as
   part of an ART regimen with either lamiVUDine or emtricitabine. Entecavir can be substituted
   for tenofovir alafenamide/tenofovir disoproxil fumarate if either is not available or not toler-
   ated. In patients 2 years and older who are already receiving ART with lamiVUDine or emtric-
   itabine, suggesting resistance to those agents, tenofovir alafenamide (preferred for 12 years of
   age and older) or tenofovir disoproxil fumarate (preferred for age less than 12 years) should
   be given as part of an ART regimen. In patients 12 years of age and older, entecavir should also
   be added to the regimen Pediatric Approved FDA Indications
   Indicated for treatment of chronic hepatis B infection in children 2 years of age or older with
   evidence of active viral replications and evidence of persistent elevations in serum aminotrans-
   ferases (ALT or AST) or histologically active disease Administration
   NIOSH Guidance: For full NIOSH guidance, see Special Considerations.

   Administer on an empty stomach (at least 2 hours before or after a meal)

   ESAs increase the risk of death, myocardial infarction, stroke, venous thromboem-

    ●   Chronic Kidney Disease:
    ●   In controlled trials, patients experienced greater risks for death, serious adverse cardiovas-
        cular reactions, and stroke when administered erythropoiesis-stimulating agents (ESAs) to

Pharmacology
   Epoprostenol, a metabolite of arachidonic acid, is a naturally occurring prostacyclin that dilates
   pulmonary and systemic arterial vascular beds and inhibits platelet aggregation. It undergoes
   rapid hydrolysis and enzymatic degradation. Extensively metabolized in the liver, with the two
   primary metabolites being active, but less so than the parent drug. Clearance through urine
   and feces is 82% and 4%, respectively. Half-life is estimated at 6 minutes or less 19,20 .

Common adverse events reported in children include diarrhea (6.5%), vomiting (2.1%), and infusion site pain (5.5%)
  and erythema (2.6%) 1 ,2 .

  Acute Graft vs Host Disease (aGVHD): Carbapenems were associated with an increased risk of grade II to IV aGVHD
  in pediatric patients (age 1 to 21 years) undergoing hematopoietic cell transplantation for acute leukemia (adjusted
  odds ratio, 24; 95% CI 02 to 51; N=2550). A sub-cohort of patients with more robust data that allowed more pre-
  cise timing and exposure analysis reported similar results (sub-hazard ratio, 31; 95% CI 99 to 72; (n=1174)) as well
  as an increased risk of grade III to IV aGVHD (subHR, 77; 95% CI, 25 to 52). Early carbapenem exposure (before
  day 0) especially impacted aGVHD risk. Sensitivity analyses revealed a consistent association between carbapenem ex-
  posure and aGVHD. There was no identified association between broad-spectrum cephalosporins and aGVHD. No sta-
  tistical difference was observed for antipseudomonal penicillins, although there was an increased risk. Median dura-
  tion of exposure to carbapenems was 5 days (range, 1 to 19 days) 9

  40 mg/mL suspension (30 mL) 2 :

  • Pre-calibrate a 2-ounce amber prescription bottle to 30 mL using purified water.

  40 mg/mL suspension (120 mL) 2 :
  • Pre-calibrate a 4-ounce amber prescription bottle to 120 mL using purified water.
  • Prepare sufficient volume of suspension vehicle by mixing 50:50 Ora-Sweet® or Ora-Sweet® SF:Ora-Plus®.

 Serious Infections: Patients treated with etanercept products are at increased risk for devel-
   oping serious infections that may lead to hospitalization or death. Most patients treated with
   etanercept products who developed these infections were taking concomitant immunosup-
   pressants such as methotrexate or corticosteroids. Etanercept-szzs should be discontinued if a
   patient develops a serious infection or sepsis. Reported Infections include: (1) Active tuberculosis, including reactivation of latent tuberculo-
   sis. Patients with tuberculosis have frequently presented with disseminated or extrapulmonary
   disease. Patients should be tested for latent tuberculosis before etanercept-szzs use and dur-
   ing therapy. Treatment for latent infection should be initiated prior to etanercept-szzs use. (2)
   Invasive fungal infections, including histoplasmosis, coccidioidomycosis, candidiasis, aspergillo-
   sis, blastomycosis, and pneumocystosis. Patients with histoplasmosis or other invasive fungal
   infections may present with disseminated, rather than localized, disease. Antigen and antibody
   testing for histoplasmosis may be negative in some patients with active infection. Empiric anti-
   fungal therapy should be considered in patients at risk for invasive fungal infections who de-
   velop severe systemic illness. (3) Bacterial, viral, and other infections due to opportunistic
   pathogens, including Legionella and Listeria.
   The risks and benefits of treatment with etanercept-szzs should be carefully considered prior
   to initiating therapy in patients with chronic or recurrent infection. Patients should be closely
   monitored for the development of signs and symptoms of infection during and after treatment
   with etanercept-szzs, including the possible development of tuberculosis in patients who
   tested negative for latent tuberculosis infection prior to initiating therapy Malignancies: Lymphoma and other malignancies, some fatal, have been reported in children
   and adolescent patients treated with tumor necrosis factor (TNF) blockers, including etaner-
   cept products Monitoring
   • Monitor CBC, creatinine, and liver enzymes at baseline and every 3 to 6 months during ther-
   apy • Evaluate patients at risk of hepatitis B virus (HBV) infection for prior evidence of infection be-
   fore initiating therapy 4

   • Closely monitor patients previously infected with HBV for clinical and laboratory signs of ac-
   tive HBV infection throughout therapy and for several months after discontinuation Active
   HBV infections have occurred during a latency period from 3 weeks to 20 months after therapy
   initiation 9/13
 • Test for latent TB and evaluate TB risk factors prior to initiating therapy and periodically dur-
   ing therapy. Monitor all patients for active TB during treatment, even if initial latent TB test is
   negative. Note that latent TB test may be falsely negative in patients receiving etanercept-szzs • Monitor patient closely for signs and symptoms of infection during and after therapy • Perform periodic skin examinations in all patients at risk of skin cancer • Monitor patients with heart failure for worsening of congestive heart failure

Common, adults: Infection (27% to 81%), injection site reaction (15% to 43%), diarrhea (3% to
   16%), rash (1% to 13%), pruritus (1% to 5%), pyrexia (1% to 3%), and urticaria (1% to 2%) Adverse reactions in pediatric patients were generally similar in frequency and type to those
   seen in adult patients Black Box Warning
   Warning: Serious Infections and Malignancies 2
   ●   Serious Infections:
   ●   •Patients treated with etanercept products are at increased risk for developing serious in-
       fections that may lead to hospitalization or death. Most patients who developed these infec-
       tions were taking concomitant immunosuppressants such as methotrexate or
       corticosteroids.
   ●   •Etanercept-ykro should be discontinued if a patient develops a serious infection or sepsis.
   ●   •Reported Infections include:
   ●   •Active tuberculosis, including reactivation of latent tuberculosis. Patients with tuberculosis
       have frequently presented with disseminated or extrapulmonary disease. Test patients for
       latent tuberculosis before etanercept-ykro use and during therapy. Treatment for latent in-
       fection prior to etanercept-ykro use.
   ●   •Invasive fungal infections, including histoplasmosis, coccidioidomycosis, candidiasis, as-
       pergillosis, blastomycosis, and pneumocystosis. Patients with histoplasmosis or other inva-
       sive fungal infections may present with disseminated, rather than localized, disease. Antigen
       and antibody testing for histoplasmosis may be negative in some patients with active infec-
       tion. Consider empiric antifungal therapy should be considered in patients at risk for inva-
       sive fungal infections who develop severe systemic illness.
   ●   •Bacterial, viral, and other infections due to opportunistic pathogens, including Legionella
       and Listeria.

 ●       •The risks and benefits of treatment with etanercept-ykro should be carefully considered
           prior to initiating therapy in patients with chronic or recurrent infection.
   ●       •Monitor patients closely for the development of signs and symptoms of infection during
           and after treatment with etanercept-ykro, including the possible development of tuberculo-
           sis in patients who tested negative for latent tuberculosis infection prior to initiating
           therapy.
   ●       Malignancies:
   ●       •Lymphoma and other malignancies, some fatal, have been reported in children and adoles-
           cent patients treated with tumor necrosis factor (TNF) blockers, including etanercept
           products.

   Monitoring
   Laboratory Parameters

   •Monitor CBC, creatinine, and liver enzymes at baseline and every 3 to 6 months during ther-
   apy •Evaluate patients at risk of hepatitis B virus (HBV) infection for prior evidence of infection be-
   fore initiating therapy 2

   •Closely monitor patients previously infected with HBV for clinical and laboratory signs of ac-
   tive HBV infection throughout therapy and for several months after discontinuation Physical Examination

   •Evaluate patients at risk of hepatitis B virus (HBV) infection for prior evidence of infection be-
   fore initiating therapy 2
   •Closely monitor patients previously infected with HBV for clinical signs of active HBV infection
   throughout therapy and for several months after discontinuation •Test for latent TB and evaluate TB risk factors prior to initiating therapy and periodically dur-
   ing therapy. Monitor all patients for active TB during treatment, even if initial latent TB test is
   negative. Note that latent TB test may be falsely negative in patients receiving etanercept-ykro •Monitor patient closely for signs and symptoms of infection during and after therapy •Perform periodic skin examinations in all patients at risk of skin cancer •Monitor patients with heart failure for worsening of congestive heart failure 5/7

drugs.uses_raw:
Coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19): The safety and effectiveness of etesevimab plus bam-
   lanivimab have not been assessed in pediatric patients. The adult dosing regimen is expected
   to result in comparable serum exposures of bamlanivimab in patients 12 years of age and
   older and weighing at least 40 kg as observed in adults, based on a pharmacokinetic modeling
   approach which accounted for effect of body weight changes associated with age on clearance
   and volume of distribution Emergency Use for COVID-19 Infection
   Etesevimab in combination with bamlanivimab is authorized for emergency use by the US
   Food and Drug Administration (FDA) for the treatment of mild to moderate COVID-19 in pedi-
   atric patients with positive results of direct SARS-CoV-2 viral testing, who are at high risk for
   progressing to severe COVID-19 and/or hospitalization Limitations of Authorized Use

   Bamlanivimab and etesevimab are not authorized for treatment of mild to moderate COVID-19
   in geographic regions where infection is likely to have been caused by a nonsusceptible SARS-
   CoV-2 variant based on available information including variant susceptibility to these drugs
   and regional variant frequency Etesevimab and bamlanivimab are NOT authorized for use in patients 1
   ●   2 years or older who are hospitalized due to COVID-19, OR
   ●   Who require oxygen therapy due to COVID-19, OR
   ●   Who require and increase in baseline oxygen flow rate due to COVID-19 in those on chronic
       oxygen therapy due to underlying non-COVID-19 related comorbidity

 Benefit of treatment with etesevimab and bamlanivimab has not been observed in patients
   hospitalized due to COVID-19. Monoclonal antibodies, such as etesevimab and bamlanivimab,
   may be associated with worse clinical outcomes when administered to hospitalized patients
   with COVID-19 requiring high flow oxygen or mechanical ventilation Emergency Use for Post-Exposure Prophylaxis of COVID-19

   Bamlanivimab plus etesevimab is authorized for emergency use by the US Food and Drug
   Administration (FDA) for post-exposure prophylaxis of COVID-19 in individuals who are at high
   risk of progression to severe COVID-19, including hospitalization or death 4

   Patients who meet the following criteria are considered at high risk of progression to severe
   COVID-19 4
   ●   Not fully vaccinated OR are not expected to mount an adequate immune response to SARS-
       CoV-2 vaccination (eg, individuals with immunocompromising conditions including those
       taking immunosuppressive medications) AND
   ●   Have been exposed to an individual infected with SARS-CoV-2 consistent with close contact
       criteria per CDC OR
   ●   Who are at high risk of exposure to an individual infected with SARS-CoV-2 because of oc-
       currence of SARS-CoV-2 infection in other individuals in the same institutional setting (eg,
       nursing homes, prisons)

   Limitations of Authorized Use
   Bamlanivimab and etesevimab are not authorized for use in geographic regions where expo-
   sure is likely to have been to a nonsusceptible SARS-CoV-2 variant based on available informa-
   tion including variant susceptibility to these drugs and regional variant frequency Post-exposure prophylaxis with bamlanivimab and etesevimab is not a substitute for vaccina-
   tion against COVID-19 Bamlanivimab and etesevimab are not authorized for pre-exposure prophylaxis for prevention
   of COVID-19 Administration

drugs.uses_raw:
Treatment of pulmonary tuberculosis, in combination with other antituberculosis drugs, in
   children 13 years of age and older 10,11 .

   Administration
   • May be administered with or without food 10 , • Concomitant use of antacids that contain aluminum hydroxide should be avoided for 4 hours
   following administration 10,11 .
   • TB: Fixed-dose combination dosage forms are preferred when available to decrease pill bur-
   den 5 ,4

   • TB: Directly observed therapy (DOT) is generally recommended in all cases, especially with in-
   termittent (not daily) dosage regimens 19/25
 Preparation
   Extemporaneous oral compounds

   100 mg/mL Suspension (100 mL) 12
   • Triturate 10 g of ethambutol to a fine powder using a mortar and pestle.
   • Add a small amount of Ora-Plus to wet the powder and mix into a fine paste.
   • Add a sufficient quantity of Ora-Plus in geometric portion to bring final volume to 100 mL.
   Transfer to a light-resistant container.

   • Label the container with "Shake well before using."
   • Stable for 90 days at room temperature or under refrigeration.

   50 mg/mL Suspension (120 mL) 13

   • Using alcohol swabs, remove the tablet coating from fifteen 400 mg ethambutol tablets.
   • Triturate the tablets into a fine powder using a mortar and pestle.
   • Add enough cherry syrup USP to coat the powder; levigate into a paste.
   • Continue adding cherry syrup USP in geometric amounts; mix thoroughly.
   • Transfer the suspension to a graduate; wash the mortar with cherry syrup USP and add to
   the graduate.

   • Add cherry syrup USP of sufficient amount to a final volume of 120 mL.
   • Label the container with "Shake well before using."
   • Stable for 30 days at room temperature.

drugs.contraindications_raw:
Adverse reactions reported include: hypersensitivity, anaphylactic/anaphylactoid reaction, der-
   matitis, pruritus, and joint pain; anorexia, nausea, vomiting, gastrointestinal upset, and ab-
   dominal pain; fever, malaise, headache, and dizziness; mental confusion, disorientation, and
   possible hallucinations; and thrombocytopenia, leukopenia, and neutropenia Numbness
   and tingling of the extremities due to peripheral neuritis have been reported rarely Monitoring
   Therapeutic Monitoring (TB Treatment)
   • Obtain acid-fast bacilli (AFB) smear and culture from sputum at least monthly until 2 consecu-
   tive culture specimens are negative. In patients with positive AFB smears upon diagnosis, ob-
   tain follow-up smears more frequently (eg, every 2 weeks until two consecutive specimens are
   negative) • In cases of known or suspected drug resistance, perform in vitro susceptibility tests with re-
   cent cultures of M. tuberculosis against pyrazinamide and the usual primary drugs using a ref-
   erence laboratory capable of performing these studies Toxic Monitoring
   • Monitor renal, hepatic, and hematopoietic function at baseline and periodically during ther-
   apy 10 , • Visual acuity (preferably with the Snellen eye chart) and color discrimination (Ishihara tests)
   should be assessed at baseline and periodically for the duration of therapy. Patients receiving
   doses greater than 15 mg/kg/day, patients receiving the drug for longer than 2 months, pa-
   tients with renal impairment 15 , and patients with HIV infection 16 should receive monthly vis-
   ual acuity and color discrimination testing . Perform ophthalmoscopy and finger perimetry
   during physical examination 10,11 .

 Therapeutic Drug Monitoring
   Peak adult ethambutol concentration target is at least 2 mg/mL in adults when measured 2
   hours after a dose of pyrazinamide Consider monitoring TB regimen drug levels in the following situations 7 :

   • Poor response despite adherence and susceptibility
   • Severe GI abnormalities such as short bowel syndrome, chronic diarrhea with malabsorption,
   severe gastroparesis
   • Drug-drug interactions
   • Impaired renal clearance
   • HIV coinfection
   • Diabetes
   • Use of second-line drugs

   Some experts use therapeutic drug monitoring for all patients with resistant TB early in treat-
   ment to identify poor responses earlier

      • Eligibility for shorter regimens: No extensive disease, no extrapulmonary disease except
      for TB lymphadenopathy, no prior exposure to any components of the regimen (exposure
      = more than 1 month of use)
      • MDR = Multidrug resistant TB, caused by strains resistant to at least both isoniazid and
      rifampin
      • RR = Rifampin resistant TB; caused by strains resistant to rifampin; may be susceptible or
      resistant to isoniazid (MDR-TB) or other first or second-line drugs
      • MDR/RR TB = caused by strains resistant to at least rifampin (RR) or at least rifampin and
      isoniazid (MDR)
      • Pre-XDR = caused by strains that meet the definition of MDR TB or RR TB plus are resis-
      tant to any fluoroquinolone
      • XDR = Extensively drug resistant TB; caused by strains that meet the definition of
      MDR/RR TB plus are resistant to any fluoroquinolone and at least 1 additional Group A
      drug (bedaquiline or linezolid).

   Longer, individualized regimens: Total duration is generally 18 to 24 months; used for those
   ineligible for shorter regimens, including those with extrapulmonary TB disease 3 ,1 ,2 . See Uses
   section for more information on regimen building.

 Tuberculosis meningitis, intensive treatment regimen; drug-susceptible

   Dosage: 17 to 5 mg/kg/dose orally once daily for 6 months; administer in combination with
   isoniazid 15 to 20 mg/kg/dose orally once daily, rifAMPin 5 to 30 mg/kg/dose orally once
   daily, and pyrazinamide 35 to 45 mg/kg/dose orally once daily 3 ,1
   Concomitant medication: Corticosteroid treatment with dexamethasone 3 to 6
   mg/kg/day or prednisolone 2 mg/kg/day (4 mg/kg/day for severe disease) for 4 weeks, fol-
   lowed by a gradual taper over 2 to 4 weeks 3 ,1 ,4 .
drugs.uses_raw:
Tuberculosis, active; drug-resistant

   Guidelines: Drug-resistant TB is treated with a combination of at least 4 or 5 drugs susceptible
   to the tuberculosis strain being treated. Shorter-course (6 to 9 months), all oral standardized
   regimens are preferred when patients meet eligibility criteria (no extensive disease, no extra-
   pulmonary disease except for TB lymphadenopathy, no prior exposure to components (expo-
   sure = more than 1 month of use). Longer course regimens are necessary for those not meet-
   ing eligibility criteria. 6 , 7 , 3 , 1 , Longer-course regimen building: Regimens are built using the World Health Organization
   groupings. Group A drugs are levofloxacin/moxifloxacin, bedaquiline, and linezolid. Group B
   drugs are clofazimine and cycloserine//terizidone. Group C drugs are ethambutol, delamanid,
   pyrazinamide, imipenem/cilastatin or meropenem (both used in combination with
   amoxicillin/clavulanate), ethionamide/prothionamide, and p-aminosalicylic acid. Injectable
   drugs such as amikacin, streptomycin, kanamycin, and capreomycin are not recommended for
   treating pediatric patients. Ethionamide/prothionamide and p-aminosalicylic acid are only to
   be used if better options are not possible or available. Regimen building is undertaken as
   follows:
   • Preferred: All 3 Group A agents and at least 1 Group B agent.

   • If only 1 or 2 Group A drugs are able to be used: Use available Group A drug(s) and both
   Group B drugs.

 • Use Group C drugs if unable to complete a 4 or 5 drug regimen using only Group A and B
   drugs.

   Treatment duration is generally 18 to 24 months total, and 15 to 17 months after culture con-
   version. Durations may be extended depending on patient response.

   TB meningitis: Take into consideration the cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) penetration of available
   drugs. Levofloxacin, moxifloxacin, linezolid, cycloserine, pyrazinamide, and
   ethionamide/prothionamide have good CSF penetration.

   Tuberculosis meningitis, intensive treatment regimen; drug-susceptible
   Guidelines: A 6-month intensive treatment regimen consisting of higher doses of isoniazid, ri-
   fampin, pyrazinamide, and ethionamide may be used for confirmed drug-susceptible TB
   meningitis in patients with a low likelihood of drug-resistant TB. Patients with HIV coinfection
   are not candidates for this regimen 3 ,1

   Pediatric FDA Approved Indication
   Treatment of active tuberculosis (TB) in patients with infections resistant to isoniazid or ri-
   fampin, or in patients with intolerance to other tuberculosis drugs. Use alone may lead to
   rapid acquisition of TB resistance; therefore, ethionamide should be used with at least one
   other drug that is susceptible to Mycobacterium tuberculosis Administration
   • Administration with a meal may reduce or eliminate gastrointestinal intolerance • Fixed-dose combination dosage forms are preferred when available to decrease pill burden
   3 ,1

   • Directly observed therapy (DOT) is generally recommended in all cases, especially with inter-
   mittent (not daily) dosage regimens

Common: Most common are gastrointestinal including nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, abdominal
   pain, excessive salivation, metallic taste, stomatitis, anorexia and weight loss Other adverse effects include nervous system effects, hepatic effects, and hypersensitivity re-

   Therapeutic Monitoring
   • Obtain acid-fast bacilli (AFB) smear and culture from sputum at least monthly until 2 consecu-

   tain follow-up smears more frequently (eg, every 2 weeks until two consecutive specimens are
   negative) 2 ,4 .

   • In cases of known or suspected drug resistance, perform in vitro susceptibility tests with re-
   cent cultures of M. tuberculosis against pyrazinamide and the usual primary drugs using a ref-
   erence laboratory capable of performing these studies 2 , Toxic Monitoring
   •Monitor blood glucose levels at baseline and periodically during therapy, especially in patients
   with diabetes •Monitor serum transaminases (SGOT, SGPT) at baseline and monthly during therapy 5

   •Evaluate thyroid function tests periotically during therapy •Perform ophthalmologic examinations (including ophthalmoscopy) at baseline and periodi-
   cally during therapy Therapeutic Drug Monitoring

 Consider monitoring TB regimen drug levels in the following situations 2 ,4 :
   • Poor response despite adherence and susceptibility
   • Severe GI abnormalities such as short bowel syndrome, chronic diarrhea with malabsorption,
   severe gastroparesis

   • Drug-drug interactions
   • Impaired renal clearance

   • HIV coinfection
   • Diabetes
   • Use of second-line drugs

   Some experts use therapeutic drug monitoring for all patients with resistant TB early in treat-
   ment to identify poor responses earlier

drugs.uses_raw:
Induction and maintenance of anesthesia: Beneficial effects on cerebral perfusion pressure
   and intracranial pressure, along with a lack of adverse hemodynamic effects, make etomidate
   a good anesthetic choice for use in patients with intracranial alterations or cardiovascular
   compromise Procedural sedation: Etomidate is used as a sedative for a variety of diagnostic and therapeu-
   tic procedures in the emergency department Retrospective studies have shown etomidate
   to be safe for use in pediatric patients as young as 6 months of age An initial dose of 1 to 4 mg/kg, along with an opioid for analgesia, has been reported safe and effective for fracture
   or major joint reduction Compared to pentobarbital, etomidate has shorter induction, se-
   dation and total exam times 13 , as well as a quicker return to baseline status, when used for
   sedation prior to CT 4 ,13 . Compared to midazolam for fracture reduction, etomidate achieved
   a higher rate of adequate sedation, along with faster mean induction and recovery times.

 Rates of desaturation were similar, but etomidate caused a higher incidence of pain on injec-
   tion In a prospective comparison of etomidate/fentanyl vs ketamine/midazolam for fracture
   reduction, the etomidate/fentanyl combination demonstrated shorter sedation and recovery
   times, and greater parent and practitioner satisfaction, but more procedural distress and a
   greater incidence of adverse effects. Myoclonus was seen in 25% of patients and, despite the
   concomitant use of lidocaine, injection site pain was seen in 17% of patients who received eto-
   midate A study of the acute hemodynamic effects of etomidate, with low-dose ketamine for
   analgesia during cardiac catheterization, revealed no adverse hemodynamic effects in patients
   with R-L shunts, making it a useful combination for procedures in the cath lab and operating
   room. In patients with L-R shunts, however, decreases in pulmonary blood flow and pul-
   monary-systemic shunt ratio make the combination a good choice for the operating room
   only, not the cath lab Due to known effects of etomidate on adrenal function, ketamine is preferred in the presence
   of profound shock when invasive procedures or intubation is necessary. Etomidate can be con-
   sidered as a second-line agent Route: While primarily used by the intravenous route, other routes have been explored due to
   the high incidence of pain on injection 16,10 . An aqueous 25% solution given rectally in doses
   of 5 to 5 mg/kg produced rapid hypnosis in preparation for inhalational anesthesia in one
   study (n=40, age 6 months to 6 years) It has also been used by the oral route in a syrup ve-
   hicle at a dose of 3 mg/kg, where it produced sedation similar to midazolam, but more rapid
   recovery Rapid sequence intubation (RSI): Due to its favorable pharmacodynamic profile in a variety
   of critically ill patients, etomidate may be the drug of choice for RSI in the emergency room Studies have reported favorable conditions for intubation (vocal cord position, patient reaction
   and jaw relaxation) in 99% of patients 7 , with 45% to 66% of first attempts and 23% to 34% of
   second attempts being successful when used in combination with various paralytics, lidocaine,
   and atropine 7 ,8 . Clinically insignificant changes in blood pressure and heart rate have been
   reported 8 ,9 , however, in one study, almost 20% of patients had a mean maximal percent de-
   crease (MMPD) in systolic BP of greater than 20%. Those patients in decompensated shock at
   the time of intubation had a lower MMPD and a higher mean maximal percent increase in sys-
   tolic BP than those not in decompensated shock, demonstrating favorable hemodynamic
   changes in this patient population The duration of effect for many paralytic agents is longer than the effect of single-dose etomi-
   date. Based upon a retrospective review of patients who received etomidate followed by long-
   acting neuromuscular blockade (NMB), the mean time to additional sedation was 44 minutes.

 Notably, 1% of patients did not receive an additional sedative for over 15 minutes and 1% received no additional sedative at all. To avoid continued paralysis without relief of pain
   and anxiety, it is recommended that additional sedation be given when long-acting NMB is
   used in combination with etomidate Pediatric Approved FDA Indications

   Induction of general anesthesia in patients 10 years or older Administration
   For IV administration only. Administer undiluted over 30 to 60 seconds Lidocaine IV adminis-
   tered immediately prior to dose may lessen injection pain

drugs.contraindications_raw:
The most commonly reported adverse reactions in pediatric patients treated with etravirine
   plus other antiretrovirals (n=101) were grade 2 or higher rash (15%) and diarrhea (at least 2%).
   Rash generally occurred in the second week of therapy, was mild to moderate, and resolved
   within one week on continued treatment Serious skin reactions: Stevens-Johnson syndrome, toxic epidermal necrolysis, and erythema
   multiforme major has been reported with etravirine use. Discontinue all ARV drugs and other
   possible causative agents if confirmed. Provide intense supportive care, including IV hydration,
   aggressive wound care, eye care, labial adhesion preventative care, pain management, and an-
   tipyretics. Parenteral nutrition and antibiotics may also be needed. Consult with a specialist to
   determine if corticosteroids and/or IVIG is appropriate. Do not reintroduce the offending medi-
   cation Drug reaction with eosinophilia and systemic symptoms (DRESS): DRESS is a rare but seri-
   ous adverse effect that has been reported with etravirine use. Discontinue all ARV drugs and
   other possible causative agents if confirmed. Consult with a specialist to determine if corticos-
   teroids and/or IVIG is appropriate. Provide supportive care of end-organ disease and do not
   reintroduce the offending agent Hypersensitivity reaction: Hypersensitivity reactions are rare but serious side effects that
   have been reported with etravirine use. Symptoms may include rash, constitutional findings,
   and sometimes organ dysfunction, including hepatic failure. If a hypersensitivity reaction is
   confirmed, discontinue all ARV drugs and rechallenging with etravirine is not recommended 3/18
