      transferase, ALT = alanine aminotransferase, BUN = blood urea nitrogen, CAB-LA
      = cabotegravir long-acting, CBC = complete blood count; DAA = direct-acting an-
      tiviral; HCV = hepatitis C virus, IN = integrase, INSTI = integrase strand transfer
      inhibitor, PrEP = pre-exposure prophylaxis

      (a) If ART is initiated soon after HIV diagnosis and entry into care, repeat baseline labora-
      tory testing is not necessary.
      (b) ART is indicated for all people with HIV and should be started as soon as possible.
      However, if ART initiation is delayed, patients should be retained in care, with periodic
      monitoring as noted above.
      (c) After 2 years of consistently suppressed HIV RNA, less frequent monitoring (eg, every 6
      months) may be considered.
      (d) After 2 years of ART with consistently suppressed viral load: CD4 count 300 to 500
      cells/mm(3), monitor every 12 months; CD4 count greater than 500 cells/mm(3), CD4 mon-
      itoring is optional.
      (e) If HIV RNA is detectable at 4 to 8 weeks, repeat every 4 to 8 weeks until viral load is
      suppressed to less than 50 copies/mL, then every 3 to 6 months.
      (f) For patients on ART, viral load is typically measured every 3 to 6 months. More frequent
      monitoring may be considered in individuals having difficulties with ART adherence or at
      risk for nonadherence. However, for adherent patients with suppressed viral load and sta-
      ble immunological status for more than 1 year, monitoring can be extended to 6-month
      intervals.
      (g) Standard genotypic drug-resistance testing in ARV-naïve persons should focus on test-
      ing for mutations in the PR and RT genes. If transmitted INSTI resistance is a concern, or if
      a person has a history of INSTI use as PrEP or treatment, or a person presents with
      viremia while on an INSTI, providers should also test for resistance mutations in the IN

 gene. In ARV-naïve patients who do not immediately begin ART, repeat testing before initi-
      ation of ART is optional if drug-resistance testing was performed at entry into care. For vi-
      rologically suppressed patients who are switching therapy for toxicity or convenience, viral
      amplification will not be possible and therefore resistance testing should not be per-
      formed. Results from prior resistance testing can be used to help in the construction of a
      new regimen.
      (h) If infected with hepatitis B virus, tenofovir disoproxil fumarate or tenofovir alafe-
      namide plus either emtricitabine or lamivudine should be used as part of the ART regimen
      to treat both hepatitis B virus and HIV infections.
      (i) If HBsAg, and HBsAb, and HBcAb are negative at baseline, administer hepatitis B vac-
      cine series. Also, consult Guidelines for Opportunistic Infections.
      (j) Typically HBV infection has resolved with loss of HBsAb despite isolated HBcAb; confirm
      with an HBV viral load if wanted. A positive HBV viral load is indicative of acute infection
      (other symptoms will be present usually) or chronic infection. Vaccinate the patient when
      viral load is negative. Also, consult Guidelines for Opportunistic Infections.
      (k) In patients with recent HCV infection (acquired in last 6 months) or advanced immun-
      odeficiency (CD4 count less than 100 cells/mm(3)), the HCV antibody test may not be ade-
      quate for screening. HCV RNA screening is indicated in persons who have been success-
      fully treated for HCV or who spontaneously cleared prior infection. HCV antibody-negative
      patients with elevated ALT may need HCV RNA testing.
      (l) At-risk populations: injection drug users, persons with a history of incarceration, men
      with HIV who have unprotected sex with men, and persons with percutaneous/parenteral
      exposure to blood in unregulated settings are at risk of HCV infection.
      (m) Serum sodium, potassium, bicarbonate, chloride, blood urea nitrogen, creatinine, glu-
      cose (preferably fasting). Monitor serum phosphorus concentrations in patients with
      chronic kidney disease who are on tenofovir-containing regimens. Renal function determi-
      nation should include creatinine monitoring and estimation of the glomerular filtration
      rate.
      (n) Consult recommendations of the HIV Medicine Association of the Infectious Diseases
      Society of America for patients with renal disease. More frequent monitoring may be indi-
      cated for patients with evidence of kidney disease (eg, proteinuria or decreased glomeru-
      lar function) or increased risk of renal insufficiency (eg. patients with diabetes or hyper-
      tension).
      (o) CBC with differential should be done when a CD4 count is performed. When CD4 count
      is no longer being monitored, the recommended frequency of CBC with differential is
      once a year. More frequent monitoring may be for patients receiving medications that po-
      tentially cause cytopenia (eg, trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole)
      (p) If random lipids are abnormal, fasting lipids should be obtained. Consult the ACA/AHA
      recommendations for diagnosis and management of patients with dyslipidemia.

 (q) If random glucose is abnormal, fasting glucose should be obtained. HgbA1C is not
      longer recommended for diagnosis of diabetes in patients with HIV on ART.
      (r) Assess urine glucose and protein before initiating tenofovir-containing regimens and
      monitor during treatment with these regimens.

drugs.dosing_raw:
Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome
   6 months or older

   Pretreatment regimen (mobilization, apheresis, reduced-intensity conditioning)
   • Mobilize hematopoietic stem and progenitor cells with granulocyte colony-stimulating factor
   and plerixafor according to established protocols • Perform apheresis to collect CD34+ cells for the manufacturing process 1

   • Collect and cryopreserve a back-up supply containing at least 3 x 106 CD34+ cells/kg; com-
   plete collection before initiating the conditioning regimen. Store for potential rescue treatment
   in cases of compromised product after conditioning regimen but before infusion, primary en-
   graftment failure, or prolonged bone marrow aplasia following treatment 1
   • Administer rituximab approximately 22 days prior to administration of etuvetidigene au-
   totemcel; provide preemptive treatment for potential lymphoproliferative disorder due to
   Epstein Barr virus infection • Administer busulfan and fludarabine for reduced intensity conditioning • Do not begin conditioning regimen until the entire dose and all infusion bags of etuvetidi-
   gene autotemcel have been received Etuvetidigene autotemcel infusion
   • Premedication: Chlorpheniramine 2 mg/kg/dose (maximum 10 mg/dose) IV once 15 to 30
   minutes prior to etuvetidigene autotemcel; may also administer an equivalent therapeutic op-
   tion 1
   • Minimum dosage: 7 x 106 CD34+ cells/kg based on body weight at the time of infusion;
   maximum volume should remain less than 20% of the patient's estimated plasma volume 1

   Post Administration
   • Following administration, irradiate any necessary blood products

 • Patients treated with etuvetidigene autotemcel should not donate blood, organs, tissues, or
   cells at any time in the future
drugs.uses_raw:
Etuvetidigene autotemcel is indicated for the treatment of pediatric patients aged 6 months or
   older and adults with Wiskott-Aldrich Syndrome (WAS) who have a mutation in the WAS gene
   and for whom hematopoietic stem cell transplantation is appropriate and no suitable human
   leukocyte antigen (HLA)-matched related stem cell donor is available 2/7
 Administration
   • For autologous use only. For single-dose IV use only • Confirm that patient's identify matches the unique patient information on the infusion bag la-
   bels prior to administration 1

   • When more than 1 bag of etuvetidigene autotemcel is needed, ensure that the volume to be
   infused is compatible with the recommended limit of the excipient dimethylsulfoxide (ie, total
   volume of dimethylsulfoxide administered should be less than 1% of the patient's estimated
   plasma volume). The maximum volume of etuvetidigene autotemcel to be administered
   should therefore remain less than 20% of the patient's estimated plasma volume • Administer etuvetidigene autotemcel via central venous catheter as soon as possible after
   thawing is complete • Ensure that the administration set consists of a blood transfusion set equipped with a 200
   micrometer filter • Infuse each bag by gravity within 2 hours of thawing, including any interruption during the in-
   fusion, to maintain maximum product viability • Infuse contents of each bag within 30 minutes with a maximum infusion rate of 5 mL/kg/hr • At the end of the infusion, flush all etuvetidigene autotemcel remaining in the infusion bag
   and any associated tubing with NS to ensure that as many cells as possible are infused into the
   patient. Consider the infusion volume in relation to the age and weight of the patient Preparation for infusion
   • Follow universal precautions and local biosafety guidelines for handling and disposal of etu-
   vetidigene autotemcel to avoid potential transmission of infectious diseases • Etuvetidigene autotemcel is supplied in 1 to 8 infusion bags (10 to 20 mL each) containing a
   frozen suspension of genetically modified autologous cells enriched for CD34+ cells. It is
   shipped from the manufacturing facility to the treatment center in a cryoshipper, which may
   contain multiple metal cassettes intended for a single patient. Each metal cassette contains
   one infusion bag with etuvetidigene autotemcel • Store etuvetidigene autotemcel in the vapor phase of liquid nitrogen at less than -130° C
   (-202° F) until ready for thawing and administration • After removing the infusion bag from the metal cassette, thaw the infusion bag in its sealed
   overwrap bag at 37° C (98.6° F) in a controlled thawing device until there is no visible ice in the

 infusion bag • Thaw etuvetidigene autotemcel one bag at a time prior to infusion. Don't thaw the next bag
   until the prior one has been completely infused • Once thawing is complete, immediately remove the bag from the thawing device • Carefully open the overwrap bag to remove the infusion bag which should be kept at room
   temperature (20° C to 25° C) until infusion. Gently massage the infusion bag to resuspend the
   cells. Inspect the content of the infusion bag for any remaining visible cellular aggregates.
   Small clumps of cellular material should disperse with gentle manual mixing. Do not shake the
   bag • Do not sample, alter, irradiate or refreeze etuvetidigene autotemcel

   Malignancy: 1 patient was diagnosed with papillary thyroid cancer 5 years after treatment.
   The patient had a family history of Graves' disease; the tumor cells did not contain viral vector
   gene sequences Management of adverse effects

   • Engraftment failure: Defined as failure to reach absolute neutrophil count greater than 500
   cells/microL associated with no evidence of bone marrow recovery by day Infuse the non-
   transduced back-up hematopoietic stem cells collected during mobilization 5/7

   serum IgG level above 5 g/L. After infusion, irradiate any required blood products • Neutropenia: For persistent neutropenia beyond 6 to 7 weeks post-infusion despite the use
   of granulocyte colony-stimulating factor, consider administration of the non-transduced back-
   up hematopoietic stem cells collected during mobilization or alternative treatments Monitoring

Afinitor® and Afinitor Disperz®: Indicated in pediatric patients 1 year or older with tuberous
   sclerosis complex (TSC) for the treatment of subependymal giant cell astrocytoma that re-
   quires therapeutic intervention but cannot be curatively resected 1 , Afinitor Disperz®: Indicated as adjunctive treatment in patients 2 years or older with TSC-as-
   sociated partial-onset seizures 1 ,2 .

   Administration
   NIOSH Guidance: For full NIOSH guidance, see Special Considerations.

 General Information: Use special handling and disposal procedures for anticancer agents. 1

   Tablets (Afinitor®)

   • Administer at the same time every day, consistently with or without food • Swallow tablets whole with a glass of water. Do not crush or break • Do not combine tablets and tablets for oral suspension to achieve the desired dose; adminis-
   ter only 1 dosage form Tablets for Suspension (Afinitor Disperz®)

   • Administer at the same time every day, consistently with or without food • Do not combine tablets and tablets for oral suspension to achieve the desired dose; adminis-
   ter only 1 dosage form • Administer tablets for oral suspension only as a suspension. Administer immediately after
   preparation and discard if not used within 60 minutes Preparation of Tablets for Suspension

   • Wear gloves if preparing suspension for another person • Prepare only with water • If using an oral syringe, add unbroken tablets to a 10-mL oral syringe. Add 5 mL of water
   only and 4 mL air to syringe, and allow the filled syringe to sit with tip upright for 3 minutes to
   suspend the tablets. Gently invert the syringe 5 times immediately prior to administration.
   After administration, add another 5 mL water and 4 mL air to suspend particles remaining in
   syringe, swirl, and administer entire contents. Do not exceed 10-mg dose per oral syringe; mix
   another syringe if required • If using a small drinking glass, add unbroken tablets to a small drinking glass (maximum
   capacity, 100 mL) that contains 25 mL of water only, and allow the glass to sit for 3 minutes to
   suspend the tablets. Stir the contents gently with a spoon immediately before drinking. After
   administration, add another 25 mL water, stir with same utensil to resuspend the remaining
   particles and administer contents. Do not exceed 10-mg dose per glass; mix another glass if
   required

drugs.pharmacokinetics_summary:
Pharmacology
   Mechanism of action

   Everolimus, a kinase inhibitor, forms a complex with FKBP-12 and the everolimus: FKBP-12
   complex binds to mammalian target of rapamycin (mTOR) complex 1 and thereby inhibits
   mTOR kinase activity. Everolimus reduces the activity of S6 ribosomal protein kinase and eu-
   karyotic elongation factor 4E-binding protein, inhibits the expression of hypoxia-inducible fac-
   tor, and reduces vascular endothelial growth factor expression 1 ,2 .

   with severe cognitive impairment requiring external assistance for recovery) (n=58) 1

   Black Box Warning
   Risk of Thyroid C-Cell Tumors

   Exenatide extended-release causes an increased incidence in thyroid C-cell tumors at clinically
   relevant exposures in rats compared to controls. It is unknown whether exenatide extended-
   release causes thyroid C-cell tumors, including medullary thyroid carcinoma (MTC), in humans,
   as the human relevance of exenatide extended-release-induced rodent thyroid C-cell tumors
   has not been determined.

   Exenatide extended-release is contraindicated in patients with a personal or family history of
   MTC and in patients with Multiple Endocrine Neoplasia syndrome type 2 (MEN 2). Counsel pa-

 tients regarding the potential risk for MTC with the use of exenatide extended-release and in-
   form them of symptoms of thyroid tumors (eg, mass in the neck, dysphagia, dyspnea, persis-
   tent hoarseness). Routine monitoring of serum calcitonin or using thyroid ultrasound is of un-
   certain value for detection of MTC in patients treated with exenatide extended-release 1

   Monitoring
   Therapeutic Monitoring

   • Monitor HbA1c every 3 months if possible. A reasonable HbA1c goal for most patients is less
   than 5%, but HbA1c goals may be more or less stringent and should be individualized to
   each patient 5 ,4

   • Perform self-monitoring of blood glucose (SMBG) as needed to assist in meeting goals of
   therapy; SMBG should be individualized to each patient 5 , Toxic Monitoring

   • Carefully monitor for signs and symptoms of pancreatitis after initiating therapy • Closely monitor for signs and symptoms of allergic reactions in patients with a history of ana-
   phylaxis or angioedema with other GLP-1 receptor agonists • Monitor for adverse reactions that may lead to hypovolemia in patients with renal transplan-
   tation and patients with mild renal impairment • If thyroid nodules are noted on physical exam or neck imaging, patient should be referred to
   an endocrinologist. Routine monitoring using thyroid ultrasound is of uncertain value • If serum calcitonin levels are elevated, patient should be referred to an endocrinologist.
   Routine monitoring of serum calcitonin is of uncertain value

drugs.uses_raw:
Hemophilia B (congenital factor IX deficiency)

 Bleeding episodes, control and prevention: Control of bleeding was achieved with 1 dose of
   coagulation factor IX Fc fusion protein recombinant in the majority of patients with factor IX
   deficiency for prophylaxis and management of bleeding episodes. Patients with severe factor
   IX deficiency (age range, 12 to 71 years old; n=123) were evaluated in trials for 2 prophylactic
   treatment regimens (fixed weekly and individualized interval prophylaxis) and an episodic (ie,
   on-demand) treatment, and to determine hemostatic efficacy of coagulation factor IX Fc fusion
   protein recombinant for bleeding episodes and perioperatively in major surgery. In the fixed
   interval prophylaxis arm, patients received an initial dose of 50 international units/kg, which
   was then dose adjusted to maintain a factor IX trough of at least 1% to 3% above baseline (me-
   dian study dose, 2 international units/kg). Patients in the individualized interval arm re-
   ceived factor IX Fc fusion protein recombinant 100 international units/kg every 10 days, with
   the dosing interval adjusted to maintain a factor IX trough of at least 1% to 3% greater than
   baseline as clinically indicated (median dosing interval, 5 days). Patients in the episodic
   treatment arm received therapy only as needed. Across all groups, 636 bleeding episodes
   were assessed in 114 patients, who received a median total dose per bleeding episode of 99 international units/kg. Most patients were treated with 1 dose (90.4%); 9% of patients
   required 2 doses, and 7% required 3 doses. At 8 to 12 hours after treatment, 7% of pa-
   tients treated with 1 dose had excellent or good response, 7% had moderate response, and 6% had no response. Bleeding, prophylaxis: In patients with factor IX deficiency, overall annualized bleeding rates
   were lower in fixed weekly and individualized weekly prophylaxis groups compared with an
   episodic (ie, on-demand) treatment group in a small study (n=123; 12 to 71 years of age). In the

drugs.uses_raw:
Clinolipid®

 Clinolipid is indicated in pediatric patients, including term and preterm neonates, as a source
   of calories and essential fatty acids for parenteral nutrition (PN) when oral or enteral nutrition
   is not possible, insufficient, or contraindicated Intralipid® and Nutrilipid®

   • Intralipid® 20% and Nutrilipid® 20% fat emulsions are indicated as a source of calories and
   essential fatty acids for parenteral nutrition when oral or enteral nutrition is not possible, in-
   sufficient, or contraindicated 11,10

   • Intralipid® 30% fat emulsion is indicated for the preparation of 3-in-1 or total nutrient admix-
   tures as a source of calories and essential fatty acids in adult and pediatric patients requiring
   parenteral nutrition for an extended time (usually more than 5 days) 13

   Smoflipid®

   • Smoflipid® (fat emulsion/fish oil/soybean oil) injectable lipid emulsion is indicated in pedi-
   atric patients, including term and preterm neonates, as a source of calories and essential fatty
   acids for parenteral nutrition when oral or enteral nutrition is not possible, insufficient, or con-
   traindicated 12

   Omegaven®

   • Omegaven® is indicated as a source of calories and fatty acids in pediatric patients with par-
   enteral nutrition-associated cholestasis (PNAC) 4

   • Omegaven® is not indicated for the prevention of PNAC. It has not been demonstrated that
   Omegaven(R) prevents PNAC in parenteral nutrition (PN)-dependent patients 4
   • It has not been demonstrated that the clinical outcomes observed in patients treated with
   Omegaven(R) are a result of the omega-6:omega-3 fatty acid ratio of the product 4

   Administration
   General Information

   • For IV infusion through a central or peripheral line only 1 ,9 ,10,11,12 .

   • Intralipid® 30%: Not for direct infusion; it must be infused as part of an admixture into a
   central or peripheral vein 13
   • Pharmacy bulk package (1000 mL container): For admixing use only and not intended for
   direct IV administration 1 ,11,10 .

 Specific Administration Information

   • Use a 2 micron in-line filter 1 ,12,11,10,13,4 .

   • Do not administer through di-2-ethylhexyl phthalate (DEHP) sets or lines 1 ,12,13,11,10,4 .

   • Can be infused concurrently into same vein as dextrose-amino acid solutions (as part of par-
   enteral nutrition) by a Y-connector located near the infusion site; flow rates should be con-
   trolled separately by individual pumps 12 , 11 , 10 , • When administered with amino acids and dextrose, the choice of central vs peripheral route
   will depend on osmolarity of the final infusate 1 ,12,4 ,11 . Admixtures greater than or equal to
   900 mOsm/L osmolarity must be infused through a central vein; osmolarity less than 900
   mOsm/L may be administered peripherally 12,4 .

   • To prevent air embolism use a nonvented infusion set or close the vent on a vented set,
   avoid multiple connections, do not connect flexible bags in series, fully evacuate residual gas in
   the bag prior to administration, do not pressurize the flexible bag to increase flow rates
   1 , 12 , 11 , For Omegaven®, use a vented infusion set when infused from the bottle • If using Nutrilipid® 20% bags for direct infusion, do not use or penetrate the blocked port

drugs.contraindications_raw:
Clinolipid®
   Adverse reactions that occurred in ≥ 5% of patients included hyperbilirubinemia, patent ductus
   arteriosus, anemia, gastroesophageal reflux disease, bradycardia, feeding intolerance, neona-
   tal intraventricular hemorrhage, increased alkaline phosphatase, atrial septal defect, hypona-

   Intralipid
   Adverse effects that occur more frequently with Intralipid-treated patients includes contamina-
   tion of the IV catheter resulting in sepsis and vein irritation by concurrently infused hypertonic
   solutions which may result in thrombophlebitis. These adverse effects are inseparable from
   the hyperalimentation procedure with or without Intralipid 19

   Nutrilipid

   Adverse effects with IV lipid emulsions include hyperlipidemia, hypercoagulability, throm-
   bophlebitis, and thrombocytopenia. Additional adverse effects reported in long-term use in-
   clude hepatomegaly, jaundice, splenomegaly, thrombocytopenia, leukopenia, liver function
   test abnormalities, brown pigmentation of the liver, and overloading syndrome Omegaven

   The most common adverse reaction with Omegaven-treated pediatric patients were vomiting
   (46%), agitation (35%), bradycardia (35%), apnea (20%), viral infection (16%), and erythema
   (12%) Smoflipid

   There was no difference in the incidence of infection between combination lipid emulsions
   (Smoflipid or Lipoplus) and standard lipid emulsions (soybean oil only) in a meta-analysis (6 tri-
   als) of neonates and infants younger than 12 months There were no significant differences in laboratory safety parameters, including liver enzymes,
   on day 29 between Smoflipid and Intralipid in a randomized, double-blind study of 28 children
   (mean age 3 and 8 months, respectively) The association between cholestasis and different lipid concentrations has not been estab-
   lished 10/18
 Monitoring
   Toxic Laboratory Monitoring
   • Carefully monitor pediatric patient's ability to eliminate the infused lipids from the circulation
   (eg, measure serum triglycerides, plasma free fatty acid levels, or both) • Obtain serum triglyceride levels before starting the infusion and regularly during therapy Additionally, check serum triglyceride levels before each dosage adjustment in patients with el-
   evated triglyceride levels • Carefully assess lab test results (eg, leukocytosis, hyperglycemia) for signs of early infection • Monitor for signs and symptoms of fat overload (eg, anemia, leukopenia, thrombocytopenia,
   coagulation disorders, hyperlipidemia, and deteriorating liver function) 4

   • Carefully monitor severely malnourished patients for signs of refeeding syndrome (eg, inter-
   cellular shifts of potassium, phosphorus, and magnesium, and thiamine deficiency) • Monitor fluid and electrolyte status, serum osmolarity, blood glucose, liver and kidney func-
   tion, coagulation parameters, and complete blood count, including platelets, throughout treat-
   ment 6 , with frequent monitoring of platelet counts in neonates 19
   • Perform liver function tests to monitor for parenteral nutrition-associated liver disease and
   other hepatobiliary disorders • Monitor for laboratory evidence of essential fatty acid deficiency; laboratory tests are avail-
   able to determine serum fatty acid levels; reference values should be consulted to help deter-
   mine adequacy of essential fatty acid status • Monitor fluid status closely in patients with pulmonary edema or heart failure Laboratory interference: Omegaven® may interfere with some laboratory blood tests (e.g.,
   hemoglobin, lactate dehydrogenase, bilirubin, and oxygen saturation) if blood is sampled be-
   fore lipids have cleared from the bloodstream. Perform these tests at least 6 hours after the
   lipid infusion is stopped 6

   Toxic Physical Monitoring

   • Monitor for signs or symptoms of hypersensitivity reactions • Carefully monitor patients for signs and symptoms of early infection (eg, fever, chills) and fre-
   quently inspect the parenteral catheter insertion site • Carefully monitor severely malnourished patients for symptoms of refeeding syndrome (eg,
   fluid retention) 11/18
 • Monitor for signs and symptoms of fat overload (eg fever, hepatomegaly, and CNS manifesta-
   tions [eg, coma]) 4

   • Monitor patients for signs and symptoms of essential fatty acid deficiency (eg, fluid retention) • Monitor fluid status throughout treatment and especially in patients with pulmonary edema
   or heart failure

   Addiction, abuse, and misuse: Because the use of transmucosal fentanyl citrate exposes pa-
   tients and other users to the risks of opioid addiction, abuse, and misuse, which can lead to
   overdose and death, assess each patient’s risk prior to prescribing and reassess all patients
   regularly for the development of these behaviors and conditions.
   Life-threatening respiratory depression: Serious, life-threatening, or fatal respiratory de-
   pression has occurred in patients treated with transmucosal fentanyl citrate, including follow-
   ing use in opioid non-tolerant patients and improper dosing. Evaluate patients for respiratory
   depression, especially during initiation of transmucosal fentanyl citrate or following a dosage
   increase. To reduce the risk of respiratory depression, proper dosing and titration of transmu-
   cosal fentanyl citrate are essential. The substitution of transmucosal fentanyl citrate for any
   other fentanyl product may result in fatal overdose. Due to the risk of respiratory depression,
   transmucosal fentanyl citrate is contraindicated in the management of acute or postoperative
   pain including headache/migraine and in opioid non-tolerant patients.
   Accidental ingestion: Accidental ingestion of even one dose of transmucosal fentanyl citrate,
   especially by children, can result in a fatal overdose of fentanyl. Death has been reported in
   children who have accidentally ingested transmucosal immediate-release fentanyl products.
   Transmucosal fentanyl citrate must be kept out of reach of children.
   Risks from concomitant use with benzodiazepines or other CNS depressants:
   Concomitant use of opioids with benzodiazepines or other central nervous system (CNS) de-
   pressants, including alcohol, may result in profound sedation, respiratory depression, coma,
   and death. Reserve concomitant prescribing of transmucosal fentanyl citrate and benzodi-
   azepines or other CNS depressants for use in patients for whom alternative treatment options
   are inadequate.
   Risk of medication errors: Substantial differences exist in the pharmacokinetic profile of
   transmucosal fentanyl citrate compared to other fentanyl products that result in clinically im-
   portant differences in the extent of absorption of fentanyl and that could result in fatal over-
   dose. When prescribing, do not convert patients on a mcg per mcg basis from any other fen-
   tanyl products to transmucosal fentanyl citrate. When dispensing, do not substitute a transmu-
   cosal fentanyl citrate prescription for other fentanyl products.

 Cytochrome P450 3A4 interaction: The concomitant use of transmucosal fentanyl citrate
   with all cytochrome P450 3A4 inhibitors may result in an increase in fentanyl plasma concen-
   trations, which could increase or prolong adverse reactions and may cause potentially fatal
   respiratory depression. In addition, discontinuation of a concomitantly used cytochrome P450
   3A4 inducer may result in an increase in fentanyl plasma concentration. Evaluate patients at
   frequent intervals receiving fentanyl citrate and any CYP3A4 inhibitor or inducer.

   Risk Evaluation and Mitigation Strategy (REMS) access program: Because of the risk for
   misuse, abuse, addiction, and overdose, transmucosal fentanyl citrate is available only through
   a restricted program required by the Food and Drug Administration, called a Risk Evaluation
   and Mitigation Strategy (REMS). Under the Transmucosal Immediate Release Fentanyl (TIRF)
   REMS Access program, outpatients, healthcare professionals who prescribe to outpatients,
   pharmacies, and distributors must enroll in the program. Further information is available at
   www.TIRFREMSAccess.com or by calling 1-866-822-1483.
   Neonatal opioid withdrawal syndrome: Prolonged use of transmucosal fentanyl citrate dur-
   ing pregnancy can result in neonatal opioid withdrawal syndrome, which may be life-threaten-
   ing if not recognized and treated, and requires management according to protocols developed
   by neonatology experts. If opioid use is required for a prolonged period in a pregnant woman,
   advise the patient of the risk of neonatal opioid withdrawal syndrome and ensure that appro-

drugs.uses_raw:
Filgrastim-txid is a biological product approved by the US FDA as a biosimilar to filgrastim.

   Filgrastim-txid is indicated for the following: 1
   • To decrease the incidence of infection associated with febrile neutropenia in patients with
   nonmyeloid malignancies receiving myelosuppressive drugs that are associated with signifi-
   cant incidence of severe neutropenia with fever.

   • To reduce the time to neutrophil recovery and the duration of fever with acute myeloid
   leukemia, following induction or consolidation therapy.

   • To reduce the duration of neutropenia and neutropenia-related clinical sequelae (febrile neu-
   tropenia) in patients with nonmyeloid malignancies who are receiving myeloablative chemo-
   therapy followed by marrow transplantation.

 • To increase survival in patients with acute exposure to myelosuppressive doses of radiation.

   • Chronic administration to reduce the incidence and duration of sequelae of neutropenia (eg,
   fever, infection, oropharyngeal ulcer) in symptomatic patients with congenital neutropenia,
   cyclic neutropenia, or idiopathic neutropenia.
   • To mobilize autologous hematopoietic progenitor cells into the peripheral blood for collec-
   tion by leukapheresis.

   Administration
   Subcutaneous

   • Remove prefilled syringe from refrigerator and allow it to reach room temperature for at
   least 30 minutes, but not longer than 24 hours, prior to administration • Discard any syringe left at room temperature for longer than 24 hours • Discard unused portion of syringes • Prefilled syringe with BD UltraSafe Passive™ Needle Guard may not accurately measure vol-
   umes less than 3 mL; direct administration of volume less than 3 mL (180 mcg) is not rec-
   ommended 1

   • Inject into outer area of upper arms, abdomen, thighs, or upper outer area of the buttock Intravenous

   • Administer as a short IV infusion (over 15 to 30 minutes) or via continuous infusion Preparation

   Intravenous

   Do not dilute in NS; may be diluted with D5W to a concentration of 15 mcg/mL Protect solutions diluted to 15 mcg/mL concentrations from adsorption to plastic materials by
   adding albumin (human) to a final concentration of 2 mg/mL Solutions diluted in D5W plus albumin are compatible with polyvinylchloride and polyolefin Store diluted solutions at room temperature for up to 14 hours, including the time during stor-
   age and duration of infusion

drugs.contraindications_raw:
Common (10% incidence or greater): Viral infection (29%), nasopharyngitis (26%), and bacte-
   rial infections (11%) 1

   Black Box Warning
   Thrombotic Events

   Serious thrombotic events have occurred in fitusiran-treated patients with risk factors for
   thromboembolism including persistent antithrombin (AT) activity less than 15%, use of fi-
   tusiran 80 mg once monthly, presence of indwelling venous catheters, and in the postopera-
   tive setting when bleed management guidelines were not followed. Monitor AT activity using
   an FDA-cleared test and target AT activity 15% to 35% to reduce the risk of thrombosis.
   Monitor patients for signs and symptoms of thrombotic events. Interrupt fitusiran in patients
   with a thrombotic event and manage as clinically indicated.

   Acute and Recurrent Gallbladder Disease

   Acute and recurrent gallbladder disease, including cholelithiasis and cholecystitis have oc-
   curred in fitusiran-treated patients, some of whom required cholecystectomy or had complica-
   tions (eg, pancreatitis) related to gallbladder disease. Monitor patients for signs and symptoms
   of acute and recurrent gallbladder disease. Consider interruption or discontinuation of fi-
   tusiran if gallbladder disease occurs. Consider alternative treatment for hemophilia in patients
   with a history of symptomatic gallbladder disease 5/9

   ally. Additional AT measurements may be considered if bleeding control is inadequate Toxic Monitoring
   • Monitor AST, ALT, and total bilirubin prior to initiating, monthly for at least the first 6 months
   of therapy, monthly for at least 6 months after a dose increase, and periodically thereafter as
   clinically indicated • Monitor for signs and symptoms of thrombotic events • Monitor for signs and symptoms of acute and recurrent gallbladder disease

drugs.contraindications_raw:
Flecainide can cause new or worsened arrhythmias, including AV block, bradycardia, ventricu-
   lar tachycardia, and torsades de pointes in children 3 ,15,4 ,17 . Higher risk of proarrhythmias in
   patients with atrial flutter or ventricular arrhythmias and structurally abnormal hearts. Cardiac
   arrest and sudden death have been reported in children with structurally abnormal hearts
   treated with flecainide. The overall incidence of proarrhythmias is approximately 7% in chil-
   dren, with serious proarrhythmias occurring in less than 1% of patients 1 ,17 . In complex ven-
   tricular arrhythmias or sustained ventricular tachycardia patients, the incidence of proarrhyth-
   mia appears to be related to the dose and to the underlying cardiac disease. Although in a ret-
   rospective review of children who received flecainide (n=369) for supraventricular tachycardias
   or ventricular arrhythmias, most proarrhythmias that occurred were not correlated with high
   dosages or plasma concentrations Has a negative inotropic effect, and may worsen heart

 failure Slows cardiac conduction and causes dose-related PR, QRS, QT interval increases.
   Nausea, dizziness, blurred vision, and headache have been reported in children 15,4 ,1 . Effect of
   drug may be altered by electrolyte abnormalities (hypokalemia or hyperkalemia); correct be-
   fore administration. Use not recommended in patients with hepatic impairment (primarily me-
   tabolized) unless potential benefits outweigh risks Black Box Warning
   An excessive mortality or non-fatal cardiac arrest rate was seen in patients (adults) with
   asymptomatic non-life-threatening ventricular arrhythmias and a history of myocardial infarc-
   tion treated with flecainide compared with that seen in patients assigned to a carefully
   matched placebo-treated group in the Cardiac Arrhythmia Suppression Trial (CAST). It is pru-
   dent to consider the risks of Class IC agents (including flecainide), coupled with the lack of any
   evidence of improved survival, generally unacceptable in patients without life-threatening ven-
   tricular arrhythmias, even if the patients are experiencing unpleasant, but not life-threatening,
   symptoms or signs. Flecainide is not recommended for use in patients with chronic atrial fibril-
   lation. Case reports of ventricular proarrhythmic effects in patients treated with flecainide for
   atrial fibrillation/flutter have included increased PVCs, VT, ventricular fibrillation (VF), and death Monitoring
   Monitor ECG continuously during initiation of therapy, as this is the most common time to see
   drug-induced arrhythmias. Obtain ECG periodically thereafter during therapy. Follow trough
   serum concentrations closely at initiation, 3 to 5 days after any dose change, and with any sig-
   nificant change in clinical status or diet. Therapeutic trough levels in children are 200 to 800
   nanograms/mL. Plasma level monitoring is especially important for patients with renal or he-
   patic impairment and patients on concurrent amiodarone therapy. Monitor electrolytes for
   any abnormalities 3 , 6 ,

   breaks at the same body site, maintenance therapy with topical corticosteroids once to twice
   weekly may reduce the rates of relapse and increase the time to first flare relative to the use of
   moisturizers alone. For long-term management, the least potent corticosteroid that is effective
   should be used to minimize the risk of adverse effects Tape: Serves as both a vehicle and an occlusive dressing. Retention of insensible perspiration
   by the tape results in hydration of the stratum corneum and improved diffusion of the medica-
   tion. The skin is protected from scratching, rubbing, desiccation, and chemical irritation. The
   tape acts as a mechanical splint to fissured skin. Since it prevents removal of the medication
   by washing or the rubbing action of clothing, the tape formulation provides a sustained action FDA approved pediatric indications: Flurandrenolide cream, lotion, ointment, and tape are

   atric patients, were nervousness, sweating, and tremor. Cough increase, dysmenorrhea, ecchy-
   mosis, emotional lability, epistaxis, manic reaction, rash, sinusitis, and weight decrease were
   each reported in 2 or more pediatric patients (and more frequently than with placebo), but
   were not observed in adults 2 , Black Box Warning

 Antidepressants increased the risk compared to placebo of suicidal thinking and behavior (sui-
   cidality) in children, adolescents, and young adults in short-term studies of major depressive
   disorder (MDD) and other psychiatric disorders. Anyone considering the use of fluvoxamine
   maleate or any other antidepressant in a child, adolescent, or young adult must balance this
   risk with the clinical need. Short-term studies did not show an increase in the risk of suicidality
   with antidepressants compared to placebo in adults beyond age 24; there was a reduction in
   risk with antidepressants compared to placebo in adults aged 65 and older. Depression and
   certain other psychiatric disorders are themselves associated with increases in the risk of sui-
   cide. Patients of all ages who are started on antidepressant therapy should be monitored ap-
   propriately and observed closely for clinical worsening, suicidality, or unusual changes in be-
   havior. Families and caregivers should be advised of the need for close observation and com-
   munication with the prescriber. FluvoxaMINE maleate is not approved for use in pediatric pa-
   tients except for obsessive-compulsive disorder Monitoring
   Monitor for clinical worsening, suicidality, and unusual changes in behavior, especially within
   the first few months of initiation and during dose increases and decreases. Monitor for sero-
   tonin syndrome during therapy and for withdrawal symptoms during drug discontinuation.
   Regularly monitor height and weight during long-term treatment. Periodically reassess need
   for continued treatment. Carefully monitor patients with controlled epilepsy for increased
   seizure frequency during use 2 ,4 .

Common, pediatric: Bleeding complications, anemia, thrombocytopenia, allergic reactions,
   generalized skin associated events, abnormal liver function, hypokalemia, and hypotension 7
   In an open-label, prospective dose-finding and pharmacokinetic study in children (n=24) re-
   ceiving fondaparinux, 2 bleeding events were reported (intracranial hemorrhage and minor,
   clinically significant gastrointestinal bleeding) In the FondaKIDS II and III studies (N= 35 and
   N=277, respectively), reported major bleeding (intracranial hemorrhage, pulmonary hemor-

 rhage, subretinal hemorrhage, blood in stool, GI bleeding, and hematuria) occurred in 5% to 6% of patients. Minor bleeding, which included blood in stool, injection site bleeding, central
   venous catheter site bleeding, tracheostomy bleeding, bleeds at other sites, and epistaxis, oc-
   curred in 4% to 19% of patients 5 ,6 .

   Although fondaparinux has a low risk of causing heparin-induced thrombocytopenia (HIT) or
   exacerbating HIT when HIT antibodies are present 9 , a case of warfarin and fondaparinux-as-
   sociated HIT with rethrombosis was reported in the literature in an 11-year-old girl. The pa-
   tient developed HIT (HIT antibodies confirmed by ELISA at 2) while being treated with unfrac-
   tionated heparin for DVT and pulmonary embolism. The case was complicated by an initial fail-
   ure of warfarin transition from bivalirudin therapy and subsequent failure on fondaparinux
   which led to rethrombosis in both instances. HIT-antibody titer was negative while on fonda-
   parinux Black Box Warning
   Epidural or spinal hematomas may occur in patients who are anticoagulated with low molecu-
   lar weight heparins (LMWH), heparinoids, or fondaparinux sodium and are receiving neuraxial
   anesthesia or undergoing spinal puncture. These hematomas may result in long-term or per-
   manent paralysis. Consider these risks when scheduling patients for spinal procedures.
   Factors that can increase the risk of developing epidural or spinal hematomas in these pa-
   tients include: use of indwelling epidural catheters, concomitant use of other drugs that affect
   hemostasis, such as NSAIDs, platelet inhibitors, or other anticoagulants, a history of traumatic
   or repeated epidural or spinal puncture, and a history of spinal deformity or spinal surgery.
   Optimal timing between the administration of fondaparinux and neuraxial procedures is not
   known. Monitor patients frequently for signs and symptoms of neurologic impairment. If neu-
   rologic compromise is noted, urgent treatment is necessary. Consider the benefits and risks
   before neuraxial intervention in patients anticoagulated or to be anticoagulated for
   thromboprophylaxis Monitoring
   Anticoagulant Monitoring
   • Measure fondaparinux-based peak anti-Xa levels 2 to 4 hours after the second or third dose,
   then weekly for 1 month, then every 1 to 3 months for the duration of fondaparinux therapy.
   Target fondaparinux-based peak anti-Xa levels are 5 to 1 mg/L 7

 • Routine coagulation tests such as prothrombin time (PT) and activated partial thromboplastin
   time (aPTT) are not useful for monitoring Toxic Monitoring

   • Monitor CBC (including platelet count) periodically • Assess stool occult blood tests periodically during therapy • Periodically monitor renal function • Closely monitor patients with hepatic impairment for signs and symptoms of bleeding • Monitor patients undergoing spinal anesthesia or spinal puncture for signs of neurological
   impairment

drugs.contraindications_raw:
Common adverse events include viral infection, bronchitis, and dyspnea. Additional adverse
   events with beta(2)-agonists include skeletal muscle tremor and cramps, tachycardia, insom-
   nia, headache, hypokalemia, and hyperglycemia Black Box Warning
   Long-acting beta2-adrenergic agonists (LABA) use increases the risk of asthma-related hospital-
   izations in pediatric and adolescent patients 3 ,4 . For pediatric and adolescent patients with
   asthma, a fixed-dose combination product containing both an inhaled corticosteroid and LABA
   is recommended to ensure compliance with combination therapy. If separate long-term ther-
   apy is required, ensure patient adherence with both treatments. LABA increase the risk of
   asthma-related death. A placebo-controlled study with another LABA (salmeterol) showed an
   increase in asthma-related deaths in patients (12 years and older; mean age 39 years) 8 receiv-
   ing salmeterol versus placebo. This finding with salmeterol is considered a class effect of LABA.
   Use of formoterol fumarate inhalation powder for the treatment of asthma without a concomi-
   tant long-term asthma control medication, such as an inhaled corticosteroid, is contraindi-
   cated. When treating patients with asthma, formoterol fumarate should only be used for pa-
   tients not adequately controlled on other asthma-controller medications or whose disease
   severity clearly warrants initiation of treatment with two maintenance therapies. Once asthma
   control is achieved and maintained, assess the patient at regular intervals and step down ther-
   apy (eg, discontinue formoterol fumarate inhalation powder) if possible without loss of asthma
   control and maintain the patient on a long-term asthma control medication. In a meta-analysis (110 studies; n=60,954 patients 4 years through greater than 65 years of
   age), there was an overall higher risk for the composite event (asthma-related deaths, intuba-
   tions, and hospitalizations) associated with LABA use compared with no LABA use (overall inci-

 dence difference of 3 events per 1000 patient-years; 95% CI, 2 to 3) for all age groups.
   The highest risk was seen in children 4 to 11 years of age (30.4 events per 1000 patient-years;
   95% CI, 7 to 1; p=0.02). This result was consistent regardless of inhaled corticosteroid use;
   however, data indicated that providing ICS and LABA as a single inhaler may decrease the risk.
   There were 9807 pediatric patients included in the meta-analysis, and the pediatric composite
   consisted primarily of asthma-related hospitalizations. Asthma-related death/intubations were
   sparse in the 4- to 17-year age groups (no LABA = 4 and LABA = 2) Monitoring
   Assess patient periodically for adequate asthma control and step down therapy if possible 1 ,2 .
   Monitor pulmonary function tests including prebronchodilator FEV1/FVC and pre- and post-
   bronchodilator FEV. Monitor severity and frequency of asthma exacerbations 1

      (e) If HIV RNA is detectable at 4 to 8 weeks, repeat every 4 to 8 weeks until viral load is

      (f) For patients on ART, viral load is typically measured every 3 to 6 months. More frequent
      monitoring may be considered in individuals having difficulties with ART adherence or at
      risk for nonadherence. However, for adherent patients with suppressed viral load and sta-
      ble immunological status for more than 1 year, monitoring can be extended to 6-month
      intervals.
      (g) Standard genotypic drug-resistance testing in ARV-naïve persons should focus on test-
      ing for mutations in the PR and RT genes. If transmitted INSTI resistance is a concern, or if
      a person has a history of INSTI use as PrEP or treatment, or a person presents with
      viremia while on an INSTI, providers should also test for resistance mutations in the IN
      gene. In ARV-naïve patients who do not immediately begin ART, repeat testing before initi-
      ation of ART is optional if drug-resistance testing was performed at entry into care. For vi-
      rologically suppressed patients who are switching therapy for toxicity or convenience, viral
      amplification will not be possible and therefore resistance testing should not be per-
      formed. Results from prior resistance testing can be used to help in the construction of a
      new regimen.
      (h) If infected with hepatitis B virus, tenofovir disoproxil fumarate or tenofovir alafe-
      namide plus either emtricitabine or lamivudine should be used as part of the ART regimen
      to treat both hepatitis B virus and HIV infections.

      cine series. Also, consult Guidelines for Opportunistic Infections.
      (j) Typically HBV infection has resolved with loss of HBsAb despite isolated HBcAb; confirm
      with an HBV viral load if wanted. A positive HBV viral load is indicative of acute infection
      (other symptoms will be present usually) or chronic infection. Vaccinate the patient when
      viral load is negative. Also, consult Guidelines for Opportunistic Infections.

drugs.pharmacokinetics_summary:
Pharmacology
   Fosamprenavir is a prodrug that is rapidly hydrolyzed to amprenavir by cellular phosphatases
   in the gut epithelium as it is absorbed. Amprenavir binds to the active site of HIV-1 protease,
   preventing the processing of viral gag and gag-pol polyprotein precursors. This interference re-
   sults in formation of immature, noninfectious viral particles. Amprenavir Tmax following oral
   administration is 5 to 4 hours (median, 5 hours). Food has no effect on the bioavailability.

drugs.contraindications_raw:
Fewer infusion-related reactions and tissue damage (eg, purple glove syndrome) compared
   with phenytoin. Hypotension and cardiac arrhythmias have been reported. Dose related ad-
   verse events include nystagmus (total level, 15 to 25 mg/L) and ataxia and mental status
   changes (total level greater than 30 mg/L). Movement disorders (bradykinesia and choreoa-
   thetosis) may also occur rarely. Minor venous irritation upon IV administration. Vomiting is
   common in children. Long-term effects of therapy include gingival hyperplasia, coarsening of
   the facies, hirsutism, hyperglycemia, and hypoinsulinemia. Fosphenytoin drug interactions are
   similar to phenytoin (ie, carbamazepine, cimetidine, corticosteroids, digoxin, furosemide, phe-
   nobarbital, and valproate) 36,17 .

   Use with caution in infants and children with hyperbilirubinemia: both fosphenytoin and biliru-
   bin displace phenytoin from protein-binding sites, resulting in increased serum free phenytoin
   concentration Serious and sometimes fatal skin reactions, including Stevens Johnson syndrome (SJS) and
   toxic epidermal necrolysis, have been reported with phenytoin therapy. Onset of symptoms is
   typically within 28 days, but can occur later. Limited data suggests that a particular human leu-
   kocyte antigen (HLA) allele, HLA-B*1502, found in patients of Asian ancestry may be a risk fac-
   tor for the development of SJS/TEN in patients taking phenytoin. Consideration should be
   given to avoiding phenytoin as an alternative for carbamazepine in patients positive for HLA-
   B*1502 Because fosphenytoin is a prodrug and is converted to phenytoin after administra-
   tion, any concern regarding this association is also applicable to fosphenytoin.

   Black Box Warning
   The rate of intravenous fosphenytoin administration should not exceed 150 mg phenytoin
   sodium equivalents (PE) per minute because of the risk of severe hypotension and cardiac ar-
   rhythmias. Careful cardiac monitoring is needed during and after administering intravenous

 fosphenytoin. Although the risk of cardiovascular toxicity increases with infusion rates above
   the recommended infusion rate, these events have also been reported at or below the recom-
   mended infusion rate. Reduction in rate of administration or discontinuation of dosing may be
   needed Solution Compatibility
   D5W, D10W and NS.

   Terminal Injection Site Compatibility
   Lorazepam, phenobarbital, and potassium chloride.

   Terminal Injection Site Incompatibility
   Midazolam.

   Monitoring
   Therapeutic Laboratory Monitoring
   • Measure serum phenytoin concentrations (the active metabolite of fosphenytoin) to guide
   dosage adjustment and achievement of target therapeutic concentrations (reference range, 10
   to 20 mcg/mL [40 to 79 mcmol/L]; unbound phenytoin, 1 to 2 mcg/mL). Peak concentrations
   are best evaluated no sooner than 2 hours after the end of IV infusion 1 ,4 or 4 hours after an
   IM injection 4 to capture full conversion of fosphenytoin to phenytoin and may aid in deter-
   mining an individual's threshold for dose-related side effects. Measure trough levels just prior
   to the next scheduled dose 1 ,4 .
   • Monitor unbound phenytoin levels in patients with renal or hepatic impairment, and in those
   with hypoalbuminemia 1 ,4 .

   • Monitor unbound phenytoin levels periodically during pregnancy (because of potential
   changes in protein binding) 1 , Toxic Laboratory Monitoring
   • Measure serum phenytoin level immediately at first sign of acute toxicity (eg, confusion, delir-
   ium, psychosis, encephalopathy) 1 ,4 .

 • Monitor phenytoin serum levels when a drug interaction is suspected 1 ,4 .
   • Measure unbound phenytoin levels in patients with renal or hepatic impairment, and in
   those with hypoalbuminemia 1 ,4 .

   • Monitor unbound phenytoin serum levels periodically during pregnancy (due to potential
   changes in protein binding) as a guide to appropriate dosage adjustment 1 , • Monitor for signs and symptoms of hyperammonemia during concomitant use of valproate Sesquient™ Closely monitor serum creatinine levels and estimated GFR (eGFR) in patients with
   severe renal impairment [eGFR 15 to 29 mL/min/1.73 m(2)] during therapy because the sul-
   fobutylether beta-cyclodextrin sodium salt is known to accumulate with renal impairment Toxic Physical Monitoring

   • Carefully monitor ECG, blood pressure, and respiratory function continuously during IV ad-
   ministration and throughout the period where maximal serum phenytoin concentrations oc-
   cur (ie, approximately 10 to 20 minutes after the end of the infusion), especially in elderly or
   critically ill patients and those with hypotension and severe myocardial insufficiency 1 , • Monitor for signs and symptoms of hyperammonemia during concomitant use of valproate Correction for Albumin (Sheiner-Tozer Equation)

   Corrected total phenytoin = total phenytoin (mcg/mL) ÷ {[albumin (g/dL)/4.4] X 9} + 1

   Free phenytoin is obtained by multiplying by 1.

   Although the correction formula above has been used to estimate corrected total and free
   phenytoin levels, inaccuracies with the formula have been shown in children. Routine mea-
   surement of free phenytoin levels is preferred in critically ill patients, patients with hypoalbu-
   minemia, and patients receiving concurrent medications that may affect phenytoin binding
   (valproate, cefazolin)

   Preparation

   IV

   • Reconstitute by injecting 10 mL of sterile water for injection into the vial. Do not use bacterio-
   static water for injection containing parabens; it is incompatible with ganciclovir and may
   cause precipitation. Shake the vial to dissolve the drug. Visually inspect the reconstituted solu-
   tion for particulate matter and discoloration prior to proceeding with infusion solution. Discard
   the vial if particulate matter or discoloration is observed.

   • Based on patient weight, remove the appropriate volume of the reconstituted solution (ganci-
   clovir concentration 50 mg/mL) from the vial and add to a compatible diluent fluid to make a fi-
   nal infusion concentration less than 10 mg/mL. Refrigerate and use within 24 hours of dilution
   to reduce the risk of bacterial contamination; do not freeze Oral

   Oral suspension 25 mg/mL (100 mL): A 25 mg/mL ganciclovir oral suspension was prepared
   with ganciclovir intravenous formulation. Reconstitute 5-500 mg vials (3 mL in each vial) of gan-

   bottle. Add 50 mL of Orasweet and shake well. Add 1 mL of 3% hydrogen peroxide and shake
   well. Add a sufficient quantity of Orasweet for a final volume of 100 mL. The suspension is sta-
   ble for 28 days at room temperature Oral suspension 100 mg/mL (200 mL): Prepare oral suspension in a vertical-flow laminar

   polyethylene terephthalate bottle. Rinse the mortar with another 50 mL of vehicle and transfer

drugs.pharmacokinetics_summary:
Pharmacology
   Mechanism of action

   Gatifloxacin's antibacterial action results from inhibition of DNA gyrase and topoisomerase IV,
   which are essential enzymes involved in the replication, transcription, repair and partitioning
   of the chromosomal DNA during bacterial cell division. Because the mechanism of action that
   differs from that of aminoglycoside, macrolide, and tetracycline antibiotics, gatifloxacin may be
   active against pathogens that are resistant to those antibiotics,

drugs.contraindications_raw:
Transient and reversible renal tubular dysfunction may occur, resulting in increased urinary
   losses of sodium, calcium, and magnesium. Vestibular and auditory ototoxicity may occur. The
   addition of other nephrotoxic and/or ototoxic medications (eg, furosemide, vancomycin) may
   increase these adverse effects. Increased neuromuscular blockade (ie, neuromuscular weak-
   ness and respiratory failure) may occur when used with pancuronium or other neuromuscular
   blocking agents and in patients with muscular disorders (myasthenia gravis or Parkinsonism).
   A Fanconi-like syndrome with amino-aciduria and metabolic acidosis has occurred in some in-
   fants treated with gentamicin. There have been occasional reports of pain at the injection site
   1 ,29
           .

   Bacterial and fungal corneal ulcers have occurred with use of the ophthalmic formulations.
   Common adverse events with the ophthalmic formulations include ocular burning and irrita-

 tion, non-specific conjunctivitis, conjunctival epithelial defects, and conjunctival hyperemia
   41,10
           .

   Black Box Warning
   Patients treated with aminoglycosides should be under close clinical observation because of
   the potential toxicity associated with their use. As with other aminoglycosides, gentamicin in-
   jection is potentially nephrotoxic. The risk of nephrotoxicity is greater in patients with impaired
   renal function and in those who receive high dosage of prolonged therapy. Neurotoxicity man-
   ifested by ototoxicity, both vestibular and auditory, can occur in patients treated with gentam-
   icin, primarily in those with pre-existing renal damage and in patients with normal renal func-
   tion treated with higher doses or for longer periods than recommended. Aminoglycoside-in-
   duced ototoxicity is usually irreversible. Other manifestations of neurotoxicity may include
   numbness, skin tingling, muscle twitching and convulsions.

   Renal and eighth cranial nerve function should be closely monitored, especially in patients
   with known or suspected reduced renal function at onset of therapy and also in those whose
   renal function is initially normal but who develop signs of renal dysfunction during therapy.
   Urine should be examined for decreased specific gravity, increased excretions of protein and
   the presence of cells or casts. BUN, serum creatinine, or CrCl should be determined periodi-
   cally. When feasible, it is recommended that serial audiograms be obtained in patients old
   enough to be tested, particularly high-risk patients. Evidence of ototoxicity (dizziness, vertigo,
   tinnitus, roaring in the ears or hearing loss) or nephrotoxicity requires dosage adjustment or
   discontinuance of the drug. As with the other aminoglycosides, on rare occasions changes in
   renal and eighth cranial nerve function may not become manifest until soon after completion
   of therapy.
   Serum concentrations of aminoglycosides should be monitored when feasible to assure ade-
   quate levels and to avoid potentially toxic levels. When monitoring gentamicin peak concentra-
   tions, dosage should be adjusted so that prolonged levels above 12 mcg/mL are avoided.
   When monitoring gentamicin trough concentrations, dosage should be adjusted so that levels
   above 2 mcg/mL are avoided. Excessive peak or through serum concentrations of aminoglyco-
   sides may increase the risk of renal and eight cranial nerve toxicity. In the event of overdosage
   or toxic reactions, hemodialysis may aid in the removal of gentamicin from the blood, espe-
   cially if renal function is, or becomes, compromised. The rate of removal of gentamicin is con-
   siderably lower by peritoneal dialysis than it is by hemodialysis.

   In the newborn infant, exchange transfusions may also be considered.
   Concurrent or sequential systemic or topical use of other potentially neurotoxic or nephrotoxic
   drugs, such as cisplatin, cephaloridine, kanamycin, amikacin, neomycin, polymyxin B, colistin.

 paromomycin, streptomycin, tobramycin, vancomycin and viomycin, should be avoided. Other
   factors which may increased patient risk of toxicity are advanced age and dehydration. The
   concurrent use of gentamicin with potent diuretics, such as ethacrynic acid or furosemide,
   should be avoided, since certain diuretics by themselves may cause ototoxicity. In addition,
   when administered intravenously, diuretics may enhance aminoglycoside toxicity by altering
   the antibiotic concentration in serum and tissue.

   Aminoglycosides can cause fetal harm when administered to a pregnant woman Solution Compatibility
   D5W, D10W, and NS.

   Terminal Injection Site Compatibility
   Acyclovir, alprostadil, amiodarone, aztreonam, caffeine citrate, cefepime, cefotaxime, cefoxitin,
   ceftazidime, ceftriaxone, cimetidine, clindamycin, dopamine, enalaprilat, esmolol, famotidine,
   fluconazole, gentamicin, heparin (concentrations of 1 unit/mL or less), insulin, linezolid, lo-
   razepam, magnesium sulfate, meropenem, metronidazole, midazolam, milrinone, morphine,
   nicardipine, pancuronium bromide, penicillin g, prostaglandin E1, ranitidine, remifentanil, ve-
   curonium, and zidovudine.

   Terminal Injection Site Incompatibility
   Amphotericin B, ampicillin, azithromycin, furosemide, imipenem/cilastatin, heparin (concentra-
   tions greater than 1 unit/mL), indomethacin, mezlocillin, nafcillin, oxacillin, propofol, and
   ticarcillin/clavulanate.

   Monitoring
   Toxic Monitoring
   • Monitoring of renal, auditory, and vestibular functions is recommended if treatment extends
   beyond 10 days • Monitor serum calcium, magnesium, and sodium periodically during therapy • Obtain urinalysis to assess for decreased specific gravity and increased excretion of protein,
   cells, and casts. Renal and auditory function should be closely monitored, especially in patients
   with renal impairment 19/26

   Measure serum concentrations periodically during therapy. Obtain peak concentration 30 min-
   utes after end of infusion or 1 hour after an intramuscular injection, and trough concentration
   just prior to the next dose When treating patients with serious infections or significantly
   changing fluid or renal status, consider measuring the serum concentration more frequently Obtaining 2 drug levels (eg, at 3 and 6 hours after start of infusion) and extrapolating the
   achieved peak and trough has been suggested; adjust dose as appropriate to achieve desired

drugs.uses_raw:
Chronic Hepatitis C Virus (HCV) Infection

   12 years or older: Overall sustained virologic response 12 weeks post-treatment (SVR12) was
   100% in adolescent patients aged 12 to less than 18 years with hepatitis C virus (HCV) infection
   without cirrhosis (N=47) who received once daily glecaprevir 300 mg/pibrentasvir 120 mg, in
   the open-label DORA (Part 1) trial. Most patients (79%) had HCV genotype 1 infection; 6% had
   genotype 2 infection, 9% had genotype 3 infection, and 6% had genotype 4 infection (no pa-
   tients had genotype 5 or 6 infection). Treatment duration was 8 weeks for 94% of patients, and
   16 weeks in 3 patients with genotype 3 infection and prior interferon treatment. As
   glecaprevir/pibrentasvir exposure is comparable between adolescents and adults, safety and
   efficacy in patients with cirrhosis, kidney transplant, liver transplant, or HCV genotype 5 or 6 in-
   fection is expected to be similar to that observed in adults 4/15
 3 to 12 years: Overall rate of sustained virologic response 12 weeks post-treatment (SVR12)
   was 96% in pediatric patients aged 3 years to less than 12 years with chronic hepatitis C (HCV)
   infection without cirrhosis (N=80; median age, 7 years) who received weight-based dosing of
   glecaprevir/pibrentasvir oral pellets in the open-label DORA (Part 2) trial. All patients were
   without cirrhosis and most patients (73%) had HCV genotype 1 infection; 3% had genotype 2
   infection, 23% had genotype 3, and 3% had HCV genotype 4 (no patients had genotype 5 or 6);
   one patient was coinfected with HIV. Treatment duration was 8 weeks for 98%, 12 weeks for 1
   patient with genotype 3 infection, and 16 weeks for another single treatment-experienced pa-
   tient with genotype 3 infection. As glecaprevir/pibrentasvir pharmacokinetics was similar be-
   tween children and adults, safety and efficacy in patients with cirrhosis, kidney transplant, liver
   transplant, or HCV genotype 5 or 6 infection are expected to be similar to that observed in
   adults Guideline Recommendations: Direct-acting antiviral (DAA) treatment with an approved regi-
   men is recommended for all children and adolescents with HCV infection 3 years or older, as
   they will benefit from antiviral therapy, regardless of disease severity. The presence of extra-
   hepatic manifestations (eg, cryoglobulinemia, rash, and glomerulonephritis) or advanced fibro-
   sis should lead to early antiviral therapy to minimize future morbidity and mortality. Selection
   of DAA and duration of therapy should take into account the patient's viral genotype, presence
   and grading of cirrhosis, and any prior treatments. Current recommendations are found in the

   Warning: Risk of Hepatitis B Virus Reactivation in Patients Coinfected with Hepatitis C

   •Test all patients for evidence of current or prior hepatitis B virus (HBV) infection before initiat-

   coinfected patients who were undergoing or had completed treatment with HCV direct-acting
   antivirals and were not receiving HBV antiviral therapy. Some cases have resulted in fulminant
   hepatitis, hepatic failure, and death. Monitor HCV/HBV coinfected patients for hepatitis flare or
   HBV reactivation during HCV treatment and post-treatment follow-up. Initiate appropriate pa-
   tient management for HBV infection as clinically indicated 11/15

drugs.pharmacokinetics_summary:
Pharmacology
   Mechanism of action: Glycerol phenylbutyrate is a triglyceride which contains 3 molecules of

drugs.uses_raw:
Ulcerative Colitis
   Guidelines: InFLIXimab should be considered for induction and maintenance of remission
   therapy in patients with chronically active or steroid-dependent ulcerative colitis uncontrolled
   by 5-aminosalicylic acid and thiopurines. Higher initial doses should be considered in children
   with low body weight (less than 30 kg) or high BMI, and in the presence of higher inflammatory
   burden and hypoalbuminemia. InFLIXimab should be given with an immunomodulator (with
   most evidence with thiopurines) to reduce the likelihood of developing inFLIXimab antibodies.
   Adalimumab and golimumab may be considered in patients intolerant to inFLIXimab or in
   those who initially respond but then lose response. Adalimumab and golimumab should not
   be used in patients with primary non-response to inFLIXimab In a retrospective review of 17 patients with moderate-to-severe ulcerative colitis, steroid-free
   remission was achieved in 4% (5/17) of patients at golimumab initiation, 4% (5/17) at
   week 10, 4% (10/14) at week 30, and 80% (8/10) at week Golimumab was discontinued in
   some patients over the course of treatment due to difficulty in maintaining remission. All pa-
   tients that failed therapy had severe colitis at least once during therapy 4
   Efficacy outcomes (ie, clinical response, clinical remission, and mucosal healing) at week 6 of
   golimumab therapy were numerically greater in serum golimumab concentrations 64
   mcg/mL or greater compared to patients that maintained concentrations less than 64
   mcg/mL in a pharmacokinetic study (N=35) In a study-extension in the patients that re-
   sponded by week 6, clinical remission and clinically meaningful changes remained stable after
   week Ten of 20 patients in the study extension were in Pediatric Ulcerative Colitis Activity
   Index (PUCAI) remission at week 110 (score less than 10) FDA Approved Pediatric Indication
   Golimumab IV injection is indicated in pediatric patients 2 years and older for the treatment of
   active polyarticular juvenile idiopathic arthritis and active psoriatic arthritis (PsA) 2

 Golimumab SUBQ injection is indicated in pediatric patients 15 kg or greater for the treatment
   of moderate to severe ulcerative colitis Administration
   • Prior to infusion, inspect for the presence of discoloration or particulate matter. Infuse IV
   over 30 minutes through in-line, low protein-binding filter (0.22-micrometer or less pore size).
   Do not administer golimumab concomitantly with any other agent through the same IV line

Common, adult: Upper respiratory tract infection, increased alanine aminotransferase, viral
   infection, increased aspartate aminotransferase, decreased neutrophil count, bronchitis, hy-
   pertension, and rash 2

 The adverse reactions observed in pediatric trials were consistent with adult patients with

   (20%) 6

   Black Box Warning
   Serious Infections and Malignancy

   Serious Infections

   Patients treated with golimumab are at increased risk for developing serious infections that
   may lead to hospitalization or death. Most patients who developed these infections were tak-
   ing concomitant immunosuppressants such as methotrexate or corticosteroids.

   Discontinue golimumab if a patient develops a serious infection.
   Reported infections with tumor necrosis factor (TNF) blockers, of which golimumab is a mem-
   ber, include:
    ●   Active tuberculosis, including reactivation of latent tuberculosis. Patients with tuberculosis
        have frequently presented with disseminated or extrapulmonary disease. Test patients for
        latent tuberculosis before golimumab use and during therapy. Initiate treatment for latent
        TB prior to golimumab use.
    ●   Invasive fungal infections, including histoplasmosis, coccidioidomycosis, candidiasis, as-
        pergillosis, blastomycosis, and pneumocystosis. Patients with histoplasmosis or other inva-
        sive fungal infections may present with disseminated, rather than localized, disease. Antigen
        and antibody testing for histoplasmosis may be negative in some patients with active infec-
        tion. Consider empiric antifungal therapy in patients at risk for invasive fungal infections
        who develop severe systemic illness.
    ●   Bacterial, viral, and other infections due to opportunistic pathogens, including Legionella
        and Listeria.

   Consider the risks and benefits of treatment with golimumab prior to initiating therapy in pa-
   tients with chronic or recurrent infection.
   Monitor patients closely for the development of signs and symptoms of infection during and
   after treatment with golimumab, including the possible development of tuberculosis in pa-
   tients who tested negative for latent tuberculosis infection prior to initiating therapy.
   Malignancy

 Lymphoma and other malignancies, some fatal, have been reported in children and adoles-
   cent patients treated with TNF-blockers, of which golimumab is a member Monitoring
   Therapeutic Laboratory Monitoring

   • Ulcerative colitis: Target trough levels during maintenance therapy are 2 mcg/mL or greater Toxic Laboratory Monitoring

   • Test patients for hepatitis B virus (HBV) infection and carrier status prior to therapy. Monitor
   HBV carriers for active hepatitis B infection throughout therapy and for several months follow-
   ing discontinuation Toxic Physical Monitoring

   • Before and during treatment, evaluate the patient for active TB, TB risk factors, and latent TB,
   including patients who had a negative tuberculin test prior to treatment and patients who
   have previously received treatment for latent or active TB • Monitor for infections during and after treatment • Monitor HBV carriers for clinical signs of active HBV infection throughout therapy and for sev-
   eral months following discontinuation • Periodically monitor all patients for the development of skin cancer, especially those with risk
   factors • Closely monitor patients with congestive heart failure (CHF) during therapy for new or wors-
   ening CHF symptoms

Routine vaccination, haemophilus influenzae type B
   ActHIB®, Hiberix® (PRP-T): 5 mL IM in the anterolateral thigh or deltoid; 4-dose series given
   at 2, 4, and 6 months of age and a booster dose at 12 to 15 months of age 1 ,2 .

   2, and 4 months of age and a booster dose at 12 to 15 months of age 1 ,3 .

   Catch-up vaccination, haemophilus influenzae type B 1
   • If dose 1 is administered at 7 to 11 months, administer the second dose at least 4 weeks later
   and 3rd (final) dose at 12 to 15 months or 8 weeks after 2nd dose (whichever is later) .
   • If dose 1 is administered at 12 to 14 months of age, administer the second (final) dose at
   least 8 weeks after the first dose .

   • If dose 1 administered before 12 months and 2nd dose before 15 months, give 3rd (final)
   dose 8 weeks after 2nd dose .
   • If 2 doses of PedvaxHIB before 12 months, administer 3rd (final) dose at 12 to 59 months and
   at least 8 weeks after 2nd dose .
   • If 1 dose is administered at 15 months or older, no further doses are needed .
   • If unvaccinated at 15 to 59 months of age, administer only 1 dose .
   • Previously unvaccinated children 60 months or older who are not considered high risk do not
   require catch-up vaccination .

   Vaccination in high-risk populations 1
   • Chemotherapy or radiation (aged 12 to 59 months): If unvaccinated or only 1 dose before
   age 12 months, give 2 doses 8 weeks apart. If 2 or more doses before age 12 months, give 1
   dose at least 8 weeks after last dose. If administered within 14 days of starting chemotherapy
   or radiation, repeat vaccine dose(s) 3 or more months after completion of therapy .

 • Hematopoietic stem cell transplant: 3 dose series administered 4 weeks apart starting 6 to
   12 months after successful transplant, regardless of previous immunization status .
   • Anatomic or functional asplenia, including sickle cell disease (aged 12 to 59 months): If
   unvaccinated or only 1 dose before age 12 months, give 2 doses 8 weeks apart. If 2 or more
   doses before age 12 months, give 1 dose at least 8 weeks after last dose .
   • Anatomic or functional asplenia, including sickle cell disease (5 years or older): If unvac-
   cinated give 1 dose .
   • Elective splenectomy (15 months or older): If unvaccinated give 1 dose, preferably at least
   14 days before procedure .

   • HIV (aged 12 to 59 months): If unvaccinated or only 1 dose before age 12 months, give 2
   doses 8 weeks apart. If 2 or more doses before age 12 months, give 1 dose at least 8 weeks af-
   ter last dose .
   • HIV (5 years or older): If unvaccinated give 1 dose .
   • Immunoglobulin deficiency, early component complement deficiency (aged 12 to 59
   months): If unvaccinated or only 1 dose before age 12 months, give 2 doses 8 weeks apart. If 2
   or more doses before age 12 months, give 1 dose at least 8 weeks after last dose .
