drugs.uses_raw:
Gilles de la Tourette's syndrome

   Haloperidol is indicated for the control of tics and vocal utterances of Tourette disorder in
   adults and children 3 years or older 1 ,4

   In a retrospective review of 120 patients with Tourette syndrome (mean age of onset, 1
   years), 83% receiving haloperidol (n=60; mean dose, 8 mg/day) experienced an overall im-
   provement. However, adverse events occurred in 50 patients and were responsible for discon-
   tinuation of therapy in 20 patients. In 23 patients who received fluphenazine following
   haloperidol, there was no significant difference in control of motor or vocal tics, but there were
   significantly fewer adverse events Haloperidol was more effective than pimozide on the
   Gilles de la Tourette syndrome severity scale and more effective than placebo on 4 of 6 mea-
   surement scales, according to a parallel and crossover study in adults and children (N=57;
   mean, 1 years; range, 8 to 46 years). Patients received once daily dosing titrated to clinical
   effect up to a maximum dose of pimozide 3 mg/kg or 20 mg, whichever was smaller,
   haloperidol 10 mg, or placebo during each of the 6-week treatment periods In a 24-week
   parallel and crossover study in patients (N=22; range, 7 to 16 years), haloperidol was not signif-
   icantly more effective compared with placebo, but pimozide was. A 70% tic reduction on the
   total Tourette Syndrome Global Scale was achieved in 64% of patients who received either pi-
   mozide (mean dose, 4 mg/day) or haloperidol (mean dose, 5 mg/day) compared with 23%
   for placebo. Haloperidol was associated with a significantly greater incidence of extrapyrami-
   dal symptoms 14

   Nonpsychotic behavior disorders, after failure to respond to non-antipsychotic medica-
   tion and psychotherapy (oral therapy only)

   Haloperidol is effective for the treatment of severe behavior problems in children of combat-
   ive, explosive hyperexcitability not accounted for by immediate provocation.. Short-term use

 of haloperidol is effective in managing hyperactive pediatric patients with excessive motor ac-
   tivity and concomitant conduct disorders such as impulsivity, difficulty sustaining attention, ag-
   gressivity, mood lability, and poor frustration tolerance which has been unresponsive to psy-
   chotherapy or non-antipsychotic medications 1 ,15

   Schizophrenia

   Haloperidol is indicated in the management of manifestations of psychotic disorders in chil-
   dren 3 years or older 1 ,15 .

   In a systematic review of 25 clinical trials, including mostly hospitalized and chronically ill
   adults with schizophrenia (1 small trial was in children aged 6 to 12 years), patients receiving
   oral haloperidol were 41% more likely to have marked overall improvement at 6 weeks (4 tri-
   als; 472 patients) and 33% more likely to have marked improvement at 6 months (8 trials; 307
   patients), compared with placebo. Once the illness was stable, haloperidol was 31% more likely
   to maintain remission (2 trials; 70 patients); however, the incidence of extrapyramidal adverse
   events was significantly increased Administration
   Long-acting IM injection
   Haloperidol decanoate injection should be administered by deep intramuscular injection. A 21
   gauge needle is recommended The maximum volume per injection site should not exceed 3 mL DO NOT administer intravenously 11

   rately monitor therapy in children. Studies have also shown invalidity in extrapolating the aPTT

   compared with adults). There are also data showing that there are significant age-related dif-
   ferences in the aPTT that correlates to an anti-factor Xa level of 35 to 7 units/mL. Many ex-
   perts prefer anti-factor Xa assays to monitor heparin therapy in children 1 ,31,32 .

   9 years or older: 5 mL IM as a 2- or 3-dose series depending on age at initiation 1

   Series Schedule 2

   • 9 to 14 years at initiation: 2-dose series of HPV vaccine on a schedule of 0 and 6 to 12
   months; minimum interval: 5 months. Repeat a dose if given too soon
   • 15 years or older at initiation: 3-dose series on a schedule of 0, 1 to 2, and 6 months; mini-
   mum intervals: 4 weeks between 1st and 2nd dose; 12 weeks between 2nd and 3rd dose; 5
   months between 1st and 3rd dose. Repeat dose(s) if given too soon

   Special populations 2
   History of sexual abuse or assault: Begin series at 9 years of age
   Immunocompromised persons: 3-dose series on a schedule of 0, 1 to 2, and 6 months as
   above, even if vaccination initiated at age 9 through 14 years
   Pregnancy: HPV vaccination is not recommended during pregnancy. If found to be pregnant
   after initiating the vaccination series, no intervention is needed. Pregnancy testing is not
   needed before HPV vaccination

drugs.pharmacokinetics_summary:
Pharmacology
   Hyaluronidase is a spreading or diffusing enzyme that modifies the permeability of connective
   tissue through the hydrolysis of hyaluronic acid, which temporarily decreases the viscosity of
   the cellular cement, promoting the diffusion/adsorption of the injected fluids or localized tran-
   sudates or exudates. Rate and extent of dispersion is directly proportional to amount of
   hyaluronidase and volume of solution

drugs.contraindications_raw:
Blood dyscrasias, including reduction in hemoglobin and red cell count, leukopenia, agranulo-
   cytosis, and purpura, have been reported. Reflex tachycardia, headache, flushing, dizziness,
   vomiting, nausea, palpitations, increased cardiac output, as well as salt and water retention
   may occur. Orthostatic hypotension occurs rarely 7 , 8 , 21 , 3 , 5 , Lupus-like syndrome has been
   reported in approximately 10% of adult patients receiving hydrALAZINE. This is more common
   in patients who are slow acetylators receiving more than 200 mg/day. Also case reports of this
   occurring in children 8 ,5 ,22 .

   Solution Compatibility
   NS.

   Terminal Injection Site Compatibility
   Dobutamine, heparin, hydrocortisone succinate, and potassium chloride.

 Terminal Injection Site Incompatibility
   Aminophylline, ampicillin, diazoxide, furosemide, and phenobarbital.

   Monitoring
   Frequent assessment of blood pressure and heart rate is recommended. CBC and antinuclear
   antibody titer determinations are recommended at baseline and periodically during long-term
   therapy

Sedation (16 to 21%), lightheadedness or feeling dizzy (12% to 22%), nightmares (2.8% to 4%),
   nausea (19% to 27%), vomiting (5% to 10%), and constipation (15% to 22%) were reported in 74
   children administered HYDROcodone/acetaminophen around-the-clock Acetaminophen: Liver toxicity occurs with excessive doses or after prolonged administration
   of therapeutic doses. There is an increased risk for development of hepatic toxicity in children
   with diabetes, children with concurrent viral infections, children with a history of hepatotoxic
   reactions, obese children, and chronically malnourished children. Initial signs of ac-
   etaminophen toxicity include anorexia, nausea, vomiting, malaise, and diaphoresis
   32 , 17 , 33 , 34 , In 2014, the FDA recommended that combination analgesics which contain more the 325 mg
   of acetaminophen per dosage unit not be prescribed or dispensed due to concerns of liver
   toxicity. Limiting the amount of acetaminophen per dosage unit could reduce the risk of se-

 vere liver injury from inadvertent overdose, a situation which can lead to liver failure, liver
   transplant, and death. At present, there are no data to support that higher amounts of ac-
   etaminophen per dosage unit provide additional benefit to outweigh the added risk of liver in-
   jury Hepatotoxicity occurred in less than 01% of children administered therapeutic doses of ac-
   etaminophen, in a systemic review (n=32,424; studies=62). The estimated risk for minor or ma-
   jor hepatic events was 031% (95% CI, 015% to 057%) No significant increases in liver
   enzymes were observed after a median duration of 60 hours (6 to 480 hours) and a median of
   9 (2 to 80) doses of IV acetaminophen in a retrospective analysis of 189 infants (1 day to 182
   days of age; 30 to 55 weeks postmenstrual age (PMA). Loading doses of 20 mg/kg, followed by
   maintenance doses of 10 mg/kg were given every 6 to 12 hours, based upon PMA Acute
   liver failure occurred in an 11-month-old boy who received therapeutic doses of oral ac-
   etaminophen for a prolonged duration (10 days) Serious skin reactions have been reported from patients who were rechallenged with ac-
   etaminophen and had a recurrence of a serious skin reaction Black Box Warning
   Warning: Addiction, abuse, and misuse; risk evaluation and mitigation strategy (REMS); life-
   threatening respiratory depression; accidental ingestion; neonatal opioid withdrawal syn-
   drome; CYP450 3A4 interaction; hepatotoxicity; and risks from concomitant use with benzodi-
   azepines or other CNS depressants 19 , 20
    ●   Risk of Medication Errors
    ●   Ensure accuracy when prescribing, dispensing, and administering
        hydrocodone/acetaminophen. Dosing errors due to confusion between mg and mL, and
        other hydrocodone/acetaminophen formulations of different concentrations can result in
        accidental overdose and death.
    ●   Addiction, Abuse, and Misuse
    ●   Hydrocodone/acetaminophen exposes patients and other users to the risks of opioid addic-
        tion, abuse, and misuse, which can lead to overdose and death. Assess each patient’s risk
        prior to prescribing hydrocodone/acetaminophen, and monitor all patients regularly for the
        development of these behaviors and conditions.
    ●   Opioid Analgesic Risk Evaluation and Mitigation Strategy (REMS)
    ●   To ensure that the benefits of opioid analgesics outweigh the risks of addiction, abuse, and
        misuse, the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) has required a REMS for these products.
        Under the requirements of the REMS, drug companies with approved opioid analgesic prod-

 ucts must make REMS-compliant education programs available to healthcare providers.
        Healthcare providers are strongly encouraged to
    ●   Complete a REMS-compliant education program,
    ●   Counsel patients and/or their caregivers, with every prescription, on safe use, serious risks,
        storage, and disposal of these products,
    ●   Emphasize to patients and their caregivers the importance of reading the Medication Guide
        every time it is provided by their pharmacist, and
    ●   Consider other tools to improve patient, household, and community safety.
    ●   Life-Threatening Respiratory Depression
    ●   Serious, life-threatening, or fatal respiratory depression may occur with use of
        hydrocodone/acetaminophen. Follow patients for signs of respiratory depression, especially
        during initiation of hydrocodone/acetaminophen or following a dose increase.
    ●   Accidental Ingestion
    ●   Accidental ingestion of hydrocodone/acetaminophen, especially by children, can result in a
        fatal overdose of hydrocodone/acetaminophen.
    ●   Neonatal Opioid Withdrawal Syndrome
    ●   Prolonged use of hydrocodone/acetaminophen during pregnancy can result in neonatal
        opioid withdrawal syndrome, which may be life-threatening if not recognized and treated,
        and requires management according to protocols developed by neonatology experts. If opi-
        oid use is required for a prolonged period in a pregnant woman, advise the patient of the
        risk of neonatal opioid withdrawal syndrome and ensure that appropriate treatment will be
        available.
    ●   Cytochrome P450 3A4 Interaction
    ●   The concomitant use of hydrocodone/acetaminophen with all Cytochrome P450 3A4 in-
        hibitors may result in an increase in hydrocodone plasma concentrations, which may cause
        potentially fatal respiratory depression. In addition, discontinuation of a concomitantly used
        Cytochrome P450 3A4 inducer may result in an increase in hydrocodone plasma concentra-
        tion. Follow patients receiving Hydrocodone Bitartrate and Acetaminophen Oral Solution
        and any Cytochrome P450 3A4 inhibitor or inducer for signs and symptoms of respiratory
        depression and sedation.
    ●   Hepatotoxicity
    ●   Acetaminophen has been associated with cases of acute liver failure, at times resulting in
        liver transplant and death. Most of the cases of liver injury are associated with the use of ac-
        etaminophen at doses that exceed 4,000 milligrams per day, and often involve more than
        one acetaminophen-containing product

 ●   Risks From Concomitant Use With Benzodiazepines Or Other CNS Depressants
    ●   Concomitant use of opioids with benzodiazepines or other central nervous system (CNS) de-
        pressants, including alcohol, may result in profound sedation, respiratory depression, coma,
        and death
    ●   Reserve concomitant prescribing of Hydrocodone Bitartrate and Acetaminophen Oral
        Solution and benzodiazepines or other CNS depressants for use in patients for whom alter-
        native treatment options are inadequate.
    ●   Limit dosages and durations to the minimum required.
    ●   Follow patients for signs and symptoms of respiratory depression and sedation.

   Monitoring
   Monitor liver and/or renal function in patients with severe hepatic or renal disease 9 ,10 . Assess
   liver function in patients taking large doses chronically or if predisposed to liver toxicity. Serum
   acetaminophen concentration is obtained only to assess toxicity in cases of suspected over-
   dose 17,18 . Closely monitor infants for respiratory depression 1 ,2 .

 Black Box Warning
   Warning: Addiction, abuse, and misuse; risk evaluation and mitigation strategy (REMS); life-
   threatening respiratory depression; accidental ingestion; neonatal opioid withdrawal syn-
   drome; CYP450 3A4 interaction; risks from concomitant use with benzodiazepines or other
   CNS depressants; serious cardiovascular and gastrointestinal events 12
    ●   Addiction, Abuse, and Misuse
    ●   HYDROcodone bitartrate and ibuprofen exposes patients and other users to the risks of
        opioid addiction, abuse, and misuse, which can lead to overdose and death. Assess each
        patient’s risk prior to prescribing HYDROcodone bitartrate and ibuprofen, and monitor all
        patients regularly for the development of these behaviors and conditions.
    ●   Opioid Analgesic Risk Evaluation and Mitigation Strategy (REMS)
    ●   To ensure that the benefits of opioid analgesics outweigh the risks of addiction, abuse, and
        misuse, the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) has required a REMS for these products.
        Under the requirements of the REMS, drug companies with approved opioid analgesic prod-
        ucts must make REMS-compliant education programs available to healthcare providers.
        Healthcare providers are strongly encouraged to
    ●   Complete a REMS-compliant education program,
    ●   Counsel patients and/or their caregivers, with every prescription, on safe use, serious risks,
        storage, and disposal of these products,
    ●   Emphasize to patients and their caregivers the importance of reading the Medication Guide
        every time it is provided by their pharmacist, and
    ●   Consider other tools to improve patient, household, and community safety.
    ●   Life-Threatening Respiratory Depression
    ●   Serious, life-threatening, or fatal respiratory depression may occur with use of
        HYDROcodone bitartrate and ibuprofen. Monitor for respiratory depression, especially dur-
        ing initiation of HYDROcodone bitartrate and ibuprofen or following a dose increase.
    ●   Accidental Ingestion
    ●   Accidental ingestion of even one dose of HYDROcodone bitartrate and ibuprofen, especially
        by children, can result in a fatal overdose of HYDROcodone.
    ●   Neonatal Opioid Withdrawal Syndrome
    ●   Prolonged use of HYDROcodone bitartrate and ibuprofen during pregnancy can result in
        neonatal opioid withdrawal syndrome, which may be life-threatening if not recognized and
        treated, and requires management according to protocols developed by neonatology ex-
        perts. If opioid use is required for a prolonged period in a pregnant woman, advise the pa-

 tient of the risk of neonatal opioid withdrawal syndrome and ensure that appropriate treat-
        ment will be available.
    ●   Cytochrome P450 3A4 Interaction
    ●   The concomitant use of HYDROcodone bitartrate and ibuprofen with all Cytochrome P450
        3A4 inhibitors may result in an increase in HYDROcodone plasma concentrations, which
        may cause potentially fatal respiratory depression. In addition, discontinuation of a con-
        comitantly used Cytochrome P450 3A4 inducer may result in an increase in HYDROcodone
        plasma concentration. Monitor patients receiving HYDROcodone bitartrate and ibuprofen
        and any Cytochrome P450 3A4 inhibitor or inducer for signs and symptoms of respiratory
        depression and sedation.
    ●   Risks From Concomitant Use With Benzodiazepines Or Other CNS Depressants
    ●   Concomitant use of opioids with benzodiazepines or other central nervous system (CNS) de-
        pressants, including alcohol, may result in profound sedation, respiratory depression, coma,
        and death
    ●   Reserve concomitant prescribing of HYDROcodone bitartrate and ibuprofen and benzodi-
        azepines or other CNS depressants for use in patients for whom alternative treatment op-
        tions are inadequate.
    ●   Limit dosages and durations to the minimum required.
    ●   Follow patients for signs and symptoms of respiratory depression and sedation.
    ●   Cardiovascular Thrombotic Events
    ●   Nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) cause an increased risk of serious cardiovas-
        cular thrombotic events, including myocardial infarction and stroke, which can be fatal. This
        risk may occur early in treatment and may increase with duration of use.
    ●   HYDROcodone bitartrate and ibuprofen is contraindicated in the setting of coronary artery
        bypass graft (CABG) surgery.
    ●   Gastrointestinal Bleeding, Ulceration, and Perforation
    ●   NSAIDs cause an increased risk of serious gastrointestinal (GI) adverse events including
        bleeding, ulceration, and perforation of the stomach or intestines, which can be fatal. These
        events can occur at any time during use and without warning symptoms. Patients with a
        prior history of peptic ulcer disease and/or GI bleeding are at greater risk for serious GI
        events.

   Monitoring

 Monitor blood pressure closely during initiation and throughout treatment. Monitor for signs
   and symptoms of gastrointestinal tract bleeding. Monitor renal function if use is required in
   patients with advanced kidney disease. Assess Hb or HCT in patients on long-term therapy
   who exhibit signs of anemia. Monitor patients with a coagulation disorder. Periodically moni-
   tor CBC and chemistry profile with long-term therapy 6 ,7 .

drugs.uses_raw:
Hydroxychloroquine sulfate is indicated to treat uncomplicated malaria when due to
   Plasmodium falciparum, P malariae, P ovale, and P vivax. Hydroxychloroquine sulfate is also indi-

 cated for malaria prophylaxis in those geographic areas where chloroquine resistance is not
   reported .
   • Concomitant therapy with an 8-aminoquinoline compound is required for the radical cure of
   infections due to P vivax and P ovale Limitations of Use

   • Hydroxychloroquine sulfate should not be administered for treatment of complicated
   malaria • Hydroxychloroquine sulfate is not effective against strains of Plasmodium species that are re-
   sistant to chloroquine or hydroxychloroquine • Hydroxychloroquine sulfate should not be used for malaria treatment or prophylaxis in cer-
   tain geographic areas where chloroquine resistance occurs or in cases when the Plasmodium
   species has not been identified • Hydroxychloroquine sulfate does not prevent relapses of P vivax or P ovale. It is not active
   against the hypnozoite forms of these species Administration
   • Take with food or milk • Do not use oral tablets in patients weighing less than 31 kg, as film-coated tablets cannot be
   divided 1

   Preparation

   Extemporaneous oral compounds

   25 mg/mL suspension (100 mL) 8 , 9
   • Place 5 tablets containing hydroxychloroquine sulfate 200 mg and crush to a fine powder
   with a mortar and pestle.

   • Add a small quantity of Oral Mix or Oral Mix SF to form a smooth paste.
   • Add additional Oral Mix or Oral Mix SF geometrically to final volume of 100 mL and mix well.

   • Package in tight, light-resistant (amber plastic) container.
   • Label bottle with "Protect from light" and "Shake well."

   • Suspension is stable for up to 90 days when stored under refrigeration (4°C) or at room tem-
   perature (25°C).

 50 mg/mL suspension (200 mL) 10
   • Weigh out 10 grams of hydroxychloroquine active pharmaceutical ingredient and add to a
   mortar.

   • Add 13 grams of SyrSpend SF PH4 ® dry powder to the mortar and triturate to homogeneity
   using a pestle. Transfer powder to a volumetric flask.
   • Add sterile water, in geometric proportions, mixing well after each addition, to a total vol-
   ume of 200 mL.

   • Transfer suspension to an amber glass container.

   • Label the container with "Shake well before using."
   • Stable for 60 days under refrigeration (2° to 8°C).

   Develops slowly Major risk factors are duration of therapy, dose greater than 5 mg/kg/day, chronic kidney dis-
   ease, and pre-existing retinal or macular disease Baseline monitoring, then annual monitoring beginning 5 years after initiation are recom-
   mended. Annual monitoring may begin sooner if major risk factors are present Monitoring
   Toxic Monitoring

   • Monitor complete blood cell counts periodically during long-term therapy • Monitor for hemolytic anemia in patients with glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase defi-
   ciency • Monitor for clinical signs and symptoms of cardiomyopathy, including use of appropriate di-
   agnostic tools, such as ECG, during treatment • Evaluate muscle strength and deep tendon reflexes periodically during prolonged treatment Ophthalmologic Screening

   • Perform a baseline ophthalmologic examination within the first year 1 in all patients begin-
   ning long-term therapy to document any complicating ocular conditions and to document the
   appearance of the fundus and functional status Include best corrected distance visual acu-
   ity (BCVA), automated threshold visual field (VF) of the central 10 degrees (central 24 degrees
   recommended if of Asian descent), and spectral domain ocular coherence tomography (SD-
   OCT) Most critical is the fundus evaluation of the macula to rule out underlying disease or
   preexisting tissue damage. Although baseline visual fields and SD-OCT are always useful, it is
   not critical to obtain at baseline unless abnormalities are present (eg, focal macular lesion,
   glaucoma, etc) that might affect screening tests • Annual ophthalmologic screening may be deferred until there have been 5 years of exposure,
   however, more frequent screening repeated annually should be considered in patients with
   significant risk factors (eg, daily dose greater than 5 mg/kg base using actual body weight, re-
   nal impairment, concomitant use of tamoxifen citrate, concurrent macular disease, or greater
   than 5 years of therapy) 7 , Including best corrected distance visual acuity (BCVA), automated

   NIOSH Guidance: For full NIOSH and safe handling guidance, see Special Considerations.

   Administration

   Tablets

   •The 100-mg tablets have 1 score line and can be split into 2 parts, 50 mg each. The 1000-mg
   tablets have 3 score lines and can be split into 4 parts, 250 mg each •Administer once daily, at the same time each day, with a glass of water 4
   •If unable to swallow tablets, may disperse immediately before use in a small quantity of water
   in a teaspoon 4

   Capsules

   •Swallow capsules whole 5
   Solution

   •Do not shake •The smaller 3 mL oral dosing syringe, marked from 5 mL to 3 mL, is for measuring doses of
   3 mL or less. The larger 10 mL oral dosing syringe, marked 1 mL to 10 mL, is for measuring
   doses greater than 3 mL •Oral solution may be taken with or after meals at any time of the day but caregivers should
   standardize the method of administration and time of day 2
   •Missed dose: Take the missed dose as soon as possible once it is noticed, but only on the
   same day. If this is not possible, the patient should skip the dose and continue with the next
   dose as prescribed. Do not take 2 doses to make up for a missed dose Extemporaneous Oral Compounds

   100 mg/mL Suspension (60 mL), using active pharmaceutical ingredient 6 ,7

 • Make a paste with 6000 mg of hydroxyurea powder with a small amount of vehicle. Vehicle is
   Ora-Plus and one of the following: Ora-Sweet, Ora-Sweet SF, Ora-Blend, or Ora-Blend SF.

   • Transfer to a glass amber bottle; do not filter..

   100 mg/mL Solution, using oral capsules 8 ,9
   • Place the contents of 500-mg hydroxyurea capsules into room-temperature sterile water of
   sufficient quantity to achieve 200 mg/mL.Do not heat the water as it results in reduced chemical
   stability by 40%.

   • Stir this solution for several hours with magnetic stirrer.

   • Filter the solution to remove insoluble excipients.

   • Add sufficient flavored syrup without color to create a 100 mg/mL solution.

   Serious: The most serious reported adverse reactions in pediatric patients included infections
   (17.8%), and blood and lymphatic system disorders (9.1%), which included serious neutropenia
   (3.2%), thrombocytopenia (3%), and anemia (3%).

 Black Box Warning
   Myelosuppression and Malignancies 2 ,1
    ●   Myelosuppression: Hydroxyurea oral tablets may cause severe myelosuppression. Do not
        give if bone marrow function is markedly depressed. Monitor blood counts at baseline and
        throughout treatment. Interrupt treatment and reduce dose as necessary.
    ●   Malignancies: Hydroxyurea is carcinogenic. Advise sun protection and monitor patients for
        malignancies.

   Monitoring
   Therapeutic Monitoring

   • Obtain fetal hemoglobin levels every 3 to 4 months to assess efficacy, monitoring for an in-
   crease of at least 2-fold over the baseline value 2 ,1 .

   Toxic Monitoring
   • Evaluate hematologic status (CBC, reticulocyte count) prior to initiation and every 2 weeks
   during dose-escalation periods 2 , Once a stable dose has been achieved, monitor every 4
   weeks for 2 months and then as clinically indicated 2 or every 2 to 3 months Follow blood
   counts on a long-term basis due to risk of leukemia • Measure markers of hemolysis if hemolytic anemia is suspected: serum lactate dehydroge-
   nase, haptoglobin, reticulocytes, unconjugated bilirubin levels, urinalysis, and direct and indi-
   rect antiglobulin (Coombs) tests 2 , • Verify pregnancy status prior to initiation of treatment if used in females of reproductive po-
   tential 2 ,1 .
   • Monitor patients for the development of secondary malignancies (skin cancer, leukemia) in
   those receiving long-term hydroxyurea treatment 2 ,1

   • Assess for signs or symptoms of hemolytic anemia, such as acute jaundice or hematuria in
   the presence of worsening anemia 2 , 1
   • Monitor for symptoms of pulmonary toxicity, especially in patients developing pyrexia, cough,
   dyspnea, or other respiratory symptoms 2

   • NSAIDs cause an increased risk of serious gastrointestinal (GI) adverse events including
   bleeding, ulceration, and perforation of the stomach or intestines, which can be fatal. These
   events can occur at any time during use and without warning symptoms. Patients with a prior

Common (pediatric): Vomiting (15%), diarrhea (9%), nausea (7%), headache (6%),
   phlebitis/infusion site reaction (5%), and rash (4%) were reported in a study of 85 pediatric pa-
   tients 0 to less than 18 years of age treated with imipenem/cilastatin/relebactam 2

   Acute graft vs host disease (aGVHD): Carbapenems were associated with an increased risk
   of grade II to IV aGVHD in pediatric patients (age 1 to 21 years) undergoing hematopoietic cell
   transplantation for acute leukemia (adjusted odds ratio, 24; 95% CI 02 to 51; N=2550). A
   sub-cohort of patients with more robust data that allowed more precise timing and exposure
   analysis reported similar results (sub-hazard ratio, 31; 95% CI 99 to 72; (n=1174)) as well
   as an increased risk of grade III to IV aGVHD (subHR, 77; 95% CI, 25 to 52). Early car-
   bapenem exposure (before day 0) especially impacted aGVHD risk. Sensitivity analyses re-
   vealed a consistent association between carbapenem exposure and aGVHD. There was no
   identified association between broad-spectrum cephalosporins and aGVHD. No statistical dif-
   ference was observed for antipseudomonal penicillins, although there was an increased risk.
   Median duration of exposure to carbapenems was 5 days (range, 1 to 19 days) Monitoring

   • Consider culture and susceptibility information, when available, for selection and modifica-
   tion of therapy Toxic Monitoring

   • Obtain medical history of previous hypersensitivity reactions to carbapenems, penicillins,
   cephalosporins, other beta lactams, and other allergens

drugs.uses_raw:
As a temporary adjunct therapy in reducing enuresis in children 6 years or older, after possible
   organic causes have been ruled out by appropriate tests 2

   For the relief of symptoms of depression. Safety and effectiveness in the pediatric population
   other than pediatric patients with nocturnal enuresis have not been established. Anyone con-

 sidering the use of imipramine in a child or adolescent must balance the potential risk with the
   clinical need 2 ,4 .

   Administration
   Preparation

   Extemporaneous oral compound

   5 mg/mL suspension (300 mL) 7

   •Weigh out 1500 mg of imipramine hydrochloride active pharmaceutical ingredient (API) and
   triturate to a fine powder using a mortar and pestle.

   •Add a small amount of SyrSpend SF PH4 to powder and mix to form a uniform paste.

   •Continue adding SyrSpend SF PH4 in geometric proportions almost to volume, thoroughly
   mixing after each addition.

   •Add sufficient amount of SyrSpend SF PH4 to bring final volume to 300 mL.

   •Transfer final product to low-actinic, light-resistant prescription bottle, and label with "Shake
   well."

   •The suspension is stable for at least 90 days at room temperature or in the refrigerator.

drugs.contraindications_raw:
Common: Weight gain, dry mouth, abdominal discomfort, sedation, tiredness, headaches,
   drowsiness, confusion, blurred vision, diaphoresis, constipation, and urinary retention 7/11
 Mood swings and nausea were the most common and limiting adverse effects in clinical prac-
   tice when treating childhood enuresis Black Box Warning
   Suicidality and Antidepressant Drugs

   Antidepressants increased the risk compared to placebo of suicidal thinking and behavior (sui-
   cidality) in children, adolescents, and young adults in short-term studies of major depressive
   disorder (MDD) and other psychiatric disorders. Anyone considering the use of imipramine or
   any other antidepressant in a child, adolescent, or young adult must balance this risk with the
   clinical need. Short-term studies did not show an increase in the risk of suicidality with antide-
   pressants compared to placebo in adults beyond age 24; there was a reduction in risk with an-
   tidepressants compared to placebo in adults aged 65 and older. Depression and certain other
   psychiatric disorders are themselves associated with increases in the risk of suicide. Patients of
   all ages who are started on antidepressant therapy should be monitored appropriately and
   observed closely for clinical worsening, suicidality, or unusual changes in behavior. Families
   and caregivers should be advised of the need for close observation and communication with
   the prescriber. Imipramine is not approved for use in pediatric patients 2 ,4 .

   Monitoring
   Toxic Monitoring

   •Perform baseline screening of sodium level and after 3 to 4 weeks in high-risk patients (eg,
   previous history of antidepressant-induced hyponatremia, low body weight, concomitant use
   of thiazides or other hyponatremia-inducing agents), especially during the first 3 weeks follow-
   ing initiation •Monitor blood pressure at baseline, with significant dose increases, and every 3 to 6 months
   once stabilized •Conduct cardiac surveillance at all dosage levels in patients with any evidence of cardiovascu-
   lar disease •Obtain baseline ECG when initiating larger-than-usual doses; repeat at appropriate intervals
   until steady state achieved 9 and throughout treatment as clinically indicated including after
   initial dose titration, with dose changes, and especially in children •Monitoring of the metabolic profile to detect early weight gain may be advisable at 3, 6, and
   12 months, then yearly, in all patients (not just in patients who are obese or overweight) and if
   receiving combination therapy, especially with atypical antipsychotics 8/11
 Depression

   •Monitor patients for clinical worsening, suicidality, or unusual changes in behavior, especially
   during the initial few months of therapy, during dosage changes, or in patients with severe de-
   pression Such monitoring should include at least weekly face-to-face contact with patients
   or their family members or caregivers during the initial 4 weeks of treatment, then visits every
   other week for the next 4 weeks, then at 12 weeks, and then as clinically indicated beyond 12
   weeks 10,11 . More frequent monitoring may be required in more severely depressed or suici-
   dal patients •Perform baseline screening (detailed psychiatric history and family history of suicide, bipolar
   disorder, and depression) prior to initiating treatment to determine if patients are at risk for
   bipolar disorder Therapeutic Drug Monitoring

   Strongly recommended during treatment for depression when titrating the dose. Therapeutic
   reference range for imipramine plus metabolite desipramine is 175 to 300 ng/mL when used
   as an antidepressant

Pharmacology
   Mechanism of Action

   The mechanism of action of imipramine is not exactly known. However, it does not act primar-
   ily by stimulation of the CNS. The clinical effect is hypothesized as being due to potentiation of
   adrenergic synapses by blocking uptake of norepinephrine at nerve endings. The mode of ac-
   tion of the drug in controlling childhood enuresis is thought to be apart of its antidepressant
   effect

   Black Box Warning
   Distant Spread of Toxin Effect
   Postmarketing reports indicate that the effects of incobotulinumtoxinA and all botulinum toxin
   products may spread from the area of injection to produce symptoms consistent with bo-
   tulinum toxin effects. These may include asthenia, generalized muscle weakness, diplopia,

 blurred vision, ptosis, dysphagia, dysphonia, dysarthria, urinary incontinence, and breathing
   difficulties. These symptoms have been reported hours to weeks after injection. Swallowing
   and breathing difficulties can be life threatening and there have been reports of death. The
   risk of symptoms is probably greatest in children treated for spasticity but symptoms can also
   occur in adults treated for spasticity and other conditions, particularly in those patients who
   have underlying conditions that would predispose them to these symptoms. In unapproved
   uses, including lower limb spasticity in children and in approved indications, cases of spread of
   effect have been reported at doses comparable to those used to treat cervical dystonia and at
   lower doses Monitoring
   Therapeutic Physical Monitoring

   • Median first onset of therapeutic effect appears within 7 days postinjection. Usual duration
   of effect is up to 12 to 16 weeks, but the effect may be shorter or longer in some patients

        corticosteroids.
    ●   Infliximab-abda should be discontinued if a patient develops a serious infection or sepsis.
    ●   Reported infections include:
    ●   Active tuberculosis, including reactivation of latent TB. Patients with tuberculosis have fre-
        quently presented with disseminated or extrapulmonary disease. Patients should be tested

 for latent TB before infliximab-abda use and during therapy. Treatment for latent infection
        should be initiated prior to infliximab-abda use.

        pergillosis, blastomycosis, and pneumocystosis. Patients with histoplasmosis or other inva-
        sive fungal infections may present with disseminated, rather than localized, disease. Antigen
        and antibody testing for histoplasmosis may be negative in some patients with active infec-

        and Listeria.

drugs.uses_raw:
Diabetic Ketoacidosis (DKA): The standard of care for DKA is continuous IV regular insulin. In
   cases when continuous IV administration is not available and in children with uncomplicated
   mild to moderate DKA, hourly or 2-hourly subcutaneous rapid-acting insulin is safe and may
   be as effective IV regular insulin infusion. Do not use this method in children whose peripheral
   circulation is impaired Type 1 diabetes mellitus: Intensive insulin therapy, either by multiple subQ injections of
   prandial and basal insulin or continuous subQ infusion, is the mainstay of treatment. Prandial
   insulin daily requirements are approximately 55% to 70% of the total daily dose, while basal in-
   sulin accounts for 30% to 45% of the total daily dose. Prepubertal children typically require 7
   to 1 units/kg/day and during puberty, the insulin requirements may rise to 1 to 2 units/kg/day.
   Rapid acting insulins such as insulin aspart should ideally be given 10 to 15 minutes before
   meals or immediately before meals to help reduce postprandial hyperglycemia and nocturnal
   hypoglycemia 6 , 7

   Type 2 diabetes mellitus: Insulin therapy should be initiated in pediatric patients presenting
   with ketosis/ketoacidosis and/or the patients HbA1c is greater than 5%. After initial treat-
   ment, insulin may be weaned off over 2 to 6 weeks by decreasing the insulin dose 30% to 50%
   with each increase in the metformin dose. If glycemic goals are not met after initial treatment
   and the addition of a glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1) agonist or empagliflozin, consider adding
   an intermediate/long-acting insulin. The starting dose of basal insulin is typically 25 to 5
   units/kg and the dose is titrated based on results of self-monitoring of blood glucose (SMBG)
   6 ,7

   well-controlled study in 777 pediatric patients with type 1 diabetes mellitus 2 to 17 years of

   Therapeutic Monitoring
   Type 1 Diabetes Mellitus

   •Routinely assess glycemic control to determine treatment effectiveness. Monitor HbA1c at
   least twice yearly in a patient who is well-controlled, every 3 months if not meeting treatment
   goals or when there is a change of therapy, or more frequently as clinically warranted. An
   HbA1c goal of less than 7% is appropriate for many children and adolescents, but HbA1c goals
   may be more or less stringent and should be individualized to each patient •Perform self-monitoring of blood glucose (SMBG) multiple times a day (6 to 10 times a day via
   meter or continuous glucose monitoring [CGM]), including prior to meals, snacks, at bedtime,
   and as needed to assist in meeting goals of therapy. Real-time or intermittently scanned CGM
   should be offered as soon as possible to children on multiple daily injections or insulin pump
   therapy Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus
   •Monitor HbA1c every 3 months if possible. A reasonable HbA1c goal for most patients is less
   than 5%, but HbA1c goals may be more or less stringent and should be individualized to
   each patient 9 , 7
   •Perform self-monitoring of blood glucose (SMBG) as needed to assist in meeting goals of ther-
   apy; SMBG should be individualized to each patient 9

   Toxic Monitoring

 •Increase the frequency of blood glucose monitoring with changes to insulin dosage (including
   strength, manufacturer, type or method of administration), coadministered glucose lowering
   medications, meal pattern, physical activity, and in patients with renal or hepatic impairment
   and hypoglycemia unawareness 4 ,2 .

   •Carefully monitor blood glucose during pregnancy 4 ,2 .

   •Monitor potassium in patients at risk for hypokalemia such as patients taking potassium-low-
   ering medications and medications that are sensitive to serum potassium concentrations 4 , •Monitor blood glucose and potassium levels closely in patients receiving IV insulin 4 ,2 .

   •Observe for signs and symptoms of heart failure 4 ,2 .

   •Routinely assess glycemic control to determine treatment effectiveness. Monitor HbA1c at

   goals or when there is a change of therapy, or more frequently as clinically warranted. An

   may be more or less stringent and should be individualized to each patient •Perform self-monitoring of blood glucose (SMBG) multiple times a day (6 to 10 times a day via

   hypo- or hyperglycemia 1 ,2

 sulin accounts for 30% to 45% of the total daily dose. Prepubertal children typically require 7

drugs.contraindications_raw:
Hypersensitivity reactions may be immediate or delayed. Some of the immediate reactions are
   manifested by hypotension, respiratory difficulty and/or cardiovascular collapse, urticaria,
   myalgia, and febrile episodes. Delayed reactions, such as myalgia, arthralgia, phlebitis, and
   lymphadenopathy, usually occur within 24 to 48 hours and resolve within 72 hours after infu-
   sion. IM use is associated with discomfort, pain, staining of the skin, tissue necrosis, tissue at-
   rophy with ulceration, and development of sarcoma at the injection site 1 , Black Box Warning
   Anaphylactic-type reactions, including fatalities, have followed parenteral administration.
   Resuscitation equipment and trained personnel must be readily available during iron dextran
   administration. Must perform test dose. Observe for signs/symptoms of anaphylactic-type
   reactions. Fatal reactions have occurred following the test dose and have occurred in situa-
   tions where the test dose was tolerated. Patients with a history of drug allergy or multiple drug
   allergies may be at increased risk of anaphylactic-type reactions Monitoring
   Monitor for signs/symptoms of anaphylactic-type reactions during administration. Obtain CBC
   (hemoglobin target level, 11 to 12 g/dL; hematocrit target level, 33% to 36%), reticulocyte
   count, liver function tests, and iron profile studies (serum ferritin, transferrin saturation) within
   4 to 8 weeks after administration to assess efficacy and toxicity 1 ,4 ,8 ,3 ,2 .

   Children with anemia of chronic kidney disease: Monitor serum ferritin (target level, 100 to
   800 nanograms/mL) and transferrin saturation (target, 20% to 50%) monthly during initial ery-

 thropoietin treatment and at least every 3 months during stable erythropoietin treatment or in
   patients with hemodialysis-dependent chronic kidney disease not treated with erythropoietin

drugs.pharmacokinetics_summary:
Pharmacology
   Iron dextran for intravenous use is a complex of ferric hydroxide and low molecular mass dex-
   tran. After administration, iron dextran is removed from the circulation by cells of the reticu-
   loendothelial system and split into iron and dextran. The iron is quickly bound to proteins to
   form hemosiderin or ferritin (or to a lesser extent, transferrin) complexes, the physiologic
   forms of iron. Hemoglobin and depleted iron stores are replenished with these iron com-

drugs.uses_raw:
• Isavuconazonium sulfate injection is indicated for the treatment of invasive aspergillosis or
   invasive mucormycosis in patients aged 1 year or older; isavuconazonium sulfate capsules are
   indicated for the treatment of invasive aspergillosis or invasive mucormycosis in pediatric pa-
   tients aged 6 years or older who weigh 16 kg or more Administration
   Intravenous

   • Administer via IV infusion over at least 1 hour; do not administer as an IV bolus injection • Use a 2 to 2 micron in-line filter • Do not infuse with other medications or IV solutions • Flush IV line with NS or D5W before and after infusion • Do not infuse with other medications or IV solutions • Infusion should be complete within 6 hours of dilution if kept at room temperature or within
   24 hours if kept under refrigeration Oral

   • Do not crush, chew, dissolve, or open capsules; swallow whole • May take with or without food 1

   Nasogastric

   • Remove cap, connect the syringe to nasogastric tube, and deliver dose. Administer three 5
   mL rinses to the nasogastric tube with water • Administer via nasogastric tube within 1 hour of reconstitution 1

   • Do not administer isavuconazonium capsules through a nasogastric tube 1

drugs.uses_raw:
Treatment for all forms of tuberculosis in which organisms are susceptible 12,13,14,6 .

   Administration
   Oral

   • Administer on an empty stomach 2

 • Crushed tablets may be mixed with low-glucose foods, such as sugar-free pudding; do not
   store for later use 2
   • Fixed-dose combination dosage forms are preferred when available to decrease pill burden
   4 ,3

   • Directly observed therapy (DOT) is generally recommended in all cases, especially with inter-
   mittent (not daily) dosage regimens Extemporaneous Oral Compound
   • Extemporaneous compounded isoniazid solution exhibited significant degradation (greater
   than 10% after 3 days) when made from tablets. Interactions occurred with excipients in the
   tablet. Isoniazid pure drug powder should be used if compounding the liquid is necessary and
   has been shown to be stable for up to 30 days 10 mg/mL Oral Suspension 11

   • Isoniazid in SyrSpend SF PH4 was stable for 90 days at 2° to 8° C and 20° to 25° C.

drugs.contraindications_raw:
Common: Adverse events include peripheral neuropathy (dose-related and more common in
   malnourished patients and those predisposed to neuritis (diabetics and alcoholics)), cerebellar
   syndrome which may include abnormal motor coordination, mild and transient liver enzyme
   elevations (10% to 20%), and gastrointestinal toxicity (nausea, vomiting, epigastric pain) 12,20 .
   Diarrhea is associated with the liquid formulation (contains sorbitol) Rare: Blood dyscrasias, neurotoxicity, and optic neuritis have been reported rarely Black Box Warning
   Severe and sometimes fatal hepatitis associated with isoniazid therapy has been reported and
   may occur or may develop even after many months of treatment. The risk of developing hep-
   atitis is age related. Approximate case rates by age are: less than 1 per 1,000 for persons un-
   der 20 years of age, 3 per 1,000 for persons in the 20 year to 34 year age group, 12 per 1,000
   for persons in the 35 year to 49 year age group, 23 per 1,000 for persons in the 50 year to 64
   year age group, and 8 per 1,000 for persons over 65 years of age. The risk of hepatitis is in-
   creased with daily consumption of alcohol. Precise data to provide fatality rate for isoniazid-re-
   lated hepatitis is not available; however, in a U.S. Public Health Service Surveillance Study of
   13,838 persons taking isoniazid, there were 8 deaths among 174 cases of hepatitis.
   Therefore, patients given isoniazid should be carefully monitored and interviewed at monthly
   intervals. For persons 35 and older, in addition to monthly symptom reviews, hepatic enzymes
   (specifically, AST and ALT (formerly SGOT and SGPT, respectively)) should be measured prior to
   starting isoniazid therapy and periodically throughout treatment. Isoniazid-associated hepati-
   tis usually occurs during the first three months of treatment. Usually, enzyme levels return to
   normal despite continuance of drug, but in some cases progressive liver dysfunction occurs.
   Other factors associated with an increased risk of hepatitis include daily use of alcohol, chronic
   liver disease and injection drug use. A recent report suggests an increased risk of fatal hepati-
   tis associated with isoniazid among women, particularly black and Hispanic women. The risk

 may also be increased during the post partum period. More careful monitoring should be con-
   sidered in these groups, possibly including more frequent laboratory monitoring. If abnormali-
   ties of liver function exceed three to five times the upper limit of normal, discontinuation of
   isoniazid should be strongly considered. Liver function tests are not a substitute for a clinical
   evaluation at monthly intervals or for the prompt assessment of signs or symptoms of adverse
   reactions occurring between regularly scheduled evaluations. Patients should be instructed to
   immediately report signs or symptoms consistent with liver damage or other adverse effects.
   These include any of the following: unexplained anorexia, nausea, vomiting, dark urine,
   icterus, rash, persistent paresthesias of the hands and feet, persistent fatigue, weakness or
   fever of greater than 3 days duration and/or abdominal tenderness, especially right upper
   quadrant discomfort. If these symptoms appear or if signs suggestive of hepatic damage are
   detected, isoniazid should be discontinued promptly, since continued use of the drug in these
   cases has been reported to cause a more severe form of liver damage.
   Patients with tuberculosis who have hepatitis attributed to isoniazid should be given appropri-
   ate treatment with alternative drugs. If isoniazid must be reinstituted, it should be reinstituted
   only after symptoms and laboratory abnormalities have cleared. The drug should be restarted
   in very small and gradually increasing doses and should be withdrawn immediately if there is
   any indication of recurrent liver involvement.

   Preventive treatment should be deferred in persons with acute hepatic diseases 12,13,14,6 .

   Monitoring
   Therapeutic Monitoring
   • Obtain acid-fast bacilli (AFB) smear and culture from sputum at least monthly until 2 consecu-
   tive culture specimens are negative. In patients with positive AFB smears upon diagnosis, ob-
   tain follow-up smears more frequently (eg, every 2 weeks until two consecutive specimens are
   negative) • Perform chest x-rays after 2 to 3 months of treatment in patients with negative initial cultures
   and at end of treatment. In patients with positive cultures at diagnosis, repeat chest x-rays af-
   ter 2 months of treatment and at completion of treatment are useful but not required. • Patients receiving twice or 3 times weekly regimens should be directly observed for compli-
   ance. Additionally, the Potts-Cozart test or isoniazid test strips are available for compliance
   monitoring 15,16,13 .

   Toxic Monitoring

 • Monitor hepatic enzymes (AST and ALT) at baseline and monthly, or more frequently if
   needed, in patients at risk for isoniazid associated hepatitis (eg, daily users of alcohol, patients
   with preexisting chronic liver disease, injection drug users, and black or Hispanic women, espe-
   cially in the postpartum period) • Consider obtaining baseline hepatic function tests in patients who have HIV infection, preg-
   nant women, and in the elderly who are taking medications for chronic medical conditions • Order baseline liver panel (or at least AST) for patients with HIV infection, liver disorders, pa-
   tients in the immediate postpartum period (within 3 months of delivery), regular alcohol users,
   injection drug use, use of medications with known possible interactions being treated with the
   combination of isoniazid and rifapentine. Subsequent testing during therapy should be per-
   formed based on abnormal baseline results or patients at risk for liver disease • Evaluate patients receiving the combination isoniazid and rifapentine regimen at least
   monthly for treatment-associated side effects (eg, icterus, liver tenderness, or rash) • Monitor closely for drug hypersensitivity reactions • Observe and interview all patients for signs and symptoms of liver toxicity every month dur-
   ing treatment • Monitor use carefully in patients with active chronic liver disease or severe renal dysfunction,
   age greater than 35, concomitant use of any chronic medication, a history of previous discon-
   tinuation of isoniazid, preexisting peripheral neuropathy or conditions that may cause neu-
   ropathy and in patients who are pregnant, HIV seropositive, IV drug users or daily users of al-
   cohol, as well as women belonging to a minority group, especially when postpartum • Periodic ophthalmologic examinations are recommended when visual symptoms occur Therapeutic Drug Monitoring
   Peak adult isoniazid concentration target is at least 3 mcg/mL in adults when measured 2
   hours after a dose of isoniazid Consider monitoring TB regimen drug levels in the following situations 2 :
   • Poor response despite adherence and susceptibility
   • Severe GI abnormalities such as short bowel syndrome, chronic diarrhea with malabsorption,
   severe gastroparesis
   • Drug-drug interactions
   • Impaired renal clearance

   • HIV coinfection

 • Diabetes
   • Use of second-line drugs
   Some experts use therapeutic drug monitoring for all patients with resistant TB early in treat-
   ment to identify poor responses earlier

Liver and intestines: Acetylation via N-acetyltransferase 2 (NAT2) and dehydrazination; signif-
   icant first-pass metabolism. Immature hepatic enzymes in neonates may impair elimination in

   Black Box Warning
   Warning: Embryo-Fetal Toxicity - Contraindicated in Pregnancy

   ISOtretinoin can cause life-threatening birth defects and is contraindicated in pregnancy.
   There is an extremely high risk that life-threatening birth defects will result if pregnancy occurs
   while taking any amount of ISOtretinoin even for short periods of time. Potentially any fetus
   exposed during pregnancy can be affected. There are no accurate means of determining pre-
   natally whether an exposed fetus has been affected. If pregnancy occurs, discontinue
   ISOtretinoin immediately and refer the patient to an obstetrician-gynecologist experienced in
   reproductive toxicity for further evaluation and counseling.

   Because of the risk of embryo-fetal toxicity, ISOtretinoin is available only through a restricted
   program under a Risk Evaluation and Mitigation Strategy (REMS) called the iPLEDGE REMS.
   Further information is available at www.ipledgeprogram.com or 1-866-495-0654 Monitoring
   Toxic Monitoring

   Evaluate blood glucose frequently during ISOtretinoin therapy in patients with increased risk
   of poor blood glucose control (eg, diabetes, obesity, increased alcohol intake, lipid metabolism

 disorder, or family history of lipid metabolism disorder) Perform hepatic function tests prior to ISOtretinoin therapy initiation and then follow-up peri-
   odically until the response to ISOtretinoin is established Perform serum lipid panel (done under fasting state with at least 36 hours between testing
   and alcohol consumption) prior to ISOtretinoin therapy initiation and then at weekly or bi-
   weekly intervals until the lipid response to ISOtretinoin is established (usually within 4 weeks)
   and more frequently in patients with increased risk of poor blood glucose control (eg, dia-
   betes, obesity, increased alcohol intake, lipid metabolism disorder, or family history of lipid
   metabolism disorder) Pregnancy Testing

   Prior to therapy initiation perform 2 pregnancy tests (urine or serum). Perform 1 test (urine or
   serum) at monthly intervals prior to each prescription refill, at completion of therapy, and at 1
   month following discontinuation Both a screening test (urine or serum) and a confirmatory test, with a sensitivity of at least 25
   milli-international units and which is Clinical Laboratory Improvement Amendment (CLIA) certi-
   fied, are required for women of childbearing potential who are being treated with ISOtretinoin
   prior to therapy initiation. The interval between the screening and confirmatory tests should
   be at least 19 days. A negative urine or serum pregnancy test is required at monthly intervals
   during therapy prior to each prescription refill, at the completion of therapy, and at 1 month
   following the last ISOtretinoin dose In patients with regular menstrual cycles, perform the confirmatory test prior to treatment ini-
   tiation during the first 5 days of the menstrual period, immediately preceding the beginning of
   ISOtretinoin therapy and after 2 forms of contraception have been used for 1 month In patients with amenorrhea, irregular cycles, or using a contraceptive method that precludes
   withdrawal bleeding, perform the confirmatory pregnancy test immediately preceding the initi-
   ation of ISOtretinoin therapy and after 2 forms of contraception have been used for 1 month

In a study of pediatric patients with chronic heart failure and dilated cardiomyopathy (6
   months to less than 18 years; mean age, 8 years), at least a 20% reduction of baseline resting
   heart rate without bradycardia or symptoms of bradycardia occurred in significantly more pa-

 tients receiving treatment with ivabradine (70%; n=73) compared with placebo (12%; n=41;
   odds ratio [OR], 24; 95% CI, 91 to 3) at 12 months. The mean reduction in resting heart
   rate was significantly greater with ivabradine compared with placebo from baseline to the end
   of the titration period (-21.2 vs -1.4 beats/min; mean difference, -18.99) and from baseline to
   12 months (-20.8 vs -3; mean difference, -16.63). There was a significantly greater increase in
   mean left ventricular ejection fraction between baseline and 12 months in patients taking
   ivabradine compared with placebo (13.5% vs 9%). Improvement in New York Heart
   Association functional class or Ross class at 12 months was 38% with ivabradine and 25% with
   placebo, which was not significantly different. There was no significant difference between
   groups in improvement in pediatric quality of life inventory (PedQOL) score at 12 months. N-
   terminal pro-B-type natriuretic peptide levels decreased significantly and similarly in both
   groups. The starting dose of ivabradine oral liquid was 02 mg/kg twice daily for patients ages
   6 to 12 months and 05 mg/kg twice daily for patients 1 year or older; tablets could be admin-
   istered to children weighing at least 40 kg with a starting dose of 5 mg twice daily. Dosages
   could be adjusted every 2 weeks for up to 8 weeks, to dosages up to 3 mg/kg or 15 mg twice
   daily based on a target heart rate reduction of at least 20% from baseline, as tolerated. The
   frequency of reported adverse events was similar between groups FDA Approved Indications:

   Ivabradine is indicated for the treatment of stable symptomatic heart failure due to dilated
   cardiomyopathy (DCM) in pediatric patients 6 months or older, who are in sinus rhythm with
   an elevated heart rate 1

drugs.uses_raw:
Coccidioidomycosis: Azole antifungals (primarily fluconazole and itraconazole) are the pre-
   ferred therapy for most chronic pulmonary and disseminated coccidioidal infections and have
   replaced amphotericin B as the treatment of choice Histoplasmosis: Ketoconazole is used rarely for histoplasmosis, but it is effective and may be
   used as a second-line alternative to itraconazole in mild cases. Ketoconazole has a higher
   number of adverse effects compared to itraconazole, which limits its use. Ketoconazole is ef-
   fective and much less expensive than itraconazole and may be used in cases of histoplasmosis
   involving mild manifestations, but not in disseminated or CNS disease 7

   FDA Pediatric Approvals
   Oral

   Indicated for the following systemic fungal infections in patients who have failed or who are in-
   tolerant to other therapies: blastomycosis, coccidioidomycosis, histoplasmosis, chromomyco-
   sis, and paracoccidioidomycosis. Ketoconazole tablets should not be used for fungal meningi-
   tis because it penetrates poorly into the cerebrospinal fluid Only use when other effective antifungal therapy is not available or tolerated and the potential
   benefits are considered to outweigh the potential risks Oral ketoconazole is no longer indicated for the treatment of onychomycosis, cutaneous der-
   matophyte infection, or Candida infections due to serious adverse events, including fatal hepa-
   totoxicity 1

   Topical
   Ketoconazole gel, and foam are indicated for the treatment of seborrheic dermatitis in im-
   munocompetent pediatric patients 12 years or older. Safety and efficacy for the treatment of

 fungal infections have not been established 3 ,2

   Administration
   Topical

   Foam

   •Dispense foam into the cap of the can, not directly onto hands 3

   •Pick up small amount and massage into affected areas until foam disappears 3

   •Part hairy areas and apply directly to skin 3

   •Avoid eye contact or other mucous membranes 3

   •Not for ophthalmic, oral, or intravaginal use 3

   Extemporaneous Oral Compound

   Ketoconazole 20 mg/mL oral suspension (300 mL) in SyrSpend SF PH4™ 4 :
   • Weigh out 6 g ketoconazole active pharmaceutical ingredient powder and transfer to a low-
   actinic prescription bottle.

   • Add SyrSpend SF PH4™ to the bottle using a volumetric pipette to achieve a final volume of
   300 mL.
   • Shake bottle until the suspension is optically uniformly dispersed.

   • Label the container with "Shake well before using" and "Protect from light."
   • Stable for up to 90 days under refrigeration (2 to 8°C) or at room temperature (20 to 25°C).

   Ketoconazole 20 mg/mL oral suspension (120 mL) 5 :

   • Comminute twelve 200 mg ketoconazole tablets to a fine powder in a mortar with pestle.

   • Add 20 mL of vehicle and mix to a paste.

   • Add vehicle by geometric dilutions with thorough mixing between each addition.
   • Suitable vehicles include a 1:1 mixture of Ora-Sweet and Ora-Plus, a 1:1 mixture of Ora-
   Sweet SF and Ora-Plus, and cherry syrup (cherry syrup concentrate diluted 1:4 with simple
   syrup).
   • Add enough vehicle to bring the final volume to 120 mL .

   • Label bottle: Shake well, Refrigerate, and Protect from light.

   • Stable for up to 60 days at 5 and 25 degrees C.

  • Give with or without food • Extended-release capsules should be swallowed whole with liquid; do not open, chew, or crush 3

 Oral Solution

  • Give with or without food • Use a calibrated measuring device for the oral solution • Discard unused oral solution 7 weeks after opening the bottle • Oral solution may be administered via a nasogastric tube or gastrostomy tube Intravenous Injection

  • May be administered IV without further dilution or mixed with NS, D5W, or LR 5

  • Preferably infuse over a period of 30 to 60 minutes; infusion durations less than 30 minutes are generally not recommended in
  pediatric patients • If diluted prior to infusion, do not store for longer than 4 hours at room temperature 5

  • Discard any unused portion 5

Common, partial-onset seizures, adjunctive therapy, adults: Dizziness (31%), headache (13%), nausea (11%), diplopia (11%),
  vomiting (9%), fatigue (9%), blurred vision (8%), ataxia (8%), somnolence (7%), and tremor (7%) 3 ,5 .

drugs.uses_raw:
Functional constipation and fecal disimpaction
   Guidelines: According to NASPGHAN guidelines, initial treatment of functional constipation in-
   cludes education, diary use (to evaluate dietary and fluid intake, especially in patients less than
   6 months), and oral treatment in patients 6 months or older. Oral medication or occasional
   suppositories may be started in patients less than 6 months if initial treatment is ineffective.
   The recommended initial treatment of choice for fecal disimpaction is polyethylene glycol
   (PEG) or enemas. For maintenance therapy, PEG with or without electrolytes is the first-line
   treatment; if PEG is not available, the recommended replacement is lactulose. Other laxatives
   (milk of magnesia, mineral oil, and stimulant laxatives) may be considered as additional or sec-
   ond-line treatments Duration of therapy: Initial therapy for fecal disimpaction should be 2 to 6 days. Maintenance
   therapy should be continued for at least 2 months or at least 1 month after a good response
   to therapy 2 , Medications should be weaned gradually and may need to be continued for
   months to years in some patients. Relapses are common and may be treated with mainte-
   nance or disimpaction therapy as needed 1

 Hepatic encephalopathy (HE): Lactulose is recommended in the treatment of HE to foster an
   intraluminal environment conducive to the conversion of ammonia (NH3) to ammonium
   (NH4+), which is less readily absorbed intestinally. The development of intracranial hyperten-
   sion is unlikely when the serum ammonia level is less than 75 micromols/L. Lactulose may be
   favored over rifaximin given its mechanism of action and shorter time to effect, but there are
   no data suggesting that therapy with either agent affects clinical outcomes Administration
   May mix oral solution with fruit juice, water, or milk

drugs.pharmacokinetics_summary:
Pharmacology
   Mechanism of action: Lactulose, a synthetic disaccharide, is degraded to lactic acid by bacte-
   ria in the colon, acetic acid and formic acid resulting in an increase in osmotic pressure and
   acidification of intestinal contents which in turn, softens the stool by promoting stool water
   content Onset of action: Up to 24 to 48 hours may be required to produce the desired bowel move-
   ment 5

   Absorption: Poorly absorbed 5

   Metabolites, active: Lactic acid, formic acid

Common: The most commonly reported adverse reactions in treatment-naive patients were
   rash (18%), headache (14%), pain (13%), diarrhea (11%), depression (11%), back pain (9%), fever
   (8%), and nausea (8%). Additional adverse reactions included abdominal pain, asthenia, dys-

   fumarate use. Consider discontinuing ARV drugs temporarily in patients with a lactate 1 to 5
   mmol/L (confirmed with second test) while conducting additional diagnostic work-up. In pa-
   tients with a lactate 5 mmol/L or greater (confirmed with second test) or 10 mmol/L (any one
   test), discontinue all ARV drugs and provide supportive therapy (eg, IV fluids, sedation, respira-
   tory support). Following resolution of clinical and laboratory abnormalities, resume therapy
   with either an NRTI-sparing regimen or a revised NRTI-containing regimen. Monitor lactate
   monthly for 3 months or more Black Box Warning
   Warning: Post Treatment Acute Exacerbations of Hepatitis B
   Severe acute exacerbations of hepatitis B have been reported in patients who are co-infected
   with hepatitis B virus (HBV) and HIV-1 and have discontinued lamiVUDine or tenofovir diso-
   proxil fumarate. Monitor hepatic function closely in these patients, and if appropriate, initiate
   anti-hepatitis B treatment 2 ,3 with both clinical and laboratory follow-up for at least several
   months in patients who discontinue lamiVUDine/tenofovir disoproxil fumarate and are co-in-
   fected with HIV-1 and HBV Monitoring

      Key: ART = antiretroviral therapy, ARV = Antiretroviral, AST = aspartate amino-
      transferase, ALT = alanine aminotransferase, BUN = blood urea nitrogen, CAB-LA
      = cabotegravir long-acting, CBC = complete blood count; DAA = direct-acting an-
      tiviral; HCV = hepatitis C virus, IN = integrase, INSTI = integrase strand transfer
      inhibitor, PrEP = pre-exposure prophylaxis

      (a) If ART is initiated soon after HIV diagnosis and entry into care, repeat baseline labora-
      tory testing is not necessary.
      (b) ART is indicated for all people with HIV and should be started as soon as possible.
      However, if ART initiation is delayed, patients should be retained in care, with periodic
      monitoring as noted above.
      (c) After 2 years of consistently suppressed HIV RNA, less frequent monitoring (eg, every 6
      months) may be considered.
      (d) After 2 years of ART with consistently suppressed viral load: CD4 count 300 to 500
      cells/mm(3), monitor every 12 months; CD4 count greater than 500 cells/mm(3), CD4 mon-
      itoring is optional.
      (e) If HIV RNA is detectable at 4 to 8 weeks, repeat every 4 to 8 weeks until viral load is
      suppressed to less than 50 copies/mL, then every 3 to 6 months.
      (f) For patients on ART, viral load is typically measured every 3 to 6 months. More frequent
      monitoring may be considered in individuals having difficulties with ART adherence or at
      risk for nonadherence. However, for adherent patients with suppressed viral load and sta-
      ble immunological status for more than 1 year, monitoring can be extended to 6-month
      intervals.
      (g) Standard genotypic drug-resistance testing in ARV-naïve persons should focus on test-
      ing for mutations in the PR and RT genes. If transmitted INSTI resistance is a concern, or if
      a person has a history of INSTI use as PrEP or treatment, or a person presents with
      viremia while on an INSTI, providers should also test for resistance mutations in the IN
      gene. In ARV-naïve patients who do not immediately begin ART, repeat testing before initi-
      ation of ART is optional if drug-resistance testing was performed at entry into care. For vi-

 rologically suppressed patients who are switching therapy for toxicity or convenience, viral
      amplification will not be possible and therefore resistance testing should not be per-
      formed. Results from prior resistance testing can be used to help in the construction of a
      new regimen.
      (h) If infected with hepatitis B virus, tenofovir disoproxil fumarate or tenofovir alafe-
      namide plus either emtricitabine or lamivudine should be used as part of the ART regimen
      to treat both hepatitis B virus and HIV infections.
      (i) If HBsAg, and HBsAb, and HBcAb are negative at baseline, administer hepatitis B vac-
      cine series. Also, consult Guidelines for Opportunistic Infections.
      (j) Typically HBV infection has resolved with loss of HBsAb despite isolated HBcAb; confirm
      with an HBV viral load if wanted. A positive HBV viral load is indicative of acute infection
      (other symptoms will be present usually) or chronic infection. Vaccinate the patient when
      viral load is negative. Also, consult Guidelines for Opportunistic Infections.
      (k) In patients with recent HCV infection (acquired in last 6 months) or advanced immun-
      odeficiency (CD4 count less than 100 cells/mm(3)), the HCV antibody test may not be ade-
      quate for screening. HCV RNA screening is indicated in persons who have been success-
      fully treated for HCV or who spontaneously cleared prior infection. HCV antibody-negative
      patients with elevated ALT may need HCV RNA testing.
      (l) At-risk populations: injection drug users, persons with a history of incarceration, men
      with HIV who have unprotected sex with men, and persons with percutaneous/parenteral
      exposure to blood in unregulated settings are at risk of HCV infection.
      (m) Serum sodium, potassium, bicarbonate, chloride, blood urea nitrogen, creatinine, glu-
      cose (preferably fasting). Monitor serum phosphorus concentrations in patients with
      chronic kidney disease who are on tenofovir-containing regimens. Renal function determi-
      nation should include creatinine monitoring and estimation of the glomerular filtration
      rate.
      (n) Consult recommendations of the HIV Medicine Association of the Infectious Diseases
      Society of America for patients with renal disease. More frequent monitoring may be indi-
      cated for patients with evidence of kidney disease (eg, proteinuria or decreased glomeru-
      lar function) or increased risk of renal insufficiency (eg. patients with diabetes or hyper-
      tension).
      (o) CBC with differential should be done when a CD4 count is performed. When CD4 count
      is no longer being monitored, the recommended frequency of CBC with differential is
      once a year. More frequent monitoring may be for patients receiving medications that po-
      tentially cause cytopenia (eg, trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole)
      (p) If random lipids are abnormal, fasting lipids should be obtained. Consult the ACA/AHA
      recommendations for diagnosis and management of patients with dyslipidemia.
      (q) If random glucose is abnormal, fasting glucose should be obtained. HgbA1C is not
      longer recommended for diagnosis of diabetes in patients with HIV on ART.

 (r) Assess urine glucose and protein before initiating tenofovir-containing regimens and
