drugs.contraindications_raw:
Rash is the most common and major concern with lamoTRIgine therapy. Other common ad-
   verse reactions associated with lamoTRIgine therapy in pediatric patients include infection,
   vomiting, fever, somnolence, accidental injury, dizziness, diarrhea, abdominal pain, tremor,
   nausea, ataxia, tremor, asthenia, bronchitis, pharyngitis, flu syndrome, diplopia 6 ,5 ,42,11 , and
   alopecia Black Box Warning
   Warning: Serious Skin Rashes

 Lamotrigine can cause serious rashes requiring hospitalization and discontinuation of treat-
   ment. The incidence of these rashes, which have included Stevens-Johnson syndrome, is ap-
   proximately 3% to 8% in pediatric patients (aged 2 to 17 years) and 08% to 3% in adults
   receiving lamotrigine. One rash-related death was reported in a prospectively followed cohort
   of 1983 pediatric patients (aged 2 to 16 years) with epilepsy taking lamotrigine as adjunctive
   therapy. In worldwide postmarketing experience, rare cases of toxic epidermal necrolysis
   and/or rash-related death have been reported in adult and pediatric patients, but their num-
   bers are too few to permit a precise estimate of the rate.
   Other than age, there are no factors identified that are known to predict the risk of occurrence
   or the severity of rash caused by lamotrigine. There are suggestions, yet to be proven, that the
   risk of rash may also be increased by (1) coadministration of lamotrigine with valproate (in-
   cludes valproic acid and divalproex sodium), (2) exceeding the recommended initial dose of
   lamotrigine, or (3) exceeding the recommended dose escalation for lamotrigine. However,
   cases have occurred in the absence of these factors.
   Nearly all cases of life-threatening rashes caused by lamotrigine have occurred within 2 to 8
   weeks of treatment initiation. However, isolated cases have occurred after prolonged treat-
   ment (eg, 6 months). Accordingly, duration of therapy cannot be relied upon as means to pre-
   dict the potential risk heralded by the first appearance of a rash.
   Although benign rashes are also caused by lamotrigine, it is not possible to predict reliably
   which rashes will prove to be serious or life threatening. Accordingly, lamotrigine should ordi-
   narily be discontinued at the first sign of rash, unless the rash is clearly not drug related.
   Discontinuation of treatment may not prevent a rash from becoming life threatening or per-
   manently disabling or disfiguring Monitoring
   Toxic Monitoring
   • Risk of rash may be diminished by keeping lamotrigine level below 38 mcmol/L at week 2 • Assess patient for emergence or worsening of depressive symptoms, suicidal thoughts or be-
   havior, or any unusual changes in mood or behavior • Monitor patient for signs of anemia and bleeding • Monitor patient for signs of meningitis (eg, nuchal rigidity, nausea and vomiting, headache) • Monitor patient for signs of unexpected infection 12/21
 Therapeutic Drug Monitoring

   • Anticonvulsant therapeutic range: 5 to 15 mcg/mL 23 ; treatment-resistant depression,
   greater than 25 mcg/mL 24

   • In a consensus guideline, the use therapeutic drug monitoring (TDM) with lamotrigine is rated
   as 2, recommended for dose titration and for special indications or problem solving. TDM will
   increase the probability of response in non-responders There is overlap in serum concen-
   trations between responders and nonresponders and between patients with or without ad-
   verse effects • There is no specific reference range for mood stabilizing effect, concentrations should be
   above 25 mcg/mL in patients with treatment-resistant depression, and the anticonvulsant
   therapeutic reference range is 3 to 15 mcg/mL with a laboratory alert level of 20 mcg/mL 24 ; in-
   cidence of toxicity increases significantly at levels greater than 15 mg/L Therapeutic refer-
   ence ranges were obtained from drug concentrations at therapeutically effective doses and re-
   lated to clinical effects; there are reports of decreased tolerability or adverse effects at
   supratherapeutic drug concentrations in blood • Saliva can be a useful alternative for therapeutic drug monitoring as drug distributes into
   saliva at concentrations that reflect non-protein-bound concentration in plasma • In a study of pediatric patients (N=32; 9 to 1 years) there was no significant correlation
   between lamotrigine blood levels and seizure frequency in children who received concomitant
   antiepileptics, except for concomitant valproic acid. Patients received valproic acid plus main-
   tenance lamotrigine doses of 1 to 3 mg/kg/day to a maximum of 200 mg/day. All effective
   cases of valproic acid plus lamotrigine were associated with levels significantly different com-
   pared with ineffective cases at 6 months and 2 years, but not at 1 year Pregnancy
   Due to the possibility of increased lamotrigine clearance during pregnancy, plasma levels
   should be monitored before, during, and after pregnancy 27,28,29,30 . Although, therapeutic
   concentrations have not been established, prepregnancy concentrations in an optimally-
   treated woman provide a reference concentration (RC) for comparison to concentrations dur-
   ing pregnancy 28,29 . The following monitoring has been suggested to minimize the risk of
   seizures in pregnant women 28 :
   • Before pregnancy: Establish the reference concentration (RC) of lamotrigine using the lowest
   effective dose and the optimal plasma level. If the patient has been receiving estrogen-contain-
   ing oral contraceptives, determine the RC and adjust the dose of lamotrigine at the same time

 the oral contraceptive is discontinued. After 1 to 2 weeks, measure the plasma concentration
   of lamotrigine and adjust the dose to reach the RC.

   • During pregnancy: Monitor lamotrigine plasma concentrations approximately every 4 weeks
   during pregnancy and adjust the dosage to maintain stable levels.
   • After pregnancy: Measure the lamotrigine plasma concentration within the first week after
   birth. If there is no increase in plasma level, recheck plasma levels after 1 to 2 weeks. If the
   lamotrigine plasma level rises above the RC, adjust the dose, and recheck plasma levels every
   1 to 2 weeks until the plasma level is stable and has reached the RC. In patients who had more
   than 3 to 4 dosage increases during pregnancy, adjust the dose on the first days after birth.
   Thereafter, if the lamotrigine plasma level rises above the RC, adjust the dose, and recheck
   plasma levels every 1 to 2 weeks until plasma level is stable and has reached the RC.

   ance to have feeding tubes unclogged or removed and replaced. Tablets may not disintegrate
   entirely when water is added to form a suspension, and/or the tablets may disintegrate but
   later form clumps which can adhere to the inside walls of the tubes. The FDA recommends
   that the Teva brand of delayed-release orally disintegrating lansoprazole tablets not be dis-
   pensed to patients with feeding tubes For administration via oral syringe: Place a 15-mg tablet in oral syringe and draw up 4 mL of
   water (10 mL for the 30-mg tablet), shake gently until tablet has dispersed, and administer
   within 15 minutes. Refill syringe with 2 mL (5 mL for the 30-mg tablet) of water, shake gently,
   and administer any remaining contents 14,15 .
   For administration via 8 French or larger nasogastric tube: Place the 15-mg tablet in a sy-
   ringe and draw up 4 mL of water (10 mL for the 30-mg tablet), shake gently and allow disper-
   sal, and inject into the stomach through the NG tube within 15 minutes. Refill the syringe with
   5 mL of water, shake gently, and flush the NG tube 14,15 . In one study attempting to provide a
   partial dose through a feeding tube, a 5 mg dose was administered successfully through an 8
   French pediatric feeding tube; however, the same dose partially clogged a 6 French pediatric
   feeding tube (was able to clear with NS flush) and completely clogged a 5 French pediatric
   feeding tube Data for successfully supplying patient-specific, partial doses of lansoprazole
   through pediatric/neonatal feeding tubes are lacking.

   Preparation

   Oral compound for suspension

   Kit contains all necessary ingredients and tools to make the suspension. The suspension is
   added to the lansoprazole powder in 2 additions; shaking well after each addition. The suspen-
   sion contains benzyl alcohol, propylene glycol and ingredients that are derived from corn Extemporaneous oral compounds

   Note: A 3 mg/mL oral suspension is available commercially through a compounding kit 19

   3 mg/mL suspension (100 mL) 20
   • Empty ten 30-mg lansoprazole capsules into a flask.

 • Mix with 100 mL of 4% sodium bicarbonate for 30 minutes using a magnetic stir plate;
   protect from light.

   • Draw up and store oral suspension in amber-colored plastic oral syringes.

   • Suspension is stable for 48 hours at room temperature and for 7 days when refrigerated.

   3 mg/mL suspension (100 mL) 21
   • Empty ten 30-mg lansoprazole capsules into a mortar.

   • If 5% pellets are used, add 5 mL of absolute ethanol to the mortar. Allow the pellets to rest
   for 5 minutes for the ethanol to soften the coating on the pellets and completely evaporate.
   • Triturate pellets into a fine powder and add it to SyrSpend SF Alka dry powder premeasured
   for 100 mL.

   • Add approximately 80 mL of purified water to mixed powders and mix thoroughly.
   • Add sufficient water to bring the final volume to 100 mL and mix thoroughly.

   • Transfer contents to low-actinic plastic bottle.

   • This formulation resulted in 10% lansoprazole loss in 8 hours at room temperature. The re-
   frigerated samples showed 4% and 12% loss at 14 days and 21 days, respectively.

Available data are limited to small studies of infants and children. Hypergastrinemia was re-

   Serious infectious disease: In pediatric patients with gastroesophageal reflux disease or
   other gastric acid-related disorders (N=1,262,424), proton pump inhibitor (PPI) use was associ-
   ated with an increased risk of serious infections overall (adjusted HR, 34; 95% CI, 32 to 36) compared with no PPI use. In sub-group analysis similar results were observed for infec-
   tions of the digestive tract (adjusted HR, 52; 95% CI, 48 to 55); ear, nose, and throat (ad-
   justed HR, 47; 95% CI, 41 to 52); lower respiratory tract (adjusted HR, 22; 95% CI, 19 to 25); kidneys or urinary tract (adjusted HR, 2; 95% CI, 15 to 25); and nervous system (ad-
   justed HR, 31; 95% CI, 11 to 54) and for both bacterial (adjusted HR, 56; 95% CI, 50 to 63) and viral infections (adjusted HR, 3; 95% CI, 28 to 33). The median follow-up time
   was 8 years, median age at index date was 84 days (range, 44 to 210 days), gestational age
   was full-term in 1%, and 8% were male. Of the children who received PPIs, the median
   duration of treatment was 118 days In a retrospective, single-center, observational, case-control study of 136 children (1 year or
   older) having protracted diarrhea and stool analysis for Clostridium difficile, the use of PPI ther-
   apy was significantly higher in the patients with C difficile-associated diarrhea compared to the
   control group (22% vs 6%; odds ratio of 5 (95% CI, 4 to 4; p=0.006)) Monitoring
   Therapeutic Monitoring

   • Observe for symptomatic improvement within 3 days. Consider intraesophageal pH monitor-
   ing to assess for efficacy (pH greater than 4) 5 ,26 .

   Toxic Monitoring
   • Consider monitoring AST, ALT, and serum gastrin levels if duration of therapy is greater than
   8 weeks • Monitor INR and PTT in patients receiving concomitant warfarin therapy 14 , • Hypomagnesemia has been reported with prolonged administration (in most cases, greater
   than 1 year). Monitor magnesium levels prior to initiation of therapy and periodically during

 therapy in patients expected to be on long-term therapy or patients receiving concomitant
   drugs, such as digoxin or those that may cause hypomagnesemia

   There are no recommendations for pediatric patients. The following are recommendations for
   adults.

   Hepatic Insufficiency: For preexisting liver disease (acute or chronic) or ALT elevations
   greater than 2 times the ULN prior to initiating treatment, use is not recommended If ALT rises to greater than 3 times the ULN, during therapy, discontinue leflunomide while the
   probable cause of the ALT elevation is investigated. If leflunomide is the likely cause for the
   ALT elevation, the cholestyramine drug-elimination procedure should be initiated to speed the
   removal of leflunomide from the body. Following discontinuation, liver function tests should
   be performed weekly until the ALT value is within the normal range. Restarting leflunomide
   may be considered if a probable cause other than leflunomide is identified Drug elimination procedure:
   There are no recommendations for pediatric patients. The following are recommendations for
   adults.

   status of patient) OR activated charcoal powder made into suspension 50 g ORALLY every 12
   hours for 11 days. Measure 2 teriflunomide concentrations 14 days apart. Course may be re-

   Leflunomide is contraindicated in pregnant women due to potential for fetal harm.
   Teratogenicity and embryo-lethality occurred in animals administered leflunomide at doses
   lower than the human exposure level. Pregnancy must be excluded before the start of treat-
   ment. Advise females of reproductive potential to use effective contraception during lefluno-
   mide treatment and during an accelerated drug elimination procedure after leflunomide treat-
   ment. Stop leflunomide and use an accelerated drug elimination procedure if pregnancy oc-
   curs Severe liver injury, including fatal liver failure, has been reported in patients treated with
   leflunomide. Leflunomide is contraindicated in patients with severe hepatic impairment.
   Concomitant use of leflunomide with other potentially hepatotoxic drugs may increase the risk
   of liver injury. Do not use in patients with acute or chronic liver disease or an ALT greater than
   2 times the ULN before treatment initiation. ALT monitoring is recommended after starting
   leflunomide. Stop leflunomide and use an accelerated drug elimination procedure if lefluno-

drugs.contraindications_raw:
In 2 studies of children with central precocious puberty treated with leuprolide (n=421), the
   most commonly reported adverse events were injection site reactions, including abscess (gen-
   erally mild to moderate; 9%), emotionally lability (5%), general pain (3%), headache (3%),
   acne/seborrhea (3%), rash including erythema multiforme (3%), and vaginitis/vaginal
   bleeding/vaginal discharge (3%) 9 ,16 .

   The most common adverse reactions reported with gonadotropin-releasing hormone agonists
   (including Lupron Depot-Ped® for 3-month administration) are injection site reactions/pain, in-
   cluding abscess, general pain, headache, emotional lability, and hot flushes/sweating Injection site pain (22.6%), headache (20.2%), pyrexia (14.3%), cough (14.3%), upper respiratory
   tract infections (11.9%), and nasal congestion (10.7%) were reported in pediatric patients
   specifically receiving the depot leuprolide 3-month pediatric preparation Monitoring
   Establish a clinical diagnosis of central precocious puberty before instituting treatment.
   Confirm with the following tests: measurement of blood concentrations of luteinizing hormone
   (LH; basal or stimulated with a gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH) analog), sex steroids,
   and assessment of bone age versus chronological age. Baseline evaluations should include the
   following: height and weight measurements, diagnostic imaging of the brain (to rule out in-
   tracranial tumor), pelvic/testicular/adrenal ultrasound (to rule out steroid secreting tumors),
   human chorionic gonadotropin levels (to rule out a chorionic gonadotropin secreting tumor),
   and adrenal steroid measurements to exclude congenital adrenal hyperplasia 9 ,5 . LH mea-
   surements are the most valuable marker for the diagnosis of CPP Monitor adherence to the prescribed drug regimen. Assess Tanner stage and growth parame-
   ters every 3 to 6 months and monitor bone age periodically 1-Month IM Depot: Perform GnRH stimulation test and obtain basal LH level or serum estra-
   diol and testosterone levels 1 to 2 months after initiating therapy and after each dose change
   to assess therapeutic response. Monitor bone age for advancement measurements every 6 to
   12 months 3-Month IM Depot: Perform GnRH stimulation test and obtain basal LH level or serum estra-
   diol and testosterone levels at 2 to 3 months, 6 months, and further during therapy to assess
   therapeutic response. Assess height (to calculate growth rate) and bone age every 6 to 12
   months 4 ,5 .

 6-Month SubQ: After 1 to 2 months of therapy, and as needed, perform GnRH stimulation test
   and a basal LH level or serum sex steroid levels to assess therapeutic response. Measure
   height every 3 to 6 months and monitor bone age periodically

drugs.contraindications_raw:
In clinical trials of pediatric patients 4 to less than 16 years of age with partial onset seizures,
   the most common adverse effects were headache (19%) nasopharyngitis (15%), vomiting
   (15%), somnolence (13%), fatigue (11%), and aggression (10%). In patients 12 years and older
   with myoclonic seizures, the most common adverse effects were somnolence (12%) and neck
   pain (8%). Nasopharyngitis (14%) and fatigue (10%) were the most commonly reported adverse
   effects in patients 4 years of age and older with primary generalized tonic-clonic seizures In clinical trials with pediatric patient less than 4 years of age, the most common adverse
   events were somnolence (13%) and irritability (12%). Other common adverse events in pedi-
   atric clinical trials (4 to 16 years of age) were fatigue (11%), aggression (10%), nasal congestion
   (9%), and decreased appetite (8%). A higher incidence of diastolic blood pressure increases
   was reported in children (1 month to less than 4 years of age) treated with levETIRAcetam
   (17%) compared with children treated with placebo (2%) Behavioral disorders (typically aggression, hostility, and nervousness) were 2-fold more likely
   in levETIRAcetam-treated compared with placebo-treated children (1 month or older) with
   epilepsy in 3 randomized studies. However, behavioral deteriorations and improvements were
   not consistently demonstrated in 10 observational studies After a 2 year follow-up, 280 infants who started antiepileptic agents as neonates experienced
   worse neurodevelopmental outcomes (cognitive and motor) with PHENobarbital compared

 with levETIRAcetam in a retrospective study Solution Compatibility
   NS, LR, and D5W.

   Diazepam, LORazepam, and valproate sodium.

   dosage changes occurred 2
   In women who plan on becoming pregnant, obtaining concentrations of levETIRAcetam before
   becoming pregnant and during the pregnancy may be beneficial. Although therapeutic con-
   centrations have not been established, prepregnancy concentrations in an optimally-treated
   woman provide a reference concentration for comparison to concentrations during preg-
   nancy, when concentrations may change 32,33 .
   Plasma concentrations of approximately 5 to 40 mcg/mL were noted in the majority of respon-

   Treatment of inhalational anthrax, post exposure, in pediatric patients 6 months or older Treatment of plague, including pneumonic and septicemic plague due to Yersinia pestis and
   prophylaxis for plague, in pediatric patients 6 months or older. Approval of this indications was
   based on an efficacy study conducted in animals .

   Ophthalmic

   Treatment of bacterial conjunctivitis in children 1 year or older caused by susceptible strains of
   the following bacteria: Corynebacterium species, Staphylococcus aureus, Staphylococcus epider-
   midis, Streptococcus pneumoniae, Streptococcus (Groups C/F), Streptococcus (Group G), Viridans
   group streptococci, Acinobacter iwoffii, Haemophilus influenzae, and Serratia marcescens In clin-
   ical studies, microbial eradication rates have been better with levoFLOXacin compared with
   ofloxacin. LevoFLOXacin provides a wider spectrum of activity compared with other
   quinolones (ofloxacin and ciprofloxacin), particularly against Streptococcus pneumoniae strains Administration
   Oral
   • Tablets may be administered without regards to food. Oral solution should be given 1 hour
   before or 2 hours after eating • Administer at least 2 hours before or 2 hours after antacids containing magnesium, alu-
   minum, as well as sucralfate, metal cations such as iron, and multivitamin preparations with
   zinc, or didanosine chewable/buffered tablets or the pediatric powder for oral solution • Tablets: If a dose of Levaquin(R) tablet is missed, take dose as soon as possible up to 8 hours
   prior to next scheduled dose. If less than 8 hours remain before the next dose, wait until next

 scheduled dose Intravenous
   • Administer by slow IV infusion not less than 60 (250- or 500-mg dose) to 90 minutes (750-mg
   dose) at a concentration of 5 mg/mL • Do not administer by rapid or bolus intravenous injection • Should not be co-administered with any solution containing multivalent cations (eg, magne-
   sium) through the same intravenous line • Maintain adequate hydration during IV levoFLOXacin to prevent formation of highly concen-
   trated urine Ophthalmic

   • Avoid contaminating the applicator tip with material from the eye, fingers or other source Preparation

   • Dilute single-use vials with a compatible diluent to achieve a final concentration of 5 mg/mL

Oral/Intravenous

   Common adverse events reported in children include vomiting and diarrhea 17 , 38 , 29/39
 CNS effects (headache and dizziness) are also commonly reported with fluoroquinolones Musculoskeletal: adverse events (arthralgia, arthritis, tendinopathy, gait abnormality) were
   reported at a higher frequency in children treated with levoFLOXacin compared with non-
   flouroquinolone therapy at a follow-up period of 60 days (2.1% vs 9%; p=0.04) and 1 year
   (3.4% vs 8%; p=0.03) in a safety analysis that included data from 3 large, multicenter efficacy
   studies (n=2233). Most musculoskeletal disorders were mild to moderate in nature and in-
   volved the weight bearing joints; arthralgia was the most common event (85%) However, a
   5-year safety analysis revealed that the cumulative long-term outcomes of children with mus-
   culoskeletal adverse events reported during the period (including ongoing arthropathy, periph-
   eral neuropathy, abnormal bone development, scoliosis, walking difficulty, myalgia, tendon
   disorder, hypermobility syndrome, and pain in the spine, hip, and shoulder) were slightly
   higher in the comparator treatment group compared with levoFLOXacin (4% vs 2%) Ophthalmic
   The most common (1% to 3%) adverse effects are transient decreased vision, fever, foreign
   body sensation, headache, transient ocular burning, ocular pain or discomfort, pharyngitis and
   photophobia 7 ,8 ,9 . Other reported reactions occurring in less than 1% of patients include aller-
   gic reactions, lid edema, ocular dryness, and ocular itching Black Box Warning
   • Fluoroquinolones, including levoFLOXacin, have been associated with disabling and poten-
   tially irreversible serious adverse reactions that have occurred together, including: ●   Tendinitis and tendon rupture
    ●   Peripheral neuropathy
    ●   Central nervous system effects
   Discontinue levoFLOXacin immediately and avoid the use of fluoroquinolones, including lev-
   oFLOXacin, in patients who experience any of these serious adverse reactions.
   • Fluoroquinolones, including levoFLOXacin, may exacerbate muscle weakness in persons with
   myasthenia gravis. Avoid in patients with known history of myasthenia gravis • Because fluoroquinolones, including levoFLOXacin, have been associated with serious ad-
   verse reactions, reserve levoFLOXacin for use in patients who have no alternative treatment
   options for the following uses: uncomplicated UTI, acute bacterial exacerbation of chronic

LEVOleucovorin Rescue, After High-dose Methotrexate for Osteosarcoma
   6 years or older: 5 mg (approximately 5 mg/m2) IV infusion every 6 hours starting 24 hours after beginning of
   methotrexate infusion. Rescue dose is based on a methotrexate dose of 12 g/m2 IV infusion
   over 4 hours. Continue LEVOleucovorin, hydration, and urinary alkalinization (pH of 7 or
   higher) until methotrexate level is less than 5 x 10-8 molar (M) (0.05 micromolar) 1 ,2 .
   Normal methotrexate elimination (serum methotrexate level at 10 micromolar at 24 hours
   after administration, 1 micromolar at 48 hours, and below 2 micromolar at 72 hours): 5 mg
   IV every 6 hours for 60 hours (total of 10 doses starting at 24 hours after start of methotrexate
   infusion) 1 ,2 .

   Delayed late methotrexate elimination (serum methotrexate level above 2 micromolar at
   72 hours and above 05 micromolar at 96 hours): 5 mg IV every 6 hours until methotrexate
   level drops below 05 micromolar Delayed early methotrexate elimination and/or acute renal injury (serum methotrexate
   level of 50 micromolar or greater at 24 hours, or 5 micromolar or more at 48 hours, or a 100%
   or greater increase in serum creatinine level at 24 hours after administration [increase from 5 to 1 mg/dL or greater]): 75 mg IV infusion every 3 hours until methotrexate level drops be-
   low 1 micromolar, then 5 mg IV infusion every 3 hours until methotrexate level is below 05
   micromolar and renal failure has resolved Dosage Adjustment
   Methotrexate toxicities: Decreased methotrexate elimination or renal impairment which are
   clinically important but less severe than the abnormalities described above can occur following
   methotrexate administration. If significant methotrexate clinical toxicity exists, but is less se-
   vere than the abnormalities described above, LEVOleucovorin should be extended for an addi-
   tional 24 hours (total of 14 doses over 84 hours) in subsequent courses of therapy 1 ,2 .

   Third-space fluid collection: Higher doses of LEVOleucovorin or prolonged administration
   may be indicated 1 , 1/6
 Other causes of delayed methotrexate elimination: Higher doses of LEVOleucovorin or
   prolonged administration may be indicated due to delay in methotrexate elimination because
   of renal insufficiency or inadequate hydration with LEVOleucovorin rescue after high-dose
   methotrexate 1 ,2 .

   Overdose of Folic Acid Antagonist or Impaired Methotrexate Elimination

   Administer as soon as possible after an overdosage of methotrexate or within 24 hours of
   methotrexate administration when methotrexate elimination is impaired.
   6 years or older: 5 mg (approximately 5 mg/m2) IV infusion every 6 hours until serum methotrexate level is
   less than 5 x 10-8 molar (M) (0.05 micromolar) 1

    ●   If the serum creatinine at 24 hours increased 50% or more compared to baseline,

   and in patients 6 years or older (Tirosint(R)) Limitations of use

   insufficient patients or for the treatment of hypothyroidism during the recovery phase of suba-
   cute thyroiditis 5 ,4 ,2 ,3 .

   Administration
   Enteral

   • Liquids are the preferred formulation for administration of drugs via enteral tubes • Tablet: In adults, crushed tablets suspended in water have been administered to patients re-
   ceiving enteral feeding through nasogastric or other tubes; for optimal absorption, wait as
   long as possible to administer the dose after interruption of feeding and wait at least 1 hour
   before resuming feeding Holding enteral feeding for 1 to 2 hours before and after adminis-
   tration has also been suggested Monitor thyroid function tests regularly (eg, weekly), as in-
   terruption of enteral feeding for 1 hour prior to and 1 hour following administration may not
   be sufficient to avoid development of hypothyroidism. Consider a small dosage increase (eg,
   25 mcg) if hypothyroidism develops, and resume original dosage once enteral feeding is dis-
   continued • Oral solution: The manufacturer suggests that levothyroxine oral solution should be admin-
   istered on an empty stomach (ie, 15 minutes prior to breakfast) 1 , however, it has been sug-
   gested that adequate absorption can be achieved when levothyroxine oral solution is adminis-
   tered directly through a feeding tube without interruption of enteral feeding IV

 Monitoring
   Therapeutic

   Laboratory
   Replacement Therapy
   •Measure both serum TSH and total or free thyroxine (T4) levels between 2 and 4 weeks after
   treatment initiation. Following dose stabilization, monitor every 3 to 12 months thereafter until
   growth is completed. May monitor more frequently as clinically indicated. Measure TSH and T4
   levels 2 weeks after any dose change. In patients with secondary and tertiary hypothyroidism,
   monitor serum free-T4 levels; maintain in the upper half of the normal range •Following initiation of therapy, serum T4 should be within the upper half of normal range
   within 2 weeks and/or serum TSH should decrease to below 20 milliUnits/L within 4 weeks •In children at least 3 years of age in whom a diagnosis of permanent hypothyroidism has not
   been made, obtain serum TSH and T4 levels after a trial period of discontinuation Suppression Therapy

   •Assess for TSH suppression to less than 1 milliUnits/L. Target TSH suppression may be lower
   (less than 01 milliUnits/L) in patients with high-risk tumors Physical Exam
   •Closely monitor patients with congenital hypothyroidism to avoid undertreatment; may have
   deleterious effects on intellectual development and linear growth •Closely monitor patients with acquired hypothyroidism to avoid undertreatment; may result
   in poor school performance due to impaired concentration and slowed mentation and in re-
   duced adult height •Perform routine clinical examination, including assessment of mental and physical growth
   and development, and bone maturation, at regular intervals Toxicity

   Laboratory

   •Monitor pediatric patients closely, including assessment of compliance, dosage administered,
   and method of administration, to avoid undertreatment and overtreatment 5 ,24,24,2 .

   •In patients with diabetes mellitus, carefully monitor glycemic control after starting, changing,
   or discontinuing thyroid hormone therapy 8/13
 Physical Exam

   •Monitor closely for cardiac symptoms following administration of levothyroxine sodium IV in
   patients who are at risk for cardiac complications or who have cardiovascular disease •Monitor patients with myxedema coma for previously undiagnosed diabetes insipidus after
   initiation of levothyroxine sodium IV therapy •Closely monitor patients with coronary artery disease during surgical procedures for develop-
   ment of cardiac arrhythmias 5 , including atrial fibrillation 24 , •Monitor patients receiving concomitant levothyroxine and sympathomimetic agents for signs
   and symptoms of coronary insufficiency •Closely monitor infants with congenital hypothyroidism during the first 2 weeks of levothyrox-
   ine therapy for cardiac overload, arrhythmias, and aspiration from avid suckling 5 ,4 .

   •Closely monitor patients with congenital hypothyroidism to avoid overtreatment; associated
   with craniosynostosis in infants, and may adversely affect the tempo of brain maturation and
   accelerate the bone age with resultant premature closure of the epiphyses and compromised
   adult stature •Closely monitor patients with acquired hypothyroidism to avoid overtreatment; may acceler-
   ate the bone age and result in premature epiphyseal closure and compromised adult stature

   • Administer at least 30 minutes prior to a meal, at approximately the same time each day • Missed dose: If a dose is missed, skip the missed dose and take the next dose at the regular
   time. Do not take 2 doses at the same time • Swallow whole; do not crush or chew capsule or capsule contents 1/4

   administered orally in either applesauce or with water or administered with water via a naso-
   gastric or gastrostomy tube. Sprinkling of beads on other soft foods or in other liquids has not
   been tested 2

   Oral administration in applesauce:

   • Place 1 teaspoonful of applesauce at room temperature into a clean container, open capsule,
   and sprinkle the entire capsule contents (beads) on the applesauce • Consume the entire mixture of beads in the applesauce immediately; do not chew the beads • Do not store the applesauce-bead mixture for future use Oral administration in water:
   • Pour approximately 1 ounce (30 mL) of bottled water at room temperature into a clean cup,
   open capsule, and sprinkle the entire capsule contents (beads) into the water • Gently swirl the beads and water for at least 20 seconds and swallow the entire mixture im-
   mediately • Add another 1 ounce of water to any remaining beads, swirl again for 20 seconds, and swal-
   low immediately • Do not store the water-bead mixture for future use Nasogastric or gastric feeding tube administration in water:
   • Open capsule and empty beads into a clean container holding approximately 1 ounce (30 mL)
   of bottled water at room temperature.

   • Gently swirl beads and water for at least 20 seconds, draw-up mixture with an appropriately
   sized catheter-tipped syringe, and apply rapid and steady pressure (10 mL/10 sec) to dispense
   the syringe contents into the tube. Add another 1 ounce of water to any remaining beads in
   the container and repeat the process.

   • After administration of the mixture, flush nasogastric or gastric tube with at least 10 mL of
   water.
   • All beads do not need to be flushed through to deliver a complete dose.

  Monitoring
  Therapeutic Monitoring (TB Treatment)

  • Monitor for clinical (eg, decrease in cough and systemic symptoms, increase in weight), radiologic, and bacteriologic response to treat-
  ment • Obtain sputum culture prior to initiation, then monthly during treatment. If cultures remain positive after 3 months, repeat susceptibility
  testing Toxic Monitoring
  • Monitor CBC weekly, especially in patients receiving linezolid for longer than 2 weeks, those with myelosuppression, those receiving con-
  current myelosuppressive drugs, or those with a chronic infection who have received previous or concomitant antibiotic therapy • TB treatment: Obtain CBC with differential prior to initiation, every 2 weeks for 2 months, then every 4 weeks for the duration of linezolid

  impairment • TB treatment: Test visual acuity at baseline and throughout treatment duration using symbol charts or "tumbling Es"; visual tracking of ob-

  • Gastrointestinal problems that may increase the risk of malabsorption

  • Concurrent HIV infection
  • Impaired renal function

  • Diabetes

   Risk of Thyroid C-Cell Tumors

   •Liraglutide causes dose-dependent and treatment-duration-dependent thyroid C-cell tumors
   at clinically relevant exposures in both genders of rats and mice. It is unknown whether liraglu-
   tide causes thyroid C-cell tumors, including medullary thyroid carcinoma (MTC), in humans, as
   the human relevance of liraglutide-induced rodent thyroid C-cell tumors has not been
   determined.
   •Liraglutide is contraindicated in patients with a personal or family history of MTC and in pa-
   tients with Multiple Endocrine Neoplasia syndrome type 2 (MEN 2). Counsel patients regarding
   the potential risk for MTC with the use of liraglutide and inform them of symptoms of thyroid
   tumors (eg a mass in the neck, dysphagia, dyspnea, persistent hoarseness). Routine monitor-
   ing of serum calcitonin or using thyroid ultrasound is of uncertain value for early detection of
   MTC in patients treated with liraglutide 3 ,1 .

Oral capsules and tablets

   Common adverse effects reported in pediatric patients during short-term clinical trials (4
   weeks), included upper abdominal pain (12%), decreased appetite (34% to 39%), dizziness (5%),
   dry mouth (4% to 5%), insomnia (13% to 23%), irritability (10%), nausea (6%), vomiting (9%), and
   decreased weight (9%) Oral solution

   Common (incidence rate 5% or greater), patients 6 to 17 years: Decreased appetite (34%
   to 39%), insomnia (13% to 22%), upper abdominal pain (12%), vomiting (9%), irritability (10%),
   decreased weight (9%), nausea (6%), dizziness (5%), dry mouth (4% to 5%) Weight loss and slowing growth rate
   Follow-up of pediatric patients aged 6 to 12 years suggests that those patients consistently
   medicated with lisdexamfetamine (ie, treatment for 7 days per week throughout the year)
   have a slowing in growth rate, measured by body weight as demonstrated by an age- and sex-
   normalized mean change from baseline in percentile of -13.4 over 1 year (average percentiles
   at baseline and 12 months were 9 and 2, respectively). Higher doses are associated with
   greater weight loss at 4 weeks of treatment. In a 4-week controlled trial of lisdexamfetamine in
   pediatric patients aged 13 to 17 years, mean weight loss from baseline to endpoint was -2.7,
   -4.3, and -4.8 pounds, respectively, for patients receiving 30 mg, 50 mg, and 70 mg Literature

   In a longer term, open-label study of children with ADHD (12 months; n=247; 6 to 12 years of
   age), these same events occurred, with the addition of cough (7%), headache (18%), influenza
   (6%), and upper respiratory infection (11%). The majority of events were documented within
   the first 4 weeks of use. Insomnia and vomiting occurred more often in patients who received
   higher doses Males may experience abdominal pain and insomnia more often than fe-
   males, while females report nausea and headache more frequently than males Cardiovascular events

 An association between the use of dextroamphetamine (and methylphenidate) and the devel-
   opment of peripheral vasculopathy has been reported in 2 separate case series (total n=8)
   17,18
         and a case-control study (n=64) In the case-control study, there was a significant asso-
   ciation between past or current use of ADHD stimulants and the presence of Raynaud syn-
   drome; there was no association with the use of other CNS medications Following the review of several case reports and the warnings issued by the FDA, the American
   Heart Association recommended screening ECGs for all patients with ADHD being considered
   for stimulant therapy. It also recommended discontinuation of stimulants in the presence of
   several CV risk factors, unless approved by a pediatric cardiologist However, since these
   recommendations were made, at least three large cohort studies of over 8 million pediatric
   patients demonstrated that stimulant medications were not associated with an increased risk
   of severe cardiovascular (CV) events with short-term use, including patients with congenital
   heart disease and other cardiac conditions. Data on possible risk from long-term use (longer
   than 2 years), however, are not available 20,21,22 . Based upon the more recent studies, the
   American Academy of Pediatrics issued a follow-up statement that screening ECGs were not
   warranted, and recommended a targeted history and physical exam as determinants for use
   and further CV evaluation Black Box Warning
   Abuse, Misuse, and Addiction

   Lisdexamfetamine dimesylate has a high potential for abuse and misuse, which can lead to the
   development of a substance use disorder, including addiction. Misuse and abuse of CNS stim-
   ulants, including lisdexamfetamine dimesylate, can result in overdose and death, and this risk
   is increased with higher doses or unapproved methods of administration, such as snorting or
   injection.

   Before prescribing lisdexamfetamine dimesylate, assess each patient’s risk for abuse, misuse,
   and addiction. Educate patients and their families about these risks, proper storage of the
   drug, and proper disposal of any unused drug. Throughout lisdexamfetamine dimesylate
   treatment, reassess each patient’s risk of abuse, misuse, and addiction and frequently monitor
   for signs and symptoms of abuse, misuse, and addiction 1 , Monitoring
   Toxic Monitoring

 • Assess the risk of abuse prior to initiation and monitor for signs of abuse and dependence
   during treatment 1 ,2
   • Evaluate for cardiac disease, including a complete physical evaluation of the patient and a
   careful evaluation for a patient or family history of sudden death or ventricular arrhythmia,
   prior to initiating therapy 1 ,2 ,14,15 . Based on the American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP) and the
   American Heart Association (AHA) consensus statements, the following cardiac monitoring rec-
   ommendations have been established to assist clinicians in the evaluation of children treated
   with stimulant drugs, including lisdexamfetamine, for ADHD 14 , 15 :
    ●   - Conduct a thorough examination prior to initiating lisdexamfetamine therapy for a diagno-
        sis of ADHD. Special attention should be given to symptoms indicative of a cardiac condi-
        tion, including palpitations, near syncope, or syncope.
    ●   - Obtain a complete family and patient history for conditions associated with sudden cardiac
        death (SCD), and determine current use of any other prescription or over-the-counter
        medications.
    ●   - Conduct a complete physical evaluation of the patient for hypertension, cardiac murmurs,
        physical findings associated with Marfan syndrome, and signs of irregular cardiac rhythms.
    ●   - Perform further evaluation if family history, patient history or physical exam is suggestive
        of cardiac disease during initial visit or at follow up visits, and if indicated, consult pediatric
        cardiologist .
    ●   - Continue to assess the patient for cardiac symptoms and any changes in family history at
        follow up visits.
    ●   - Blood pressure and heart rate should be evaluated at baseline, during routine follow-up
        within 1 to 3 months, and at follow up visits every 6 to 12 months. Increases in blood pres-
        sure and heart rate have been reported with stimulant use.

   • Monitor for the emergence of serotonin syndrome during initiation and dosage titration 1 ,2
   • Evaluate for bipolar disorder and screen for risk factors associated with developing a manic
   episode prior to initiating therapy 1 ,2 .

drugs.contraindications_raw:
Common side effects: Fine hand tremor, polyuria and mild thirst may occur during initiation
   of treatment during acute manic phase and may persist through treatment. Transient and mild
   nausea and general discomfort may also appear during the first few days of lithium treatment.
   A temporary reduction of dose or discontinuation may be necessary, but some side effects
   may subside with continued treatment Endocrine and metabolic: Thyrotropin concentration was elevated in lithium treated pedi-
   atric patients compared with placebo treated (3 milli-international units/L vs -0.1 milli-interna-
   tional units/L; p less than 001) Lithium toxicity: The likelihood of lithium toxicity increases with rising serum lithium levels
   (particularly levels greater than 5 mEq/L). Patients sensitive to lithium may exhibit toxicity at
   lower levels. Early signs of toxicity include diarrhea, vomiting, drowsiness, muscular weakness,

 and coordination difficulties. At levels 2 mEq/L or more giddiness, ataxia, blurred vision, tinni-
   tus, and large output of dilute urine may develop. Levels above 3 mEq/L involve multiple or-
   gans and organ systems 3 ,10,11,12 .

   Black Box Warning
   Lithium toxicity is closely related to serum lithium levels, and can occur at doses close to thera-
   peutic levels. Facilities for prompt and accurate serum lithium determinations should be avail-
   able before initiating therapy 3 ,10

   Monitoring
   Laboratory
   •During the acute phase, measure serum lithium trough (drawn 12 hours after the last oral
   dose) concentrations 3 days after starting lithium, and regularly until patient is stabilized 1 , During maintenance for uncomplicated bipolar disorder, regularly measure serum trough con-
   centrations. Serum should be drawn immediately prior to the next dose. Additionally, monitor
   after any change in dosage, concurrent medication (e.g. diuretics, NSAIDs, renin-angiotensin
   system antagonists, or metronidazole), marked increase or decrease in routinely performed
   strenuous physical activity, and in the event of a concomitant disease 1 ,2 . Obtain trough levels
   a minimum of 7 days after dose change Goal: 6 to 2 mEq/L lithium trough concentration 4 , 7 , 9 ; maximum was 4 mEq/L The
   manufacturer recommends 8 to 2 mEq/L for the acute goal 1 ,2 (do not exceed 2 mEq/L
   during the acute treatment phase) 3 and 8 to 1 mEq/L for the maintenance goal 1 ,2 .

   •Carefully monitor thyroid function in patients with hypothyroidism during the acute phase
   and maintenance treatment 3 , 10 , 11 , 12
   •Carefully monitor serum lithium concentrations in pregnant women during pregnancy and af-
   ter delivery due to changes in clearance and vascular volume 1 ,2 .
   •Assess kidney function prior to and during therapy; assess routine urinalysis, other tests to
   assess tubular function (e.g. urine specific gravity or osmolality following a period of water de-
   privation, or 24-hour urine volume), and glomerular function (e.g. serum creatinine, creatinine
   clearance, or proteinuria) 3 ,10,11,12 .

   Physical Findings

 •Monitor for evidence of neurologic toxicity in patients receiving a neuroleptic (ie, haloperidol)
   or patients with organic brain syndrome or other CNS impairment 3 ,11,12 .

   •Monitor for emergence of serotonin syndrome

   The specific mechanism of action of lithium is known. According to preclinical studies, lithium

drugs.uses_raw:
Lopinavir/ritonavir is indicated in combination with other antiretroviral agents for the treat-
   ment of HIV-1 infection in patients 14 days of age or older Administration

 Administer oral solution with food. Use a calibrated dosing syringe or the supplied calibrated
   cup to administer the oral solution dose. Administration of the oral solution before or after ice
   chips, sweet or tangy foods, chocolate syrup, or peanut butter may partially improve taste.
   Tablets may be administered without regard to meals but may be better tolerated when ad-
   ministered with meal or snack. Tablets should be swallowed whole, and should not be chewed,
   broken, or crushed Compatible feeding tubes include silicone and polyvinyl chloride (PVC) If the tablets are used together with didanosine, administer both without food. If the oral solu-
   tion is used together with didanosine, give didanosine 1 hour before or 2 hours after
   lopinavir/ritonavir dose Oral solution not recommended for use with polyurethane feeding tubes due to ethanol and
   propylene glycol content and potential for incompatibility. Compatible feeding tubes include
   silicone and polyvinyl chloride (PVC)

drugs.contraindications_raw:
Common, 6 months to 12 years: In a study of pediatric patients 6 months to 12 years of age
   (n=100), taste aversion (22%), vomiting (21%), and diarrhea (12%) were the most commonly re-
   ported events in patients treated for up to 48 weeks. Rash of moderate to severe intensity was
   reported in 3% of patients Other selected adverse events include gastrointestinal intoler-
   ance, nausea, and hyperlipidemia, especially hypertriglyceridemia, along with elevations in
   liver transaminases, hyperglycemia, PR interval prolongation, QT interval prolongation, and
   Torsades de Pointes. CNS Depression: Global CNS depression (eg, abnormal EEG, altered stated of consciousness,
   somnolence) has been reported with lopinavir/ritonavir. Discontinue use if confirmed.
   Lopinavir/ritonavir oral solution contains ethanol and propylene glycol as excipients. If needed,
   reintroduction of lopinavir/ritonavir may be considered when the patient is outside the vulner-
   able period (ie, postmenstrual age of 42 weeks and a postnatal age of 14 days or more) 3
   Dyslipidemia: Dyslipidemia has been reported with the use of protease inhibitors. Assess all
   patients with dyslipidemia for additional atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease (ASCVD) risk
   factors (patients with HIV are considered at moderate risk for ASCVD). Consider ARV regimen
   changes, especially if the patient is receiving an older protease inhibitor (eg, lopinavir/ritonavir)

 and/or ritonavir-boosting. If LDL-C is 130 mg/dL or more but less than 250 mg/dL, refer to the
   NHLBI guidelines on a treatment approach with lifestyle modifications and drug therapy.
   Persistent dyslipidemia may lead to premature ASCVD Central lipodystrophy/lipo-accumulation: Central lipohypertrophy or lipo-accumulation has
   been reported with darunavir use. Counsel patient on lifestyle modification and dietary inter-
   ventions. Consider using an INSTI instead of lopinavir/ritonavir Osteopenia and osteoporosis: Osteopenia and osteoporosis has been reported with
   lopinavir/ritonavir. To help prevent osteopenia or osteoporosis from occurring, ensure that the
   patient has sufficient intake and levels of calcium and vitamin D, encourage weight-bearing ex-
   ercise, minimize modifiable risk factors (eg, smoking, low BMI, use of steroids or medroxypro-
   gesterone), and consider switching from lopinavir/ritonavir to rilpivirine or an unboosted
   INSTI. If osteopenia or osteoporosis does occur, consider switching the ARV regimen and sup-
   plementing with vitamin D3 to raise serum 25-OH-vitamin D concentrations to 30 nanograms
   (ng)/mL Serious skin reactions: Stevens-Johnson syndrome, toxic epidermal necrolysis, and erythema
   multiforme major has been reported with lopinavir/ritonavir use. Discontinue all ARV drugs
   and other possible causative agents if confirmed. Provide intense supportive care, including IV
   hydration, aggressive wound care, eye care, labial adhesion preventative care, pain manage-
   ment, and antipyretics. Parenteral nutrition and antibiotics may also be needed. Consult with a
   specialist to determine if corticosteroids and/or IVIG is appropriate. Do not reintroduce the of-
   fending medication Monitoring

      transferase, ALT = alanine aminotransferase, BUN = blood urea nitrogen, CAB-LA
      = cabotegravir long-acting, CBC = complete blood count; DAA = direct-acting an-

      inhibitor, PrEP = pre-exposure prophylaxis

      (a) If ART is initiated soon after HIV diagnosis and entry into care, repeat baseline labora-
      tory testing is not necessary.
      (b) ART is indicated for all people with HIV and should be started as soon as possible.
      However, if ART initiation is delayed, patients should be retained in care, with periodic
      monitoring as noted above.
      (c) After 2 years of consistently suppressed HIV RNA, less frequent monitoring (eg, every 6
      months) may be considered.
      (d) After 2 years of ART with consistently suppressed viral load: CD4 count 300 to 500

 cells/mm(3), monitor every 12 months; CD4 count greater than 500 cells/mm(3), CD4 mon-
      itoring is optional.
      (e) If HIV RNA is detectable at 4 to 8 weeks, repeat every 4 to 8 weeks until viral load is
      suppressed to less than 50 copies/mL, then every 3 to 6 months.
      (f) For patients on ART, viral load is typically measured every 3 to 6 months. More frequent
      monitoring may be considered in individuals having difficulties with ART adherence or at
      risk for nonadherence. However, for adherent patients with suppressed viral load and sta-
      ble immunological status for more than 1 year, monitoring can be extended to 6-month
      intervals.
      (g) Standard genotypic drug-resistance testing in ARV-naïve persons should focus on test-
      ing for mutations in the PR and RT genes. If transmitted INSTI resistance is a concern, or if
      a person has a history of INSTI use as PrEP or treatment, or a person presents with
      viremia while on an INSTI, providers should also test for resistance mutations in the IN
      gene. In ARV-naïve patients who do not immediately begin ART, repeat testing before initi-
      ation of ART is optional if drug-resistance testing was performed at entry into care. For vi-
      rologically suppressed patients who are switching therapy for toxicity or convenience, viral
      amplification will not be possible and therefore resistance testing should not be per-
      formed. Results from prior resistance testing can be used to help in the construction of a
      new regimen.
      (h) If infected with hepatitis B virus, tenofovir disoproxil fumarate or tenofovir alafe-
      namide plus either emtricitabine or lamivudine should be used as part of the ART regimen
      to treat both hepatitis B virus and HIV infections.
      (i) If HBsAg, and HBsAb, and HBcAb are negative at baseline, administer hepatitis B vac-
      cine series. Also, consult Guidelines for Opportunistic Infections.
      (j) Typically HBV infection has resolved with loss of HBsAb despite isolated HBcAb; confirm

   12 years of age and older: Initial, 2 to 3 mg/day orally, divided twice daily to three times daily.
   Usual range is 2 to 6 mg/day, with daily doses ranging from 1 to 10 mg/day. A larger dose may
   be taken before bedtime 5 , Discontinuation of therapy or dosage reduction: Gradually taper dose; if withdrawal reac-
   tions occur, consider pausing the taper or increasing the dosage to the previous tapered
   dosage level and subsequently decrease the dosage more slowly Iatrogenic benzodiazepine withdrawal syndrome: Limited data available. Optimal weaning
   protocol has not been established.

   Pediatric ICU: One protocol in a pediatric ICU used the following weaning schedule 8 :

   Starting dose of LORazepam: Multiply current midazolam drip rate by 5 to approximate the
   mg/kg/dose of LORazepam to be administered orally every 6 hours for 4 doses (maximum: 2 mg/kg/dose, up to 4 mg/dose). Give first dose of LORazepam 24 to 48 hours prior to dis-
   continuing midazolam infusion. Decrease midazolam infusion by 25% of the starting rate every
   6 hours after the second dose of LORazepam.
   Midazolam infusion for 5 to 13 days: After 4 doses of LORazepam, wean by 20% of the starting
   dose and give every 6 hours for 4 doses (24 hours). Wean to every 8 hours for 3 doses (24
   hours). Wean to every 12 hours for 2 doses (24 hours). If dose is greater than 05 mg/kg/dose,
   wean by 20% of the starting dose every 24 hours until dose is less than 05 mg/kg/dose, then
   discontinue.
   Midazolam infusion for 14 days or greater: After 8 doses of LORazepam, wean by 20% of the
   starting dose and give every 6 hours for 8 doses (48 hours). Wean to every 8 hours for 6 doses

 (48 hours). Wean to every 12 hours for 4 doses (48 hours). If dose is greater than 05
   mg/kg/dose, wean by 20% of the starting dose every 48 hours until dose is less than 05
   mg/kg/dose, then discontinue.
   Managing withdrawal: If Withdrawal Assessment Tool-1 (WAT-1) score is 3 or greater, give a res-
   cue dose of LORazepam 05 mg/kg/dose (max of 4 mg/dose) and reassess in 1 hour. If patient
   requires 4 or more rescue doses in a 12 hour period, consider returning to previous dosing
   schedule.
   Pediatric Cardiac ICU: One protocol in a pediatric cardiac ICU used the following weaning
   schedule 9 :
   Starting dose of LORazepam: If midazolam infusion rate is greater than 24 mg/kg/hr, wean in-
   fusion to 24 mg/kg/hr before starting LORazepam at 25 mg/kg/dose IV or orally every 4
   hours (maximum: 4 mg/dose). If midazolam infusion rate is less than 24 mg/kg/hr, multiply
   current midazolam drip rate by 83 to approximate the mg/kg/dose of LORazepam to be ad-
   ministered IV or orally every 4 hours (maximum: 4 mg/dose). This dose may also be adminis-
   tered as a rescue dose.
   Midazolam infusion for 5 to 7 days: Wean LORazepam by 20% of the starting dose every 24
   hours for a total wean duration of 5 days.

   Midazolam infusion for 8 to 30 days: Wean LORazpam by 20% of the starting dose every 48
   hours for a total wean duration of 10 days.
   Midazolam infusion for greater than 30 days: Wean LORazepam by 10% of the starting dose ev-
   ery 48 hours for a total wean duration of at least 20 days.
   Managing withdrawal: Administer rescue dose of LORazepam if patient has a WAT-1 score of 4
   or greater and greater than 2 above baseline. If patient requires three or more rescue doses of
   LORazepam in 24 hours, consider holding wean. If patient requires 5 or more rescue doses of
   LORazepam in 24 hours, consider returning to the previous dosing schedule. If patient has a
   WAT-1 score of 4 or greater and greater than 2 above baseline and rescue dose of LORazepam
   does not have a sustained benefit, consider delirium and continue wean.

   Insomnia:

   12 years of age and older: A single daily dose of 2 to 4 mg orally, usually given at bedtime 5 ,6 .

   Discontinuation of therapy or dosage reduction: Gradually taper dose; if withdrawal reac-
   tions occur, consider pausing the taper or increasing the dosage to the previous tapered
   dosage level and subsequently decrease the dosage more slowly Procedural sedation/amnesia:

 Usual dose: 05 mg/kg (range, 02 to 09 mg/kg; maximum 2 mg/dose)
   orally/sublingually/IV 30 to 60 minutes prior to procedure 2 ,10,11,12 .

   Sedation for critically ill patients in ICU
   Less than 50 kg: Loading dose, 05 to 1 mg/kg IV maximum 2 to 4 mg, followed by initial
   infusion of 03 mg/kg/hr IV 13

   50 kg or more: Loading dose, 05 to 1 mg/kg IV maximum 2 to 4 mg, followed by initial in-
   fusion of 2 mg/hr IV 13

   Status epilepticus: 1 mg/kg/dose IV 14 (range 05 to 1 mg/kg; maximum dose 4 mg);
   may repeat dose in 5 to 10 minutes if seizure continues. Has also been given rectally at the
   same dose in children with no IV access 15,16,17,18,19,20,21,22 .

   Risks From Concomitant Use With Opioids; Abuse, Misuse, and Addiction; and
   Dependence and Withdrawal Reactions: 35
    ●   Concomitant use of benzodiazepines and opioids may result in profound sedation, respira-
        tory depression, coma, and death. Reserve concomitant prescribing of these drugs in pa-
        tients for whom alternative treatment options are inadequate. Limit dosages and durations
        to the minimum required. Follow patients for signs and symptoms of respiratory depression
        and sedation.

 ●   The use of benzodiazepines, including lorazepam injection, exposes users to risks of abuse,
        misuse, and addiction, which can lead to overdose or death. Abuse and misuse of benzodi-
        azepines commonly involve concomitant use of other medications, alcohol, and/or illicit
        substances, which is associated with an increased frequency of serious adverse outcomes.
        Before prescribing lorazepam injection and throughout treatment, assess each patient’s risk
        for abuse, misuse, and addiction.
    ●   The continued use of benzodiazepines for several days to weeks may lead to clinically signif-
        icant physical dependence. The risks of dependence and withdrawal increase with longer
        treatment duration and higher daily dose. Although lorazepam injection is indicated only for
        intermittent use, if used more frequently than recommended, abrupt discontinuation or
        rapid dosage reduction of lorazepam injection may precipitate acute withdrawal reactions,
        which can be life-threatening. For patients using lorazepam injection more frequently than
        recommended, to reduce the risk of withdrawal reactions, use a gradual taper to discon-
        tinue lorazepam injection.

   • Use of the COMFORT-B Scale, State Behavioral Scale, or Richmond Agitation-Sedation Scale

 One case of hypotension and one case of reduced glomerular filtration rate occurred with
   losartan in a study of 99 children (6 months to 6 years of age). Abnormal serum sodium, potas-
   sium, creatinine, and hemoglobin occurred in 1%, 24%, 3%, and 2% of children, respec-
   tively. There were no early withdrawals due to adverse events 3
   A case was reported of a 7-year-old boy who developed acute renal failure and hypotension
   following treatment with combination therapy of losartan and lisinopril for proteinuria 26

   kidney disease, 7 children experienced significant hyperkalemia (mean potassium increase
   from 3 to 5). Close monitoring of potassium levels is recommended Adult

   Common (2% or greater than placebo): Dizziness, upper respiratory infection, nasal conges-
   tion, back pain 4

   Black Box Warning
   Fetal Toxicity

   When pregnancy is detected, discontinue losartan as soon as possible. Drugs that act directly
   on the renin-angiotensin system can cause injury and death to the developing fetus 4 ,5 .

   Monitoring
   • Monitor blood pressure during dose titration and periodically thereafter. Monitor for signs
   and symptoms of hypotension • In patients receiving concomitant therapy with losartan and other agents that affect the
   renin-angiotensin system, closely monitor blood pressure, renal function, and electrolytes • Monitor renal function (BUN and serum creatinine) and electrolytes (particularly potassium) 1
   week after therapy initiation, 1 week after any dose change, and every 3 to 6 months during
   long-term therapy

   In a meta-analysis of 6 randomized, double-blind trials in pediatric patients with familial hyper-
   cholesterolemia, statins reduced LDL, total cholesterol, triglycerides, and increased HDL. As
   compared with placebo, the pooled effect size was a reduction of 01% and 11% for LDL and
   total cholesterol, respectively, and an increase of 12% for HDL Data suggests that statin use in those 8 to 18 years of age had similar adverse-event profiles
   and efficacy when compared to adult studies 2 , however, randomized controlled trials in chil-
   dren have been limited to patients with hereditary familial hypercholesterolemia for a maxi-
   mum duration of 2 years. Data are lacking for children with secondary dyslipidemias. Long-
   term safety, especially with regard to growth and sexual development, is unknown Heterozygous Familial Hypercholesterolemia
   Statin therapy for 6 to 96 weeks significantly improved LDL-C and other lipid parameters (ex-
   cept triglycerides) and was well-tolerated in a metaanalysis of 9 studies in 1191 pediatric pa-
   tients (mean age, 3 +/- 5 years; mean BMI, 3 +/- 7 kg/m(2) based on 6 studies) with
   heterozygous familial hypercholesterolemia. At the end of treatment, the observed differences
   in lipid parameters for statins vs placebo were: Total cholesterol (9 studies) -79.3 mg/dL (95%
   CI, -93.9 to -64.7 mg/dL); LDL-C (9 studies) -78.5 mg/dL (95% CI, -93.2 to -63.8 mg/dL);
   Triglycerides (8 studies) -4.8 mg/dL (95% CI, -9.7 to 1 mg/dL); Apolipoprotein B (8 studies)
   -49.6 mg/dL (95% CI, -60.4 to -38.8 mg/dL); HDL-C (8 studies) 2 mg/dL (95% CI, 08 to 29
   mg/dL). In subgroup analysis, statins showed a dose-dependent effect on achievement of the
   LDL-C target. Important differences among studies may affect the validity of the total choles-
   terol, LDL-C, and apolipoprotein B results. Lovastatin 10 to 40 mg/day was given in 2 studies,
   pravastatin 10 to 40 mg/day in 2 studies, simvastatin 10 to 40 mg/day in 2 studies, pitavastatin
   1 to 4 mg/day in 1 study, atorvastatin 10 to 20 mg/day in 1 study, and rosuvastatin 5 to 20
   mg/day in 1 study Pediatric FDA approved indication:

   Heterozygous Familial Hypercholesterolemia in Pediatric Patients (10 to 17 years of age)

   Lovastatin significantly decreased plasma levels of total-C, LDL-C, and apolipoprotein B during
   double-blind, placebo-controlled clinical studies in boys (study 1) and postmenarchal girls
   (study 2) 10 to 17 years of age. In study 1, the mean achieved LDL-C value was 9 mg/dL in
   the lovastatin group compared with 8 mg/dL in the placebo group. In study 2, the mean
   achieved LDL-C value was 5 mg/dL in the lovastatin group compared with 5 mg/dL in
   the placebo group. Long-term reduction of morbidity and mortality into adulthood is unknown 3/8
 Administration
   Administer once daily with the evening meal

drugs.uses_raw:
Migraine prophylaxis: A 16-week randomized study of patients 3 to 17 years (N=118; 86 pa-
   tients completed study) with at least a 4 week history of at least weekly migraines reported
   that headache frequency and severity may be reduced with magnesium oxide prophylaxis
   compared with placebo. The decrease in headache frequency was sustained over the 16-week
   study period in the magnesium oxide group, while the placebo group initially had a decrease
   in frequency that then began to increase after about 6 weeks. Magnesium oxide dosage was 9
   mg/kg/day of elemental magnesium divided into 3 daily doses given with food. Diarrhea was
   reported by 19% in the magnesium oxide group compared with 7% in the placebo group Pain intensity and frequency of migraine headaches without aura were significantly reduced
   when magnesium 400 mg orally was used prophylactically among patients who received either
   acetaminophen or ibuprofen for acute relief (N=160; 5 to 16 years). Measurements were evalu-
   ated at 3 and 18 months, and intensity was measured by a visual analog scale. Patients taking
   magnesium plus acetaminophen experienced significantly faster relief than those on ac-
   etaminophen alone, but a similar difference was not found in the ibuprofen groups Guidelines

   • Absorption of oral magnesium products varies by salt form. Bioavailability and absorption
   may be more complete with the aspartate, citrate, chloride, and lactate forms than with oxide
   or sulfate • The following conditions increase the risk of magnesium deficiency because of decreased in-
   take, reduced absorption, or increased loss from the body 2
    ●   Alcohol dependence
    ●   Concomitant medications that alter magnesium status
    ●   Decreased absorption and increased renal excretion in older adults
    ●   Gastrointestinal diseases such as Crohn disease, gluten-sensitive enteropathy (celiac dis-
        ease), regional enteritis, resection or bypass of the small intestine
    ●   Type 2 diabetes or insulin resistance

   Limitations of Use

   Caution is advised when used in patients with kidney disease 1 , 2/4
 Administration
   Take tablet orally 1

   Inhalation

   Inhaled dry powder mannitol is indicated for assessment of bronchial hyperresponsiveness in
   patients 6 years or older without clinically apparent asthma Limitations of Use
   Mannitol inhalation powder is not a standalone test or a screening test for asthma. Bronchial
   challenge testing with mannitol should be used only as part of an overall assessment of
   asthma Administration
   Inhalation:

   •Do not swallow capsules •Only use with the provided inhaler •When performing a bronchial challenge test, the patient should be supervised at all times
   during the test •Administer a standard dose of a short-acting inhaled beta-agonist for positive response and
   significant respiratory symptoms 7/17
 •Discontinue the bronchial challenge test and administer a bronchodilator, if a patient has a
   10% or greater FEV1 reduction with 0 mg capsule •A nose clip may be used if preferred. If used, apply the nose clip and direct the patient to
   breath though the mouth •Insert the 0 mg capsule in the provided inhaler device. Depress buttons on side of device
   slowly to puncture capsule, once only; a second puncture may fragment the capsules •The patient should exhale completely, before inhaling from device in a controlled deep inspi-
   ration •At the end of deep inspiration, start 60 second timer; the subject should hold breath for 5 sec-
   onds and exhale through mouth before removing nose clip •At the end of 60 seconds, measure the FEV1 in duplicate (the measurement after inhaling the
   0 mg capsule is the baseline FEV1) •Repeat the administration steps until the patient has a positive response or negative test •All remaining unused blister packs and the inhaler should be properly discarded at the com-
   pletion of the test Injection:

   •For IV infusion, preferably into a central vein •Do not administer simultaneously with blood products through the same administration set
   because of the possibility of pseudoagglutination or hemolysis •Use administration sets with a final in-line filter because of potential for crystals to form •Use a non-vented infusion set or close the vent on a vented set, avoid multiple connections,
   and do not connect flexible containers in series to prevent air embolism 8
   •Fully evacuate residual gas in the container prior to administration and do not pressurize the
   flexible container to increase flow rates to prevent air embolism 8
   •If administration is controlled by a pumping device, turn off pump before the container runs
   dry to prevent air embolism 8

   •For single use only. Discard unused portion

drugs.uses_raw:
Indicated in combination with other antiretroviral agents for the treatment of CCR5-tropic HIV-
   1 infection in patients weighing at least 2 kg. Not recommended in patients with dual/mixed-
   or CXCR4- tropic HIV-1 infection Administration
   May take with or without food 1

   For pediatric patients unable to swallow tablets, administer the oral solution using the in-
   cluded bottle adapter and oral dosing syringe. For doses 5 mL or less, use the 3-mL syringe;
   for doses greater than 5 mL, use the 10-mL syringe Use care when measuring neonate doses due to the small volume of oral solution

      Key: ART = antiretroviral therapy, ARV = Antiretroviral, AST = aspartate amino-
      transferase, ALT = alanine aminotransferase, BUN = blood urea nitrogen, CAB-LA
      = cabotegravir long-acting, CBC = complete blood count; DAA = direct-acting an-
      tiviral; HCV = hepatitis C virus, IN = integrase, INSTI = integrase strand transfer
      inhibitor, PrEP = pre-exposure prophylaxis

      (a) If ART is initiated soon after HIV diagnosis and entry into care, repeat baseline labora-
      tory testing is not necessary.
      (b) ART is indicated for all people with HIV and should be started as soon as possible.
      However, if ART initiation is delayed, patients should be retained in care, with periodic
      monitoring as noted above.
      (c) After 2 years of consistently suppressed HIV RNA, less frequent monitoring (eg, every 6
      months) may be considered.
      (d) After 2 years of ART with consistently suppressed viral load: CD4 count 300 to 500

 cells/mm(3), monitor every 12 months; CD4 count greater than 500 cells/mm(3), CD4 mon-
      itoring is optional.
      (e) If HIV RNA is detectable at 4 to 8 weeks, repeat every 4 to 8 weeks until viral load is
      suppressed to less than 50 copies/mL, then every 3 to 6 months.
      (f) For patients on ART, viral load is typically measured every 3 to 6 months. More frequent
      monitoring may be considered in individuals having difficulties with ART adherence or at
      risk for nonadherence. However, for adherent patients with suppressed viral load and sta-
      ble immunological status for more than 1 year, monitoring can be extended to 6-month
      intervals.
      (g) Standard genotypic drug-resistance testing in ARV-naïve persons should focus on test-
      ing for mutations in the PR and RT genes. If transmitted INSTI resistance is a concern, or if
      a person has a history of INSTI use as PrEP or treatment, or a person presents with
      viremia while on an INSTI, providers should also test for resistance mutations in the IN
      gene. In ARV-naïve patients who do not immediately begin ART, repeat testing before initi-
      ation of ART is optional if drug-resistance testing was performed at entry into care. For vi-
      rologically suppressed patients who are switching therapy for toxicity or convenience, viral
      amplification will not be possible and therefore resistance testing should not be per-
      formed. Results from prior resistance testing can be used to help in the construction of a
      new regimen.
      (h) If infected with hepatitis B virus, tenofovir disoproxil fumarate or tenofovir alafe-
      namide plus either emtricitabine or lamivudine should be used as part of the ART regimen
      to treat both hepatitis B virus and HIV infections.
      (i) If HBsAg, and HBsAb, and HBcAb are negative at baseline, administer hepatitis B vac-
      cine series. Also, consult Guidelines for Opportunistic Infections.
      (j) Typically HBV infection has resolved with loss of HBsAb despite isolated HBcAb; confirm
      with an HBV viral load if wanted. A positive HBV viral load is indicative of acute infection
      (other symptoms will be present usually) or chronic infection. Vaccinate the patient when
      viral load is negative. Also, consult Guidelines for Opportunistic Infections.
      (k) In patients with recent HCV infection (acquired in last 6 months) or advanced immun-
      odeficiency (CD4 count less than 100 cells/mm(3)), the HCV antibody test may not be ade-
      quate for screening. HCV RNA screening is indicated in persons who have been success-
      fully treated for HCV or who spontaneously cleared prior infection. HCV antibody-negative
      patients with elevated ALT may need HCV RNA testing.
      (l) At-risk populations: injection drug users, persons with a history of incarceration, men
      with HIV who have unprotected sex with men, and persons with percutaneous/parenteral
      exposure to blood in unregulated settings are at risk of HCV infection.
      (m) Serum sodium, potassium, bicarbonate, chloride, blood urea nitrogen, creatinine, glu-
      cose (preferably fasting). Monitor serum phosphorus concentrations in patients with
      chronic kidney disease who are on tenofovir-containing regimens. Renal function determi-

 nation should include creatinine monitoring and estimation of the glomerular filtration
      rate.
      (n) Consult recommendations of the HIV Medicine Association of the Infectious Diseases
      Society of America for patients with renal disease. More frequent monitoring may be indi-
      cated for patients with evidence of kidney disease (eg, proteinuria or decreased glomeru-
      lar function) or increased risk of renal insufficiency (eg. patients with diabetes or hyper-
      tension).
      (o) CBC with differential should be done when a CD4 count is performed. When CD4 count
      is no longer being monitored, the recommended frequency of CBC with differential is
      once a year. More frequent monitoring may be for patients receiving medications that po-
      tentially cause cytopenia (eg, trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole)
      (p) If random lipids are abnormal, fasting lipids should be obtained. Consult the ACA/AHA
      recommendations for diagnosis and management of patients with dyslipidemia.
      (q) If random glucose is abnormal, fasting glucose should be obtained. HgbA1C is not
      longer recommended for diagnosis of diabetes in patients with HIV on ART.
      (r) Assess urine glucose and protein before initiating tenofovir-containing regimens and
      monitor during treatment with these regimens.
      (s) In women with child-bearing potential.

   Product-Specific Monitoring

   Perform a highly sensitive tropism assay prior to initiation of maraviroc therapy Additional liver function test monitoring may be warranted in patients with pre-existing liver
   dysfunction or who are co-infected with hepatitis B or C Monitoring for cardiovascular adverse events may be warranted in patients with cardiovascu-
   lar comorbidities, risk factors for postural hypotension, or receiving concomitant medications
   that lower blood pressure Monitor patients closely during therapy for evidence of infections

   12 years or older and weighing at least 35 kg: 400 mg orally twice daily 1

drugs.uses_raw:
Maribavir is indicated for the treatment of adults and pediatric patients (12 years or older and
   at least 35 kg) with post-transplant cytomegalovirus (CMV) infection/disease that is refractory
   to treatment (with or without genotypic resistance) with ganciclovir, valganciclovir, cidofovir, or
   foscarnet 1

   Administration
   Oral

   • Administer orally with or without food • Swirl container gently to keep the particles from settling, administer the suspension before it
   settles; the mixture will have a bitter taste; rinse container with 15 mL of drinking water and
   administer the rinse water; repeat until no particles are left in container Nasogastric Tube or Orogastric Tube
   • Once the tablets are completely dispersed in the syringe, administer via NG or OG tube be-
   fore the dispersion settles • Draw 15 mL of water using the same syringe and flush NG or OG tube; repeat until no parti-
   cles are left in syringe • For doses of 800 mg (four 200-mg tablets) and 1200 mg (six 200-mg tablets), repeat adminis-
   tration steps until prescribed dose is reached

    ●   Cardiovascular Thrombotic Events
    ●   NSAIDs cause an increased risk of serious cardiovascular thrombotic events, including my-
        ocardial infarction and stroke, which can be fatal. This risk may occur early in treatment and
        may increase with duration of use.
    ●   Meloxicam is contraindicated in the setting of CABG surgery.
    ●   Gastrointestinal Bleeding, Ulceration, and Perforation
    ●   NSAIDs cause an increased risk of serious gastrointestinal (GI) adverse reactions including
        bleeding, ulceration, and perforation of the stomach or intestines, which can be fatal. These
        events can occur at any time during use and without warning symptoms. Patients with a
        prior history of peptic ulcer disease and/or GI bleeding are at greater risk for serious GI
        events.

   therapy 2 ,3 .

   Titration: Adjust to a dose that provides adequate analgesia and minimizes adverse reactions;
   continually re-evaluate use. Use the lowest effective dosage for the shortest duration consis-
   tent with individual treatment goals 2 , 3
   Discontinuation: Do not abruptly discontinue in physically dependent patients. Gradually ta-
   per dose by 25% to 50% every 2 to 4 days; if signs or symptoms of withdrawal occur during ta-
   per, increase to the previous dose level and taper more slowly 2 ,3 .

   Preoperative medication
   Usual dosage: 1 to 2 mg/kg/dose IM or subQ administered 30 to 90 minutes before begin-
   ning of anesthesia; maximum dosage, 100 mg Rigors, postoperative
