drugs.uses_raw:
Attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD)
   Guidelines: The recommended first-line treatment for children and adolescents with ADHD is
   age dependent. For children 4 to 6 years, parent training in behavioral management (PTBM)
   and/or behavioral classroom interventions is the treatment of choice. In moderate-to-severe
   cases, methylphenidate may be considered if the behavioral interventions are unsuccessful.
   For children 6 to 12 years, the combined treatment of an FDA-approved stimulant drug for
   ADHD and PTBM and/or behavioral classroom intervention (preferably both) is preferred. In
   children 12 years or older, the preferred treatment is an FDA-approved stimulant drug A meta-analysis that included 6 trials with 216 participants 6 to 17 years old given tricyclic an-
   tidepressants (TCA; desipramine and nortriptyline) demonstrated that TCAs improve the core
   symptoms of ADHD as assessed by parents, teachers, and clinicians, but their use is limited
   due to adverse effects and lack of comprehensive study. All studies evaluated the severity of
   ADHD symptoms but trial investigators used different scales and raters, making it difficult to
   combine results. In 3 trials, the Clinical Global Impression (CGI) response rates for TCAs were
   more efficacious than placebo (OR 5, 95% CI 29 to 39); the calculated number needed
   to treat for benefit was 2, which was consistent for both TCAs. The authors note that other
   first-line pharmacological interventions for ADHD (methylphenidate, amphetamine derivatives,
   atomoxetine, alpha agonists) have been studied comprehensively for this indication and
   should be considered before TCAs due to their safer side-effect profile Major depressive disorder: The American Academy of Pediatrics recommends that patients
   10 to 21 years old with major depressive disorder in the primary care setting should receive
   psychotherapy (eg, cognitive behavioral therapy or interpersonal psychotherapy for adoles-
   cents) and/or treatment with an SSRI. Tricyclic antidepressants were not included in the most
   recent guidelines because of a lack of efficacy demonstrated in clinical trials for this class of
   antidepressants 2/8
 FDA Approved Indications

   Safety and effectiveness in the pediatric population have not been established. Anyone consid-
   ering the use of nortriptyline hydrochloride in a child or adolescent must balance the potential
   risks with the clinical need Nortriptyline is indicated for the relief of symptoms of depression. Endogenous depressions
   are more likely to be alleviated than other depressive states

drugs.contraindications_raw:
Common: Weight gain, dry mouth, abdominal discomfort, sedation, tiredness, headaches,
   drowsiness, confusion, blurred vision, diaphoresis, constipation, and urinary retention 1

   Black Box Warning
   Suicidality and Antidepressant Drugs

 Antidepressants increased the risk compared to placebo of suicidal thinking and behavior (sui-
   cidality) in children, adolescents, and young adults in short-term studies of major depressive
   disorder (MDD) and other psychiatric disorders. Anyone considering the use of nortriptyline
   hydrochloride or any other antidepressant in a child, adolescent, or young adult must balance
   this risk with the clinical need. Short-term studies did not show an increase in the risk of suici-
   dality with antidepressants compared to placebo in adults beyond age 24; there was a reduc-
   tion in risk with antidepressants compared to placebo in adults aged 65 and older. Depression
   and certain other psychiatric disorders are themselves associated with increases in the risk of
   suicide. Patients of all ages who are started on antidepressant therapy should be monitored
   appropriately and observed closely for clinical worsening, suicidality, or unusual changes in be-
   havior. Families and caregivers should be advised of the need for close observation and com-
   munication with the prescriber. Nortriptyline hydrochloride is not approved for use in pedi-
   atric patients 2 ,13 .

   Monitoring
   Toxic Monitoring
   •Perform baseline screening of sodium level and after 3 to 4 weeks in high-risk patients (eg,
   older than 65 years, previous history of antidepressant-induced hyponatremia, low body
   weight, concomitant use of thiazides or other hyponatremia-inducing agents), especially dur-
   ing the first 3 weeks following initiation and regularly in the elderly •Monitor blood pressure at baseline, with significant dose increases, and every 3 to 6 months
   once stabilized •Screen for risk of bipolar disorder prior to initiation in patients with depressive symptoms (eg,
   detailed psychiatric history, including a family history of suicide, bipolar disorder, and depres-
   sion ) •Evaluate ECG for QT prolongation at baseline, at steady state, after initial dose titration, with
   dose changes, and especially with higher doses and in children and the elderly •Monitor patients receiving antidepressants for worsening of depression, suicidality, or un-
   usual changes in behavior, especially at the initiation of therapy or when the dose increases or
   decreases Such monitoring should include at least weekly face-to-face contact with patients
   or their family members or caregivers during the initial 4 weeks of treatment, then visits every
   other week for the next 4 weeks, then at 12 weeks, and then as clinically indicated beyond 12
   weeks. Families and caregivers should be advised of the need for close observation (ie, daily
   observation) of patients and communication with the prescriber More frequent monitoring
   may be required in more severely depressed or suicidal patients 5/8
 •Patients who experience symptoms of anxiety, agitation, panic attacks, insomnia, irritability,
   hostility, impulsivity, akathisia, hypomania, or mania may be at an increased risk for worsening
   depression or suicidality •Monitor patients with a history of seizure, since nortriptyline lowers the seizure threshold •Monitor for the emergence of serotonin syndrome •Consider ophthalmologic evaluation for susceptibility to angle closure •Metabolic profile may be advisable to detect early weight gain at 3, 6, and 12 months, then
   yearly, in all patients (not just in patients who are obese or overweight) and if receiving combi-
   nation therapy, especially with atypical antipsychotics

drugs.pharmacokinetics_summary:
Pharmacology
   Mechanism of Action
   The exact mechanism of mood elevation by tricyclic antidepressants is unknown. Nortriptyline
   is not a monoamine oxidase inhibitor. It inhibits the activity of histamine, 5-hydrox-
   ytryptamine, and acetylcholine. It increases the pressor effect of norepinephrine but blocks
   the pressor response from phenethylamine. It is suggested that nortriptyline interferes with
   the transport, release, and storage of catecholamines 2

drugs.uses_raw:

   drome, odevixibat was associated with a significant improvement in pruritus with a change
   from baseline in average scratching score of -1.7 compared with -0.8 with placebo for a mean
   difference of -0.9 (95% CI, -1.4 to -0.3) at month Scratching severity was assessed on a 5-
   point ordinal response scale, with scores ranging from 0 (no scratching) to 4 (worst possible
   scratching). The most common adverse reactions were diarrhea (29%), abdominal pain (14%),
   hematoma (9%), and decreased weight (6%). No patients discontinued treatment due to an ad-
   verse reaction. Patients were randomized to receive odevixibat 120 mcg/kg once daily (n=35)
   or placebo (n=17). The median age was 1 years (range, 7 to 5 years) in the odevixibat
   group and 2 years (range, 5 to 3 years) in the placebo group; 5 patients were older than
   12 years. Of the 52 patients, 52% were male and 83% were white; 92% of patients had the JAG1
   mutation and 8% had the NOTCH2 mutation. The mean scratching score in the 2 weeks prior

 to baseline was 9. Baseline mean estimated GFR was 159 mL/min/1.73 m(2). Baseline median
   ALT, AST, and total bilirubin were 152 units/L, 135 units/L, and 2 mg/dL, respectively Pruritus: Odevixibat reduced serum bile acid levels and improved pruritus and sleep in 20 pa-
   tients (mean age 5 +/- 6 years) with cholestatic liver disease. There were 5 sequentially es-
   calating dose cohorts comprised of 10 mcg/kg, 30 mcg/kg, 60 mcg/kg, 100 mcg/kg, or 200
   mcg/kg. Serum bile acid, sleep, and multiple itch assessments were measured at baseline and
   at the end of the 4-week treatment period. Mean change in serum bile acid levels was -123.1
   +/- 118 micromol/L (range, -394 to 15) in the full analysis set and -165.1 micromol/L (range -394
   to -1.2) in patients with PFIC. Improvements in pruritus (3 scales) and sleep were reported in all
   cohorts at the end of treatment compared to baseline, with the greatest improvement seen in
   the 100 mcg/kg cohort. Reduced pruritus correlated significantly with reduced serum bile
   acids. Odevixibat was well tolerated, and all patients completed treatment FDA Approved Indications

   older with Alagille syndrome 1

   breast milk, infant formula, or other age-appropriate liquids 4/9
 • Unable to swallow soft foods: Administer via oral syringe only; do not administer via "sippy
   cup" or bottle. Place the tip of the syringe into the front of the patient’s mouth between the
   tongue and the side of the mouth, and then gently push the plunger down to squirt the mix-
   ture between the child's tongue and the side of the mouth. Do not squirt mixture in the back
   of the child's throat because this could cause gagging or choking. Follow dose with breast milk,
   infant formula, or other age-appropriate liquids. If any pellet/liquid mixture remains in mixing
   cup, withdraw remaining liquid into oral syringe and administer; repeat until all pellet/liquid
   mixture has been administered Oral Capsules

   with a small amount of soft food or an age-appropriate liquid. Mix until well dispersed and ad-
   minister entire dose immediately; do not store mixture for future use

drugs.uses_raw:
Post Transplant Steroid Resistant Nephrotic Syndrome: Ofatumumab has been used to
   treat FSGS recurrence after kidney transplant in several case reports. In one case series which
   included 5 pediatric cases (4 years and older) and 2 adult cases, reduction in proteinuria was
   achieved by 4/5 pediatric patients by 6 to 9 months post-transplant and by all patients by 12
   months. However, 2 of the 5 patients received either steroids or liquid apheresis during treat-
   ment which was closely associated with urinary remission. Additionally, another patient re-
   ceived only 2 doses of ofatumumab since graft function and proteinuria were normalized prior
   to ofatumumab administration. The only infusion related adverse effects reported were itching
   in 1 patient and urticaria developing in another; both events subsided with supportive treat-
   ment and the patients tolerated further infusions with no complications The second case se-
   ries included 2 pediatric patients which 1 patient achieved complete and sustained remission
   of proteinuria and the other patient only achieved partial remission. In patient #1, proteinuria
   decreased moderately after the first ofatumumab dose. Plasmapheresis was started 7 months
   after the first dose was given and a second ofatumumab dose was given 10 months after.
   Within 2 months of the second ofatumumab dose, the patient had achieved complete remis-
   sion which persists at the time of publication. In patient #2, the first dose of ofatumumab

 failed to improve proteinuria. A second dose was given 2 months afterwards which produced a
   substantial reduction of proteinuria to non-nephrotic levels (partial remission). Patients were
   given ofatumumab after no or partial response to plasmapheresis and rituximab Administration
   •(Arzerra®) Do not administer as an IV push, IV bolus, or subQ 2

   Bioterrorism: Following a bioterrorism event, treat symptomatic patients with 2 antimicrobial
   agents from different classes, with at least 1 being considered a first-line therapy (see table be-

   naturally occurring Yersinia pestis, engineered resistance is possible with strains used for

   cerning symptoms. For asymptomatic patients likely exposed, rapidly distribute post-exposure
   prophylaxis. Duration of post-exposure prophylaxis is 7 days Naturally occurring Y. pestis infections: Treatment duration for all infection types is 10 to 14
   days, or longer for ongoing fever or concerning symptoms. Antimicrobial resistance is ex-
   tremely rare. Specific recommendations are below: 4
   • Pneumonic or septicemic plague: May initiate treatment with 1 antimicrobial agent for
   mild/moderate disease; for severe disease, initiate dual therapy with 2 antimicrobial agents
   from different classes and narrow therapy to a single agent after clinical improvement occurs.
   If the diagnosis of plague is uncertain, include antimicrobial coverage for community-acquired
   pneumonia until results are available.
   • Bubonic or pharyngeal plague: Initiate treatment with 1 antimicrobial agent for primary dis-
   ease in stable patients with no signs or symptoms of secondary pneumonic or septicemic
   plague. If primary bubonic or pharyngeal plague has progressed to secondary pneumonic or
   septicemic plague, follow treatment recommendations for pneumonic/septicemic plague.
   • Meningitis: Dual therapy with chloramphenicol and either levoFLOXacin or moxifloxacin is rec-
   ommended. For secondary meningitis in patients already receiving antimicrobial therapy, add
   chloramphenicol to the existing regimen. Once chloramphenicol has been added, continue the
   full treatment regimen for an additional 10 days. Chloramphenicol is an appropriate choice for

 treating plague meningitis despite a relative contraindication for use in children younger than
   6 months due to the severity of the infection.

   • Pre-exposure prophylaxis: Pre-exposure prophylaxis is generally unnecessary as long as stan-
   dard and droplet precautions are maintained. Consider pre-exposure prophylaxis in cases of
   surgical mask shortages, patient overcrowding, or poor hospital ventilation. Discontinue pre-
   exposure prophylaxis 48 hours after last perceived exposure.
   • Post-exposure prophylaxis: Consider post-exposure prophylaxis for those with close (less than
   6 feet) contact with a patient with pneumonic plague who were not wearing adequate per-
   sonal protective equipment, lab workers accidentally exposed to infectious materials of not
   following standard precautions, and those in close or direct contact with infected animals (eg,
   vet staff, pet owners, hunters). Duration of post-exposure prophylaxis is 7 days.

   Breastfeeding: Mothers with pneumonic plague may continue to breastfeed if they are being
   treated and the infant is being treated or receiving post-exposure prophylaxis. If the infant is

The most common adverse effects reported for OLANZapine and placebo in adolescents were
   weight gain (29.6% vs 6%), somnolence (24.6% vs 4%), increased appetite (24% vs 6%), se-
   dation (19% vs 6%), and dry mouth (6.1% vs 0%) in a pooled analysis (n=268) Other ad-
   verse events reported in adolescents were dizziness, fatigue, headache, abdominal pain, and
   pain in extremity. Adolescents were more likely than adults to gain more weight, experience
   increased sedation, and have greater increases in laboratory values (total cholesterol, triglyc-
   erides, LDL cholesterol, prolactin, and hepatic aminotransferase) 2 , After a minimum of 24 weeks of OLANZapine, adolescents experienced a mean change in fast-
   ing glucose of 1 mg/dL 2 ,3 . The odds ratio for cumulative type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM)
   risk was 09 (95% CI, 5 to 9) in antipsychotic-exposed youth compared with psychiatric
   controls in a meta-analysis (n=7 studies); although the absolute incidence rate of T2DM com-
   pared with all controls (3.09 cases (95% CI, 35 to 82) per 1000 patients-years) was small
   over the mean follow-up period of 7 years (n=13 studies). Important differences among stud-
   ies included may affect the validity of this finding. The majority of antipsychotic agents were
   second-generation agents (risperiDONE, QUEtiapine, ARIPiprazole, and OLANZapine) Weight gain of more than 7% of baseline was more common in the OLANZapine compared
   with placebo group (45.8% vs 7%, p=0.002) in a randomized, 6-week trial (n=107); mean
   weight gain of 3 kg vs 1 kg The mean increases in weight, height, body mass index, stan-
   dardized percentiles, and z scores were greater (p less than 05) in the OLANZapine-treated
   adolescents compared with US standardized growth curves in a pooled analysis (n=268) 10/15
 Average weight gain in 45 pediatric patients treated with either OLANZapine, risperidone, or
   clozapine after 6 weeks was 6 kg, 8 kg, and 5 kg, respectively 30 and after 45 weeks in 33
   patients (9 to 3 years of age) was 2 kg, 2 kg, and 5 kg, respectively The metabolic values that statistically increased more from baseline in the OLANZapine group
   than placebo group were fasting triglycerides (41.6 mg/dL vs 4 mg/dL) and uric acid (32.7
   mcmol/L vs -5.7 mcmol/L) in a randomized, 6-week trial (n=107) Black Box Warning
   There are serious risks, including profound sedation, respiratory depression, coma, and/or
   death, associated with combined use of opioids and benzodiazepines, other drugs that de-
   press the CNS, or alcohol. Concomitant use should be reserved for patients with no alternative
   treatment. If necessary, use the lowest initial dose and titrate based on clinical response.
   Monitor patients closely for sedation and respiratory depression. Screen patients for risk of
   substance-use disorders Monitoring
   Closely monitor high-risk patients for suicidal tendencies during treatment 15,2 ,3 .

   Measure fasting blood glucose, fasting lipid profile, and blood pressure at baseline and after 3
   months of treatment. When results are normal after 3 months, then follow-up values should
   be obtained annually for blood pressure and every 6 months for glucose and lipids Monitor
   for symptoms of hyperglycemia (ie, polydipsia, polyuria, polyphagia, or weakness) or worsen-
   ing of glucose control 15,2 ,3 .

   Regularly monitor for weight gain during treatment 15,2 ,3 . Assess body mass index at baseline,
   at 4, 8, and 12 weeks, and a minimum of every 3 months while on OLANZapine Monitor CBC frequently during the first few months of treatment in patients with a history of
   clinically significant low WBC or drug-induced leukopenia/neutropenia. Monitor for fever or
   signs of infection in neutropenic patients. Patients with severe neutropenia (absolute neu-
   trophil count less than 1000/mm3) should discontinue OLANZapine and have their WBC fol-
   lowed until recover 15,2 ,3 .
   Obtain a baseline electrocardiogram, followed by routine electrolyte and QTc interval monitor-
   ing, in patients receiving haloperidol for treatment of ICU delirium

• Omalizumab-igec is a biological product approved by the US FDA as biosimilar to
   omalizumab.
   • Omalizumab-igec is indicated for adults and pediatric patients 6 years of age and older with
   moderate to severe persistent asthma who have a positive skin test or in vitro reactivity to a
   perennial aeroallergen and whose symptoms are inadequately controlled with inhaled corti-
   costeroids • Omalizumab-igec is indicated for the reduction of allergic reactions (Type I), including ana-
   phylaxis, that may occur with accidental exposure to one or more foods in adult and pediatric
   patients aged 1 year and older with IgE-mediated food allergy; to be used in conjunction with
   food allergen avoidance • Omalizumab-igec is indicated for the treatment of chronic idiopathic urticaria in adults and
   adolescents (12 years or older) who remain symptomatic despite H1 antihistamine therapy Limitations of Use
   • Omalizumab-igec is not indicated for the relief of acute bronchospasm or status asthmaticus • Omalizumab-igec is not indicated to treat other forms of urticaria • Omalizumab-igec is not indicated for the emergency treatment of allergic reactions, including
   anaphylaxis 14/21
 Administration
   • Gently pinch and a fold of skin and insert needle SUBQ at 45 to 90 degree angle with a quick
   motion. Administer slowly (may take up to 15 seconds) into thigh or abdomen, avoiding the 2-
   inch area around the navel. The outer area of the upper arm may be used by a caregiver or
   healthcare professional. Do not inject into moles, scars, bruises, or areas with tender, red,
   hard, or broken skin. If more than 1 injection is required, administer each injection at least 1
   inch apart from other injection sites. Do not touch the plunger rod while inserting the needle
   into the skin. Slowly push the plunger rod all the way down until the full dose of medicine gets
   injected, and the syringe is empty. If the plunger rod is not fully pressed, the needle shield will
   not extend to cover the needle when it is removed • Do not rub the injection site. If the medicine comes into contact with skin, wash that area
   with water • Prefilled Syringe information is described in the table below 1 :

   and epistaxis Black Box Warning
   Anaphylaxis
   Anaphylaxis, presenting as bronchospasm, hypotension, syncope, urticaria, and/or an-
   gioedema of the throat or tongue, has been reported to occur after administration of omal-
   izumab products. Anaphylaxis has occurred as early as after the first dose of omalizumab
   products, but also has occurred beyond 1 year after beginning regularly administered treat-
   ment. Because of the risk of anaphylaxis, initiate omalizumab-igec therapy in a healthcare set-
   ting and closely observe patients for an appropriate period of time after omalizumab-igec ad-
   ministration. Health care providers administering omalizumab-igec should be prepared to
   manage anaphylaxis that can be life-threatening. Inform patients of the signs and symptoms

 of anaphylaxis and instruct them to seek immediate medical care should symptoms occur.
   Selection of patients for self-administration of omalizumab-igec should be based on criteria to
   mitigate risk from anaphylaxis Monitoring
   Therapeutic Monitoring

   • Evaluate baseline serum total IgE levels to use in combination with body weight to determine
   dose and dosing frequency. Total IgE levels will rise with treatment and remain elevated for 1
   year after discontinuation of therapy. Retesting levels during treatment cannot be used for
   dose determination. If therapy is interrupted for 1 year or longer, retest total serum IgE levels • In patients with allergic asthma or nasal polyps, monitor for significant changes in body
   weight • Periodically reassess the need for continued treatment 1

   Toxic Monitoring
   • Closely monitor for anaphylaxis both during and after administration. Anaphylaxis has oc-
   curred following the first dose with time to onset ranging from 90 minutes to 2 hours in clinical
   studies, but has also occurred 1 year following initiation of regular treatment . 1

   • Evaluate for systemic eosinophilia (eosinophilia, vasculitic rash, worsening pulmonary symp-
   toms, cardiac complications, neuropathy), especially during oral corticosteroid dose reduc-
   tions. Systemic eosinophilia sometimes presents with clinical features of vasculitis consistent
   with Churg-Strauss syndrome • Monitor for parasitic helminth infection (eg, roundworm, hookworm, whipworm, thread-
   worm) during therapy in patients with high risk. Duration of monitoring required after discon-
   tinuation of therapy is not known

   Mild, Child-Pugh A: No dose adjustment needed 1

   Moderate, Child-Pugh B: Reduce dosage to 100 mg once daily and closely monitor for ad-
   verse reactions; consider lowering to 50 mg once daily if adverse reactions emerge. If hepatic
   function improves to mild impairment or normal function, initiation of omaveloxolone at the
   approved recommended dosage may be considered 1
   Severe, Child-Pugh C: Avoid use; if hepatic function improves to moderate impairment, mild
   impairment, or normal function, initiation of omaveloxolone at the approved recommended
   dosage may be considered 1
   Concomitant use
   Moderate CYP3A4 inhibitors: Avoid concomitant use. If coadministration cannot be avoided,
   reduce omaveloxolone to 100 mg orally once daily and closely monitor for adverse reactions; if
   adverse reactions emerge, reduce omaveloxolone to 50 mg orally once daily 1

   Strong CYP3A4 inhibitors: Avoid concomitant use. If coadministration cannot be avoided, re-
   duce omaveloxolone to 50 mg orally once daily and closely monitor for adverse reactions; if
   adverse reactions emerge, coadministration with strong CYP3A4 inhibitors should be discon-
   tinued 1

   Strong or moderate CYP3A4 inducers: Avoid concomitant use 1

 Elevated transaminases
   Greater than 5x the ULN, or greater than 3x the ULN with evidence of liver dysfunction
   [eg, elevated bilirubin]: Immediately discontinue omaveloxolone and repeat liver function
   tests; if transaminase levels stabilized or resolve, omaveloxolone may be reinitiated with in-
   creased liver function monitoring 1

   Fluid overload/heart failure: May require discontinuation 1

drugs.contraindications_raw:
Generally well-tolerated, although available data are limited to small studies of infants and
   children. Common adverse events in both adults and pediatric patients were headache, ab-
   dominal pain, nausea/vomiting, diarrhea, and flatulence; fever and respiratory system events
   were the most frequently reported reactions in pediatric studies. Hypergastrinemia was re-
   ported in children who received omeprazole for extended periods of time (greater than 1
   year). Mild transaminase elevations have also been reported 7 ,30,31,32,33,34 .
   Frequently reported adverse events in pediatric clinical trials included: adverse reactions of the
   respiratory system, 1 month to 16 years of age; otitis media, 1 month to less than 1 year of
   age; fever, 1 to less than 2 years of age; accidental injuries, 2 to 16 years of age 1 ,2 .

   Serious infectious disease: In pediatric patients with gastroesophageal reflux disease or
   other gastric acid-related disorders (N=1,262,424), proton pump inhibitor (PPI) use was associ-
   ated with an increased risk of serious infections overall (adjusted HR, 34; 95% CI, 32 to 36) compared with no PPI use. In sub-group analysis similar results were observed for infec-
   tions of the digestive tract (adjusted HR, 52; 95% CI, 48 to 55); ear, nose, and throat (ad-
   justed HR, 47; 95% CI, 41 to 52); lower respiratory tract (adjusted HR, 22; 95% CI, 19 to

                                                          7/13 25); kidneys or urinary tract (adjusted HR, 2; 95% CI, 15 to 25); and nervous system (ad-
   justed HR, 31; 95% CI, 11 to 54) and for both bacterial (adjusted HR, 56; 95% CI, 50 to 63) and viral infections (adjusted HR, 3; 95% CI, 28 to 33). The median follow-up time
   was 8 years, median age at index date was 84 days (range, 44 to 210 days), gestational age
   was full-term in 1%, and 8% were male. Of the children who received PPIs, the median
   duration of treatment was 118 days In a retrospective, single-center, observational, case-control study of 136 children (1 year or
   older) having protracted diarrhea and stool analysis for Clostridium difficile, the use of PPI ther-
   apy was significantly higher in the patients with C difficile-associated diarrhea compared to the
   control group (22% vs 6%; odds ratio of 5 (95% CI, 4 to 4; p=0.006)) Monitoring

   •Consider intraesophageal pH monitoring to assess for efficacy (pH greater than 0) •Observe for symptomatic improvement within 3 days Toxic Monitoring

   than 1 year). Monitor magnesium levels prior to initiation of therapy and periodically during
   therapy in patients expected to be on long-term therapy or patients receiving concomitant
   drugs such as digoxin or those that may cause hypomagnesemia 18

   riodically during treatment in patients with a preexisting risk of hypocalcemia (eg, hy-
   poparathyroidism) 19

   Black Box Warning
   Distant Spread of Toxin Effect

   The effects of onabotulinumtoxinA and all botulinum toxin products may spread from the area
   of injection to produce symptoms consistent with botulinum toxin effects. These symptoms
   have been reported hours to weeks after injection. Swallowing and breathing difficulties can
   be life threatening and there have been reports of death. The risk of symptoms is probably
   greatest in children treated for spasticity but symptoms can also occur in adults, particularly in
   those patients who have an underlying condition that would predispose them to these symp-
   toms Monitoring
   Physical Exam
   • Prior to treatment for sialorrhea, careful assessment should be performed in patients with
   Gross Motor Function Classification System V when dysphagia is present • Closely monitor patients with peripheral motor neuropathic disease, amyotrophic lateral
   sclerosis, or neuromuscular junction disorders (eg, myasthenia gravis or Lambert-Eaton syn-
   drome) for clinically significant adverse events, including severe dysphagia and respiratory
   compromise • Monitor for reduced lung function in patients with compromised respiratory status treated
   for upper limb spasticity 10/14

   Intrathecal injection
   • Prior to administration, remove 3 mL of cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) using a lumbar puncture
   needle to create space for injection volume • Administer onasemnogene abeparvovec-brve as an intrathecal bolus injection over approxi-
   mately 1 to 2 minutes through the lumbar puncture needle • Place patient in Trendelenburg position (head down at 30 degrees for 15 minutes). Adjust pa-
   tient positioning and duration based on the patient’s clinical status to enhance distribution

   • For single-dose intrathecal injection only; should only be administered by healthcare profes-
   sionals (eg, interventional radiologist or neurologist) experienced in performing lumbar punc-
   tures • Thaw in the refrigerator for approximately 4 hours, or at room temperature for approxi-
   mately 1 hour. If thawed in the refrigerator, remove from refrigerator on day of dosing. Bring
   to room temperature prior to injection; do not use unless thawed. Do not shake and do not re-
   freeze • Immediately prior to dosing, draw the content from the vial into the syringe, remove air from
   syringe, confirm the dose volume of 3 mL in the syringe, cap syringe and deliver to patient in-
   jection location • Once dose is drawn into the syringe, it may be held in the refrigerator at 2° to 8° C (36° to 46°
   F) for up to 24 hours, including a 5-hour maximum time out-of-refrigeration allowance within
   the 24-hour period. Discard the vector-containing syringe if not injected within this time period Compatible material components

   IV.

drugs.uses_raw:
Treatment of uncomplicated acute illness due to influenza A and B infection in pediatric patients 2 weeks and older who have been symptomatic
  for no more than 2 days 1 ,2 .

  Prophylaxis of influenza A and B in pediatric patients 1 year or older 1 ,2 ..

  Limitations of use

  • Not a substitute for annual influenza vaccination 1 ,2

  • Consider available information on influenza drug susceptibility patterns and treatment effects when deciding whether to use 1 ,2

  • Not recommended for patients with end-stage renal disease not undergoing dialysis 1 ,2

  Administration
  May be given with or without food. Food may increase tolerability in some patients 1 ,2 .
  For pediatric patients who cannot swallow capsules, oseltamivir oral suspension is the preferred formulation. However, if the oral suspension
  product is not available, oseltamivir capsules may be opened and mixed with sweetened liquids such as regular or sugar-free chocolate syrup,
  corn syrup, caramel topping, or light brown sugar (dissolved in water) 1 ,2 .

  Because of possible interference with immune response, live attenuated influenza vaccine should not be given within 2 weeks before or 48
  hours after administration of oseltamivir. Trivalent inactivated influenza vaccine may be given at any time, regardless of oseltamivir use 1 ,2 .

  Preparation
  Oral powder for suspension

  Tap the closed bottle several times to loosen powder Measure 55 mL of water in a graduated cylinder and to bottle 4/8
 Close bottle and shake well for 15 seconds. Final concentration of reconstituted suspension is 6 mg/mL Label with "Shake well before use" Use reconstituted suspension within 17 days if stored under refrigeration (2 to 8°C/36 to 46°F) or within 10 days if stored at room temperature
  (25°C/77°F) Extemporaneous oral compound

  Note: A 6 mg/mL oral suspension is available commercially. During emergency situations and when neither the oral-suspension or age-appro-
  priate strengths of capsules are available, an emergency supply of oral suspension may be compounded from the 75 mg capsules. The com-
  pounded suspension yields a 6 mg/mL concentration (same as commercially available 6 mg/mL suspension) and total volume adequate for 1 pa-
  tient for a 5-day course of treatment or a 10-day course of prophylaxis 6 mg/mL suspension 1

  • Determine dose, required number of 75 mg oseltamivir capsules, and total volume required for compounding. For a dose of 15 mg or less, 3
  capsules are required and total volume is 5 mL; for 30 mg, 6 capsules are required and total volume is 75 mL; for 45 mg, 8 capsules are re-
  quired and total volume is 100 mL; for 60 mg, 10 capsules are required and total volume is 125 mL; for 75 mg, 12 capsules are required and total
  volume is 150 mL. If the dose is between these doses, default to the next greater dose and volume.

  • Place specified amount of water into a polyethyleneterephthalate (PET) or glass bottle: 5 mL for 3 capsules; 5 mL for 6 capsules; 7 mL for 8
  capsules; 8 mL for 10 capsules; 10 mL for 12 capsules.
  • Transfer contents of required number of oseltamivir 75 mg capsules into the PET or glass bottle and gently swirl for at least 2 minutes to wet
  the powder.
  • Slowly add the specified volume of vehicle to the bottle: 5 mL for 3 capsules (total volume, 5 mL); 69 mL for 6 capsules (total volume, 75
  mL); 91 mL for 8 capsules (total volume, 100 mL); 115 mL for 10 capsules (total volume, 125 mL); 137 mL for 12 capsules (total volume, 150 mL).
  Vehicle options include cherry syrup, Ora-Sweet SF®, or simple syrup.

  • Close the bottle and shake well for 30 seconds to dissolve active drug.
  • Label with "Shake well before use."
  • Stable for 35 days when refrigerated (2 to 8°C/36 to 46°F) or for 5 days at room temperature.

drugs.uses_summary:
Oxaprozin is indicated for the relief of signs and symptoms of juvenile rheumatoid arthritis
   (JRA) 1 , 2 , 3

   Administration
   Once-a-day dosing is suggested, however divided doses may be considered in patients unable
   to tolerate single doses 1 ,2 ,3 .

   Weight 22 to 31 kg: 600 mg orally once daily; adjust dose and frequency if necessary after ob-
   serving the initial response 1 ,2 ,3 .
   Weight 32 to 54 kg: 900 mg orally once daily; adjust dose and frequency if necessary after ob-
   serving the initial response 1 ,2 ,3 .

   Weight 55 kg or greater: 1200 mg once daily; adjust dose and frequency if necessary after ob-
   serving the initial response 1 , 2 , Maximum dose: 1200 mg/day 1

   Dose Adjustment
   Renal impairment, severe
   Initiate with 600 mg orally once daily; if insufficient relief of symptoms, may cautiously increase
   dose to 1200 mg with close monitoring 1 ,2 ,3 .

   Hepatic Impairment
   No specific recommendations are available; monitor patients with severe impairment for ad-
   verse reactions 1 , 2 , Drug reaction with eosinophilia and systemic symptoms (DRESS)

   Discontinue use immediately if signs or symptoms occur 1 ,2 ,3
   Gastrointestinal event, serious

 Discontinue use until event is ruled out; may include inflammation, bleeding, ulceration, and
   perforation of the stomach or intestines 1 ,2 ,3
   Hepatic disease
   Discontinue use if clinical signs and symptoms or systemic manifestations (eg, eosinophilia or
   rash) occur 1 ,2 ,3

   Hypersensitivity

   Discontinue use at first appearance of symptoms 1 , 2 , 3
   Low body weight
   Initiate with 600 mg orally once daily; if insufficient relief of symptoms, may cautiously increase
   dose to 1200 mg with close monitoring 1 ,2 ,3 .
   Skin reactions, serious
   Discontinue use at first appearance of symptoms; may include exfoliative dermatitis, Stevens-
   Johnson Syndrome, and toxic epidermal necrolysis 1 ,2 ,3

drugs.contraindications_raw:
Common, incidence greater than 3%: Constipation, diarrhea, dyspepsia, nausea, and rash Black Box Warning
   Black Box Warning

   Nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) cause an increased risk of serious cardiovascu-
   lar thrombotic events, including myocardial infarction and stroke, which can be fatal. This risk
   may occur early in treatment and may increase with duration of use. Oxaprozin is contraindi-
   cated in the setting of coronary artery bypass graft (CABG) surgery. NSAIDs can also cause an
   increased risk of serious gastrointestinal (GI) adverse events, including bleeding, ulceration,
   and perforation of the stomach or intestines, which can be fatal. These events can occur at any
   time during use and without warning symptoms. Elderly patients and patients with a prior his-
   tory of peptic ulcer disease and/or GI bleeding are at greater risk for serious GI events 1 , Monitoring
   Toxic Laboratory Monitoring

   Consider periodic monitoring of CBC and chemistry profiles in patients on long-term therapy 5/9
 Monitor renal function in patients with renal or hepatic impairment, heart failure, dehydration,
   or hypovolemia during treatment If use is necessary in advanced renal disease, observe patients for worsening renal function Toxic Physical Monitoring
   Monitor for signs and symptoms of serious cardiovascular thrombotic events, including my-
   ocardial infarction, cardiac ischemia, and stroke, throughout the treatment course Monitor for signs and symptoms of gastrointestinal ulceration and bleeding during therapy Monitor blood pressure during initiation and throughout treatment course Assess patients with preexisting severe heart failure for signs and symptoms of worsening

   ders If use is necessary in patients with a recent myocardial infarction, monitor patients for signs of

   tions in elderly patients during therapy Monitor for adverse reactions in patients with severe hepatic dysfunction In women who are pregnant, if treatment is necessary between about 20 and 30 weeks' gesta-

   hours

drugs.contraindications_raw:
The most commonly reported adverse events associated with OXcarbazepine extended-re-
   lease tablets in pediatric patients 4 to 16 years (n=18) previously treated with other antiepilep-

 tic drugs were similar to those reported in adults, which included dizziness, somnolence,
   headache, balance disorder, tremor, vomiting, diplopia, and asthenia (5% or greater and more
   frequent than with placebo) The most commonly observed adverse reactions associated with immediate-release
   OXcarbazepine use in pediatric patients 4 years or older previously treated with other
   antiepileptic drugs (n=171) were vomiting (33%), somnolence (31%), headache (31%), dizziness
   (28%), nausea (19%), diplopia (17%), ataxia (13%), fatigue (13%), abnormal vision (13%), nystag-
   mus (9%), abnormal gait (8%), and tremor (6%) Infections and infestations were more frequently reported with immediate-release
   OXcarbazepine use in pediatric patients 1 month to younger than 4 years previously or not
   previously treated with other antiepileptic drugs compared with older children and adults. The
   most commonly reported (5% or greater) adverse reactions in this population were similar to
   other patients of any age In a randomized study of cognitive function in patients with newly diagnosed partial seizures
   (n=112; age range 6 to 16 years), there were no differences demonstrated in cognitive tests be-
   tween OXcarbazepine and carbamazepine or valproic acid over a 6 month period Monitoring
   Monitor serum sodium during maintenance treatment, particularly among patients receiving
   concurrent mediations known to decrease serum sodium levels and if symptoms of hypona-
   tremia develop. Monitor patient for the emergence or worsening of depression, suicidal
   thoughts or behavior, and/or any unusual changes in mood or behavior. Monitor therapeutic
   response during pregnancy and through the postpartum period as OXcarbazepine and its ac-
   tive metabolite levels may decrease during pregnancy 3 ,1 .

   Monitor plasma levels of the concomitant AEDs during OXcarbazepine immediate-release titra-
   tion period, especially at OXcarbazepine immediate-release doses greater than 1200 mg/day Consider testing for the presence of HLA-B*15:02 allele prior to initiation of treatment in pa-
   tients with ancestry in genetically at-risk populations (most common in patients of Han
   Chinese, Thai, Filipino, Malaysian, Korean, or eastern Indian descent) 10

   pedis reported mycological cure rates of 77% (oxiconazole twice daily), 79% (oxiconazole once
   daily), and 33% (vehicle). Treatment success was reported in 52%, 43%, and 14%, respectively.
   The studies included 95 pediatric patients 10 years or younger, with 1 reported case of red-
   dening of skin and 1 case of eczema-like skin alterations 1

   Dermatologic: Serious skin reactions have been reported from patients who were rechal-
   lenged with acetaminophen and had a recurrence of a serious skin reaction Hepatic: Liver toxicity occurs with excessive doses or after prolonged administration of thera-
   peutic doses. There is an increased risk for development of hepatic toxicity in children with di-
   abetes, children with concurrent viral infections, children with a history of hepatotoxic reac-
   tions, obese children, and chronically malnourished children. Initial signs of acetaminophen
   toxicity include anorexia, nausea, vomiting, malaise, and diaphoresis 33,20,34,35,36 .

   In 2014, the FDA recommended that combination analgesics which contain more the 325 mg
   of acetaminophen per dosage unit not be prescribed or dispensed due to concerns of liver
   toxicity. Limiting the amount of acetaminophen per dosage unit could reduce the risk of se-
   vere liver injury from inadvertent overdose, a situation which can lead to liver failure, liver
   transplant, and death. At present, there are no data to support that higher amounts of ac-
   etaminophen per dosage unit provide additional benefit to outweigh the added risk of liver in-
   jury Hepatotoxicity occurred in less than 01% of children administered therapeutic doses of ac-
   etaminophen, in a systemic review (n=32,424; studies=62). The estimated risk for minor or ma-
   jor hepatic events was 031% (95% CI, 015% to 057%) No significant increases in liver
   enzymes were observed after a median duration of 60 hours (6 to 480 hours) and a median of
   9 (2 to 80) doses of IV acetaminophen in a retrospective analysis of 189 infants (1 day to 182
   days of age; 30 to 55 weeks postmenstrual age (PMA). Loading doses of 20 mg/kg, followed by
   maintenance doses of 10 mg/kg were given every 6 to 12 hours, based upon PMA Acute
   liver failure occurred in an 11-month-old boy who received therapeutic doses of oral ac-
   etaminophen for a prolonged duration (10 days) Respiratory: Epidemiological evidence demonstrated an association between acetaminophen
   use and asthma 41 , atopy 42 , rhinoconjunctivitis, and eczema Confirmatory studies are
   needed; however, in a meta-analysis the odds ratio (OR) was 6 (95% CI, 48 to 74) for the
   risk of asthma in children among users of acetaminophen in the year prior to asthma diagno-
   sis and the first year of life and 96 (95% CI, 5 to 56) for the risk of wheezing and ac-
   etaminophen use in the previous year of life In 2 observational studies, the OR was 61

 (95% CI, 33 to 77) for atopy and acetaminophen exposure before the age of 15 months 42 ,
   up to 39 (95% CI, 24 to 55) for rhinoconjunctivitis symptoms or 99 (95% CI, 82 to 16)
   for eczema symptoms and acetaminophen exposure in the previous 12 months in adolescents OxyCODONE: Adverse effects reported after oxyCODONE were abdominal pain (7%), difficulty
   walking (23%), dizziness (20%), dry mouth (38%), itching (16%), sweating (9%), tiredness (66%),
   and vomiting (3%) in a single-dose study (n=51; 10 to 12 years of age) After a single 1
   mg/kg IV oxyCODONE dose, none of the 6 infants (1 day to 6 months of age) who received it
   experienced apnea or hypoventilation that required assistance during the study Black Box Warning
   Warnings: Addiction, abuse, and misuse; risk evaluation and mitigation strategy (REMS); life-
   threatening respiratory depression; accidental ingestion; neonatal opioid withdrawal syn-
   drome, CYP3A4 interaction; hepatoxicity, and risks from concomitant use with benzodi-
   azepines or other CNS depressants 22 , 23
    ●   Addiction, Abuse, and Misuse:
    ●   oxyCODONE/acetaminophen exposes patients and other users to the risks of opioid addic-
        tion, abuse, and misuse, which can lead to overdose and death. Assess each patient’s risk
        prior to prescribing oxyCODONE/acetaminophen, and monitor all patients regularly for the
        development of these behaviors and conditions.
    ●   Opioid Analgesic Risk Evaluation and Mitigation Strategy:
    ●   To ensure that the benefits of opioid analgesics outweigh the risks of addiction, abuse, and
        misuse, the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) has required a REMS for these products.
        Under the requirements of the REMS, drug companies with approved opioid analgesic prod-
        ucts must make REMS-compliant education programs available to healthcare providers.
        Healthcare providers are strongly encouraged to:
    ●   Complete a REMS-compliant education program,
    ●   Counsel patients and/or their caregivers, with every prescription, on safe use, serious risks,
        storage, and disposal of these products,
    ●   Emphasize to patients and their caregivers the importance of reading the Medication Guide
        every time it is provided by their pharmacist, and
    ●   Consider other tools to improve patient, household, and community safety.
    ●   Life-Threatening Respiratory Depression

 ●   Serious, life-threatening, or fatal respiratory depression may occur with use of
        oxyCODONE/acetaminophen. Monitor for respiratory depression, especially during initia-
        tion of oxyCODONE/acetaminophen or following a dose increase.
    ●   Accidental Ingestion
    ●   Accidental ingestion of oxyCODONE/acetaminophen, especially by children, can result in a
        fatal overdose of oxyCODONE/acetaminophen.
    ●   Neonatal Opioid Withdrawal Syndrome
    ●   Prolonged use of oxyCODONE/acetaminophen during pregnancy can result in neonatal opi-
        oid withdrawal syndrome, which may be life-threatening if not recognized and treated, and
        requires management according to protocols developed by neonatology experts. If opioid
        use is required for a prolonged period in a pregnant woman, advise the patient of the risk
        of neonatal opioid withdrawal syndrome and ensure that appropriate treatment will be
        available.
    ●   Cytochrome P450 3A4 Interaction
    ●   The concomitant use of oxyCODONE/acetaminophen with all cytochrome P450 3A4 in-
        hibitors may result in an increase in oxycodone plasma concentrations, which could in-
        crease or prolong adverse reactions and may cause potentially fatal respiratory depression.
        In addition, discontinuation of a concomitantly used cytochrome P450 3A4 inducer may re-
        sult in an increase in oxyCODONE plasma concentration. Monitor patients receiving
        oxyCODONE/acetaminophen and any CYP3A4 inhibitor or inducer.
    ●   Hepatotoxicity
    ●   Acetaminophen has been associated with cases of acute liver failure, at times resulting in
        liver transplant and death. Most of the cases of liver injury are associated with the use of ac-
        etaminophen at doses that exceed 4000 mg per day, and often involve more than one ac-
        etaminophen-containing product.
    ●   Risks From Concomitant Use With Benzodiazepines Or Other CNS Depressants
    ●   Concomitant use of opioids with benzodiazepines or other central nervous system (CNS) de-
        pressants, including alcohol, may result in profound sedation, respiratory depression, coma,
        and death
    ●   Reserve concomitant prescribing of oxyCODONE/acetaminophen and benzodiazepines or
        other CNS depressants for use in patients for whom alternative treatment options are
        inadequate.
    ●   Limit dosages and durations to the minimum required.
    ●   Follow patients for signs and symptoms of respiratory depression and sedation.

 Monitoring
   Monitor patients for serious adverse events during therapy, including respiratory depression,
   severe hypotension, and hepatotoxicity. Monitor postoperative patients for decreased bowel
   motility 12,13 .
   Monitor patients susceptible to the intracranial effects of carbon dioxide retention (eg, evi-
   dence of increased intracranial pressure or brain tumors) for signs and symptoms of sedation
   and respiratory depression, particularly during initiation of therapy. Monitor patients with
   acute pancreatitis or other biliary tract disease for worsening symptoms. Monitor patients with
   a history of seizure disorder for worsened control 19

   Assess for signs of pain. Monitor temperature. Assess liver function in patients taking large
   doses chronically or if predisposed to liver toxicity. Serum acetaminophen concentration is ob-
   tained only to assess toxicity in cases of suspected overdose 20 ,

   Black Box Warning

   Embryo-Fetal Toxicity

   Palovarotene is contraindicated in pregnancy. Palovarotene may cause fetal harm. Because of
   the risk of teratogenicity and to minimize fetal exposure, palovarotene is to be administered
   on if conditions for pregnancy prevention are met.

   Premature Epiphyseal Closure
   Premature epiphyseal closure occurs in growing pediatric patients treated with palovarotene,
   close monitoring is recommended 1

   Monitoring
   Toxic Laboratory Monitoring

   Obtain a negative pregnancy test in patients of childbearing age within one week of therapy
   initiation and periodically during therapy Toxic Physical Monitoring

   Monitor linear growth in growing pediatric patients Assess baseline skeletal maturity via hand/wrist and knee x-rays, standard growth curves and
   pubertal staging in all growing pediatric patients. Continue monitoring every 6 to 12 months
   until patients reach skeletal maturity (eg, epiphyseal closure) or final adult height Assess for spinal fracture periodically using radiologic method Monitor for new or worsening psychiatric symptoms during therapy

drugs.dosing_raw:
Critical Dosing Note: As of March 2024, there are 5 FDA-approved pancreatic enzyme products
   available: Creon®, Zenpep®), Pancreaze®, Pertzye®, and Viokace®. These products are not in-
   terchangeable. When switching from one pancreatic enzyme product to another, monitor pa-
   tients for clinical symptoms of exocrine pancreatic insufficiency and titrate the dosage as
   needed 1 ,2 ,3 ,4 ,5 .
   Use either actual body weight or fat ingestion-based dosing scheme. Initiate at the lowest rec-
   ommended dosage and individualize dosage based on clinical symptoms, degree of steator-
   rhea present, and fat content of diet 1 ,3 ,4 ,5 .

   Exocrine Pancreatic Insufficiency

   12 months or younger

   Pancreaze®: 2600 lipase units orally per 120 mL of formula or per breastfeeding 3

   Creon® or Zenpep®: 3000 lipase units orally per 120 mL of formula or per breastfeeding 5 ,1
   Pertzye®: 4000 lipase units orally or via gastrostomy tube per 120 mL of formula or per
   breastfeeding 4

   Older than 12 months to younger than 4 years

   Creon®, Pancreaze®, Pertzye®, or Zenpep®: Begin with 1000 lipase units/kg/meal orally
   (Creon®, Pancreaze®, Pertzye®, or Zenpep®) or via gastrostomy tube (Pertzye®); administer
   approximately half the mealtime dose with a snack. Total daily dosage should reflect approxi-
   mately 3 meals plus 2 or 3 snacks per day 1 , 3 , 4 , Dosage titration: Titrate dosage as needed; if signs and symptoms of malabsorption persist,
   increase the dosage. Changes in dosage may require an adjustment period of several days. If
   doses are to exceed maximum dosage, investigation is warranted; such doses should only be
   used if they are documented to be effective by fecal fat measures or an improvement in signs
   or symptoms of malabsorption including measures of nutritional status 1 ,3 ,4 ,5 .

 Maximum dosage: 2500 lipase units/kg/meal, 10,000 lipase units/kg/day, or 4000 lipase
   units/g fat ingested/day 1 ,3 ,4 ,5

   Older than 4 years
   Creon®, Pancreaze®, Pertzye®, or Zenpep®: Begin with 500 lipase units/kg/meal orally
   (Creon®, Pancreaze®, Pertzye®, or Zenpep®) or via gastrostomy tube (Pertzye®); administer
   approximately half the mealtime dose with a snack. Total daily dosage should reflect approxi-
   mately 3 meals plus 2 or 3 snacks per day 1 ,3 ,4 ,5 .

   Dosage titration: Titrate dosage as needed; if signs and symptoms of malabsorption persist,
   increase the dosage. Changes in dosage may require an adjustment period of several days. If
   doses are to exceed maximum dosage, investigation is warranted; such doses should only be
   used if they are documented to be effective by fecal fat measures or an improvement in signs
   or symptoms of malabsorption including measures of nutritional status 1 , 3 , 4 , Maximum dosage: 2500 lipase units/kg/meal, 10,000 lipase units/kg/day, or 4000 lipase
   units/g fat ingested/day 1 ,3 ,4 ,5

   Dose Adjustment

   Renal Impairment: Specific recommendations are not available 1 ,3 ,4 ,5

   Hepatic Impairment: Specific recommendations are not available 1 , 3 , 4 , 5
drugs.uses_raw:
Creon(R), Pancreaze(R), Pertzye(R), and Zenpep(R) are indicated for the treatment of exocrine
   pancreatic insufficiency 1 ,3 ,4 ,5 .

   Administration
   Gastrostomy Tube (Pertzye®)
   • Only use contents of 4000 USP lipase unit capsule for gastrostomy tube administration (14
   French or larger); do not administer contents of more than 2 capsules at one time 6

 • Open 1 or 2 capsules and mix contents with at least 10 mL of applesauce; do not crush mi-
   crospheres 6
   • Administer the suspension through gastrostomy tube via syringe immediately after mixing,
   then flush tube with 10 mL water 6

   •Discard any unused mixture and do not save for later use 6

   If dose required more than 2 capsules, repeat above steps until prescribed dose is achieved Oral Route (Creon®, Pancreaze®, Pertzye®, or Zenpep®)
   Up to 12 months of age:

   • Administer immediately prior to feeding; do not mix pancrelipase capsule contents directly
   into formula or breast milk, contents of the capsule may be 1) sprinkled on a small amount of
   soft acidic food with a pH of 5 or less (eg, applesauce, bananas, plain Greek yogurt, pears)
   being careful not to crush the capsule contents (the entire mixture should be given to the in-
   fant immediately), or 2) sprinkled directly into the infants mouth. Immediately administer addi-
   tional breast milk or formula after administration to ensure complete swallowing of the cap-
   sule contents. Visually inspect the infants mouth to ensure that no drug is retained in the
   mouth 1 ,3 ,4 ,5 .

   • Missed dose: If a dose is missed, administer the next dose with the next feeding 1 , 3 , 4 , 12 months or older:

   • Administer with meals and snacks, with sufficient fluid. Discard any unused portion of cap-
   sule contents. Swallow capsule whole, do not crush or chew. Ensure contents are not retained
   in mouth. For patients having difficulty swallowing, capsules may be opened and added to
   a small quantity apple sauce or of acidic soft food (pH 5 or less), dispersed equally, swal-
   lowed immediately and followed by sufficient fluid. Keep the container tightly closed between
   use to protect from moisture 1 ,3 ,4 ,5 .

   • Missed dose: If a dose is missed, take the next dose with the next meal or snack 1 ,3 ,4 ,5 .

   dizziness (6.3% vs 0%), respiratory/thoracic/mediastinal disorders (12.5% vs 2%), and cough

   placebo treated-patients, respectively 4/8
 Pancreaze™: In a study of pediatric patients 6 to 30 months of age (n=17), the most commonly
   reported adverse events with pancrelipase therapy were gastrointestinal, including diarrhea
   and vomiting. In children older than 8 years of age the type and incidence of adverse events
   were similar to adults; most common events were gastrointestinal complaints Pertzye™: The safety in children 8 years and older and adults were similar with the most com-
   mon adverse reactions of diarrhea, dyspepsia, and cough Ultresa™: In a study of patients 7 to 11 years of age (n=9), adverse events reported with pan-
   crelipase were nasal congestion (14%), neck pain (14%), beta-hemolytic streptococcal infection
   (11%), ear pain (11%), and lymphadenopathy (11%) Zenpep®: The most commonly reported adverse events in pediatric patients 1 to 6 years of
   age (n=19) during treatment were gastrointestinal, including abdominal pain and steatorrhea In children 7 years of age and older (n=24) during a crossover study, the type and incidence
   of adverse events were similar to adults and included abdominal pain (18%), flatulence (6%),
   headache (15%), contusion (6%), decreased weight (6%), cough (6%), and early satiety (6%)

   Toxic Laboratory Monitoring

   Monitor uric acid levels in patients with hyperuricemia, gout, or renal impairment Toxic Physical Monitoring

   Monitor patients with a known hypersensitivity reaction to proteins of porcine origin during
   treatment 2

Hypoxemia may occur because of inadequate mechanical ventilation and deterioration in pul-

   Intravenous pantoprazole is indicated for treatment of gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD)
   and a history of erosive esophagitis (EE) for up to 7 days in pediatric patients aged 3 months or
   older 8

   Limitations of Use

   The safety and effectiveness of pantoprazole IV for the treatment of upper gastrointestinal
   bleeding have not been established in adult or pediatric patients 8

   Administration
   Intravenous

   • Flush IV line before and after administration with NS or D5W • Infuse IV over a period of approximately 15 minutes through a dedicated line or through a Y-
   site • Compatible with NS or D5W when administering through a Y-site; stop Y-site administration
   immediately if precipitation or discoloration occurs Nasogastric or Gastric Tube

   Delayed-Release Suspension: 5
   • Remove the plunger from the barrel of a 60-mL catheter-tip syringe. Connect the catheter tip
   of the syringe to a 16 French (or larger) tube. Hold the syringe attached to the tubing as high as
   possible while giving to prevent any bending of the tubing.

 • Empty the contents of the packet into the barrel of the syringe and add 10 mL of apple juice;
   gently tap and/or shake the barrel of the syringe to help rinse the syringe and tube.

   • Repeat at least twice more using the same amount of apple juice (10 mL) each time. No gran-
   ules should remain in the syringe.

   Extemporaneously Prepared 2 mg/mL Pantoprazole Suspension

   • If using an extemporaneously prepared 2 mg/mL pantoprazole suspension compounded us-
   ing sodium bicarbonate solution, administer through a 16 French nasogastric tube followed by
   a 20-mL water flush Oral

   Delayed-Release Tablets:

   • Swallow whole with or without food. Concomitant antacid use does not affect absorption 5

   Delayed-Release Suspension: • Administer approximately 30 minutes prior to a meal via oral administration in apple juice or
   applesauce. Do not administer in liquids other than apple juice, or foods other than
   applesauce.
   • For administration in applesauce, sprinkle granules on 1 teaspoonful of applesauce. Do not
   crush or chew the granules; use within 10 minutes of preparation. Take sips of water to wash
   granules down into stomach.

   • For administration in apple juice, empty granules into 5 mL of apple juice and stir for 5 sec-
   onds; granules will not dissolve. Use immediately after preparation. Rinse the container once
   or twice with apple juice and swallow immediately to ensure the entire dose has been
   administered.

   • Do not divide the 40-mg suspension packet to create a 20-mg dose for pediatric patients who
   are unable to take the tablet formulation

   Preparation

   Intravenous, 15-minute Infusion
   3 Months to Less than 1 Year of Age

   • Reconstitute the 40-mg powder for injection vial with 10 mL of NS; store reconstituted solu-
   tion up to 6 hours at room temperature up to 30°C (86° F) prior to further dilution • Further dilute the contents of the vial with 21 mL NS to a final concentration of approximately 3 mg/mL; store diluted solution at room temperature up to 30°C (86°F); must be used within
   24 hours from the time of initial reconstitution 6/18
 • Withdraw the desired dose of the diluted pantoprazole solution and discard any unused por-
   tion 1 to 17 Years of Age

   • Reconstitute the 40-mg powder for injection vial with 10 mL of NS; store reconstituted solu-
   tion up to 6 hours at room temperature up to 30°C (86°F) prior to further dilution • Further dilute the contents of the vial with 100 mL of NS or D5W to a final concentration of
   approximately 4 mg/mL; store diluted solution at room temperature up to 30°C (86°F); must
   be used within 24 hours from the time of initial reconstitution • Withdraw the desired dose of the diluted pantoprazole solution and discard any unused por-
   tion Extemporaneous Suspension for Nasogastric Administration (2 mg/mL) 17

   • Triturate one 40-mg pantoprazole tablet into a fine powder with a mortar and pestle.
   • Transfer powder to a glass container, rinse the mortar and pestle twice with 5 mL aliquots of 2% sodium bicarbonate solution, and add rinsings to container with powder.
   • Close container and mix for 10 minutes until a uniform suspension forms.
   • Transfer contents to a 20-mL polypropylene syringe. Rinse glass container 2 times with 5 mL
   of 2% sodium bicarbonate solution, adding rinsings to syringe for a total volume of 20 mL.
   • Protect from light;
   • Stable at room temperature for at least 24 hours, stable for 2 weeks at 5°C, and for up to 3
   months at –20°C.

   Extemporaneous Oral Suspension (2 mg/mL) 18
   • Remove imprint from twenty 40-mg pantoprazole tablets and allow to dry.
   • Triturate the tablets, transfer to a beaker and add 340 mL of sterile water for irrigation, and
   place the beaker on a magnetic stirrer.
   • Add 8 g of sodium bicarbonate powder and stir for about 20 minutes until the tablet rem-
   nants have disintegrated and the coating has dissolved.

   • While stirring, add another 8 g of sodium bicarbonate powder and stir for about five min-
   utes until the powder dissolves.
   • Add enough sterile water for irrigation to bring the final volume to 400 mL and mix well.

   •Suspension is stable for 62 days under refrigeration. Shake well before using.

   Black Box Warning
   Antidepressants increased the risk of suicidal thoughts and behaviors in pediatric and young
   adult patients in short-term studies. Closely monitor all antidepressant-treated patients for
   clinical worsening, and for emergence of suicidal thoughts and behaviors. Paroxetine hy-
   drochloride is not approved for use in the pediatric population Monitoring

 Monitor for clinical worsening, suicidality, and unusual changes in behavior, especially within
   the first few months of drug initiation and during dose increases and decreases. Monitor for
   serotonin syndrome during therapy and for withdrawal symptoms during drug discontinua-
   tion. Periodically monitor height and weight and for the need for continued treatment.
   Monitor for mania and hypomania during treatment 9 ,10,11 .
   When treating depression, monitor patient at least monthly during the continuation phase of
   treatment

drugs.uses_raw:
Peanut Allergy: Of patients 4 to 17 years old (n=499), 2% who received peanut allergen-
   dnfp were able to ingest a single-dose of at least 600 mg of peanut protein during the exit food
   challenge compared with 4% of placebo patients (between-group difference, 2%; 95% CI,
   53% to 73%) in a randomized trial (N=555); there was no significant difference in tolerance of
   exit 600-mg peanut protein challenge in subjects 18 to 55 years old (41.5% vs 3%). An signif-
   icantly greater number of patients in the peanut allergen-dnfp group tolerated the 300-mg
   (76.6% vs 1%) and the 1000-mg (50.3% vs 4%) peanut protein dose during the exit food
   challenge. The maximum severity of symptoms was moderate in 25% with peanut allergen-
   dnfp and 59% with placebo (severe, 5% vs 11%); 10% in the peanut allergen-dnfp group re-
   ceived epinephrine compared with 53% for placebo during the exit food challenge. There was
   no significant between-group difference among patients 4 to 17 years for peanut-specific IgE
   from baseline to the end of the trial. Adverse events were reported in 7% of patients 4 to 17
   years in the peanut allergen-dnfp group and 2% for placebo (mild, 7% vs 7%; moder-
   ate, 50% vs 4%; severe, 3% vs 8%, respectively). Adverse events more common with
   peanut allergen-dnfp included gastrointestinal (GI) events (85.8% vs 4%), respiratory tract
   (81.2% vs 8%), and immune system (66.9% vs 9%). Withdrawal from the trial due to ad-
   verse events occurred in 6% for peanut allergen-dnfp and 4% for placebo; 3% in the
   peanut allergen-dnfp was due to dose-limiting GI symptoms. In the peanut allergen-dnfp
   group, 2% experienced a systemic adverse reaction (1 event severe) vs 2% for placebo.
   Enrolled patients had a serum peanut-specific IgE of at least 35 kUA/L and/or a mean wheal
   diameter at last 3 mm larger than the negative control on skin-prick testing for peanut FDA Approved Pediatric Indication

   Peanut (Arachis hypogaea) allergen powder-dnfp is indicated in conjunction with a peanut-
   avoidant diet for the mitigation of allergic reactions, including anaphylaxis, that may occur with

 accidental exposure to peanut. It is approved for use in patients with a confirmed diagnosis of
   peanut allergy. Initial Dose Escalation may be administered to patients 4 through 17 years old.
   Up-Dosing and Maintenance may be continued in patients 4 years and older Limitation of use: Not indicated for the emergency treatment of allergic reactions, including
   anaphylaxis Administration

Common, pediatric and adult: Infusion related reactions (25% vs 23% with placebo), pyrexia
   (19% vs 10%), nasopharyngitis (18% vs 12%), influenza (11%) vs 5%, cough (10% vs 2%), and
   nausea (10% vs 7%) 1

   Black Box Warning
   Warning: Serious Infections Caused by Encapsulated Bacteria

   Pegcetacoplan, a complement inhibitor, increases the risk of serious infections, especially
   those caused by encapsulated bacteria, such as Streptococcus pneumoniae, Neisseria meningi-
   tidis, and Haemophilus influenzae type B. Life-threatening and fatal infections with encapsulated
   bacteria have occurred in patients treated with complement inhibitors. These infections may
   become rapidly life-threatening or fatal if not recognized and treated early.

   Complete or update vaccination for encapsulated bacteria at least 2 weeks prior to the first
   dose of pegcetacoplan, unless the risks of delaying therapy with pegcetacoplan outweigh the
   risk of developing a serious infection. Comply with the most current Advisory Committee on
   Immunization Practices (ACIP) recommendations for vaccinations against encapsulated bacte-
   ria in patients receiving a complement inhibitor. See Warnings and Precautions for additional
   guidance on the management of the risk of serious infections caused by encapsulated
   bacteria.

   Patients receiving pegcetacoplan are at increased risk for invasive disease caused by encapsu-
   lated bacteria, even if they develop antibodies following vaccination. Monitor patients for early
   signs and symptoms of serious infections and evaluate immediately if infection is suspected.

   Because of the risk of serious infections caused by encapsulated bacteria, EMPAVELI is avail-
   able only through a restricted program under a Risk Evaluation and Mitigation Strategy (REMS)
   called the EMPAVELI REMS 4/8

   mediately if infection is suspected • Monitor patients for infusion-related reactions • Closely monitor for signs and symptoms of hemolysis and other reactions for at least 8
   weeks after discontinuation of treatment. Hemolysis may be identified by reappearance of
   symptoms such as fatigue, hemoglobinuria, abdominal pain, dyspnea, major adverse vascular
   events (including thrombosis), dysphagia, or erectile dysfunction

The most common adverse effects when given in combination with ribavirin were usually mild
   to moderate in severity and included influenza-like illness (91%), upper respiratory tract infec-
   tion (60%), headache (64%), gastrointestinal disorder (56%), skin disorder (47%), and injection-
   site reaction (45%). The events that resulted in discontinuation of mono- or combination ther-
   apy (7 out of 114 children) was depression, psychiatric evaluation abnormal, transient blind-
   ness, retinal exudates, hyperglycemia, type 1 diabetes mellitus, and anemia. Serious, acute hy-
   persensitivity reactions and cutaneous eruptions, including Stevens-Johnson syndrome (ery-
   thema multiforme major), have been reported When ribavirin is combined with either peginterferon alfa-2a or alfa-2b for the treatment of
   chronic hepatitis C in children, hematologic effects such as leukopenia (52%), neutropenia
   (32%), anemia (11%), and thrombocytopenia (5%) were reported in a meta-analysis of 8 clinical
   trials 10/14
 In a clinical study (n=14) of 2 to 8 year old patients receiving peginterferon alfa-2a monother-
   apy for 48 weeks, the most commonly experienced adverse events were pyrexia (79%),
   headache (43%), low absolute neutrophil count (36%) requiring dose adjustment, fatigue (21%),
   vomiting (21%), nausea (14%), injection-site reactions (14%), and irritability (14%) In a study (n=107) of pediatric patients 5 to 18 years of age, peginterferon alfa-2a with or with-
   out ribavirin resulted in a decrease in weight-for-age z-scores (WAZ), BMI-for-age (BMIZ), and
   height-for-age (HAZ) as well as body composition at 48 weeks of therapy. Subjects treated for
   24 or 48 weeks of therapy returned to baseline normal growth parameters by the 2-year fol-
   low-up date. In patients treated for 72 weeks (n=11), the HAZ remained significantly different
   from baseline at 96 weeks post-treatment 14,4 .

   Documented serious eye complications (n=4), of ischemic retinopathy, uveitis, and temporary
   monocular blindness, developed in children during a study (n=114) that performed prospec-
   tive comprehensive ophthalmic examinations at enrollment and after 24 and 48 weeks of
   treatment Black Box Warning
   Black Box Warning

   Alpha interferons, including peginterferon alfa-2a, may cause or aggravate fatal or life-threat-
   ening neuropsychiatric, autoimmune, ischemic, and infectious disorders. Patients should be
   monitored closely with periodic clinical and laboratory evaluations. Therapy should be with-
   drawn in patients with persistently severe or worsening signs or symptoms of these condi-
   tions. In many, but not all cases, these disorders resolve after stopping peginterferon alfa-2a
   therapy Monitoring
   At baseline: perform eye exam, CBC, liver function tests, bilirubin, renal function tests, neu-
   ropsychiatric exam, pregnancy test, and ECG if preexisting cardiac abnormalities 11,12,4 .

   During therapy: monitor hematological and chemistry assessments at 1, 3, 5, and 8 weeks,
   then every 4 weeks; TSH every 12 weeks; ECG (if preexisting cardiac abnormalities); renal func-
   tion tests; periodic ophthalmologic exams (if preexisting ophthalmologic disorders); and preg-
   nancy testing monthly if of childbearing potential throughout treatment and for 6 months fol-
   lowing discontinuation. Monitor liver function test more frequently if patient experiences ALT

 flares. Closely monitor patient's clinical status and monitor for serious adverse reactions, in-
   cluding evidence of depression, during treatment

Pre-exposure Prophylaxis of COVID-19
   Pemivibart may be effective for pre-exposure prophylaxis of COVID-19 in the authorized popu-
   lation. The range of titers achieved with pemivibart for 3 months following administration of
   4500 mg IV were consistent with the titer levels associated with clinical efficacy in prior clinical
   trials evaluating certain monoclonal antibodies for the prevention of COVID-19 HIV co-infection: Pemivibart should be considered in children 12 years or older and weighing
   40 kg or greater with HIV with severe immunosuppression for the prevention of COVID-19, re-
   gardless of COVID-19 vaccination status. Pemivibart may be considered in patients with mod-
   erate to no immunosuppression in whom COVID-19 vaccines are contraindicated or unavail-

 able. Monoclonal antibodies, including pemivibart, are not a substitute for vaccination in peo-
   ple who are eligible for COVID-19 vaccines Emergency Use Authorization
   The US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) has issued an Emergency Use Authorization (EUA)
   for the emergency use of the unapproved product pemivibart for the pre-exposure prophy-
   laxis of COVID-19 in adults and adolescents aged 12 years or older and 40 kg or greater 1 :

   •Who are not currently infected with SARS-CoV-2 and who have not had a known recent expo-
   sure to an individual infected with SARS-CoV-2 AND
   •Who have moderate-to-severe immune compromise due to a medical condition or receipt of
   immunosuppressive medications or treatments and are unlikely to mount an adequate re-
   sponse to COVID-19 vaccination
   Medical conditions or treatments that may result in moderate-to-severe immune compromise
   and an inadequate immune response to COVID-19 vaccination include 1 :
   •Active treatment for solid tumor and hematologic malignancies
   •Hematologic malignancies associated with poor responses to COVID-19 vaccines regardless of
   current treatment status (eg, chronic lymphocytic leukemia, non-Hodgkin lymphoma, multiple
   myeloma, acute leukemia)

   •Receipt of solid-organ transplant or an islet transplant and taking immunosuppressive
   therapy
   •Receipt of chimeric antigen receptor (CAR)-T-cell or hematopoietic stem cell transplant (within
   2 years of transplantation or taking immunosuppressive therapy)
   •Moderate or severe primary immunodeficiency (eg, common variable immunodeficiency dis-
   ease, severe combined immunodeficiency, DiGeorge syndrome, Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome)

   •Advanced or untreated HIV infection (people with HIV and CD4 cell counts less than
   200/mm(3), history of an AIDS-defining illness without immune reconstitution, or clinical mani-
   festations of symptomatic HIV)

   •Active treatment with high-dose corticosteroids (ie, 20 mg or greater of prednisone or equiva-
   lent per day when administered for 2 weeks or longer), alkylating agents, antimetabolites,
   transplant-related immunosuppressive drugs, cancer chemotherapeutic agents classified as
   severely immunosuppressive, and biologic agents that are immunosuppressive or immuno-
   modulatory (eg, B-cell depleting agents)

   Limitations of Authorized Use

 Pemivibart is not authorized for use for treatment of COVID-19, or for post-exposure prophy-
   laxis of COVID-19 in individuals who have been exposed to someone infected with SARS-CoV-2 Pre-exposure prophylaxis with pemivibart is not a substitute for vaccination in individuals for
   whom COVID-19 vaccination is recommended. Individuals for whom COVID-19 vaccination is
   recommended, including individuals with moderate-to-severe immune compromise who may
   derive benefit from COVID-19 vaccination, should receive COVID-19 vaccination In individuals who have recently received a COVID-19 vaccine, administer pemivibart at least 2
   weeks after vaccination Administration
   •Administer immediately after preparation •If immediate administration is not possible, may store the diluted solution at room tempera-
   ture under ambient light for up to 4 hours. Do not shake the diluted solution •Attach infusion set including inline 2-micron filter to prepared IV bag, then prime the infu-
   sion set •Administer the entire 50-mL infusion using infusion pump or gravity infusion set over a mini-
   mum of 60 minutes. Due to potential overfill, administer the entire contents of prepared IV
   bag to avoid underdosing •Once infusion is complete, flush line with NS

  Inhibits synthesis of bacterial cell wall. Dissolves slowly at site of injection with hydrolysis to penicillin G. Distributes widely into body tissues.
  Highest concentration in the kidneys, with smaller amounts in the liver, skin, and intestines. Approximately 60% bound to serum protein.
  Excreted rapidly by tubular excretion. In young infants and patients with renal impairment, excretion is prolonged

  For IM injection only. Avoid injection into or near an artery or nerve. Administer by deep IM injection in the upper, outer quadrant of the

  Needle may be blocked if injection is not made at a slow, steady rate due to high concentration of suspended material in the product 1/2

drugs.pharmacokinetics_summary:
Pharmacology
   Penicillin V potassium, an analog of penicillin G, is bactericidal against penicillin-susceptible or-
   ganisms through inhibition of cell wall synthesis. Not active against penicillinase-producing or-
   ganisms, including many strains of staphylococci. Displays high in-vitro activity against staphy-
   lococci (except penicillinase-producing strains) streptococci, and pneumococci. Penicillin V
   potassium is not inactivated by gastric secretions (advantage over penicillin G).
