   Monitoring
   Toxic Laboratory Monitoring

   • Monitor blood glucose levels 7 daily prior to initiation, daily during therapy, and several times
   after treatment 7 , • Monitor BUN and serum creatinine 7 prior to initiation, daily during therapy, and after treat-
   ment • Monitor CBC and platelet count 7 prior to initiation, during therapy, and several times after
   treatment • Monitor liver function tests 7 , including serum bilirubin, AST, and ALT prior to initiation, dur-
   ing therapy, and after treatment • Monitor serum calcium 7 prior to initiation, during therapy, and after treatment • Monitor patient closely for development of hyperkalemia Toxic Physical Monitoring

   • Monitor blood pressure closely 7 during administration and several times thereafter until
   blood pressure is stable 1

   • Monitor ECG 7 prior to initiation, during therapy, and after treatment • Monitor patient closely for development of hyperglycemia 7 or hypoglycemia 7 , • Monitor patient closely for development of pancreatitis 7 ,1 .

   • Monitor patient closely for development of Stevens-Johnson syndrome

 Black Box Warning
   Concomitant use: There are serious risks, including profound sedation, respiratory depres-
   sion, coma, and/or death, associated with combined use of opioids and benzodiazepines,
   other drugs that depress the CNS, or alcohol. Concomitant use should be reserved for patients
   with no alternative treatment. If necessary, use the lowest initial dose and titrate based on clin-
   ical response. Monitor patients closely for sedation and respiratory depression. Screen pa-
   tients for risk of substance-use disorders Neurologic: Brain development in children may be affected by repeated or lengthy use of gen-
   eral anesthetic and sedation drugs during surgeries or procedures, especially in children
   younger than 3 years or in fetuses of pregnant women during the third trimester; balance ap-
   propriate anesthesia use and timing of elective procedures that can be delayed against poten-
   tial risks in children younger than 3 years and pregnant women, particularly with procedures

drugs.contraindications_raw:
Extravasation causes tissue inflammation and necrosis due to high pH and osmolality.
   Propylene glycol content of the intravenous formulation has been associated with seizures and
   may potentiate the cardiovascular effects of phenytoin. Purple glove syndrome can occur with
   IV use (even without extravasation). Hypotension and cardiac arrhythmias have been reported.
   May increase the risk of suicidal thoughts or behavior. High serum concentrations are associ-
   ated with seizures. Dose related adverse events include nystagmus (total level 15 to 25 mg/L)
   and ataxia and mental status changes (total level greater than 30 mg/L). Movement disorders

 (bradykinesia and choreoathetosis) may also occur rarely. Hypersensitivity reactions have
   been reported in infants. Long-term effects of phenytoin include gingival hyperplasia, coarsen-
   ing of the facies, hirsutism, hyperglycemia, and hypoinsulinemia. Cutaneous side effects in-
   clude maculopapular exanthema, drug-induced lupus, and pigmentary alterations. Phenytoin
   interacts with carbamazepine, cimetidine, corticosteroids, digoxin, furosemide, phenobarbital,
   and valproate 39,52,19 .

   Folic acid 5 mg/day orally was associated with a significantly lower rate of gingival hyperpla-
   sia (21% vs. 9% for placebo) in children 6 to 15 years of age taking phenytoin in a 6-month,
   randomized, double-blind, placebo controlled study (N=120) Black Box Warning
   The rate of intravenous phenytoin administration should not exceed 1 to 3 mg/kg/min (or 50
   mg per minute, whichever is slower) in pediatric patients because of the risk of severe hy-
   potension and cardiac arrhythmias. Careful cardiac monitoring is needed during and after ad-
   ministering intravenous phenytoin. Although the risk of cardiovascular toxicity increases with
   infusion rates above the recommended infusion rate, these events have also been reported at
   or below the recommended infusion rate. Reduction in rate of administration or discontinua-
   tion of dosing may be needed Solution Compatibility
   NS only.

   Solution Incompatibility
   D5W and D10W.

   Terminal Injection Site Compatibility
   Esmolol, famotidine, and fluconazole.

   Terminal Injection Site Incompatibility

   tanyl, heparin, hyaluronidase, hydrocortisone succinate, insulin, lidocaine, linezolid,

 methadone, micafungin, morphine, nitroglycerin, pentobarbital, potassium chloride, pro-
   cainamide, propofol, sodium bicarbonate, and vitamin K1.

   Monitoring
   Monitor electrocardiogram, blood pressure, and respiratory function continuously during infu-
   sion, and for 15 minutes to 1 hour after infusion 39,15 . Measure serum phenytoin concentra-
   tion approximately 2 hours after IV loading dose. For maintenance therapy, a trough measure-
   ment is suggested. Therapeutic serum phenytoin concentration is 10 to 20 mg/L for total
   phenytoin and 1 to 2 mg/L for unbound phenytoin. Monitor for emergence or worsening of de-
   pression, suicidal thoughts or behavior, and/or any unusual changes in mood and behavior
   14,15
           .

   Correction for Albumin (Sheiner-Tozer Equation)

   Corrected total phenytoin = total phenytoin (mcg/mL) ÷ {[albumin (g/dL)/4.4] X 9} + 1

   Free phenytoin is obtained by multiplying by 1.

   Although the correction formula above has been used to estimate corrected total and free
   phenytoin levels, inaccuracies with the formula have been shown in children and adults.
   Routine measurement of free phenytoin levels is preferred in critically ill patients, patients with
   hypoalbuminemia, and patients receiving concurrent medications that may affect phenytoin

   percent free phenytoin was increased to approximately 22% In critically ill patients (1

   population pharmacokinetic study (n=32), the free phenytoin was 12%

   Initial dosing frequency: Every 3 days. Obtain a baseline plasminogen activity level; if patient
   is receiving fresh frozen plasma, allow for a 7-day washout period before obtaining Determination of dosing frequency on day 3:

   • Obtain a trough plasminogen activity level about 72 hours after the initial dose and before
   the second dose (same time of day as initial dosing). If plasminogen activity level is less than
   10% above baseline, increase frequency to every 2 days. If plasminogen activity level is 10% to
   20% above baseline, maintain frequency at every 3 days. If plasminogen activity level is more
   than 20% above baseline, decrease frequency to every 4 days. Maintain this dosing frequency
   for 12 weeks while treating active lesions Determination of dosing frequency at week 12:
   • If lesions do not resolve by week 12 or there are new or recurrent lesions, increase dosing
   frequency in 1-day increments every 4 to 8 weeks up to every 2 days while reassessing clinical
   improvement until lesion resolution or until lesions stabilize without further worsening. If de-
   sired clinical improvement does not occur by 12 weeks, check trough plasminogen activity
   level • If plasminogen activity level is 10% or more above baseline trough level, consider other treat-
   ment options (eg, surgical removal of lesion in addition to plasminogen treatment). If trough
   plasminogen activity level is less than 10% above baseline trough level, obtain a second level to
   confirm; if confirmed in combination with no clinical efficacy, consider discontinuing plasmino-
   gen treatment due to possibility of neutralizing antibodies • If lesions resolve by 12 weeks, continue at same dosing frequency and monitor for new or re-
   current lesions every 12 weeks

 Routine vaccination, pneumococcal disease: The CDC Advisory Committee on Immunization
   Practices (ACIP) recommends a routine vaccination series with a pneumococcal conjugate vac-
   cine (PCV) consisting of 4 doses at 2, 4, 6, and 12 to 15 months of age. Either PCV 15-valent
   (PCV15) or PCV 20-valent (PCV20) may be used 1 ,2 .If the PCV series was started with PCV 13-va-
   lent (PCV13), the series may be completed with PCV15 or PCV20 without giving additional
   doses. A supplemental dose of PCV15 or PCV20 is not indicated for healthy children without
   risk factors who have completed an age-appropriate PCV schedule For infants born at less
   than 37 weeks gestation who are medically stable enough to be vaccinated, pneumococcal
   conjugate vaccine should be administered at the recommended age concurrent with other
   routine vaccinations Catch-up vaccination, pneumococcal disease: The CDC Advisory Committee on
   Immunization Practices (ACIP) recommends 1 to 4 doses of pneumococcal conjugate vaccine
   (PCV) depending on patient age and previous vaccination administration. Either PCV 15-valent
   (PCV15) or PCV 20-valent (PCV20) may be used. Catch-up vaccination is recommended for all
   healthy children less than 5 years of age and for all children less than 18 years of age with cer-
   tain conditions that increase the risk of pneumococcal disease. Risk conditions include cere-
   brospinal fluid leak; chronic heart disease; chronic kidney disease (excluding maintenance dial-
   ysis and nephrotic syndrome, which are included in immunocompromising conditions);
   chronic liver disease; chronic lung disease (including moderate persistent or sever persistent
   asthma); cochlear implant; diabetes mellitus; immunocompromising conditions (on mainte-
   nance dialysis or with nephrotic syndrome); congenital or acquired asplenia or splenic dys-
   function; congenital or acquire immunodeficiencies; disease and conditions treated with im-
   munosuppressive drugs or radiation therapy, including malignant neoplasms, leukemias, lym-
   phomas, Hodgkin disease, and solid organ transplant; HIV infection; and sickle cell disease or
   other hemoglobinopathies. See current immunization guidelines for full recommendations 1 ,2 .

   Supplemental vaccination, children with any risk conditions: Supplemental doses of either
   pneumococcal conjugate vaccine 20-valent (PCV20) or pneumococcal polysaccharide vaccine
   23-valent (PPSV23) may be recommended depending on patient age and prior pneumococcal
   conjugate vaccine (PCV) history for children less than 18 years of age with certain conditions
   that increase the risk of pneumococcal disease 1 ,2 :

   • For patients with any risk condition who have previously received at least 1 dose of PCV20, no
   further PCV20 or PPSV23 doses are needed.

   • For patients with chronic medical conditions (cerebrospinal fluid leak; chronic heart disease;
   chronic kidney disease (excluding maintenance dialysis and nephrotic syndrome, which are in-
   cluded in immunocompromising conditions); chronic liver disease; chronic lung disease (in-

 cluding moderate persistent or sever persistent asthma); cochlear implant; diabetes mellitus)
   who previously completed a recommended PCV series with pneumococcal conjugate vaccine
   13-valent (PCV13) or pneumococcal conjugate vaccine 15-valent (PCV15), either a dose of
   PCV20 or a dose of PPSV23 is recommended at least 8 weeks after the most recent PCV dose.

   • For patients with immunocompromising conditions (on maintenance dialysis or with
   nephrotic syndrome; congenital or acquired asplenia or splenic dysfunction; congenital or ac-
   quire immunodeficiencies; disease and conditions treated with immunosuppressive drugs or
   radiation therapy, including malignant neoplasms, leukemias, lymphomas, Hodgkin disease,
   and solid organ transplant; HIV infection; and sickle cell disease or other hemoglobinopathies)
   who previously completed a recommended PCV series with PCV13 or PCV15, either a dose of
   PCV20 or a dose of PPSV23 is recommended at least 8 weeks after the most recent PCV dose.
   If PPSV23 is used, either a dose of PCV20 or a second dose of PPSV23 is recommended at least
   5 years after the first PPSV23 dose.

   Supplemental vaccination, hematopoietic stem cell transplant (HSCT) Children who re-
   ceived HSCT are recommended to receive three doses of pneumococcal conjugate vaccine 20-
   valent (PCV20) 4 weeks apart beginning 3 to 6 months after HSCT. A fourth PCV20 dose is rec-
   ommended at least 6 months after the 3rd PCV20 dose or at least 12 months after HSCT,
   whichever is later. If the pneumococcal vaccine series was started with pneumococcal conju-
   gate vaccine 13-valent (PCV13) or pneumococcal conjugate vaccine 15-valent (PCV15), the se-
   ries may be completed with PCV20 without giving extra doses. If PCV20 is not available, admin-
   ister PCV15 as a 3-dose series, followed by a dose of pneumococcal polysaccharide vaccine 23-
   valent (PPSV23) at least 12 months after HSCT. As patients with chronic graft-versus host dis-

   Prademagene zamikeracel is for autologous topical application on wounds only. The sheets
   are administered surgically by a qualified healthcare provider using the following steps 1

   • Verify patient’s identity.

 • Prepare wound by debridement under general or other appropriate anesthesia.
   • Before surgical application, pick up prademagene zamikeracel sheet with forceps by grasping
   the titanium ligating clips. Handle sheets only with forceps and only by the titanium ligating
   clips.
   • Do not trim sheets.
   • Apply unaltered prademagene zamikeracel sheets onto the wound bed only (nylon suture on
   the prademagene zamikeracel sheet facing away from wound) by affixing via resorbable su-
   tures. Do not suture prademagene zamikeracel onto healthy intact skin. Do not overlap sheets
   on wounds.

   • Apply all selected sheets in a single surgical session.
   • Cover area of application of prademagene zamikeracel sheets with non-adhesive dressings
   and topical antibiotic ointment.
   • Instruct patient to leave the treated area undisturbed for 5 to 10 days at the discretion of the
   physician based on individual needs for immobilization of treated areas and post-surgical
   recovery.
   • Instruct patient to keep dressings dry and not submerge the treated area in water until the
   gauze of the prademagene zamikeracel product falls off the treatment site. Gauze backing
   should fall off within 2 to 3 weeks of surgical application.

drugs.uses_raw:
Pralidoxime chloride is indicated as an antidote with concomitant atropine for the treatment
   of poisoning due to those pesticides and chemicals of the organophosphate class which have
   anticholinesterase activity 1

   Treatment is most effective if initiated immediately after poisoning; efficacy is severely dimin-
   ished if given more than 36 hours after exposure to poison 1

   Limitations of Use

 Pralidoxime is not effective in treating poisoning caused by phosphorus, inorganic phosphates,
   or organophosphates with no anticholinesterase activity Pralidoxime is not indicated for the treatment of pesticides in the carbamide class, as it may in-
   crease carbaryl toxicity Administration
   Slow IV administration is preferred; if not feasible, IM may be used IV (continuous infusion): Administer loading dose over 15 to 30 minutes (not to exceed 200
   mg/minute); administer continuous infusion at a rate of 10 to 20 mg/kg/hr 1
   IV (intermittent infusion): Administer doses over 15 to 30 minutes; do not exceed a rate of
   200 mg/minute 1

   IV (fluid restriction or rapid administration): Administer a more concentrated 50 mg/mL so-
   lution over at least 5 minutes; do not exceed a rate of 200 mg/minute 1

   IM: Administer in the anterolateral thigh to avoid the nerve, artery, vein, and femur 1

drugs.contraindications_raw:
In a 2-year double-blind, placebo-controlled study in children 8 to 18 years of age, the safety
   and tolerability profile of pravastatin was generally similar to that of placebo; influenza and
   headache were common in both groups In short-term, placebo-controlled studies in adults, the most commonly reported adverse ef-
   fects in adults were musculoskeletal pain (10.1%), nausea/vomiting (7.4%), upper respiratory
   infection (5.9%), diarrhea (6.7%), and headache (6.3%) During long-term placebo-controlled trials, the most commonly reported adverse effects in
   adults were musculoskeletal pain (24.9%), upper respiratory tract infection (21.2%), muscu-
   loskeletal traumatism (10.2%), chest pain (10%), influenza (9.2%), fatigue (8.4%), cough (8.2%),
   dizziness (7.3%), rash (7.2%), and sinus abnormality (7%) Statins were well tolerated and adverse events were mostly unrelated to statin therapy in a
   meta-analysis of 9 studies in 1191 pediatric patients (mean age, 3 +/- 5 years; mean BMI, 3 +/- 7 kg/m(2) based on 6 studies) with heterozygous familial hypercholesterolemia.
   Treatment-related adverse events were reported in 0% to 15%. Myalgia that resolved during
   continuation of treatment was reported in 2 studies (2.7% of patients receiving rosuvastatin
   and 1% receiving pitavastatin). There were no reports of life-threatening adverse events, and
   permanent discontinuation due to adverse events was 0% in 4 studies and 7% to 9% in 3
   studies. There was no significant difference compared with placebo in transaminase and crea-
   tine kinase levels, and there was no effect on growth or sexual development Monitoring

   ual maturation, and development •Measure baseline creatinine kinase, ALT, and AST •After 4 weeks, measure ALT, and AST; if normal, recheck in 8 weeks and then in 3 months.
   During maintenance, every 3 to 4 months in the first year, then every 6 months or as clinically

Oral, short-term use

   • Adverse effects with short-term use include reversible abnormalities in glucose metabolism,
   increased appetite, fluid retention, weight gain, mood alteration, hypertension, peptic ulcer,
   and rarely aseptic necrosis • Bradycardia: In pediatric patients with severe Kawasaki disease, 1% developed bradycar-

   or admission to the intensive care unit occurred Oral, long-term use

   • Adverse effects with long-term use include adrenal axis suppression, growth suppression,
   dermal thinning, hypertension, diabetes, Cushing's syndrome, cataracts, muscle weakness,
   and rarely immune function impairment • Decreased linear growth rate: Corticosteroids have been associated with a decreased rate
   of growth in children especially with high-dose, long-term treatment. Corticosteroids decrease

 the quantity of growth hormone released and also decrease the sensitivity of tissues to its ef-
   fect. The effect on growth suppression may be minimized by using the lowest effective dose of
   the corticosteroid and using alternate day therapy, if possible. In patients deficient in growth
   hormone, human growth hormone may also increase growth rate 96,97,98 .
   • Neurodevelopmental outcomes: PrednisoLONE and methylPREDNISolone use for more
   than 28 days was associated with lower Bayley Scales of Infant Development-Third Edition
   (BSID-III) motor scores (adjusted mean difference -7.9, 95% CI -14.2 to -0.9). After adjusting for
   predetermined variables (small for gestational age, respiratory support at 14 days, maternal
   education, and serious adverse events), length of exposure was no longer associated with mo-
   tor outcomes. There was also no linear association between exposure duration and BSID-III
   scores at corrected age 2 years (n=54) Ophthalmic use
   • Glaucoma with optic nerve damage, visual acuity and field defects, posterior subcapsular
   cataract formation, secondary ocular infections, delayed wound healing, and perforation of the

 • MDR = Multidrug resistant TB, caused by strains resistant to at least both isoniazid and
      rifampin
      • RR = Rifampin resistant TB; caused by strains resistant to rifampin; may be susceptible or
      resistant to isoniazid (MDR-TB) or other first or second-line drugs
      • MDR/RR TB = caused by strains resistant to at least rifampin (RR) or at least rifampin and
      isoniazid (MDR)
      • Pre-XDR = caused by strains that meet the definition of MDR TB or RR TB plus are resis-
      tant to any fluoroquinolone
      • XDR = Extensively drug resistant TB; caused by strains that meet the definition of
      MDR/RR TB plus are resistant to any fluoroquinolone and at least 1 additional Group A
      drug (bedaquiline or linezolid).

drugs.uses_raw:
Tuberculosis, active; drug-resistant: Drug-resistant TB is treated with a combination of at
   least 4 or 5 drugs susceptible to the tuberculosis strain being treated. Shorter-course (6 to 9
   months), all oral standardized regimens are preferred when patients meet eligibility criteria
   (no extensive disease, no extrapulmonary disease except for TB lymphadenopathy, no prior
   exposure to components (exposure = more than 1 month of use). A 6-month regimen of pre-
   tomanid, linezolid, bedaquiline, and moxifloxacin (if fluoroquinolone-susceptible) can be used
   in patients 14 years or older. Longer course regimens are necessary for those not meeting eli-
   gibility criteria. 2 ,5 ,3 ,6 ,7 .

   Tuberculosis, active, drug-resistant- HIV coinfection: Bedaquiline, pretomanid, linezolid,
   and moxifloxacin (BPaLM) for 6 months is the preferred regimen for treating rifamycin-resis-
   tant TB in adolescents with HIV coinfection. Treatment may be extended to 9 months if spu-
   tum cultures are positive between 4 to 6 months. Discontinue moxifloxacin (BPaL) if strain is
   fluoroquinolone-resistant FDA Approved Pediatric Uses: Pretomanid is not FDA approved for use in pediatric patients Administration
   • Administer by directly observed therapy • Take with food • Swallow tablets whole with water • If unable to swallow tablets, may choose 1 of the 2 following options:
   • Crush and suspend: Crush tablet, then suspend in 5 mL of room temperature water; stir vigor-
   ously to mix. Administer immediately and do not store for later use. Rinse the cup with an ad-
   ditional 5 mL of water and administer to ensure no residue is left in the cup • Soak and crush: Soak tablet in 5 mL of room temperature water for 4 to 5 minutes in a drink-
   ing cup, then crush any remaining solid contents. Stir vigorously to mix. Administer immedi-
   ately and do not store for later use. Rinse the cup with an additional 5 mL of water and admin-
   ister to ensure no residue is left in the cup • Missed dose: If the combination regimen of pretomanid, bedaquiline, and linezolid is inter-
   rupted by a healthcare provider for safety reasons, missed doses can be made up at the end

 of the treatment; doses of linezolid alone missed due to linezolid adverse reactions should not
   be made up Extemporaneous oral compound

   20 mg/mL Suspension (100 mL) 8

   • Triturate 10 200-mg tablets of pretomanid to a fine powder using a glass mortar and pestle.
   • Add approximately 15 mL of simple syrup to wet the powder and mix into a fine paste.
   • Add an additional 77 mL of simple syrup in geometric proportions while mixing thoroughly,
   to bring the total volume in the mortar to 100 mL.
   • Transfer to an appropriately sized amber bottle.
   • Label the container with "Shake well before using."

   • Stable for 30 days at room temperature (22 to 24°C) or at 30°C.

   Sugar-free oral compound

   20 mg/mL Suspension (100 mL) 8
   • Prepare Thick & Easy® vehicle by adding 5 grams Thick & Easy® Instant Food and
   Beverage Thickening Powder to 236 mL distilled water; mix with a spoon for 30 seconds and
   let the mixture sit for at least 5 minutes before use. Mix again just prior to use.
   • Triturate 10 200-mg tablets of delamanid to a fine powder using a glass mortar and pestle.

   • Add the following to the ground tablets in the mortar: Methylparaben 100 mg, potassium sor-
   bate 100 mg, citric acid 125 mg, and sodium saccharin 125 mg. Mix all the powders well using
   the pestle.

   • Add 20 mL of distilled water to the mortar and mix well to form a uniform suspension.
   • Transfer contents of mortar to a 100-mL graduated cylinder. Rinse mortar and pestle with an
   additional 30 mL distilled water in 5 to 10 mL increments; pour washings into graduated
   cylinder.
   • Add 30 mL of prepared Thick & Easy® vehicle to the graduated cylinder and mix well. Add
   any additional amount needed of the Thick & Easy® vehicle to achieve a total volume of 100
   mL, and mix well.
   • Transfer to an appropriately sized amber bottle.
   • Label the container with "Shake well before using."

   • Stable for 30 days at room temperature (22 to 24°C) or at 30°C.

drugs.contraindications_raw:
Common, adult: Peripheral neuropathy (22%), increased transaminases (24%), acne (13%),
   pleuritic pain (9%), neutropenia (7%), and pruritus (7%) were reported 1 with the guideline-pre-
   ferred regimen of pretomanid, bedaquiline, and linezolid (600 mg dose) Incidences of these
   adverse effects, plus the appearance of several likely linezolid-related effects, were reported
   with a regimen of pretomanid, bedaquiline, and linezolid (1200 mg dose) Hepatic enzyme elevations: ALT elevations between 3 and 5x ULN, 5 and 8x ULN, and
   greater than 8x ULN were reported in 7%, 0%, and 2%, respectively, treated with pretomanid,
   bedaquiline, and linezolid 600 mg (n=45). AST elevations between the same parameters were
   reported in 0%, 0%, and 2%. Total bilirubin elevations greater than 1 to 2x ULN and greater
   than 2x ULN were reported in 2% and 2%, respectively Monitoring
   Therapeutic Monitoring

 • Monitor for clinical (eg, decrease in cough and systemic symptoms, increase in weight), radio-
   logic, and bacteriologic response to treatment 7
   • Obtain sputum culture prior to initiation, then monthly during treatment. If cultures remain
   positive after 3 months, repeat susceptibility testing • Monitor body weight monthly; adjust doses accordingly 6

   Toxic Monitoring
   • Monitor CBC a minimum at baseline, at 2 weeks, and then monthly in patients receiving line-
   zolid as part of the combination regimen of pretomanid, bedaquiline, and linezolid • Monitor liver function tests (ALT, AST, alkaline phosphatase, and bilirubin) at a minimum at
   baseline, at 2 weeks, and then monthly while on treatment and as needed. If evidence of new
   or worsening liver dysfunction occurs, test for viral hepatitides 1

   • Monitor for symptoms of hepatoxicity (eg fatigue, anorexia, nausea, jaundice, dark urine, liver
   tenderness, and hepatomegaly) 1
   • Obtain an ECG before initiation of treatment, and at least 2, 12, and 24 weeks after starting
   treatment with the combination regimen of pretomanid, bedaquiline, and linezolid. Obtain
   serum potassium, calcium, and magnesium at baseline and monitor these electrolytes if QT
   prolongation is detected 1

   Therapeutic Drug Monitoring

   Consider monitoring therapeutic drug concentrations in patients with the following conditions
   7
       :

   • Gastrointestinal problems that may increase the risk of malabsorption
   • Concurrent HIV infection

   • Impaired renal function
   • Diabetes
   Some experts use therapeutic drug monitoring for all patients with resistant TB early in treat-
   ment to identify poor responses earlier

   Malaria; Prophylaxis
   Guideline dosage: 5 mg/kg base (0.8 mg/kg salt) orally once daily; MAX dose 30 mg base
   (52.6 mg salt) 2

   Duration of therapy: Begin treatment 1 to 2 days before traveling to malaria-endemic areas.
   Take daily at the same time each day while in malaria-endemic areas and continue treatment
   for an additional 7 days after leaving endemic areas for primary prophylaxis and 14 days for
   terminal prophylaxis (presumptive antirelapse therapy) 2

   Guideline dosage: 5 mg/kg base (0.8 mg/kg salt) orally once daily for 14 days 1
   Concomitant medications: Primaquine should be used with one of the following antimalarial
   agents: chloroquine, hydroxychloroquine, artemether-lumefantrine, atovaquone-proguanil,
   quinine, or mefloquine 1

   Guideline dosage, children: Primaquine base 3 mg/kg orally once daily plus clindamycin 10
   mg/kg/dose IV or orally every 6 hours has been used in adults. Data for use in children are not
   available. Dosing for children is based on use of these drugs for treating other infections Concomitant medication, children: Adjunctive corticosteroids are recommended for PaO2
   less than 70 mmHg on room air or alveolar-arterial O2 gradient greater than 35 mmHg:
   PredniSONE day 1 to 5, 1 mg/kg orally twice daily; day 6 to 10, 5 to 1 mg/kg orally twice a day;
   day 11 to 21, 5 mg/kg orally once daily. Alternatively, methylprednisolone 1 mg/kg/dose IV

   every 6 hours or 600 mg every 8 hours. For moderate to severe infections, may use IV clin-

   21, 20 mg orally once daily. Alternatively, methylprednisolone IV may be given at 75% of the
   prednisone doses Duration of therapy: 21 days 3 ,4

   Glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD) deficiency (intermediate): 45 mg orally once

   PALS guidelines: Procainamide may be considered to treat SVT in pediatric patients with car-
   diopulmonary compromise who are unresponsive to vagal maneuvers and adenosine Comparison with amiodarone: A small retrospective study (N=40 episodes of SVT) reported
   full treatment success (immediate conversion within 1 hour without further recurrences) in
   50% of the 14 episodes of SVT treated with procainamide and 15% of the 26 episodes treated
   with amiodarone. Amiodarone was switched to procainamide in 8 patients, with 4 achieving
   full success after conversion. Most patients were also given other antiarrhythmic medications
   before and during the study. Age of included patients ranged from 1 day to 19 years (median,
   34 days), with 54% younger than 30 days. Congenital heart disease was present in 65% SVT
   subtypes included were orthodronic reciprocating tachycardia (ORT), intra-atrial reentrant
   tachycardia (IART), and ectipic atrial tachycardia (EAT).. Median initial amiodarone dose was 5
   mg/kg (range, 1 to 10 mg/kg), followed by a continuous infusion of 5 mcg/kg/min (range, 5 to

 15 mcg/kg/min) in 54% of amiodarone-treated patients. Median procainamide initial dose was
   10 mg/kg (range, 5 to 10 mg/kg) followed by a continuous infusion of 20 mcg/kg/min (range,
   10 to 40 mcg/kg/min) in 79% of procainamide-treated patients Junctional tachycardia:In a study of pediatric patients 1 day or older with postoperative junc-
   tional tachycardia, combined hypothermia plus procainamide was effective in 80% of treated
   subjects (n=30) compared with efficacy rates of 32% with hypothermia alone (n=38) and 22%
   with procainamide alone (n=9). Mean procainamide level for the hypothermia plus pro-
   cainamide group was 6 mcg/mL. Efficacy was defined as achieving a heart rate less than 170
   beats per minute within 2 hours of initiation with no heart rate rebound to greater than 170
   beats per minute. Procainamide was given as a bolus dose of 5 to 15 mg/kg over 15 to 30 min-
   utes followed by a continuous infusion of 20 to 80 mcg/kg/min; target serum procainamide
   level was 4 to 10 mcg/mL Junctional tachycardia: Procainamide monotherapy was safe and effective for rapid rate con-
   trol of postoperative junctional tachycardia (JT) occurring in children following surgical repair
   of congenital heart defects. Two procainamide dosing protocols were used. In protocol A (n=5),
   following a loading dose of 3 mg/kg IV over 20 minutes, a continuous infusion was initiated at a

drugs.uses_raw:
Anesthesia induction and maintenance: Propofol is used for induction and maintenance of
   anesthesia 16,17 , although pain on injection may limit usefulness for induction, despite pre-
   medication or concomitant use of lidocaine 2 , Procedural sedation:

   Propofol has been used safely, by intermittent bolus or IV infusion, in a variety of settings out-
   side of the operating room where management of movement (eg, diagnostic imaging) and/or
   or pain due to procedures or instrumentation (eg, bronchoscopy, fracture reduction, lumbar
   puncture) are considerations 18,19,20 . Painful procedures require concomitant use of an anal-
   gesic, such as an opioid or ketamine • Propofol vs Dexmedetomidine: Propofol bolus plus continuous infusion in pediatric pa-
   tients requiring procedural sedation was associated with a significantly shorter induction plus
   study time compared with dexmedetomidine, likely due to the 10-minute infusion requirement
   for dexmedetomidine induction doses (N=2432; age range 1 month to 17 years). Propofol was
   also associated with a significantly shorter recover time (34.3 minutes vs 6 minutes). Airway

 obstruction and desaturation were reported more frequently with propofol, but no patients
   required intubation; changes in heart rate or blood pressure occurred more frequently with
   dexmedetomidine • Propofol plus Ketamine vs Ketamine Monotherapy: A meta-analysis (6 studies, 693 sub-
   jects) of pediatric patients administered ketamine-propofol combination or ketamine
   monotherapy for procedural sedation reported significantly lower incidences of cardiovascular
   adverse events, psychomimetic adverse events, and nausea/vomiting with ketamine-propofol
   combination compared ketamine monotherapy. Time endpoints, such as procedure time and
   recovery time, were unable to be assessed due to significant heterogeneity Convulsive Status Epilepticus: Propofol is a third-line agent for the treatment of status
   epilepticus, to be used in refractory cases. Use cautiously in young children and avoid use of
   high doses for prolonged periods of time due to the risk of adverse effects 22 , 23 , In several case series, propofol controlled seizure activity in patients who were refractory to
   standard therapy. In an initial case series (n=5; age 9 months to 19 years), maximum propofol
   infusion rates of 5 to 18 mg/kg/hr were used to control seizures activity; in 2 cases, pentobar-
   bital coma had failed prior to administration of propofol Propofol 3 mg/kg IV bolus, fol-
   lowed by an infusion of 100 mcg/kg/min (6 mg/kg/hr) was successfully used in a 9-month-old
   infant with RSE after failure of benzodiazepines, phenobarbital, and phenytoin A series of
   14 of 22 patients with refractory status epilepticus given propofol 1 to 2 mg/kg IV bolus, fol-
   lowed by an infusion of 1 to 5 mg/kg/hr (17 to 83 mcg/kg/min), achieved adequate control of
   seizure activity. In 4 cases, propofol was discontinued due to adverse effects, including hyper-
   triglyceridemia and rhabdomyolysis Given the retrospective nature of these reports and
   the potential for severe metabolic and organ system dysfunction with prolonged, high dose in-
   fusions of propofol 16 , other treatments with proven efficacy and greater safety should be con-
   sidered prior to use of propofol.

   Sedation in critically ill patients, Guidelines:

   Propofol may be considered as a second-line agent for sedation in critically ill pediatric pa-
   tients (alpha 2-agonists are considered first-line). To minimize the risk of propofol-related infu-
   sion syndrome development, continuous propofol sedation is recommended at doses less
   than 4 mg/kg/hr (67 mcg/kg/min) and for less than 48 hours Short-term (less than 48 hours) continuous propofol sedation may be a useful adjunct during
   the peri-extubation period to facilitate weaning of other analgosedative agents prior to extuba-
   tion 8

 Sedation in ICU for mechanical ventilation: While propofol is approved in adults, neither
   the FDA or the manufacturer recommends use of propofol for sedation in pediatric ICU pa-
   tients due to safety concerns. In an unpublished clinical trial of 327 pediatric patients, mortality
   was greater in patients who received propofol versus those who received standard sedative
   agents (SSA), such as chloral hydrate, fentanyl, ketamine, lorazepam, morphine, and phenobar-
   bital. Of the patients who died, the mortality for propofol 2%, propofol 1% and SSA was 11%,
   8%, and 4%, respectively The trial was terminated early due to this increase in mortality 27 ;
   however, further analysis of the data did not reveal a drug or disease-related pattern to the
   deaths 16 , and propofol has been used safely for this indication in pediatric patients 28,29 . A
   dosing protocol, based upon pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic parameters, was devel-
   oped in mechanically-ventilated pediatric patients. A bolus dose (2.5 mg/kg), followed by a de-
   creasing, continuous infusion (7.6 mg/kg/hr down to 3 mg/kg/hr over 4 hours, maintained at
   this dose for duration of desired sedation), was recommended for achievement of a target
   blood propofol level of 1 mg/L Tracheal intubation: Propofol in doses of 5 to 3 mg/kg allowed for excellent intubation
   conditions in greater than 90% of patients who received sevoflurane +/- nitrous oxide inhala-
   tion anesthesia (age range, 5 to 7 years) 30,31,32 . In one study, a lower dose was required in
   those patients who received higher concentrations of sevoflurane Pediatric Approved FDA Indications

drugs.contraindications_raw:
Side effects reported most frequently include apnea, arrhythmia, tachycardia, hypotension, hy-
   pertension, movement, burning/stinging or pain, pruritus, and rash 16,44,45,18 . Agitation, flush-
   ing (hands and feet), hyperirritability, and tremor, along with higher incidences of agitation,
   bradycardia, and jitteriness may accompany abrupt discontinuation of drug Propofol infusion syndrome: Propofol infusion syndrome (PIS), a rare but potentially fatal
   condition comprised of metabolic and organ system dysfunction (metabolic acidosis, hyper-
   kalemia, lipemia, rhabdomyolysis, hepatomegaly, hepatic and renal failure), may occur when
   used for sedation and/or anesthesia.

   Risk factors for PIS include 16 , 46 , 27 , 27 , 37 :
   • age less than 12 years
   • decreased delivery of oxygen to tissues
   • upper respiratory infection

 • serious neurologic injury
   • sepsis

   • inadequate carbohydrate intake or stores
   • high doses of inotropic agents, steroids, or vasoconstrictors

   • prolonged, high dose infusions (greater than 4 mg/kg/hr for more than 48 hours duration)
   • subclinical mitochondrial disease

   Emergent treatment should focus on the clinical features shown to be associated with mor-
   tality: ECG changes, hyperkalemia, hypotension, and fever. Various ECG changes have been re-
   ported, and their treatment should follow standard treatment for the arrhythmia in question.
   Consider hemofiltration if hyperkalemia, acidosis, or fever do not respond adequately to con-
   ventional measures. Extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (ECMO) has also been reported to
   be beneficial in some cases where response to vascular compartment filling, vasopressors,
   and inotropes was inadequate. 47
   Case Reports
   A 10-month old requiring a propofol infusion for sedation at a mean rate of 10 mg/kg/hr for 5 hours developed severe symptoms of metabolic acidosis and bradydysrhythmia. Based
   on worsening symptoms resistant to treatment, plasmaphereses followed by continuous veno-
   venous hemofiltration (CVVH) was done. Acidosis improved over a 12-hour period using a bi-
   carbonate predilution fluid. CVVH was discontinued after 2 days and the child made a com-
   plete recovery A 2-year-old who developed PIS after receiving a propofol for over 72 hours (an average hourly
   rate of 2 mg/kg) was successfully treated with hemofiltration resulting in an improvement in
   metabolic acidosis and cardiac function A 4-year-old requiring titration of propofol to 6 mg/kg/hr for refractory status epilepticus
   developed symptoms of PIS after 48 hours. Treatment with partial-exchange blood transfusion
   (PEBT) was initiated in small aliquots to avoid severe hemodynamic disturbances. Cardiac ab-
   normalities were corrected and patient became hemodynamically stable enough to permit
   continuous veno-venous hemodialysis for renal failure and removal of toxins A 16-year-old male receiving propofol infusion over 67 hours developed symptoms of PIS.
   Treatment with therapeutic plasma exchange (TPE) resulted in immediate reduction of triglyc-
   eride levels at three hours, resolution of acidosis at 24 hours, and normalization of blood lac-
   tate within 48 hours. Creatine phosphokinase continued to increase after treatment, peaking
   four days after TPE and subsequently falling to normal levels within two weeks 9/18

 Monitoring
   Laboratory Monitoring

   • Propofol Infusion Syndrome (PRIS): monitor patients for signs and symptoms of metabolic
   derangements and organ system failures. Patients may develop severe metabolic acidosis, hy-
   perkalemia, lipemia, rhabdomyolysis, hepatomegaly, cardiac and renal failure following the
   use of propofol injectable emulsion infusions. This syndrome most often occurs following pro-
   longed, high-dose infusions (greater than 5 mg/kg/h for greater than 48 hours); however, this
   syndrome may also occur following large-dose, short-term infusions during surgical anesthesia • Suggested monitoring and screening for PRIS during continuous propofol sedation includes
   intermittent measurement of lactic acid, triglycerides, creatine kinase, serum creatinine, and
   liver function studies 8
   • Patients at risk of hyperlipidemia should be monitored for increases in serum triglycerides or
   serum turbidity especially when propofol is administered for long periods of time or in pa-
   tients with inadequate fat clearance • Urinalysis and urine sediment should be evaluated in patients at risk of renal impairment
   prior to propofol therapy initiation and monitored on alternate days during sedation. The
   EDTA component of the propofol formulation has been known to be toxic to renal tubules • Urine zinc levels should be monitored especially when propofol is administered for longer
   than 5 days. The EDTA component of the propofol formulation may increase urinary zinc loss
   especially in patients predisposed to deficiency (burns, diarrhea, major sepsis).

   Physical Exam
   • Anaphylactic reactions (eg. angioedema, bronchospasm, erythema, and hypotension) should
   be monitored, especially in patients with an unknown allergy to eggs, egg products, soybeans,
   or soy products (use is contraindicated).
   • Cardiorespiratory depressive effects (blood pressure, pulse oximetry, and electrocardiogram)
   should be monitored in patients for early signs of hypotension and/or bradycardia, apnea, air-
   way obstruction, and/or oxygen desaturation. These effects are more likely to occur following
   rapid bolus administration or rapid increases in infusion rates, especially in the elderly, debili-
   tated, ASA-PS III or IV patients, patients receiving concomitant drugs with additive cardiorespi-
   ratory depressive effects. Apnea persisting for more than 60 seconds during induction of anes-
   thesia requiring ventilatory assistance should be monitored. Patients with preexisting primary
   hyperlipoproteinemia, diabetic hyperlipemia, and pancreatis are at greater risk of apnea 11/18
 • Fever, infection/sepsis, other life-threatening illness, and/or death may occur following ad-
   ministration of a contaminated product Patients who develop fever, chills, and body aches
   or other symptoms of an acute febrile reaction shortly after receiving propofol should be eval-
   uated for bacterial sepsis • Assessment of the level of sedation in mechanically ventilated pediatric patients is recom-
   mended, using the Comfort-B Scale, State Behavioral Scale, or Richmond Agitation-Sedation
   Scale 8
   • All pediatric patients requiring mechanical ventilation should be assigned a target depth of
   sedation and evaluated at least once daily with a validated sedation assessment tool 8
   • Continuous electrocardiogram monitoring is recommended during continuous propofol se-
   dation to screen/monitor for Propofol Infusion Syndrome (PRIS) 8

   • Increased intracranial pressure or impaired cerebral circulation leading to decreases in mean
   arterial pressure and cerebral perfusion pressure should be monitored when propofol is ad-
   ministered to neurosurgical patients.
   • Seizures during recovery from anesthesia occurs with greater frequency in epileptic patients.
   • Weaning of sedation level is recommended. The signs and symptoms of rapid awakening fol-
   lowing abrupt discontinuation including anxiety, agitation, and resistance to mechanical
   ventilation.

Adverse effects are related to beta-receptor blockade. Significant reductions in myocardial
   function and hypotension resulting in cardiac compromise have been reported in association
   with beta-blockers, especially during IV administration in infants. May cause AV block.

   drawal syndrome (nervousness, tachycardia, sweating, hypertension) has been associated with
   sudden cessation of the drug 2 ,67,68,1 ,38,72 .

   Infantile hemangioma: The most common (10% or more) adverse events in infants treated
   for infantile hemangioma were sleep disorders, aggravated respiratory tract infections, periph-
   eral coldness, agitation, diarrhea, somnolence, nightmare, irritability, decreased appetite, ab-
   dominal pain, and vomiting Asymptomatic and symptomatic hypoglycemia, requiring hospitalization, have been reported
   in infants receiving propranolol for the treatment of infantile hemangioma. Infants less than 3
   months of age are at increased risk 73 , 74 , Hypoglycemia including hypoglycemic seizures

      • RR = Rifampin resistant TB; caused by strains resistant to rifampin; may be susceptible or

      isoniazid (MDR)

      tant to any fluoroquinolone
      • XDR = Extensively drug resistant TB; caused by strains that meet the definition of
      MDR/RR TB plus are resistant to any fluoroquinolone and at least 1 additional Group A

   abusers) • Monitor serum uric acid levels prior to starting therapy, periodically during treatment, and if
   any clinical signs or symptoms occur during therapy • Monitor for symptoms and clinical signs of liver injury; especially in patients with preexisting
   liver disease or those at increased risk for drug-related hepatitis (eg, alcohol abusers) Therapeutic Drug Monitoring

   Peak adult pyrazinamide concentration target is at least 20 mcg/mL in adults when measured
   2 hours after a dose of pyrazinamide Consider monitoring TB regimen drug levels in the following situations 5 :

   • Poor response despite adherence and susceptibility
   • Severe GI abnormalities such as short bowel syndrome, chronic diarrhea with malabsorption,
   severe gastroparesis
   • Drug-drug interactions
   • Impaired renal clearance
   • HIV coinfection

   • Diabetes
   • Use of second-line drugs
   Some experts use therapeutic drug monitoring for all patients with resistant TB early in treat-
   ment to identify poor responses earlier

drugs.pharmacokinetics_summary:
Pharmacology
   Mechanism of action

   PyRIDostigmine bromide, an analog of neostigmine, inhibits acetylcholinesterase. It inhibits
   the breakdown of acetylcholine by cholinesterase 9 , thus, facilitating free transmission of

 nerve impulses across the neuromuscular junction. PyRIDostigmine is characterized by a long
   duration of action and fewer gastrointestinal adverse effects than neostigmine 1 ,11 .

drugs.pharmacokinetics_summary:
Pharmacology
   Pyridoxine is a coenzyme in amino acid and carbohydrate metabolism required for the conver-
   sion of tryptophan to both niacin and neurotransmitter serotonin and conversion of dopa to
   dopamine. It is also required for the synthesis of the inhibitory neurotransmitter gamma-
   aminobutyric acid (GABA). Pyridoxine-dependent seizures are a result of defective binding of
   pyridoxine in the formation of GABA. They typically present in the neonatal period or early in-
   fancy;

 Extended-Release Tablets

   Hepatic Impairment: Initiate therapy at a dose of 25 mg/day then increase daily in incre-
   ments of 25 to 50 mg/day to an effective and tolerable dose for immediate-release tablets Initiate therapy with 50 mg/day; may be increased in increments of 50 mg/day depending on
   patient response and tolerance for extended-release tablets Coadministration with CYP3A4 Inhibitors: Reduce QUEtiapine dose to one-sixth the original
   dose when using concurrently with a strong CYP3A4 inhibitor (eg, ketoconazole, itraconazole,
   indinavir, ritonavir, nefazodone). When the CYP3A4 inhibitor is discontinued, increase
   QUEtiapine dose by 6-fold 2 ,3 .
   Coadministration with CYP3A4 Inducers: Increase QUEtiapine dose by as much as 5-fold
   during chronic (greater than 7 to 14 days) coadministration with a strong CYP3A4 inducer (eg,
   phenytoin, carbamazepine, rifampin, avasimibe, St John's wort), titrating dose based on clinical
   response and tolerability. When the CYP3A4 inducer is discontinued, reduce QUEtiapine to the
   original dose within 7 to 14 days 2 ,3 .

   Switching from Immediate-Release to Extended-Release Tablets: The equivalent total daily
   dose of the immediate-release QUEtiapine may be taken as extended-release once daily 2 , Reinitiation of Quetiapine: There are no specific data on reinitiation; but it's recommended
   to follow the initial dose schedule for patients who stopped QUEtiapine more than a week pre-
   viously. If less than a week has passed, then gradual dose escalation may not be needed 2 ,3 .
   Switching from Antipsychotics: There are no specific data on switching from or concomitant
   use with other antipsychotics. Some patients may need gradual discontinuation whereas, oth-
   ers may be able to abruptly discontinue the previous antipsychotic agent. Either way, minimize
   the time of overlapping antipsychotic administration. For patients on depot antipsychotics, ini-
   tiate QUEtiapine in place of the next scheduled injection. The need for continuing existing ex-
   trapyramidal syndrome medication should be re-evaluated periodically .

   Extended-Release Tablets

   Swallow tablets whole. Do not crush, chew, or split Immediate-Release Tablets

   May be given without regard to food . 2

   Preparation
   Extemporaneous oral compounds

   40 mg/mL suspension (100 mL) 6 :

   • Mix the following powders together in a mortar: quetiapine fumarate 4000 mg, saccharin
   sodium 100 mg, butylated hydroxytoluene 100 mg, and silica gel, micronized 3000 mg.
   • Add about 50 mL of sweet almond oil and 3 mL peppermint oil to the powders and mix well .

   • Transfer mixture to a tight, light-resistant container.

   • Add sufficient quantity of sweet almond oil to reach a final volume of 100 mL.

   • Suspension is stable up to 6 months.

   10 mg/mL suspension (40 mL) 7 :

 • Grind a 400 mg immediate-release quetiapine tablet to a fine powder using a mortar and
   pestle

   • Add 2 mL propylene glycol to the mortar and mix to form a paste. Add a 2 to 5 mL Ora-Blend
   to mortar and mix until a uniform paste forms.
   • Continue adding Ora-Blend (no more than 50% of total volume) until a pourable mixture
   forms.

   • Transfer contents of mortar to an amber bottle. Wash the mortar with Ora-Blend (no more
   than 15% of total volume each wash) and pour contents into amber bottle.

   • Repeat wash as necessary. Ensure final volume of 40 mL.

   • Stable at room temperature for up to 60 days.

   The odds ratio for cumulative type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM) risk was 09 (95% CI, 5 to 9) in antipsychotic-exposed youth compared with psychiatric controls in a meta-analysis (n=7
   studies); although the absolute incidence rate of T2DM compared with all controls (3.09 cases
   (95% CI, 35 to 82) per 1000 patients-years) was small over the mean follow-up period of 7
   years (n=13 studies). Important differences among studies included may affect the validity of

 this finding. The majority of antipsychotic agents were second-generation agents (risperiDONE,
   QUEtiapine, ARIPiprazole, and OLANZapine) In an open-label, 8-week study (n=34) in pre-adolescents, the most common adverse effects

   testinal disturbance, and decreased energy in school age children (6 to 15 years of age) Black Box Warning
   There are serious risks, including profound sedation, respiratory depression, coma, and/or
   death, associated with combined use of opioids and benzodiazepines, other drugs that de-
   press the CNS, or alcohol. Concomitant use should be reserved for patients with no alternative
   treatment. If necessary, use the lowest initial dose and titrate based on clinical response.
   Monitor patients closely for sedation and respiratory depression. Screen patients for risk of
   substance-use disorders QUEtiapine fumarate and QUEtiapine fumarate XR are not approved for the treatment of pa-
   tients younger than 10 years. There is an increased risk of suicidal thoughts and behavior in
   children, adolescents and young adults taking antidepressants. Monitor patients closely for
   clinical worsening and emergence of suicidal thoughts and behaviors 2 ,3 .

   mal after 3 months of treatment, then monitor annually Other experts recommend moni-
   toring fasting plasma glucose at 3 and 6 months and there is only weak evidence to support
   monitoring at 12 months for QUEtiapine. Beyond 1 year monitoring is based on previous val-
   ues 8/13

   and weakness 2 ,3 .

   mal after 3 months, then monitor at least every 5 years Other experts recommend moni-
   toring fasting LDL, fasting HDL, and fasting triglycerides at baseline and 3 months; however,
   there is only weak evidence to support monitoring at 6 and 12 months for QUEtiapine. For to-
   tal cholesterol they recommend monitoring at baseline, 3 and 6 months; however there is only

   sults Regularly monitor weight 2 ,3 . Monitor body mass index at baseline and at 4, 8, and 12 weeks,
   and at least every 3 months thereafter, or more often as indicated Obtain complete CBC frequently during the first few months of therapy in patients with preex-
   isting low white blood cell counts or a past history of drug-induced leukopenia or neutropenia

         .
   Evaluate for abnormal movements (eg, dystonia, akathisia, tardive dyskinesia) and neuroleptic
   malignant syndrome However, there is weak evidence to recommend monitoring for neu-
   rological signs and symptoms for QUEtiapine Carefully monitor for recurrence of neuroleptic malignant syndrome in patients with past his-
   tory 2 , Evaluate patient for risk of abuse or misuse and monitor for symptoms during treatment 2 ,3 .

   Measure blood pressure at the beginning of treatment and periodically thereafter 2 ,3 .

   Perform ophthalmic examination of the lens to detect cataract formation at initiation of treat-
   ment and every 6 months thereafter 2 , 3

      transferase, ALT = alanine aminotransferase, BUN = blood urea nitrogen, CAB-LA
      = cabotegravir long-acting, CBC = complete blood count; DAA = direct-acting an-

      inhibitor, PrEP = pre-exposure prophylaxis

      (a) If ART is initiated soon after HIV diagnosis and entry into care, repeat baseline labora-
      tory testing is not necessary.
      (b) ART is indicated for all people with HIV and should be started as soon as possible.
      However, if ART initiation is delayed, patients should be retained in care, with periodic
      monitoring as noted above.
      (c) After 2 years of consistently suppressed HIV RNA, less frequent monitoring (eg, every 6
      months) may be considered.
      (d) After 2 years of ART with consistently suppressed viral load: CD4 count 300 to 500
      cells/mm(3), monitor every 12 months; CD4 count greater than 500 cells/mm(3), CD4 mon-
      itoring is optional.
      (e) If HIV RNA is detectable at 4 to 8 weeks, repeat every 4 to 8 weeks until viral load is
      suppressed to less than 50 copies/mL, then every 3 to 6 months.
      (f) For patients on ART, viral load is typically measured every 3 to 6 months. More frequent
      monitoring may be considered in individuals having difficulties with ART adherence or at
      risk for nonadherence. However, for adherent patients with suppressed viral load and sta-
      ble immunological status for more than 1 year, monitoring can be extended to 6-month
      intervals.
      (g) Standard genotypic drug-resistance testing in ARV-naïve persons should focus on test-
      ing for mutations in the PR and RT genes. If transmitted INSTI resistance is a concern, or if
      a person has a history of INSTI use as PrEP or treatment, or a person presents with
      viremia while on an INSTI, providers should also test for resistance mutations in the IN
      gene. In ARV-naïve patients who do not immediately begin ART, repeat testing before initi-
      ation of ART is optional if drug-resistance testing was performed at entry into care. For vi-

 rologically suppressed patients who are switching therapy for toxicity or convenience, viral
      amplification will not be possible and therefore resistance testing should not be per-
      formed. Results from prior resistance testing can be used to help in the construction of a
      new regimen.
      (h) If infected with hepatitis B virus, tenofovir disoproxil fumarate or tenofovir alafe-
      namide plus either emtricitabine or lamivudine should be used as part of the ART regimen
      to treat both hepatitis B virus and HIV infections.
      (i) If HBsAg, and HBsAb, and HBcAb are negative at baseline, administer hepatitis B vac-
      cine series. Also, consult Guidelines for Opportunistic Infections.
      (j) Typically HBV infection has resolved with loss of HBsAb despite isolated HBcAb; confirm
      with an HBV viral load if wanted. A positive HBV viral load is indicative of acute infection
      (other symptoms will be present usually) or chronic infection. Vaccinate the patient when
      viral load is negative. Also, consult Guidelines for Opportunistic Infections.
      (k) In patients with recent HCV infection (acquired in last 6 months) or advanced immun-
      odeficiency (CD4 count less than 100 cells/mm(3)), the HCV antibody test may not be ade-
      quate for screening. HCV RNA screening is indicated in persons who have been success-
      fully treated for HCV or who spontaneously cleared prior infection. HCV antibody-negative
      patients with elevated ALT may need HCV RNA testing.
      (l) At-risk populations: injection drug users, persons with a history of incarceration, men
      with HIV who have unprotected sex with men, and persons with percutaneous/parenteral
      exposure to blood in unregulated settings are at risk of HCV infection.
      (m) Serum sodium, potassium, bicarbonate, chloride, blood urea nitrogen, creatinine, glu-
      cose (preferably fasting). Monitor serum phosphorus concentrations in patients with
      chronic kidney disease who are on tenofovir-containing regimens. Renal function determi-
      nation should include creatinine monitoring and estimation of the glomerular filtration
      rate.
      (n) Consult recommendations of the HIV Medicine Association of the Infectious Diseases
      Society of America for patients with renal disease. More frequent monitoring may be indi-
      cated for patients with evidence of kidney disease (eg, proteinuria or decreased glomeru-
      lar function) or increased risk of renal insufficiency (eg. patients with diabetes or hyper-
      tension).
      (o) CBC with differential should be done when a CD4 count is performed. When CD4 count
      is no longer being monitored, the recommended frequency of CBC with differential is
      once a year. More frequent monitoring may be for patients receiving medications that po-
      tentially cause cytopenia (eg, trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole)
      (p) If random lipids are abnormal, fasting lipids should be obtained. Consult the ACA/AHA
      recommendations for diagnosis and management of patients with dyslipidemia.
      (q) If random glucose is abnormal, fasting glucose should be obtained. HgbA1C is not
      longer recommended for diagnosis of diabetes in patients with HIV on ART.

 (r) Assess urine glucose and protein before initiating tenofovir-containing regimens and
      monitor during treatment with these regimens.
      (s) In women with child-bearing potential.

Crying and irritability: In otherwise healthy term infants, histamine2 receptor antagonists or
   proton pump inhibitors should not be used for the treatment of crying and distress Prevention of stress ulcers and GI hemorrhage in critically ill patients 3 , 5 , 4 , Gastroesophageal Reflux (GER): In otherwise healthy term infants, histamine2 receptor an-
   tagonists or proton pump inhibitors should not be used for the treatment of visible regurgita-
   tion Gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD): Proton pump inhibitors (PPIs) are the first-line
   agents for erosive esophagitis in infants and children with GERD. Histamine2 receptor antago-
   nists are the second-line agent if PPIs are not available or are contraindicated. A duration of
   treatment for 4 to 8 weeks for GERD symptoms is recommended. Regularly reassess the need
   for long-term acid suppression. If no response after 4 to 8 weeks, then re-evaluate for other
   causes of symptoms. H2RAs and PPIs are not recommended for extraesophageal symptoms
   (e.g. cough, wheezing, asthma), unless GERD symptoms are present and/or GERD has been di-
   agnosed A trial use of PPIs as a diagnostic test for GERD is not recommended in infants or in patients
   presenting with extraesophageal symptoms. However, in children with typical GERD symp-
   toms, a trial of 4 to 8 weeks with a PPI may be used as a diagnostic test Administration

 IV bolus: Dilute in NS to a maximum concentration of 5 mg/mL and give over at least 5 min-
   utes (maximum 4 mL/minute) Intermittent IV infusion: Dilute in D5W or other compatible solution to a concentration of no
   greater than 5 mg/mL and give over 15 to 20 minutes (maximum 5 to 7 mL/minute) Standard concentrations that may be used are 1, 2, 5 mg/mL Continuous IV infusion: Dilute in D5W or other compatible solution to a concentration of 5
   mg/mL or less Standard concentrations that may be used are 5, 1, 5 mg/mL IM: No dilution necessary Oral effervescent tablets (Zantac®25 EFFERdose®): Do not chew, swallow whole, or dis-
   solve on the tongue. Dissolve 1 tablet in 5 mL of water and wait until the tablet is completely
   dissolved before administration in a medicine dropper or oral syringe; may be given with or
   without food Oral syrup and tablets: May be given with or without food

drugs.contraindications_raw:
General: RaNITIdine is well tolerated and has a low incidence of adverse effects, including
   rash, headache, fatigue, irritability, dizziness, nausea, constipation, and diarrhea, that are usu-
   ally mild. Elevations in hepatic enzymes, leukopenia, thrombocytopenia, and bradycardia have
   been reported in adults. Transient pain at the site of IM injection and transient local burning or
   itching with IV administration have been reported. RaNITIdine has been reported to affect the
   bioavailability of other drugs such as atazanavir, delavirdine, gefitinib, glipizide, ketoconazole,
   midazolam, procainamide, triazolam, and warfarin, 10,2 ,12 .

   Solution Compatibility
   D5W, D10W, and NS.

   Terminal Injection Site Compatibility
   Acyclovir, acetazolamide, amikacin, aminophylline, ampicillin, atropine, aztreonam, cefazolin,
   cefepime, cefoxitin, ceftazidime, chloramphenicol, clindamycin, dexamethasone, digoxin,
   dobutamine, dopamine, enalaprilat, epinephrine, erythromycin lactobionate, fentanyl, flucona-
   zole, flumazenil, furosemide, gentamicin, glycopyrrolate, heparin, insulin, isoproterenol, lido-
   caine, linezolid, lorazepam, meropenem, metoclopramide, midazolam, milrinone, morphine,
   nicardipine, nitroprusside, pancuronium bromide, penicillin G, piperacillin,
   piperacillin/tazobactam, potassium chloride, propofol, protamine, remifentanil, tobramycin,
   vancomycin, vecuronium, vitamin K1, and zidovudine.

   Terminal Injection Site Incompatibility
   Amphotericin B, pentobarbital, and phenobarbital.

   Monitoring
   •Gastric pH may be measured to assess efficacy (pH greater than 4) •Monitor renal and hepatic function 2 ,10,19 .

 •Monitor prothrombin time in patients taking warfarin 2 ,10,19 .

drugs.uses_raw:
Increased Uric Acid Levels- Tumor Lysis Syndrome (TLS): 2
    ●   High risk* patients should be offered prophylaxis with rasburicase along with increased hy-
        dration (Grade 1B recommendation).
    ●   Rasburicase is contraindicated in patients with G6PD deficiency. Instead treatment should
        consist of fluids and allopurinol, and monitored carefully (Grade 2C recommendation)
    ●   Urate assays while patients are receiving rasburicase, must be sent to the laboratory on ice
        to prevent falsely low assay results (Grade 1B recommendation).
    ●   In high-risk children, in the absence of established clinical or laboratory TLS, prophylaxis can
        be achieved in many patients using a single dose of rasburicase 2 mg/kg. Treatment needs
        to be followed by close laboratory and clinical monitoring for evidence of progressive TLS
        (Grade 2C recommendation).

 ●   In established TLS, administer rasburicase. The duration is dependent on the clinical re-
        sponse (Grade 1B recommendation).
    ●   When rasburicase is being used in the treatment or prophylaxis of TLS, allopurinol is unnec-
        essary and may reduce the effectiveness of rasburicase (Grade 2C recommendation).
    ●   * High risk is defined as (1) acute lymphoblastic or myeloid leukemia with WBC greater than
        100 x 10(9)/L, (2) Burkitt lymphoma or lymphoblastic lymphoma, or (3) high-grade lym-
        phoma (diffuse large B-cell lymphoma and T-cell non-Hodgkin lymphoma) with bulky dis-
        ease (LDH greater than 2 x ULN or tumor bulk on CT scan)

   Dose Comparison: A systematic review identified 1 randomized trial (N=30) that compared
   rasburicase 15 mg/kg with rasburicase 2 mg/kg both administered IV over 30 minutes daily
   for 5 days to pediatric patients with newly diagnosed hematological malignancies and hyper-
   uricemia or high tumor burden. There was no significant between-group difference in percent-
   age of normalization of serum uric acid with 5 weeks of follow-up, reduction in serum uric acid
   level at 4 hours, or in the frequency of adverse effects Fixed-Dose: A single dose of rasburicase 6-mg fixed dose compared with rasburicase weight-
   based dosing (0.15 to 2 mg/kg) produced nonsignificantly different rates of normalization of
   uric acid levels (less than 5 mg/dL) within 24 hours of treatment (81% vs 85%) in a retrospec-
   tive review of 48 pediatric patients (mean age, 6 years) weighing 30 kg or more. Mean uric
   acid levels at 24 hours were not significantly different: 17 mg/dL with fixed dosing versus 57 mg/dL with weight-based dosing. Four patients in each dosing group required additional
   dose(s). Adverse events with fixed versus weight-based dosing included nausea (24% vs 63%),
   vomiting (14% vs 26%), abdominal pain (10% vs 44%), and acute kidney injury (20% vs 11%) Comparison to Allopurinol: In a randomized trial in children, rasburicase (N=27; 3 to 17
   years of age) compared with allopurinol (N=25; 5 to 16 years of age) significantly reduced
   plasma uric acid at 4 hours after the first dose (86% vs 12%; p less than 0001) in patients with
   leukemia or lymphoma receiving chemotherapy at high risk for developing tumor lysis syn-
   drome. Rasburicase 2 mg/kg/day IV or allopurinol 300 mg/m2/day orally or 10 mg/kg/day di-
   vided every 8 hours was administered for 5 to 7 days. In a subgroup analysis of patients with
   hyperuricemia at baseline, all patients treated with rasburicase (n=10) and no patients treated
   with allopurinol (n=5) achieved a uric acid concentration of less than 8 mg/dL at 4 hours. Over
   the first 96 hours of therapy, creatinine levels in hyperuricemic patients improved (from 144%
   to 102% of mean for age and gender) in patients receiving rasburicase and worsened (from
   132% to 147% of mean for age and gender) in patients receiving allopurinol 2/6
 FDA Pediatric Approval: Rasburicase is indicated for the initial management of plasma uric
   acid levels in patients with leukemia, lymphoma, and solid tumor malignancies who are receiv-
   ing anti-cancer therapy expected to result in tumor lysis and subsequent elevation of plasma
   uric acid. Rasburicase is indicated only for a single course of treatment 1

   Administration
   •Final volume for infusion should be 50 mL in 9% sodium chloride •Infuse the diluted rasburicase solution intravenously over 30 minutes; do not administer as a
   bolus infusion •Do not filter •Flush the line with at least 15 mL of normal saline before and after the rasburicase infusion or
   infuse in a separate line

   Hypersensitivity Reactions

 •Rasburicase can cause serious and fatal hypersensitivity reactions including anaphylaxis.
   Immediately and permanently discontinue rasburicase in patients who experience a serious
   hypersensitivity reaction Hemolysis
   •Do not administer rasburicase to patients with glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD)
   deficiency. Immediately and permanently discontinue rasburicase in patients developing
   hemolysis. Screen patients at higher risk for G6PD deficiency (eg, patients of African or
   Mediterranean ancestry) prior to starting rasburicase Methemoglobinemia

   •Rasburicase can result in methemoglobinemia in some patients. Immediately and perma-
   nently discontinue rasburicase in patients developing methemoglobinemia Interference with Uric Acid Measurements

   •Rasburicase enzymatically degrades uric acid in blood samples left at room temperature.
   Collect blood samples in pre-chilled tubes containing heparin and immediately immerse and
   maintain sample in an ice water bath. Assay plasma samples within 4 hours of collection Monitoring
   Laboratory Parameters

   •Perform pretreatment screening for patients at a higher risk for glucose-6-phosphate dehy-
   drogenase (G6PD) deficiency (eg, patients of African or Mediterranean ancestry) 6

   •For uric acid samples, collect blood samples in pre-chilled tubes containing heparin and im-
   mediately immerse and maintain sample in an ice water bath. Assay plasma samples within 4
   hours of collection 1

   Physical Exam

   •Monitor for signs and symptoms of a severe allergic reaction (eg, bronchospasm, chest pain
   and tightness, dyspnea, hypoxia, hypotension, shock, and/or urticaria)

drugs.uses_raw:
Atypical Hemolytic Uremic Syndrome

   A complete thrombotic microangiopathy (TMA) response was achieved in 71% of patients after
   26 weeks of ravulizumab-cwvz treatment in an interim analysis of the single-arm ALXN1210-
   aHUS-312 trial (N=14) of pediatric patients (median age, 2 years (range, 9 to 3 years)
   with atypical hemolytic uremic syndrome (aHUS) who were naïve to eculizumab. Complete
   TMA response was defined as normalization of platelet count and LDH and at least a 25% im-
   provement in serum creatinine, which had to be met a 2 separate assessments at least 28 days
   apart. Median time to complete TMA response was 30 days (range, 15 to 88 days), and median
   duration of complete response was 08 months (range, 08 to 54 months) Paroxysmal Nocturnal Hemoglobinuria

   In an unblinded study of pediatric patients 9 to 17 years old with paroxysmal nocturnal
   hemoglobinuria (PNH) who were eculizumab experienced (n=8) or complement inhibitor naïve
   (n=5), the percent change from baseline in LDH was nonsignificant in the treatment naïve
   group -47.9% (95% CI, -113.4% to 5%) and in the experienced group 7% (95% CI, -36.7% to
   46%). There was a significant change in transfusion avoidance in both the eculizumab experi-

 enced group (60%; 95% CI, 7% to 7%) and naïve group (100%; 95% CI, 1% to 100%)
   and in hemoglobin stabilization for experienced 60% (95% CI, 7% to 7%) and naïve 75%
   (95% CI, 9% to 8%); change in FACIT-Fatigue was nonsignificant from baseline in both
   groups FDA Approved Pediatric Indication

   • Ravulizumab-cwvz is indicated to treat adults and pediatric patients 1 month or older with
   atypical hemolytic uremic syndrome (aHUS) to inhibit complement-mediated thrombotic mi-
   croangiopathy (TMA). • Ravulizumab-cwvz is indicated for the treatment of adult and pediatric patients 1 month or
   older with paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria (PNH) Limitations of Use: Ravulizumab-cwvz is not indicated to treat patients with Shiga toxin
   Escherichia coli-related hemolytic uremic syndrome (STEC-HUS) Administration

drugs.contraindications_raw:
Common, pediatric, atypical hemolytic uremic syndrome (aHUS): Pyrexia (50%), upper res-
   piratory tract infection (44%), diarrhea (38%), headache (31%), constipation (25%), vomiting
   (25%), hypertension (25%) 1
   Common, pediatric, paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria (PNH): Upper respiratory tract
   infection (54%), anemia (23%), abdominal pain (23%), and headache (23%) 1

   Black Box Warning
   Warning: Serious Meningococcal Infections

   Life-threatening meningococcal infections/sepsis have occurred in patients treated with
   ravulizumab-cwvz. Meningococcal infection may become rapidly life-threatening or fatal if not
   recognized and treated early.
    ●   Comply with the most current Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices (ACIP) recom-
        mendations for meningococcal vaccination in patients with complement deficiencies.
    ●   Immunize patients with meningococcal vaccines at least 2 weeks prior to administering the
        first dose of ravulizumab-cwvz, unless the risks of delaying ravulizumab-cwvz therapy out-
        weigh the risk of developing a meningococcal infection.
    ●   Vaccination reduces, but does not eliminate, the risk of meningococcal infection. Monitor
        patients for early signs of meningococcal infections and evaluate immediately if infection is
        suspected.
   Because of the risk of serious meningococcal infections, ravulizumab-cwvz is available only
   through a restricted program under a Risk Evaluation and Mitigation Strategy (REMS) called
   Ultomiris REMS Monitoring

 Toxic Laboratory Parameters
   • Monitor closely for early signs of meningococcal infection and evaluate patients immediately
   if infection is suspected • Monitor closely for signs of worsening infection in patients with active systemic infection • Monitor closely following discontinuation of therapy for at least 12 months for signs of
   thrombotic microangiopathy complications, including platelet count decrease of 25% or more
   compared to baseline or peak count during treatment, and serum creatinine or LDH increase
   of 25% or more compared to baseline or nadir during treatment Toxic Physical Exam
   • Monitor closely for early symptoms of meningococcal infection and evaluate patients imme-
   diately if infection is suspected • Monitor closely for symptoms of worsening infection in patients with active systemic infec-
   tion • Monitor closely following discontinuation of therapy for at least 12 months for signs of
   thrombotic microangiopathy complications, including changes in mental status, seizures,
   angina, dyspnea, thrombosis, or increasing blood pressure • Monitor for signs and symptoms of infusion-related reactions for at least 1 hour following
   completion of the injection

   without meningitis. For cutaneous anthrax, antitoxin use is only recommended when antimi-
   crobial agents are not available or not appropriate. Raxibacumab and obiltoxaximab are pre-
   ferred, and anthrax immune globulin is an alternative. Raxibacumab and obiltoxaximab may
   also be used for postexposure prophylaxis when antimicrobial agents are not available or not
   appropriate 1

   FDA Approve

Anthrax: Anthrax antitoxins are recommended for all patients with systemic anthrax, with or
   without meningitis. For cutaneous anthrax, antitoxin use is only recommended when antimi-
   crobial agents are not available or not appropriate. Raxibacumab and obiltoxaximab are pre-
   ferred, and anthrax immune globulin is an alternative. Raxibacumab and obiltoxaximab may
   also be used for postexposure prophylaxis when antimicrobial agents are not available or not
   appropriate 1

   FDA Approved Pediatric Uses
   Raxibacumab is indicated for the treatment inhalational anthrax due to Bacillus anthracis, in
   combination with appropriate antibacterial drugs. It is also indicated for prophylaxis of inhala-
   tional anthrax when alternative therapies are not available or are not appropriate 2

   Limitations of Use
   • The effectiveness of raxibacumab is based solely on efficacy studies in animal models, as
   controlled clinical trials with intentional exposure of humans to inhalational anthrax are not
   ethical or feasible 2
   • Safety and pharmacokinetics (PK) of raxibacumab have been studied in adult healthy volun-
   teers. There have been no trials of safety or PK of raxibacumab in the pediatric population. An
   extrapolation approach was used to derive dosing regimens that are predicted to provide pe-
   diatric patients with exposure comparable to the observed exposure in adults 2
   • Raxibacumab binds to the protective antigen of Bacillus anthracis. It does not cross the
   blood-brain barrier, and does not prevent or treat meningitis. Raxibacumab should be used in
   combination with appropriate antibacterial drugs 2
