drugs.uses_raw:
COVID-19:

   Non-hospitalized patients: In a randomized double-blind trial in non-hospitalized patients
   (pediatric patients 12 years or older, n=8) with mild-to-moderate COVID-19 with at least 1 risk
   factor for progression to hospitalization (N=562), 3 days of remdesivir treatment was associ-
   ated with a significantly lower rate of COVID-19-related hospitalization/all-cause mortality com-
   pared with placebo. The composite endpoint of COVID-19-related hospitalization/all-cause
   mortality through day 28 occurred in 7% of those in the remdesivir group compared with 3% in the placebo group for a HR of 134 (95% CI, 031 to 586); hospitalization was de-
   fined as at least 24 hours of acute care. No deaths were observed in either group through day
   28 • Per National Institutes of Health guidelines, remdesivir is suggested as an alternative option
   for the treatment of COVID-19 in adults who are not hospitalized who are at high risk of pro-
   gression to severe COVID-19; nirmatrelvir/ritonavir is the preferred treatment in this popula-
   tion 5
   Hospitalized patients: In a randomized, open-label trial in patients aged 12 years or older
   hospitalized with severe COVID-19 (N=397), 5- or 10-day courses of remdesivir were similar
   with regard to clinical improvement at 14 days compared with baseline (using a 7-point ordinal
   scale), after adjustment for baseline clinical status. The median age (interquartile range) at
   baseline was 61 (50 to 69) and 62 (50 to 71) years in the 5-day and 10-day groups. No further
   details were provided on age of adolescent patients in the study. Baseline clinical status of pa-

 tients in the 10-day group was significantly worse compared with those in the 5-day group;
   35% had a score of 2 or 3 in the 10-day group, while 26% had a score of 2 or 3 in the 5-day
   group (see details about scores below). In the 5-day group, 86% of patients completed the full
   5-day course of remdesivir therapy while 44% of patients in the 10-day course completed the
   full course; treatment course was not completed due to discharge from hospital (8% for 5-day
   and 35% for 10-day), adverse events (4% for 5-day and 11% for 10-day), or death (0% for 5-day
   and 6% for 10-day). In patients who had 5 days of remdesivir treatment, 65% had clinical im-
   provement of at least 2 points at day 14, while 54% of those who received 10 days of treat-
   ment had improved scores of at least 2 points; the distribution of clinical status scores were
   similar at day 14 between groups. At day 14, observed rates between the 5- and 10-day treat-
   ment groups were 70% vs 59% for modified clinical recovery, and 8% vs 11% for mortality.
   Remdesivir dosage was 200 mg IV on day 1 and 100 mg IV daily for the subsequent 4 or 9 days,
   depending on the assigned treatment group. A total of 5% and 6% of patients discontinued
   remdesivir treatment due to aminotransferase elevations in the 5-day and 10-day groups In
   a phase 2/3 open-label trial in hospitalized pediatric patients aged at least 28 days and weigh-
   ing at least 3 kg with confirmed SARS-CoV-2 infection and mild to severe COVID-19 (N=53),
   treatment with up to 10 days of remdesivir was associated with improvement in clinical status
   compared with baseline; this result is descriptive only as this was primarily a pharmacokinetic
   and safety trial • Per National Institutes of Health guidelines, remdesivir is suggested for use in the treatment
   of COVID-19 in patients who are hospitalized and require minimal supplemental oxygen.
   Consider addition of dexamethasone to remdesivir therapy with increasing oxygen require-
   ments (eg, high-flow device or noninvasive ventilation). Do not use remdesivir as monotherapy
   in patients who have recently been intubated; consider remdesivir plus dexamethasone in this
   population 5

   COVID-19 Infection - HIV Co-infection Guidelines

   Outpatient setting: Remdesivir may be considered in the outpatient setting for treatment of
   laboratory-confirmed or clinically suspected mild to moderate COVID-19 in children with HIV
   28 days or older and weighing at least 3 kg who are at high risk of progressing to severe
   COVID-19 due to advanced or untreated HIV, or another high risk condition defined by the
   CDC. It should be initiated within 7 days of symptom onset, but may be considered in those se-
   verely immunosuppressed with more than 7 days of symptoms. For pediatric patients 12 years
   or older, nirmatrelvir/ritonavir is the preferred treatment option, but remdesivir may be con-
   sidered if nirmatrelvir/ritonavir is unavailable or contraindicated Inpatient setting: Remdesivir should be considered in the inpatient setting for treatment of
   laboratory-confirmed or clinically suspected mild to moderate COVID-19 in children with HIV
   28 days or older and weighing at least 3 kg who are receiving supplemental oxygen. It should

 be administered to pediatric patients who are severely or critically ill, have a rapidly increasing
   oxygen requirement, and/or are at high risk of progressing to severe COVID-19 due to ad-
   vanced or untreated HIV or another high-risk condition as defined by CDC. It should be initi-
   ated within 7 days of symptom onset, but may be considered in those severely immunosup-
   pressed with more than 7 days of symptoms FDA Approved Pediatric Indication

   Remdesivir is indicated in pediatric patients (from birth and at least 5 kg) who are hospital-
   ized, or who are not hospitalized and have mild-to-moderate COVID-19 and are at high risk for
   progression to severe COVID-19 (including hospitalization or death) Remdesivir may only be administered in settings in which healthcare providers have immedi-
   ate access to medications to treat a severe infusion or hypersensitivity reaction, such as ana-
   phylaxis, and the ability to activate the emergency medical system (EMS), as necessary 3

   Administration
   • 5 kg to less than 40 kg: Infuse over 30 to 120 minutes; calculate infusion rate based on to-
   tal infusion volume and infusion time • 40 kg or greater; infusion volume 250 mL: Infuse over 30 minutes (rate of 33 mL/min), 60
   minutes (rate of 17 mL/min), or 120 minutes (2.08 mL/min) • 40 kg or greater, infusion volume 100 mL: Infuse over 30 minutes (rate of 33 mL/min), 60
   minutes (rate of 67 mL/min), or 120 minutes (0.83 mL/min) • Remdesivir may only be administered in settings in which healthcare providers have immedi-
   ate access to medications to treat a severe infusion or hypersensitivity reaction, such as ana-
   phylaxis, and the ability to activate the emergency medical system (EMS), as necessary • Administer by intravenous infusion only. Do not administer by any other route • Administer immediately after preparation when possible • Do not administer simultaneously with any other medication as IV compatibility with other
   solutions is unknown Preparation

   • Remdesivir powder for injection must be reconstituted with Sterile Water for Injection, then
   further diluted with NS 4/10
 • Reconstitute the vial by adding 19 mL sterile water for injection to vial; shake for 30 seconds
   and allow to settle for 2 to 3 minutes, repeating as necessary until complete dissolution. The
   resulting solution contains 5 mg/mL. Further dilute with NS according to the patient's weight,
   as detailed below 1.5 kg to less than 40 kg.
   • Further dilute reconstituted solution with NS to a final concentration of 25 mg/mL; gently
   invert 20 times to mix (do not shake). Use a syringe pump for infusion volumes less than 50
   mL • If using a prefilled NS IV bag for infusion, withdraw and discard the amount of diluent equal
   to the volume of reconstituted solution needed plus a quantity sufficient to achieve a 25
   mg/mL final volume concentration of remdesivir diluted solution, then withdraw the required
   volume of reconstituted remdesivir solution into an appropriately sized syringe and transfer to
   the infusion bag; invert the bag 20 times to mix (do not shake) • If using an empty infusion bag for infusion, transfer the required volume of reconstituted
   remdesivir solution to the bag, followed by a volume of NS sufficient to achieve a 25 mg/mL
   final volume concentration of remdesivir diluted solution • If using a syringe for infusion, select an appropriately sized syringe equal to or larger than the
   calculated total infusion volume of 25 mg/mL remdesivir solution needed and withdraw the
   required volume of reconstituted remdesivir solution from the vial into the syringe based on
   patient’s calculated dose, followed by the required volume of NS needed to achieve a 25
   mg/mL final volume concentration of remdesivir diluted solution; invert syringe 20 times to
   mix (do not shake) and use immediately 40 kg or greater:

   • For a 200-mg dose (2 vials), withdraw 40 mL of NS from a 100-mL or 250-mL infusion bag and
   discard; transfer the reconstituted remdesivir solution (2 x 20 mL) into the infusion bag. For a
   100-mg dose (1 vial), withdraw 20 mL of NS from a 100-mL or 250-mL infusion bag and discard;
   transfer the reconstituted remdesivir solution (20 mL) into the infusion bag. Gently invert 20
   times to mix (do not shake) • After dilution, the prepared solution may be stored at a room temperature between 20 and
   25° (68 and 77° F) for up to 24 hours or refrigerated between 2 and 8° C (36 and 46° F) for up
   to 48 hours. Discard unused portion and do not reuse or save diluted solution for future use

   Remifentanil hydrochloride is a mu-opioid agonist exhibiting analgesic effects with a rapid on-
   set and a short duration of action. Unlike fentanyl, duration of action does not increase with

   state Vd of 350 mL/kg. Rapid and slow distribution half-life are 1 and 6 minutes, respectively.

drugs.contraindications_raw:
Oral ribavirin in combination with pegylated or non-pegylated interferon alfa: The most
   common adverse events in pediatric patients treated with combination therapy during clinical
   trials (n=221) were influenza-like illness (91%), fever (80%), headache (51% to 62%), abdominal
   pain (12% to 21%), nausea/vomiting (18% to 27%), anorexia/loss of appetite (11% to 29%), fa-
   tigue (25% to 30%), injection-site reactions (29% to 44%), neutropenia (33%), and muscu-
   loskeletal pain (17% to 35%) 4 ,1 .
   When combined with either peginterferon alfa-2a or alfa-2b for the treatment of CHC in chil-
   dren, hematologic effects such as leukopenia (52%), neutropenia (32%), anemia (11%), and
   thrombocytopenia (5%) were reported in a meta-analysis of 8 clinical trials Inhalation/nebulization: No common adverse effects were reported during clinical trials in
   infants who received ribavirin. Rash and conjunctivitis, which resolved within hours of discon-
   tinuation of therapy, have been associated with aerosolized ribavirin. Serious events in infants
   include worsening of respiratory status, bronchospasm, pulmonary edema, hypoventilation,
   cyanosis, dyspnea, bacterial pneumonia, pneumothorax, apnea, atelectasis, ventilator depen-
   dence, cardiac arrest, hypotension, bradycardia and digitalis toxicity. In patients with coexist-
   ing congenital heart disease, bigeminy, bradycardia, and tachycardia have been reported.
   Among direct caregivers who reported adverse effects in postmarketing surveillance (total
   events=350), the most common events were headache (51%), conjunctivitis (32%), and rhinitis,
   nausea, rash, dizziness, pharyngitis or lacrimation (10% to 20% each). Black Box Warning
   Oral Capsule, Tablet, and Solution
   Ribavirin is not effective for monotherapy treatment of chronic hepatitis C virus infection. The
   primary toxicity is hemolytic anemia, which may result in worsening of cardiac disease and fa-
   tal and nonfatal myocardial infarctions. Avoid use in patients with significant or unstable car-
   diac disease. Significant teratogenic and/or embryocidal effects have been demonstrated in all
   animal species exposed to ribavirin. Ribavirin is contraindicated in women who are pregnant
   and in male partners of women who are pregnant. Use 2 reliable forms of contraception and
   avoid pregnancy during therapy and for 6 months after completion of treatment in both fe-
   male patients and in female partners of male patients who are taking ribavirin 4 ,1 .

   Inhalation/Nebulization Solution

   Use in patients requiring mechanical ventilator assistance should be undertaken only by physi-
   cians and support staff familiar with the specific ventilator being used and this mode of drug
   administration. Strict attention must be paid to procedures that have been shown to minimize
   the accumulation of drug precipitate, which can result in mechanical ventilator dysfunction

 and associated increased pulmonary pressures. Use caution when administering aerosolized
   ribavirin to patients requiring mechanical ventilator assistance. Sudden deterioration of respi-
   ratory function has been associated with initiation of aerosolized ribavirin in infants. Monitor
   respiratory function during treatment. Discontinue use if sudden deterioration of respiratory
   function occurs and only reinitiate with extreme caution. Inhalation/nebulization ribavirin is
   not indicated for use in adults. Ribavirin has been shown to produce testicular lesions in ro-
   dents and to be teratogenic in all animal species in which adequate studies have been con-
   ducted (rodents and rabbits) Monitoring
   Oral Capsule, Tablet, and Solution
   Patients with chronic hepatic C should be seen monthly for the first 12 weeks of therapy, fol-
   lowed by visits at 8 to 12 weeks intervals thereafter until the end of therapy. Side effects, medi-
   cation adherence and possible depression should be assessed at each visit. Lab monitoring
   should include CBC, serum creatinine, ALT, and HCV RNA at baseline, and then at weeks 4, 12
   and 24 weeks, and then at 4 to 12 week intervals thereafter until end of therapy. Labs should
   be repeated again at 24 weeks following completion of therapy. Thyroid function should moni-
   tored every 12 weeks during therapy. Patients who achieve a sustained viral response, but
   have cirrhosis, should continue to be monitored periodically, including screening for hepato-
   cellular carcinoma 4 ,1 ,5 .

   In female patients of childbearing potential, exclude pregnancy prior to treatment initiation
   and on a monthly basis during and for 6 months after therapy discontinuation 1 , Perform an ECG in patients with preexisting heart disease 1 ,4 . Perform an eye examination at
   baseline in all patients, and periodically during therapy in patients with preexisting ophthalmo-
   logic disorders. Regular dental examinations should be performed Inhalation/nebulization Solution
   Monitor respiratory function and fluid status carefully. Monitor pulmonary pressures every 2
   to 4 hours in infants requiring mechanical ventilation. In infants receiving ventilation, an in-
   crease in expiratory pressures can occur if the flow through the aerosol generator is not ad-
   justed properly, if the expiratory valve is not frequently cleaned, and if one-way valves and fil-
   ters are not used with ventilator lines. Continuously monitor aerosol therapy to prevent these
   complications

   Mechanism of Action

 Riboflavin 5'-phosphate sodium is the precursor of two coenzymes, flavin adenine dinucleotide
   and flavin mononucleotide, which catalyze oxidation and reduction reactions in a number of
   metabolic pathways. When used for corneal collagen cross-linking, riboflavin 5'-phosphate

drugs.contraindications_raw:
Common adverse events reported in pediatric patients include neutropenia, leukopenia, gas-
   trointestinal complaints, and rash. Corneal deposits, not affecting vision, have also been re-
   ported Monitoring
   Therapeutic Monitoring, TB
   • Obtain acid-fast bacilli (AFB) smear and culture from sputum at least monthly until 2 consecu-
   tive culture specimens are negative. In patients with positive AFB smears upon diagnosis, ob-
   tain follow-up smears more frequently (eg, every 2 weeks until two consecutive specimens are
   negative) • Perform chest x-rays after 2 to 3 months of treatment in patients with negative initial cultures
   and at end of treatment. In patients with positive cultures at diagnosis, repeat chest x-rays af-
   ter 2 months of treatment and at completion of treatment are useful but not required. Toxic Monitoring

   •Monitor hematologic tests periodically during therapy 13 , 7
   •Carefully monitor patients with severe renal impairment for rifabutin-associated adverse ef-
   fects 13
   •Closely monitor patients for signs and symptoms of uveitis, especially with coadministration
   of macrolide antibiotics or fluconazole and related compounds •Monitor for signs or symptoms of hypersensitivity reaction •Routine ophthalmic examinations are recommended 14,15

   Therapeutic Drug Monitoring, TB

   Consider monitoring TB regimen drug levels in the following situations 3 :

 • Poor response despite adherence and susceptibility

   • Severe GI abnormalities such as short bowel syndrome, chronic diarrhea with malabsorption,
   severe gastroparesis
   • Drug-drug interactions

   • Impaired renal clearance
   • HIV coinfection
   • Diabetes

   • Use of second-line drugs

drugs.uses_raw:
Treatment of all forms of tuberculosis (in combination with appropriate antitubercular agents) Treatment of asymptomatic carriers of N meningitidis to eliminate meningococci from the na-
   sopharynx Administration
   Intravenous: Administer by intermittent IV infusion over 30 minutes to 3 hours at a concen-
   tration not exceeding 6 mg/mL. Avoid extravasation during infusion Oral:

   • Administer either 1 hour before or 2 hours after a meal with a full glass of water • TB: Fixed-dose combination dosage forms are preferred when available to decrease pill bur-
   den 35,36
   • TB: Directly observed therapy (DOT) is generally recommended in all cases, especially with in-
   termittent (not daily) dosage regimens Preparation
   IV

 • Reconstitute 600-mg vial with 10 mL sterile water for injection and swirl gently to dissolve.
   Reconstituted 60 mg/mL solution is stable for up to 30 hours at room temperature 38
   • Further dilute by withdrawing a volume equivalent to the dose to be administered from the
   reconstituted vial and adding to D5W or NS, with a final concentration not to exceed 6 mg/mL.
   Mix well. Dilutions in D5W are stable for 8 hours at room temperature, and dilutions in NS are
   stable for 6 hours at room temperature. Precipitation may occur after these time frames Extemporaneous oral compounds

   25 mg/mL Suspension (120 mL) using Ora-Sweet, Ora-Plus, or cherry syrup 39
   • Empty ten 300-mg capsules OR twenty 150-mg capsules into a mortar.
   • Add 20 mL of vehicle to the powder and mix until a uniform paste has formed. Vehicle op-
   tions are a 1:1 mixture of Ora-Sweet and Ora-Plus, a 1:1 mixture of Ora-Sweet SF and Ora-
   Plus, or cherry syrup.
   • Continue to add vehicle in geometric portions until almost to volume; mix thoroughly after
   each addition.

   • Add the contents of the mortar to a prescription bottle. Rinse mortar with vehicle and trans-
   fer to container.
   • Add sufficient amount of vehicle to a final volume of 120 mL.
   • Label the container with "Shake well before using."
   • Stable for 28 days at room temperature or under refrigeration.

   25 mg/mL Suspension (200 mL) using SyrSpend SF 40
   • Add 5 grams rifampin powder to a 250 mL amber bottle.
   • Add 200 mL of SyrSpend SF to bottle while hand stirring to prevent bubbles from forming in
   the suspension.
   • Divide suspension into 2 bottles, each containing 100 mL.

   • Label the container with "Shake well before using."
   • Stable for 60 days at room temperature (18 to 26°C) or under refrigeration (2 to 8°C) and pro-
   tected from light.

   A 10 mg/mL rifAMPin oral suspension can be prepared in a similar fashion to the 25 mg/mL
   suspension, with the following vehicle options: Syrup NF, Simple syrup (Humco™), fruit fla-
   vored syrup (Syrpalta®, Emerson), raspberry syrup (Humco™. Stable for 4 weeks at room tem-
   perature or under refrigeration 29/41

   RifAMPin diluted to 33 mg/mL:
   Vancomycin (40 mg/mL).
   RifAMPin diluted to 6 mg/mL:

   Amiodarone (12.5 mg/mL), amoxicillin/clavulanate (10/2 mg/mL), bumetanide (0.5 mg/mL), mi-
   dazolam (0.1 mg/mL), pantoprazole (8 mg/mL), and vancomycin (40 mg/mL).

   Terminal Injection Site Incompatibility
   Diltiazem and tramadol.

   Monitoring
   Therapeutic Monitoring, TB
   • Obtain acid-fast bacilli (AFB) smear and culture from sputum at least monthly until 2 consecu-
   tive culture specimens are negative. In patients with positive AFB smears upon diagnosis, ob-
   tain follow-up smears more frequently (eg, every 2 weeks until two consecutive specimens are
   negative) • Perform chest x-rays after 2 to 3 months of treatment in patients with negative initial cultures
   and at end of treatment. In patients with positive cultures at diagnosis, repeat chest x-rays af-
   ter 2 months of treatment and at completion of treatment are useful but not required. Toxic Laboratory Monitoring

   •Monitor liver function tests, especially ALT and AST levels, prior to starting therapy; continue
   follow-up monitoring every 2 to 4 weeks during therapy in patients with impaired liver function
   or receiving other hepatotoxic drugs 32/41
 •Evaluate a bilirubin level, serum creatinine level, and a CBC panel (including a platelet count)
   prior to starting therapy and continue follow-up monitoring in patients who have laboratory
   abnormalities. Pediatric patients do not require baseline testing unless there is a known or
   suspected complicating condition •Monitor coagulation tests (prothrombin time and other coagulation tests) in patients at risk of
   vitamin K deficiency (eg, those with chronic liver disease, poor nutritional status, on prolonged
   antibacterial drugs or anticoagulants) •If concomitant use of rifampin and cefazolin cannot be avoided in patients who have an in-
   creased risk of bleeding, closely monitor prothrombin time and other coagulation tests as clini-
   cally indicated Toxic Physical Monitoring
   •Monitor for signs or symptoms of hypersensitivity reactions (eg, fever, rash, urticaria, an-
   gioedema, hypotension, acute bronchospasm, conjunctivitis, thrombocytopenia, neutropenia,
   elevated liver transaminases, or flulike syndrome) 47,48 .
   •Monitor for symptoms and clinical signs of liver injury, especially with prolonged use or con-
   comitant use of other hepatotoxic agents 49,50 .

   •Cytochrome P450 inducer which may decrease serum levels of certain drugs; monitor for pos-
   sible drug interactions 28

   Therapeutic Drug Monitoring, TB
   Peak adult rifAMPin concentration target is at least 8 mcg/mL in adults when measured 2
   hours after a dose of isoniazid Consider monitoring TB regimen drug levels in the following situations 33 :

   • Poor response despite adherence and susceptibility
   • Severe GI abnormalities such as short bowel syndrome, chronic diarrhea with malabsorption,
   severe gastroparesis
   • Drug-drug interactions
   • Impaired renal clearance
   • HIV coinfection
   • Diabetes
   • Use of second-line drugs

      (a) If ART is initiated soon after HIV diagnosis and entry into care, repeat baseline labora-
      tory testing is not necessary.
      (b) ART is indicated for all people with HIV and should be started as soon as possible.
      However, if ART initiation is delayed, patients should be retained in care, with periodic
      monitoring as noted above.
      (c) After 2 years of consistently suppressed HIV RNA, less frequent monitoring (eg, every 6
      months) may be considered.
      (d) After 2 years of ART with consistently suppressed viral load: CD4 count 300 to 500
      cells/mm(3), monitor every 12 months; CD4 count greater than 500 cells/mm(3), CD4 mon-
      itoring is optional.
      (e) If HIV RNA is detectable at 4 to 8 weeks, repeat every 4 to 8 weeks until viral load is
      suppressed to less than 50 copies/mL, then every 3 to 6 months.
      (f) For patients on ART, viral load is typically measured every 3 to 6 months. More frequent
      monitoring may be considered in individuals having difficulties with ART adherence or at
      risk for nonadherence. However, for adherent patients with suppressed viral load and sta-
      ble immunological status for more than 1 year, monitoring can be extended to 6-month
      intervals.
      (g) Standard genotypic drug-resistance testing in ARV-naïve persons should focus on test-
      ing for mutations in the PR and RT genes. If transmitted INSTI resistance is a concern, or if
      a person has a history of INSTI use as PrEP or treatment, or a person presents with
      viremia while on an INSTI, providers should also test for resistance mutations in the IN
      gene. In ARV-naïve patients who do not immediately begin ART, repeat testing before initi-
      ation of ART is optional if drug-resistance testing was performed at entry into care. For vi-
      rologically suppressed patients who are switching therapy for toxicity or convenience, viral
      amplification will not be possible and therefore resistance testing should not be per-
      formed. Results from prior resistance testing can be used to help in the construction of a
      new regimen.
      (h) If infected with hepatitis B virus, tenofovir disoproxil fumarate or tenofovir alafe-
      namide plus either emtricitabine or lamivudine should be used as part of the ART regimen
      to treat both hepatitis B virus and HIV infections.
      (i) If HBsAg, and HBsAb, and HBcAb are negative at baseline, administer hepatitis B vac-
      cine series. Also, consult Guidelines for Opportunistic Infections.
      (j) Typically HBV infection has resolved with loss of HBsAb despite isolated HBcAb; confirm
      with an HBV viral load if wanted. A positive HBV viral load is indicative of acute infection
      (other symptoms will be present usually) or chronic infection. Vaccinate the patient when
      viral load is negative. Also, consult Guidelines for Opportunistic Infections.

 (k) In patients with recent HCV infection (acquired in last 6 months) or advanced immun-
      odeficiency (CD4 count less than 100 cells/mm(3)), the HCV antibody test may not be ade-
      quate for screening. HCV RNA screening is indicated in persons who have been success-
      fully treated for HCV or who spontaneously cleared prior infection. HCV antibody-negative
      patients with elevated ALT may need HCV RNA testing.
      (l) At-risk populations: injection drug users, persons with a history of incarceration, men
      with HIV who have unprotected sex with men, and persons with percutaneous/parenteral
      exposure to blood in unregulated settings are at risk of HCV infection.
      (m) Serum sodium, potassium, bicarbonate, chloride, blood urea nitrogen, creatinine, glu-
      cose (preferably fasting). Monitor serum phosphorus concentrations in patients with
      chronic kidney disease who are on tenofovir-containing regimens. Renal function determi-
      nation should include creatinine monitoring and estimation of the glomerular filtration
      rate.
      (n) Consult recommendations of the HIV Medicine Association of the Infectious Diseases

   studies); although the absolute incidence rate of T2DM compared with all controls (3.09 cases
   (95% CI, 35 to 82) per 1000 patients-years) was small over the mean follow-up period of 7
   years (n=13 studies). Important differences among studies included may affect the validity of
   this finding. The majority of antipsychotic agents were second-generation agents (risperiDONE,
   QUEtiapine, ARIPiprazole, and OLANZapine) Black Box Warning
   There are serious risks, including profound sedation, respiratory depression, coma, and/or
   death, associated with combined use of opioids and benzodiazepines, other drugs that de-

   treatment. If necessary, use the lowest initial dose and titrate based on clinical response.

drugs.dosing_raw:
Critical Dosing Note
   • Screen patients for TB before starting therapy. Ritlecitinib should not be given to patients
   with active TB. For patients with latent TB or those with a negative latent TB test who are at
   high risk for TB, initiate preventive therapy for latent TB prior to initiation • Screen for viral hepatitis in accordance with clinical guidelines. Initiation is not recommended
   in patients with hepatitis B or hepatitis C • Perform absolute lymphocyte count (ALC) and platelet counts prior to initiation. Should not
   be initiated in patients with an ALC of less than 500/mm(3) or a platelet count of less than
   100,000/mm(3) • Update immunizations according to current immunization guidelines Alopecia areata, severe

   12 year or older: 50 mg orally once daily 1

   Interruption of treatment: If treatment interruption is indicated, a temporary treatment in-
   terruption for less than 6 weeks is not expected to result in significant loss of regrown scalp
   hair Dose Adjustment Title
   Renal Impairment
   No clinically significant differences were observed in patients with severe impairment (esti-
   mated GFR less than 30 mL/min); no studies were done for mild or moderate impairment as a
   clinically relevant increase in exposure is not expected Hepatic Impairment
   Mild (Child-Pugh A) or Moderate (Child-Pugh B) impairment: No dose adjustment is re-
   quired 1

   Severe (Child-Pugh C) impairment: Use not recommended 1
   Other Adjustments

 Aminotransferase (ALT and AST) elevations: Interrupt treatment if increases in ALT or AST
   are observed and a drug-induced injury is suspected, until this diagnosis is excluded Hypersensitivity reactions: Discontinue if a clinically significant reaction occurs Hematologic abnormalities, platelets: Discontinue if platelet count is less than 50,000/mm3.
   1

   Hematologic abnormalities, lymphocytes: Interrupt if absolute lymphocyte count (ALC) is
   less than 500/mm3. Treatment may be restarted once the ALC returns above this value Serious infection: Interrupt if a patient develops a serious or opportunistic infection; may be
   resumed once the infection is controlled Herpes zoster: Interrupt treatment if a patient develops herpes zoster, until the episode re-
   solves Major adverse cardiovascular events: Discontinue in patients that have experienced a my-
   ocardial infarction or stroke 1

   Thromboembolic events: Interrupt treatment if symptoms or thrombosis or embolism occur,
   evaluate promptly and treat appropriately

   Black Box Warning
   Warning: Serious Infections, Mortality, Malignancy, Major Adverse Cardiovascular
   Events (MACE) and Thrombosis

 Increased risk of serious bacterial, fungal, viral and opportunistic infections leading to hospital-
   ization or death, including tuberculosis (TB). Interrupt treatment if serious infection occurs un-
   til the infection is controlled. Ritlecitinib should not be given to patients with active tuberculo-
   sis. Test for latent TB before and during therapy; treat latent TB prior to use. Monitor all pa-
   tients for active TB during treatment, even patients with initial negative, latent TB test.

   Higher rate of all-cause mortality, including sudden cardiovascular death with another Janus ki-
   nase inhibitor (JAK) vs TNF blockers in rheumatoid arthritis (RA) patients. Ritlecitinib is not ap-
   proved for use in RA patients.

   Malignancies have occurred in patients treated with ritlecitinib. Higher rate of lymphomas and
   lung cancers with another JAK inhibitor vs TNF blockers in RA patients.

   Higher rate of MACE (defined as cardiovascular death, myocardial infarction, and stroke) with
   another JAK inhibitor vs. TNF blockers in RA patients.
   Thrombosis has occurred in patients treated with ritlecitinib. Increased incidence of pul-
   monary embolism, venous and arterial thrombosis with another JAK inhibitor vs. TNF blockers Monitoring
   Toxic Laboratory Monitoring
   • Prior to initiation screen for viral hepatitis in accordance with clinical guidelines prior to initi-
   ating and during therapy • Monitor patients for the development of signs and symptoms of infection during and after
   treatment • Prior to initiation preform absolute lymphocyte count and platelet count • Evaluate liver enzyme elevations at baseline and thereafter according to routine patients
   management Toxic Physical Monitoring

   • Monitor for signs and symptoms of infection during and after treatment • Evaluate for active and latent TB before treatment initiation and monitor for signs and symp-
   toms of active TB during treatment in high risk patients • Perform periodic skin examination in high risk patients of skin cancer • Prior to initiating or continuing therapy with Janus kinase (JAK) inhibitors, evaluate the bene-
   fits and risks of treatment in patients, especially who are current or past smokers, those with

 other cardiovascular risk factors, those who develop a malignancy, and those with a known
   malignancy other than a successfully treated nonmelanoma skin cancer • Evaluate the risks and benefits of treatment prior to initiating therapy in patients with chronic
   or recurrent infection, with a history of a serious or an opportunistic infection, who have been
   exposed to TB, who have resided or traveled in areas of endemic TB or endemic mycoses and
   in those with underlying conditions that may predispose them to infection. Carefully monitor
   patients during and after treatment for the signs and symptoms of infections • Prior to initiating or continuing therapy, evaluate the benefits and risks of major adverse car-
   diovascular events (MACE) defined as cardiovascular death, non-fatal myocardial infarction
   (MI), and non-fatal stroke, especially in patients who are current or past smokers, those with
   other cardiovascular risk factors, those who develop a malignancy, and those with a known

      Key: ART = antiretroviral therapy, ARV = Antiretroviral, AST = aspartate amino-
      transferase, ALT = alanine aminotransferase, BUN = blood urea nitrogen, CAB-LA
      = cabotegravir long-acting, CBC = complete blood count; DAA = direct-acting an-
      tiviral; HCV = hepatitis C virus, IN = integrase, INSTI = integrase strand transfer
      inhibitor, PrEP = pre-exposure prophylaxis

      (a) If ART is initiated soon after HIV diagnosis and entry into care, repeat baseline labora-
      tory testing is not necessary.
      (b) ART is indicated for all people with HIV and should be started as soon as possible.
      However, if ART initiation is delayed, patients should be retained in care, with periodic
      monitoring as noted above.
      (c) After 2 years of consistently suppressed HIV RNA, less frequent monitoring (eg, every 6
      months) may be considered.
      (d) After 2 years of ART with consistently suppressed viral load: CD4 count 300 to 500
      cells/mm(3), monitor every 12 months; CD4 count greater than 500 cells/mm(3), CD4 mon-
      itoring is optional.
      (e) If HIV RNA is detectable at 4 to 8 weeks, repeat every 4 to 8 weeks until viral load is
      suppressed to less than 50 copies/mL, then every 3 to 6 months.
      (f) For patients on ART, viral load is typically measured every 3 to 6 months. More frequent
      monitoring may be considered in individuals having difficulties with ART adherence or at
      risk for nonadherence. However, for adherent patients with suppressed viral load and sta-
      ble immunological status for more than 1 year, monitoring can be extended to 6-month
      intervals.
      (g) Standard genotypic drug-resistance testing in ARV-naïve persons should focus on test-
      ing for mutations in the PR and RT genes. If transmitted INSTI resistance is a concern, or if
      a person has a history of INSTI use as PrEP or treatment, or a person presents with
      viremia while on an INSTI, providers should also test for resistance mutations in the IN
      gene. In ARV-naïve patients who do not immediately begin ART, repeat testing before initi-
      ation of ART is optional if drug-resistance testing was performed at entry into care. For vi-
      rologically suppressed patients who are switching therapy for toxicity or convenience, viral
      amplification will not be possible and therefore resistance testing should not be per-
      formed. Results from prior resistance testing can be used to help in the construction of a

 new regimen.
      (h) If infected with hepatitis B virus, tenofovir disoproxil fumarate or tenofovir alafe-
      namide plus either emtricitabine or lamivudine should be used as part of the ART regimen
      to treat both hepatitis B virus and HIV infections.
      (i) If HBsAg, and HBsAb, and HBcAb are negative at baseline, administer hepatitis B vac-
      cine series. Also, consult Guidelines for Opportunistic Infections.
      (j) Typically HBV infection has resolved with loss of HBsAb despite isolated HBcAb; confirm
      with an HBV viral load if wanted. A positive HBV viral load is indicative of acute infection
      (other symptoms will be present usually) or chronic infection. Vaccinate the patient when
      viral load is negative. Also, consult Guidelines for Opportunistic Infections.
      (k) In patients with recent HCV infection (acquired in last 6 months) or advanced immun-
      odeficiency (CD4 count less than 100 cells/mm(3)), the HCV antibody test may not be ade-
      quate for screening. HCV RNA screening is indicated in persons who have been success-
      fully treated for HCV or who spontaneously cleared prior infection. HCV antibody-negative
      patients with elevated ALT may need HCV RNA testing.
      (l) At-risk populations: injection drug users, persons with a history of incarceration, men
      with HIV who have unprotected sex with men, and persons with percutaneous/parenteral
      exposure to blood in unregulated settings are at risk of HCV infection.
      (m) Serum sodium, potassium, bicarbonate, chloride, blood urea nitrogen, creatinine, glu-
      cose (preferably fasting). Monitor serum phosphorus concentrations in patients with
      chronic kidney disease who are on tenofovir-containing regimens. Renal function determi-
      nation should include creatinine monitoring and estimation of the glomerular filtration
      rate.
      (n) Consult recommendations of the HIV Medicine Association of the Infectious Diseases
      Society of America for patients with renal disease. More frequent monitoring may be indi-
      cated for patients with evidence of kidney disease (eg, proteinuria or decreased glomeru-
      lar function) or increased risk of renal insufficiency (eg. patients with diabetes or hyper-
      tension).
      (o) CBC with differential should be done when a CD4 count is performed. When CD4 count
      is no longer being monitored, the recommended frequency of CBC with differential is
      once a year. More frequent monitoring may be for patients receiving medications that po-
      tentially cause cytopenia (eg, trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole)
      (p) If random lipids are abnormal, fasting lipids should be obtained. Consult the ACA/AHA
      recommendations for diagnosis and management of patients with dyslipidemia.
      (q) If random glucose is abnormal, fasting glucose should be obtained. HgbA1C is not
      longer recommended for diagnosis of diabetes in patients with HIV on ART.
      (r) Assess urine glucose and protein before initiating tenofovir-containing regimens and
      monitor during treatment with these regimens.
      (s) In women with child-bearing potential.

   were used 2 ,3 ,4 ,5 ,6 ,7 .

   Induction: 375 mg/m2 IV infusion once weekly for 4 weeks 1
   Induction concomitant medication: MethylPREDNISolone 30 mg/kg (not to exceed 1 g/day)
   IV once daily for 3 days starting prior to the first rituximab infusion, then continue oral steroids
   per clinical practice 1
   Concomitant medication: Give Pneumocystis jiroveci pneumonia prophylaxis during riTUX-
   imab treatment and for at least 6 months following the last riTUXimab infusion 1

   Followup treatment (if disease is controlled following induction and a rituximab product
   was used for induction of active disease): 250 mg/m(2) IV within 24 weeks but no sooner
   than 16 weeks after last rituximab product induction infusion or based on clinical evaluation,
   then 250 mg/m(2) IV 2 weeks later, and 250 mg/m2 IV every 6 months thereafter as clinically
   indicated 1

   Infections: Eight (14.5%) pediatric patients with juvenile rheumatoid arthritis treated with riT-
   UXimab developed infections (adenoiditis (4), sinusitis (1), otitis (3), exacerbation of herpes in-
   fection (4), skin infection (6), and acute focal pneumonia (8)) Infusion-related reactions: When administered per manufacturer's recommendations 20 , in-

   tory problems, nausea, hypotension, and chills) occurred in 8% of pediatric patients. Most
   reactions occur with the first dose of a new cycle (39.2%), thereafter the reactions were less
   common (2.7%). Reactions were mild and associated with an elevated absolute lymphocyte
   count. Out of the 43 reactions, 27 required treatment with acetaminophen, diphenhydramine,
   and/or corticosteroids; 16 reactions required a short discontinuation of the infusion Severe Events: Severe neutropenia with absolute neutrophil count below 500/microliter (n=3)
   and acute focal pneumonia (n=8) occurred in patients treated with riTUXimab for juvenile idio-
   pathic arthritis (n=55) Black Box Warning
   Warning: Fatal Infusion-relate Reactions, Severe Mucocutaneous Reactions Hepatitis B Virus
   (HBV) Reactivation, and Progressive Multifocal Leukoencephalopathy

   RiTUXimab administration can result in serious, including fatal, infusion-related reactions.
   Deaths within 24 hours of riTUXimab infusion have occurred. Approximately 80% of fatal infu-
   sion reactions occurred in association with the first infusion. Monitor patients closely.
   Discontinue riTUXimab infusion for severe reactions and provide medical treatment for Grade
   3 or 4 infusion-related reactions.
   Severe, including fatal, mucocutaneous reactions can occur in patients receiving riTUXimab.

   HBV reactivation can occur in patients treated with riTUXimab, in some cases resulting in ful-
   minant hepatitis, hepatic failure, and death. Screen all patients for HBV infection before treat-
   ment initiation and monitor patients during and after treatment with riTUXimab. Discontinue
   riTUXimab and concomitant medications in the event of HBV reactivation.
   Progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy (PML), including fatal PML, can occur in patients
   receiving riTUXimab 1

drugs.uses_raw:
EINSTEIN Jr Trial

   The randomized EINSTEIN Jr trial compared rivaroxaban (n=355) with standard anticoagulants
   (n=165) for treatment of VTE in children 0 to 17 years old. Treatment duration was 3 months,
   except in children younger than 2 years with catheter-related VTE who had a treatment dura-
   tion of 1 month.
   Recurrent VTE: There was no significant difference in the incidence of symptomatic recurrent
   VTE with rivaroxaban versus standard anticoagulants (1% vs 3%; HR, 4; 95% CI, 11 to 41);
   however, due to the low incidence of VTE, a powered noninferiority study was not feasible.
   Non-catheter-related VTE developed in 4 patients in each study group, and cerebral vein and
   sinus thrombosis developed in 1 patient who received standard anticoagulation; there were no
   cases of catheter-related VTE or fatal VTE. Median follow-up was 91 days in patients with a
   treatment duration of 3 months (n=463) and 31 days with a treatment duration of 1 month

 (n=37). The composite of recurrent VTE and deterioration on repeat imaging was reported in
   1% with rivaroxaban and 4% with standard anticoagulation (HR, 41; 95% CI, 12 to 36).

   Bleeding events: Major or clinically relevant non-major bleeding was reported in 3% of the ri-
   varoxaban group and 2% of the standard anticoagulation group. There was no major bleeding
   in the rivaroxaban group, and 1 case of pulmonary bleeding and 1 case of intracranial bleeding
   in the standard anticoagulation group. Clinically relevant non-major bleeding was reported in
   3% versus 1%.

   Net clinical benefit: The composite of recurrent VTE or major bleeding was significantly reduced
   with rivaroxaban (1% vs 4%; HR, 3; 95% CI, 08 to 93).
   Dosing protocols: Children were randomized to rivaroxaban or standard anticoagulants after 5
   to 9 days of anticoagulation with unfractionated heparin, low molecular weight heparin, or
   fondaparinux. Rivaroxaban dosing was weight-based to match an equivalent exposure in
   adults of 20 mg once daily; rivaroxaban tablet or suspension was administered 1, 2, or 3 times
   daily. The standard anticoagulation group continued heparin or switched to a vitamin K antag-
   onist EINSTEIN Jr CVT Trial

   In a substudy of the EINSTEIN-Jr phase 3 trial, an analysis of the safety and efficacy of rivaroxa-
   ban and standard anticoagulants was performed in a predetermined subgroup of 114 children
   who presented with cerebral venous thrombosis. The study treatment period was 3 months.

   Recurrent VTE: None of the rivaroxaban recipients and 1 of the standard anticoagulant recipi-
   ents had symptomatic recurrent VTE after 3 months (absolute risk difference, 4%; 95% CI -2.6
   to 5).
   Bleeding events: Major or clinically relevant non-major bleeding occurred in 8% of the rivarox-
   aban recipients and 5% of the standard anticoagulation recipients (absolute risk difference in
   favor of standard anticoagulation 4%; 95% CI -6.7 to 4). There was no major bleeding in
   the rivaroxaban group, and 1 case of intracranial bleeding occurred in the standard anticoagu-
   lation group.

   Sinus recanalization: Complete recanalization occurred in 25% of rivaroxaban recipients and in
   15% of standard anticoagulation recipients (OR, 63; 95% CI 78 to 41). Incomplete recanal-
   ization occurred in 53% and 59%, respectively.
   Net clinical benefit: Children with central venous thrombosis treated with rivaroxaban or stan-
   dard anticoagulation had a low risk of recurrent VTE and clinically relevant bleeding.

   Dosing protocols: Children were randomized to rivaroxaban or standard anticoagulants after 5
   to 9 days of anticoagulation with unfractionated heparin, low molecular weight heparin, or
   fondaparinux. Rivaroxaban dosing was weight-based to match an equivalent exposure in

 adults of 20 mg once daily and was administered as either a tablet or suspension 1, 2, or 3
   times daily depending on patient weight. The standard anticoagulation group continued hep-
   arin or switched to a vitamin K antagonist UNIVERSE Trial

   In the randomized part B of the UNIVERSE study, patients 2 to 8 years old with single-ventricle
   congenital heart disease who had an initial Fontan procedure within 4 months were random-
   ized to rivaroxaban oral suspension (n=66) or aspirin (n=34) for 12 months. Thrombotic and
   bleeding events were adjudicated by an independent committee.

   Thrombotic events: A thrombotic event was reported in 2% of patients with rivaroxaban and 9%
   of patients with aspirin. With rivaroxaban, the thrombotic event was pulmonary embolism.
   With aspirin, thrombotic events were ischemic stroke (n=1) and VTE (n=2). The study was not
   powered to detect a difference in thrombotic events.

   Bleeding events: Major bleeding events occurred in 1 patient (2%) with rivaroxaban and 0% with
   aspirin; the single event of major bleeding with rivaroxaban was epistaxis that required a
   blood transfusion. Clinically relevant nonmajor bleeding was reported in 6% versus 9%, and
   trivial bleeding in 33% versus 35%.

   Adverse events: Adverse events were reported in 86% with rivaroxaban and 85% with aspirin;
   serious adverse events were reported in 28% and 24%, respectively.

   Dosing protocols: Rivaroxaban oral suspension dosing was weight-based to match equivalent
   exposure in adults receiving 10 mg once daily for thromboprophylaxis and was administered
   orally or through NG tube twice daily. Aspirin dosage was approximately 5 mg/kg once daily FDA approved uses: Rivaroxaban is indicated to treat VTE and reduce the risk of recurrent VTE
   in pediatric patients from birth to less than 18 years after at least 5 days of initial parenteral
   anticoagulant treatment, and is also indicated for thromboprophylaxis in pediatric patients 2
   years or older with congenital heart disease who have undergone the Fontan procedure Administration
   VTE treatment and risk reduction of recurrent VTE:

   • Take with food or feedings Post-Fontan procedure thromboprophylaxis:

   • Take with or without food or feedings Vomit or spit up of dose:

 • If the patient vomits or spits up within 30 minutes after a dose, give a new dose. If the pa-
   tients vomits more than 30 minutes after a dose, do not readminister and give next dose as
   scheduled. If repeated vomit or spit up occurs, the caregiver should contact the healthcare
   provider Oral suspension:
   • For children unable to swallow 10-, 15-, or 20-mg whole tablets, the oral suspension should
   be used • May be administered through NG or gastric feeding tube. Flush the feeding tube with water
   after administration Tablets:

   • Rivaroxaban 5 mg tablets are not recommended for pediatric patients. Do not split
   tablets in an attempt to provide a fraction of a dose • Crush tablets (any strength) and suspend in 50 mL of water; crushed tablets are stable in wa-

   Black Box Warning
   Premature Discontinuation of Rivaroxaban Increases the Risk of Thrombotic Events
   Premature discontinuation of any oral anticoagulant, including rivaroxaban, increases the risk
   of thrombotic events. If anticoagulation with rivaroxaban is discontinued for a reason other
   than pathological bleeding or completion of a course of therapy, consider coverage with an-
   other anticoagulant Spinal/Epidural Hematoma

   Epidural or spinal hematomas have occurred in patients treated with rivaroxaban who are re-
   ceiving neuraxial anesthesia or undergoing spinal puncture. These hematomas may result in
   long-term or permanent paralysis. Consider these risks when scheduling patients for spinal
   procedures. Factors that can increase the risk of developing epidural or spinal hematomas in
   these patients include:
    ●   Use of indwelling epidural catheters
    ●   Concomitant use of other drugs that affect hemostasis, such as nonsteroidal antiinflamma-
        tory drugs (NSAIDs), platelet inhibitors, other anticoagulants
    ●   A history of traumatic or repeated epidural or spinal punctures
    ●   A history of spinal deformity or spinal surgery
    ●   Optimal timing between the administration of rivaroxaban and neuraxial procedures is not
        known.

   Monitor patients frequently for signs and symptoms of neurological impairment. If neurologi-
   cal compromise is noted, urgent treatment is necessary

 Consider the benefits and risks before neuraxial intervention in patients anticoagulated or to
   be anticoagulated for thromboprophylaxis Monitoring
   Coagulation Tests

   • Monitoring the anticoagulation effect of rivaroxaban using a clotting test (prothrombin time,
   INR or activated partial thromboplastin time) or anti-factor Xa activity is not recommended • Routine monitoring is not required. Coagulation test monitoring may be performed to ensure
   efficacy in those with a history of nonadherence, drug interactions, assess bleeding potential
   (renal failure, overdose), and to assist in drug-selection decisions • If necessary, chromogenic anti-FXa assay is the preferred method for quantitative assess-
   ment 7 ,8 ,9 . It is a precise, sensitive, and accurate test with a concentration-dependent inhibi-
   tion of FXa activity. However, it must be calibrated for a specific anticoagulant and cannot be
   used to assess the anticoagulation effect of other agents not previously calibrated. Low and
   high plasma concentrations can be measured with acceptable interlaboratory precision.
   Trough range for rivaroxaban was 6 to 239 mcg/mL. In the absence of a calibrated test, a stan-
   dard chromogenic anti-FXa assay calibrated to unfractionated or low molecular weight hep-
   arins may be used for qualitative assessment to measure the presence or absence of anticoag-
   ulant effect Drug Levels
   • Plasma concentrations of rivaroxaban can be measured using liquid chromatography-tan-
   dem mass spectrometry. At steady state the mean peak and trough concentrations for rivarox-
   aban 20 mg/day was 274 and 129 nanograms/mL The Biophen DiXaI has also been shown to
   accurately estimate rivaroxaban plasma concentrations greater than 30 nanogram/mL (70
   nanomol/L); however, at lower levels, liquid chromatography-tandem mass spectrometry
   should be employed as a detection method Laboratory Tests
   • Evaluate liver function at baseline and periodically monitor tests for any significant change in
   function. In general, healthy patients may be monitored yearly, however more frequent moni-
   toring may be required in patients at risk of hepatic dysfunction • Evaluate baseline CBC during initiation and at regular intervals (at least yearly) to assess any
   trends in hemoglobin/hematocrit. Evaluate more frequently if needed, especially in patients
   with active bleeding symptoms 10/14
 Renal Evaluation

   • Assess renal function prior to initiation of therapy and periodically during treatment.
   Frequency of monitoring depends on individual patient factors, including baseline renal func-
   tion, concomitant drug therapy, comorbidities, and age, but it is recommended to monitor re-
   nal function at least every 6 months and every 3 to 6 months in patients with renal impairment
   (CrCl less than 60 mL/min) or during an acute illness that may worsen renal function (infec-
   tions, acute heart failure). In the frail, increased monitoring is recommended • Patients younger than 1 year: Use SCr to determine renal function • Patients 1 year or older: Obtain eGFR using the updated Schwartz formula [eGFR = (0.413 x
   height in cm) divided by SCr (mg/dL)] if SCr is measured by an enzymatic creatinine method
   calibrated to be traceable to isotope dilution mass spectrometry (IDMS). If SCr is measured
   with routine methods (eg, the traditional Jaffe reaction), use the original Schwartz formula
   [eGFR = (k x height in cm) divided by Scr (mg/dL)]. The proportionality constant (k) is 55 in all
   children 1 to 13 years and in girls older than 13 years, and 7 in boys older than 13 years Physical Evaluation
   • Closely monitor for signs and symptoms of blood loss, especially in patients with renal im-
   pairment • Frequently monitor for neurological impairment (ie, midline back pain, sensory or motor
   deficits, or bowel or bladder dysfunction) in patients undergoing neuraxial anesthesia (epidu-
   ral or spinal anesthesia) or spinal puncture • All patients on indefinite antithrombotic therapy for secondary prevention of recurrent VTE
   should be reevaluated at least annually for changes in bleeding risk factors and assessed for
   new bleeding complications • Monitor weight regularly to ensure therapeutic dose is maintained

drugs.uses_raw:
Migraine headache: An initial treatment option in children and adolescents is ibuprofen oral
   solution 10 mg/kg. In adolescents, the following triptans were found to be the most effective in
   a systematic review: sumatriptan/naproxen oral tablets (10/60 mg, 30/180 mg, 85/500 mg),
   zolmitriptan nasal spray (5 mg), sumatriptan nasal spray (20 mg), rizatriptan oral disintegrating
   tablet (5 or 10 mg), or almotriptan oral tablet (6.25 or 5 mg). Ibuprofen or naproxen may be
   added if the triptan does not provide complete response. The triptans that were the most
   likely to provide pain-free relief at 2 hours were sumatriptan plus naproxen (any dose) and
   zolmitriptan nasal spray (5 mg). For ineffective pain relief, an alternative triptan may be tried A 2008 meta-analysis of acute migraine treatments, which included sumatriptan, rizatriptan,
   zolmitriptan, ergots, and analgesics (n=11 studies), concluded that only ibuprofen and suma-
   triptan (4 out of 5 studies used the nasal route) were effective at 2 hours post-dose for
   headache relief (respective number needed to treat (NNT), 4 and 4) and for complete relief
   (respective NNT, 4 and 9), but recommended ibuprofen as first line therapy due to a
   smaller NNT and lower cost Triptan efficacy trials in the pediatric population have been hampered by high placebo re-
   sponse rates 7 , 8 , In an early randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial (n=296; age 12 to 17 years), pain
   relief at 2 hours post-dose was achieved in 66% and pain freedom in 32% of patients following
   a 5 mg dose, versus 56% and 28% for those who received placebo; neither result reached sta-
   tistical significance. Both treatment groups improved nausea, phonophobia, and functional im-
   pairment; however, rizatriptan was statistically better compared with placebo at 1 hour to at
   least 4 hours for nausea, at 4 hours for phonophobia, and 1 and 2 hours for functional impair-
   ment When used on non-school or non-camp days, a 5 mg dose produced pain relief at 2
   hours, however, there was no difference from placebo when pain relief and pain-free response
   at 2 hours were compared over all treatment days. There were slight improvements in func-
   tionality and associated symptoms with rizatriptan, but these were not statistically significant
   (n=476; age 12 to 17 years) The primary efficacy measure in both of these studies was pred-
   icated on results from adults 11 , In a later, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled, 2-stage, enhanced-design trial (n=116:
   age 6 to 17 years), rizatriptan oral disintegrating tablets produced headache relief at 2 hours
   (primary outcome) and pain freedom 2 hours after administration. Response rate for
   headache relief was 72% vs 39% (p less than 001). Ability to function also returned. Results
   were not statistically significant when younger patients (6 to 11 years) were considered as a
   separate group. Rizatriptan dose was based upon weight; those less than 40 kg received 5 mg
   and those 40 kg or greater received 10 mg These results were confirmed in a larger, more

 recent, similarly designed trial (n=770; age 6 to 17 years), in which pain freedom was the pri-
   mary outcome measure. Response rates for rizatriptan and placebo were 6% vs 22%
   (p=0.025), respectively, for patients 12 to 17 years of age and 33% vs 2% (p=0.01), respec-
   tively, for patients 6 to 17 years of age. Absence of vomiting was 9% vs 5% (p less than 05), respectively, in 12 to 17 year old subjects Pediatric FDA Approved Indications Oral tablets are approved for the acute treatment of mi-
   graine headaches with or without aura in patients 6 to 17 years of age 2 ,3 . Rizatriptan oral film
   is indicated for the acute treatment of migraine with or without aura in patients 12 to 17 years
   of age weighing 40 kg or greater Limitations of Use

   • Rizatriptan oral film should only be used where a clear diagnosis of migraine has been estab-
   lished. If a patient has no response for the first migraine attack treated with rizatriptan oral
   films, the diagnosis of migraine should be reconsidered before rizatriptan oral films are ad-
   ministered to treat any subsequent attacks • Rizatriptan oral film is not indicated for the preventive treatment of migraine • Safety and effectiveness have not been established for cluster headache Administration
   For patients with risk factors predictive of coronary artery disease, consider administration of
   first dose in a medically-supervised setting 2 ,3 .
   Oral disintegrating tablets: Remove blister pack from outer aluminum pouch right before
   dosing, then peel open blister pack with dry hands. Place tablet on tongue and allow to disinte-
   grate, then swallow. Administration with liquid not needed 2 ,3 .

   Oral film: Administration with liquid is not necessary. Place the oral film on the tongue, where
   it will disintegrate within approximately 2 minutes and be swallowed with saliva

   rocuronium with general anesthetic agents can prolong the QTc interval. Most pediatric pa-
   tients anesthetized with halothane who did not receive atropine for induction experienced a
   transient increase (30% or greater) in heart rate after intubation, whereas only 1 of 19 infants

   resistance, so caution is appropriate in patients with pulmonary hypertension. Extravasations
   cause local tissue irritation. In studies worldwide, tachycardia occurred in 3% of patients, 4% of which was judged as related by investigators. The package insert statement that

   Warning: Serious Infections, Mortality, Malignancy, Major Adverse Cardiovascular
   Events, and Thrombosis 3
   Serious Infections

   Patients treated with oral Janus kinase inhibitors for inflammatory conditions are at risk for de-
   veloping serious infections that may lead to hospitalizations or death.
   Reported infections include: active tuberculosis, which may present with pulmonary or extra-
   pulmonary disease; invasive fungal infections, including candidiasis and pneumocystosis; and
   bacterial, viral, and other infections due to opportunistic pathogens.

 Avoid use of ruxolitinib in patients with an active, serious infection, including localized infec-
   tions. If a serious infection develops, interrupt ruxolitinib until the infection is controlled.

   The risks and benefits of treatment with ruxolitinib should be carefully considered prior to ini-
   tiating therapy in patient with chronic or recurrent infection.
   Patients should be closely monitored for the development of signs and symptoms of infection
   during and after treatment with ruxolitinib.
   Mortality
   Higher rate of all-cause mortality, including sudden cardiovascular death have been observed
   in patients treated with oral Janus kinase inhibitors for inflammatory conditions.
   Malignancies
   Lymphoma and other malignancies have been observed in patients with Janus kinase in-
   hibitors for inflammatory conditions.
   Major Adverse Cardiovascular Events (MACE)
   Higher rate MACE (including cardiovascular death, myocardial infarction, and stroke) has been
   observed in patients treated with Janus kinase inhibitors for inflammatory conditions.
   Thrombosis

   Thrombosis, including deep vein thrombosis, pulmonary embolism, and arterial thrombosis
   has been observed at an increased incidence in patients treated with oral Janus kinase in-
   hibitors for inflammatory conditions compared to placebo. Many of these adverse reactions
   were serious and some resulted in death. Patients with symptoms of thrombosis should be
   promptly evaluated.

   Monitoring
   Acute Graft Versus Host Disease

   tion indicates efficacy Toxic Laboratory Parameters Monitoring

drugs.contraindications_raw:
Common adverse events include headache, pharyngitis, rash, and urticaria. Additional adverse
   effects with beta(2)-agonists include skeletal muscle tremor and cramps, tachycardia, insom-
   nia, hypokalemia, and hyperglycemia Black Box Warning
   Long-acting beta2-adrenergic agonists (LABA) use increases the risk of asthma-related hospital-
   izations in pediatric and adolescent patients 10,6 . For pediatric and adolescent patients with
   asthma, a fixed-dose combination product containing both an inhaled corticosteroid and LABA
   is recommended to ensure compliance with combination therapy. If separate long-term ther-
   apy is required, ensure patient adherence with both treatments. LABA increase the risk of
   asthma-related death. A placebo-controlled study (12 years and older; mean age 39 years) 10
   with salmeterol showed an increase in asthma-related deaths in patients receiving salmeterol
   versus placebo. Use of salmeterol inhalation powder for the treatment of asthma without a
   concomitant long-term asthma control medication, such as an inhaled corticosteroid, is con-
   traindicated. When treating patients with asthma, salmeterol should only be used for patients
   not adequately controlled on other asthma-controller medications or whose disease severity
   clearly warrants initiation of treatment with two maintenance therapies. Once asthma control
   is achieved and maintained, assess the patient at regular intervals and step down therapy (eg,
   discontinue salmeterol fumarate inhalation powder) if possible without loss of asthma control
   and maintain the patient on a long-term asthma control medication In a meta-analysis (110 studies; n=60,954 patients 4 years through greater than 65 years of
   age), there was an overall higher risk for the composite event (asthma-related deaths, intuba-
   tions, and hospitalizations) associated with LABA use compared with no LABA use (overall inci-
   dence difference of 3 events per 1000 patient-years; 95% CI, 2 to 3) for all age groups.
   The highest risk was seen in children 4 to 11 years of age (30.4 events per 1000 patient-years;
   95% CI, 7 to 1; p=0.02). This result was consistent regardless of inhaled corticosteroid use;
   however, data indicated that providing ICS and LABA as a single inhaler may decrease the risk.
   There were 9807 pediatric patients included in the meta-analysis, and the pediatric composite
   consisted primarily of asthma-related hospitalizations. Asthma-related death/intubations were
   sparse in the 4- to 17-year age groups (no LABA = 4 and LABA = 2) Monitoring
   Assess patient periodically for adequate asthma control and step down therapy if possible 1 , Monitor pulmonary function tests including prebronchodilator FEV1/FVC and pre- and post-
   bronchodilator FEV. Monitor severity and frequency of asthma exacerbations 1 4/6

drugs.contraindications_raw:
Common: In a clinical study of 93 pediatric patients with polyarticular juvenile idiopathic
   arthritis (pJIA), the most common adverse effects were nasopharyngitis (36.6%), upper respira-
   tory tract infection (14%), injection site erythema (9.7%), and neutropenia (5.4%) Black Box Warning
   Risk of serious infections 1

   Patients treated with sarilumab are at increased risk for developing serious infections that may
   lead to hospitalization or death. Opportunistic infections have also been reported in patients
   receiving sarilumab. Most patients who developed infections were taking concomitant im-
   munosuppressants such as methotrexate or corticosteroids.
   Avoid use of sarilumab in patients with an active infection.

   Reported infections include:

   •Active tuberculosis, which may present with pulmonary or extrapulmonary disease. Patients
   should be tested for latent tuberculosis before sarilumab use and during therapy. Treatment
   for latent infection should be initiated prior to sarilumab use

   •Invasive fungal infections, such as candidiasis, and pneumocystis. Patients with invasive fun-
   gal infections may present with disseminated, rather than localized, disease.

   • Bacterial, viral and other infections due to opportunistic pathogens.

   Closely monitor patients for signs and symptoms of infection during treatment with sarilumab.
   If a serious infection develops, interrupt sarilumab until the infection is controlled.

   Consider the risks and benefits of treatment with sarilumab prior to initiating therapy in pa-
   tients with chronic or recurrent infection.

   Monitoring
   Toxic Laboratory Monitoring

   • Monitor neutrophil counts and platelets prior to initiation of therapy, 4 to 8 weeks after treat-
   ment initiation and approximately every 3 months thereafter. When considering dosage modi-
   fication, use results obtained at the end of the dosing interval • Monitor ALT and AST levels prior to initiation of therapy, 4 to 8 weeks after treatment initia-
   tion and approximately every 3 months thereafter. If clinically indicated, consider monitoring
   other liver function tests (ie, bilirubin) 4/6
 • Assess lipid parameters approximately prior to initiation of therapy, 4 to 8 weeks after treat-
   ment initiation and at approximately 6 month intervals thereafter Toxic Physical Monitoring

   • Test for latent TB prior to initiation. Monitor all patients for active TB during treatment, even
   if initial latent TB test is negative 1

   • Monitor patient closely for signs and symptoms of infection during and after therapy 1

Postoperative nausea and vomiting
   Guidelines: Scopolamine is not currently recommended for management of postoperative
   nausea and vomiting (PONV) in pediatric patients. Recommendations for the prophylaxis of
   PONV are guided by the amount of risk factors (eg, 3 years or older, strabismus surgery, sur-
   gery time over 30 minutes, post-operative long-term opioid use, etc) present in a patient. Low
   risk patients (no risk factors) may receive a 5-HT3 antagonist, dexamethasone, or no prophy-
   laxis. Patients at medium risk (1 or 2 risk factors) for PONV should receive a 5-HT3 antagonist
   plus dexamethasone as prophylaxis; for high risk patients (3 or more risk factors), total intra-
   venous anesthesia (TIVA) with propofol may be considered in addition to a 5-HT3 antagonist
   and dexamethasone. TIVA is an effective treatment in children but the risk of bradycardic
   events is increased. Glycopyrrolate administration may help reduce the risk of bradycardia and
   also reduces nausea and vomiting. If PONV prophylaxis has failed, patients should receive an-
   other antiemetic agent from a different pharmacological class. Administering repeated doses
   of antiemetics of the same class within 6 hours does not provide additional therapeutic bene-
   fits when compared with placebo. Alternative medications include droperidol, promethazine,
   dimenhydrinate, and metoclopramide Literature: Transdermal scopolamine significantly reduced postoperative nausea and vomit-
   ing compared with placebo in patients 6 to 14 years old undergoing abdominal surgery (N=40).
   The patches were applied after anesthesia induction and before the start of surgery and were
   removed when patient-controlled analgesia with morphine was discontinued. Scopolamine
   was associated with significantly more incidences of excessive sedation compared to placebo.
   Scopoderm TTS providing scopolamine 5 mg/3 days was used 1

 Limitations of use
   The safety and effectiveness of transdermal scopolamine have not been established in pedi-
   atric patients. Pediatric patients are particularly susceptible to the anticholinergic adverse re-
   actions of scopolamine, including neurologic and psychiatric adverse reactions, serious hyper-
   thermic reactions, and drug withdrawal syndrome Administration
   Do not cut the transdermal system; only 1 transdermal system should be worn at a time Apply the transdermal system to skin in the postauricular area (hairless area behind 1 ear).
   After application, wash hands thoroughly with soap and water and dry hands If the transdermal system becomes displaced, discard it and apply a new 1 on the hairless area
   behind the other ear Upon removal, fold the used transdermal system in half with the sticky side together and dis-
   card in household trash in a manner that prevents accidental contact or ingestion by children,
   pets, or others

drugs.uses_raw:
Pulmonary arterial hypertension: Selexipag is a selective oral prostacyclin receptor agonist
   that may provide some benefits over other prostacyclin analogs in certain pediatric patients.
   Patients may experience fewer side effects because of its selectivity, and the oral formulation
   may provide a treatment option when parenteral administration is not feasible (ie, central line
   concerns, frequent central line infections, lack of resources or support, quality of life issues,
   etc) 7 , • A systematic review of 14 studies (13 case reports/series, 1 prospective observational study)
   synthesized results from patients as young as 6 months of age with pulmonary hypertension
   treated with selexipag. Selexipag was initiated as add-on therapy in 30 patients, and 28 pa-
   tients were transitioned from other prostacyclin analogs to selexipag. Dosing and titration
   were variable, but generally lower-weight patients were initiated at 50 mcg twice daily, and
   those weighing 25 kg or greater generally were initiated at 100 to 200 mcg twice daily. Titration
   occurred anywhere from every 1 day to every 4 weeks. Overall, individual results were vari-
   able, but generally showed improvement, maintenance, or non-deterioration of noninvasive
   and invasive parameters. Some patients and/or caregivers in the add-on therapy group re-
   ported improved quality of life, while all patients/caregivers in the transition group reported
   improved quality of life. At follow-up, 3 patients in the add-on therapy group had disease pro-
   gression; in the transition group, 3 patients failed transition and restarted treprostinil, and 1
   patient had disease progression • A retrospective study of 87 pediatric patients with pulmonary hypertension treated with se-
   lexipag found that patients using selexipag as add-on therapy (n=32; first exposure to a
   prostacyclin agonist) had a significant improvement in PVRI/SVRi ratio (pulmonary vascular
   resistance/systemic vacular resistance ratio), stable echocardiography results (including right
   ventricular function), and stable functional testing results (eg, NT pro BNP, 6-minute-walk-dis-

 tance, WHO functional class). Patients who transitioned to selexipag from another prostacyclin
   analog had a significantly increased cardiac index, stable echocardiography results (including
   right ventricular function), and stable functional testing results except for a significantly re-
   duced V02 max (maximal oxygen consumption during cardiopulmonary exercise testing) and
   significantly increased NT pro BNP results. Selexipag was initiated 50 mcg twice daily for those
   less than 25 kg; 100 or 200 mcg twice daily for those 25 to 50 kg; and 200 mcg twice daily for
   those greater than 50 kg. Doses were titrated as tolerated to a median maximum dose of 5
   mcg/kg/dose twice daily. Median follow-up was 623 days; 17 patients had discontinued selexi-
   pag (2 for adverse effects, 15 for clinical worsening) FDA Approved Pediatric Indications: Selexipag is not approved for use in pediatric patients.
   In adults, it is indicated for the treatment of WHO Group 1 pulmonary arterial hypertension
   (PAH) to delay disease progression and reduce the risk of hospitalization for PAH Administration

drugs.uses_raw:
Neurofibromatosis Type 1 (NF1): Selumetinib treatment resulted in a confirmed partial re-
   sponse (decrease in target neurofibroma volume of at least 20%) in 70% of children and a
   durable response lasting for at least 12 cycles in 56% of children with neurofibromatosis type
   1, who had inoperable, measurable plexiform neurofibromas in stratum 1 of the single-arm,
   open label, SPRINT trial (N=50). The median change in neurofibroma volume at best response
   was −27.9% (range, −55.1% to 2%). The median progression-free survival was not reached,
   with progression-free survival of 84% at 3 years. There was no correlation between change in
   neurofibroma size and patient-reported outcomes or function. Included patients (median age 5 years) had a median of 3 neurofibroma-related complications (disfigurement [n=44], motor
   dysfunction [n=33], pain [n=6]). Discontinuation due to adverse events occurred in 10% of pa-
   tients and included Grade 3 diarrhea (cycle 3), Grade 3 weight gain (cycle 9), Grade 3 parony-
   chia (cycle 15), Grade 4 skin ulceration (cycle 19), and Grade 4 elevated creatinine (cycle 8).
   Patients received selumetinib 25 mg/m(2) orally twice daily approximately every 12 hours in
   continuous 28-day cycles. Results in age-matched controls in the NCI natural-history study of
   neurofibromatosis type 1, 78% of patients had a neurofibroma volume increase of at least 20%
   over 2 years, with a median progression-free survival of 3 years (95% CI, 1 to 6), and
   progression-free survival was 15% at 3 years FDA Approved Pediatric Indication
   Selumetinib is indicated for the treatment of pediatric patients 1 year of age or older with neu-
   rofibromatosis type 1 (NF1) who have symptomatic, inoperable plexiform neurofibromas 9/15

   Black Box Warning
   Warning: Immunosuppression, Use is Not Recommended in Liver or Lung Transplant
   Patients

   Immunosuppression, use is not recommended in liver or lung transplant patients.

   Increased susceptibility to infection and the possible development of lymphoma and other
   malignancies may result from immunosuppression.
    ●   Increased susceptibility to infection and the possible development of lymphoma may result
        from immunosuppression. Only physicians experienced in immunosuppressive therapy and
        management of renal transplant patients should use sirolimus for prophylaxis of organ re-
        jection in patients receiving renal transplants. Patients receiving the drug should be man-
        aged in facilities equipped and staffed with adequate laboratory and supportive medical re-
        sources. The physician responsible for maintenance therapy should have complete informa-
        tion requisite for the followup of the patient.

 The safety and efficacy of sirolimus as immunosuppressive therapy have not been established
   in liver or lung transplant patients, and therefore, such use is not recommended.

   Liver Transplantation – Excess Mortality, Graft Loss, and Hepatic Artery Thrombosis (HAT)
    ●   The use of Rapamune in combination with tacrolimus was associated with excess mortality
        and graft loss in a study in de novo liver transplant patients. Many of these patients had evi-
        dence of infection at or near the time of death.
    ●   In this and another study in de novo liver transplant patients, the use of Rapamune in com-
        bination with cyclosporine or tacrolimus was associated with an increase in HAT; most cases
        of HAT occurred within 30 days post-transplantation and most led to graft loss or death.

   Lung Transplantation – Bronchial Anastomotic Dehiscence
    ●   Cases of bronchial anastomotic dehiscence, most fatal, have been reported in de novo lung
        transplant patients when sirolimus has been used as part of an immunosuppressive

drugs.contraindications_summary:
Bicarbonate administered during inadequate ventilation increases PCO2, thereby decreasing
   pH. Rapid infusion of hypertonic solution is linked to intracranial hemorrhage in neonates and
   infants. Extravasation may cause local tissue necrosis at IV site. Fluid overload, hypocalcemia,
   hypokalemia, and hypernatremia may occur. Aggressive therapy may result in metabolic alka-
   losis (associated with muscle twitching, irritability, and tetany) 3 ,9 ,7 .

   Solution Compatibility
   D5W, D10
