   Mechanism of Action: When bicarbonate is administered, buffering of hydrogen ions occurs,
   leading to increased production of carbon dioxide and water. Animal studies of resuscitation
   demonstrate that poor coronary perfusion leads to carbon dioxide accumulation within the
   myocardium, leading to decreased myocardial contractility 12,9 .

   Pharmacodynamics

   Onset: 15 minutes 1

   thiosulfate may be used. It is also reasonable to consider using sodium thiosulfate in combina-
   tion with hydroxocobalamin to enhance cyanide elimination 1/6
 Evidence: The efficacy and safety of sodium nitrite/sodium thiosulfate was based primarily on
   published case reports. No randomized control trials exist. Sodium thiosulfate was always
   used with sodium nitrite in the available data. Dosing recommendations were derived from
   theoretical calculations of antidote detoxifying potential, extrapolation from animal experi-
   ments, and a small number of human case reports FDA Approved Pediatric Uses
   Sodium nitrite and sodium thiosulfate are indicated for the treatment of acute cyanide poison-
   ing that is judged to serious or life-threatening Carefully weigh risks and benefits in patients with an uncertain diagnosis of cyanide poisoning,
   especially if the patient is not in extremis Regional poison center may be contacted at 1-800-222-1222 Administration
   Administer by slow IV injection 1

   Warning: Life Threatening Hypotension And Methemoglobin Information

   Sodium nitrite can cause serious adverse reactions and death in humans, even at doses less
   than twice the recommended therapeutic dose. Sodium nitrite causes hypotension and
   methemoglobin formation, which diminishes oxygen carrying capacity. Hypotension and

 methemoglobin formation can occur concurrently or separately. Because of these risks,
   sodium nitrite should be used to treat acute life-threatening cyanide poisoning and be used
   with caution in patients where the diagnosis of cyanide poisoning is uncertain Patients should be closely monitored to ensure adequate perfusion and oxygenation during
   treatment with sodium nitrite Alternative therapeutic approaches should be considered in patients known to have dimin-
   ished oxygen or cardiovascular reserve (eg, smoke inhalation victims, preexisting anemia, car-
   diac or respiratory compromise), and those at higher risk of developing methemoglobinemia
   (eg, congenital methemoglobin reductase deficiency) as they are at greater risk for potentially
   life-threatening adverse events related to the use of sodium nitrite Monitoring

   apy for adequacy of oxygenation and perfusion. Oxygen saturation measurements using stan-
   dard pulse oximetry and calculated oxygen saturation values based on measured PO2 are not
   reliable when methemoglobinemia is present • Monitor patient for at least 24 to 48 hours after administration of therapy for recurrent signs
   and symptoms of cyanide toxicity Toxic Monitoring

   • Obtain hemoglobin and hematocrit upon treatment initiation • Closely monitor methemoglobin concentrations during treatment using co-oximetry and

   ments in patients with anemia • Measure oxyhemoglobin and carboxyhemoglobin levels by pulse oximetry or other measure-
   ments in patients that present with evidence of smoke inhalation • Monitor patients with known or suspected glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency

 Black Box Warning
   Warning: Central Nervous System Depression and Misuse and Abuse
   Central Nervous System Depression

   Sodium oxybate is a CNS depressant In clinical trials at recommended doses, obtundation
   and clinically significant respiratory depression occurred in adult patients treated with sodium
   oxybate Many patients who received sodium oxybate during clinical trials in narcolepsy
   were receiving central nervous system stimulants 2 , Abuse and Misuse

   Sodium oxybate is the sodium salt of gamma-hydroxybutyrate (GHB). Abuse or misuse of illicit
   GHB, either alone or in combination with other CNS depressants, is associated with CNS ad-
   verse reactions, including seizure, respiratory depression, decreases in the level of conscious-
   ness, coma, and death 2 ,1 .

   Restricted Access Program

   Because of the risks of CNS depression and abuse and misuse, sodium oxybate is available
   only through a restricted program under a Risk Evaluation and Mitigation Strategy (REMS)
   called the Xywav, Xyrem and Lumryz 2 REMS 2 ,1 .

   Monitoring
   • Monitor for emergence of depressive symptoms in patients with a previous history of a de-
   pressive illness and/or suicide attempt • Monitor for emergence of psychiatric events • Monitor for impaired motor/cognitive function

   Monitoring
   Measure plasma ammonia levels every hour during dialysis until levels stabilize to less than
   200 to 300 micromoles/L. Capillary blood should not be used for monitoring ammonia levels.
   Monitor blood glucose, electrolytes (especially potassium), and acid-base status closely during
   the acute phase (eg, every 4 hours). Toxicity due to ammonia scavenging drugs presents as ke-
   toacidosis. An anion gap that is greater than 15 mEq/L or has increased by greater than 6
   mEq/L from baseline may indicate drug accumulation. Monitor amino acids daily to assess the
   effectiveness of citrulline/arginine replacement and glutamine removal. Assess AST and ALT

   fundoscopic evidence of cerebral edema, and/or of gray matter and white matter damage to
   assess patient response to treatment. Monitor infusion site closely during infusion for signs of
   extravasation

drugs.uses_raw:
Management of urea cycle metabolism disorders (UCD): Long-term treatment of patients
   (UCD) involves the restriction of dietary protein, supplementation with essential amino acids,
   and administration of compounds to augment excretion of waste nitrogen Sodium phenyl-
   butyrate has been used successfully for long-term management of hyperammonemia in a vari-
   ety of urea cycle disorders, including arginase deficiency, carbamoyl phosphate synthetase de-
   ficiency, N-acetyl-glutamate synthase deficiency 7 ,6 , argininosuccinic acid synthetase deficiency
   6,8
      , and ornithine transcarbamylase deficiency 7 , 6 , 9 , According to a cross-sectional study
   from the UCD Consortium of the Rare Diseases Clinical Research Network, sodium phenylbu-
   tyrate is used in 37% of patients in the United States having UCD Another product, glycerol
   phenylbutyrate, was approved in 2013 for management of UCD. In two open-label, cross-over,
   comparative studies (total n=26; age 2 months to 17 years), glycerol phenylbutyrate was found
   to be non-inferior to sodium phenylbutyrate with respect to ammonia control when used at
   equivalent doses 12,13 . Signs and symptoms associated with UCD or its treatment either de-
   creased or resolved after 10 days of treatment with glycerol phenylbutyrate following a switch
   from the sodium product When asked, study patients expressed a preference for the glyc-
   erol product A further pooled analysis of 77 patients, which compared glycerol and sodium
   phenylbutyrate (n=77; 51 adults and 26 children age 6 to 17 years), also demonstrated non-in-
   feriority of the glycerol product. Analysis of non-inferiority was consistent among the subpopu-
   lations examined, including age, gender, age at onset, and UCD type. In addition, significantly
   lower serum ammonia and glutamine levels were obtained with the glycerol as compared with
   the sodium product. Of particular note, improvements in executive function were seen among
   the pediatric patients Induction of fetal hemoglobin synthesis in sickle cell disease: Increased levels of fetal he-
   moglobin (HbF) was associated with less severe disease and increased survival in patients with
   sickle cell disease (HbSS) In a pilot study of children with HbSS (n=8; age 4 to 13 years), sodium phenylbutyrate doubled
   the percentage of fetal reticulocytes in 75% of patients given daily doses ranging from 9 to 7 gm/m2/day; an apparent linear dose-response relationship was noted. After an initial rise,
   however, reticulocyte levels fell in 63% of patients after 3 to 11 weeks of therapy. Alterations in
   gene expression or tachyphylaxis with daily dosing were suggested as possible causes The
   same investigative group later reported that pulsed dosing, rather than daily use, may over-
   come the subsequent fall in reticulocyte levels seen in the first study. Weekly pulses consisting
   of 5 g/day, given for 4 out of 7 days each week, produced a sustained elevation of fetal reticu-
   locyte and HbF levels in a child from the pilot study who had then switched to pulsed dose
   therapy. Increases were maintained over a period of 3 years, when the patient opted to dis-
   continue therapy due to pill burden 2/11
 Pediatric FDA Approved Indication

   Oral Tablet and Powder
   Sodium phenylbutyrate oral tablet and oral powder is indicated as adjunct therapy to dietary
   protein restriction and occasionally essential amino acid supplementation in urea cycle disor-
   ders with neonatal-onset (complete enzyme deficiency and presents within the first 28 days of
   life) or late-onset (partial deficiency occurring after the first month of life) involving deficiencies
   of carbamylphosphate synthetase, argininosuccinic acid synthetase, or ornithine transcar-
   bamylase Oral Suspension

   Sodium phenylbutyrate oral suspension is indicated as adjunctive therapy to standard of care,
   which includes dietary management, for the chronic management of pediatric patients weigh-
   ing 20 kg or greater and with a body surface area (BSA) of 2 m2 or greater, with urea cycle
   disorders (UCDs) involving deficiencies of carbamylphosphate synthetase (CPS), ornithine tran-
   scarbamylase (OTC), or argininosuccinic acid synthetase (AS) Limitation of Use
   • Episodes of acute hyperammonemia may occur in patients while on sodium phenylbutyrate.
   Sodium phenylbutyrate is not indicated for the treatment of acute hyperammonemia, which
   can be a life-threatening medical emergency that requires rapid acting interventions to reduce
   plasma ammonia levels 4 , Administration
   Powder
   • Each level teaspoon (included) dispenses 2 g of powder and 3 g sodium phenylbutyrate;
   each level tablespoon (included) dispenses 1 g of powder and 6 g sodium phenylbutyrate • Mix powder with water, solid food, or liquid food prior to administration. Administer immedi-
   ately after mixture with food. If mixed with water, suspension may be stored up to 1 week at
   room temperature or refrigerated. May be administered via mouth, gastrostomy, or nasogas-
   tric tube. Lightly shake before use Tablets

   • Tablets are for use in patients 20 kg or greater 3

 Pellets

   • Administer orally; administration via gastrostomy or nasogastric tubes has not been evalu-
   ated • Schedule dosages at the same time as food consumption (meal or snack) • Use the calibrated dosing spoon to measure oral pellets. The dosing spoon is directly cali-
   brated in grams of sodium phenylbutyrate • Swallow the coated oral pellets with a drink (eg, water, fruit juices, protein-free infant formu-
   las) or sprinkle onto spoonful of apple sauce or carrot puree. Do not chew oral pellets directly
   or mix into liquids • Swallow immediately to minimize dissolution of coating • Missed dose: Take missed dose as soon as possible. There should be at least 3 hours be-
   tween 2 doses and doses should not be doubled to make up for the missed dose Suspension
   • Pour the entire contents of the Mix-Aid packet into approximately 4 oz of water in a cup and
   stir, forming a suspension 4
   • Pour the entire content of the sodium phenylbutyrate packet(s) into the suspension and stir;
   the entire packet should be administered within 5 minutes after stirring to minimize dissolu-
   tion of the coating • After 30 minutes, the suspension should be discarded • Pour another 4 oz of water into the cup and administer to make sure that any sodium
   phenylbutyrate remaining in the cup is consumed • Sodium phenylbutyrate oral suspension is for oral administration only; do not administer via
   gastrostomy or nasogastric tubes. Take with food • Missed dose: Take the missed dose as soon as possible on the same day 4

   Preparation

   Extemporaneous oral compound

   Note: Pellets for reconstitution to an oral suspension are commercially available.

   200 mg/mL Suspension (60 mL) 5
   • Triturate 12 g of sodium phenylbutyrate powder to a fine powder using a glass mortar and
   pestle.

 • Geometrically add 30 mL of vehicle until a smooth suspension is formed. Vehicle options are
   a 1:1 mixture of Ora-Plus and Ora-Sweet or a 1:1 mixture of Ora-Plus and Ora-Sweet SF.

   • Transfer mixture into a 2 ounce amber plastic bottle.

   • Rinse mortar with enough vehicle to bring final volume to 60 mL.

   • Label the container with "Shake well before using."
   • Stable for 90 days at room temperature (23 to 25C). Use of a masking agent (chocolate syrup
   or peanut butter) before and after administration is recommended.

drugs.uses_raw:
Successful colon cleansing, defined as "excellent" or "good" according to the Aronchick scale,
   was comparable between sodium picosulfate/magnesium oxide/citric acid and polyethylene
   glycol in pediatric patients 9 years or older in a randomized study (N=78). "Excellent" was de-
   fined as greater than 90% of mucosa seen, mostly liquid stool, and minimal suctioning needed
   for adequate visualization. "Good" was defined as greater than 90% of mucosa seen, mostly
   liquid stool, and significant suctioning needed for adequate visualization. In patients aged 9 to
   12 years, successful colon cleansing was achieved in 88% of patients receiving sodium
   picosulfate/magnesium oxide/citric acid (95% CI, 62% to 98%) and in 81% in patients receiving
   polyethylene glycol (95% CI, 54% to 96%). For patients aged 13 to 16 years, successful colon
   cleansing was achieved in 81% of patients receiving sodium picosulfate/magnesium
   oxide/citric acid (95% CI, 54% to 96%) and in 86% in patients receiving polyethylene glycol (95%
   CI, 57% to 98%). Of the 32 patients that received sodium picosulfate/magnesium oxide/citric
   acid, 9 patients received the split dose regimen (doses received the evening before and day of
   colonoscopy) and 23 patients received the day before regimen (doses received the
   afternoon/early evening and late evening before day of colonoscopy) 3 ,2

   Pediatric FDA Approval
   The combination of sodium picosulfate, magnesium oxide, and citric acid as an oral solution is
   indicated for cleansing the colon as a preparation for colonoscopy for pediatric patients 9
   years or older 3 , 2

   Administration
   Prepopik®

   •Reconstitute immediately before each administration •Fill dosing cup with cold water up to the 5-ounce line, pour in contents of 1 packet, and stir for
   2 to 3 minutes • Do not refrigerate or add ice to the solution •Consume a variety of only clear liquids on the day prior to the colonoscopy; should include
   balanced electrolyte solution. Additional clear liquids include black coffee, tea, clear broth or

 bouillon, clear juices without pulp, ginger ale and other sodas, plain jello, and frozen juice bars,
   and up until 2 hours before the time of the procedure; stop consumption of all fluids at least 2
   hours prior to the procedure •Do not eat solid food or dairy, consume red or purple liquids, consume alcohol, or take other
   laxatives and do not take oral medications within 1 hour of beginning the cleansing •Separate the administration of tetracycline or fluoroquinolone antibiotics, iron, digoxin, chlor-
   promazine, or penicillamine by at least 2 hours before and not less than 6 hours after adminis-
   tration of sodium picosulfate, magnesium oxide, and citric acid oral solution Clenpiq®

   •Dilution not required, one bottle is equal to 1 dose •Consume a variety of only clear liquids on the day prior to the colonoscopy; should include

drugs.contraindications_raw:
Common (greater than 5%): Nausea, vomiting, and abdominal pain 1 ,2

   Anaphylaxis and other hypersensitivity reactions have been reported postmarketing There have been rare reports of serious arrhythmias associated with the use of ionic osmotic
   laxative products for bowel preparation; use caution in patients at increased risk of arrhyth-
   mias (eg, patients with a history of prolonged QT interval, uncontrolled arrhythmias, recent
   myocardial infarction, unstable angina, congestive heart failure, or cardiomyopathy) and con-
   sider predose and post-colonoscopy ECGs in patients at increased risk of serious cardiac ar-
   rhythmias There have been reports of generalized tonic-clonic seizures with the use of bowel preparation
   products in patients with no prior history of seizures. The seizure cases were associated with
   electrolyte abnormalities (eg, hyponatremia, hypokalemia, hypocalcemia, and hypomagne-
   semia) and low serum osmolality. The neurologic abnormalities resolved with correction of
   fluid and electrolyte abnormalities. Use caution in patients with a history of seizures and in pa-
   tients at risk of seizure, such as patients taking medications that lower the seizure threshold
   (eg, tricyclic antidepressants), patients withdrawing from alcohol or benzodiazepines, patients
   with known or suspected hyponatremia Significant vomiting or signs of rehydration, including signs of orthostatic hypotension may oc-
   cur. Approximately 20% of pediatric patients experienced orthostatic changes with Prepopik(R)
   compared with 7% of those who received polyethylene glycol. Post-colonoscopy lab test (elec-
   trolytes, creatinine, and BUN) should be considered in those who become symptomatic.
   Symptoms could occur up to 5 days post colonoscopy 2

   effectiveness in children has not been established Should not be used for emergency treat-
   ment of life-threatening hyperkalemia due to its delayed onset of action Administration
   Oral: Shake well before use. Sodium polystyrene sulfonate suspension may be delivered into
   the stomach through a plastic tube and, if desired, given with a diet appropriate for a patient
   in renal failure When using the powder, mix in a small quantity of water or syrup. Mix with 3
   to 4 mL per gram of resin Separate dosing of other oral medications by at least 3 hours (before or after other oral medi-
   cations). Patients with gastroparesis or other conditions resulting in delayed emptying of food

drugs.contraindications_summary:
Adverse effects associated with sodium polystyrene sulfonate include anorexia, nausea, gastric
   irritation, diarrhea, and vomiting. Constipation may occur, especially with high doses.
   Hypokalemia, hypocalcemia, hypomagnesemia and significant sodium retention may occur.
   Intestinal obstruction due to concretions of aluminum hydroxide, when used in combination
   with sodium polystyrene sulfonate, have been reported. Rare instances of intestinal necrosis
   have been reported Post-marketing

Adverse effects associated with sodium polystyrene sulfonate include anorexia, nausea, gastric
   irritation, diarrhea, and vomiting. Constipation may occur, especially with high doses.
   Hypokalemia, hypocalcemia, hypomagnesemia and significant sodium retention may occur.
   Intestinal obstruction due to concretions of aluminum hydroxide, when used in combination
   with sodium polystyrene sulfonate, have been reported. Rare instances of intestinal necrosis
   have been reported Post-marketing events include fecal impaction following rectal administration, particularly in
   children, and gastrointestinal concretions (bezoars) following oral administration. Other re-
   ports were ischemic colitis and gastrointestinal tract ulceration or necrosis which could lead to
   intestinal perforation. Rare cases of acute bronchitis and/or bronchopneumonia associated
   with inhalation of particles of polystyrene sulfonate Monitoring
   Monitor for electrolyte disturbances including potassium, calcium, and magnesium. Especially
   monitor serum potassium levels every 24 hours to avoid hypokalemia; early signs of severe hy-
   pokalemia include irritability, confusion, and delayed thought processes. Late signs include se-
   vere muscle weakness, which may progress to paralysis

Results from the Safety and Appropriateness of Growth Hormone Treatment in Europe
   (SAGhE) study (n=6928) demonstrated an increase in all-cause mortality in adults with GH use
   in childhood than would be expected based on year, age, and gender. Patients who received
   higher doses (greater than 05 mg/kg/day) or were shorter at the start of treatment had
   higher mortality rates. There was an increase in mortality due to diseases of the circulatory
   system or due to ill-defined conditions
drugs.contraindications_raw:
Results from the Safety and Appropriateness of Growth Hormone Treatment in Europe
   (SAGhE) study (n=6928) demonstrated an increase in all-cause mortality in adults with GH use
   in childhood than would be expected based on year, age, and gender. Patients who received
   higher doses (greater than 05 mg/kg/day) or were shorter at the start of treatment had
   higher mortality rates. There was an increase in mortality due to diseases of the circulatory
   system or due to ill-defined conditions, whereas other causes of mortality, including neo-
   plasms, were not more frequent. There was a 5-fold increase in the number of deaths due to
   bone tumors and a 7 fold increase in deaths related to cerebral or subarachnoid hemor-
   rhage Results from the National Cooperative Growth Study (NCGS) revealed 4084 adverse events
   (AEs) and 1559 serious adverse events (SAEs), including 174 deaths, among its 54,996 regis-
   trants over a 20 year period. Of the 174 deaths reported, only 19 (11%) were felt to be related
   to GH therapy. Twelve of the 19 deaths were due to neoplasms (primary CNS tumors), with the
   remaining due to isolated cases due to other causes. There was no increase in new malignan-
   cies or recurrences of CNS tumors, nor was there an increased incidence of leukemia, in pa-
   tients without risk factors for these conditions. The highest incidence of overall AEs, SAEs, and
   deaths occurred in patients having organic growth hormone deficiency (OGHD) and chronic re-
   nal insufficiency (CRI); patients with idiopathic short stature (ISS) had the lowest incidence of all
   events. Specific groups which were identified as being at risk for sudden death include those
   with Turner Syndrome (aortic dissection and rupture), Prader-Willi Syndrome (respiratory fail-
   ure), and ACTH-deficiency (adrenal insufficiency). The incidence of targeted events associated
   with or exacerbated by GH therapy (scoliosis, pancreatitis, slipped capital femoral epiphysis, in-

 tracranial hypertension, diabetes mellitus, and adrenal insufficiency) was reported as less than
   or equal to 1% Significant side effects in children are very rare and include arthralgia, edema, benign intracra-
   nial hypertension, and prepubertal gynecomastia; a transient reduction in dose or temporary
   discontinuation of GH therapy may be indicated Adverse reactions reported in pediatric patients receiving somatropin include injection site re-
   actions, hypersensitivity to the diluent, and hypothyroidism Headache and gynecomastia
   have been reported with somatropin use in children 4 ,7 .

   Leukemia has been reported postmarketing in a small number of patients Somatropin use in pediatric patients has been associated with injection site discomfort and an
   increased risk of otitis media (43% vs 26%) and ear disorders (18% vs 5%) compared with
   placebo 6 , In a 12-month study of pediatric patients who received somatropin 053 mg/kg/day for
   growth hormone deficiency (n=98), the most commonly reported adverse reactions included
   headache (10.2% vs 3%), pyrexia (9.2% vs 3%), cough (5.1% vs 1%), respiratory tract in-
   fection (5.1% vs 2%), diarrhea (3.1% vs 2%), vomiting (4.1% vs 2%), and pharyngitis (3.1% vs 2%) compared with an active somatropin control (n=49). The most commonly reported ad-
   verse events in pediatric patients with Turner syndrome receiving somatropin 37
   mg/kg/week (n=30) were respiratory tract infection (13.3%) and ear infection (6.7%) In 2 studies in pediatric patients with Prader-Willi syndrome, edema, aggressiveness, arthral-
   gia, benign intracranial hypertension, hair loss, headache, and myalgia were reported in soma-
   tropin-treated patients. In 2 studies in pediatric patients with Turner syndrome, the most fre-
   quently reported adverse events with somatropin treatment were respiratory illnesses (in-
   fluenza, tonsillitis, otitis, sinusitis), joint pain, and urinary tract infection. Joint pain was the only
   treatment-related adverse event reported in more than 1 patient. In 2 open-label studies in pe-
   diatric patients with idiopathic short stature, the most commonly reported adverse events in-
   cluded upper respiratory tract infections, influenza, tonsillitis, nasopharyngitis, gastroenteritis,
   headaches, increased appetite, pyrexia, fracture, altered mood, and arthralgia 7 ,9 .

   In clinical studies of pediatric patients with growth hormone deficiency (GHD) who received
   Omnitrope® cartridge (n=86), elevated HbA1c, eosinophilia, and hematoma were reported in
   14%, 12%, and 9% of patients, respectively. Adverse events reported with Omnitrope® for in-
   jection (n=44) included hypothyroidism (16%), eosinophilia (11%), elevated HbA1c (9%),
   hematoma (9%), headache (7%), hypertriglyceridemia (5%), and leg pain (5%) 12/20
 The most frequently reported adverse effects associated with Norditropin® treatment in pedi-
   atric patients were common childhood diseases. In Noonan syndrome patients 3 to 14 years of
   age (n=21), upper respiratory infection, gastroenteritis, ear infection, and influenza were re-
   ported. Among Turner syndrome patients, influenza-like illness, upper respiratory tract infec-
   tion, otitis externa, gastroenteritis, eczema, and otitis media were reported. Cases of otitis me-

drugs.dosing_raw:
To minimize the risk of induced arrhythmia, hospitalize patients initiating or re-initiating therapy for
   at least 3 days or until steady-state drug levels are reached, in a facility that can provide cardiac re-
   suscitation and continuous ECG monitoring. Obtain QT interval and normalize serum potassium
   and magnesium prior to initiation. Calculate estimated CrCl to determine appropriate dosing inter-
   val. Withdraw other antiarrhythmic therapy (for a minimum of 2 to 3 plasma half-lives if possible)
   prior to initiation 1 ,2 ,3 ,4 .
   Do not start therapy if the baseline QTc interval is greater than 450 milliseconds (JT greater than 330
   milliseconds if QRS is over 100 milliseconds) 1 ,4 ,2 ,3 .

   Oral
   Weight-based dosing
   Initial: 2 mg/kg/day orally in 2 or 3 divided doses (divided every 8 to 12 hours). Gradually in-
   crease as needed in 1 to 2 mg/kg/day increments every 3 to 5 days until stable rhythm is main-
   tained 5 , 6 , 7 , 8 , Higher initial doses (up to 3 to 4 mg/kg/day) have also been used in children
   10,11
           .
   Maintenance: Usual maintenance dose ranges from 2 to 8 mg/kg/day orally in 2 or 3 divided
   doses 12,5 ,10,11,6 ,7 ,8 ,9 .

   Maximum recommended daily dose is 160 mg twice daily In a prospective, multiple-dose pharmacokinetics/pharmacodynamics study (n=76), an age-
   specific dosing regimen was derived. For infants and children less than 6 years of age, an initial
   dose of 3 mg/kg/day orally in divided doses every 8 hours with a target dose of 6 mg/kg/day is
   recommended. For children greater than 6 years of age, an initial dose of 2 mg/kg/day orally in
   divided doses every 8 hours with a target dose of 4 mg/kg/day is recommended. The dosing
   regimen was based on a 50% (initial dose) and 95% (target dose) probability to achieve conver-
   sion into sinus rhythm Body surface area (BSA) dosing

 Initial: 90 to 100 mg/m2/day orally in 2 or 3 divided doses (divided every 8 to 12 hours).
   Gradually increase as needed every 3 to 5 days until stable rhythm is maintained 15,13,16 .
   Lower (50 mg/m2/day) and higher (200 mg/m2/day) initial doses have also been used 17,9 .

   Maintenance: Usual maintenance dose ranges from 100 to 250 mg/m2/day in 2 or 3 divided
   doses, although lower or higher doses may be needed 15 , 13 , 16 , 18 , In one study (n=66) in chil-
   dren, a child with ventricular tachycardia required a maintenance dose of 350 mg/m2/day In
   a retrospective study (n=10) in infants requiring combination therapy with flecainide and so-
   talol for refractory supraventricular tachycardia, the median effective dose was 175
   mg/m2/day (range, 100 to 250 mg/m2/day) Infants with a BSA less than 33 m2 receiving BSA-normalized doses were found to have
   greater drug exposure and more pronounced beta-blocking and Class III effects than infants
   and children with a BSA greater than 33 m2 Dose interval
   Studies with sotalol in children have shown that an every 8-hour regimen is preferred over an
   every 12-hour regimen to prevent breakthrough arrhythmias and decrease the wide fluctua-
   tions between peak and trough concentrations 14,19,20,18 .

   Intravenous
   Loading dose: 1 mg/kg IV over 10 minutes was used in a retrospective chart review in 83 pa-
   tients (mean age, 3 years; range, 10 days to 14 years) Maintenance dose: 5 mg/kg/day IV was used in a retrospective chart review in 83 patients
   (mean age, 3 years; range, 10 days to 14 years). Continue for 1 to 24 hours after transition to
   sinus rhythm then switch to oral therapy In patients unable to take oral sotalol, intravenous sotalol may be used as a substitute. Data
   regarding the use of the intravenous formulation in pediatric patients are lacking. In adults,
   the recommended intravenous dose is approximately 94% of the oral dose and is given at the
   same frequency. For example, a patient receiving 80 mg sotalol orally twice daily should re-
   ceive 75 mg sotalol intravenously twice daily
drugs.uses_raw:
Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (HCM): Beta-blockers are recommended as first-line treat-
   ment for HCM, including obstructive HCM, nonobstructive HCM with preserved ejection frac-
   tion, HCM with atrial fibrillation, and HCM with ventricular arrhythmias. Sotalol has been
   shown to be safe and is commonly prescribed for children with HCM and atrial fibrillation. In
   children with HCM and recurrent ventricular arrhythmias despite beta-blocker use, antiar-
   rhythmic drug therapy (eg, amiodarone, mexiletine, sotalol) is recommended. Treatment
   choice should be guided by age, underlying comorbidities, severity of disease, patient prefer-
   ence, and a balance of safety and efficacy Ventricular/supraventricular tachyarrhythmias

   Refractory supraventricular tachycardia (PALS guidelines): Sotalol, procainamide, and
   amiodarone may be considered to treat SVT refractory to vagal maneuvers and adenosine in
   pediatric patients with cardiopulmonary compromise Treatment of refractory ventricular and supraventricular tachyarrhythmias 17,29,16,5 ,10,30,7 ,9 .
   Sotalol is most effective for reentrant SVT with efficacy rates of 63% to 100% reported in clini-
   cal studies. Highest efficacy seen for atrioventricular reentrant tachycardia and Wolff-
   Parkinson-White syndrome 12,7 ,9 . In 83 patients (mean age, 3 years; range, 10 days to 14
   years) with persistent tachycardias, there was no significant difference in rates of conversion
   to sinus rhythm with use of IV sotalol based on type of tachycardia: 57% with atrioventricular
   reentrant tachycardia, 67% with persistent atrial tachycardia, 44% with atrial flutter, 67% with
   atrial fibrillation, and 60% with sustained ventricular tachycardia. An additional 15% of patients
   converted with addition of propafenone. Mean time to conversion was significantly faster for
   atrioventricular reentrant tachycardia (1 hour) versus atrial tachycardia (13.7 hours) or atrial
   flutter (11.5 hours). Neither sinus arrest, hypotension, nor treatment-related arrhythmias oc-
   curred. Use was not recommended in children with severely impaired cardiac function. Two studies in pediatric patients have shown lower success rates for the treatment of ventricu-
   lar tachycardia. In one study, the success rate was only 17%, while in the other study, the suc-
   cess rate was 64% (compared with 93% for SVT) 7 ,9 .

 For atrial tachycardias, efficacy rates of 73% to 85% have been reported 10,11 .

   In adults, sotalol is indicated for the treatment of life-threatening, documented ventricular ar-
   rhythmias, such as sustained ventricular tachycardia. Its use in patients with less severe ar-
   rhythmias, even if the patients are symptomatic, is generally not recommended. Avoid treat-
   ment of patients with asymptomatic ventricular premature contractions 3 ,2 .

   In adults, sotalol is indicated for the maintenance of normal sinus rhythm (delay in time to re-
   currence of atrial fibrillation/atrial flutter (AFIB/AFL)) in patients with symptomatic AFIB/AFL
   who are currently in sinus rhythm. Because sotalol can cause life-threatening ventricular ar-
   rhythmias, reserve its use for patients in whom AFIB/AFL is highly symptomatic. Patients with
   paroxysmal AFIB that is easily reversed (by Valsalva maneuver, for example) should usually not
   be given Betapace/Betapace AF 3 , Administration

   May administer without regard to meals. Separate administration of aluminum- or magne-
   sium- containing antacids with sotalol by 2 hours Intravenous

   mends infusing over 5 hours Sotalol has been administered over 10 minutes in 83 pediatric
   patients In adults, sotalol has been infused in 5 minutes or less When used for substitution of oral sotalol, to match the exposure to oral sotalol, use the same
   dosing frequency with IV administration and infuse the adjusted dose over 5 hours When used for a loading dose prior to initiation or dose escalation of oral sotalol, infuse the
   loading dose over 1 hour 1

   venient for administration and consistent with fluid restriction Extemporaneous oral compounds

   Note: A 5 mg/mL oral solution is available commercially.

   To minimize the risk of drug-induced arrhythmia, initiate or reinitiate oral sotalol in a facility
   that can provide cardiac resuscitation and continuous electrocardiographic monitoring. Sotalol
   can cause life threatening ventricular tachycardia associated with QT interval prolongation.

 Calculate creatinine clearance to determine appropriate dosing. If the QT interval prolongs to
   500 msec or greater, reduce the dose, lengthen the dosing interval, or discontinue the drug 2 ,3
   Do not initiate intravenous sotalol therapy if the baseline QTc is longer than 450 ms Solution Compatibility
   D5W, NS, and Lactated Ringer's.

   Ventricular Arrhythmias

   utilizing a suitable method (eg, programmed electrical stimulation (PES) or Holter monitoring)
   prior to continuing the patient on chronic sotalol therapy 4 ,32,22 .

   younger who can take a longer time to reach steady-state 32 , Toxic Laboratory Monitoring

   mias) prior to and during every gradual upward dose titration, especially in patients with se-

   Mechanism of Action

   Spironolactone/hydroCHLOROthiazide is a combination of two diuretic agents with different
   but complementary mechanisms and sites of action, thereby providing additive diuretic and

   spironolactone is mediated through its action as a specific pharmacologic antagonist

drugs.uses_raw:
Dravet Syndrome:

 Stiripentol (n=12) significantly improved response rates (50% or greater decrease in seizure
   frequency; 67% vs 1%) compared with placebo (n=11) in a randomized study in patients with
   Dravet syndrome inadequately controlled on clobazam and valproate. Mean percentage
   change in seizure frequency also significantly improved with stiripentol compared with
   placebo (-74% vs -13%). Patients (3 to less than 18 years; with at least 4 generalized clonic or
   tonic-clonic seizures per month) received either stiripentol 50 mg/kg/day in divided doses or
   placebo in addition to their prior treatment of clobazam and valproate In a randomized trial (n=41), stiripentol added to valproate and clobazam significantly reduced
   clonic and tonic-clonic seizure frequency compared with placebo added to valproate and
   clobazam in children with severe myoclonic epilepsy in infancy (mean, 35 years). Overall, 71%
   in the stiripentol group had at least a 50% reduction in seizure frequency (clonic or tonic-
   clonic) compared with 5% in the placebo group. Seizure-free rate was significantly better with
   stiripentol (n=9) compared with none in the control group. Seizure frequency decreased 69%
   from baseline among stiripentol-treated children and increased 7% among controls; median
   number of seizures in 1 month was 5 and 14 in stiripentol- and placebo-treated children. One
   patient in each group had status epilepticus. Overall, 5 of 20 patients in the control group ex-
   perienced an adverse event compared with 21 of 21 patients in the stiripentol group (drowsi-
   ness and loss of appetite most common). However, when dosing of clobazam was decreased,
   the adverse effect disappeared in 12 of 21 of the stiripentol group. Stiripentol was given for 2
   months at a dose of 50 mg/kg 2 or 3 times a day (mean 3 mg/kg/day). Seizure rates were
   measured during the second month and recorded in a diary by parents and caretakers.
   Maximum doses were valproate 30 mg/kg/day and clobazam 5 mg/kg/day. Clobazam dosing
   was reduced during the study from mean 5 to 38 mg/kg/day in the stiripentol group (val-
   proate dose did not change) FDA Pediatric Approval

   Indicated for the treatment of seizures associated with Dravet syndrome (DS) in patients 6
   months or older, weighing 7 kg or greater, who are taking clobazam. There are no clinical data
   to support the use of stiripentol as monotherapy in DS 2

   Capsules

   •Should be swallowed whole with a glass of water during a meal •Do not open or break capsules Suspension

 •Should be mixed with a glass of water (100 mL) and taken immediately after mixing during a
   meal •Add a small amount of water (25 mL) to the drinking cup and drink all of the remaining mix-
   ture to assure no medicine is left in the glass

drugs.uses_raw:
Brucellosis: Combination therapy is recommended to reduce the incidence of relapse. For
   children 8 years or younger, first-line therapy is oral sulfamethoxazole/trimethoprim in combi-
   nation with rifAMPin. For children older than 8 years, first-line therapy is oral doxycycline or
   tetracycline in combination with rifAMPin. Sulfamethoxazole/trimethoprim may be substituted
   if tetracyclines are contraindicated. Add gentamicin or streptomycin for the first 14 days of
   therapy for complicated cases (eg, endocarditis, meningitis, osteomyelitis). Duration of therapy
   is at least 6 weeks, and can be extended to 4 to 6 months for life-threatening infections, such
   as meningitis or endocarditis Plague
   Bioterrorism: Following a bioterrorism event, treat symptomatic patients with 2 antimicrobial
   agents from different classes, with at least 1 being considered a first-line therapy (see table be-
   low), until sensitivity results are available. While antimicrobial resistance is extremely rate with
   naturally occurring Yersinia pestis, engineered resistance is possible with strains used for
   bioterrorism events. Treatment duration is 10 to 14 days, or longer for ongoing fever or con-
   cerning symptoms. For asymptomatic patients likely exposed, rapidly distribute post-exposure
   prophylaxis. Duration of post-exposure prophylaxis is 7 days Naturally occurring Y. pestis infections: Treatment duration for all infection types is 10 to 14
   days, or longer for ongoing fever or concerning symptoms. Antimicrobial resistance is ex-
   tremely rare. Specific recommendations are below: 3
   • Pneumonic or septicemic plague: May initiate treatment with 1 antimicrobial agent for
   mild/moderate disease; for severe disease, initiate dual therapy with 2 antimicrobial agents
   from different classes and narrow therapy to a single agent after clinical improvement occurs.
   If the diagnosis of plague is uncertain, include antimicrobial coverage for community-acquired
   pneumonia until results are available.

   • Bubonic or pharyngeal plague: Initiate treatment with 1 antimicrobial agent for primary dis-
   ease in stable patients with no signs or symptoms of secondary pneumonic or septicemic
   plague. If primary bubonic or pharyngeal plague has progressed to secondary pneumonic or
   septicemic plague, follow treatment recommendations for pneumonic/septicemic plague.

   • Meningitis: Dual therapy with chloramphenicol and either levoFLOXacin or moxifloxacin is rec-
   ommended. For secondary meningitis in patients already receiving antimicrobial therapy, add
   chloramphenicol to the existing regimen. Once chloramphenicol has been added, continue the
   full treatment regimen for an additional 10 days. Chloramphenicol is an appropriate choice for
   treating plague meningitis despite a relative contraindication for use in children younger than
   6 months due to the severity of the infection.

   • Pre-exposure prophylaxis: Pre-exposure prophylaxis is generally unnecessary as long as stan-
   dard and droplet precautions are maintained. Consider pre-exposure prophylaxis in cases of

 surgical mask shortages, patient overcrowding, or poor hospital ventilation. Discontinue pre-
   exposure prophylaxis 48 hours after last perceived exposure.

   • Post-exposure prophylaxis: Consider post-exposure prophylaxis for those with close (less than
   6 feet) contact with a patient with pneumonic plague who were not wearing adequate per-
   sonal protective equipment, lab workers accidentally exposed to infectious materials of not
   following standard precautions, and those in close or direct contact with infected animals (eg,
   vet staff, pet owners, hunters). Duration of post-exposure prophylaxis is 7 days.

   Breastfeeding: Mothers with pneumonic plague may continue to breastfeed if they are being
   treated and the infant is being treated or receiving post-exposure prophylaxis. If the infant is
   not being treated or received prophylaxis, mothers should avoid breastfeeding until they have
   received treatment for at least 48 hours and demonstrated clinical improvement CDC first-line and alternative treatment and prophylaxis options for children 1 month or

   FDA Approved Pediatric Uses: Streptomycin is approved to treat the following infections
   caused by organisms susceptible to the drug but not susceptible or amenable to potentially
   less toxic antimicrobials: Tuberculosis; infections caused by Yersinia pestis (plague); Francisella
   tularensis (tularemia); Brucella; Calymmatobacterium granulomatis (donovanosis, granuloma in-
   guinale); H. ducreyi (chancroid); H. influenzae (in combination with another antimicrobial); K.
   pneumoniae pneumonia (in combination with another antimicrobial); urinary tract infections
   caused by E. coli, Proteus, A. aerogenes, K. pneumoniae, or Enterococcus faecalis; endocarditis due

 to Streptococcus viridans or E. faecalis (in combination with a beta-lactam); bacteremia caused
   by Gram-negative bacilli (in combination with another antimicrobial) Administration
   IM

   • The preferred IM administration site is the midlateral muscles of the thigh; may use the pe-
   riphery of the upper outer quadrant of the gluteal region in infants and small children only
   when needed. Administer into deltoid only if it is well-developed; use caution to avoid nerve in-
   jury. Do not administer into lower or mid-third of the upper arm. Alternate injection sites IV

   • Administer IV over 30 minutes 5
   • Although not approved for IV use, many patients who require the drug may not have suffi-
   cient muscle mass to tolerate IM injections. Preparation, IM

   • Reconstitute vial with sterile water for injection. Add 2 mL for a final concentration of 200
   mg/mL; add 2 mL for a final concentration of 250 mg/mL; or add 8 mL for a final concentra-
   tion of 400 mg/mL • Reconstituted solution may be stored for 1 week at room temperature and protected from
   light Preparation, IV

   • Reconstitute vial with sterile water for injection. Add 2 mL for a final concentration of 200
   mg/mL; add 2 mL for a final concentration of 250 mg/mL; or add 8 mL for a final concentra-
   tion of 400 mg/mL • Dilute with NS or D5W to a total volume of 100 mL 5

   • Diluted solution is stable for 24 hours 5

drugs.contraindications_raw:
Common: Vestibular ototoxicity (nausea, vomiting, vertigo), paresthesia of face, rash, fever, ur-
   ticaria, angioneurotic edema, eosinophilia 1

 Ototoxicity

   • Vestibular dysfunction is dose- and duration-related. In adults, doses of 8 to 2 grams/day
   are likely to lead to vestibular dysfunction in a large percentage of adults. Risk is increased
   with renal impairment or concomitant administration of other ototoxic medications (eg,
   furosemide, mannitol, ethacrynic acid) • Symptoms appear early and are usually reversible if streptomycin is discontinued. Most
   symptoms disappear within 2 to 3 months of discontinuation, except for the relative inability
   to walk in total darkness or on very rough terrain • There is more potential for vestibular dysfunction compared with cochlear injury. Vestibular
   dysfunction is characterized by headache, nausea, vomiting, and disequilibrium. Early cochlear
   injury is characterized by loss of high-frequency hearing • Monitoring via caloric and audiometric tests is to be completed before, during, and after in-
   tensive streptomycin therapy to facilitate early detection and drug discontinuation in order to
   prevent irreversible damage • Some cases of ototoxicity associated with aminoglycosides may be related to certain variants
   in the mitochondrially encoded 12S rRNA gene (MT-RNR1), particularly the m.1558>G variant.
   This variant is present in less than 1% of the US population, and may result in ototoxicity with
   serum aminoglycoside concentrations in the therapeutic range. In patients with a known ma-
   ternal of ototoxicity caused by aminoglycosides, consider alternative options if possible Black Box Warning
   • The risk of severe neurotoxic reactions is sharply increased in patients with impaired renal
   function or prerenal azotemia. These include disturbances of vestibular and cochlear function,
   optic nerve dysfunction, peripheral neuritis, arachnoiditis, and encephalopathy may also oc-
   cur. The incidence of clinically detectable, irreversible vestibular damage is particularly high in
   patients treated with streptomycin.
   • Renal function should be monitored carefully; patients with renal impairment and/or nitro-
   gen retention should receive reduced doses. The peak serum concentration in individuals with
   kidney damage should not exceed 20 to 25 mcg/mL.

   • The concurrent or sequential use of other neurotoxic and/or nephrotoxic drugs with strepto-
   mycin, including neomycin, kanamycin, gentamicin, cephaloridine, paromomycin, viomycin,
   polymyxin B, colistin, tobramycin, and cyclosporine should be avoided.

   • The neurotoxicity of streptomycin can result in respiratory paralysis from neuromuscular
   blockage, especially when the drug is given soon after the use of anesthesia or muscle

 relaxants.

   • The administration of streptomycin in parenteral form should be reserved for patients where
   adequate laboratory and audiometric testing facilities are available during therapy Monitoring
   Therapeutic Monitoring

   • Perform culture and susceptibility testing when available Toxic Monitoring

   • Monitor renal function carefully • Perform caloric stimulation and audiometric tests at baseline, during, and following intensive
   streptomycin treatment • When treating venereal infections (eg, granuloma inguinale, chancroid) and concomitant
   syphilis is suspected, perform suitable laboratory procedures such as dark field examination
   prior to initiation, then monthly for at least 4 months Therapeutic Drug Monitoring
   • Consider monitoring serum drug concentrations patients with renal impairment; peak levels
   should not exceed 20 to 25 mcg/mL in this population

• Renal excretion: 29 to 89% of a dose is excreted in the urine within 24 hours • Hemodialysis: Hemodialysis removes significant amounts of streptomycin. Blood levels may

drugs.contraindications_raw:
Cardiac arrest, malignant hyperthermia, arrhythmias, bradycardia, tachycardia, hypertension,
   hypotension, hyperkalemia, prolonged respiratory depression, and apnea have been reported Black Box Warning
   Ventricular Dysrhythmias, Cardiac Arrest, and Death from Hyperkalemic
   Rhabdomyolysis in Pediatric Patients 18
    ●   Acute rhabdomyolysis with hyperkalemia followed by ventricular dysrhythmias, cardiac ar-
        rest, and death has occurred after the administration of succinylcholine to apparently
        healthy pediatric patients who were subsequently found to have undiagnosed skeletal mus-
        cle myopathy, most frequently Duchenne muscular dystrophy.

 ●   When a healthy appearing pediatric patient develops cardiac arrest within minutes after ad-
        ministration of succinylcholine chloride, not felt to be due to inadequate ventilation, oxy-
        genation or anesthetic overdose, immediate treatment for hyperkalemia should be insti-
        tuted. In the presence of signs of malignant hyperthermia, appropriate treatment should be
        instituted concurrently.
    ●   Reserve the use of succinylcholine chloride in pediatric patients for emergency intubation or
        instances where immediate securing of the airway is necessary, eg, laryngospasm, difficult
        airway, full stomach, or for intramuscular use when a suitable vein is inaccessible.

   Monitoring
   Therapeutic Physical Monitoring

   Train-of-four (TOF) monitoring with clinical assessment, rather than TOF monitoring alone, is
   recommended in critically ill pediatric patients in the ICU Toxic Laboratory Monitoring

   Obtain a preoperative creatine kinase Toxic Physical Monitoring

   Monitor oxygen saturation, heart rate, and blood pressure continuously Closely monitor ECG for peaked T-waves, an early sign of potential cardiac arrest secondary to
   acute rhabdomyolysis with hyperkalemia Obtain a history and physical to identify developmental delays suggestive of a myopathy Assess patients for previous anaphylactic reactions to other neuromuscular blocking agents
   prior to therapy Monitor temperature and expired carbon dioxide continuously for early recognition of malig-
   nant hyperthermia Observe for early signs of malignant hyperthermia, including jaw muscle spasm, acidosis, or
   generalized rigidity to initial administration of succinylcholine for tracheal intubation, or failure
   of tachycardia to respond to deepening anesthesia Assess for the presence of a Phase II block, manifesting as prolonged respiratory muscle paral-
   ysis or weakness, by using peripheral nerve stimulation Monitor neuromuscular transmission and the development of fasciculations during therapy 6/9
 Monitor patients for clinical signs of vomiting and aspiration during induction of anesthesia
   and neuromuscular blockade Monitor patients to ensure that the level of anesthesia is adequate

drugs.pharmacokinetics_summary:
Pharmacology
   Mechanism of Action: The mechanism of action for sucralfate is not completely understood.
   However, it is known that the effects of sucralfate are the result of a local action by forming an
   ulcer-adherent complex with proteinaceous exudate at the ulcer site. This action is thought to
   cover the ulcer site and prevent against future attacks from acid, pepsin, and bile salts 3 ,4 .

   Absorption and Excretion: Sucralfate is minimally absorbed from the gastrointestinal tract

drugs.pharmacokinetics_summary:
Pharmacology
   Sucrose administration provides a calming effect and reduces acute procedural pain in infants.
   The potential mechanism of these effects includes activation of the endogenous opioid system
   through taste receptors on the tip of the tongue. The time to maximal effect is approximately 2
   minutes and the duration of effect is approximately 5 to 10 minutes. The beneficial effects of
   sucrose can be improved by nonnutritive sucking 3 ,11 .

drugs.uses_raw:
Acinetobacter baumannii infection, carbapenem-resistant (CRAB): Guidance from the
   Infectious Disease Society of America (IDSA) recommends a sulbactam-containing agent in
   combination with a second agent for the treatment of infections caused by CRAB.
   Sulbactam/durlobactam in combination with imipenem/cilastatin or meropenem is preferred.
   If sulbactam/durlobactam is unavailable, high-dose ampicillin/sulbactam in combination with
   polymyxin B, high-dose minocycline, tigecycline, or cefiderocol is an alternative. If prolonged
   therapy is necessary (eg, osteomyelitis), the second agent may be discontinued after clinical
   improvement occurs and the sulbactam-containing agent continued as monotherapy for the
   rest of the duration of therapy. Nebulized antibiotics are not recommended. In general, dura-
   tion of therapy is the same as for infections caused by more susceptible organisms. If suscepti-
   bility testing results indicate that empiric therapy was not active against the organism, dura-
   tion of therapy is counted starting from initiation of a susceptible agent or regimen 1 ,2 .

   FDA Approved Pediatric Uses: Sulbactam and durlobactam are not approved for use in pedi-
   atric patients. In adults it is approved to treat hospital-acquired bacterial pneumonia and ven-
   tilator-associated bacterial pneumonia caused by susceptible isolates of Acinetobacter bauman-
   nii-calcoaceticus complex Administration
   • Bring the prepared solution to ambient room temperature (over 15 to 30 minutes) prior to in-
   fusion • Administer all doses via IV infusion over 3 hours • Compatibility for administration with solutions containing other drugs or diluents other than

   drugs • Use the prepared solution within 24 hours when stored refrigerated at 2 to 8°C (36 to 46°F);
   discard unused portion Preparation

   gle-dose vials of durlobactam 5 g as sterile powders that must be reconstituted and further

   gently shake to dissolve. Each reconstituted vial contains 1 g of sulbactam per 5 mL of clear,

 colorless to slightly yellow solution. The reconstituted solution is not for direct injection and
   must be diluted before IV infusion; dilute within 1 hour of reconstitution • Reconstitute each durlobactam 5 g single-dose vial with 5 mL of Sterile Water for Injection
   and gently shake to dissolve. Each reconstituted vial contains 5 g of durlobactam per 5 mL

   and must be diluted before intravenous infusion; dilute within 1 hour of reconstitution • To prepare the required dose, withdraw 5 mL of reconstituted sulbactam and 5 mL of recon-

drugs.uses_raw:
Toxoplasmosis
   • Pyrimethamine, sulfADIAZINE, and folinic acid are first-line therapy for pediatric patients with
   confirmed/strongly suspected congenital toxoplasmosis (including asymptomatic toxo-
   plasmosis), active toxoplasmic chorioretinitis, and severe primary (acute) toxoplasmosis
   (including immunocompromised patients and reactivation of latent infection) • Strongly consider empiric therapy in newborns born to mothers with symptomatic toxoplas-
   mosis during pregnancy, regardless of whether the mother was treated 7
   • If pyrimethamine and sulfADIAZINE (first-line therapy) are not available, may use
   trimethoprim/sulfamethoxazole until they are available 1

   FDA approved pediatric indications

   SulfADIAZINE is contraindicated in infants younger than 2 months of age except as adjunctive
   therapy with pyrimethamine in the treatment of congenital toxoplasmosis 3

   SulfADIAZINE is indicated to treat the following conditions: 3
   •Chancroid

   •Trachoma
   •Inclusion conjunctivitis

   •Norcardiosis
   •Urinary tract infections, in the absence of obstructive uropathy or foreign bodies, when
   caused by susceptible strains/organisms
   •Toxoplasmosis encephalitis, in patients with or without acquired immunodeficiency syn-
   drome, as adjunct therapy with pyrimethamine

   •Malaria due to chloroquine-resistant strains of Plasmodium falciparum, as adjunct therapy

   •Meningococcal meningitis, treatment and prophylaxis
   •Acute otitis media due to Haemophilus influenzae, when used with penicillin

 •H influenzae meningitis, as adjunct therapy with streptomycin

   •Recurrent rheumatic fever, prophylaxis

   Administration
   •Administer each sulfADIAZINE dose with 8 ounces of water 3

   Preparation

   Extemporaneous oral formulations

   100 mg/mL suspension in SyrSpend™ SF PH4 (300 mL) 4 :

   • Weigh 30 g of sulfADIAZINE active pharmaceutical ingredient and triturate in a mortar to a
   fine powder.
   • Add a small amount of SyrSpend™ SF PH4 liquid and mix to form a uniform paste.

   • Add aliquots of SyrSpend™ SF PH4 liquid in geometric proportions, mixing with each
   addition.

   • Transfer to a low actinic prescription bottle and fill to final volume of 300 mL with SyrSpend™
   SF PH4, shake to mix thoroughly.

   • Protect from light; shake well before use.

   • Stable at room temperature (20 to 25° C) or under refrigeration (2 to 8° C) for up to 90 days.

   100 mg/mL suspension in simple syrup 5 :
   • Calculate number of sulfADIAZINE 500 mg tablets required for volume of suspension to be
   made; pulverize in a mortar for 3 minutes.
   • Measure the amount of liquid required, made up of simple syrup as vehicle with methylcel-
   lulose 1% as suspending agent; add half the volume to the mortar and mix until a smooth
   paste is formed.
   • Transfer mixture to a light-protected prescription bottle.

   • Slowly add vehicle up to final volume, mixing with each addition.

   • Protect from light; shake well before use.

   • Stable at room temperature (20 to 25° C) for up to 14 days.

   100 mg/mL suspension in Ora-Plus/Ora-Sweet (100 mL) 6 :
   • Weigh 10 g sulfADIAZINE powder and place into a mortar.

 • Measure out 50 mL Ora-Plus liquid, and add to mortar in small portions, mixing after each
   addition, to form a smooth mixture.

   • Transfer to a prescription bottle and add sufficient Ora-Sweet to final volume of 100 mL in
   portions, and mix well
   • Protect from light; shake well before use.

   • Stable at room temperature or under refrigeration for up to 60 days.

 • Weigh 30 g of sulfaSALAzine active pharmaceutical ingredient and triturate in a mortar to a

   minutes).

   • Levigate the tablets until a smooth paste is formed. Add more vehicle to the mixture until a
   liquid is formed.

   • Transfer the contents to the graduated cylinder; use additional vehicle to rinse remaining
   drug from mortar and add to cylinder.

   shaking.

   • Shake well for at least 15 seconds before use.

   • Store at room temperature (59 to 86° F); do not freeze.

 • Discard after 30 days.

drugs.contraindications_raw:
Adverse effects reported at an incidence 2% or more and higher than placebo in a random-
   ized, controlled trial of adolescents (n=490) included hot flash (up to 2%) and tightness in neck
   of jaw (up to 2%) In a long-term, open-label study of adolescents (n=622), common treat-
   ment-related adverse events were nausea (7%), dizziness (3%), muscle tightness (3%), and
   chest discomfort (3%). A higher proportion of younger (12 to 14 years) than older (15 to 17
   years) subjects reported neck pain (6% vs 2%). In addition, a higher proportion of females than
   males reported nausea (12% vs 4%) During a long-term, open-label study of adolescents (n=622), only 1 subject with a normal
   blood pressure (BP) at baseline had a follow-up BP that met the definition of clinical hyperten-
   sion Black Box Warning
   NSAIDs cause an increased risk of serious cardiovascular thrombotic events, including myocar-
   dial infarction and stroke, which can be fatal. This risk may occur early in treatment and may
   increase with duration of use. SUMAtriptan/naproxen is contraindicated in the setting of coro-
   nary artery bypass graft (CABG) surgery. NSAIDs cause an increased risk of serious gastroin-
   testinal (GI) adverse events including bleeding, ulceration, and perforation of the stomach or
   intestines, which can be fatal. These events can occur at any time during use and without
   warning symptoms. Patients with a prior history of peptic ulcer disease and/or GI bleeding are
   at greater risk for serious GI events Monitoring
   Perform a cardiovascular evaluation in patients with multiple cardiovascular risk factors at
   baseline. Consider ECG upon administration of first dose in patients with cardiovascular risk
   factors who have a negative cardiovascular evaluation; furthermore, consider periodic cardio-
   vascular evaluation in intermittent long-term users 1

   Monitor patients for chest pain following administration Monitor renal function in patients with dehydration, mild to moderate renal impairment, or
   preexisting kidney disease 6/9
 Assess hepatic function in patients with symptoms suggestive of hepatic dysfunction or abnor-
   mal liver tests 1
   Monitor for signs and symptoms of gastrointestinal ulceration and bleeding; especially in pa-
   tients receiving concomitant low-dose aspirin for cardiac prophylaxis Monitor hematocrit and hemoglobin in patients on long-term NSAIDS and showing signs or
   symptoms suggestive of anemia 1
   Carefully monitor platelets and bleeding time in patients who may be affected by changes in
   platelet function (ie, coagulation disorders, concomitant anticoagulants) 1

   Monitor blood pressure during treatment 1

   dose based on tolerability 4

   Preparation
   Extemporaneous oral compound

   5 mg/mL suspension (60 mL) 6
   • Triturate fifteen 20-mg tablets of tadalafil to a fine powder using a mortar and pestle.
   • Mix 30 mL of Ora-Plus® with 30 mL of Ora-Sweet® to create a vehicle.

 • Add approximately 30 mL of vehicle to the mortar via geometric dilution, mix well, and trans-
   fer mixture to a 2 oz amber container.
   • Rinse mortar with vehicle and transfer to container.
   • Add enough vehicle to container to bring final volume to 60 mL.
   • Label the container with "Shake well before using."
   • Stable for 91 days at room temperature (24°C).

Tafenoquine plus chloroquine significantly lowered the risk of recurrent Plasmodium vivax
   parasitemia at 6 months by 87% (risk ratio (RR) 13; 95% CI, 08 to 22) compared with
   chloroquine alone in a meta-analysis of 3 studies (N=250). The risk of recurrence was also sig-
   nificantly lower when tafenoquine (including doses up to 2100 mg) plus chloroquine was com-
   pared to primaquine (15 mg/day over 14 days) plus chloroquine (RR 3; 95% CI, 15 to 59, 2
   trials, N=215), however there was no significant difference when 300 mg tafenoquine was used
   (RR 41; 95% CI, 15 to 14, one study). One of the 3 studies included patients aged 16 years
   or older; all trials excluded patients with G6PD deficiency, pregnant females and children The risk of recurrence at month 6 for tafenoquine plus chloroquine was reduced by 76% com-
   pared with placebo plus chloroquine (odds ratio, 24; 95% CI, 15 to 38) in a double-blind,
   randomized, controlled study. Recurrence-free efficacy was reported in 60% of patients
   treated with tafenoquine (n=260) and in 26% of patients treated with placebo (N=133). All pa-
   tients received chloroquine phosphate 600-mg free base on days 1 and 2 and 300-mg free
   base on day 3 and then either received tafenoquine 300 mg on day 1 or 2, active control, or
   placebo. The mean age of patients was 35 years (range, 16 to 79 years) Pediatric FDA Approval: Tafenoquine is indicated for the radical cure (prevention of relapse)
   of Plasmodium vivax malaria in patients 16 years or older who are receiving appropriate anti-

 malarial therapy for acute P vivax infection Not indicated for the treatment of acute P vivax as a single agent Administration

   patient’s risk prior to prescribing tapentadol and reassess all patients regularly for the devel-

   Life-Threatening Respiratory Depression:
   • Serious, life-threatening, or fatal respiratory depression may occur with use of tapentadol
   oral tablets, especially during initiation or following a dose increase. To reduce the risk of res-
   piratory depression, proper dosing and titration of tapentadol tablets are essential.
   Accidental Ingestion:

   • Accidental ingestion of even 1 dose of tapentadol oral tablets, especially by children, can re-
   sult in a fatal overdose of tapentadol.
   Risks from Concomitant Use with Benzodiazepines or Other CNS Depressants:

   • Concomitant use of opioids with benzodiazepines or other CNS depressants, including alco-
   hol, may result in profound sedation, respiratory depression, coma, and death. Reserve con-
   comitant prescribing tapentadol tablets and benzodiazepines or other CNS depressants for
   use in patients for whom alternative treatment options are inadequate.

   Neonatal Opioid Withdrawal Syndrome
   • If opioid use is required for an extended period of time in a pregnant woman, advise the pa-
   tient of the risk of NOWS, which may be life-threatening if not recognized and treated. Ensure

 the management by neonatology expert will be available at delivery.
   Opioid Analgesic Risk Evaluation and Mitigation Strategy (REMS)

   • Healthcare providers are strongly encouraged to complete a REMS-compliant education pro-
   gram and to counsel patients and caregivers on serious risks, safe use, and the importance of
   reading the Medication Guide with each prescription Monitoring
   Therapeutic Laboratory Monitoring

   • Continually reevaluate the maintenance of pain control • Evaluate the continued use of tapentadol on an ongoing basis in pediatric patients Toxic Physical Monitoring

   • Continually reevaluate the maintenance of pain control and the presence of adverse reac-
   tions • Assess risk for addiction, abuse, or misuse prior to prescribing and reassess for the develop-
   ment of these behaviors during therapy • Regularly evaluate for respiratory depression in patients with chronic pulmonary disease,
   cachectic, or debilitated patients, especially during initiation, and during titration and when
   given concomitantly with other drugs that depress respiration • Regularly evaluate for severe hypotension during initiation and titration • Monitor for sedation and respiratory depression in patients with increased intracranial pres-
   sure, brain tumors, head injury, or impaired consciousness, especially when initiating therapy • Monitor patients with hepatic impairment closely for respiratory and central nervous depres-
   sion • Monitor patients with biliary tract disease, including acute pancreatitis, for worsening symp-
   toms • Monitor patients with a history of seizure disorders for worsened seizure control during ther-
   apy

   • Disease resulting in airway compromise or affecting the nervous system

   • Ocular or periorbital infection, regardless of the time since infection onset

drugs.uses_raw:
A 24-week trial evaluated subQ teduglutide in pediatric patients 1 through 17 years of age with
   short bowel syndrome (SBS) who were dependent on parenteral support (PS). Patients re-
   ceived teduglutide 05 mg/kg/day (n=26), teduglutide 025 mg/kg/day (n=24), or standard of
   care (n=9). In patients who received teduglutide 05 mg/kg/day, 69% had a reduction in PS
   volume of at least 20%, and 12% achieved enteral autonomy. A reduction in PS infusion of at
   least 1 day/week was reported in 38%, and the mean decrease from baseline in PS volume was
   23 mL/kg/day (42% reduction). In an extension study of patients who responded (n=15), addi-
   tional treatment with 05 mg/kg/day was provided for patients who deteriorated or stopped
   improving after discontinuation of prior teduglutide treatment. Efficacy results after an addi-
   tional 24 weeks (mean total treatment, 40 weeks) were similar to those at the end of the origi-
   nal 24-week study, and 1 additional patient achieved enteral autonomy A 12-week trial evaluated 3 doses of subQ teduglutide (0.05 mg/kg/day, n=15; 025
   mg/kg/day, n=14; 0125 mg/kg/day, n=8) and standard of care (n=5) in patients 1 through 17

 years old with at least a 12-month history of SBS who were dependent on PN (parenteral nutri-
   tion and/or IV fluids). In patients who received teduglutide 05 mg/kg/day and those who re-
   ceived standard of care, respectively, results after 12 weeks showed a median PN volume re-
   duction of 3 L/week compared with no change, a daily PN infusion time of 3 fewer hours/day
   compared with no change, and a PN calorie reduction of 17 versus 1 kcal/kg/day.
   Independence from PN was achieved in 20% of patients who received teduglutide 05
   mg/kg/day. The most common adverse reactions with teduglutide 05 mg/kg/day were vomit-
   ing (47%) and fever (47%). The study was not powered for comparisons of efficacy or safety
   outcomes Pediatric FDA Approved Indictions
   Treatment of pediatric patients 1 year or older with short bowel syndrome (SBS) who are de-
   pendent on parenteral support 2

   Administration
   •For subQ injection only; do not administer by IV or IM injection Do not use the 5-mg kit in pediatric patients weighing less than 10 kg •Reconstitute with 5 mL of sterile water for injection (provided in prefilled syringe) and let
   stand for 30 seconds •Gently roll vial between palms for 15 seconds and then let stand for about 2 minutes; do not
   shake •If undissolved powder is visible, gently roll vial again; do not use product if it remains undis-
   solved after second attempt •Administer within 3 hours of reconstitution; discard unused portion 2

   •Alternate injection sites (eg, arms, thighs, and quadrants of the abdomen) 2

   •If a dose is missed, take as soon as possible on that day. Do not take 2 doses on the same day

drugs.contraindications_raw:
Adverse reactions in pediatric subjects were consistent with those observed in adults during
   clinical studies. In HIV-infected adults, common adverse reactions were rash, diarrhea,
   headache, pain, depression, asthenia, nausea (all with an incidence of greater than or equal to
   10% and grade 2 to 4 in severity) 5 , and flatulence.

   Lactic acidosis
   Lactic acidosis has been reported with tenofovir disoproxil fumarate use. Consider discontinu-
   ing ARV drugs temporarily in patients with a lactate 1 to 5 mmol/L (confirmed with second
   test) while conducting additional diagnostic work-up. In patients with a lactate 5 mmol/L or

 greater (confirmed with second test) or 10 mmol/L (any one test), discontinue all ARV drugs
   and provide supportive therapy (eg, IV fluids, sedation, respiratory support). Following resolu-
   tion of clinical and laboratory abnormalities, resume therapy with either an NRTI-sparing regi-
   men or a revised NRTI-containing regimen. Monitor lactate monthly for 3 months or more Musculoskeletal
   Osteopenia and osteoporosis has been reported with tenofovir disoproxil fumarate. To help
   prevent osteopenia or osteoporosis from occurring, ensure that the patient has sufficient in-
   take and levels of calcium and vitamin D, encourage weight-bearing exercise, minimize modifi-
   able risk factors (eg, smoking, low BMI, use of steroids or medroxyprogesterone), consider us-
   ing rilpivirine or an unboosted protease inhibitor with tenofovir disoproxil fumarate, consider
   switching tenofovir disoproxil fumarate to tenofovir alafenamide when possible, and consider
   measuring vitamin D levels and supplementing with vitamin D3 if a deficiency is identified. If
   osteopenia or osteoporosis does occur, consider switching the ARV regimen and supplement-
   ing with vitamin D3 to raise serum 25-OH-vitamin D concentrations to 30 nanograms (ng)/mL Gastrointestinal
   Pancreatitis has been reported with the use of NRTIs and ritonavir-boosted PIs; discontinue
   the offending agent and avoid reintroduction Black Box Warning
   Posttreatment exacerbation of hepatitis: Severe acute exacerbations of hepatitis have been re-
   ported in HBV-infected patients who have discontinued anti-hepatitis B therapy, including
   tenofovir disoproxil fumarate. Hepatic function should be monitored closely with both clinical
   and laboratory follow-up for a least several months in patients who discontinue anti-hepatitis
   B therapy. If appropriate, resumption of anti-hepatitis B therapy may be warranted Monitoring

      (a) If ART is initiated soon after HIV diagnosis and entry into care, repeat baseline labora-
      tory testing is not necessary.
      (b) ART is indicated for all people with HIV and should be started as soon as possible.
      However, if ART initiation is delayed, patients should be retained in care, with periodic
      monitoring as noted above.
      (c) After 2 years of consistently suppressed HIV RNA, less frequent monitoring (eg, every 6
      months) may be considered.
      (d) After 2 years of ART with consistently suppressed viral load: CD4 count 300 to 500
      cells/mm(3), monitor every 12 months; CD4 count greater than 500 cells/mm(3), CD4 mon-
      itoring is optional.
      (e) If HIV RNA is detectable at 4 to 8 weeks, repeat every 4 to 8 weeks until viral load is
      suppressed to less than 50 copies/mL, then every 3 to 6 months.
      (f) For patients on ART, viral load is typically measured every 3 to 6 months. More frequent
      monitoring may be considered in individuals having difficulties with ART adherence or at
      risk for nonadherence. However, for adherent patients with suppressed viral load and sta-
      ble immunological status for more than 1 year, monitoring can be extended to 6-month
      intervals.
      (g) Standard genotypic drug-resistance testing in ARV-naïve persons should focus on test-
      ing for mutations in the PR and RT genes. If transmitted INSTI resistance is a concern, or if
      a person has a history of INSTI use as PrEP or treatment, or a person presents with
      viremia while on an INSTI, providers should also test for resistance mutations in the IN
      gene. In ARV-naïve patients who do not immediately begin ART, repeat testing before initi-
      ation of ART is optional if drug-resistance testing was performed at entry into care. For vi-
      rologically suppressed patients who are switching therapy for toxicity or convenience, viral

 amplification will not be possible and therefore resistance testing should not be per-
      formed. Results from prior resistance testing can be used to help in the construction of a
      new regimen.
      (h) If infected with hepatitis B virus, tenofovir disoproxil fumarate or tenofovir alafe-
      namide plus either emtricitabine or lamivudine should be used as part of the ART regimen
      to treat both hepatitis B virus and HIV infections.
      (i) If HBsAg, and HBsAb, and HBcAb are negative at baseline, administer hepatitis B vac-
      cine series. Also, consult Guidelines for Opportunistic Infections.
      (j) Typically HBV infection has resolved with loss of HBsAb despite isolated HBcAb; confirm
      with an HBV viral load if wanted. A positive HBV viral load is indicative of acute infection
      (other symptoms will be present usually) or chronic infection. Vaccinate the patient when
      viral load is negative. Also, consult Guidelines for Opportunistic Infections.
      (k) In patients with recent HCV infection (acquired in last 6 months) or advanced immun-
      odeficiency (CD4 count less than 100 cells/mm(3)), the HCV antibody test may not be ade-
      quate for screening. HCV RNA screening is indicated in persons who have been success-
      fully treated for HCV or who spontaneously cleared prior infection. HCV antibody-negative
      patients with elevated ALT may need HCV RNA testing.
      (l) At-risk populations: injection drug users, persons with a history of incarceration, men
      with HIV who have unprotected sex with men, and persons with percutaneous/parenteral
      exposure to blood in unregulated settings are at risk of HCV infection.
      (m) Serum sodium, potassium, bicarbonate, chloride, blood urea nitrogen, creatinine, glu-
      cose (preferably fasting). Monitor serum phosphorus concentrations in patients with
      chronic kidney disease who are on tenofovir-containing regimens. Renal function determi-
      nation should include creatinine monitoring and estimation of the glomerular filtration
      rate.
      (n) Consult recommendations of the HIV Medicine Association of the Infectious Diseases
      Society of America for patients with renal disease. More frequent monitoring may be indi-
      cated for patients with evidence of kidney disease (eg, proteinuria or decreased glomeru-

      tension).

Pharmacology
   Tenofovir disoproxil fumarate is a nucleotide analog HIV-1 and HBV reverse transcriptase in-
   hibitor and is a prodrug that is rapidly hydrolyzed to tenofovir via plasma esterases following
   oral absorption Tenofovir is structurally, and has actions similar to adefovir 17,18 . Steady-

drugs.contraindications_raw:
Common: Nervousness (16.9% to 35%), tremor (7.8% to 38%), headache (7.5% to 8%), som-
   nolence (5.5% to 7%), and palpitations (5% to 9%) 2 ,1

   IV terbutaline decreased systolic and diastolic blood pressures by 7% to 14% and 14% to 26%,
   respectively, compared to baseline, in a retrospective review (N=124). The most pronounced
   reduction was noted in patients 0 to 6 years after 4 hours of treatment. Significant increases in
   heart rate were also observed after the first hour of administration but there were no differ-
   ences after 4 hours. Eight percent of patients required vasoactive medication to support their
   blood pressure during terbutaline infusion 10
   Hypokalemia was also reported with IV terbutaline administration. Mean potassium levels
   dropped 16% to 18% after the first 24 hours of administration; no patients required potassium
   replacement Black Box Warning
   Prolonged Tocolysis
   Terbutaline sulfate has not been approved and should not be used for prolonged tocolysis (be-
   yond 48 to 72 hours). In particular, terbutaline sulfate should not be used for maintenance to-
   colysis in the outpatient or home setting. Serious adverse reactions, including death, have
   been reported after administration of terbutaline sulfate to pregnant women. In the mother,
   these adverse reactions include increased heart rate, transient hyperglycemia, hypokalemia,
   cardiac arrhythmias, pulmonary edema and myocardial ischemia. Increased fetal heart rate
   and neonatal hypoglycemia may occur as a result of maternal administration 2 ,1 .
