 plague. If primary bubonic or pharyngeal plague has progressed to secondary pneumonic or
   septicemic plague, follow treatment recommendations for pneumonic/septicemic plague.

   • Meningitis: Dual therapy with chloramphenicol and either levoFLOXacin or moxifloxacin is rec-
   ommended. For secondary meningitis in patients already receiving antimicrobial therapy, add
   chloramphenicol to the existing regimen. Once chloramphenicol has been added, continue the
   full treatment regimen for an additional 10 days. Chloramphenicol is an appropriate choice for
   treating plague meningitis despite a relative contraindication for use in children younger than
   6 months due to the severity of the infection.
   • Pre-exposure prophylaxis: Pre-exposure prophylaxis is generally unnecessary as long as stan-
   dard and droplet precautions are maintained. Consider pre-exposure prophylaxis in cases of
   surgical mask shortages, patient overcrowding, or poor hospital ventilation. Discontinue pre-
   exposure prophylaxis 48 hours after last perceived exposure.

   • Post-exposure prophylaxis: Consider post-exposure prophylaxis for those with close (less than
   6 feet) contact with a patient with pneumonic plague who were not wearing adequate per-
   sonal protective equipment, lab workers accidentally exposed to infectious materials of not
   following standard precautions, and those in close or direct contact with infected animals (eg,
   vet staff, pet owners, hunters). Duration of post-exposure prophylaxis is 7 days.
   Breastfeeding: Mothers with pneumonic plague may continue to breastfeed if they are being
   treated and the infant is being treated or receiving post-exposure prophylaxis. If the infant is
   not being treated or received prophylaxis, mothers should avoid breastfeeding until they have

   Small intestinal bacterial overgrowth (SIBO)

   Patients presenting with signs and symptoms of SIBO pose a challenge, as there is no clear
   consensus on the definition of SIBO or optimal treatment strategies. The most commonly used
   diagnostic tests for SIBO include glucose/lactulose breath testing (non-invasive) and small
   bowel aspirate cultures (gold standard) Antibiotics used to treat SIBO include those that
   target mainly gram negative aerobic and anaerobic species (eg, Bacteroides, Enterococci,
   Coliforms, Lactobacillus). The most commonly prescribed first-line medications in SIBO include
   rifAXIMin and metroNIDAZOLE. Other common antibiotics include
   trimethoprim/sulfamethoxazole, amoxicillin/clavulanic acid, ciprofloxacin, neomycin, gentam-
   icin, doxycycline and tetracycline 9 ,18 . Repeat antibiotic courses are often needed when treat-
   ing SIBO, especially in patients with small bowel syndrome (SBS) or pediatric chronic intestinal
   pseudo-obstruction (PIPO); however, repeating antibiotic courses is based on anecdotal evi-
   dence and expert opinion. Typical antibiotic courses are given for 10 to 14 days, followed by 10
   to 14 days of an antibiotic-free period. Switching to another antibiotic or antibiotic cycling may
   be considered if there is no response to the first treatment 19,9 .
   Antibiotic cycling: Antibiotic cycling may be considered if there is no response to the initial
   treatment choice. Some example regimens include (1) 7 to 10 days of an antibiotic, followed by
   7 to 10 days with a different antibiotic and then 7 to 10 days antibiotic free, (2) 7 to 10 days of
   an antibiotic, followed by 7 to 10 days with a different antibiotic and then 7 to 10 days with an-
   other antibiotic, (3) 7 to 10 days of an antibiotic, followed by 7 to 10 days with a different an-
   tibiotic FDA Approved Pediatric Uses: Tetracycline is approved for children older than 8 years for the
   treatment of a variety of infections caused by organisms susceptible to tetracycline Administration
   Administer with an adequate amount of fluid to prevent esophageal irritation or ulceration Preparation

drugs.pharmacokinetics_summary:
Pharmacology
   THAM (Tris-Hydroxymethyl Aminomethane) is a proton acceptor that generates NH3+ and
   HCO3- without generating CO2. Volume of distribution equivalent to total body water.
   Undergoes minimal metabolism. The protonated R-NH3+ is eliminated by the kidneys.
   Approximately 75% of the dose is excreted in the urine after 8 hours. Unlike bicarbonate,
   THAM does not require an open system for CO2 elimination in order to exert its buffering ef-
   fect 1 ,2 ,3 .

drugs.uses_raw:
Thiamine deficiency disorder
   Currently there are no evidence based recommendations for treating thiamine deficiency dis-
   orders (TDD), and the doses used in practice vary widely depending on clinical manifestations
   and locally available preparations and drug dilutions in low-resource settings. The response to
   thiamine is rapid in patients presenting with cardiovascular manifestations of TDDs, with reso-
   lution of shock, irritability, tachycardia, normalization of breastfeeding, and apparent recovery
   within hours of thiamine administration. The general dosage range of thiamine in studies with
   cardiovascular-associated TDDs includes 100 mg daily to 75 mg twice daily. Results are compa-
   rable when treating patients with neurologic-associated TDDs with similar dosages. However,
   there have been cases reported of high-dose thiamine (500 mg three times daily for over 2
   months) being required for Wernicke's encephalopathy in adolescents. These findings suggest
   that higher doses and longer durations of treatment may be required for neurological mani-
   festations of TDDs 3
   Thiamine responsive disorders
   In a prospective study developing a predictive model for thiamine responsive disorders (TRD)
   in infants and young children showing signs of thiamine deficiency disorders (TDD; N=420), the
   most likely predictors of TRD and their associated increased risk in a low-resource setting in-
   cluded hoarse voice/loss of voice (58% increased risk), exclusively or predominantly breastfed
   (99% increase), cyanosis (44% increase), no eye contact (39% increase), and no diarrhea in pre-
   vious 2 weeks (59% increase). The high-resource model retained the same predictors of the
   low-resource model, with the addition of cranial ultrasound (50% increase) and the exception
   of no diarrhea in the previous 2 weeks. Infants and young children 21 days to less than 18
   months that presented with at least 1 sign or symptom consistent with TDD were eligible for
   inclusion and received thiamine 100 mg IV for at least 3 days Refeeding syndrome

   The ASPEN guidelines recommend treatment of established refeeding syndrome should be di-
   rected to correcting the underlying electrolyte abnormalities to prevent sequelae and may ad-
   ditionally include either a reduction in calories or a slowing of advancement in calories to-
   wards eventual goals. Consideration of the severity and rapidity of the electrolyte decrement
   and risk for refeeding syndrome may determine whether electrolytes should be corrected be-
   fore initiation of any calories or calorie increase. Thiamine should be administered before
   feeding commences or before initiating IV fluids containing dextrose in high-risk patients FDA-approved pediatric indications
   Thiamine is effective for the treatment of thiamine deficiency or beriberi whether of the dry
   (major symptoms related to the nervous system) or wet (major symptoms related to cardio-

 vascular system) variety. Thiamine should be used when rapid restoration of thiamine is nec-
   essary (eg, Wernicke's encephalopathy, infantile beriberi with acute collapse, CV disease due to
   thiamine deficiency, or neuritis of pregnancy if vomiting is severe Thiamine is indicated in patients with established thiamine deficiency who cannot take thi-
   amine orally due to coexisting severe anorexia, nausea, vomiting, or malabsorption Administration
   Intravenous: Infuse over at least 30 minutes to reduce the risk of anaphylactic or anaphylac-
   toid reactions Refeeding syndrome: Thiamine should be administered before feeding commences or before
   initiating IV fluids containing dextrose in patients at high-risk of refeeding syndrome Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome: If administering a glucose drip or carbohydrate load, give IV
   or IM thiamine first to prevent acute Wernicke encephalopathy Preparation for Administration

   Initiate treatment 12 weeks prior to onset of each grass pollen season and continue treatment
   throughout each season 5 years or older: One tablet SL once daily For sustained effectiveness for one grass pollen season after cessation of treatment, the tablet may
   be taken daily for 3 consecutive years
drugs.uses_raw:
Allergic rhinitis, grass pollen-induced: Subcutaneous or sublingual specific immunotherapy
   is suggested for children with allergic rhinitis First-line drug treatment includes oral antihis-
   tamines (long-acting and non-sedating) or intranasal corticosteroids 3 ,2 . Intranasal antihis-
   tamines may be considered for seasonal allergic rhinitis In a randomized, double-blind trial (n=1501), patients treated with Phleum pratense pollen ex-
   tract had significantly reduced self-rated allergic rhinoconjunctivitis symptoms and use of res-
   cue medications compared with patients who received placebo. Patients (age range, 5 to 65
   years; 9% younger than 18 years) with confirmed sensitivity to Timothy grass pollen and a
   history of grass pollen induced rhinitis, with or without conjunctivitis, received either Phleum
   pratense pollen extract or placebo SL once daily, starting approximately 3 months prior to on-
   set of the grass pollen season and continuing for the entire pollen season. Patients were al-
   lowed symptom-relieving medications such as antihistamines or corticosteroids. The daily total
   combined score (TCS) was composed of a daily symptom score and a daily medication use
   score. During the study, the daily TCS for the entire group was 23% lower in the allergen ex-
   tract treated-group compared with the placebo treated-group. In a subgroup analysis of chil-

 dren (n=283; 5 to younger than 18 years) the TCS score was 32% lower in the allergen com-
   pared with placebo group Pediatric FDA Approved Indications: Indicated in persons 5 years to 65 years of age as im-
   munotherapy for the treatment of grass pollen-induced allergic rhinitis with or without con-
   junctivitis confirmed by positive skin test or in vitro testing for pollen-specific IgE antibodies for
   Timothy grass or cross-reactive grass pollens Administration
   First dose should be administered under physician supervision, with patient observa-
   tion for at least 30 minutes after administration. Consider discontinuation of treatment in
   patients with persistent and escalating local reactions in the mouth and throat For sublingual use only. Remove tablet from blister pack immediately prior to administration.
   Place tablet under tongue and hold there until completely dissolved (approximately 1 minute),
   then swallow. Do not take tablet with food or beverages and avoid such intake for 5 minutes
   following dissolution of tablet. Wash hands after handling tablet(s)

The most common adverse effects were oral pruritus (24.4% vs 1% placebo), mouth edema
   (9.8% vs 2% placebo), and throat irritation (21.3% vs 5% placebo) in 881 pediatric patients
   (5 to 17 years of age). Systemic allergic reaction, requiring epinephrine, occurred in 1 out of
   447 pediatric patients Black Box Warning
   Timothy Grass Pollen Allergen Extract can cause life-threatening allergic reactions such as ana-
   phylaxis and severe laryngopharyngeal restriction. Do not administer Timothy Grass Pollen
   Allergen Extract to patients with severe, unstable or uncontrolled asthma, and observe pa-
   tients in the office for at least 30 minutes following the initial dose. Prescribe auto-injectable
   epinephrine, instruct and train patients on its appropriate use, and instruct patients to seek
   immediate medical care upon its use. Timothy Grass Pollen Allergen Extract may not be suit-
   able for patients with certain underlying medical conditions (eg, compromised lung function,
   significant arrhythmia) that may reduce their ability to survive a serious allergic reaction, or in
   patients who may be unresponsive to epinephrine or inhaled bronchodilators (eg, those taking
   beta-blockers, alpha-adrenergic blockers, ergot alkaloids, tricyclic antidepressants) Monitoring
   Reevaluate patients with recurrent asthma exacerbations and consider discontinuation of
   treatment

Treatment of the following infections in children older than 3 years of age 1 :

    ●   Intestinal amebiasis caused by Entamoeba histolytica.

   Administration
   • Administer with food • Tablets: May be crushed and mixed in artificial cherry syrup Preparation
   Extemporaneous oral compound 7 mg/mL oral suspension (30 mL) 1
   • Triturate four 500-mg tablets of tinidazole to a fine powder using a mortar and pestle.

   • Add approximately 10 mL of cherry syrup, mix well, and transfer mixture to a graduated am-
   ber container.
   • Transfer any remaining drug in the mortar using cherry syrup rinses to a final volume of 30
   mL.
   • Label the container with "Shake well before using."

   • Stable for 7 days at room temperature (24°C).

   Black Box Warning
   Carcinogenicity has been seen in mice and rats treated chronically with metronidazole, an-
   other nitroimidazole agent . Although such data have not been reported for tinidazole, the two
   drugs are structurally related and have similar biologic effects. Limit use of tinidazole to ap-
   proved indication only. Avoid chronic use Monitoring
   Total and differential leukocyte counts are recommended if re-treatment is required. Closely
   monitor patients if therapy continues beyond 3 days

   Risk of Thyroid C-Cell Tumors

   In rats, tirzepatide causes dose-dependent and treatment-duration-dependent thyroid C-cell
   tumors at clinically relevant exposures. It is unknown whether tirzepatide causes thyroid C-cell
   tumors, including medullary thyroid carcinoma (MTC), in humans as human relevance of
   tirzepatide induced rodent thyroid C-cell tumors has not been determined.

   Tirzepatide is contraindicated in patients with a personal or family history of MTC or in pa-
   tients with Multiple Endocrine Neoplasia syndrome type 2 (MEN 2). Counsel patients regarding
   the potential risk for MTC with the use of tirzepatide and inform them of symptoms of thyroid
   tumors (eg, a mass in the neck, dysphagia, dyspnea, persistent hoarseness). Routine monitor-
   ing of serum calcitonin or using thyroid ultrasound is of uncertain value for early detection of
   MTC in patients treated with tirzepatide Monitoring

 Therapeutic Monitoring

   • Monitor HbA1c at least twice yearly in patients who are well-controlled, every 3 months if not
   meeting treatment goals or when there is a change of therapy, or more frequently as clinically
   warranted •Perform blood glucose monitoring as needed to assist in meeting goals of therapy Toxic Monitoring

   • If serum calcitonin levels are elevated, patient should be further evaluated. Routine monitor-
   ing of serum calcitonin is of uncertain value • Monitor renal function when initiating or escalating doses and in patients reporting severe
   adverse gastrointestinal reactions, especially in patients with renal impairment that could lead
   to volume depletion • Monitor oral medications with a narrow therapeutic index (eg, warfarin) and those depen-
   dent on threshold concentrations for efficacy when used concomitantly with tirzepatide • If thyroid nodules are noted on physical exam or neck imaging, patient should further evalu-
   ated. Routine monitoring using thyroid ultrasound is of uncertain value • Carefully observe patients for signs and symptoms of pancreatitis, including persistent se-
   vere abdominal pain, sometimes radiating to the back with or without vomiting • Monitor patients with a history of diabetic retinopathy for progression of disease

   with tobramycin inhalation solution compared with placebo-treated patients In patients
   treated with either tobramycin inhalation powder or inhalation solution, more patients treated
   with tobramycin inhalation powder developed cough (48.4% vs 1%), lung disorder (33.8% vs 1%; including pulmonary or cystic fibrosis exacerbations), dyspnea (15.6% vs 4%), pyrexia
   (15.6% vs 4%), oropharyngeal pain (14% vs 5%), dysphonia (13.6% vs 8%), chest discom-
   fort (6.5% vs 9%), or throat irritation (4.5% vs 9%) than patients administered tobramycin
   inhalation solution Common adverse reactions (less than 3%) associated with the ophthalmic preparations are hy-
   persensitivity and localized ocular toxicity, including lid itching and swelling, and conjunctival
   erythema Black Box Warning
   Warnings
   •Patients treated with tobramycin injection and other aminoglycosides should be under close
   clinical observation, because these drugs have an inherent potential for causing ototoxicity

 and nephrotoxicity •Neurotoxicity, manifested as both auditory and vestibular ototoxicity, can occur. The auditory
   changes are irreversible, are usually bilateral, and may be partial or total. Eighth nerve impair-
   ment and nephrotoxicity may develop, primarily in patients having preexisting renal damage
   and in those with normal renal function to whom aminoglycosides are administered for longer
   periods or in higher doses than those recommended. Other manifestations of neurotoxicity
   may include numbness , skin tingling, muscle twitching, and convulsions. The risk of aminogly-
   coside-induced hearing loss increases with the degree of exposure to either high peak or high
   trough serum concentrations. Patients who develop cochlear damage may not have symptoms
   during therapy to warn them of eighth-nerve toxicity, and partial or total irreversible bilateral
   deafness may continue to develop after the drug has been discontinued •Rarely, nephrotoxicity may not become apparent until the first few days after cessation of
   therapy. Aminoglycoside-induced nephrotoxicity usually is reversible •Renal and eighth-nerve function should be closely monitored in patients with known or sus-
   pected renal impairment and also in those whose renal function is initially normal but who de-
   velop signs of renal dysfunction during therapy. Peak and trough serum concentrations of
   aminoglycosides should be monitored periodically during therapy to assure adequate levels
   and to avoid potentially toxic levels. Prolonged serum concentrations above 12 mcg/mL should
   be avoided. Rising trough levels (above 2 mcg/mL) may indicate tissue accumulation. Such ac-
   cumulation, excessive peak concentrations, advanced age, and cumulative dose may contrib-
   ute to ototoxicity and nephrotoxicity. Urine should be examined for decreased specific gravity
   and increased excretion of protein, cells, and casts. Blood urea nitrogen, serum creatinine, and
   creatinine clearance should be measured periodically. When feasible, it is recommended that
   serial audiograms be obtained in patients old enough to be tested, particularly high-risk pa-
   tients. Evidence of impairment of renal, vestibular, or auditory function requires discontinua-
   tion of the drug or dosage adjustment •Tobramycin injection should be used with caution in premature and neonatal infants because
   of their renal immaturity and the resulting prolongation of serum half-life of the drug •Concurrent and sequential use of other neurotoxic and/or nephrotoxic antibiotics, particularly
   other aminoglycosides (e.g., amikacin, streptomycin, neomycin, kanamycin, gentamicin, and
   paromomycin), cephaloridine, viomycin, polymyxin B, colistin, cisplatin, and vancomycin,
   should be avoided. Other factors that may increase patient risk are advanced age and dehy-
   dration •Aminoglycosides should not be given concurrently with potent diuretics, such as ethacrynic
   acid and furosemide. Some diuretics themselves cause ototoxicity, and intravenously adminis-

 tered diuretics enhance aminoglycoside toxicity by altering antibiotic concentrations in serum
   and tissue •Aminoglycosides can cause fetal harm when administered to a pregnant woman Solution Compatibility
   D5W, D10W, and NS.

   Terminal Injection Site Compatibility
   Acyclovir, alprostadil, amiodarone, aztreonam, calcium gluconate, cefoxitin, ceftazidime, clin-
   damycin, dopamine, enalaprilat, esmolol, fluconazole, furosemide, insulin, heparin (concentra-
   tions less than or equal to 1 unit/mL), linezolid, magnesium sulfate, metronidazole, midazolam,
   milrinone, morphine, nafcillin, nicardipine, ranitidine, remifentanil, theophylline, and
   zidovudine.

   Terminal Injection Site Incompatibility
   Ampicillin, azithromycin, cefepime, imipenem/cilastatin, indomethacin, heparin (concentra-
   tions greater than 1 unit/mL), mezlocillin, oxacillin, penicillin G, propofol, and
   ticarcillin/clavulanate.

   Monitoring
   Measure serum concentrations after 2 or 3 doses and at 3 to 4 day intervals during treatment.
   Obtain peak concentration 30 minutes after end of infusion or 1 hour after an intramuscular
   injection, and trough concentration just prior to the next dose For once-daily dosing, a
   peak/MIC ratio of at least 10:1 has been suggested For once-daily dosing in CF patients, an
   AUC target of 100 mg x hr/mL, or a trough less than 1 mcg/mL has been suggested 42,5 .
   Obtaining one level at least one hour after a 1-hour infusion and another level 8 to 12 hours
   later and extrapolating data to determine peak and trough has also been suggested When
   treating patients with serious infections or significantly changing fluid or renal status, consider
   measuring the serum concentration more frequently Monitor serum calcium, magnesium, and sodium periodically during therapy. Obtain urinalysis
   to assess for decreased specific gravity and increased excretion of protein, cells, and casts.

 Renal and auditory function should be closely monitored, especially in patients with renal im-
   pairment. Serial audiograms are recommended for patients old enough to be tested Inhalation:
   One hour after administration of the inhalation solution, serum levels range from 06 to 89
   mcg/mL in patients with normal renal function; routine monitoring is not necessary. Patients
   with impaired renal function may require monitoring of serum levels 35,34 .

   One hour after administration of the inhalation powder, serum tobramycin concentrations are
   approximately 1 to 2 mcg/mL . Routine monitoring is not necessary; however, discontinue

   Risk of Serious Infection

   for developing serious infections that may lead to hospitalization or death. Most patients who
   developed these infections were taking concomitant immunosuppressants such as methotrex-
   ate or corticosteroids • If a serious infection develops, interrupt tocilizumab-aazg until the infection is controlled • Reported infections include: Active tuberculosis, which may present with pulmonary or ex-
   trapulmonary disease. Patients should be tested for latent tuberculosis before tocilizumab-
   aazg use and during therapy. Treatment for latent infection should be initiated prior to
   tocilizumab-aazg use. Invasive fungal infections, including candidiasis, aspergillosis, and
   pneumocystosis. Patients with invasive fungal infections may present with disseminated,
   rather than localized, disease. Bacterial, viral and other infections due to opportunistic
   pathogens • The risks and benefits of treatment with tocilizumab-aazg should be carefully considered
   prior to initiating therapy in patients with chronic or recurrent infection • Patients should be closely monitored for the development of signs and symptoms of infec-
   tion during and after treatment with tocilizumab-aazg, including the possible development of
   tuberculosis in patients who tested negative for latent tuberculosis infection prior to initiating
   therapy Monitoring

   cate liver injury • Monitor for signs and symptoms of infection, including TB, during and after treatment • During treatment for polyarticular juvenile idiopathic arthritis, monitor absolute neutrophil
   count, platelet count, ALT levels, and AST levels at the time of second infusion and every 4 to 8

   or corticosteroids.
   • If a serious infection develops, interrupt tocilizumab-bavi until the infection is controlled.

   tocilizumab-bavi use. Invasive fungal infections, including candidiasis, aspergillosis, and
   pneumocystosis. Patients with invasive fungal infections may present with disseminated,
   rather than localized, disease. Bacterial, viral and other infections due to opportunistic
   pathogens.

   prior to initiating therapy in patients with chronic or recurrent infection.

   tion during and after treatment with tocilizumab-bavi, including the possible development of
   tuberculosis in patients who tested negative for latent tuberculosis infection prior to initiating
   therapy Monitoring

   • Monitor absolute neutrophil and platelet counts at the time of second infusion and every 2 to

   • Evaluate for TB risk factors and test for latent TB prior to initiation • Monitor for signs and symptoms of infection, including TB, during and after treatment • Monitor for signs and symptoms of demyelinating disorders • Evaluate new onset abdominal symptoms for development of gastrointestinal perforation 1
   • Observe for symptoms that may indicate liver injury, including fatigue, anorexia, right upper
   abdominal discomfort, dark urine, or jaundice

Common, adult: Upper respiratory tract infection, nasopharyngitis, diarrhea, headache, hy-
   pertension 3
   Adverse drug reactions in patients with polyarticular course juvenile idiopathic arthritis were
   consistent with those seen in adult rheumatoid arthritis patients 3

   Black Box Warning
   Serious Infections 1
    ●   Patients treated with tofacitinib are at increased risk for developing serious infections that
        may lead to hospitalization or death. Most patients who develop these infections were tak-
        ing concomitant immunosuppressants such as methotrexate or corticosteroids.
    ●   If a serious infection develops, interrupt tofacitinib until the infection is controlled.
    ●   Reported infections include:
    ●   Active tuberculosis, which may present with pulmonary or extrapulmonary disease. Patients
        should be tested for latent tuberculosis before tofacitinib use and during therapy.
        Treatment for latent infection should be initiated prior to tofacitinib use.
    ●   Invasive fungal infections, including cryptococcosis and pneumocystosis. Patients with inva-
        sive fungal infections may present with disseminated, rather than localized, disease.
    ●   Bacterial, viral, including herpes zoster, and other infections due to opportunistic
        pathogens.
    ●   The risks and benefits of treatment with tofacitinib should be carefully considered prior to
        initiating therapy in patients with chronic or recurrent infection.
    ●   Patients should be closely monitored for the development of signs and symptoms of infec-
        tion during and after treatment with tofacitinib, including the possible development of tu-
        berculosis in patients who tested negative for latent tuberculosis infection prior to initiating
        therapy.

   Mortality 1

 ●   In a large, randomized, postmarketing safety study in rheumatoid arthritis (RA) patients 50
        years of age and older with at least one cardiovascular (CV) risk factor comparing tofacitinib
        5 mg twice a day or tofacitinib 10 mg twice a day to tumor necrosis factor (TNF) blockers, a
        higher rate of all-cause mortality, including sudden cardiovascular death, was observed with
        tofacitinib 5 mg twice a day or tofacitinib 10 mg twice a day. Tofacitinib oral tablets/oral so-
        lution 10 mg twice daily (or a tofacitinib extended-release tablet 22 mg once daily) dosage is
        not recommended for the treatment of RA or PsA.

   Malignancies 1
    ●   Malignancies, including lymphomas and solid tumors, have occurred in patients treated
        with tofacitinib and other Janus kinase inhibitors used to treat inflammatory conditions. In
        RA patients, a higher rate of malignancies (excluding NMSC) was observed in patients
        treated with tofacitinib 5 mg twice a day or tofacitinib 10 mg twice a day compared with TNF
        blockers.
    ●   Lymphomas and lung cancers were observed at a higher rate in patients treated with tofaci-
        tinib 5 mg twice a day or tofacitinib 10 mg twice a day in RA patients compared to those
        treated with TNF blockers. Patients who are current or past smokers are at additional in-
        creased risk.

   Major Adverse Cardiovascular Events 1
    ●   RA patients 50 years of age and older with at least one cardiovascular risk factor, treated
        with tofacitinib 5 mg twice daily or tofacitinib 10 mg twice daily, had a higher rate of major
        adverse cardiovascular events (MACE) (defined as cardiovascular death, myocardial infarc-
        tion, and stroke), compared to those treated with TNF blockers. Patients who are current or
        past smokers are at additional increased risk. Discontinue tofacitinib in patients that have
        experienced a myocardial infarction or stroke.

   Thrombosis 1
    ●   Thrombosis, including pulmonary embolism, deep venous thrombosis, and arterial throm-
        bosis have occurred in patients treated with tofacitinib and other Janus kinase inhibitors
        used to treat inflammatory conditions. Many of these events were serious and some re-
        sulted in death. RA patients 50 years of age and older with at least one cardiovascular risk
        factor treated with tofacitinib 5 mg twice daily or tofacitinib 10 mg twice daily compared to
        TNF blockers had an observed increase in incidence of these events. Avoid tofacitinib in pa-
        tients at risk. Discontinue tofacitinib and promptly evaluate patients with symptoms of
        thrombosis

drugs.contraindications_raw:
In epilepsy clinical trials, cognitive/neuropsychiatric adverse reactions (ie, psychomotor
   slowing, concentration/attention difficulty, speech disorders/related speech problems, and
   language problems) were reported more often in adults than pediatric patients. In pediatric
   patients, the most frequently reported neuropsychiatric reactions were somnolence and fa-
   tigue (adjunctive therapy) and headache, dizziness, anorexia, and somnolence (monotherapy) .
   In migraine studies, cognitive adverse effects (most commonly, difficulty with
   concentration/attention) were dose-dependent, particularly at the 200 mg dose. The effects
   occurred more often in younger patients (6 to 11 years of age) compared with older patients
   (12 to 17 years of age). Although most common during titration phase, at times it persisted
   into the maintenance phase. The data suggests topiramate may result in psychomotor slowing
   and decreased verbal fluency 1 ,7 ,8 . Topiramate 100 mg/day demonstrated worsening of 5-
   choice reaction time (p=0.028), pattern recognition memory (p=0.027), and rapid visual infor-
   mation processing (p=0.04) as compared with placebo based upon results from the Cambridge
   Neuropsychological Test Automated Battery (CANTAB) administered at baseline and study end
   in a randomized, placebo-controlled, double-blind trial of migraineurs (n=103; age 12 to 17
   years). A dose of 50 mg/day caused worsening of the controlled oral word association (ani-
   mals) portion of the CANTAB (p=0.012) as compared with placebo In children 2 to 16 years of age who received recommended doses of topiramate, the most
   common adverse effects reported were aggressive reaction (9%), abnormal gait (8%), anorexia
   (9% to 24%), ataxia (6%), diarrhea (2% to 98%), concentration/attention difficulty (2% to 15%),
   difficulty with memory (3% to 8%), dizziness (4% to 6%), fatigue (7% to 16%), fever (1% to 12%),
   insomnia (2% to 9%), nausea (6% to 8%), mood problems (1% to 8%), personality
   disorder/behavior problems (3% to 11%), nervousness (14%), paresthesia (3% to 382%), pur-
   pura (8%), rhinitis (5% to 8%), somnolence (2% to 26%), upper respiratory infection (16% to
   26%), and weight loss (7% to 17%) 1 , 7 , In infants less than 2 years of age, appetite loss,
   drowsiness, lethargy, hyperthermia (during summer months), irritability, nervousness, and
   weight loss were observed 16,17,18,19 .
   Eating disorders developed or were exacerbated in 7 female adolescents after starting topira-
   mate for the treatment of migraine or chronic headache Persistent treatment-emergent decreases in serum bicarbonate (metabolic acidosis) have
   been reported in 89% of infants (5 months to 3 years) 56 , up to 67% of children (2 to 16
   years), and up to 77 of adolescents receiving topiramate Abnormally low serum bicarbonate
   levels (absolute value less than 17 mEq/L and greater than 5 mEq/L decrease from baseline)
   occurred in 33% of infants 56 , 1% to 11% of children, and 2% to 6% of adolescents receiving
   topiramate Effects on acid-base balance appear to be dose-related 56 , Compensated, nor-
   mal anion gap, metabolic acidosis, and hypokalemia were reported during long-term treat-
   ment (greater than 12 months) with topiramate in a study of 24 children (4.6 to 19 years). No

 significant correlations were found between topiramate dosage or duration and bicarbonate
   or potassium levels Asymptomatic kidney stones were reported to develop in 2% of children who had received
   topiramate for at least 12 months in an observational study from Saudi Arabia (n=96; mean
   age 9 +/- 8 years). Of note, all the children who developed stones were younger than 7
   years. The baseline prevalence of kidney stones in this populations is 367% Monitoring
   Monitor for hyperthermia and decreased sweating, especially in hot weather. Monitor for new-
   onset or worsening depression, suicidal thoughts or behavior, and/or any unusual changes in
   mood or behavior. Measure serum bicarbonate levels at baseline and periodically during treat-
   ment. Seizures or increased seizure frequency should be monitored in patients with or without
   a history of epilepsy if rapid withdrawal of topiramate therapy is required. Examination of am-
   monia levels is recommended in any patient experiencing unexplained lethargy, vomiting, or
   changes in mental status, which may be indicative of hyperammonemia with or without en-

In a study of single-dose traMADol for postsurgical pain in children (n=80; age range, 7 to 16
   years), the incidence of adverse events was small with the following as the most commonly re-
   ported events: vomiting (10%), nausea (9%), fever (7%), pruritus (7%), and rash (4%) Other
   effects reported in children include somnolence, constipation, and urinary retention 28,11 .

   Black Box Warning
   Warnings Addiction, abuse, and misuse; risk evaluation and mitigation strategy (REM); life-
   threatening respiratory depression; accidental ingestion; ultra-rapid metabolism of tramadol
   and other risk factors for life-threatening respiratory depression in children; neonatal opioid
   withdrawal syndrome; interactions with drugs affecting CYP P450 isoenzymes; and risks from
   concomitant use with benzodiazepines or other CNS depressants 19 , 20 :
    ●   Addiction, Abuse, and Misuse
    ●   Tramadol hydrochloride exposes patients and other users to the risks of opioid addiction,
        abuse, and misuse, which can lead to overdose and death. Assess each patient's risk prior
        to prescribing tramadol hydrochloride, and monitor all patients regularly for the develop-
        ment of these behaviors and conditions
    ●   Opioid Analgesic Risk Evaluation and Mitigation Strategy (REMS)

 ●   To ensure that the benefits of opioid analgesics outweigh the risks of addiction, abuse, and
        misuse, the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) has required a REMS for these products.
        Under the requirements of the REMS, drug companies with approved opioid analgesic prod-
        ucts must make REMS compliant education programs available to healthcare providers.
        Healthcare providers are strongly encouraged to:
    ●   complete a REMS-compliant education program,
    ●   counsel patients and/or their caregivers, with every prescription, on safe use, serious risks,
        storage, and disposal of these products,
    ●   emphasize to patients and their caregivers the importance of reading the Medication Guide
        every time it is provided by their pharmacist, and
    ●   Consider other tools to improve patient, household, and community safety
    ●   Life-Threatening Respiratory Depression
    ●   Serious, life-threatening, or fatal respiratory depression may occur with use of tramadol hy-
        drochloride. Monitor for respiratory depression, especially during initiation of tramadol hy-
        drochloride or following a dose increase. Instruct patients to swallow tramadol extended re-
        lease formulas intact, and not to cut, break, chew, crush or dissolve the tablets or capsules
        to avoid exposure to a potentially fatal dose of tramadol.
    ●   Accidental Ingestion
    ●   Accidental ingestion of tramadol hydrochloride, especially by children, can result in a fatal
        overdose of tramadol. One dose of extended-release tramadol can be fatal, particularly in
        children.
    ●   Ultra-Rapid Metabolism Of Tramadol And Other Risk Factors For Life-Threatening
        Respiratory Depression In Children
    ●   Life-threatening respiratory depression and death have occurred in children who received
        tramadol. Some of the reported cases followed tonsillectomy and/or adenoidectomy; in at
        least one case, the child had evidence of being an ultra-rapid metabolizer of tramadol due
        to a CYP2D6 polymorphism. Tramadol hydrochloride is contraindicated in children younger
        than 12 years of age and in children younger than 18 years of age following tonsillectomy
        and/or adenoidectomy. Avoid the use of tramadol hydrochloride in adolescents 12 to 18
        years of age who have other risk factors that may increase their sensitivity to the respiratory
        depressant effects of tramadol
    ●   Neonatal Opioid Withdrawal Syndrome
    ●   Prolonged use of tramadol hydrochloride during pregnancy can result in neonatal opioid
        withdrawal syndrome, which may be life-threatening if not recognized and treated, and re-
        quires management according to protocols developed by neonatology experts. If opioid use

 is required for a prolonged period in a pregnant woman, advise the patient of the risk of
        neonatal opioid withdrawal syndrome and ensure that appropriate treatment will be
        available
    ●   Interactions with Drugs Affecting Cytochrome P450 Isoenzymes
    ●   The effects of concomitant use or discontinuation of cytochrome P450 3A4 inducers, 3A4 in-
        hibitors, or 2D6 inhibitors with tramadol are complex. Use of cytochrome P450 3A4 induc-
        ers, 3A4 inhibitors, or 2D6 inhibitors with tramadol hydrochloride requires careful consider-
        ation of the effects on the parent drug, tramadol, and the active metabolite, M1
    ●   Risks from Concomitant Use with Benzodiazepines or Other CNS Depressants
    ●   Concomitant use of opioids with benzodiazepines or other central nervous system (CNS) de-
        pressants, including alcohol, may result in profound sedation, respiratory depression, coma,
        and death.
    ●   Reserve concomitant prescribing of tramadol hydrochloride and benzodiazepines or other
        CNS depressants for use in patients for whom alternative treatment options are
        inadequate.
    ●   Limit dosages and durations to the minimum required.
    ●   Follow patients for signs and symptoms of respiratory depression and sedation

   Monitoring
   Monitor patients for respiratory depression, particularly within the first 24 to 72 hours of ther-
   apy initiation and after dose increases, and especially in the cachectic, debilitated, and those
   with chronic pulmonary disease or with concomitant use of other drugs that cause respiratory
   depression Monitor for signs and symptoms of hypotension following treatment initiation or titration in
   patients with compromised ability to maintain blood pressure (eg, reduced blood volume or
   concurrent CNS depressant treatment) Assess for worsened seizure control in patients with history of seizure disorders 18

   Assess patient for suicidal ideation and unusual behavior or worsening depression Monitor for signs of sedation and respiratory depression in patients susceptible to intracranial
   effects of carbon dioxide retention (eg, preexisting intracranial pressure, brain tumors, or head
   injuries), especially during initiation of therapy Monitor for worsening of symptoms in patients with biliary tract disease, including acute pan-
   creatitis 5

drugs.uses_raw:
Chronic Insomnia in Neurodevelopmental Disorders (NDDs)

   Unspecified NDDs: First-line therapy for chronic insomnia in children with NDDs are sleep hy-
   giene strategies, which should be continued when pharmacotherapy is added. Choice of ther-
   apy is typically determined on a case-by-case basis; traZODone may be considered in select
   children with NDDs refractory to other agents TraZODone was the third-most frequently
   prescribed medication for children with chronic insomnia and NDDs, after melatonin and non-

 prescription antihistamines. Anecdotal reports suggest traZODone may be helpful for patients
   with midnight and terminal insomnia, specifically Insomnia in Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD): Data about efficacy of traZODone for treat-
   ment of insomnia in ASD patients are scarce, but its use is common; one clinicians' survey
   found that traZODone was used in 5% of cases. TraZODone may be effective for insomnia
   in ASD, especially in children who have not benefited from other sleep medications; it in-
   creases slow-wave sleep, shortens sleep latency, and improves sleep continuity, with limited
   REM suppression. The hypnotic effect of traZODone occurs at lower doses than those used for
   antidepressant effects 4

   Insomnia and Rage Attacks in Opsoclonus-Myoclonus Syndrome: Oral traZODone signifi-
   cantly improved insomnia and reduced rage attacks in an observational study of children with
   opsoclonus-myoclonus syndrome (N=51). Hours of sleep per night increased from 7 hours at
   baseline to 8 hours post-treatment. The number of nighttime awakenings was reduced from 1 to 97, and rage scores (index of frequency/severity of rage attacks) decreased from 3 to 2. The mean traZODone dose was 3 mg/kg/day and patients were treated for a mean of 1
   years. TraZODone was well-tolerated across all ages (mean, 3 years old; range, 7 to 17
   years old) FDA-Approved Pediatric Indications

   Safety and effectiveness in pediatric patients have not been established 1 ,8

   Administration
   •Swallow whole; tablets may be broken in half at the score line; do not crush or chew 1 ,8 .

   •Take shortly after a meal or light snack 1 , •May administer a major portion of the daily dose at bedtime or reduce dose to minimize
   drowsiness 1 ,8 .

   Preparation
   Extemporaneous oral compound

   10 mg/mL suspension (100 mL) 9

   • Measure and/or weight out 1000 mg of trazodone tablets.

   • Triturate tablets into a fine powder in a mortar with a pestle.

   • Incorporate 100 mL of cherry syrup in geometric portions to the powder. Mix well.

 • Package in a tight, light resistant container with a beyond use date of 30 days.

drugs.uses_raw:
Atopic dermatitis, active inflammatory disease: For acute flares, use of topical corticos-
   teroids is recommended daily until inflammatory lesions are significantly improved and less
   thick, for up to several weeks at a time. During significant flares, the use of mid- or higher po-
   tency topical corticosteroids for short courses may be appropriate to gain rapid control of
   symptoms Atopic dermatitis, relapse prevention: In patients who experience frequent, repeat out-
   breaks at the same body site, maintenance therapy with topical corticosteroids once to twice
   weekly may reduce the rates of relapse and increase the time to first flare relative to the use of

 moisturizers alone. For long-term management, the least potent corticosteroid that is effective
   should be used to minimize the risk of adverse effects Infantile hemangioma

   Guidelines: Intralesional injection of betamethasone or triamcinolone or a combination of
   both may be used to treat focal, bulky infantile hemangiomas during proliferation or in certain
   critical anatomic locations, such as the lip or nose. Local skin adverse effects, such as dermal
   atrophy or pigmentary changes, failure to thrive, and transient Cushingoid features are com-
   mon adverse events with intralesional administration Evidence:

   •A meta-analysis of 22 studies found that 71% of subjects treated with intralesional corticos-
   teroid injection (mostly with triamcinolone monotherapy or triamcinolone plus betametha-
   sone) achieved greater than 75% regression in infantile hemangioma size •The combination of a high-potency steroid (betamethasone) and a long-acting steroid (triam-
   cinolone) may maximize early regression and decrease rebound growth 5 , as well reduce the
   required number of injections and risk of side effects FDA-approved pediatric indications

   Cream, lotion, ointment, or spray: Triamcinolone cream, lotion, ointment, and spray are ap-
   proved for the relief of inflammatory and pruritic symptoms of corticosteroid-responsive der-
   matoses 8 , 10 , 12 , Triamcinolone injection is approved for the following indications when oral therapy is not
   feasible 3 :
   •Severe allergic conditions nonresponsive to conventional therapy including: seasonal or
   perennial allergic rhinitis, asthma, atopic or contact dermatitis, drug hypersensitivity reactions
   and serum sickness, and transfusion reactions 3

   •Dermatologic diseases: Bullous dermatitis herpetiformis, exfoliative erythroderma, mycosis
   fungoides, pemphigus, severe erythema multiforme (Stevens-Johnson syndrome) 3
   •Intralesional treatment of alopecia areata, keloids, discoid lupus erythematosus, localized hy-
   pertrophic, infiltrated, inflammatory lesions of granuloma annulare, lichen planus, lichen sim-
   plex chronicus (neurodermatitis), and psoriatic plaques, necrobiosis lipoidica diabeticorum 13
   •Endocrine disorders: Congenital adrenal hyperplasia, hypercalcemia associated with cancer,
   and nonsuppurative thyroiditis 3

 •Gastrointestinal diseases: Regional enteritis and ulcerative colitis, to tide the patient over a
   critical part of the disease 3
   •Hematologic disorders: Autoimmune hemolytic anemia, Diamond-Blackfan anemia, pure red
   cell aplasia, and selected cases of secondary thrombocytopenia 3

   •Trichinosis with neurologic or myocardial involvement 3
   •Tuberculosis meningitis with subarachnoid block or impending block when used in conjunc-
   tion with appropriate antituberculous therapy 3

   •Neoplastic diseases: Palliative management of lymphomas or leukemias 3

   •Nervous system diseases: Acute exacerbations of multiple sclerosis, cerebral edema associ-
   ated with primary or metastatic brain tumor or craniotomy 3
   •Ophthalmic diseases: Sympathetic ophthalmia, temporal arteritis, uveitis, and ocular inflam-
   matory conditions unresponsive to topical corticosteroids 3
   •Renal diseases: To induce diuresis or remission of proteinuria in patients with idiopathic
   nephrotic syndrome or that due to lupus erythematosus 3

   •Respiratory diseases: Berylliosis, fulminating or disseminating pulmonary tuberculosis when
   used concurrently with appropriate antituberculosis chemotherapy, idiopathic eosinophilic
   pneumonias, and symptomatic sarcoidosis 3
   •Rheumatic disorders: Short-term administration in the treatment of acute rheumatic carditis,
   ankylosing spondylitis, psoriatic arthritis, dermatomyositis, and polymyositis; systemic lupus
   erythematosus 3
   •Intraarticular injection is indicated for the adjunctive short-term treatment of acute and suba-
   cute bursitis 3

   •Intraarticular injection is indicated for the adjunctive short-term treatment of tenosynovitis or
   epicondylitis 3
   • IM or intraarticular administration is indicated as adjunctive, short-term therapy in acute
   gouty arthritis to tide the patient over an acute episode or exacerbation 3
   •IM or intraarticular administration is indicated as adjunctive therapy for the short-term treat-
   ment of rheumatoid arthritis 3

   • IM or intraarticular administration is indicated as adjunctive therapy for the short-term treat-
   ment of synovitis of osteoarthritis 3

   Administration

 Injectable suspension

   General information

   •Not for IV, intradermal, intraocular, epidural, or intrathecal use 14
   •Shake vial well before using; use immediately after withdrawing from vial to prevent settling
   in the syringe 3

   Intralesional Injection

   •Determine volume needed to deliver drug throughout lesion 15
   •Infantile hemangioma: Inject directly into lesion, around the edge of the lesion, or both, using a
   27- or 30-gauge needle; multiple injections at different sites may be needed for a single lesion.
   Advance needle tip into lesion, withdraw plunger gently, and if no blood returns, slowly inject
   the steroid over 1 minute. Apply pressure to stop any bleeding •Other skin lesions: Inject using tuberculin syringe with 23- to 25 gauge needle Intramuscular injection

   •Inject deeply into gluteal muscle; minimum needle length for nonobese adults is 5 inches 3

   •Rotate injection sites for subsequent injections 3

   Local Injection

   •Intraarticular: If excessive synovial fluid in joint, remove some, but not all, prior to steroid in-
   jection. Prior local anesthetic use may be desirable. Avoid injecting suspension into tissues sur-
   rounding site as this may cause tissue atrophy •Epicondylitis: Infiltrate suspension into area of greatest tenderness •Tenosynovitis: Inject into tendon sheath, not the tendon substance Topical
   General information

   •Massage gently after application until medication disappears 8 ,10,12,11

   •Do not use with occlusive dressings unless directed by a physician 8 , 10 , 12 , 11

   •Avoid contact with eyes 8 ,10,12,11
   Spray

   •Do not use on the underarm or groin areas unless directed by a physician 12

 •When using spray on face, cover eyes and avoid inhalation of the spray 12
   •Aerosol spray is flammable; avoid heat, flame, or smoking during and immediately following
   application 12

drugs.pharmacokinetics_summary:
Pharmacology
   Mechanism of action: Triamcinolone is a synthetic steroid with anti-inflammatory, antipru-
   ritic, and vasoconstrictive actions. The mechanism of anti-inflammatory activity of the topical
   corticosteroids is unclear but involves activity on T lymphocytes, monocytes, macrophages,
   and dendritic cells, interfering with antigen processing and suppressing the release of pro-in-
   flammatory cytokines 2 ,8 ,10,12,11 .

   fined as a resolution of symptoms, normalization of eosinophil count, and improvement in ul-
   trasound appearances at 3 months post-treatment. At the day of discharge from hospital (day
   10), the percentage of patients that were free of abdominal pain was significantly lower in the
   triclabendazole group compared to the artesunate group (88% vs 100%). Patients were ran-
   domized to receive either 2 doses of triclabendazole 10 mg/kg given 12 hours apart with food
   or artesunate 4 mg/kg/day for 10 days 2

   FDA Pediatric Approved Indictions

   Triclabendazole is indicated for the treatment of fascioliasis in patients 6 years or older Administration
   •Take with food 1

   Guidelines: Topical therapies are recommended as first-line agents for mild, moderate, or se-
   vere acne as initial or maintenance monotherapy or in combination with other topical or oral
   agents. When managing acne with topical therapies, multimodal therapy combining multiple
   mechanisms of action is recommended to optimize efficacy and to reduce the risk of antibiotic
   resistance. Topical agents with strong recommendations include topical retinoids, benzoyl per-
   oxide, and topical antibiotics. Agents with conditional recommendations include clascoterone,
   salicylic acid, and azelaic acid In 2 large randomized trials of patients 9 years or older with moderate facial and truncal acne,
   12 weeks of treatment with topical trifarotene compared with vehicle significantly improved fa-
   cial success rates (29.4% vs 5% in PERFECT 1 [N=1208] and 3% vs 7% in PERFECT 2
   [N=1212]) and truncal success rates (35.7% vs 25% and 6% vs 9%). Facial success was de-
   termined by Investigator’s Global Assessment (IGA) and truncal success was determined by
   Physician’s Global Assessment (PGA); both IGA and PGA successes were defined as a rating of
   clear or almost clear and at least a 2-grade change from baseline. IGA facial success rates were
   significantly improved with trifarotene at week 4 in PERFECT 1 and week 8 in PERFECT 2, and
   PGA truncal success rates were significantly improved with trifarotene at 8 weeks in both trials.
   Facial and truncal lesions counts were also significantly reduced with trifarotene (see table).

   Black Box Warning
   Serious Infections, Mortality, Malignancy, Major Adverse Cardiovascular Events, and
   Thrombosis
   Serious Infections
    ●   Patients treated with upadacitinib are at increased risk for developing serious infections
        that may lead to hospitalization or death. Most patients who developed these infections
        were taking concomitant immunosuppressants such as methotrexate or corticosteroids. If a
        serious infection develops, interrupt upadacitinib until the infection is controlled. Reported
        infections include:
    ●   Active tuberculosis, which may present with pulmonary or extrapulmonary disease. Patients
        should be tested for latent tuberculosis before upadacitinib use and during therapy.
        Treatment for latent infection should be considered prior to upadacitinib use.
    ●   Invasive fungal infections, including cryptococcosis and pneumocystosis.
    ●   Bacterial, viral, including herpes zoster, and other infections due to opportunistic
        pathogens.
    ●   The risks and benefits of treatment with upadacitinib should be carefully considered prior
        to initiating therapy in patients with chronic or recurrent infection.
    ●   Patients should be closely monitored for the development of signs and symptoms of infec-
        tion during and after treatment with upadacitinib, including the possible development of tu-
        berculosis in patients who tested negative for latent tuberculosis infection prior to initiating
        therapy
   Mortality
    ●   In a large, randomized, postmarketing safety study in rheumatoid arthritis (RA) patients 50
        years of age and older with at least one cardiovascular risk factor comparing another Janus
        kinase (JAK) inhibitor to tumor necrosis factor (TNF) blockers, a higher rate of all-cause mor-
        tality, including sudden cardiovascular death, was observed with the JAK inhibitor.

 Malignancies
    ●      Lymphoma and other malignancies have been observed in patients treated with upadaci-
           tinib. In RA patients treated with another JAK inhibitor, a higher rate of malignancies (exclud-
           ing non-melanoma skin cancer (NMSC)) was observed when compared with TNF blockers.
           Patients who are current or past smokers are at additional increased risk.

   Major Adverse Cardiovascular Events
    ●      In RA patients 50 years of age and older with at least one cardiovascular risk factor treated
           with another JAK inhibitor, a higher rate of major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE) (de-
           fined as cardiovascular death, myocardial infarction, and stroke), was observed when com-
           pared with TNF blockers. Patients who are current or past smokers are at additional in-
           creased risk. Discontinue upadacitinib in patients that have experienced a myocardial in-
           farction or stroke.
   Thrombosis
    ●      Thrombosis, including deep venous thrombosis, pulmonary embolism, and arterial throm-
           bosis have occurred in patients treated with JAK inhibitors used to treat inflammatory condi-
           tions. Many of these adverse events were serious and some resulted in death. In RA pa-
           tients 50 years of age and older with at least one cardiovascular risk factor treated with an-
           other JAK inhibitor, a higher rate of thrombosis was observed when compared with TNF
           blockers. Avoid upadacitinib in patients at risk. Patients with symptoms of thrombosis
           should discontinue upadacitinib and be promptly evaluated.
   2 ,9

   Monitoring
   Laboratory Monitoring:

   • Verify pregnancy status of females of reproductive potential prior to initiation • Screen for viral hepatitis prior to initiation and monitor for reactivation during treatment • Evaluate neutrophil count, lymphocyte count, and hemoglobin at baseline and thereafter ac-
   cording to routine patient management • Evaluate liver enzymes at baseline and thereafter according to routine patient management • Measure lipid levels 12 weeks after initiation of therapy and thereafter according to lipid
   management guidelines 7/11
 • Monitor for signs and symptoms of infection, including active tuberculosis (even in patients
   who test negative prior to therapy), during and after treatment Physical Exam:

   • Monitor patients who may be at risk for gastrointestinal perforation (eg, patients with a his-
   tory of diverticulitis and those taking concomitant medications including NSAIDs or corticos-
   teroids) • Monitor clinically for inadequate therapeutic response in patients who repeatedly observe
   medication residue in their stool • Evaluate and test patients for latent and active TB infection prior to administration • Monitor for signs and symptoms of infection, including active tuberculosis (even in patients
   who test negative prior to therapy), during and after treatment • Perform periodic skin examinations in patients at increased risk for skin cancer • Prior to initiating or continuing therapy with JAK inhibitors, evaluate the benefits and risks of
   treatment in patients, especially who are current or past smokers, those with other cardiovas-
   cular risk factors, those who develop a malignancy, and those with a known malignancy other
   than a successfully treated nonmelanoma skin cancer

Pharmacology
   Ursodiol is a hydrophilic bile acid that decreases both the secretion of cholesterol from the
   liver and its intestinal absorption. After conjugation with taurine or glycine, it then enters the
   enterohepatic circulation where it is excreted into the bile and intestine. It is hydrolyzed back
   to the unconjugated form or converted to lithocholic acid which is excreted in the feces.

drugs.uses_raw:
For the treatment of cold sores (herpes labialis) in pediatric patients 12 years or older 1
   For the treatment of chickenpox in immunocompetent pediatric patients aged 2 years to less
   than 18 years 1

   Limitations of Use

   The safety and efficacy of valacyclovir has not been established in: 1

   • Immunocompromised patients other than for the suppression of genital herpes in HIV-1 in-
   fected patients with a CD4+ cell count greater than or equal to 100 cells/mm3

 • Patients aged less than 12 years with cold sores (herpes labialis)
   • Patients aged less than 2 years or greater than 18 years with chicken pox
   • Patients aged less than 18 years with genital herpes
   • Patients aged less than 18 years with herpes zoster
   • Neonates and infants as suppressive therapy following neonatal herpes simplex virus (HSV)
   infection

   Administration
   • Administer with or without food 1

   Preparation
   Extemporaneous oral compound

   50 mg/mL suspension (180 mL) 2

   • Triturate eighteen 500-mg caplets of valacyclovir to a fine powder using a mortar and pestle.
   • Add 40 mL of chosen suspension vehicle in 5-mL aliquots, mixing thoroughly between each
   addition. Suspension vehicle options areOra-Plus.or Syrpalta.

   • Pour mixture into a 180-mL amber glass bottle.
   • Rinse mortar and pestle with 10 mL of suspension vehicle (Ora-Plus® or Syrpalta) and pour
   into bottle; repeat 4 more times (5 total rinses of 10 mL each).
   • Add enough syrup (Ora-Sweet®, Ora-Sweet® SF, or Syrpalta) to bottle to bring final vol-
   ume to 180 mL.

   • Label the container with "Shake well before using" and "Refrigerate."
   • Suspensions made with Ora-Sweet® or Ora-Sweet® SF are stable for 21 days at 4°C; sus-
   pensions made with Syrpalta are stable for 35 days at 4°C.

   25 or 50 mg/mL suspension (100 mL) 1
   • Prepare Suspension Structured Vehicle (SSV) according to the USP-NF.

   • Using a pestle and mortar, grind the required number of valacyclovir 500 mg tablets until a
   fine powder is produced (5 tablets for 25 mg/mL suspension; 10 tablets for 50 mg/mL
   suspension).
   • Gradually add 5-mL aliquots of SSV to the mortar and triturate the powder until a paste has
   been produced. Ensure the powder has been adequately wetted.

 • Continue to add 5-mL aliquots of SSV to the mortar, mixing thoroughly between additions,
   until a concentrated suspension is produced, to a minimum total quantity of 20 mL SSV and a
   maximum total quantity of 40 mL SSV for both the 25 mg/mL and 50 mg/mL suspensions.

   • Transfer the mixture to a suitable 100-mL measuring flask.
   • Add cherry flavor (add amount as instructed by supplier) to the mortar and dissolve in 5 mL
   of SSV. Once dissolved, add to the measuring flask.
   • Rinse the mortar at least 3 times with approximately 5-mL aliquots of SSV, transferring the
   rinsing to the measuring flask between additions.

   • Make the suspension to volume (100 mL) with SSV and shake thoroughly to mix.
   • Transfer the suspension to an amber glass medicine bottle with a child-resistant closure.

   • Label the container with "Shake well before using."
   • Stable for 28 days when refrigerated (2 to 8°C or 36 to 46°F)

drugs.dosing_raw:
Congenital CMV Infection, Symptomatic

   29 days to 1 year of age: 16 mg/kg per dose orally every 12 hours. Treat for a minimum of 6
   weeks; longer-term treatment may be appropriate 1 ,2 . Studies have reported continuing pro-
   phylaxis for 3 or 6 months 3 ,4 .

   Dosing applies only to pharmaceutical grade valGANciclovir. Data are not available for extem-
   poraneous formulations.
   Dose Adjustment for Hematologic Toxicity: If absolute neutrophil count (ANC) less than 500
   cells/mm3 (confirm by repeat count), hold drug until ANC greater than 750 cells/mm3. If the
   ANC falls again to less than 750 cells/mm3, reduce the dosage by 50%. If ANC again falls to less
   than 500 cells/mm3, discontinue the drug CMV Disease, Prophylaxis- High-Risk Kidney Transplant
   4 months to 16 years of age: Dose is once daily orally and is based on body surface area
   (BSA) and creatinine clearance (CrCl; derived from a modified Schwartz formula); begin therapy
   within 10 days of transplantation and continue through day 200 post-transplantation. The
   maximum dose is 900 mg daily CMV Disease, Prophylaxis- High-Risk Heart Transplant

   1 month to 16 years of age: Dose is once daily orally and is based on body surface area (BSA)
   and creatinine clearance (CrCl; derived from a modified Schwartz formula); begin therapy
   within 10 days of transplantation and continue through day 100 post-transplantation. The
   maximum dose is 900 mg daily Pediatric Dose (mg) = 7 x BSA x CrCl (using modified Schwartz formula), where:
   Mosteller BSA (m2) = square root of {Ht (cm) x Wt (kg)}/3600; and
   Schwartz CrCl (mL/min/1.73 m2) = {k x Ht (cm)}/SCr (mg/dL)
   where k=

 ● 33 for patients younger than 1 year with low birth weight for gestational age
    ● 45 for patients younger than 1 year with birth weight appropriate for gestational age
    ● 45 for patients 1 to younger than 2 years
    ● 55 for boys ages 2 to younger than 13 years and girls ages 2 to younger than 16 years, and
    ● 7 for boys ages 13 to 16 years
    ●   Ht = height; Wt = weight; Scr = serum creatinine
    ●   k values are based on Jaffe method of measuring serum creatinine, and may require correc-
        tion when enzymatic methods are used.

   If the calculated CrCl exceeds 150 mL/min/1.73 m(2), then a maximum value of 150
   mL/min/1.73 m(2) should be used in the dose equation All calculated doses in children should be rounded to the nearest 10-mg increment for the ac-
   tual deliverable dose up to a maximum dose of 900 mg once daily. The oral solution is the
   preferred formulation in children, but the tablets may be used if the calculated dose is within
   10% of the available tablet strength (450 mg) Older than 16 years : 900 mg once daily; begin therapy within 10 days of transplantation and
   continue through day 100 post-heart-transplantation 5 , 6 or for 200 days post-kidney-trans-
   plantation Cytomegalovirus Disease, Prophylaxis-Hematopoietic Cell Transplant (HCT) (40 kg or
   greater):

   Preemptive Therapy (less than 100 days post-HCT): induction therapy, 900 mg orally twice
   daily for 7 to 14 days (allogeneic HCT) or 7 days (autologous HCT), followed by maintenance
   therapy with 900 mg orally once daily for a minimum of 2 weeks (when 14 days of induction
   given) or 3 weeks (when 7 days of induction given) and indicator test is negative 7

   Preemptive Therapy (greater than 100 days post-HCT): induction therapy, 900 mg orally
   twice daily for 7 to 14 days, followed by maintenance therapy with 900 mg orally once daily for
   1 to 2 weeks or until indicator test is negative 7

   Symptomatic Congenital CMV Disease

drugs.uses_raw:
Prevention of CMV disease in kidney transplant patients age 4 months to 16 years at high risk
   and heart transplant patients 1 month to 16 years of age at high risk. ValGANciclovir is not FDA
   approved for use in liver transplant patients Administration
   NIOSH Guidance: For full NIOSH guidance, see Special Considerations.

 Oral

   Administer with food.Do not break or crush tablets • Handle and dispose of according to guidelines for antineoplastic drugs; drug is potentially
   carcinogenic and mutagenic 5

   • Avoid direct contact of broken or crushed tablets, the powder for oral solution, and the re-
   constituted oral solution with the skin or mucous membranes Preparation

   Reconstitution of Oral Solution: Valcyte® for oral solution must be constituted by the phar-
   macist prior to dispensing to the patient. To prepare the oral solution measure 91 mL of puri-
   fied water in a graduated cylinder. Shake the Valcyte® bottle to loosen the powder. Remove
   the cap and add approximately half the total amount of water for constitution to the bottle
   and shake the closed bottle well for about 1 minute. Add the remainder of water and shake
   the closed bottle well for about 1 minute. This prepared solution contains 50 mg of valGANci-
   clovir free base per 1 mL Extemporaneous Oral Compounds

   ValGANciclovir Oral Suspension 30 mg/mL (120 mL) 10

   • Place 8 valGANciclovir 450 mg tablets into a mortar. Triturate into a fine powder.

   • In 1 mL increments, add Ora-Plus to the powder, mixing to form a paste.

   • Through the process of geometric dilution, add a total of 60 mL of Ora-Plus, mixing well after
   each addition.

   • Add the mixture to an amber glass bottle; scrape mortar and pestle for leftover residue and
   add to bottle.

   • Rinse mortar and pestle with 10 mL of Ora-Sweet and add to bottle; repeat the rinsing
   process four times.

   • Add enough Ora-Sweet to the bottle to bring the total volume to 120 mL; shake well.

   • Label the bottle with "Shake Well Before Use" and "Refrigerate."
   • Stable for 35 days when refrigerated (4 degrees C)

   ValGANciclovir Oral Suspension 60 mg/mL (120 mL) 10
   • Place 16 valGANciclovir 450 mg tablets into a mortar. Triturate into a fine powder.

 • In 1 mL increments, add Ora-Plus to the powder, mixing to form a paste.
   • Through the process of geometric dilution, add a total of 60 mL of Ora-Plus, mixing well after
   each addition.

   • Add the mixture to an amber glass bottle; scrape mortar and pestle for leftover residue and
   add to bottle.

   • Rinse mortar and pestle with 10 mL of Ora-Sweet and add to bottle; repeat the rinsing
   process four times.
   • Add enough Ora-Sweet to the bottle to bring the total volume to 120 mL; shake well.

   • Label the bottle with "Shake Well Before Use" and "Refrigerate."

   • Stable for 35 days when refrigerated (4 degrees C)

   ValGANciclovir Oral Suspension 90 mg/mL (225 mL) 11 :
   • Triturate 45 valGANciclovir 450 mg tablets into a fine powder in a glass mortar.

   • Slowly add 45 mL of the sodium benzoate solution * and work the powder into a smooth
   paste using a pestle. All film coating should dissolve
   • Add 50 mL of the cherry-chocolate vehicle **, mix well, and transfer to a beaker that has
   been calibrated to 225 mL with a graduated cylinder.

   • Rinse mortar and pestle with two 50 mL portions of the cherry-chocolate vehicle and transfer
   the liquid from each rinse into the beaker.

drugs.uses_raw:
Indicated as monotherapy and adjunctive therapy in the treatment of patients with complex
   partial seizures that occur either in isolation or in association with other types of seizures. Also
   indicated for use as sole and adjunctive therapy in the treatment of simple and complex ab-
   sence seizures, and adjunctively in patients with multiple seizure types which include absence
   seizures 13,14,12,15

 Limitations of Use

   Because of the risk to the fetus of decreased IQ, neurodevelopmental disorders, neural tube
   defects, and other major congenital malformations, which may occur very early in pregnancy,
   valproate should not be used to treat women with epilepsy or bipolar disorder who are preg-
   nant or who plan to become pregnant unless other medications have failed to provide ade-
   quate symptom control or are otherwise unacceptable. Valproate should not be administered
   to a woman of childbearing potential unless other medications have failed to provide ade-
   quate symptom control or are otherwise unacceptable. For prophylaxis of migraine
   headaches, valproate is contraindicated in women who are pregnant and in women of child-
   bearing potential who are not using effective contraception 13,14,12,15 .

   Note: Depakote ER® is only approved for children 10 years and older. Depakene®,
   Depakote®, and Depakote® sprinkle capsules are approved for children 10 years and older
   for complex partial seizures and for all children with simple and complex absence seizures and
   multiple seizure types. Depacon® injection is approved for all children with complex partial
   seizures, simple and complex absence seizures, and multiple seizure types when oral therapy
   is not feasible.

   Administration
   NIOSH Guidance: For full NIOSH guidance, see Special Considerations.

   Intravenous:

   • Divide total daily dose if exceeds 250 mg/day • Infuse over 60 minutes or a maximum rate of 20 mg/min • May administer as an IV bolus over 5 to 10 minutes. Rapid IV infusions of 2 to 6
   mg/kg/minute have been given safely in children 8 ,6 ,10 . For intermittent IV, a standard concen-
   tration was 30 mg/mL or 50 mg/mL Manufacturer recommends diluting dose in at least 50
   mL (D5 W, NS, or LR) and infusing over 60 minutes Preparation

   • Dilute with 50 mL of D5W, NS, or LR Compatibility and Stability

   solutions for at least 24 hours when stored in glass or polyvinyl chloride (PVC) bags at a con-
   trolled room temperature between 15 and 30 degrees C (59 and 86 degrees F): 12
    ●   dextrose (5%) injection
    ●   sodium chloride (0.9%) injection
    ●   lactated ringer's injection
   Oral
   • Capsules should be swallowed whole without chewing to avoid local irritation of the mouth
   and throat 15

   • Capsules: Give in divided doses if the total daily dose exceeds 250 mg 15
   • Capsules: Slow titration from initial dose and giving with food may help decrease GI irritation
   15

   • Extended-release formulations are for once-daily dosing and should be swallowed whole and

 promised patient 54 and significant hypotension in another patient receiving intravenous val-
   proate Black Box Warning
   Warning: Life Threatening Adverse Reactions 13 , 14 , 15
    ●   Hepatotoxicity
    ●   General Population: Hepatic failure resulting in fatalities has occurred in patients receiving
        valproate. These incidents usually have occurred during the first six months of treatment.
        Serious or fatal hepatotoxicity may be preceded by non-specific symptoms such as malaise,
        weakness, lethargy, facial edema, anorexia, and vomiting. In patients with epilepsy, a loss of
        seizure control may also occur. Patients should be monitored closely for appearance of
        these symptoms. Serum liver tests should be performed prior to therapy and at frequent in-
        tervals thereafter, especially during the first 6 months.
    ●   Children under the age of 2 years are at a considerably increased risk of developing fatal
        hepatotoxicity, especially those on multiple anticonvulsants, those with congenital meta-
        bolic disorders, those with severe seizure disorders accompanied by mental retardation,
        and those with organic brain disease. When valproic acid products are used in this patient
        group, they should be used with extreme caution and as a sole agent. The benefits of ther-
        apy should be weighed against the risks. The incidence of fatal hepatotoxicity decreases
        considerably in progressively older patient groups.
    ●   Patients with Mitochondrial Disease: There is an increased risk of valproate-induced acute
        liver failure and resultant deaths in patients with hereditary neurometabolic syndromes
        caused by DNA mutations of the mitochondrial DNA Polymerase gamma (POLG) gene (e.g.
        Alpers Huttenlocher Syndrome). Valproic acid is contraindicated in patients known to have
        mitochondrial disorders caused by POLG mutations and children under two years of age
        who are clinically suspected of having a mitochondrial disorder. In patients over two years
        of age who are clinically suspected of having a hereditary mitochondrial disease, valproic
        acid should only be used after other anticonvulsants have failed. This older group of pa-
        tients should be closely monitored during treatment with valproic acid for the development
        of acute liver injury with regular clinical assessments and serum liver testing. POLG muta-
        tion screening should be performed in accordance with current clinical practice.
    ●   Fetal Risk
    ●   Valproate can cause major congenital malformations, particularly neural tube defects (e.g.,
        spina bifida). In addition, valproate can cause decreased IQ scores and neurodevelopmental
        disorders following in utero exposure.

 ●   Valproate is therefore contraindicated for prophylaxis of migraine headaches in pregnant
        women and in women of childbearing potential who are not using effective contraception.
        Valproate should not be used to treat women with epilepsy or bipolar disorder who are
        pregnant or who plan to become pregnant unless other medications have failed to provide
        adequate symptom control or are otherwise unacceptable.
    ●   Valproate should not be administered to a woman of childbearing potential unless other
        medications have failed to provide adequate symptom control or are otherwise unaccept-
        able. In such situations, effective contraception should be used.
    ●   A Medication Guide describing the risks of valproate is available for patients.
    ●   Pancreatitis
    ●   Cases of life-threatening pancreatitis have been reported in both children and adults receiv-
        ing valproate. Some of the cases have been described as hemorrhagic with a rapid progres-
        sion from initial symptoms to death. Cases have been reported shortly after initial use as
        well as after several years of use. Patients and guardians should be warned that abdominal
        pain, nausea, vomiting, and/or anorexia can be symptoms of pancreatitis that require
        prompt medical evaluation. If pancreatitis is diagnosed, valproate should ordinarily be dis-
        continued. Alternative treatment for the underlying medical condition should be initiated as
        clinically indicated

   • In a consensus guideline, the use therapeutic drug monitoring (TDM) with valproic acid is
   rated as 1, strongly recommended for dose titration and for special indications. The highest

 probability of response or remission can be expected at drug concentrations within the re-
   ported therapeutic reference range • The therapeutic reference range for valproic acid when used as a mood stabilizer or anticon-
   vulsant is 50 to 100 mcg/mL, with a laboratory alert level of 120 mcg/mL; however, 120
   mcg/mL has been clinically tolerated in acute mania. Reported therapeutic reference ranges
   are established. Controlled clinical trials have shown beneficial effects of TDM. Reports on de-
   creased tolerability or intoxications exist • Monitor valproic acid plasma concentrations periodically to assist in achieving satisfactory
   clinical response, especially during the early course of therapy and with the addition or discon-
   tinuation of concomitant antiepileptic drugs Samples for valproic acid levels should be
   drawn before the morning dose due to its short half-life to insure proper interpretation of con-
   centration 44

   Toxic Laboratory Monitoring

   • Measurements of 25-hydroxy-vitamin D levels should be assessed regularly in children to de-
   tect early osteopenia • Perform liver function tests prior to the initiation of therapy and at frequent intervals there-

Pharmacology
   Valsartan is an angiotensin receptor blocker which blocks the vasoconstrictor and aldosterone-
   secreting effects of angiotensin II by selectively blocking the binding of angiotensin II to the
   AT1 receptor in many tissues, such as vascular smooth muscle and the adrenal gland. Its ac-
