drugs.uses_raw:
• Treatment of serious or severe infections (septicemia, bone infections, lower respiratory tract infections, and skin and skin structure infec-
  tions) caused by susceptible strains of methicillin-resistant (beta-lactam-resistant) staphylococci. Also indicated for penicillin-allergic pa-
  tients, for patients who cannot receive or who failed to respond to other therapy, and for infections caused by vancomycin-susceptible or-
  ganisms resistant to other antimicrobial drugs 1 ,2 .
  • Treatment of endocarditis caused by susceptible isolates of MRSA, Viridans group Streptococcus gallolyticus, Enterococcus species,
  Corynebacterium species, and early-onset prosthetic valve endocarditis due to Staphylococcus epidermis. Also indicated for penicillin-allergic
  patients or those patients who cannot receive or failed to respond to other drugs 1 ,2 .
  • Pseudomembranous colitis due toC difficile and staphylococcal enterocolitis (oral administration only). Not effective by the oral route
  for any other infection 36,2 .

  Administration
  Intravenous
  • Administer by intermittent IV infusion over 60 to 120 minutes (no more than 10 mg/minute) at a concentration not to exceed 5
  mg/mL 1 ,2 .

 • Concentrations up to 10 mg/mL have been used in fluid restricted patients; use of higher concentrations may increase the risk of infusion
  related reactions • Administer prior to IV anesthetic agents to reduce the risk of infusion-related adverse events 1 ,2 .

  • Tyzavan™ is a ready-to-administer product. If the required dose does not equal 500 mg, 750 mg, 1 g, 25 g, 5 g, 75 g, or 2 g, this prod-
  uct is not recommended, and an alternative form of vancomycin should be considered Extravasation management: Although not pediatric-specific, the following are recommendations for extravasation of acidic or alkaline,
  like vancomycin, agents 35 :
  • General
   ●   Stop and disconnect infusion; do not remove the cannula or needle
   ●   Attempt to gently aspirate as much extravasated agent as possible; avoid manual pressure
   ●   Remove cannula or needle
   ●   Dry heat and elevation
   ●   Closely monitor for signs of coagulation and ischemia
   ●   Avoid attempt at pH neutralization (vancomycin - pH 4)
   ●   Monitor and consider the need for surgical management such as surgical flushing with normal saline or debridement and excision of
       necrotic tissue (especially if pain persists for 1 to 2 weeks). In cases of compartment syndrome, surgical decompression may be required
  • Refractory events:
   ●   Hyaluronidase 15 units intradermally along injection site and edematous area. Give as five, 2-mL intradermal injections along extrava-
       sation site and edematous tissue.

  • Inadvertent intraarterial administration:
   ●   Leave inadvertent intraarterial line in place for diagnostics
   ●   Systemic heparin titrated to therapeutic anticoagulant effect.
   ●   Stellate ganglion block

  Intraventricular

  • When administering via a ventricular drain, clamp the drain for 15 to 60 minutes to allow the agent to equilibrate throughout the CSF Oral
  Powder for oral solution

  • Shake reconstituted solution before each use Diluted IV solution

  • Intravenous powder for solution may be administered orally or via nasogastric tube Preparation

  Intravenous powder for solution
  • Reconstitute 500-mg and 1-g vial with 10 mL and 20 mL of sterile water for injection, respectively, to a concentration of 50 mg/mL.
  Reconstituted solution stable for 14 days under refrigeration • Dilute prior to administration using D5W or NS to a maximum concentration of 5 mg/mL (concentrations up to 10 mg/mL may also be
  used in fluid restricted patients) • Solutions diluted with D5W or NS are stable for 14 days under refrigeration. Solutions diluted with the following infusion fluids are stable
  for 96 hours under refrigeration: D5NS; LR; D5LR; D5W and Normosol®-M; and acetated ringer's injection • Standard Concentrations: Some institutions use standard concentrations of 5 and 10 mg/mL Intraventricular

  • Dilute to a concentration of 2 to 5 mg/mL in preservative free normal saline 38,39,8 ,10 .

 Oral
  Powder for oral solution

  • Each kit contains 1 bottle of vancomycin hydrochloride USP powder and 1 bottle of pre-measured grape-flavored diluent. Once the diluent
  is added to the powder, the final concentration of the reconstituted solution is 25 mg/mL or 50 mg/mL • Store reconstituted solution under refrigeration (2 to 8°C) and discard after 14 days, or if solution appears hazy or contains particulate
  matter Diluted IV solution

  • Intravenous powder for solution may be diluted in 1 ounce of water and given orally. Flavoring syrup may be added to improve taste Extemporaneous oral compounds
  Note: Powder for oral solution is commercially available in a concentration of 25 mg/mL or 50 mg/mL.

  25 mg/mL oral solution (100 mL) 40
   ●   Reconstitute 5 g vancomycin hydrochloride for injection.
   ●   Using a 1:1 mixture of Ora-Sweet® and purified water, add sufficient quantity for a total volume of 100 mL to 5 g of vancomycin.
   ●   Mix well and package into a light-resistant bottle.
   ●   Stable for 75 days when refrigerated or 26 days when stored at room temperature.

  50 mg/mL oral solution (100 mL) 41
   ●   Add 250 mg of vancomycin USP raw powder or pharmacy bulk product to a 500 mL volumetric flask.
   ●   Add 100 mL SyrSpend® SF and stir on a stir plate while adding another 300 mL of SyrSpend® SF.
   ●   Add sufficient volume of SyrSpend® SF for a total volume of 500 mL and stir until homogenous preparation.
   ●   Store in amber prescription bottle. Stable for 90 days when refrigerated (2°C to 8°C).

  Ophthalmic

  31 mg/mL ophthalmic solution (15 mL) 42,43
   ●   Ophthalmic solution should be compounded using aseptic technique under a class 100 laminar-airflow hood to ensure sterility.
   ●   Add 5 mL of preservative-free Sterile Water for Injection (USP) to 500 mg vancomycin hydrochloride for injection; shake well (concentra-
       tion of 100 mg/mL).
   ●   Remove 6 mL from artificial tears (Tears Naturale) bottle.
   ●   When the vancomycin has dissolved, draw up 6 mL of vancomycin with a syringe; transfer to the artificial tears bottle.
   ●   Shake well.
   ●   Label with "For Ophthalmic Use" and with proper expiration date.
   ●   Stable for 10 days when refrigerated (4 degrees C) and 7 days when kept at room temperature (25 degrees C).

drugs.contraindications_raw:
Common: Anaphylaxis, vancomycin infusion reactions, acute kidney injury, hearing loss, neutropenia Infusion reactions: Rapid bolus administration may result in anaphylactoid reactions, including hypotension, wheezing, dyspnea, urticaria,
  or pruritus. Rash and hypotension (vancomycin infusion reaction) may appear rapidly and resolve within minutes to hours. Such events are
  rare if vancomycin is administered by slow infusion over 60 minutes at a rate of 10 mg/min or less. Should a reaction occur, lengthening in-
  fusion time usually eliminates risk for subsequent doses 2 ,53 .

  Hematologic: Neutropenia has been reported after prolonged administration, usually starting 1 week or more after onset of therapy or af-
  ter a total dosage of 25 g, and appears to be promptly reversible with discontinuation of vancomycin. Thrombocytopenia has also been
  rarely reported. Reversible agranulocytosis has been rarely reported, but a causal relationship has not been established Nephrotoxicity has been reported; may be enhanced by aminoglycoside therapy 31,53 . and may occur with oral vancomycin during or af-
  ter completion of therapy Nephrotoxicity (50% or more increase in serum creatinine) was experienced in 19 out of 291 (6.5%) patients 3 months to younger than 19
  years treated with vancomycin for at least 48 hours. Nephrotoxicity was associated with trough concentration of 15 mg/dL or more (OR, 49; 95% CI, 2 to 1) and concurrent use of piperacillin/tazobactam (OR, 14; 95% CI, 02 to 6) A greater risk of acute kidney injury was associated with the use of combination vancomycin IV plus piperacillin/tazobactam IV (OR, 4; 95%
  CI, 26 to 14) compared with vancomycin plus other antipseudomonal beta-lactam antibiotics in a retrospective cohort study of 1915 chil-
  dren 6 months to 18 years of age The use of concurrent furosemide and vancomycin was associated with an increased risk of acute kidney injury (AKI) (adjusted OR, 52;
  95% CI, 88 to 62) in pediatric patients (0 to 18 years of age) in the intensive care unit in a retrospective study (n=265). The rate of AKI was 4% Late AKI was associated with durations of vancomycin for 8 days or longer in 13% of children receiving vancomycin 40 to 60 mg/kg/day in a
  retrospective study (n=167). Children younger than 1 year were more likely to experience AKI 17/24
 Oral administration: Common adverse events reported in adults (N=260) treated with vancomycin oral powder for solution include nau-
  sea (17%), abdominal pain (15%), and hypokalemia (13%) Systemic absorption of orally administered formulation may occur in some patients (eg, those with renal insufficiency or colitis); monitoring
  of serum concentrations may be warranted Ototoxicity has been reported; may be enhanced by aminoglycoside therapy 31,53 and has been reported most frequently with high IV
  doses or underlying hearing loss Phlebitis: Inflammation at the injection site has been reported. Phlebitis may be minimized by slow infusion and dilution of the drug 2 ,53 .

  Solution Compatibility
  D5W, D10W, and NS.

  Terminal Injection Site Compatibility
  Acyclovir, alprostadil, amikacin, ampicillin, aminophylline, amiodarone, aztreonam, caffeine citrate, calcium gluconate, caspofungin, cimeti-
  dine, enalaprilat, esmolol, famotidine, fluconazole, heparin (concentrations of 1 unit/mL or less), hydrocortisone succinate, insulin, linezolid,
  lorazepam, magnesium sulfate, meropenem, midazolam, milrinone, morphine, nicardipine, pancuronium bromide, potassium chloride,
  propofol, ranitidine, remifentanil, sodium bicarbonate, vecuronium, and zidovudine.

  Terminal Injection Site Incompatibility
  Cefazolin, cefepime, cefotaxime, cefoxitin, ceftazidime, ceftriaxone, chloramphenicol, dexamethasone, heparin (concentrations greater than
  1 unit/mL), mezlocillin, nafcillin, pentobarbital, phenobarbital, piperacillin, piperacillin/tazobactam, ticarcillin, and ticarcillin/clavulanate.

  Monitoring
  Toxic Monitoring

  • To minimize the risk of ototoxicity, auditory function monitoring should be considered in patients receiving concomitant ototoxic drugs • Monitor renal function for nephrotoxicity 1 ,2 .
  • Periodic monitoring of white blood cell count should be done to screen for neutropenia in patients on prolonged therapy with vancomycin
  or those who are receiving concomitant drugs that may cause neutropenia • Monitor for infusion-related events, including hypotension and vancomycin infusion reaction 1 ,2 .

  Therapeutic Drug Monitoring

  AUC/MIC ratio
  Suspected or serious MRSA infections: In general, target a vancomycin AUC of 400 mg x hr/L, assuming vancomycin MIC of 1 mg/L
  (AUC/MIC ratio of 400); may potentially target a higher AUC of 600 mg x hr/L Begin therapeutic monitoring within 24 to 48 hours of vancomycin initiation for serious MRSA infections AUC-guided monitoring is recommended for all pediatric age groups, including neonates. Trough-only monitoring, with a target of 15 to 20
  mg/L, is no longer recommended in patients with serious infections due to MRSA Bayesian software programs for AUC monitoring with a trough concentration are recommended; however, 2 pharmacokinetic samples (ie,
  1 to 2 hours post infusion and at the end of the dosing interval) may improve accuracy and precision of AUC estimates compared with using
  only a trough concentration. Another approach is collection of 2 concentrations (obtained near the steady-state, post-distributional peak
  concentration at 1 to 2 hours after infusion and trough at end of dosing interval), preferably but not required during the same dosing inter-
  val (if possible) and utilizing first-order pharmacokinetic equations to estimate the AUC Vancomycin AUC less than 800 mg x hr/L and trough less than 15 mg/mL may reduce risk of acute kidney injury Obesity: Perform early and frequent therapeutic monitoring, guided by AUC 18/24
 Dialysis: Obtain predialysis vancomycin serum concentrations not less than weekly; complete within 24 hours after initiating continuous re-
  nal replacement therapy Trough concentrations

  Trough-only monitoring, with a target of 15 to 20 mg/L, is no longer recommended in patients with serious infections due to MRSA A trough concentration range of 10 to 15 mg/L for less severe infections 48 and for children (older than neonates) with endocarditis is rec-
  ommended. In the presence of MRSA with MIC of greater than 1 mg/L or when there is a lack of microbiological response, then 15 to 20
  mg/L may be required The following recommendations are based on primarily adult data. Based on the pharmacodynamic properties of vancomycin and their
  presumed similarity among different age groups 49 , these recommendations may be applicable to pediatric patients.

  serum vancomycin levels at therapeutic levels for systemic infection treatment have been reported after multiple oral doses of vancomycin;

   Black Box Warning
   Warning: Drug-Induced Liver Injury and Liver Failure 1

 • Elevated transaminases have been observed in patients treated with
   vanzacaftor/tezacaftor/deutivacaftor. Cases of serious and potentially fatal drug-induced liver
   injury and liver failure were reported in patients who were taking a fixed-dose combination
   drug containing elexacaftor, tezacaftor, and ivacaftor, which contains the same or similar ac-
   tive ingredients as vanzacaftor/tezacaftor/deutivacaftor. Liver injury has been reported within
   the first month of therapy and up to 15 months following initiation of
   elexacaftor/tezacaftor/ivacaftor.

   • Assess liver function (ALT, AST, alkaline phosphatase, and bilirubin) in all patients prior to ini-
   tiating vanzacaftor/tezacaftor/deutivacaftor, every month during the first 6 months of treat-
   ment, then every 3 months for the next 12 months, then at least annually thereafter. Consider
   more frequent monitoring for patients with a history of liver disease or elevated liver function
   tests at baseline.

   • Interrupt vanzacaftor/tezacaftor/deutivacaftor for significant elevations in liver function tests
   or in the event of signs or symptoms of liver injury. Consider referral to a hepatologist. Follow
   patients closely with clinical and laboratory monitoring until abnormalities resolve. If abnor-
   malities resolve, resume treatment only if the benefit is expected to outweigh the risk. Closer
   monitoring is advised after resuming vanzacaftor/tezacaftor/deutivacaftor.

   • Vanzacaftor/tezacaftor/deutivacaftor should not be used in patients with severe hepatic im-
   pairment (Child-Pugh Class C). Vanzacaftor/tezacaftor/deutivacaftor is not recommended in
   patients with moderate hepatic impairment (Child-Pugh Class B) and should only be consid-
   ered when there is a clear medical need, and the benefit outweighs the risk. If used, monitor
   patients closely.

drugs.uses_raw:
Acute graft-versus-host disease, gastrointestinal

   Vedolizumab was evaluated for gastrointestinal (GI) acute graft-versus-host disease (aGVHD) in
   a case series of 13 children (median age, 3 years; range, 7 to 9 years); cases were rated
   as mild/ moderate (n=7) or severe (n=6). After a median follow-up time of 12 months (range, 3
   to 30 months), 8 patients recovered completely, 2 had ongoing chronic colitis, and 3 patients
   died. Patients with milder disease had more rapid symptom improvement (some within 7
   days). Resolution of diarrhea in more severe patients occurred relatively late after starting
   vedolizumab and required multiple concomitant treatments. During vedolizumab treatment,
   38 infectious episodes were noted; most were GI-related. Severe adverse reactions included
   posterior reversible encephalopathy syndrome attributed to calcineurin inhibitor use (n=2), GI
   perforations (n=2), and septic shock (n=5; 1 fatal) In 3 cases of GI-aGVHD in children (1.5 to 4 years old), vedolizumab dosed at 177 mg/m(2)
   BSA/dose was significantly effective for 2 patients. One patient underwent bone marrow trans-
   plant (BMT) and developed GI-aGVHD on day 26 post-transplant. Symptoms improved dramat-
   ically within 14 days of the first vedolizumab dose on day 100 post-transplant; he received re-
   peat doses at weeks 2 and 6, then every 8 weeks thereafter. Methylprednisolone was tapered

 and successfully discontinued on day 759 post-transplant. A second BMT patient received a
   similar series of vedolizumab infusions, with immediate improvement of diarrhea and signifi-
   cant improvement on colonoscopy .Mycophenolate and steroids were successfully discontin-
   ued on day 330 post-transplant. A third patient received 2 doses of vedolizumab without
   symptom improvement; his condition worsened and he required a second bone marrow
   transplant. No serious side effects of vedolizumab were reported in any patient Inflammatory bowel disease (Crohn's disease/ulcerative colitis)

   Vedolizumab was evaluated for children with Crohn's disease (CD) and ulcerative colitis (UC) in
   a systematic review (10 studies, N=455). The pooled clinical remission rates in CD were 25%
   (19/75) at 6 weeks, 28% (25/85) at 14 weeks, 32% (17/53) at 22 weeks, and 46% (43/92) at 1
   year. For UC, the pooled clinical remission rates were 36% (25/70) at 6 weeks, 48% (52/101) at
   14 weeks, 53% (24/45) at 22 weeks, and 45% (50/112) at 1 year. Mucosal healing was found in
   17% to 39% of CD patients and 15% to 34% of UC patients. A serious adverse event was re-
   ported in 6% of subjects In prospective study of vedolizumab (N=142, mean age, 6 years) 32% of children with CD
   and 42% of children with UC were in clinical remission (steroid-free and exclusive enteral nutri-
   tion-free) at week Higher drug concentrations predicted a better response in children who
   weighed less than 30 kg; the optimal drug concentrations in this group were greater than 25
   mcg/mL at week 6, and greater than 7 mcg/mL at week 14, corresponding to a dose of 200
   mg/m(2) BSA.. Overall, vedolizumab was well-tolerated, with 32 children reporting at least one
   adverse event. The most common adverse events were headache (n=5), myalgia (n=4), and
   fever (n=3) At week 54, complete remission was reported in 25% of children with CD and 47%
   with UC. Steroid-free and exclusive enteral-nutrition free remission (clinical remission) was
   noted in 34% of CD patients (22 of 64 patients) and in 53% of UC patients (39 of 74 patients).
   Remission was more common in patients with mild disease and in those achieving a therapeu-
   tic response or clinical remission at week The dose administered to patients in the study was
   177 mg/m2/dose. Based on a dose-response analysis of the data, the optimal dose is sug-
   gested to be 200 mg/m2/dose (or 10 mg/kg/dose) with a maximum of 300 mg/dose.
   Vedolizumab was discontinued before week 54 of the follow-up period in 53% patients (34 of
   64 patients) in the CD group and 26% of patients (19 of 73 patients) in the UC group. Reasons
   for discontinuation included surgery (7 of 137 patients), inadequate response (35 of 137 pa-
   tients), adverse events (2 of 137 patients), and lost to follow-up (9 of 137 patients). Adverse
   events occurred in 21% of children, most commonly headache, myalgia, and fever In a retrospective cohort study of pediatric patients with UC refractory to an anti-TNF agent,
   treatment with vedolizumab (n=262) or ustekinumab (n=74) was associated with 6-month cor-
   ticosteroid-free clinical remission rates of 3% and 8%, respectively. General clinical re-
   sponse was achieved in 7% of patients on vedolizumab and 30% of patients on ustek-

 inumab. Efficacy and safety parameters did not differ significantly between treatment groups Limitations of Use

   Safety and effectiveness of vedolizumab have not been established in pediatric patients Administration
   IV

   • Infuse over 30 minutes and flush line with 30 mL NS or LR upon completion • Do not administer as IV push or bolus • Discard any unused infusion solution SubQ

   • Administer each subQ injection at a different anatomic location (ie, thighs, any quadrant of
   abdomen, or upper arms) than the previous injection. Do not inject into moles, scars, bruises,
   or areas where the skin is tender, erythematous, or indurated Preparation
   IV

   • Reconstitute 300 mg vial with 8 mL sterile water for injection, NS, or LR at room tempera-
   ture 20 to 25 degrees C (68 to 77 degrees F) using a syringe with a 21- to 25-gauge needle •Gently swirl for at least 15 seconds to dissolve; do not invert or shake vigorously • Allow reconstituted solution to rest at room temperature between 20 to 25 degrees C (68 to
   77 degrees F) for up to 20 minutes to settle any foam (the vial can be swirled and inspected for
   dissolution during this time); do not use solution if not fully dissolved in 30 minutes • Reconstituted solution in the vial may be stored in the refrigerator at 2 to 8 degrees C (36 to
   46 degrees F) for up to 8 hours, but should be used immediately if stored at room temperature • Once dissolved, gently invert vial 3 times then immediately withdraw 5 mL of reconstituted
   solution using the syringe with the 21- to 25-gauge needle; discard any solution remaining in
   vial • Dilute the 5 mL of reconstituted solution in 250 mL NS or LR; do not add other drugs to the
   admixture 4/10
 • Use infusion solution as soon as possible after preparation or store solutions diluted with NS
   for up to 12 hours at room temperature between 20 to 25 degrees C (68 to 77 degrees F) or up
   to 24 hours in the refrigerator (including up to 12 hours at room temperature) between 2 and
   8 degrees C (36 to 46 degrees F); solutions diluted with LR may be stored for up to 6 hours in
   the refrigerator and cannot be stored at room temperature; any time that the reconstituted
   solution remained in the vial should be subtracted from the time that the solution may be
   stored in the infusion bag SubQ

   • Prefilled syringe and pen should be a clear to moderately opalescent, colorless to slightly yel-
   low solution. Do not use prefilled syringes or pens with visible particulate matter or discol-
   oration

drugs.contraindications_raw:
Common adverse events reported with venlafaxine extended-release (ER) in trials for anxiety
   (n=610) were abnormal behavior (4%), accidental injury (11%), anorexia (13% to 22%), asthenia
   (20%), mydriasis (4%), nausea (11% to 23%), pharyngitis (9%), and weight loss (11%) 2 ,3 . In a
   comparative trial of venlafaxine ER and SSRIs (n=334), adverse events were aches (13.9% vs 3%), accident/injury (4.2% vs 1%), flu-like symptoms (12.7% vs 5%), gastrointestinal
   symptoms (4.2% vs 4%), irritability (4.8% vs 8%), musculoskeletal symptoms (6% vs 6%),
   skin (mostly itching and rash) (7.8% vs 8%), sleep disturbances (7.2% vs. 3%), suicidality (suici-
   dal ideation, suicide attempt, or self-injurious behavior) (22.3% vs. 5%), and suicide at-
   tempts (6.6% vs. 6%) Extended-release venlafaxine treatment in pediatric patients 6 to 17 years of age resulted in a
   significant decrease in average growth compared with placebo in one 8-week study (0.3 cm
   [n=122] vs 1 cm [n=132]; p=0.041) but not in another 8-week study (0.8 cm [n=146] vs 7 cm
   [n=147]). In a 6-month study, pediatric patients who received venlafaxine had less-than-ex-
   pected increases in height based on age- and sex-matched peers; growth rate differences were

 larger for patients younger than 12 years compared with older than 12 years. Decreased ap-
   petite was reported more often with venlafaxine treatment compared with placebo in both 8-
   week studies (10% vs 3%); no discontinuations due to anorexia or weight loss were reported Pediatric patients 6 to 17 years of age (n=666) had an average weight loss of 45 kg com-
   pared with an average gain of 77 kg in placebo-treated patients. A weight loss of at least 5% was reported more often with venlafaxine compared with placebo (18% to 47% vs 6%
   to 14%; p less than 001). With venlafaxine use up to 6 months, the difference in actual and
   expected weight gain was larger in patients younger than 12 years than older than 12 years.
   Clinically relevant increases in blood pressure and serum cholesterol levels have been re-
   ported in pediatric patients (6 to 17 years of age) who received venlafaxine; rates were similar
   to that observed in adults 10,9 ,8 .

   Black Box Warning
   Tablet and Tablet, Extended-release
   Antidepressants increased the risk compared to placebo of suicidal thinking and behavior (sui-
   cidality) in children, adolescents, and young adults in short-term studies of Major Depressive
   Disorder (MDD) and other psychiatric disorders. Anyone considering the use of venlafaxine hy-
   drochloride or any other antidepressant in a child, adolescent, or young adult must balance
   this risk with the clinical need. Short-term studies did not show an increase in the risk of suici-
   dality with antidepressants compared to placebo in adults beyond age 24; there was a reduc-
   tion in risk with antidepressants compared to placebo in adults aged 65 and older. Depression
   and certain other psychiatric disorders are themselves associated with increases in the risk of
   suicide. Patients of all ages who are started on antidepressant therapy should be monitored
   appropriately and observed closely for clinical worsening, suicidality, or unusual changes in be-
   havior. Families and caregivers should be advised of the need for close observation and com-
   munication with the prescriber. Venlafaxine is not approved for use in pediatric patients 7 , Capsule, Extended-release
   Antidepressants increased the risk of suicidal thoughts and behavior in pediatric and young
   adult patients in short-term studies. Closely monitor all antidepressant-treated patients for
   clinical worsening, and emergence of suicidal thoughts and behaviors. Venlafaxine hydrochlo-
   ride is not approved for use in pediatric patients Monitoring

 Monitor for clinical worsening, suicidality, and unusual changes in behavior, especially within
   the first few months of initiation and during dose increases and decreases. Monitor for sero-
   tonin syndrome and neuroleptic malignant syndrome during therapy and for withdrawal
   symptoms during drug discontinuation. Monitoring of serum cholesterol levels during long-
   term treatment may be warranted. Regularly monitor blood pressure, height, and weight dur-
   ing use. Monitor patients with raised intraocular pressure. Periodically reassess for need for
   continued treatment 10,9 ,8 . When treating depression, monitor patient at least monthly during
   the continuation phase of treatment

   Black Box Warning
   Permanent vision loss 6 ,2
    ●   Vigabatrin can cause permanent bilateral concentric visual field constriction, including tun-
        nel vision that can result in disability. In some cases, vigabatrin also can damage the central
        retina and may decrease visual acuity.
    ●   The onset of vision loss from vigabatrin is unpredictable, and can occur within weeks of
        starting treatment or sooner, or at any time after starting treatment, even after months or
        years.
    ●   Symptoms of vision loss from vigabatrin are unlikely to be recognized by patients or care-
        givers before vision loss is severe. Vision loss of milder severity, while often unrecognized by
        the patient or caregiver, can still adversely affect function.
    ●   The risk of vision loss increases with increasing dose and cumulative exposure, but there is
        no dose or exposure known to be free of risk of vision loss.

 ●   Vision assessment is recommended at baseline (no later than 4 weeks after starting vigaba-
        trin), at least every 3 months during therapy, and about 3 to 6 months after the discontinua-
        tion of therapy.
    ●   Once detected, vision loss due to vigabatrin is not reversible. It is expected that, even with
        frequent monitoring, some patients will develop severe vision loss.
    ●   Consider drug discontinuation, balancing benefit and risk, if vision loss is documented.
    ●   Risk of new or worsening vision loss continues as long as vigabatrin is used. It is possible
        that vision loss can worsen despite discontinuation of vigabatrin.
    ●   Because of the risk of vision loss, vigabatrin should be withdrawn from patients with refrac-
        tory complex partial seizures who fail to show substantial clinical benefit within 3 months of
        initiation and within 2 to 4 weeks of initiation for patients with infantile spasms, or sooner if
        treatment failure becomes obvious. Patient response to and continued need for vigabatrin
        should be periodically reassessed.
    ●   Vigabatrin should not be used in patients with, or at high risk of, other types of irreversible
        vision loss unless the benefits of treatment clearly outweigh the risks.
    ●   Vigabatrin should not be used with other drugs associated with serious adverse ophthalmic
        effects such as retinopathy or glaucoma unless the benefits clearly outweigh the risks.
    ●   Use the lowest dosage and shortest exposure to vigabatrin consistent with clinical
        objectives.
    ●   Because of the risk of permanent vision loss, vigabatrin is available only through a restricted
        program under a Risk Evaluation and Mitigation Strategy (REMS) called the Vigabatrin REMS
        Program. Further information is available at www.vigabatrinREMS.com or 1-866-244-8175.

   Monitoring
   Periodically evaluate the need for continued therapy, as substantial clinical benefit should be
   seen within 2 to 4 weeks (or sooner) of initiation for infantile spasms and within 3 months for
   refractory complex partial seizures For infantile spasms, discontinue vigabatrin and initiate
   other treatment if the infant has not demonstrated clinical improvement after 2 weeks of an
   initial trial or dosage escalation Perform ophthalmologic examinations, including threshold visual field evaluation and dilated
   indirect retina ophthalmoscopy, at baseline (no later than 4 weeks after therapy initiation), at
   least every 3 months during treatment, and approximately 3 to 6 months following treatment
   discontinuation. In cooperative pediatric patients, consider electrophysiology (eg, elec-
   troretinography), retinal imaging (eg, optical coherence tomography), or other patient-appro-

 priate vision evaluation methods. Repeat abnormal or uninterpretable ophthalmic assess-
   ments. Patients formally exempted from vision testing may continue treatment with clinical
   judgment and patient counseling. Periodic vision monitoring or formal exemptions must be
   documented under the SHARE program Monitor patients for new-onset or worsening of depression, suicidal thoughts or behavior, or
   any unusual changes in mood or behavior Monitor for symptoms of anemia 5 ,

drugs.uses_raw:
Recombinant von Willebrand factor is approved for on-demand treatment and control of
   bleeding episodes and perioperative management of bleeding in pediatric patients 1 year of
   age and older Administration
   • Each vial is labeled with the actual amount of recombinant von Willebrand factor (rVWF) activ-
   ity in international units (IU), as measured with the Ristocetin cofactor assay (VWF:RCo) • Administer von Willebrand factor within 3 hours after reconstitution • Draw air equal to the amount of reconstituted solution into an empty plastic syringe • Connect the syringe to the clear plastic connector and push the entire amount of air into the
   vial • While keeping the syringe plunger pressed in, flip the syringe and vial so that the vial is on
   top • Draw the solution into the syringe. Do not push and pull the solution back and forth between
   the syringe and vial as this may adversely affect the integrity of the product • No more than 2 vials may be pooled into a single syringe. Pooling of more than 2 vials may
   result in formation of filaments, which requires discarding of the solution in the syringe • If a patient is to receive more than 1 vial of von Willebrand factor, leave syringe attached to
   the vial or cover syringe tip with a suitable sterile cap until ready to infuse to reduce risk of
   contamination • Administer IV at a rate up to a maximum of 4 mL per minute, ensuring comfort of patient. If
   tachycardia occurs, slow infusion rate or interrupt administration • If also administering recombinant factor VIII, administer the complete dose of recombinant
   von Willebrand factor followed by recombinant factor VIII within 10 minutes Preparation
   • Allow vial(s) of von Willebrand factor and sterile water for injection diluent to reach room
   temperature 8/13
 • If more than one vial is required for the dose, reconstitute each separately Some flakes or particles may remain in the reconstituted vial. The Mix2Vial filter will remove
   extraneous flakes or particles, and the resulting solution should be clear and colorless • Do not use the solution in the syringe if it is cloudy or contains flakes or particles after filtra-
   tion from vial to syringe • Remove the plastic caps from the vial and clean with a sterile alcohol swab • Peel back the cover of the Mix2Vial transfer set while leaving the Mix2Vial device in the clear
   plastic packaging • Firmly hold diluent vial on a level surface and invert the Mix2Vial over the diluent vial, then
   push the blue plastic cannula of the Mix2Vial firmly and straight down through the rubber
   stopper • Remove the plastic packaging carefully to leave the Mix2Vial firmly attached to the diluent vial • Firmly hold the von Willebrand factor vial on a level surface. Quickly invert the diluent vial
   with the Mix2Vial attached and push the transparent plastic cannula firmly straight down
   through the stopper of the von Willebrand factor vial • Verify that the diluent was drawn into the von Willebrand factor vial. Do not use if vacuum
   has been lost • Gently swirl the attached vials to mix or allow the reconstituted product to sit for 5 minutes
   then gently swirl, ensuing powder dissolves completely. Do not shake, as this will adversely af-
   fect integrity of product • Once the powder is completely dissolved, unscrew the Mix2Vial into two separate pieces and
   discard the empty diluent vial and the blue part of the Mix2Vial • Do not refrigerate after reconstitution

Common adverse effects in pediatric patients with oral voriconazole were nausea (44%), ab-
   dominal pain (28%), vomiting (18%), skin rash (10%), hepatic toxicity (8%), headache (8%),

 seizure (4%), visual complaints (2%), and hypokalemia (2%) Visual disturbances have been

   tors included white race, cystic fibrosis, cumulative treatment time, and cumulative dose. Out
   of the 87 children who experienced phototoxicity, 4 (4.6%) developed non-melanoma skin can-
   cer 44

   Hepatic: Transient elevations in liver function tests have been commonly reported In a ret-
   rospective study (n=200) in adult and pediatric hematopoietic stem cell transplant recipients
   receiving voriconazole, 34% of patients developed hepatoxicity at a median of 26 days after
   treatment initiation; most reactions were mild and reversible Neurologic: A significant correlation existed between plasma voriconazole concentration
   greater than 5 mg/L and neurological side effects and skin side effects in a pharmacokinetic

   an inverse correlation (higher mg/kg/day doses in younger children) shown in studies of war-
   farin in children 6 ,2 ,7 . In a prospective, cohort study (n=59) in children receiving warfarin, me-
   dian therapeutic warfarin doses were 26 mg/kg, 063 mg/kg, and 08 mg/kg for children 1
   to 5 years of age, 5 to 10 years of age, and 10 years and older, respectively In another
   prospective study (n=319) in children, mean warfarin maintenance doses were 33, 15, 13,
   and 09 mg/kg/day for children less than 1 year of age, 1 to 5 years of age, 6 to 13 years of
   age, and 13 years and older, respectively In a prospective study in children receiving warfarin, 79% of children achieved their target INR
   within 7 days with this protocol Maintenance doses of warfarin in children who have undergone a Fontan procedure have
   been shown to be 25% less than children with other congenital heart diseases Conversion From Heparin to Warfarin Therapy
   Conversion to warfarin may begin concurrently with heparin or may be delayed 3 to 6 days.
   Full dose heparin therapy and warfarin overlap for 4 to 5 days is recommended and until ther-
   apeutic INR is achieved. After this, heparin therapy may be discontinued. Due to the effect of
   heparin on the INR, an INR should not be obtained until at least 5 hours after the last bolus in-
   travenous dose of heparin, 4 hours after discontinuation of heparin infusion, and at least 24
   hours after the last subcutaneous dose of heparin 2/13

 Warfarin can cause major or fatal bleeding. Regular monitoring of INR should be performed on
   all treated patients. Drugs, dietary changes, and other factors affect INR levels achieved with
   warfarin sodium therapy. Instruct patients about prevention measures to minimize risk of
   bleeding and to report signs and symptoms of bleeding Monitoring
   Monitor INR daily following the initial warfarin dose until the INR is stabilized to the therapeu-
   tic range; then periodically based on clinical need, generally every 1 to 4 weeks. Perform addi-
   tional INR testing when other warfarin products are interchanged with Coumadin(R) or when
   other drugs (including botanicals) are initiated, discontinued, have dosages changed, or are
   taken irregularly. Monitor INR more frequently in patients with high risk of bleeding, when
   starting or stopping other drugs (including those for short-term use), changing dosages of
   other drugs, and in patients with renal impairment After stabilization, monitor INR fre-
   quently in children to ensure target INR is achieved and maintained 8 , Children, especially in-
   fants, require more frequent INR measurements compared to adults 12,2 ,3 . In a prospective
   study (n=115) in children receiving warfarin, children required a mean of 4 INR measurements
   per month with 5 dose adjustments. Only a small number of children (n=7) could be man-
   aged safely with monthly INR measurements In another prospective study (n=319) in chil-

   ume of xenon gas is 250 mL to 750 mL, the fraction of xenon Xe 129 isotopic enrichment is

   129 gas blend, is indicated for use with magnetic resonance imaging for evaluation of lung
   ventilation in adults and pediatric patients aged 6 years or older Limitations of Use

   • Xenon Xe 129 hyperpolarized has not been evaluated for use with lung perfusion imaging • Safety and effectiveness have not been established in patients less than 6 years of age 1

 Administration
   • Administer dose within 5 minutes of dose equivalent (DE) measurement, and within 60 min-
   utes of filling dose delivery bag. After 60 minutes, do not use and discard the dose • Administer according to the directions provided in the HPX Hyperpolarization System
   Operator’s Manual, Administering Xenoview™ • Once the patient has inhaled the full dose, begin MRI scanning immediately. Upon scan com-
   pletion, instruct the patient to breathe normally 1
   • Concomitant use of supplemental oxygen may decrease image quality; withhold supplemen-
   tal oxygen for 2 breaths prior to xenon Xe 129 hyperpolarized inhalation. Oxygen may be re-
   sumed immediately following breath hold Preparation
   Each Dose Delivery Bag contains at least 75 mL Dose Equivalent (DE) of hyperpolarized xenon
   Xe 129 measured within 5 minutes of administration, in a volume of 250 mL to 750 mL total
   xenon with additional nitrogen, NF (99.999% purity) added to reach a total volume of the Dose
   Delivery Bag • Select an appropriate dose delivery bag based on the patient’s Total Lung Capacity (TLC). If
   TLC is not available at the time of the procedure, select dose delivery bag based on patient’s
   forced vital capacity (FVC). If neither TLC nor FVC values are available, select the dose delivery
   bag based on estimates of the patient’s TLC using American Thoracic Society-endorsed
   plethysmography-based predictive equations based on sex and height • If TLC is less than 2 L or FVC is less than 5 L, use a 300 mL dose delivery bag. If TLC is 2 to
   less than 3 L or FVC is 5 to less than 5 L, use a 500 mL dose delivery bag. If TLC is 3 to
   less than 5 L or FVC is 5 to less than 8 L, use a 750 mL dose delivery bag. If TLC is 5 L or
   greater or FVC is 8 L or greater, use a 1000 mL dose delivery bag • Prepare hyperpolarized xenon Xe 129 in the HPX Hyperpolarizer from the Xenon Xe 129 gas
   blend and add Nitrogen, NF (99.999% purity) as necessary to fill the remaining volume in the
   Xenoview™ dose delivery bag, according to the HPX Hyperpolarization System Operator’s
   Manual • Measure the volume and DE in the Xenoview™ dose delivery bag using the HPX polarization
   measurement station no more than 5 minutes prior to administration. The DE measurement
   should be at least 75 mL. Do not use and discard the dose if the volume is determined to be
   outside of the acceptable range or the DE is less than 75 mL 2/5

   Although not preferred, zafirlukast is an alternative to ICS for mild persistent asthma and can
   be used as adjunctive therapy in combination with ICS in pediatric patients younger than 12
   years of age; a long-acting beta2-agonist is the preferred adjunctive therapy for adolescents.
   All asthmatic patients should have a SABA available to treat acute exacerbations, regardless of
   long-term controller therapy Zafirlukast 20 mg twice daily reduced daytime asthma symptom scores and improved FEV1 in a
   randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial of patients 12 years of age or older with
   mild to moderate asthma (n=762; 16% pediatric), 45% of whom also had seasonal and peren-
   nial allergic rhinitis. Patients also experienced fewer nighttime awakenings, fewer mornings
   with asthma symptoms, and used fewer puffs of SABA. Improvements in outcome measures
   were evident as early as 2 days after treatment initiation. Peak expiratory flow rates (PEFR) in
   the morning increased from baseline, although evening measurements did not. Improvements
   in FEV1 and PEFR appeared to be related to the degree of airflow obstruction at baseline Outcome measures were consistent during a 39-week open-label extension (n=443; 16% pedi-
   atric). An overall treatment failure rate of 1% occurred; the failure rate decreased over time
   from 2% to 3% In a subgroup analysis of results from 4 randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trials
   clinical trials in patients 12 years or older with mild to moderate asthma (n=1484; approxi-
   mately 20% pediatric), zafirlukast 20 mg twice daily resulted in improvements in morning and
   evening PEFR, FEV1, and FEV1 % predicted, asthma symptoms score, nighttime awakenings,
   mornings with asthma and use of SABA. There was a greater reduction in rescue SABA use
   with older versus younger patients and in those using more than 8 puffs/day at baseline ver-
   sus those using less. Treatment effects were most pronounced in patients with greater asthma
   severity as defined by baseline pulmonary function. The overall treatment failure rate was 9% with zafirlukast compared with 4% with placebo; the likelihood of an asthma exacerba-
   tion leading to treatment failure was greater in those patients having greater pulmonary im-
   pairment at baseline In the Accolate Clinical Experience and Pharmacoepidemiology Trial (ACCEPT), zafirlukast 20
   mg twice daily improved FEV1 by at least 10% in 71% of subjects and by at least 15% in 63% of
   subjects with mild to severe asthma aged 12 years and older (n=3759; 3% pediatric), the ma-
   jority of whom had moderate to severe asthma and were taking one or more medications for
   asthma control at baseline. Improvement was observed within 1 week of drug initiation and in-
   creased weekly over the 12-week treatment period. At study end, mean asthma symptoms
   score had improved by 30%, nighttime awakenings by 47%, and mornings with asthma by 39%,
   while use of SABA was reduced by 24%; changes from baseline were greater for patients with

 mild and moderate asthma compared with severe asthma. Asthma worsening occurred in 3% of patients. A preference for zafirlukast over other asthma medications was indicated by
   74% of patients; 70% of these had a preference for oral medication Zafirlukast 10 mg twice daily improved the percent of predicted FEV1 from baseline in pooled
   results from 2 randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trials in children with mild asthma
   (n=411; age 5 to 11 years). Other outcome measures, including morning and evening PEFR,
   peak flow variability, and use of SABA, also showed improvement over the study period; those
   with more frequent SABA use at baseline had a greater reduction in the use of rescue medica-
   tion at study end. Zafirlukast has been shown to be less effective than fluticasone in patients with persistent
   asthma 10 , In a randomized, double-blind, double-dummy trial of patients previously
   treated with SABA alone (n=451; age 12 to 68 years), zafirlukast produced a lower mean in-
   crease in morning FEV1 compared to low-dose fluticasone. In addition, there was less improve-
   ment in FVC, morning and evening PEFR, symptom-free days, nighttime awakenings, SABA use,
   and rescue-free days In another randomized, double-blind, double-dummy trial of patients
   with mild asthma who were previously controlled on low doses of other ICS and switched
   (n=437; age 12 to 81 years), zafirlukast resulted in less improvement in morning FEV1 com-
   pared with low dose inhaled fluticasone; this difference was apparent during the first week of
   the 6-week study. The zafirlukast group was also nearly 3 times more likely to have a decrease
   in FEV1 of 10% or more, while the fluticasone group was almost twice as likely to have an in-
   crease in FEV1 of 10% or more. In addition, more patients in the zafirlukast experienced an ex-
   acerbation and more withdrew from the study due to lack of efficacy compared with fluticas-
   one Doses used in both studies were zafirlukast 20 mg twice daily and fluticasone 88 mcg
   inhaled twice daily Chronic idiopathic/spontaneous urticaria, adjunct: The guideline for management of
   chronic urticaria from the World Allergy Organization and other professional groups recom-
   mends nonsedating antihistamines as first line therapy, with dose escalation, up to 4 times the
   usual dose, if needed. If symptoms continue, a different nonsedating antihistamine or an addi-
   tion of a leukotriene antagonist is recommended. Zafirlukast should not be used as monother-
   apy because the risks outweigh the benefits In a retrospective review of patients with chronic idiopathic urticaria (n=18; age 9 to 60 years),
   the addition of either zafirlukast or montelukast produced dramatic improvement in 10/18 pa-
   tients within 1 week, with resolution of symptoms within 1 month. The dose of zafirlukast was
   20 mg twice daily 5/9

   dence to recommend for or against the routine chronic use of leukotriene modifiers to im-
   prove lung function or reduce exacerbations in children 6 years or older 14 and children 2

drugs.contraindications_raw:
Common adverse events reported during pediatric trials were fever and cough. Other adverse
   events were hepatomegaly, nausea and vomiting, diarrhea, nasal discharge or congestion, skin
   rashes, lymphadenopathy .

 Endocrine and metabolic: Insulin resistance, asymptomatic hyperglycemia, and diabetes mel-
   litus have been reported with zidovudine use. Counseling patients on lifestyle modifications
   (eg, implementing diet low in saturated fat, cholesterol, trans fat, and refined sugars, increas-
   ing physical activity, smoking cessation) may be beneficial. If a patient experiences any of these
   symptoms, consider switching zidovudine to tenofovir alafenamide, tenofovir disoproxil fu-
   marate, or abacavir. Patients with a fasting plasma glucose less than 100 mg/dL does not rule
   out insulin resistance; recheck fasting plasma glucose in 6 to 12 months. In patients with a
   fasting plasma glucose 100 mg/dL or greater, consult an endocrinologist Lactic acidosis: Lactic acidosis has been reported with zidovudine use. Consider discontinuing
   ARV drugs temporarily in patients with a lactate 1 to 5 mmol/L (confirmed with second test)
   while conducting additional diagnostic work-up. In patients with a lactate 5 mmol/L or greater
   (confirmed with second test) or 10 mmol/L (any one test), discontinue all ARV drugs and pro-
   vide supportive therapy (eg, IV fluids, sedation, respiratory support). Following resolution of
   clinical and laboratory abnormalities, resume therapy with either an NRTI-sparing regimen or a
   revised NRTI-containing regimen. Monitor lactate monthly for 3 months or more Pancreatitis: Pancreatitis has been reported with the use of NRTIs and ritonavir-boosted PIs;
   discontinue the offending agent and avoid reintroduction Serious skin reactions: Stevens-Johnson syndrome, toxic epidermal necrolysis, and erythema
   multiforme major has been reported with lopinavir/ritonavir use. Discontinue all ARV drugs
   and other possible causative agents if confirmed. Provide intense supportive care, including IV
   hydration, aggressive wound care, eye care, labial adhesion preventative care, pain manage-
   ment, and antipyretics. Parenteral nutrition and antibiotics may also be needed. Consult with a
   specialist to determine if corticosteroids and/or IVIG is appropriate. Do not reintroduce the of-
   fending medication Black Box Warning
   Zidovudine has been associated with hematologic toxicity, including neutropenia and severe
   anemia, particularly in patients with advanced HIV disease. Prolonged use of zidovudine has
   been associated with symptomatic myopathy. Lactic acidosis and severe hepatomegaly with
   steatosis, including fatal cases, have been reported. Suspend treatment if clinical or laboratory
   findings suggestive of lactic acidosis or pronounced hepatotoxicity occur Solution Compatibility
   D5W and NS.

      transferase, ALT = alanine aminotransferase, BUN = blood urea nitrogen, CAB-LA

      (a) If ART is initiated soon after HIV diagnosis and entry into care, repeat baseline labora-
      tory testing is not necessary.
      (b) ART is indicated for all people with HIV and should be started as soon as possible.
      However, if ART initiation is delayed, patients should be retained in care, with periodic
      monitoring as noted above.
      (c) After 2 years of consistently suppressed HIV RNA, less frequent monitoring (eg, every 6
      months) may be considered.
      (d) After 2 years of ART with consistently suppressed viral load: CD4 count 300 to 500
      cells/mm(3), monitor every 12 months; CD4 count greater than 500 cells/mm(3), CD4 mon-
      itoring is optional.
      (e) If HIV RNA is detectable at 4 to 8 weeks, repeat every 4 to 8 weeks until viral load is
      suppressed to less than 50 copies/mL, then every 3 to 6 months.
      (f) For patients on ART, viral load is typically measured every 3 to 6 months. More frequent
      monitoring may be considered in individuals having difficulties with ART adherence or at
      risk for nonadherence. However, for adherent patients with suppressed viral load and sta-
      ble immunological status for more than 1 year, monitoring can be extended to 6-month
      intervals.
      (g) Standard genotypic drug-resistance testing in ARV-naïve persons should focus on test-
      ing for mutations in the PR and RT genes. If transmitted INSTI resistance is a concern, or if
      a person has a history of INSTI use as PrEP or treatment, or a person presents with
      viremia while on an INSTI, providers should also test for resistance mutations in the IN
      gene. In ARV-naïve patients who do not immediately begin ART, repeat testing before initi-
      ation of ART is optional if drug-resistance testing was performed at entry into care. For vi-
      rologically suppressed patients who are switching therapy for toxicity or convenience, viral
      amplification will not be possible and therefore resistance testing should not be per-
      formed. Results from prior resistance testing can be used to help in the construction of a

 new regimen.
      (h) If infected with hepatitis B virus, tenofovir disoproxil fumarate or tenofovir alafe-
      namide plus either emtricitabine or lamivudine should be used as part of the ART regimen
      to treat both hepatitis B virus and HIV infections.
      (i) If HBsAg, and HBsAb, and HBcAb are negative at baseline, administer hepatitis B vac-
      cine series. Also, consult Guidelines for Opportunistic Infections.
      (j) Typically HBV infection has resolved with loss of HBsAb despite isolated HBcAb; confirm
      with an HBV viral load if wanted. A positive HBV viral load is indicative of acute infection
      (other symptoms will be present usually) or chronic infection. Vaccinate the patient when
      viral load is negative. Also, consult Guidelines for Opportunistic Infections.
      (k) In patients with recent HCV infection (acquired in last 6 months) or advanced immun-
      odeficiency (CD4 count less than 100 cells/mm(3)), the HCV antibody test may not be ade-
      quate for screening. HCV RNA screening is indicated in persons who have been success-
      fully treated for HCV or who spontaneously cleared prior infection. HCV antibody-negative
      patients with elevated ALT may need HCV RNA testing.
      (l) At-risk populations: injection drug users, persons with a history of incarceration, men
      with HIV who have unprotected sex with men, and persons with percutaneous/parenteral
      exposure to blood in unregulated settings are at risk of HCV infection.
      (m) Serum sodium, potassium, bicarbonate, chloride, blood urea nitrogen, creatinine, glu-
      cose (preferably fasting). Monitor serum phosphorus concentrations in patients with
      chronic kidney disease who are on tenofovir-containing regimens. Renal function determi-
      nation should include creatinine monitoring and estimation of the glomerular filtration
      rate.
      (n) Consult recommendations of the HIV Medicine Association of the Infectious Diseases
      Society of America for patients with renal disease. More frequent monitoring may be indi-
      cated for patients with evidence of kidney disease (eg, proteinuria or decreased glomeru-
      lar function) or increased risk of renal insufficiency (eg. patients with diabetes or hyper-
      tension).
      (o) CBC with differential should be done when a CD4 count is performed. When CD4 count
      is no longer being monitored, the recommended frequency of CBC with differential is
      once a year. More frequent monitoring may be for patients receiving medications that po-
      tentially cause cytopenia (eg, trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole)
      (p) If random lipids are abnormal, fasting lipids should be obtained. Consult the ACA/AHA
      recommendations for diagnosis and management of patients with dyslipidemia.
      (q) If random glucose is abnormal, fasting glucose should be obtained. HgbA1C is not
      longer recommended for diagnosis of diabetes in patients with HIV on ART.
      (r) Assess urine glucose and protein before initiating tenofovir-containing regimens and
      monitor during treatment with these regimens.

drugs.uses_raw:
Bipolar I Disorder, as Monotherapy of Manic or Mixed Episodes
   Guideline Recommendations: Ziprasidone has been recommended as a second-line treat-
   ment for acute mania in Bipolar Disorder, although only after unsuccessful trials of multiple
   first-line strategies. Atypical antipsychotics including ziprasidone have demonstrated efficacy
   in treating classic mania, mixed mania, and in manic patients with mixed features. In patients
   who are inadequately responsive to first-line agents, second-line choices include monotherapy
   with olanzapine, carbamazepine, ziprasidone, or haloperidol, or combination therapy with
   olanzapine plus lithium or divalproex. Trials with ziprasidone as adjunct therapy to lithium or
   divalproex have showed lack of efficacy 1/10
 Literature: In a 4-week randomized controlled trial of children ages 10 to 17 years with bipo-
   lar I disorder (N=168), ziprasidone was associated with a significant decrease in Young Mania
   Rating Scale (YMRS) scores compared with placebo (mean between-group difference at week 4,
   -4.23; 95% CI -7.14 to -1.32). Significant reductions in the mean YMRS scores were evident be-
   ginning at week 1 and continued throughout the study, with 2% of ziprasidone-treated pa-
   tients and 5% receiving placebo classified as responders (ie, at least a 50% decrease in
   YMRS score). The mean Clinical Global Improvement-S (CGI-S) score was significantly reduced
   in the ziprasidone group at weeks 1 and 3 versus placebo, but was not maintained at week 4 A 26-week open-label extension phase was conducted (N=23) to evaluate longer-term safety
   parameters. During the study, the Child Depression Rating Scale Revised (CDRS-R) decreased
   from baseline for all participants; no patients experienced a sustained depressive mood. All-
   causality treatment-emergent adverse events were reported in 19 participants (82.6%); most
   were mild or moderate in intensity, with 2 severe events reported (suicidal ideation and fa-
   tigue). The mean weight gain from baseline to week 26 was 08 kg; no treatment-related ele-
   vations in glucose or insulin were reported. Mean changes in YMRS and CGI-S scores were sec-
   ondary outcome measures. On both ratings tools, participants who continued ziprasidone
   treatment into the extension study (n=10) maintained or improved their response, and partici-
   pants who initiated ziprasidone in the extension study (n=13) showed improved scores Ziprasidone was more effective than placebo (Young Mania Rating Scale [YMRS] score, -13.81
   vs -8.61) in a 4-week, randomized trial of pediatric outpatients (10 to 17 years; N=237) currently
   in a manic or mixed episode. Significant reductions in the mean YMRS scores were evident be-
   ginning at week 1 and continued throughout the study, with 53% of ziprasidone-treated pa-
   tients and 22% receiving placebo classified as responders. In a 26-week, open-label extension
   phase (N=162), the mean change in YMRS score remained improved from week 4 (-3.3). There
   was a higher incidence of somnolence and sedation in this population compared with that
   seen in adult study populations FDA Approved Pediatric Uses: Safety and effectiveness in pediatric patients have not been
   established Administration
   NIOSH Guidance: For full NIOSH guidance, see Special Considerations.

   Oral Capsules

   Take with food 4

   Swallow capsules whole; do not open, crush, or chew 2/10
 Preparation

   Extemporaneous oral compound 5 mg/mL suspension (60 mL) 5
   • Reconstitute 8 ziprasidone 20-mg vials with 2 mL distilled water per vial and shake vigor-
   ously to dissolve; final concentration for each vial is 20 mg/mL.

   • Transfer 5 mL of reconstituted ziprasidone solution to an appropriately sized graduated
   cylinder.
   • Add enough Ora-Sweet® to achieve a final volume of 60 mL and transfer to a brown plastic
   bottle.

   • Label the container with "Shake well before using" and "Protect from light."
   • Stable for 6 weeks under refrigeration (5°C).

   Perform CBC frequently for the first few months of treatment in patients with preexisting low
   WBC or history of drug-induced leukopenia or neutropenia CBC monitoring should also in-

   with diabetes mellitus should be regularly monitored for worsening of glucose control • Measure fasting lipid profile at baseline, at week 12, and then every 5 years thereafter.

   Examine patient for tardive dyskinesia before initiation and then annually. Patients at high risk
   for tardive dyskinesia (ie, patients who have experienced acute dystonic reactions, akathisia, or
   other clinically significant extrapyramidal side effects) should be examined every 6 months
   throughout the duration of treatment Complete fall risk assessment in patients with conditions or concomitant medications that may
   exacerbate antipsychotic effects (eg, somnolence, orthostatic hypotension, motor instability)
   when initiating treatment and recurrently in patients on long-term therapy Closely monitor patients for suicidality during therapy due to the increased risk of suicide at-

   at each visit until stable, then yearly 6/10

   To reduce the development of drug-resistant bacteria and maintain the effectiveness of an-

   or strongly suspected to be caused by susceptible bacteria. When culture and susceptibility in-
   formation are available, they should be considered in selecting or modifying antibacterial ther-

   to the empiric selection of therapy Administration
   • Take with food if weight is 50 kg or greater. Take 1 hour before or 2 hours after food if weight
   is 35 to less than 50 kg 1
   • Mix with water before administering. Do not take in dry form, and do not mix with other liq-
   uids or sprinkle on food 1

   • Measure 60 mL of water in provided mixing container 1
   • Add the entire contents of 1 unit-dose packet in mixing container. Close with provided lid and
   shake vigorously for 60 seconds or longer until all granules are suspended and a uniform sus-
   pension is achieved 1

   • Remove the lid from the container and administer 1

   • To ensure administration of the full dose, add an additional 60 mL of water to the same mix-
   ing container, shake, and administer 1
   • Administer within 15 minutes of mixing; if not administered within 15 minutes, a new dose
   must be prepared 1

Nasal Spray: In a single, multicenter, double-blind, randomized, placebo-controlled study, ad-
   verse reactions reported in pediatric patients (12 to 17 years of age) administered
   ZOLMitriptan 5 mg nasal spray (n=171), compared with placebo were taste disturbance (6.5%

   use, a limited number of clinically serious adverse events, similar to those reported rarely in
   adults, were reported in pediatric patients Oral Tablet: In one randomized, placebo-controlled study, adverse reactions reported in pedi-
   atric patients (12 to 17 years of age) administered ZOLMitriptan 5 mg, 5 mg, and 10 mg oral
   tablets (n=699) compared with placebo were tightness (3% to 11% vs 1%), dizziness (5% to 9%
   vs 2%), nausea (3% to 8% vs 1%), paresthesia (2% to 6% vs 0%), asthenia (1% to 5% vs 1%), and
   pain (2% to 5% vs 0%) The most common adverse events reported from an open-label,
   pharmacokinetic and safety study in adolescents (n=21) were headache, nausea, dizziness,
   neck pain, and flushing There were no clinically significant changes in vital signs, ECG, phys-
   ical examination or clinical evaluation following administration in a study (n=21) Monitoring
   Perform a cardiovascular evaluation prior to first use in triptan-naive patients with multiple
   cardiovascular risk factors (eg, diabetes, hypertension, smoking, obesity, strong family history
   of CAD). Consider ECG upon administration of first dose in patients with cardiovascular risk
   factors who have a negative cardiovascular evaluation 2 ,3 . Monitor patients for chest pain fol-

 lowing administration Consider periodic cardiovascular evaluation in intermittent, long-
   term users with risk factors. Conduct cardiac evaluation in patients at high cardiac risk if sensa-
   tions of tightness, pain, pressure, and heaviness occur in the chest, throat, neck, or jaw.
   Monitor blood pressure during therapy 2 ,3 , especially in patients with moderate or severe he-
   patic impairment. Evaluate patients for CAD or a predisposition to Prinzmetal variant angina if
   signs or symptoms of angina occur following administration. Monitor ECG if similar symptoms
   recur with subsequent dosing
